The people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering at his delay in the temple. When he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realised that he had seen a vision in the temple. He kept making signs to them and remained mute. When his time of service was ended, he went to his home.

And the people were waiting for Zechariah. Luke takes the camera outside for three verses, and it is one of the small perfect touches in his Gospel. The crowd is waiting, and they have begun to look at one another. The incense offering did not take long, and the priest who offered incense normally came out quickly and pronounced the priestly blessing over the people from the temple steps. A long delay was worrying. The Holy Place was dangerous, and a priest who offended God could die there (Leviticus 16:2, 13). The whole architecture of the place rested on the assumption that a sinful man in a holy room might not come out again. They were wondering at his delay.

He was unable to speak to them. The priest could not give the blessing: the Aaronic blessing, some of the oldest words in Israel’s worship. The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace (Numbers 6:24–26). Zechariah opens his mouth and nothing comes out. Consider what that congregation took home. The blessing was not pronounced. The service ended wrong. A man came out of the Holy Place gesturing with his hands like somebody who had seen something, and there was no benediction in Jerusalem that day.

The blessing on its way. Israel had waited four hundred years for God to speak, and on the day he finally did, the man appointed to bless them was struck dumb, because the LORD was about to make his face shine upon them in a way no formula could carry. The old order falls silent; a new blessing is coming. The blessing was not cancelled. It was on its way in person. At the very end of Luke’s Gospel, Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his disciples (24:50–51), the blessing the priest could not give. Luke has bookended his whole Gospel with it: a priest who cannot bless, and a Priest who blesses as he ascends.

And they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. Something had happened. They could not know what, but they knew God had done something in that room.

When his time of service was ended, he went to his home. He finished his week of duty, faithful even in his silence. He stayed. He finished his course. He served out the rest of his days in silence, doing everything that did not require a voice, with the greatest news in four centuries locked inside him and no way of telling a soul. His home was in the hill country of Judea (v. 39). There is a whole doctrine of faithfulness in that sentence. Obedience is largely what a person keeps doing after the moment of glory has passed and he is back on the roster with nothing to show for it.

In a sentence. Zechariah came out of the temple unable to speak or give the blessing, and the people realised he had seen a vision; after his week of service, he went home.

On a Tuesday. Even under God’s discipline, keep doing your duty faithfully. Zechariah finished his service. After the conference, the retreat, the moving Sunday, the ordinary week comes back. Turn up to it. Do the things that do not need a voice. Faithfulness after the high point is where most of the Christian life is lived.

For worship. The blessing that died on Zechariah’s lips came to Israel in person. The LORD has made his face shine upon us in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). He lifted up his hands over his disciples and was carried into heaven still blessing them, and he has never lowered them. Every believer now lives under the raised hands of the risen Priest.
verseByVerse.note: The people waited for the priest to come out and pronounce the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, 'Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying: thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.

His wife Elizabeth conceived. Just as the angel said. God’s word comes true, despite Zechariah’s doubt.

And for five months she kept herself hidden. Elizabeth conceives, and then does the last thing anyone would expect. She disappears for five months. We are not told why, and readers have guessed for centuries. Perhaps for private worship and thanksgiving. Perhaps because no one would believe her until the pregnancy was visible. Perhaps in obedience to the Nazirite rules. The likeliest reading is the simplest. She is an old woman in a small village where everyone has known for forty years that she cannot have children. A pregnancy at her age would first be doubted, then discussed, then examined by every neighbour with an opinion. She waits until the thing is past argument, until the God who did it is the only possible explanation, and only then lets herself be seen. The sixth month will be when Gabriel comes to Mary (v. 26), and her pregnancy will be Mary’s sign (v. 36).

Not every mercy needs announcing. There is wisdom in that worth borrowing. Some works of God are still soft when they happen, and putting them straight in front of a crowd that will handle them roughly can damage them. Elizabeth sits with hers for five months, alone with God, before she gives it to anybody else. The instinct to publish everything immediately is not faith. Very often it is only noise.

Thus the Lord has done for me. She knows exactly who has done it. Her first words are praise, and what comes out is pure theology. Not “we have had wonderful news”. Not a word about herself. The Lord did it; the Lord looked.

In the days when he looked on me. “Looked on”: with favour, with grace. God had seen her all along. It is the look of Exodus, when God saw the affliction of his people in Egypt and came down to do something about it (Exodus 3:7–8). It is not casual noticing. It is the look that ends in action.

To take away my reproach among people. The shame of barrenness. Rachel said the same: God has taken away my reproach (Genesis 30:23). God lifts the shame of his people. And notice what she says was taken away. Not the barrenness: the reproach. Oneidos: the disgrace, the thing people said. That is the wound she reports, and it tells you where the injury actually lay. She had lost the child she never had. She had also lost forty years of standing in a room: every wedding she attended, every festival, every conversation that changed direction as she came in. What God took away that morning was not only a medical condition. It was a sentence a whole village had passed on her, and which she had heard them pass.

The only verdict recorded. She had lived under other people’s verdict for four decades. It turned out that the only verdict ever actually recorded about her was the one in verse 6, and it had read righteous before God the whole time.

What about shame that God has not yet removed? Some shame is the echo of other people’s cruelty, like Elizabeth’s; some is the right sting of our own sin. Christ deals with both. For our sin, he bore the shame of the cross, despising it (Hebrews 12:2), so that the guilt is gone and the shame no longer defines us. For the shame others put on us, he gives a verdict that outweighs theirs. You may still feel it, and the feeling may take years to fade. But the feeling is not the verdict. In Christ, God has looked on you with favour, and those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed (Psalm 34:5).

In a sentence. Elizabeth conceived and stayed in seclusion five months, praising God for looking on her with favour and removing her shame.

On a Tuesday. Whatever shame you carry, God sees you and is able to take it away. Give him the praise when he does. When good news comes, consider whether it needs time alone with God before it goes on social media. And watch your words about others: never be the voice whose verdict someone has to live under for forty years.

For worship. The Lord looked, and the look ended in action. He saw Hagar in the desert, Israel in Egypt and Elizabeth in the hill country, and he has looked on us in Christ, who bore our reproach outside the gate so that we might never be put to shame. Other people’s verdicts fade. His stands for ever: righteous before God.

parallels.desc: Rachel: God has taken away my reproach

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six months after the annunciation to Zechariah, Gabriel is sent again — this time not to a priest in the temple but to a young woman in Galilee. The contrast is everything Luke is about. The gospel does not move from centre to periphery, from the established to the marginal, from the important to the overlooked. It moves the other way.

The temple in Jerusalem is where Gabriel went first; a village in Galilee, to a girl betrothed to a builder, is where he goes next. Nazareth was small and undistinguished — so undistinguished that Nathanael would later ask whether anything good could come out of it (John 1:46). The answer, it turns out, is everything.

Gabriel's greeting is without precedent in Jewish literature. Nobody else in the Bible is greeted this way. Mary is “favoured” — the graced one, the one on whom divine favour has freely fallen.

Roman Catholic theology has developed from this greeting the doctrines of Mary's immaculate conception and sinlessness; the Reformed reading takes the word as referring to God's gracious choice of Mary for this specific task rather than to any inherent quality in her. The distinction matters, and Mary settles it herself at v. 47 when she calls God her Saviour. In Luke's account the wonder is never Mary's worthiness. It is God's freedom.

The announcement of Jesus's birth is the most theologically dense passage in the chapter. Gabriel says four things: he will be great; he will be called Son of the Most High; the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father; he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

These claims are simultaneously royal and divine. The throne of David identifies him as the Messiah of Israel's hope; the title Son of the Most High and the endless kingdom move beyond anything a merely human king could claim. Gabriel is announcing the fulfilment of 2 Samuel 7:12-16 and the inauguration of the kingdom of Daniel 7:14. The Messiah Israel expected and the Son of God the disciples would confess are one and the same person.

Mary's question is entirely different in character from Zechariah's request for a sign. She does not doubt; she asks for clarification. The mechanism puzzles her, not the possibility. And Gabriel's answer is the most direct statement of the incarnation in the Synoptic Gospels: the Holy Spirit will come upon her, the power of the Most High will overshadow her, and the child will be called holy, the Son of God.

The language of overshadowing recalls the cloud of divine presence that covered the tabernacle (Exod. 40:35) — the presence of God taking up residence. Mary is the new tabernacle, the place where God chooses to dwell. And her response, “Let it be to me according to your word,” is the finest answer to divine grace in the New Testament. Not resignation. Not reluctant compliance. Surrender that is also worship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “Son of the Most High” places Jesus in direct relationship to the God of Israel's covenant. In Daniel 7:18-27 it is the saints of the Most High who receive the kingdom; here the kingdom is given to the Son of the Most High himself. Gabriel is announcing not merely that Jesus will be the greatest of Israel's kings but that he is the figure Daniel saw receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will not be destroyed.

The Davidic covenant and the everlasting kingdom of Daniel meet in this child — and a thousand years of promise, apparently stalled since the exile, resume in a single sentence spoken in a village house.

The Holy Spirit's role in the conception is the New Testament's clearest statement that the incarnation is a divine act and not a human achievement. Mary supplies the humanity; the Spirit supplies the initiative that makes this birth unlike every other.

The result is not a demigod — a being partly divine and partly human — but a fully human being who is at the same time the eternal Son of God. This is what the church has confessed from the beginning: two natures, one person, without confusion or mixture. Gabriel does not explain the mechanics of the mystery. He announces the reality.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary's “Let it be to me according to your word” is the model response to a divine call that exceeds comprehension. She does not understand how this will happen. She does not know what it will cost. She cannot see Simeon's sword or the hill called Golgotha. She says yes to a future she cannot see, on the strength of the word of a God she trusts.

That is what faith is — not the confident feeling that everything will be easy, but the willingness to place yourself in the hands of the One who has spoken.

The contrast between Gabriel's errand to the temple in Jerusalem and his errand to a house in Nazareth is Luke's first great declaration that the gospel is for everyone. The most important conversation in human history took place not in a palace or a sanctuary but in the home of an ordinary girl in a town nobody thought much of.

God's greatest gifts consistently arrive through the most unlikely channels — which means no person, no place and no circumstance is too small or too obscure to be the site of divine grace.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin’s name was Mary.

The contrast. Six months later Gabriel is sent again, and Luke means the reader to feel the drop. The first annunciation was in Jerusalem, in the temple, in the Holy Place, at the hour of prayer, to an ordained priest of the line of Aaron in the middle of the liturgy, about a child born to a barren woman. The second is in a village in despised Galilee, in a house, to a girl with no title, no office and no lineage worth recording, about a child born to a virgin. Same angel, same errand, opposite ends of the world. The first is wonderful; the second is greater. John is great; Jesus is greater.

In the sixth month. Of Elizabeth’s pregnancy. Luke dates the coming of the Son of God by the swelling of an old woman’s body in the hill country.

A city of Galilee named Nazareth. “City” here means a town. Nazareth was a small, obscure village in the hills of lower Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus or in the rabbinic lists of Galilean towns. Archaeology suggests a settlement of a few hundred people, farming and quarrying, on a ridge off the main road. Nathanael’s famous question, Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46), is less snobbery than bewilderment. It is the sound a man makes on being told the Messiah comes from a place he has to think for a moment to locate. God chose the insignificant.

To a virgin. Parthenos, a young unmarried woman who has not had sexual relations. Luke makes this unmistakable: he says virgin twice in this verse, and Mary herself says she has not known a man (v. 34). This echoes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:23).

Betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph. Jewish marriage had two stages. Betrothal was a binding agreement, made before witnesses, usually when the girl was perhaps twelve to fourteen. It was not an engagement in the modern sense. The couple were legally husband and wife, unfaithfulness counted as adultery, and breaking the betrothal required a divorce (Matthew 1:19). But they did not yet live together or have sexual relations; the woman remained in her father’s house. About a year later came the wedding, when the bride was brought to her husband’s home. So Mary is legally bound to Joseph and still living at home, which is exactly the condition in which a pregnancy is a catastrophe.

Of the house of David. Joseph was a descendant of King David. As Jesus’ legal father, he gave him the legal right to David’s throne (3:23–31; Matthew 1:1–16). One note for the reader tracking the promise: of the house of David attaches to Joseph, and Joseph is not going to be this child’s father. How the son of Mary comes to hold David’s throne is a real question, and Luke takes it up when he sets out the genealogy in chapter 3. In Israel a legal son, named and received by his father, was a true heir. For now it is enough to see that God has been steering towards this house for a thousand years, and that the heir of David is a builder in a small town who does not yet know what he is about to be told.

And the virgin’s name was Mary. Greek Mariam, from Hebrew Miriam, the name of Moses’ sister. One of the most common names among Jewish women of the time.

Round the back. Luke’s whole Gospel is in this contrast, and he will go on making it: shepherds before scholars, a Samaritan before a priest, a tax collector before a Pharisee, a dying thief before the men who arranged the cross. God’s gifts do not come in at the front door. They arrive round the back, through people nobody thought to ask.

In a sentence. In the sixth month, Gabriel was sent to Nazareth, to a virgin named Mary, betrothed to Joseph, a descendant of David.

On a Tuesday. God works through obscure places and ordinary people. No village is too small, and no person too ordinary, for his purposes. If you live somewhere nobody has heard of, in a job nobody notices, in a church of thirty people, you are standing on exactly the kind of ground God likes to choose. Do the work in front of you as if heaven were watching, because it is.

For worship. The eternal Son did not choose a palace or a capital. He chose a village people had to think to locate, and a girl with nothing but faith. The Lord of glory is not impressed by what impresses us, and that is the best news the overlooked have ever heard. He who chose Nazareth chooses the nobodies still, and makes them his own.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hills of Galilee. Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; the couple did not yet live together.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to her and said, 'Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!' But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to her and said: greetings, O favoured one, the Lord is with you! But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.

Greetings. Chaire, the ordinary Greek greeting, literally rejoice. There may be an echo of the prophets’ calls to the daughter of Zion to sing and rejoice, because the King of Israel, the LORD, is in her midst (Zephaniah 3:14–17; Zechariah 9:9). Nobody else in the Bible is greeted like this.

O favored one. Kecharitōmenē, from charis, grace: one who has been graced, one who has received favour. It repays taking apart, because a great deal has been built on it. Its form is a perfect passive participle, which in Greek means: something was done to her, and the result of it stands. Not gracious one, as though describing her character. Not full of grace in the sense of a vessel with grace to hand out. The plainest English is: you who have been graced. Somebody else is the actor here. Mary is the one it happened to. The same verb is used of all believers in Ephesians 1:6: his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us (literally graced us) in the Beloved. Mary is the recipient of God’s grace, chosen freely by him. She has not earned it.

Where Christians differ: full of grace. The Latin Vulgate translated the word gratia plena, full of grace, giving the familiar Hail Mary, full of grace. Roman Catholic teaching has understood Mary as filled with grace from her conception, and so preserved from original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854), as remaining sinless all her life, and as one who can dispense grace to others and may be prayed to. Protestants should say what they can say warmly before they say what they cannot. Mary is the most highly favoured woman who ever lived; the Reformers said so without embarrassment. Verdict: the Greek word means one who has been shown favour, not one who is a source of grace. Grace, by definition, is not owed and not earned; the greeting tells you that Mary received something, which is exactly what a woman needing nothing could not do. Mary was a sinner saved by grace, who calls God my Saviour (v. 47). Only the drowning have any use for a lifeboat. She is to be honoured as the most blessed of women, the mother of our Lord, and a model of faith and obedience (v. 45). But she is not to be prayed to, and she does not dispense grace. Grace comes from God alone, through Christ alone.

The Lord is with you. The promise given to the great servants of God when he called them: Moses, Joshua, Gideon (Judges 6:12), Jeremiah. God is about to give her a task.

But she was greatly troubled at the saying. Not by the angel (as Zechariah was), but by his words. Luke is careful about it. Gabriel has not yet mentioned a child. All he has said is that she is graced and that God is with her. Why would God’s favour rest on her? Humility.

And tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. “Discern” (dielogizeto): she thought it through, considered it, turned the sentence over, working out what on earth it could mean. Mary is thoughtful (2:19, 51). This is not a passive girl. The first thing Luke tells us about her mind is that it went to work.

Favoured does not mean comfortable. Favoured is one of the most misread words in the Christian vocabulary. It did not mean an easy life was coming. Being the favoured one of God bought Mary a pregnancy nobody would believe, a fiancé who nearly divorced her, a birth among animals, a refugee run into Egypt with a killer behind her, a son whose neighbours tried to throw him off a cliff, and an old man in the temple telling her that a sword would pierce through her own soul. God’s favour is not a promise of comfort. It is a promise of God, which is a far better thing to be given, and a far heavier thing to carry.

If God favours me, why is my life so hard? Because his favour is not a promise of ease but of himself. Mary was the most favoured woman in history, and her favour brought scandal, poverty, exile and a sword through her soul at the cross. Hardship is not evidence that God has withdrawn his favour; often it is the very road his favour takes. Look at what the favour was for: Christ came to her and through her. In your hard place, the question is not whether God has stopped favouring you, but what he is bringing to you, and through you, in it. And the Lord is with you is said to every believer (Matthew 28:20).

In a sentence. Gabriel greeted Mary as one favoured by God’s grace and assured her that the Lord was with her, and she was deeply perplexed by the greeting.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, you too have been graced (Ephesians 1:6). God’s favour rests on you, not because you deserve it, but because he is gracious. When the day goes badly, do not read it as a change in his face towards you. Say it over to yourself: I have been graced, and the Lord is with me.

For worship. Grace is God’s word, not ours. He looked on a girl in Nazareth and on every sinner who believes and said: graced, in the Beloved. All the favour any of us will ever receive flows from the Son Mary carried, and none of it flows through anyone but him. He is the fountain, and we are all, Mary first among us, cups held out to be filled.

parallels.desc: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valour”

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to her, 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel said to her: do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favour with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.

For you have found favor with God. Gabriel now explains the greeting he opened with, and the explanation is not about Mary at all. She has found favour. It is the phrase used of Noah in a world God had already decided to flood: Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8). Nobody manufactures that. A man does not find what he produced himself. God’s free choice and grace.

You will conceive in your womb and bear a son. The words come in the plainest form imaginable, and they echo Isaiah 7:14: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. Luke does not quote it, but the echo is clear, and Matthew makes it explicit (Matthew 1:22–23). Notice too how ordinary the mechanics are. She will conceive; she will carry; she will bear. There is no suggestion that the pregnancy will be shortened, or painless, or visibly supernatural to anybody watching. The eternal Son enters the world through nine months of nausea, backache and swollen ankles in a house with a dirt floor. God did not arrange a dignified entrance. He arranged a real one.

Did Isaiah really say virgin? The Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14, ʿalmah, means a young woman of marriageable age, who would be expected to be a virgin; the Greek translation of the Old Testament, made long before Jesus, rendered it virgin (parthenos). Matthew quotes it in that form (Matthew 1:23). Matthew and Luke both say plainly that Mary conceived without a man (v. 34), so the question of the word does not touch the fact. And the sign Isaiah promised was meant to be a wonder, a child who would be called God with us.

The hinge of the Bible. This is the hinge on which the whole Bible turns. From the promise in Eden that a woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), through the covenant sworn to Abraham, through the throne promised to David, through every prophet who said the virgin shall conceive and to us a child is born, the entire weight of it comes down on one sentence spoken in a back room in Galilee.

And you shall call his name Jesus. “Jesus” is the Greek form of Joshua (Yeshua), meaning the LORD saves, or the LORD is salvation. Matthew gives the meaning: for he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). It was a common name; there are several in Josephus. But this child would fulfil it as no one else. Joshua led Israel into the promised land; Jesus brings his people into God’s eternal rest (Hebrews 4:8–10). The name is already the whole sermon, and it is worth hearing what it does not say. The child is not called the LORD reigns, or the LORD comes, or the LORD judges, all of which would have been true. He is called the LORD saves. And the naming is done before he is conceived, which means the rescue was decided before the rescuer had a body.

Saves from what? First and most deeply, from our sins: from their guilt, which he carried in our place on the cross, bearing the punishment we deserved; from their power, which his Spirit breaks in us; and finally from their presence, when he returns. He also saves from everything sin has brought: death, the fear of death, and the judgement to come. People often want a Jesus who rescues them from loneliness, debt or anxiety, and he cares about all of those. But the name points to the root. If he saves you from your sins, everything else is on its way to being put right.

In a sentence. Gabriel told Mary not to fear, for God had shown her favour: she would conceive and bear a son, and name him Jesus, the LORD saves.

On a Tuesday. When you sin today, do not hide from him and do not try to pay it off with a better afternoon. Go to him by name. His name is the LORD saves, and he has never yet changed it for anyone.

For worship. The name of Jesus is the gospel in a word: the Lord saves. Call on his name, for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). The Word by whom the world was made was going to be knitted together inside a girl. He who holds the stars in their courses would have to be carried. He who feeds every living thing would need to be fed. Heaven’s answer to a ruined world was not a decree issued from a safe distance but a Son, sent, named before conception, called the LORD saves because that is what he came to do, and there has never yet been a soul who came to him for it and was turned away.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

verseByVerse.quote: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

Four claims, and they climb. Gabriel now describes the child, and each phrase is higher than the last: great, Son of the Most High, heir of David’s throne, king of an endless kingdom.

He will be great. John was to be great before the Lord (v. 15); the measuring rod was named because John needed one. Jesus is simply great, without qualification, because there is nothing to measure him against. This is the language used of God himself: Great is the LORD (Psalm 48:1).

And will be called the Son of the Most High. “The Most High” (Hypsistos) is a name for God (Genesis 14:18–20; Psalm 91:1). “Called” in Hebrew idiom means will be: he will be, and be recognised as, God’s Son. The title is not conferred so much as recognised. Israel’s kings were spoken of as God’s sons by adoption at their coronation (Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14). This one is the Son before anybody crowns him.

And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David. The fulfilment of God’s covenant with David, made a thousand years earlier: I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever; I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Samuel 7:12–16; also Psalm 89; Isaiah 9:6–7). The last real Davidic king had been dragged off to Babylon six centuries before. The throne had stood empty so long that an Idumean client of Rome was sitting in the palace. Every Jew longed for the Son of David, the Messiah. Gabriel says the promise is not dead. It was waiting for the right heir. This child is he.

And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. Jacob was renamed Israel; the house of Jacob is God’s people. And it now includes all who belong to Christ by faith, Jew and Gentile: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29; 6:16).

And of his kingdom there will be no end. Here the language stops being merely royal. Daniel had watched one like a son of man come to the Ancient of Days and receive an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14); Isaiah had promised a child of the increase of whose government there will be no end (Isaiah 9:6–7). No merely human king ever gets that sentence, for the plain reason that human kings die. David’s earthly dynasty ended with the exile. This king’s reign is eternal.

Where Christians differ: has the throne been given yet? A reader will fairly ask whether this has happened. Jesus never sat on a throne in Jerusalem. Israel is not restored as a kingdom. Sincere Christians answer this differently, and both answers love the same Bible and read it with the same seriousness. Many, including teachers a reader may know and value, such as John MacArthur, hold that the promise is literal and still ahead: Christ will reign in Jerusalem over a restored Israel for a thousand years after his return, and Gabriel’s words will be fulfilled as plainly as they were spoken. Others, in the Reformed tradition, hold that the reign began at the resurrection, when God seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority (Ephesians 1:20–21), and point out that Peter said as much at Pentecost: God had sworn to David to set one of his descendants on his throne, and this Jesus God raised up and exalted (Acts 2:30–36). Verdict: the second reading is the more likely, since Peter applies David’s throne to the risen and ascended Christ: the promise is being fulfilled now. Gabriel’s kingdom is not an earthly, political kingdom confined to a thousand years, but an everlasting one. He reigns now at God’s right hand, gathering his people from every nation, and will reign for ever when he returns to make all things new. And both readings agree on everything Gabriel actually says here: that the throne is his, that the kingdom is real, and that it has no end. Whatever else is still to come, no future is coming in which he is not King.

If Jesus reigns now, why is the world such a mess? Because his reign, for now, is carried on in the way he chose: by his word and Spirit, gathering and ruling a people, while he patiently delays the final judgement so that more may repent (2 Peter 3:9). Psalm 110 shows the King seated at God’s right hand in the midst of his enemies, until they are made his footstool. So the evil you see is real but not sovereign; it is the rebellion of a defeated enemy on borrowed time. Christ is already Lord of every power (Matthew 28:18), and the day is fixed when every knee will bow. You live in the middle: the King has come, and the King is coming.

In a sentence. Mary’s son would be great, the Son of the Most High, and God would give him David’s throne, to reign over God’s people for ever in a kingdom without end.

On a Tuesday. Live today as a subject of the King whose kingdom has no end. Before the news, the deadlines and the opinions of powerful people take their place in your mind, put him in his: on the throne. Then ask what it would look like for him to be King over your money, your tongue and your time this week.

For worship. Jesus reigns now, and for ever. Thrones have risen and fallen, Herod’s and Caesar’s among them, and his has not moved. The promise God swore to David waited a thousand years and was not one word short when it came. Every other kingdom has an end written into it. His alone has none, and his people will reign with him in it, world without end.

parallels.desc: on the throne of David, no end
a kingdom that shall not be destroyed

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said to the angel, 'How will this be, since I am a virgin?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary said to the angel: how will this be, since I am a virgin?

How will this be. Literally she says, since I do not know a man. Not doubt, but a sincere question. She does not ask for a sign, as Zechariah did. She asks how God will do it. Gabriel does not rebuke her.

Since I am a virgin. Literally since I do not know a man, the Hebrew idiom for sexual relations that runs right back to Genesis 4:1. And the tense matters: it is present. She is not only saying I never have; she is saying that is not my situation. She is betrothed, but not yet married, and the obvious answer would have been: you will be married within the year, and this is how children ordinarily arrive. She does not give it. Something in Gabriel’s you will conceive has landed on her as immediate, and she understands the angel to mean that she will conceive now, before her marriage to Joseph.

Same words, opposite postures. Sixteen verses earlier a priest asked a question and lost his voice. Why is she answered warmly? The words look similar. The postures are opposite. Zechariah asked how shall I know this? and then produced his evidence, for I am an old man, which is not a question but a rebuttal. Mary asks how will this be? and produces nothing at all. She raises no objection, offers no counter-argument, requests no proof. She has accepted that it will happen and wants to know how. The difference is not the intelligence of the question but the direction it faces. One is asking God to justify himself; the other is asking God to explain himself. God has never once refused the second.

There is no forbidden question. That distinction is worth keeping, because honest believers regularly go quiet in prayer for fear of asking the wrong thing. There is no forbidden question in this chapter. What Gabriel meets with silence is not enquiry but the settled decision that God’s word has already been weighed against the facts and found wanting. Ask anything. The line is only crossed when the asking has stopped being asking.

What will people say? There is something else in her question that ought to be said out loud, because it is easy to miss underneath the theology. She does not ask what will people say? That question was coming, and it was going to cost her more than anyone else in this chapter. A betrothed girl visibly pregnant had, under the law, put herself within reach of stoning (Deuteronomy 22:23–24); at best she faced a quiet divorce and a lifetime of whispering. It simply is not what she asks first. Her mind goes to God’s method before it goes to her own reputation, and she has perhaps ten seconds in which to think.

What it does not mean. Not, as Augustine and later Roman Catholic interpreters have argued, that Mary had taken a vow of lifelong virginity, and so could not imagine having a child even after marriage. Nothing in the text suggests a vow; she was betrothed to Joseph to be married in the normal way. Her question is simply about how she can conceive now, before the marriage. Matthew says Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (Matthew 1:25), and the Gospels speak of Jesus’ brothers and sisters (Mark 6:3). The more likely reading is that Mary and Joseph lived as husband and wife after Jesus’ birth, and that their marriage was a good and holy thing.

In a sentence. Mary asked how she could have a child, since she had never had relations with a man.

On a Tuesday. It is not wrong to ask God how. Faith asks questions; unbelief demands proofs. Take the question you have been afraid to bring to God and bring it today, in the posture Mary used: I believe you will do what you say; show me how.

For worship. God is not offended by the questions of his children. He who stooped to explain himself to a girl in Nazareth is the God who reasons with us, invites us to ask, and gives wisdom generously without reproach (James 1:5). He is patient with the slow, gentle with the bewildered, and never weary of a trusting question.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered her, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel answered her: the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God.

Gabriel does not explain the biology. He describes an action of God, in two lines of Hebrew-style parallelism, and then names the result.

The Holy Spirit will come upon you. The answer to how: by the direct creative power of God. Not by any human father. As the Spirit hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), the Spirit will bring about a new creation in Mary’s womb. Jesus is the beginning of the new humanity, the second Adam (3:38; 1 Corinthians 15:45).

And the power of the Most High will overshadow you. “Overshadow” (episkiasei) is not a euphemism. It is temple language. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud that settled on the tabernacle so that even Moses could not go in, because the glory of the LORD filled it (Exodus 40:35). It is the word for the cloud on the mountain of transfiguration (9:34). Wherever this verb appears, God is taking up residence. God’s own presence will rest on her. Mary is being told, in the only vocabulary Israel possessed for it, that she is about to become the place where God dwells, the tabernacle in which God comes to dwell with his people: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, literally tabernacled (John 1:14).

The virgin conception. This is the teaching of the virgin birth, more precisely the virginal conception: Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, without a human father. It is taught plainly by both Matthew and Luke, independently, and confessed by the church in every creed.

Did it really happen, or is it a legend? A modern reader deserves the blunt question put plainly. Two things need saying. First, Luke means it literally. The word is parthenos, and Mary’s own question settles the sense: she is betrothed, and says she has not known a man. This is a claim about biology, made in a culture that knew perfectly well where babies come from. Second, it does not read like legend. The pagan tales sometimes offered as parallels, a god taking a mortal woman, a hero fathered by Zeus, are lurid couplings producing half-divine hybrids. This is their opposite: no union, no partner, a quiet overshadowing, and a wholly human child. And nobody inventing a Messiah’s origin would have invented this one, because it left Mary a betrothed girl visibly pregnant before her wedding. That was not a badge of honour but a scandal she would carry, and her son with her: years later men would sneer at him in public, we were not born of sexual immorality (John 8:41). Legends are built to impress. This account cost the family its reputation, and the Gospels record it soberly anyway, because it was true.

Why it matters. Not as a conjuring trick to prove he was special, but because of who was being born. It shows that salvation is God’s work, not human achievement. The one conceived here is not a new person who began in Nazareth. He is the eternal Son, and the virgin conception is how the eternal Son took a real human nature, born of woman, genuinely one of us (Galatians 4:4), without simply becoming one more son of Adam, produced by ordinary generation and heir to Adam’s ruined line. It shows that Jesus is both truly God and truly human: born of a woman, fully human; conceived by the Spirit, the eternal Son taking our nature. And it means that he was not born under the guilt of Adam’s sin, but was holy from conception. Take away the miracle and you do not have a simpler Christ. You have a different one.

Therefore the child to be born will be called holy. Set apart, sinless: holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26). Only a holy one could be the sacrifice for the unholy. A lamb with a blemish could not be offered, and a Saviour with sin of his own could not bear ours.

The Son of God. Not because the Spirit was his father in a physical sense, as pagan myths told of gods fathering children. Luke means that the eternal Son, who already existed (John 1:1–14; Philippians 2:6–7), took human nature in Mary’s womb by the Spirit’s power. The conception does not make him the Son; it is the way the Son became man.

Does it matter if a Christian doubts the virgin birth? Yes, more than people think. A believer who is confused about it is not thereby lost, and should be taught patiently. But to deny it is to deny the plain testimony of two Gospels and the faith of the whole church, and it loosens the doctrine of who Christ is. If Scripture is wrong here, where it speaks so plainly, on what ground do we trust it about the resurrection? And the miracle carries the gospel: our salvation began not with human effort but with God coming down. Hold it gladly. It is not an embarrassment to be explained away but a glory to be adored.

In a sentence. The angel explained that the Holy Spirit would come upon Mary and the power of God would overshadow her, so that her child would be holy, the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. When you say the creed on Sunday, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary, slow down and mean it. Then carry it into the week: the God who began your salvation without any human help is the God who will finish it without your help either.

For worship. The eternal Son of God became a tiny human being in a virgin’s womb, for us. The Word by whom everything that exists was made became an embryo. The Son who had no beginning acquired a birthday. He who fills heaven and earth was, for a season, a few millimetres long, in the dark, under a girl’s heart, in a village nobody had heard of. Angels long to look into this and cannot exhaust it (1 Peter 1:12), and no creature has ever measured the distance he came down.
verseByVerse.note: “Overshadow” recalls the cloud of God’s presence overshadowing the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: the cloud settled on the tent

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. For nothing will be impossible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. For nothing will be impossible with God.

And behold, your relative Elizabeth. A sign, offered without being asked for. Mary could go and see it for herself (v. 39). That is worth noticing: the man who demanded evidence got silence, and the girl who demanded nothing got a relative six months pregnant in the hill country. God is generous with confirmation to people who were not holding out for it. We are not told exactly how they were related. “Relative” (syngenis) is a general word. Elizabeth was of Aaron’s line; Mary’s ancestry is not stated, though some think Luke’s genealogy is hers.

In her old age has also conceived a son. If God can do this, he can do the greater thing.

And this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. Luke lets the village nickname be heard. That is what Elizabeth had been called for forty years, and Gabriel repeats it in the same breath as the news that it is finished. The very thing people called her has been reversed.

For nothing will be impossible with God. Read it in Greek and the sense sharpens considerably. What is translated nothing is literally no word: rhēma, a spoken word, a declared thing, an utterance. No word God speaks will fail to do what it was sent to do. Gabriel is not making an open-ended claim about everything a human being can imagine. He is making a claim about what God has said. And he is quoting, too. This is very nearly what the LORD said to Abraham when Sarah laughed behind the tent door: Is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). The God who gave Isaac to Sarah has given John to Elizabeth, and will give Jesus to Mary. Jesus will say the same of salvation: what is impossible with man is possible with God (18:27).

A signature, not a blank cheque. That distinction matters most to the person most likely to need it. This verse gets written on cards and handed to families in hospital corridors, and it is heard as a promise that the outcome they are desperate for is available if only they can believe hard enough. Then the outcome does not come, and a grieving person concludes either that God let them down or that their faith was too small. Both conclusions are false, and the verse never said what they were told it said. It is not a blank cheque with the amount left for us to fill in. It is a signature under what God has already put in writing. Which is better, not worse. A God who did anything anybody asked would be a God run by whoever prayed last. What is guaranteed here is stronger and steadier: not that everything we want is possible, but that nothing God has promised can fail. He said a barren woman would conceive, and she is in her sixth month. He said a virgin would bear a son, and the room is about to go quiet.

So what has God put in writing? If the request you are carrying is not among the things God has promised, that is not the end of the matter. Look hard at the list of things he has written down: that he will never leave you nor forsake you; that nothing in all creation can separate you from his love; that he works all things together for good for those who love him; that he will finish what he began in you; that he will raise your body on the last day (John 6:40; Romans 8:28, 38–39; Philippians 1:6; Hebrews 13:5). Not one of those is negotiable, and not one of them depends on the strength of your grip. Pray boldly for the healing, the job, the child, the prodigal, because God is able. Rest your weight on the promises, because God is faithful.

In a sentence. Gabriel told Mary that her elderly, barren relative Elizabeth was six months pregnant, for no word of God is impossible.

On a Tuesday. What has God promised in his word that seems impossible to you? Nothing he says will fail. Write down one of those promises and carry it with you this week. When the situation looks impossible, read it again: not what you hope, but what he has said.

For worship. No word of God has ever fallen to the ground. He spoke to Abraham, and Isaac came; to Elizabeth, and John came; to Mary, and the Son of God came. The universe itself stands on his word. Our safety is not the strength of our faith but the faithfulness of the One who speaks, and he has never once failed to do what he said.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.' And the angel departed from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary said: behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word. And the angel departed from her.

Behold, I am the servant of the Lord. “Servant” (doulē): literally slave, a female bond-servant, the feminine of doulos. It is not modesty. It is a legal category, and it describes somebody with no right of refusal, whose time and body and future belong to another. Total submission. She belongs to God, and he may do with her as he wills. Hannah used the same word of herself (1 Samuel 1:11). Mary reaches for the strongest available word for belonging entirely to somebody else, and applies it to herself before she has been told anything more about what is coming.

The cost. Mary’s yes was costly. Count what she agrees to in that half-second. An unmarried pregnant girl in a small village faced disgrace, gossip and suspicion that would follow her and her son for life (John 8:41), in a village of a few hundred people where everyone would do the arithmetic. She might lose Joseph: Matthew tells us his mind was made up to divorce her before an angel changed it (Matthew 1:19–20). Under the law, she could even face death for adultery (Deuteronomy 22:20–24), and she will have read it. Her explanation will be that an angel came. There is no version of this in which she is believed. She said yes anyway.

Let it be to me according to your word. Faith and obedience together. “Let it be” is a single word, genoito, and its form in Greek is the mood of wishing: not a shrug of resignation but a reaching towards. She is not saying I suppose it must happen. She is saying let it happen. She takes God at his word and submits to it. Her response is the opposite of Zechariah’s, and the model for every believer’s response to God. Elizabeth will praise her for exactly this: blessed is she who believed (v. 45). Jesus will later say that those who hear the word of God and keep it are more blessed even than his mother as his mother (11:27–28).

The shape of every real obedience. She is not being held up here as something the rest of us are expected to reproduce; nobody else will ever be asked this. But the shape of it is the shape of every real obedience. She is asked to say yes to a future she cannot see, on the strength of a word from a God she can trust. That is what faith always is. It is never the confident feeling that things will turn out comfortably. It is the decision to trust the character of the one who is speaking, at the precise moment when the content of what he has said has made everything harder.

And the angel departed from her. The conversation is over. The yes is given to a messenger who is about to leave, after which there is nobody in that room but a girl and the God she has just handed her life to. Now she must live by faith in the word, without the angel.

Another garden, another woman. There was another garden and another woman, and a word from outside asking to be believed. That one weighed God’s word against the evidence in front of her, the fruit looked good and the serpent had a point, and reached out her hand. This one weighs nothing and reaches for nothing, and simply says: let it be to me according to your word. The long ruin that began with a woman disbelieving God had begun to be undone by a woman believing him.

What if I cannot say yes to God about something? Be honest with him about it; he knows already. Tell him what you fear, what it will cost and why you are holding back. Then look at the one asking. Mary said yes not because the road looked easy but because she trusted the character of the God who spoke. Ask him for the will to obey, because it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). Take the next step you can see, even a small one. And remember that the perfect yes was spoken by her Son in Gethsemane: not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). Your yes rests on his.

In a sentence. Mary humbly accepted God’s will as his servant, asking that it be done to her according to his word.

On a Tuesday. Make Mary’s words your own prayer today, whatever it costs: I am the Lord’s servant; let it be to me according to your word. Say it over the part of your life you have been keeping back from him, and then do the first thing obedience requires.

For worship. Behind Mary’s yes stands a greater yes. The eternal Son said to the Father, Behold, I have come to do your will (Hebrews 10:7), and took the body Mary’s yes made room for, and carried that yes all the way to the cross. Every promise of God finds its Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). He is the servant of the Lord who never once held anything back, and he is our Saviour.

parallels.desc: let your servant find favour in your eyes

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mary leaves for the hill country of Judah “with haste” — the word suggests urgency, even a kind of breathless joy. She has just received the most overwhelming news in history, and the angel has told her that her elderly relative is also pregnant. She goes at once, not to tell the story but to be with somebody who might understand it: someone else visited by grace in a way that makes no human sense.

The moment Mary's greeting reaches Elizabeth, the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps. John recognises Jesus before either of them has been born. This is not sentimental detail; it is Luke's first testimony to what the Baptist's whole ministry will be. Jesus is the one who is coming, and John exists to point towards him. Even in the womb, before any conscious act of faith, John responds to the presence of the Lord.

The Holy Spirit fills Elizabeth in that moment and she speaks with prophetic clarity. Mary is blessed; the fruit of her womb is blessed; and Elizabeth marvels that “the mother of my Lord” should come to her. That exclamation is the first confession of Jesus's lordship in Luke's Gospel, and it comes from a woman who cannot know it by any natural means. The Spirit has revealed it.

Lord on Elizabeth's lips is the title Israel's Scriptures give to God himself. She is not saying “the mother of an important person.” She is saying “the mother of the one who is LORD.” The full theological weight of the title is present from the beginning.

And the section does not end with the confession. It ends with a beatitude, and the beatitude is about faith: “blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord” (v. 45). Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, does not finally commend Mary's womb, her lineage or her purity. She commends her trust.

That is the section's real climax, and it sets Mary directly against Zechariah, who heard the same angel in the same six months and did not believe. Luke has framed his whole opening around a single question: the word of God has come — will it be received?
verseByVerse.theology:
John's leap at the sound of Mary's greeting is a pre-natal act of recognition that is also a pre-natal act of worship. The Reformed tradition reads this, alongside Jeremiah 1:5 and the Baptist's filling with the Spirit from the womb, as a sign that divine grace and knowledge precede human consciousness. The child does not decide to leap; the Spirit moves him.

This is the grace that goes before us — that calls and shapes and prepares before we are capable of any response. It is not an argument for conscious infant faith. It is a sign of the sovereign grace of God that precedes every human act.

Elizabeth's blessing of Mary — “blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” — applies the Old Testament's blessing language to the New Testament's supreme moment of grace. Mary stands in the line of those through whom God has worked unexpected deliverance.

But she surpasses them all, because the one she carries is not a deliverer of Israel only but the Saviour of the world. And v. 45 keeps even that from becoming a cult of the mother: what the Spirit singles out in her is not her body but her believing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary goes to Elizabeth with haste — not to process her experience alone, not to work things out in private, but to be with somebody who can understand. The instinct is exactly right. The grace of God is not meant to be received and kept in isolation.

The community of the gospel is the community of those who have all, in one way or another, been visited by unexpected grace, and who find in each other's company the confirmation and the joy that private reflection cannot produce. An isolated believer is a believer at risk.

Elizabeth's question — “Why is this granted to me?” — is the question of someone who has not lost the astonishment grace produces. She has been told by an angel that she will bear a child; she is herself six months into an impossible pregnancy; and when she hears Mary's greeting her first response is wonder at the privilege of the moment.

The soul still capable of asking “why me?” in the face of God's gifts is a soul grace is still shaping. The moment we begin to feel we have earned the visit, something essential has been lost. And notice what is entirely absent from Elizabeth: any trace of comparison with the younger woman whose portion is plainly larger than her own.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah. She entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.

Mary arose and went with haste. In those days: immediately. Mary does not sit down to process. She packs. Eager to see the sign (v. 36), and to share her news with the one person who would understand. She is not going in order to break the news; Gabriel has already told her that Elizabeth knows something like it from the inside. She is going to be with the one other person on earth who will not think she has lost her mind.

Into the hill country, to a town in Judah. The highlands around Jerusalem. The town is unnamed; tradition says Ein Karem, about five miles (8 km) west of Jerusalem. From Nazareth it was a journey of 80–100 miles (130–160 km), four or five days on foot, through or around Samaria, over rough country, in the first weeks of a pregnancy, by a girl probably in her mid-teens. A young girl would probably have travelled with a group. Luke does not say who went with her. He says she went with haste.

Grace looks for company. That instinct is exactly right and deserves naming. Grace that has just landed on a person is heavy, and the first thing it looks for is somebody else who has been under the same weight. This is a good deal of what the church is for, and it is why an isolated believer is a believer at risk. Neither of these two women could have explained her situation to anybody else in Israel. Each of them could explain it to the other in a sentence.

And greeted Elizabeth. The ordinary greeting, peace. Mary calls out a greeting at the door and, before Elizabeth has understood anything, the child inside her moves.

The baby leaped in her womb. Not just a normal movement. The verb skirtaō is the one the Greek Old Testament uses of hills skipping like rams (Psalm 114:4) and of the twins struggling inside Rebekah (Genesis 25:22). John, filled with the Spirit from the womb (v. 15), recognises the presence of his Lord, himself an unborn child, perhaps only days or weeks after conception. Elizabeth interprets it: he leaped for joy (v. 44). John’s ministry of pointing to Jesus has begun before either is born. There may be an echo, too, of David leaping and dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:16): the ark of the covenant was the place of God’s presence, and the presence has come to the hill country of Judah again, in a girl.

The first to recognise him. And the order of Luke’s sentence is precise and deliberate. The baby leaps first; then Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit. The mother’s prophecy comes second. The first person in the New Testament to recognise Jesus Christ was a six-month-old unborn child who could not see, could not reason, and had no idea what he was doing. John’s entire ministry will consist of pointing away from himself towards somebody else. He began it before he was born, in the dark, at the sound of a voice, and he did it without a single thought in his head. Which is a fair picture of how anybody comes to recognise him: by the Spirit, before we understand.

The unborn. Luke, who was a physician, chooses his word for that child carefully. He calls him brephos. It is the same word he uses of the newborn Jesus lying in the manger (2:12, 16), and the same word he uses of the infants people brought to Jesus to be touched (18:15). Unborn at six months, newborn in the straw, babe in arms: one word, three stages, no seam anywhere. The unborn child is a person. And Jesus was a person, the incarnate Lord, from his conception. Luke does not pause to argue the point. It is simply how he saw it, and how he wrote it.

And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. And so she speaks as a prophet.

Does this mean an unborn baby can have faith? Luke is describing something unique: John’s Spirit-given recognition of the Lord as part of his special calling as forerunner. It is not a general rule about all unborn children. But it does show that God is not limited by age or understanding, that the Spirit can work in a person before birth, and that the unborn are persons with whom God deals. That is why believing parents may pray for their children from the womb, and why the Reformed confessions speak of elect infants being regenerated by the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3).

In a sentence. Mary hurried to visit Elizabeth, and at her greeting, the unborn John leaped in Elizabeth’s womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. When God works in your life, share it with a fellow believer who can rejoice with you. And look around your church for the person carrying something heavy that only another believer could understand. Make the journey to them. A visit can be the place where the Spirit moves.

For worship. Before Jesus could speak, he was already being recognised; before John could reason, he was already rejoicing. The presence of Christ makes the unborn leap, the old prophesy and the young sing. Wherever he comes, even hidden, even small, joy breaks out, because he is the Lord, and the Spirit will not let him go unhonoured.
verseByVerse.note: The hill country of Judea was the highland around Jerusalem, some 80 miles or more from Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: and she exclaimed with a loud cry, 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
She exclaimed with a loud cry: blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?

She exclaimed with a loud cry. Elizabeth does not greet Mary. She shouts. Spirit-filled, overflowing joy. This is not a decorous welcome at the door. An old woman has been overtaken by the Holy Spirit in her own hallway and comes out of it at the top of her voice.

Blessed are you among women. The construction is a Hebrew superlative: most blessed of all women, because of the child she carries. Jael was praised in similar words for delivering Israel (Judges 5:24). Mary will bear the Deliverer.

And blessed is the fruit of your womb. Mary is blessed because her child is blessed. Her honour comes from him. And note the order: she blesses Mary, then moves immediately past her to the child, and returns to Mary only to commend her faith (v. 45). Almost every word after this is about him.

And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? A remarkable confession. This is the first human confession of Jesus as Lord in Luke’s Gospel, and it is made by a pregnant old woman in a village house about an embryo she cannot see. “Lord” (kyrios) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s own name, and on the lips of a daughter of Aaron steeped in that Bible it is not a courtesy title. Elizabeth is not saying the mother of somebody important. By the Spirit, she is saying that the child inside her young relative is the LORD.

The elder bows. Now look at who is speaking and to whom. Elizabeth is the elder by decades. She is the priest’s wife, the daughter of Aaron, the one with the angelic visitation in her own household, pregnant with a great prophet, a miracle six months advanced. Mary is a teenager from Galilee engaged to a builder. By every measure a human being naturally reaches for, the seniority runs one way, and Elizabeth’s first instinct is to humble herself and ask why she has been granted the privilege of the visit. Why? Because Mary’s child is my Lord.

No trace of comparison. There is not a trace of comparison in her, and that is rarer than any miracle in this chapter. Two people are blessed at the same moment, unequally, and the one with the smaller share is the one who is delighted. Most of us can manage to be pleased for somebody else right up to the point where their gift is visibly larger than ours, and then something goes quiet inside. The Spirit filled Elizabeth, and what came out was joy at another woman’s greater portion. Her son will say the same thing thirty years later: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

Where Christians differ: Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus (AD 431) gave Mary the title Theotokos, God-bearer or Mother of God. It was meant as a statement about Christ: the one Mary bore is truly God, one person, not two, not a man who later became divine. Protestants have generally accepted the doctrine while being wary of the title, because it has been used to exalt Mary. Verdict: the doctrine is true and important: the child in Mary’s womb was the eternal Son of God made man, Elizabeth’s Lord. But it does not mean that Mary is the source of his deity, or that she should be honoured above other believers. Mother of my Lord is the biblical phrase, and Mary’s honour is always derived from her Son. The title, rightly used, says something about him.

Still astonished. Her question, why is this granted to me?, belongs to a person who has not lost her astonishment. She has had an angel in the family and an impossible pregnancy of her own, and she is still amazed to be visited. Familiarity with grace is the occupational hazard of everyone who has known God a long time. The moment the visit stops being a surprise, something has begun to harden.

How do I stop envying a fellow Christian? Start where Elizabeth started: with the Lord, not the comparison. Her eyes were on the child, and so the difference in gifts did not matter. Envy grows when we measure our share against someone else’s; it shrinks when we remember that every gift, theirs and ours, is grace we never deserved. Thank God aloud, specifically, for the thing in your brother or sister that you envy. Then serve them in it. And remember the body: their greater gift is given for your good as well (1 Corinthians 12:26).

In a sentence. Filled with the Spirit, Elizabeth blessed Mary and her child, and humbly marvelled that the mother of her Lord should visit her.

On a Tuesday. Think of the believer whose gifts or blessings outshine yours, the one that makes something in you go quiet. Today, find a way to say the equivalent of Elizabeth’s sentence to them, and mean it.

For worship. Elizabeth called an unborn child my Lord, and she was right. He was Lord in the womb, Lord in the manger, Lord on the cross and Lord on the throne. The God whose name Israel would not pronounce had come to the hill country hidden in a girl, and the Spirit gave an old woman eyes to see him. May he give us the same eyes, and the same astonishment, that he should come to us.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.

The baby in my womb leaped for joy. Elizabeth explains what happened at the door. She interprets her own child’s movement, and she does it under the filling of the Spirit, so this is not a mother’s fond guess. “Joy” (agalliasei): exultation, the joy of the messianic age, the gladness that cannot sit still. Gabriel had promised Zechariah joy and gladness at the boy’s birth (v. 14). The joy has already begun.

And blessed is she who believed. Then Elizabeth pronounces a beatitude, the first in Luke’s Gospel, spoken by a woman, some months before Jesus is born. Read what she actually commends. Not Mary’s purity. Not her lineage. Not her womb; she has just blessed that, and now she moves to something else and gives it the emphatic final position. What the Holy Spirit singles out in the mother of the Lord is that she believed. Mary is blessed because she trusted God’s word. Faith is what makes anyone blessed (11:28).

The chapter’s whole argument. Her faith is the contrast with Zechariah’s unbelief (v. 20), in Elizabeth’s own house, where her husband still sat silent. Two people receive an announcement from the same angel in the same six months. One does not believe, and is silenced. One believes, and is blessed. Luke is not moralising about temperament. He is showing, before Jesus has drawn breath, what this entire Gospel is going to be about: the word of God comes, and everything turns on whether it is received.

Blessed rather. Luke will come back to this and make it explicit. Later a woman in a crowd calls out to Jesus, Blessed is the womb that bore you, the natural thing to say, and very close to what Elizabeth says here. And Jesus answers her: Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it (11:27–28). He is not disowning his mother. He is redirecting the blessing onto the thing his mother actually did, which is exactly what Elizabeth commends in this verse, and exactly what stands open to anybody reading this page.

That there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord. God’s word will be fulfilled. Faith rests on that. And notice when she believed. Not once the pregnancy showed. Not after Joseph came round, or Simeon confirmed it, or the shepherds turned up with their story. Mary believed that there would be a fulfilment: future, unseen, unverified, and about to make her life extremely difficult. Faith is not the conclusion reached once the evidence is safely in. It is trust extended across the gap while the evidence is still on its way. Everything else in the Christian life stands downstream of whether that gap can be crossed.

Is my faith strong enough to make me blessed? The blessing does not rest on the size of your faith but on the faithfulness of the one you trust. Mary was blessed because she believed God’s word, and the power was in the word, not in her believing. A trembling hand that holds Christ receives all of Christ. If your faith is weak, take it to the word: read the promise again, pray it back to God, and ask him to strengthen what he has begun. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves; strong faith in anything else does not.

In a sentence. Elizabeth explained that her baby had leaped for joy at Mary’s greeting, and blessed Mary for believing that God’s word to her would be fulfilled.

On a Tuesday. Blessed are those who believe God’s word. Which of his promises do you need to believe today? Choose one, and live this day as though it were true before you can see it, because it is.

For worship. The blessing of the gospel is open to every hearer: not only to the woman who carried Christ, but to everyone who hears his word and keeps it. God has spoken, and his word cannot fail. He gives the faith that receives it, he keeps the promise it rests on, and he fills those who believe with a joy that leaps.

parallels.desc: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–56 — Mary's Song of Praise: The Magnificat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Magnificat — named from the first word of its Latin translation, “My soul magnifies the Lord” — is the New Testament's greatest hymn and one of the most theologically rich passages in Scripture. It is modelled so closely on Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2:1-10 that some have argued Luke originally assigned it to Elizabeth; but the text is clear, and the reasons for it belonging to Mary are overwhelming.

Mary is the New Testament's Hannah — the woman through whom God's greatest act of salvation is brought into the world. And like Hannah she responds not with private gratitude but with public theology: a proclamation of what God is like, what he has done, and what he always does.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 46-50) is personal. Mary sings of what God has done for her: he has looked on the humble estate of his servant; he has done great things for her; his mercy extends to those who fear him. The second (vv. 51-55) is cosmic and historical: God has scattered the proud, brought down the mighty, exalted the humble, filled the hungry, sent the rich away empty, and helped his servant Israel.

Those verbs are past tense — the Greek aorist, expressing completed action — even though none of it has yet visibly happened. Mary sings in the prophetic past: what God is going to do in Jesus is so certain that she sings it as already accomplished. This is the faith that sees the invisible reality and speaks it before it is seen.

The theology of the Magnificat is the theology of the great reversal — the consistent pattern in which God works through what the world considers weak, low, foolish and despised, to accomplish what power and wisdom cannot. The proud are scattered; the mighty brought down; the humble exalted; the hungry filled; the rich sent away empty.

This is not a manifesto for violent revolution — every verb has God as its subject — but the testimony of a God whose ways are not our ways, who chooses the foolish things of the world to shame the wise (1 Cor. 1:27). Mary has understood it because she has lived it: she is herself the lowly servant God has honoured beyond imagining.

And the song ends where the story began, with Abraham (vv. 54-55) — the reversals are not God changing his policy but God keeping an old appointment. Then, with no transition at all, Luke notes that Mary stayed three months and went home (v. 56). She walked back to Nazareth visibly pregnant, to a fiancé who would decide to divorce her. The extraordinary is set down in the middle of the ordinary, and the ordinary is where it has to be carried.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Magnificat's use of the past tense for events that have not yet occurred — he has scattered the proud, he has brought down the mighty — is the linguistic form of prophetic certainty. The prophets of Israel consistently spoke of future events in the past tense when the certainty of God's word made the outcome as sure as if it had already happened.

Isaiah 53 does exactly this, narrating the Servant's suffering and vindication in the past tense centuries before either occurred. Mary's song places her in that prophetic line — not as one who has received a vision of the future but as one who has received the seed of the future in her own body and understands what it means.

The “humble estate” of Mary is a condition of insignificance and social unimportance. God has looked upon it — deliberately noticed — not despite it but through it. This is the theology of election that runs from Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, and David the youngest over his brothers, to Galilee over Jerusalem and Mary over every princess in Israel.

God's choices consistently invert the world's criteria. The reason is not that the lowly are inherently virtuous. It is that the glory of a grace which chooses them cannot possibly be confused with a favour granted on the basis of merit.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Magnificat has been sung in Christian worship since the earliest centuries — in the evening prayer of the church, in the liturgies of East and West, in the hymns of the Reformation — and set to music by composers from Monteverdi to Bach. It is not merely a beautiful poem. It is the church joining Mary's song, declaring that the God who did great things for her is doing great things still.

Every Christian who sings it stands in the line of Mary's witness: scattering the proud, filling the hungry, keeping covenant with his people, is what he is still doing.

It is also among the most politically subversive texts in the New Testament — not because it calls for revolution but because it announces a King whose reign will outlast every human empire, whose justice will overturn every human injustice, and whose mercy will outlive every human cruelty.
