It happens, and Scripture does not hide it: Isaiah speaks of one who fears the LORD and walks in darkness and has no light, and tells him to trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isaiah 50:10). Darkness in a believer’s feelings is not the same as being outside the light. The sun has risen whether or not clouds cover it today. Keep to the means of grace, tell a pastor or trusted friend, and seek medical help if the darkness is depression; that is not a lack of faith. And wait for him, as those who watch for the morning (Psalm 130:6). He has never failed to bring it.

In a sentence. Through God’s tender mercy, the Messiah will dawn on us like the sunrise from heaven, bringing light to those in darkness and death, and guiding us into peace.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you know who is sitting in the dark this week, grieving, depressed, far from God. You cannot make the sun rise for them, but you can sit with them, pray for them and tell them that the light is coming from above. Go.

For worship. Four hundred years of night, and a world sitting in the shadow of death since a garden gate closed behind it. And then over the eastern rim, without a sound, without permission, without one hand raised anywhere to help it: the light. Not a torch, not a candle carried by a prophet, but the Dayspring himself, the Branch of David, the Sun of Righteousness rising with healing in his wings, to give light to people who had long since stopped looking for it and to set their feet, one by one, in the way of peace. He rose then. He has not set since.

parallels.desc: the sun of righteousness shall rise
light on those in the land of deep darkness

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

One verse, thirty years. Luke has spent seventy-nine verses on nine months, and now he covers three decades in a sentence and moves on. Everything a biography would want, the boy’s education, his father’s teaching, when Zechariah and Elizabeth died and left him, how he came to be in the desert at all, is simply absent.

And the child grew and became strong in spirit. Similar words are used of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:21, 26) and of Jesus (2:40, 52). Growth in body and in spirit, by the Spirit with whom he was filled. Something is being formed that will not be visible until it is needed.

And he was in the wilderness. The wilderness of Judea, the barren desert between the hill country and the Dead Sea. It is not sand. It is a wasteland of limestone ridges and dry gorges falling away towards the Dead Sea: brutally hot, almost waterless, and empty. Zechariah and Elizabeth were old and probably died while John was young. The wilderness was where Israel had been formed, where Elijah had fled, and where the prophets had said God would make a way (Isaiah 40:3). That is where the son of a Jerusalem priest spent his twenties. He had a hereditary right to serve in the temple: the courses, the incense, the rota his own father had drawn the lot in. He never took it up.

Was John connected with Qumran? Some have suggested that John was raised by the Essene community at Qumran, near the Dead Sea, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, who took in boys and also lived in the wilderness and quoted Isaiah 40:3; this is possible but unproved. Luke says nothing of it, and John’s message, a call to all Israel to repent and a baptism given once, was quite unlike the separatist community’s repeated washings. He was in the wilderness because God was preparing him there.

Until the day of his public appearance to Israel. About thirty years later (3:1–2). Years of hidden preparation for a short public ministry. God is not in a hurry. The greatest man born of women, by Christ’s own reckoning, spent thirty of his thirty-odd years doing, so far as the record goes, nothing whatever.

The waiting room. That is a hard verse for anybody whose life currently feels like a waiting room: the years that count for nothing on any visible ledger, the training that has never been used, the gifts nobody has asked for, the long stretch in which a person is plainly being prepared for something that shows no sign of arriving. Luke’s one-line summary of thirty such years is worth having: they were not lost. Every element of what John eventually was came out of them. The plain speech that could not be bought, the total indifference to being liked, the ability to look a king in the face and tell him the truth about his marriage: none of that is learned in a city. It is what the desert does to a man, and it cannot be got any other way, or in any less time.

Not knowing how long. It has to be said as well that John did not know how long the wilderness would last. There was no calendar with the date circled. He was there until the day, and the day was in God’s diary, not his. That is the real condition of the waiting: not knowing whether this is preparation, or simply what the rest of life is going to look like.

What if my wilderness never ends in public ministry? Then it was still not wasted. Most of God’s servants never have a public appearance to Israel; their whole life is the hidden part, and God counts it. The point of John’s desert was not that it led to fame but that God was with him in it and forming him for whatever he had appointed. Your hidden years may be preparing you for a single conversation, a child raised in the faith, a quiet faithfulness that holds a church together, or simply for heaven. Nothing done for God in obscurity is lost (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 15:58).

In a sentence. John grew strong in body and spirit and lived in the wilderness until the day he appeared publicly to Israel.

On a Tuesday. God prepares his servants in hidden places, often for many years. Don’t despise your wilderness years. Ask not when this will end, but what God is forming in you while it lasts, and give yourself to that today.

For worship. The desert years did end, and when they did the whole country went out to hear him. But the sentence that mattered had been written long before any of that: the hand of the Lord was with him (v. 66), and it was with him in the wilderness for thirty years, while nothing whatever appeared to be happening. The God who shaped John in secret also sent his own Son through thirty hidden years in Nazareth before he showed himself. He is never in a hurry and never late, and he wastes nothing.

parallels.desc: the word of God came to John in the wilderness

1.text: <sup>1</sup> Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, <sup>2</sup> just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, <sup>3</sup> it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, <sup>4</sup> that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught. <sup>5</sup> In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. <sup>6</sup> And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. <sup>7</sup> But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years. <sup>8</sup> Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, <sup>9</sup> according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. <sup>10</sup> And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. <sup>11</sup> And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. <sup>12</sup> And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. <sup>13</sup> But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. <sup>14</sup> And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, <sup>15</sup> for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb. <sup>16</sup> And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, <sup>17</sup> and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.” <sup>18</sup> And Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.” <sup>19</sup> And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. <sup>20</sup> And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.” <sup>21</sup> And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. <sup>22</sup> And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. <sup>23</sup> And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home. <sup>24</sup> After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, <sup>25</sup> “Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.” <sup>26</sup> In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, <sup>27</sup> to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary. <sup>28</sup> And he came to her and said, “Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!” <sup>29</sup> But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. <sup>30</sup> And the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. <sup>31</sup> And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. <sup>32</sup> He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, <sup>33</sup> and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” <sup>34</sup> And Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?” <sup>35</sup> And the angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God. <sup>36</sup> And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. <sup>37</sup> For nothing will be impossible with God.” <sup>38</sup> And Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her. <sup>39</sup> In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, <sup>40</sup> and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. <sup>41</sup> And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, <sup>42</sup> and she exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! <sup>43</sup> And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? <sup>44</sup> For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. <sup>45</sup> And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.” <sup>46</sup> And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, <sup>47</sup> and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, <sup>48</sup> for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; <sup>49</sup> for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. <sup>50</sup> And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation. <sup>51</sup> He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; <sup>52</sup> he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; <sup>53</sup> he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. <sup>54</sup> He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, <sup>55</sup> as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” <sup>56</sup> And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home. <sup>57</sup> Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. <sup>58</sup> And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her. <sup>59</sup> And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, <sup>60</sup> but his mother answered, “No; he shall be called John.” <sup>61</sup> And they said to her, “None of your relatives is called by this name.” <sup>62</sup> And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. <sup>63</sup> And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they all wondered. <sup>64</sup> And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. <sup>65</sup> And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, <sup>66</sup> and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. <sup>67</sup> And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, <sup>68</sup> “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people <sup>69</sup> and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, <sup>70</sup> as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, <sup>71</sup> that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; <sup>72</sup> to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, <sup>73</sup> the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us <sup>74</sup> that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, <sup>75</sup> in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. <sup>76</sup> And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, <sup>77</sup> to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins, <sup>78</sup> because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high <sup>79</sup> to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.” <sup>80</sup> And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

2.title: The Birth of the King
2.overview:
Chapter 2 of Luke is the world's most familiar story — and precisely because of that familiarity, it is the story most easily received without being heard. We have heard the angels and the manger and the shepherds so many times that the shocking strangeness of the events has been smoothed away by repetition. Luke is a careful historian, and he intends these details to be astonishing: the Emperor of Rome issues a decree, and the decree unwittingly fulfils a prophecy he knows nothing about. The Son of God is born not in a palace but in the place where animals feed. Heaven's armies appear not to priests or rulers but to shepherds — the lowest of the low in first-century Jewish society. The incarnation is not a dignified event. It is a scandal.

The chapter moves through four scenes: the birth in Bethlehem (vv. 1–7), the angels and the shepherds (vv. 8–20), the presentation in the temple with Simeon and Anna (vv. 21–40), and the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple (vv. 41–52). Together they establish three things about the child: he is born in the line of David and in fulfilment of Scripture; he is recognised by the Spirit-filled as the one Israel has been waiting for; and he understands himself, from the earliest age, as defined by a unique relationship with the Father that supersedes even the claims of family.

The presentation in the temple (vv. 21–40) is one of Luke's most theologically dense passages. In Simeon's song — the Nunc Dimittis — the scope of the child's significance is made explicit for the first time: he is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.” He is not merely the Messiah of Israel; he is the fulfilment of the universal promise of Isaiah (42:6; 49:6), the Servant who is to be the light of the nations. And the shadow of the cross falls even here: Simeon tells Mary that a sword will pierce her soul, that this child is set for the falling and rising of many, that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed. The manger casts the shadow of the cross from the very beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Birth of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of Jesus is introduced by one of the most politically freighted sentences in the New Testament: “In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus.” Augustus was the most powerful man in the world — the man who had ended a century of Roman civil war and inaugurated the Pax Romana. He called himself divi filius, son of the deified Julius. The Roman world hailed him as saviour, as lord, as the bringer of peace and of good news.

Luke places that decree at the head of the story of the one who is the true Son of God, the true Saviour, the true Lord, the true bringer of peace and good news. The contrast is not accidental. Luke's Gospel is, among other things, a counter-narrative to the propaganda of Rome — and it never once raises its voice to say so.

Augustus's census serves God's purposes without Augustus knowing it. He orders a registration for taxation; God uses it to bring a Galilean couple to Bethlehem, where Micah had said the ruler of Israel would be born (Mic. 5:2). The most powerful man on earth is, unwittingly, the instrument for keeping a seven-hundred-year-old promise.

This is the biblical theology of providential history. God works through the ordinary and sometimes brutal machinery of human politics to accomplish his purposes, and neither the emperor's ignorance nor his indifference can obstruct it. Nor does God remove the cost: the couple still walk ninety miles, and Mary still walks them at the end of a pregnancy.

The manger is the detail that has shaped two thousand years of Christian imagination, and rightly. Mary wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no place for them in the inn. The word rendered “inn” (katalyma) more often means the guest room of a private house — it is the word used of the upper room at the Last Supper (22:11) — and the likeliest picture is a crowded family home whose guest room was already full.

Either way the scene is the same: the one who is the bread of life is laid in the box the animals eat from; the one who made every star has nowhere to be put. The incarnation is the ultimate act of self-emptying, and Luke communicates it not with theological abstraction but with the concrete detail of the trough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The juxtaposition of Caesar Augustus and the infant Jesus is a statement about the nature of true power. Augustus commanded armies, controlled the Mediterranean, and issued decrees that moved millions across the empire. The child in the manger will command no army for thirty years, will spend his public life in a small region of a minor province, and will die as a criminal.

And yet it is the child, not the emperor, who is worshipped two thousand years later — whose kingdom, as Zechariah sang, has no end. Luke is asking his reader to see, from the first chapter onward, that the power which actually runs the universe does not look like the power that runs an empire.

The swaddling cloths are not merely a practical detail; they are a sign. When the shepherds are told they will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger, the cloths are part of the identifier. They say: he is truly human, wrapped as every newborn was wrapped, indistinguishable at a glance from any other child in Bethlehem.

The manger says the other half: that his humanity is received in the most vulnerable and dependent form imaginable. The eternal Son of God becomes a baby who cannot feed himself, cannot move himself, and cannot survive an hour without his mother.
verseByVerse.examples:
The census that brings Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem is a reminder that God uses inconvenient, uncomfortable, even oppressive circumstances to accomplish his purposes. Joseph and Mary did not choose to travel ninety miles at the end of a pregnancy. The Roman state imposed it. And in the imposition, the plan of God was fulfilled.

The Christian who finds himself in circumstances he did not choose — a redundancy that opens a door, a move that leads to an unexpected church, a disruption that turns out to have been an appointment — is living in the pattern of the incarnation. Being in the centre of God's will has never meant being outside other people's decisions.

The manger has been the comfort of every Christian who has ever felt overlooked, marginalised, or without a place. The Son of God did not insist on suitable accommodation. He took what was available, in the circumstances Providence had arranged, and made it holy.

No circumstance is too humble, and no situation too undignified, to be the place where God chooses to be present. The God who was born in a stable is found in the most improbable places — which is exactly where his people most often need to find him.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration, when Quirinius was governor of Syria.

Meaning first. Luke 2 tells of the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, the announcement to shepherds by an army of angels, the presentation of the infant in the temple where Simeon and Anna recognise him, and the one story we have of his boyhood, when at twelve he stayed behind in his Father’s house. The whole chapter holds two things together: the glory of who this child is, Saviour, Christ the Lord, God’s salvation, a light for the nations, and the lowliness of how he came, in a feeding trough, to a poor family, under the law, growing up unseen in Nazareth. The emperor issues decrees and thinks he rules the world; the true King is wrapped in strips of cloth, and God moves the empire to bring him to the right town.

The setting. Luke sets the birth of Jesus on the stage of world history, inside the machinery of empire, and he does it with a name that would have made a first-century reader sit up. The most powerful man in the world issues a decree, and without knowing it, moves a poor couple to the very town where the prophet Micah said the Messiah would be born (Micah 5:2). God rules the emperors.

Caesar Augustus. Octavian, the great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar, who ended a century of Rome’s civil wars and became the first Roman emperor, ruling from 27 BC to AD 14. The Senate gave him the title Augustus, revered one. His official title was divi filius, son of the deified one, son of god. He was hailed in inscriptions as saviour and lord, and a famous decree in Asia Minor called his birthday the beginning of the good news (euangelia) for the world. He was credited with bringing peace, the Pax Romana. Luke’s readers would notice the contrast: every one of those words is about to be given to somebody else in this chapter, by an angel, over a field of sheep. The angels announce good news of a true Saviour, Christ the Lord, and true peace (vv. 10–14), born in a feeding trough. Luke is quietly staging the two claims side by side and letting the reader decide which one held. One of these men issued a decree that moved the world. The other could not yet hold up his own head.

That all the world should be registered. “All the world” (oikoumenē) means the Roman Empire. A registration, or census, was taken for taxation and military purposes. Augustus ordered several censuses in various provinces during his reign.

How providence works. And notice what the decree actually accomplishes. Augustus wants a tax register. God wants a Galilean couple in Bethlehem, because Micah had said seven hundred years earlier that the ruler of Israel would come from there. The most powerful man on earth signs an order, and without the least idea what he is doing, he serves a prophecy he has never read, about a God he does not worship, on behalf of a child he will never hear of. That is how providence works. God governs history by means of people who are convinced they are governing it themselves.

This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria. A well-known historical puzzle, and the difficulty is real and is better faced than dodged. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius is known to have been governor of Syria from AD 6, when he conducted a census in Judea after it came under direct Roman rule; Luke himself mentions the revolt of Judas the Galilean that it provoked (Acts 5:37). But Jesus was born before Herod died in 4 BC. On the face of it Luke is a decade out. Several solutions have been proposed. Quirinius may have held an earlier office in Syria, perhaps as a military commander, during which an earlier census began; there is some evidence he was active in the region then. Or the Greek may be read, as the ESV footnote allows, as: this was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria, distinguishing it from the famous later census. That is the simplest answer. A provincial registration may also simply have taken years to work through.

Did Luke make a mistake? Weigh this before concluding that he blundered. Luke plainly knew about the AD 6 census, since he reports its consequences himself, so he is hardly the man to have muddled it with another. He was a careful historian (1:3), and wherever this writer can be checked he proves unusually accurate, getting a mass of shifting local titles exactly right where a careless man would have stumbled. Such a man has earned the benefit of the doubt at the one point where our own records happen to be thin. The puzzle is not settled, but it is not a proof of error, and honesty serves better here than invented certainty.

In a sentence. The emperor Augustus decreed a census of the empire, the first, when Quirinius was governor of Syria.

On a Tuesday. The decisions of governments, however powerful, serve God’s purposes. He is working even through what seems like bureaucratic inconvenience. When the news is full of powerful men and their decrees, remember who moved Augustus’s pen, and pray for those in authority without fearing them (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

For worship. The God who rules the emperors is the God who came as a baby. He turned the census of the most powerful man on earth into a road for a pregnant girl, so that a seven-hundred-year-old promise would land in the right town on the right night. Caesar’s titles have crumbled into museum stones. The child he never heard of is Saviour and Lord for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Augustus ruled the Roman Empire from 27 BC to AD 14. The ESV notes that verse 2 can also be read “This was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria” — the dating of this census is debated.

parallels.desc: the revolt “in the days of the census”

verseByVerse.quote: And all went to be registered, each to his own town. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone went to be registered, each to his own town. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.

Each to his own town. The town of his family’s origin, or where he held property. An Egyptian census edict from AD 104 similarly required people to return to their home districts.

And Joseph also went up from Galilee. “Up” because Judea is higher, and Jerusalem is always up. Ninety miles, and Luke gives it a sentence.

The road was not shortened. From Nazareth to Bethlehem is four or five days on foot for people who are not pregnant. Mary is in the last stage of a first pregnancy. The road runs south through hill country, and every mile of it was ordered by a man in Rome who wanted his revenue figures. Nobody asked whether it was a convenient time. The Christmas story is regularly told as though God arranged a gentle providence for the holy family. He did not. He arranged a tax census, a long walk, and an overcrowded town. The plan of salvation ran straight through a bureaucratic imposition that everyone involved would have described as a nuisance, and God did not remove one inch of the road to spare the mother of his Son.

To the city of David, which is called Bethlehem. Bethlehem, about five miles (8 km) south of Jerusalem, was David’s home town (1 Samuel 16:1; 17:12). The name means house of bread: the Bread of Life is born there (John 6:35). Micah had prophesied: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2). Jerusalem was usually called the city of David; Luke gives the title to humble Bethlehem.

Because he was of the house and lineage of David. Jesus’ legal descent from David came through Joseph (1:27). Luke gives the reason for the journey twice over, because it is the point. A thousand years earlier a shepherd boy had been anointed in that town (1 Samuel 16:1–13); six centuries earlier the line had been cut off and carried to Babylon; and now the heir of David walks back into his ancestral town to be counted as a taxpayer of a foreign empire. The dynasty had come to this. And it is precisely here that Micah’s promise lands.

With Mary, his betrothed, who was with child. Still betrothed: Matthew tells us Joseph had taken her as his wife but had no union with her until the child was born (Matthew 1:24–25). Luke’s wording is not a contradiction; it is a witness’s exactness. This is what their situation looked like to everyone who saw them on that road, and very likely how the register recorded it: a woman heavily pregnant, travelling with a man she was not yet fully married to, in a culture where everybody counted the months. Why did she go? Perhaps she was also required to register, or perhaps Joseph would not leave her alone in Nazareth to face gossip. The journey of about 80–90 miles (130–145 km) would have taken several days, hard for a woman near the end of pregnancy.

The cost went on. They walked ninety miles under that. There is no record of either of them complaining about it. Whatever else the yes at 1:38 cost, it went on costing all the way to Bethlehem, and the cost was not glorious. It was tiredness, and dust, and the way people looked at them at the wells.

What about my life being pushed around by other people’s decisions? This is worth remembering by anybody whose life is currently being moved about by decisions taken in rooms they will never enter: a restructure, a policy, a landlord, a letter from an office. Being inside God’s will has never meant being outside other people’s decisions. Joseph and Mary were in the exact centre of the plan of God and were also, at the same moment, two more names on a Roman list. You may appeal, object or plan around the decision where that is right. But you need not believe that the people in the room are the ones in control. Your Father is, and he can turn their decree into your road.

In a sentence. Because of the census, Joseph, a descendant of David, travelled from Nazareth to Bethlehem, David’s town, with Mary his betrothed, who was pregnant.

On a Tuesday. God fulfilled a prophecy seven centuries old by means of a tax census. He is faithful to his word in ways you would never expect. When the form arrives, the transfer comes through, the plan is cancelled, walk the road without bitterness. You do not know what promise it is carrying you towards.

For worship. The heir of David walked into his father’s town as a nobody on a Roman list, and the God of Micah’s prophecy was steering every step. He did not spare his Son’s mother the road, and he did not spare his Son the greater road that lay ahead. He keeps his promises through dust and decrees, and he is never more in control than when the powerful think they are.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth to Bethlehem is a journey of roughly 80–90 miles.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were there, the time came for her to give birth. She gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.

And while they were there. We do not know how long they had been there. The tradition that she gave birth on the night they arrived is not in the text.

She gave birth to her firstborn son. Told with the greatest simplicity. The most important birth in the history of the world is recorded in a handful of words, with no adjectives. The eternal Son of God was born as a human baby. Luke, a physician, records no complication, no cry, no drama. There is a strong argument that Mary herself is the source for these chapters, and the restraint sounds like her. “Firstborn” carries the meaning of legal rights and of being consecrated to God (v. 23; Exodus 13:2). And Christ is the firstborn of all creation and the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:15, 18).

Where Christians differ: did Mary have other children? Luke could have written her son. That he writes her firstborn son is, on the plainest reading, the ordinary way of speaking of a woman’s first child, and it naturally implies others came after, though it does not require it. Read it alongside Matthew’s note that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth (Matthew 1:25), and alongside the four brothers and the sisters named later in the Gospels (Matthew 13:55–56; Mark 6:3). Rome and the Orthodox East read it differently, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life and that the brothers were cousins or Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. The word alone does not settle the argument: firstborn was also a legal term for the son who opened the womb and carried the firstborn’s rights, which is exactly the status that sends this family to the temple fifteen verses later. Verdict: the natural reading is the right one, and nothing in Scripture requires straining past it: Mary and Joseph went on to have a family in the ordinary way. Nor is anything precious lost by taking it plainly. Mary’s honour never rested on what happened after Bethlehem. It rests on the virgin conception, on the child she bore, and on the faith with which she received him.

And wrapped him in swaddling cloths. Strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn, to keep the limbs straight and warm. Not a sign of poverty: it is what every mother in that world did with a newborn. Normal care, done by Mary herself, without a midwife, it seems. He was not neglected (Ezekiel 16:4). It is the ordinary, competent care of a baby by somebody who knows what she is doing. And it is the first sign of something Luke will not let go of: this is a real infant, with real limbs that need binding. Solomon was swaddled too, as an old Jewish writing outside the Bible recalls (Wisdom of Solomon 7:4–5): even the greatest king began like this.

And laid him in a manger. A feeding trough for animals, perhaps of stone or wood. Luke says it three times in ten verses, which is his way of underlining. The one who would say I am the bread of life was laid, on the first night, in the box the animals ate out of. The tradition of a stable or a cave (from the second century) comes from the manger. Many houses had an area at the lower end, or a cave beneath, where animals were kept at night, with mangers.

Because there was no place for them in the inn. “Inn” (katalyma) is not the word for a commercial inn; that is pandocheion, which Luke uses in the parable of the good Samaritan (10:34). Katalyma means a lodging place or guest room, the same word as the upper room of the Last Supper (22:11). The likeliest picture is not a hard-faced innkeeper with a full register but a crowded family house in Bethlehem, its one guest room already taken, perhaps by other relatives in town for the census, and a couple put in the lower part of the house where the animals were brought in at night. It is a smaller and sadder scene than the pantomime. Nobody turned them away. There simply was no room, and the family made do. Either way, the point stands: the Lord of glory was born in the humblest circumstances. No room. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Does it matter whether it was an inn or a guest room? Not to the gospel, but it helps us read honestly. The popular picture of a cruel innkeeper is not in the text, and preaching against him misses the point. Luke’s emphasis is not on someone’s unkindness but on God’s chosen lowliness: the Son of God did not merely suffer rejection at the door of an inn; he entered the world at the bottom of an ordinary crowded house, among the animals. It also means the Christmas story is closer to home than we thought. He came into the kind of overcrowded, makeshift family arrangement many people know.

In a sentence. In Bethlehem, Mary gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in strips of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the guest room.

On a Tuesday. Make room for him. Not only at Christmas, but in the crowded house of your week: the schedule already full, the guest room taken by other things. Give him the first part of the day, not what is left in the lower room.

For worship. There it is. The Word who was in the beginning with God, by whom all things were made, is lying in straw in a back room in an overcrowded village, wrapped in strips of cloth by a teenager, with the smell of animals in the air and nobody in the world aware of it except a few shepherds who have not been told yet. He who upholds the universe by the word of his power is being held up by his mother, because he cannot hold his own head. There is no distance in the universe like the distance he came, and he came all of it.
verseByVerse.note: Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn. A manger is a feeding trough. The word for “inn” can mean a guest room — the same word used for the upper room in 22:11.

parallels.desc: though he was rich, he became poor

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — The Shepherds and the Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The announcement of the birth is made not to the emperor, not to the high priest, not to the Sanhedrin, not to the scholars who could have quoted the prophecy from memory — but to shepherds keeping watch over their flocks in a field at night.

In first-century Jewish society shepherds occupied the lowest rungs of the ladder. Their work made ritual purity nearly impossible to maintain; later rabbinic rulings counted their testimony unreliable; and the settled respectable classes regarded them with suspicion. It is to these men, in this field, at this hour, that the glory of the Lord appears — the same glory that had filled the tabernacle and had not been seen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple.

The angel's announcement is one of the most compressed theological summaries in the New Testament: “For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.” Three titles in seven words. Saviour — the one who rescues; a title Caesar also claimed and could not fulfil. Christ (Christos) — the Anointed One, the fulfilment of Israel's whole prophetic tradition. Lord (kyrios) — the title Israel's Scriptures give to God himself. All three at once, all three together, all three true.

The sign given to confirm it is the inverse of every sign of power in human history: a baby, wrapped as every baby was wrapped, lying in a feeding trough. Kings are found in palaces and gods in temples. This one is identified by the humblest container in the village.

Then the sky fills. The heavenly host is a military picture — the armies of heaven drawn up over a hillside, praising God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.”

That last phrase is sometimes rendered “peace, good will toward men,” following a variant reading behind the older English versions. The better-attested text is the one the ESV follows: the peace comes to the people of God's good pleasure. That is not a colder reading but a warmer one — a goodwill announced to everyone in general is guaranteed to no one in particular, whereas this peace rests on the sovereign choice of God, which does not move.

The section ends where it must. The shepherds go with haste, find exactly what they were told they would find, tell everybody, and go back to work — glorifying and praising God, with the sheep still to be watched and nothing whatever in their circumstances altered.
verseByVerse.theology:
The choice of shepherds is Luke's first major instance of the great reversal that runs through his whole Gospel: the last are first, the humble are exalted, and those the world dismisses are the ones God chooses to honour. God shows here, in advance, the design he later carried out when he chose poor and uneducated fishermen for apostles.

The good news comes first to those who have nothing — no status, no ritual purity, no legal standing — because the good news is precisely that God's grace is not distributed on the basis of any of those things.

The sign given to the shepherds requires a different kind of looking than a sign of glory would have required. A God who appears in unexpected humility can be walked past. The shepherds do not go looking for what they would have expected; they go looking for exactly what they were told to expect, and they find it.

And Luke is careful about the response of everyone else. The neighbours wondered — a word he uses often and never confuses with faith. Wonder is a doorway and not a destination. Mary, in the same room, does something different with the same information (v. 19), and the contrast is the point of the paragraph.
verseByVerse.examples:
The shepherds' response — “Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened” — is the model of responsive faith. They do not debate the vision. They do not wait for a second confirmation. They do not propose considering the matter carefully before acting. They go with haste, and they find exactly what they were told they would find.

The gap between hearing the word of God and acting on it is where faith most often quietly dies — not by a decision to disobey, but by a perfectly reasonable delay that becomes permanent. The shepherds closed the gap in about ten seconds.

They then became the first evangelists of the New Testament. Fishermen would follow; a tax collector would follow; a persecutor would follow. But the first to announce the birth of the Saviour were men whose word counted for little and who had nothing to commend them except that they had seen what they had seen.

That is the pattern of Christian witness in every generation: not credentials, not eloquence, not social standing, but the testimony of those who have met God and cannot keep quiet about it. And note what they proclaimed — not their experience of the light and the fear, but “the saying that had been told them.” The message, not the sensation.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And an angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. An angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.

Shepherds out in the field. Luke leaves the manger and takes the reader out into the dark, and the choice of company is deliberate. Shepherds were humble working men, not the gentle figures of the Christmas card. In first-century Jewish society they were near the bottom. The work made ritual purity practically impossible; they were out with animals for days at a time, away from the washings and the synagogue. In later rabbinic writings they were often looked down on, regarded as unreliable and unable to keep the ceremonial law, and grouped with tax collectors as men whose testimony was not accepted in court, on the assumption that a man grazing flocks on other people’s land was probably grazing them where he should not.

The announcement goes to a night shift. These are the men to whom the birth of the Son of God is announced. Not the emperor whose decree opened the chapter. Not the high priest, a few miles away in Jerusalem, nor Herod. Not the scholars who could have quoted Micah 5:2 from memory and who, when Herod asked them in Matthew’s account, did exactly that and then did nothing about it. God shows here, in advance, what he would do later when he chose fishermen for apostles. The news comes first to men with no standing, no purity and no legal credibility, because the news is precisely that God’s grace is not distributed on the basis of any of those things. The good news is for the lowly (1:52). And David, the shepherd king, was from Bethlehem; Jesus is the good shepherd (John 10:11).

Keeping watch over their flock by night. Taking turns to guard against thieves and wild animals. Somebody stayed awake while the others slept. This is not a spiritual retreat. It is work, at an hour when everybody with a choice is in bed. Some suggest these flocks near Bethlehem were raised for temple sacrifices.

What does this do to the date of Christmas? Flocks were kept in the open from spring to autumn, and sometimes all year in the milder Judean climate, so Luke’s detail does not fix the season. The date of 25 December was chosen by the church centuries later; we do not know the time of year, and no doctrine hangs on it. Christians may gladly celebrate the birth of Christ on that day, as long as they do not mistake a tradition for a command. What Luke does tell us is the hour, night, and he means it, because the whole chapter is about a light arriving in the dark.

And the glory of the Lord shone around them. That phrase is the heaviest in the verse. The shining brightness of God’s presence, the kabod, the weight of God’s own glory, which filled the tabernacle so Moses could not enter and settled on the temple so the priests could not stand (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11). That glory had not been seen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple and go out over the Mount of Olives before the exile (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Six centuries later it comes back, and it comes back in a field, to men who could not have gone into the temple courts without a wash and a change of clothes.

And they were filled with great fear. Literally they feared a great fear. Of course they did. This is what happens every time. And the first word out of heaven’s mouth is spoken to deal with it.

In a sentence. To shepherds keeping watch over their flock at night near Bethlehem, an angel appeared and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.

On a Tuesday. God came first to working men on the night shift. However ordinary your work, he can meet you there. If you work nights, care for animals, clean offices or drive the early bus, you are in exactly the company God chose for the first announcement of his Son.

For worship. The glory that left the temple came back in a sheep field. God did not wait for his people to climb up to him; he brought the weight of his presence down to the bottom of the social ladder, in the dark, to men who could not have entered his courts. That is the gospel before a word of it is spoken: the holy God has come to the unclean, and come to save.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds were humble working men, often looked down on.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel said to them: fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.

Fear not. Again, the first word is comfort. Before any content, the terror is addressed. God’s habit of opening with that sentence is worth noticing: he knows exactly what his presence does to people, and he never leaves them standing in it.

I bring you good news. One verb in Greek, euangelizomai, the verb from which comes gospel. This is the gospel. The noun form was Roman public vocabulary: an euangelion was the dispatch announcing a victory, an heir, an emperor’s accession. Heaven takes the empire’s word for a state announcement and puts it in the mouth of an angel over a sheep field.

Of great joy. Joy is the response to the gospel throughout Luke.

That will be for all the people. “The people” (laos) usually means Israel in Luke. But the joy will spread beyond (v. 32). Not for the qualified. Luke will spend twenty-two more chapters showing what all means: a Samaritan, a centurion, a sinful woman, a tax collector, a thief on a cross.

For unto you is born. Two small words in the middle of the sentence: unto you. For shepherds. For you. Not merely a Saviour has been born, but a Saviour has been born for you, said to men whose word counted for little.

This day. “Today” (sēmeron) is a key word in Luke: today this Scripture has been fulfilled (4:21); today salvation has come to this house (19:9); today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). The gospel is never a rumour about the distant past or a hope for the vague future. It is today.

In the city of David. Bethlehem, as promised (Micah 5:2).

A Savior. The title the empire gave to Augustus. Augustus was hailed as saviour of the world for ending the civil wars. He had saved people from each other for a while. He could do nothing at all about what was actually killing them. This is the true Saviour, who saves from sin (Matthew 1:21; Acts 5:31). It is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus is called Saviour at his birth.

Who is Christ the Lord. Three titles in one breath, and two of them were being claimed for Caesar Augustus that year. “Christ” (Christos): the Anointed One, the Messiah, the promised king from David’s line, everything Israel had been promised, gathered into one man. “Lord” (Kyrios): the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s own name, Yahweh. Caesar took that title too. Only one of the two was entitled to it. A newborn baby is the Saviour, the Messiah, and the Lord God. The unique combination Christ the Lord appears only here in the New Testament. The baby in the manger is God.

Joy for a hard December. Good news of great joy is a hard sentence to be handed in a hard season. There are people for whom Christmas is mainly an empty chair, the first one after a funeral, or the twentieth. There are marriages being held together for the sake of a day. There are people who will sing about joy on Sunday morning and cry in the car park afterwards. So read what the angel actually says, and notice that it is not an instruction. He does not command anyone to feel joyful. He reports an event: unto you is born this day. The joy in this verse is not a mood the shepherds are told to work up. It is a fact about something that has happened outside them, in a village down the road, whether they feel it tonight or not. That is the only kind of joy that survives a bad year. A joy that depends on the state of your heart will go down with your heart. A joy that rests on a birth that has already occurred, in a place you could walk to, cannot be taken away by grief; it can only be temporarily hidden by it.

So what do I do if I cannot feel the joy this year? Do not fake it, and do not conclude that you have lost your faith. Let the joy rest where the angel put it: on the fact that a Saviour has been born for you. Go to church anyway, and let others sing the words you cannot. Tell a friend or pastor how hard it is. Weep if you need to; Jesus wept at a grave. Read the angel’s words slowly, and say them back to God: this is true, even tonight. The feeling may come later, or not this year. The fact does not depend on it, and he will carry you until it returns.

In a sentence. The angel announced the good news of great joy: in Bethlehem a Saviour had been born that day, the Messiah and Lord.

On a Tuesday. Receive the news as good news, for you, today, and rejoice. When you tell someone about Jesus this week, tell it as an announcement, not advice: not try harder, but a Saviour has been born.

For worship. Unto us a Saviour is born, who is Christ the Lord. The empire had its saviour and its lord, and he died in his bed at Nola like any other man. Ours was laid in a feeding trough, nailed to a cross, raised from the tomb, and he reigns. He saves from what no emperor could touch, and he was born for shepherds, and for us.
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah; “Lord” was the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

parallels.desc: he will save his people from their sins
to us a child is born
the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.

And this will be a sign for you. A way to recognise him. The shepherds are given a way of identifying the child, and the identifier is the strangest thing in the chapter. In every other place in Scripture where God gives a sign, the sign is remarkable: a burning bush, a fleece, a shadow going backwards on a sundial, a virgin conceiving. Here the sign is a baby in a feeding trough.

A baby wrapped in swaddling cloths. That was normal. Every newborn was swaddled. The cloths say: he is completely human. Every baby in Bethlehem was wrapped that way; nothing about him looked other than ordinary, and that is the point. There was no halo.

And lying in a manger. That was not. No one laid a baby in a feeding trough. This would identify him among all the babies of Bethlehem. Consider what they were not told. They were not given a street, a house, a family name, or the name of the child. They were told to look for an ordinary newborn in a wholly unsuitable container, and in a village the size of Bethlehem that was enough, because there would be exactly one. The manger says: his humanity has been received in the most dependent form there is. A child in a feeding trough cannot feed himself, cannot move himself, cannot survive an hour without somebody else.

The sign is the opposite of what you would expect. The Saviour, Christ the Lord, will be found not in a palace in silk, but in an animal’s feeding trough. That is the sign: his lowliness. Kings are found in palaces. Warriors are found in fortresses. Gods are found in temples. This King is found in the place the animals eat from, and the shepherds are told so in advance, so that when they see it they will not conclude they have come to the wrong house. It points to the whole shape of his life and death. And it meant the shepherds could come. They would not have been allowed into a palace; they could go into a place with animals.

A sign, not a scene. That is worth taking hold of by anyone who has been waiting a long time for God to make himself unmistakable. There is a way of asking for a sign which is really asking for a scene: something loud enough to end the possibility of doubt. God does give signs; he gave one here, and it was a sign that could be walked past by anybody not told what to look for. The pattern has not changed. What God offers his people is not usually a blaze in the sky but a set of appointed ordinary things: bread, wine, water, a book, a gathering of unimpressive people. The world looks at that and sees a feeding trough. Faith looks at the same feeding trough and sees exactly what it was told it would find.

Should I ask God for a sign? Not as a condition of believing what he has already said. The shepherds were given a sign by God; they did not demand one. Jesus refused to perform signs for those who wanted proof on their own terms (11:29). We have something better than they had: the full record of his life, death and resurrection in Scripture. In making decisions, ask God for wisdom (James 1:5), study his word, seek counsel and pray; do not lay out fleeces as a test. And look for him where he has promised to be found: in his word, his people and his ordinances.

In a sentence. The sign by which the shepherds would recognise the Saviour was a newborn baby lying in a feeding trough.

On a Tuesday. God’s greatest work is often found in the lowliest places. Look for Christ among the humble. This Sunday, when the bread and the cup are passed, or the Bible is opened in an unimpressive room, see it as the shepherds saw the manger: exactly what you were told you would find.

For worship. The shepherds were not asked to work anything out. They were told what to look for, and they went and looked. That is the whole of their part in it, and it turned out to be enough. God hid his glory in a feeding trough so that the lowliest could find it and the proudest would walk past. He still does. Blessed are the eyes that see him there.

parallels.desc: the LORD himself will give you a sign

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!

A multitude of the heavenly host. One angel had been enough to terrify them. Now the sky opens. “Host” (stratia) means an army. Not a choir in the modern sense but the massed host of heaven, the armies of the LORD of hosts (1 Kings 22:19), drawn up over a field outside a village of a few hundred people. The armies of heaven have come not to fight but to sing. The armies of heaven announce peace. And Luke does not say they sang; he says they were praising God and saying. Whatever the sound was, the words were plain enough to be written down. The song has two lines, and they run from the top of the universe to the bottom.

Glory to God in the highest. In Latin, Gloria in excelsis Deo, sung in Christian worship for centuries. The birth of Jesus brings glory to God, in the highest heavens. The first purpose of the incarnation is God’s glory. Heaven’s first response to the incarnation is not relief, or congratulation, or wonder at the mechanism. It is glory given to God, which means the angels understood at once what the human race would take centuries to argue about: that this birth is not chiefly about us. It is about him. Something has just happened that shows God to be more magnificent than the angels had yet seen him, and they say so.

And on earth peace. Peace with God, reconciliation, the end of hostility between the holy God and rebellious humanity (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14–17), and the shalom that flows from it. Not the political peace of the Pax Romana, imposed by armies, built out of roads and legions and crucifixion, which lasted as long as the legions did. Not the absence of conflict either: the child in the trough will say plainly that he did not come to bring that sort (12:51). It is the ending of a war between heaven and earth, the peace Christ makes by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1).

Among those with whom he is pleased. Literally among men of his good pleasure (en anthrōpois eudokias). “His good pleasure” is God’s: those on whom God’s favour rests, whom he has chosen in his grace; Ephesians 1:5 and 9 use the same word for God’s choosing will. The peace is not for all people indiscriminately, nor for those who are good enough to please God, but for those whom God, in his sovereign grace, has chosen to favour.

Textual note. The King James Version, following later manuscripts, reads: on earth peace, good will toward men. The difference is one letter in Greek (eudokia or eudokias). One family of manuscripts has eudokia, good will, standing on its own as a third item; the other has eudokias, of good pleasure, attached to the men. The earliest and best manuscripts have eudokias, giving the ESV’s reading. The old reading is familiar from carols, but the better text points to God’s good pleasure.

A warmer reading, not a colder one. The difference in sense is worth having clearly. The first reading makes the announcement a general benevolence broadcast over the earth. The second makes it a specific grant to particular people, given because God chose to give it. That is not a colder reading; it is a warmer one. A goodwill announced to everybody in general is a goodwill guaranteed to nobody in particular. What the angels announce is peace that has an owner’s name on it, resting not on how the recipients turn out but on the good pleasure of God, which is the one foundation that does not move.

How do I know if God’s good pleasure rests on me? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by looking to Christ. The gospel is offered freely to everyone: whoever comes to him, he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have come to Christ, trusting him and turning from your sin, that is the evidence that God’s favour rests on you, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Election is not a locked door to worry about; it is the reason the door was opened to you. If you are not sure you have come, come now. The peace is for all who believe.

In a sentence. A vast army of angels praised God, giving him glory in the highest and announcing peace on earth for those on whom his favour rests.

On a Tuesday. Join the angels: give glory to God for the birth of Christ. Then live in the peace he has made. If you are carrying guilt, anxious that God is against you, hear the angels: the war is over for those on whom his favour rests. Make peace, too, with the brother you are at odds with; the peace of heaven is meant to reach earth.

For worship. Glory in the highest, and peace at the bottom. Between the two lies the whole distance the Son of God travelled that night, and the angels sing at both ends of it, because the God who is glorified in the highest heaven has just made peace at the lowest point of the world. If we have peace with God, it is because his good pleasure rests on us, by grace, and there is nothing in creation that has ever cost more or been given more freely.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV’s “among those with whom he is pleased” follows the better manuscripts; older translations read “good will toward men.”

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.' And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us. They went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.

Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened. The sky closes. The light goes. And the shepherds, standing in a field that is suddenly very dark and very quiet, say the only sensible thing anyone has said so far in this chapter. “Thing” is literally word (rhēma), meaning both the event and the message. They act on the word at once. They do not doubt like Zechariah, but obey like Mary.

What is not in that sentence. No debate about whether the vision was genuine. No suggestion of waiting for daylight, or for a second confirmation, or for somebody more qualified. No one says, but who will watch the sheep?, and that is not a small point, because those sheep were somebody’s property and the shepherds were answerable for them.

Which the Lord has made known to us. They knew the angel’s message came from the Lord. They get the theology exactly right in passing. They do not say the angel told them. They say the Lord did. They understood that a messenger is a mouth and not a source.

And they went with haste. Leaving their flocks. The phrase has been used once already in this Gospel, of Mary going up to the hill country (1:39). Luke reserves it for people whose response to a word from God is to start moving.

The interval where faith dies. The gap between hearing something from God and acting on it is where a great deal of faith quietly dies. It is rarely closed by a decision to disobey. It is closed by delay: by the entirely reasonable interval in which a thing is considered, and weighed, and put off until the season is better, and then no longer feels urgent, and then is not mentioned again. What is remarkable about these men is not their piety. It is that the interval was about ten seconds long.

And found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger. Exactly as the angel said. The sign was fulfilled. Every word of God comes true. They walked into a crowded house in the middle of the night with a story that must have sounded insane, and there in the animals’ quarters was precisely what they had been told they would find. That is the reward of obedience in this story, and it is worth naming because it is so unglamorous. They were not given a further revelation. They were given confirmation of the one they already had. God’s word, acted on, led them to exactly what it said it would, which is the only proof of it anybody ever gets, and the only one anybody needs.

But is it not wise to wait and think before acting? Yes, about many decisions; Scripture commends counsel and care (Proverbs 15:22). But where God has spoken plainly, waiting is usually a polite form of not obeying. You do not need to pray about whether to forgive, to tell the truth, to come to Christ, or to be baptised as a believer; he has already said. Think hard about how; do not linger over whether. And with the call of the gospel itself, delay is the most dangerous thing of all: now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

In a sentence. When the angels left, the shepherds hurried to Bethlehem and found Mary, Joseph and the baby in the manger, just as they had been told.

On a Tuesday. When God speaks, respond at once. Go and see for yourself what he has done in Christ. Think of the thing God has made plain to you in his word that you have been weighing for months. Close the interval today.

For worship. God’s word does not mislead. He sent shepherds into a crowded house in the night on the strength of a sentence, and the sentence was exact to the last detail. He has never yet sent anyone to look for Christ and let them come back empty. Seek, and you will find (11:9), because he has first sought us.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.

They made known the saying that had been told them. They cannot keep it in. Nobody commissioned these men. There is no instruction anywhere in the angel’s message to go and tell people; they were told where to look, and that was all. But having looked, they told everyone. The shepherds became the first evangelists, telling what they had heard and seen. Men whose testimony would not be accepted in court were God’s first witnesses to the birth of Christ, as women would be to the resurrection.

The pattern Luke keeps to. Fishermen will follow them. A tax collector will follow. A persecutor of the church will follow. Not one of the great preachers of the New Testament had credentials at the point where God took hold of him. What the shepherds had was not eloquence or standing. It was that they had seen what they had seen, and there is no substitute for it and no way of manufacturing it.

The message, not the sensation. Notice also what they told. Not their experience: not the light, or the fear, or how the sky had looked. They made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. Their testimony was the message, not the sensation. Which is still the right order: what happened to me is interesting to precisely nobody, and what has happened in Bethlehem is news for everybody.

And all who heard it wondered. “Wondered” (ethaumasan): were amazed. A frequent response in Luke, and he is very exact about it. Wondering is not believing. It is the emotion of a person for whom something has been genuinely interesting and not yet decisive. Crowds marvel at Jesus all through this Gospel, and marvelling saves nobody. The people in that house went to bed amazed, and we do not hear of what became of them.

Amazed, and nothing more. That is a sobering thing to hold beside a Christmas service. It is entirely possible to be moved by this story every December for fifty years, to find it beautiful, to feel something at the carols, to be genuinely glad it is true, and to remain, at the end, exactly where those neighbours were: amazed, and nothing more. Wonder is a doorway, and it is a good one; Luke never sneers at it. But a doorway is for walking through. A verse from now Mary will do something different with the same information, and the difference is the whole point of the paragraph.

What should I say when I tell someone about Jesus? Start with him, not with yourself. Your story matters as a witness to what he has done, but the heart of it is the message: who Jesus is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he calls everyone to turn and trust him. Say it simply, as the shepherds did. You do not need answers to every objection; you can say, I do not know, but I know this. And do not be discouraged if people only wonder. Your task is to tell; it is the Spirit’s work to turn wonder into faith.

In a sentence. Having seen the child, the shepherds told everyone what had been said about him, and all who heard were amazed.

On a Tuesday. You don’t need credentials to tell others about Jesus. Tell what you have heard and seen. And examine your own wonder: has it ever gone through the doorway? If you love the Christmas story but have never bowed to the child in it, do it today.

For worship. God chose men whose word counted for nothing to carry the first news of his Son, so that the power would plainly be his and not theirs. He still sends ordinary witnesses, and he still opens hearts. The message they carried has outlived the empire that despised them: a Saviour is born, and he is Christ the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.

But Mary. A contrast with the general amazement. The but is doing real work. Everybody else in the room wondered; Mary did something else, and Luke marks the contrast deliberately. Mary goes deeper.

Treasured up all these things. “Treasured up” (synetērei): kept carefully, preserved, held on to, the way a person stores something valuable rather than leaving it out. “Things” is again rhēmata, words and events. She kept them in her memory. This is probably one of Luke’s hints at his source: who else could have told him these things, but Mary herself (1:2–3)? If she is the source behind these two chapters, and the intimacy of the detail suggests she is, then this verse is her own account of what she was doing while everybody else was exclaiming, and Luke is telling us how his material came to survive at all.

Pondering them in her heart. “Pondering” (symballousa): literally throwing together, putting together, comparing, thinking through, seeking the meaning. It is the word a person would use for comparing two accounts, or matching a piece to the pattern. So this is not vague reverie. Mary is doing something specific and strenuous. She now has in her possession an angel’s announcement, a relative’s prophecy, her own song, a birth in a stranger’s animal quarters, and a group of shepherds at midnight with a story about an army in the sky. She cannot make one picture of it yet. She lays the pieces alongside each other and keeps turning them. She did not understand everything (v. 50), but she reflected on it. Mary is a model of meditation on God’s word and works.

A believer’s inner method. This is one of the few places in Scripture that shows a believer’s inner method rather than describing it. Something happens that has God’s fingerprints on it and no available explanation. The two usual responses are to force a meaning onto it at once, or to let it go as nothing. Mary does neither. She holds it, unexplained, and works at it. That means keeping a record, mentally or otherwise, of what God has actually done and said, so that it is still there in five years when a piece arrives that makes sense of it. It means resisting the urge to tidy providence into a lesson while it is still happening. And it means being willing to carry an unresolved thing for a long time without either abandoning it or pretending it is resolved.

What does Christian meditation look like? It is not emptying the mind, as in Eastern practices, but filling it with God’s word and turning it over. Take a short passage, read it slowly several times, and ask: what does this say about God? About Christ? About me? What does it command, promise or warn? Connect it to other things you know of Scripture, as Mary connected the angel’s words with the shepherds’ story. Then turn it into prayer and praise. Ten unhurried minutes on a few verses will often do more than an hour of skimming. Psalm 1 calls the man blessed who meditates on God’s law day and night.

In a sentence. Mary carefully kept all these things and kept thinking them over in her heart.

On a Tuesday. Don’t just be amazed by Christ. Treasure and ponder what God has said and done. Take time today to reflect on a passage of Scripture. And keep the record: write down the thing God did this year that you still do not understand, and come back to it.

For worship. She was still doing it twelve years later at verse 51, and there is no sign she had it all worked out even then. The mother of the Lord lived most of her life holding things she did not yet understand, and that is not a failure of faith. It is what faith looks like from the inside, over time. And the God who gave her the pieces gave her, at the cross and the empty tomb, the whole picture. He does not leave his ponderers in the dark for ever.

parallels.desc: his father kept the saying in mind

verseByVerse.quote: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.

And the shepherds returned. To their flocks, to their ordinary work. Their circumstances were the same; they were not. That is the sentence, and it deserves to be felt. These men had seen the glory of God break over a hillside, heard the armies of heaven, walked into a house and found the Messiah of Israel lying in a feeding trough, and told everybody in the village. And when the night was over there was nothing for them to do except go back out to the flock, take the next watch, and get on with a job that had not changed in any respect. Luke does not record that any of them left their trade. There is no suggestion that the shepherds became preachers, or moved to Jerusalem, or were ever heard of again.

Glorifying and praising God. They join the angels’ song (v. 14). That is the note to hold. The night did not deliver them from the ordinary. It went with them into it.

Down from the mountaintop. There is something here for everybody who has come down from a mountaintop. The conference ends, the retreat closes, the funeral service that felt like heaven touching the room gives way to Tuesday, and the temptation is to conclude that the real thing was up there and this down here is the interval between. The shepherds’ testimony is the opposite. The glory came to them at work, at night, in the middle of a shift, and it sent them back to the same shift with the same sheep, and they went praising.

For all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them. Heard (from the angel) and seen (the child): everything matched. The word of God and the facts agreed. Luke closes the section by underlining that last clause once more. The word came; they acted on it; they found it exactly as promised; and their praise is specifically for the correspondence between the two. That is what the whole chapter has been about since verse 1. A decree was signed in Rome, a prophecy was kept in Bethlehem, an announcement was made in a field, and every part of it fitted.

Should a new believer leave his job to serve God? Usually not. Paul told the Corinthians that each should remain in the condition in which he was called, and serve God there (1 Corinthians 7:17–24). God calls some to leave their nets and preach, and the church should test such a call.
