But most believers glorify God by going back to the sheep: doing their ordinary work honestly, well and joyfully, for the Lord and not for men (Colossians 3:23). The question is not whether your job is spiritual enough, but whether you do it with praise.

In a sentence. The shepherds went back to their work praising God for all they had heard and seen, exactly as they had been told.

On a Tuesday. Go back to your ordinary work today glorifying and praising God. Christ is born, and everything is as he said. Take one moment in the shift, the commute or the washing-up to say aloud what you have heard and seen of him.

For worship. The shepherds went home in the dark, singing, to a job nobody respected, which is very nearly a definition of the Christian life. Of everyone in Bethlehem that night, they were the only ones who had both heard and obeyed. And the God they praised had made every word of his promise fit: the decree, the town, the trough, the song. He is the God whose word and works agree, and he goes with his people back into the ordinary, and fills it with praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The presentation is the scene where the old covenant meets the new — where the long story of Israel's worship, sacrifice and waiting encounters the one the whole system had been pointing at.

Joseph and Mary come to Jerusalem for two duties, both required by the law: the purification of the mother forty days after the birth of a son (Lev. 12:1-8), and the presentation of the firstborn to the LORD (Exod. 13:2, 12-15; Num. 18:15-16). They bring the offering of the poor — two birds rather than a lamb and a pigeon — which tells us plainly what the family's circumstances were. The King of heaven and earth was raised in poverty.

Simeon is described in the language of the faithful remnant: righteous, devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit upon him. That phrase, the consolation of Israel, comes from Isaiah 40 — “Comfort, comfort my people” — the promised end of exile and return of God to his people. Simeon has been waiting inside that chapter his whole life, and the Spirit has promised him he will not die before he sees the Lord's Christ.

Now, as a young couple with the offering of the poor come into the courts, the Spirit moves him. He takes the child into his arms, and everything he has spent his life waiting for is a warm weight in his hands.

His song — the Nunc Dimittis — is among the most moving passages in Luke. The verbs are those of a sentry being stood down after a long watch. He can go now: his eyes have seen God's salvation, and the salvation he is holding is not for Israel only but “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” — the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs (42:6; 49:6) and the universal scope of the gospel announced before it has begun.

And then the shadow falls. The child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, a sign to be opposed; and a sword will pierce Mary's own soul. Joy and sorrow are not opposites in Luke's Gospel. They are twins, born of the same truth. The one who is the light of the world will be rejected, and the one whose birth the angels celebrated will die on a cross. Simeon holds the baby and sees all of it.

Anna is the second witness the law required (Deut. 19:15) — a daughter of Asher, one of the tribes long written off as lost, who has given decades of widowhood to fasting and prayer in that building and who arrives at exactly the right hour. And the section closes with the family's return to Nazareth and a single sentence covering the boy's whole childhood: he grew, became strong, was filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon's announcement that the child is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (v. 32) is the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs and the theological seed of the entire Gentile mission of Acts. From the moment of the presentation, Luke's Gospel contains within it the global church. The child in Simeon's arms is not merely the king of the Jews; he is the light of the world.

This is why Luke, writing for a Gentile reader, is the Gospel that most fully develops the universal reach of the good news. The trajectory is established here, in the temple courts, by an old man who has waited his whole life to say what he now says and who is ready to die.

Simeon's warning to Mary — that a sword will pierce her own soul — has been understood in the tradition as pointing to her presence at the crucifixion (John 19:25-27). The word is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, and Simeon does not soften it. The sword is the sword of grief, of the suffering that participation in the Son's mission inevitably involves.

But the clause “that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed” shows a wider purpose. The coming of Jesus forces a crisis of decision in every heart; he does not leave people neutral. He is “appointed for the fall and rising of many” — the stone of Isaiah 8:14 laid in the middle of the road. His presence divides, and in dividing it discloses what was already there.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simeon's “now you are letting your servant depart in peace” is the model of a death well prepared for — not the resignation of a man who has given up, but the discharge of a sentry who has received what he was waiting for. And notice what his peace does not rest on: not on achievement (we are told nothing of what he accomplished), not on longevity, but on what his eyes have seen.

The Christian who has seen that same salvation — not with physical eyes but with the eyes of faith, and has taken hold of it — has precisely what Simeon had, and may face death on precisely the same terms. Not because death is nothing, but because what lies beyond it is the same Christ known in life.

Anna is Luke's portrait of long faithfulness. She had been waiting most of her adult life — decades of widowhood — for the redemption of Jerusalem. She did not give up, did not grow cynical, and did not stop praying because the answer had not come. When it came, she was exactly where she had always been.

Her years were not the waiting room for her ministry; they were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family's arms when everyone around her saw a queue — and who knew, by name, everyone in Jerusalem who was waiting to be told. The reward of patient faithfulness is rarely glamorous. It is being in the right place when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

When he was circumcised. On the eighth day, as the law required (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), like John (1:59). Eight days old, and the first blood he ever shed was shed in obedience to the law he had written. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham. It marked a boy as belonging to the covenant people, under its promises and under its obligations. And it was, for an infant, a real wound, the first shedding of his blood.

Under the law, all the way down. Stop there for a moment, because Luke gives it half a verse and it is worth more. The Son of God enters his own creation and, before he is nine days old, is cut with a knife in submission to a requirement he himself laid down. He does not stand outside the law and gesture at it from a distance. He steps under it, all the way down: born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). There was no way to redeem people who were under something except by getting under it with them. From the beginning he fulfilled it perfectly, on our behalf (Matthew 5:17).

He was called Jesus. The LORD saves (1:31). It was a common enough name; there are several men of that name in Josephus, and that is part of the point. The name over the cross would be an ordinary name from an unremarkable town.

The name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. Mary and Joseph obeyed exactly. Luke is careful with that clause. The naming was not a family decision made in the weeks after the birth; it was settled by Gabriel before there was anything to name. The name was not their choice but God’s.

The knife and the name. Hold the two halves of the verse together, because Luke has put them in one sentence for a reason. On the same day the child is cut into the covenant, he is given the name that says how the covenant will finally be kept. The knife and the name arrive together, and they will arrive together again at the end: the blood and the saving, the wound and the rescue, in the same event.

Why did Jesus need to keep the law for us? Because we have not kept it, and God’s law still stands. Christ did two things for his people. He bore the penalty for our disobedience on the cross, and he lived the perfect obedience we owed, from the eighth day to the last. Both are counted to everyone who trusts him: our sins to him, his righteousness to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is why a believer can stand before God not merely pardoned but accepted as righteous. Your record before God is not your week; it is his life.

In a sentence. On the eighth day Jesus was circumcised and named Jesus, as the angel had commanded before he was conceived.

On a Tuesday. Jesus kept God’s law from his first week of life, for you. His obedience is counted as yours. When you fail today, do not try to cover it with extra effort. Confess it, and rest on the obedience that began in Bethlehem and was finished on the cross.

For worship. And notice who obeys here. Jesus does nothing in this verse; it is done to him. He is carried, held, named and cut, entirely passive, at eight days old. The first thing the Saviour ever did about our salvation, he did by being handed over to somebody else’s hands, and the last thing he did about it, he did the same way. The Lord of the law became its subject, so that its subjects might become sons.

parallels.desc: the name given by the angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, 'Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord') and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord) and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

Two ceremonies. Forty days after the birth the family goes up to Jerusalem, and Luke combines two separate requirements of the law into one visit.

The time came for their purification. After giving birth to a son, a mother was ceremonially unclean for forty days, and then brought an offering to the priest: a lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or dove for a sin offering. If she could not afford a lamb, she could bring two doves or pigeons instead (Leviticus 12:1–8). This was never a statement that childbirth was sinful; it belonged to a whole system of laws about blood and life and the boundary between the holy and the ordinary, teaching Israel by repetition that God is not to be approached casually.

Why their purification? A reader with Leviticus open will trip over the pronoun. The law prescribes purification for the mother alone. The child needs none; Joseph needs none. Luke is almost certainly describing the family’s observance as a whole, the household going up together to discharge what the law laid on them, so that the pronoun covers the journey rather than the rite. It may include Joseph, or the family, or simply be loose phrasing. Some later copies smoothed it to her, which is where the older English reading comes from; but their is the harder and better-attested wording, and a copyist is far likelier to have tidied a difficulty than to have created one.

To present him to the Lord. Every firstborn son belonged to God, because God had spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover, when the firstborn of Egypt were not (Exodus 13:2, 12–15). The firstborn had to be redeemed, bought back, by a payment of five shekels to a priest (Numbers 18:15–16). Luke does not mention the payment, but speaks of presenting him, as Hannah presented Samuel to the Lord for his service (1 Samuel 1:22–28). Jesus is truly holy to the Lord, given wholly to God. What Luke shows is the firstborn handed over to the Lord, who will himself pay a much larger price, not have it paid for him.

Nothing to be purified from. The oddity is worth sitting with, because the whole scene is saying it. Of every person in the temple courts that day, this forty-day-old child is the one with nothing whatever to be purified from. He is holiness itself, carried in a girl’s arms, and he is brought in anyway, counted in with the rest, circumcised on the eighth day and presented on the fortieth like any other son of Israel.

A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8). Leviticus asks for a lamb and a pigeon. It adds that if a woman cannot afford a lamb, two birds will do. Mary brings the birds. Mary and Joseph could not afford a lamb. That single detail tells us what the family’s finances were, and it should be allowed to land. Jesus was born into a poor family. The King of heaven and earth was raised by people who could not afford the standard offering. He grew up in a house where the cheaper option was chosen because it had to be. Anyone who has ever stood at a counter and taken the smaller thing because the larger one was out of reach has stood where Mary stood that morning, and the child she was carrying grew up in that house on purpose.

Was Mary a sinner? The law required a mother to bring a sin offering after childbirth (Leviticus 12:6–8), and Mary brought it, as every mother did. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary was preserved from all sin. But Mary herself calls God my Saviour (1:47), and Scripture says all have sinned (Romans 3:23) with the single exception of her Son. She shared the common need of all people for a Saviour, and obeyed the law that provided for it. She too was a sinner needing atonement, and her atonement was in her arms.

Does Jesus understand money worries? Yes, from the inside. He grew up in a house that counted coins, worked with his hands for a living, later had nowhere to lay his head, and depended on the gifts of others (8:3; 9:58). He is not a distant Lord who cannot sympathise. Bring your bills, your fears about the rent and your shame about being poor to him in prayer; he knows the counter where you take the cheaper thing. And if you are not poor, remember that the Lord himself was raised by people who chose the two birds. Look out for those in your church who are choosing them now.

In a sentence. Forty days after his birth, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple to present their firstborn to the Lord and to offer the poor family’s sacrifice for Mary’s purification.

On a Tuesday. Jesus grew up in a poor family. He understands financial hardship. And everything you have, including your children, belongs to God. Present them to him in prayer today, by name, as Mary and Joseph did.

For worship. They could not afford a lamb, but they brought the Lamb of God (John 1:29). She could not afford a lamb. She was carrying one. The God who required a lamb from every mother provided the one Lamb for every sinner, and laid him in the arms of a poor girl who brought two birds. He who was rich became poor, so that we through his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days after the birth of a son the mother brought a purification offering. Firstborn sons belonged to the LORD and were redeemed. Two birds instead of a lamb was the offering of the poor.

parallels.desc: every firstborn is holy to the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

A man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon. Luke turns the camera away from the family to an old man crossing the temple courts, and he tells us four things about him in a single verse. He is not said to be a priest; an ordinary godly man. Tradition makes him old, though Luke does not say so (v. 29 implies it).

Righteous and devout. “Righteous” toward God’s law; “devout” (eulabēs), careful, reverent, conscientious in religion. The same covenant vocabulary used of Zechariah and Elizabeth in chapter 1.

Waiting for the consolation of Israel. “Consolation” (paraklēsin): comfort, encouragement. The phrase has an address. It comes from the great turn in Isaiah: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God (Isaiah 40:1), the announcement that the exile is over, that the warfare is ended, that God is coming back to his people along a road made straight in the desert. The comfort God had promised his people, the coming of the Messiah to end their suffering and exile. Simeon has been living inside that chapter. He is not waiting for a general improvement in the national mood. He is waiting for God to keep a specific promise in a specific book. He was one of the faithful remnant who were waiting, like Anna (v. 38) and Joseph of Arimathea (23:51).

And the Holy Spirit was upon him. The Spirit, who had been silent in Israel, is now active: on Elizabeth, Zechariah, Mary, John and Simeon. Three times in three verses Luke mentions the Spirit in connection with Simeon (vv. 25, 26, 27): upon him, revealing to him, moving him into the temple. Israel had had no prophet for four centuries, and now the Spirit is everywhere in this Gospel’s opening. The silence is not merely being broken. It is being flooded.

That he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. A personal promise. “The Lord’s Christ”: the Messiah who belongs to God, God’s anointed one (Psalm 2:2). We are not told when that promise was given, or how long ago. It had been revealed, and it stood. Which means Simeon had been carrying a private word from God for years, possibly for decades, with no way of proving it to anybody, no date attached, and a body that was visibly running out of time. Every year that passed made the promise harder to hold and closer to fulfilment, and he had no means of telling which.

The promise not yet kept. That is a position a good many older believers know from the inside: the thing God once made you sure of, which has still not happened, and which you have long since stopped mentioning to people because of the way they look at you. Simeon’s promise was kept. It was kept at the last possible end of a long life, in a place he had walked through a thousand times, on a morning that began like every other.

Should I expect personal promises from God like Simeon’s? Simeon lived at a unique moment, when the Spirit was announcing the Messiah’s arrival, and his revelation was part of that. Today God speaks to us through his completed word, and its promises are ours in Christ: they are more sure than any private impression (2 Peter 1:19). Be careful about treating a strong feeling as a promise from God; many have been badly hurt by doing so. But the shape of Simeon’s life is ours: we too are waiting, for Christ’s return, on the strength of God’s word, and that promise will be kept as surely as his was.

In a sentence. Simeon, a righteous and devout man in Jerusalem waiting for God’s promised comfort, had been told by the Holy Spirit that he would see the Messiah before he died.

On a Tuesday. Waiting on God is not wasted time. Wait faithfully, as Simeon did, for what God has promised. Fill the waiting with what filled his: the Scriptures, the house of God, prayer, and an eye open for Christ.

For worship. He was not waiting for a sign in the sky. He was waiting for a person. And the reason he did not miss him, when he finally came in through the gate in the arms of a poor couple carrying two pigeons, is that he had spent his whole life learning what to look for. The God of all comfort kept his word to one old man, and in keeping it, kept his word to the world.
verseByVerse.note: “The consolation of Israel” means the comfort God had promised his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms, blessed God and said:

And he came in the Spirit into the temple. Luke does not say Simeon decided to go to the temple that morning; he says he came in the Spirit. Led by the Spirit at exactly the right moment. God’s timing is precise. Something moved him, and he went, on a day when the courts were full of people.

When the parents brought in the child Jesus. Into the temple courts, perhaps the Court of the Women. One poor couple among many, with a baby. No one else noticed. Consider the arithmetic of that morning. The temple complex covered something like thirty-five acres. Mary and Joseph had come to do a small, ordinary thing that dozens of families did every week. They were not expecting to be met. Simeon did not know who he was looking for; he had a promise, not a description. And out of all that crowd the old man walks straight to the right child.

Most appointments look like this. Neither party is aware of what is about to happen. That is worth sitting with, because most of the appointments God keeps are like that from the inside. There is no sense in the room of a scene being staged. There is an old man following an impulse, a young couple doing their duty, a queue for the offerings, and a providence that has been arranging this meeting for longer than anyone present has been alive.

He took him up in his arms. The old man takes the baby in his arms. The long wait ends in an embrace. It is one of the great pictures of Scripture, and it is easy to hurry past because it is so quiet. Here is the old covenant, in the person of a man near the end of his life, standing in the temple that had been the centre of Israel’s worship for a thousand years, and it reaches out and takes the new covenant into its arms, in the form of a six-week-old baby. Everything the temple existed to do, everything the sacrifices had been pointing at, everything the prophets had been promising, is now a warm weight in an old man’s hands. The whole system is holding the thing it was built to announce, and the thing it was built to announce is going to make the system unnecessary.

And blessed God. Praise is his first response. Not a speech to the crowd. Not an announcement to the priests. The first response of a man who has just received what he waited a lifetime for is to turn away from the gift and speak to the Giver.

How can I know the Spirit is leading me? The Spirit leads above all through the Scriptures he inspired, and he never leads contrary to them. He also guides through godly counsel, through providence, and through desires he shapes in a heart soaked in his word, as Simeon’s was. Most of his leading is not felt as a dramatic impulse at the time; it is seen afterwards, when you notice that you were in the right place. So do not wait for a sensation before you act. Walk in obedience to what is written, pray for guidance, and trust that he is ordering your steps even when you cannot feel it.

In a sentence. Led by the Spirit into the temple just as Jesus’ parents brought him in, Simeon took the child in his arms and praised God.

On a Tuesday. When God gives you a good gift today, do what Simeon did: before you speak about it to anyone, speak about it to him.

For worship. Simeon held God’s salvation in his arms. By faith we hold Christ too. That is what a life of waiting had made of him: he held the Christ, and looked past him to the Father, which is precisely what the Christ himself would spend his ministry teaching people to do. Blessed be the God who put his Son into an old man’s arms, and puts him into ours.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.

The Nunc Dimittis. Simeon’s song is called the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin (now you dismiss). It has been sung at evening services for something like fifteen hundred years, and it is the shortest of the three songs in Luke’s opening. It is also the only one sung by somebody who is about to die.

Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace. Two words carry the picture. “Lord” here is not the usual kyrios but despotēs, Master, the word for the master of a household with absolute authority over his slaves, the word a slave used of his owner; and servant is doulos, the slave himself. “Depart” (apolyeis): release, dismiss, discharge, stand a man down, as a master releases a slave from duty, or as a watchman is relieved at the end of his shift. A sentry who has been posted, who has held the position through the night, and who is now formally relieved. Simeon had been on watch for the Messiah. Now he has seen him, and he can be released: he can die in peace. He is not saying he wants to die. He is saying his watch is over and he may go off duty. A man who has seen Christ is ready to die.

According to your word. The promise of verse 26 has been kept.

For my eyes have seen your salvation. Simeon looks at a forty-day-old baby and says: I have seen your salvation. He does not say I have seen the one who will bring salvation. He says he has seen salvation itself. In his arms. Salvation is not a thing, an idea or a system. It is a person. To see Jesus is to see God’s salvation. All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God (Isaiah 52:10).

That you have prepared in the presence of all peoples. Not only for Israel. Prepared by God, in the sight of all the nations.

A light for revelation to the Gentiles. This is where the song opens out, and the moment ought to be felt. Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, where the LORD says it is too small a thing for the Servant merely to restore Israel: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth. In the temple of Israel, at the presentation of a Jewish baby, under the law of Moses, a devout old Jewish man announces that this child is salvation for the Gentiles. Before Jesus has spoken a word, before a single disciple is called, the global reach of the gospel is announced in the temple courts by a man who is ready to die. This is the theme of Luke and Acts: the gospel goes from Jerusalem to the nations (24:47; Acts 1:8; 13:47, where Paul quotes the same verse). Every Gentile who has ever come to Christ came in through a door that Simeon saw standing open.

And for glory to your people Israel. The Messiah is Israel’s greatest glory, the one in whom all her history and hope are fulfilled: from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all (Romans 9:5).

A death well prepared for. This passage is read at more funerals than almost any other in Luke. Simeon is the picture of a death well prepared for, and notice what it does not depend on. Not on achievement: we are told nothing whatever about what he accomplished. Not on longevity, or on being ready in some general sense. He can go because my eyes have seen your salvation. His peace rests entirely on something outside himself which he has laid hold of. That is available. Nobody now will hold the infant Christ in the temple. But the salvation Simeon saw with his eyes is the same salvation offered to faith, and the man or woman who has taken hold of it has exactly what Simeon had, and may be discharged on exactly the same terms.

What happens to a believer at death? Depart in peace is exactly right. The believer’s soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no purgatory to pass through, because Christ has already made full purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3), and no sleep of the soul in between: the dying thief was promised, today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). The body rests in the grave until Christ returns and raises it in glory (Westminster 32.1). So a Christian may face death as Simeon did, not with bravado but with peace, because his watch is over and his Master is calling him home.

In a sentence. Simeon praised God that he could now die in peace, for he had seen God’s salvation, a light to reveal God to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.

On a Tuesday. If you have seen Christ by faith, you can face death in peace. Pray Simeon’s prayer at the end of the day, as the church has done for centuries at evening prayer. Every night’s sleep is a small rehearsal of the last one; go to it in the same peace.

For worship. He asked for nothing else. He had been given a promise and he had waited on it, and when it was kept he wanted no extension. There is a whole doctrine of contentment in an old man who holds the Christ and says: that will do. Now let your servant go. The salvation he held was prepared before all peoples, and it reached us. Christ is our light, and in him we may lie down in peace.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon’s song is known as the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin.

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth
all the ends of the earth shall see

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His father and his mother marvelled at what was said about him.

His father. Luke calls Joseph Jesus’ father, as Mary does (v. 48). He has spent a chapter and a half establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father. Now he calls him one, without comment. There is no contradiction and no carelessness. He was his legal father, who raised him, though not his biological father (3:23: as was supposed). Joseph is the father of this boy in every way that a life is lived: he named him, presented him, taught him a trade, protected him, and raised him, and Luke is content to use the ordinary word for it.

Marveled at what was said about him. Even after angels and shepherds, they were amazed. Perhaps especially by the words about the Gentiles. They were learning, step by step, who this child was. These two have had more supernatural confirmation than anyone in Scripture since Moses. Mary has had an angel in her room, a prophecy from Elizabeth, and a song of her own. Joseph has had an angel in a dream. There have been shepherds at the manger with an account of an army in the sky. And now, six weeks later, a total stranger in the temple takes their baby in his arms and says things about him that leave them astonished. They marvelled. Which means they had not exhausted this. There was more in the child than they had grasped, and they knew it.

Never exhausted. That is a curiously encouraging verse for anyone who has been a Christian for a long time and quietly suspects everyone else understands more than they do. If the mother of Jesus, forty days in, with Gabriel’s words still ringing, could be astonished by something a stranger said about her own son, then the ordinary experience of finding that Christ keeps exceeding your account of him is not a sign of immaturity. It is a sign of accuracy.

A word for stepfathers and adoptive fathers. Which is worth noticing by any man raising a child who is not his by blood. The Son of God was brought up by one, and Scripture calls that man his father without a footnote. The work you do in naming, providing, teaching and protecting is real fatherhood in God’s eyes. And it is a picture of the gospel itself: God adopts sons who were not his by nature, and is not ashamed to be called their Father.

In a sentence. Joseph and Mary were amazed at what Simeon said about Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The more you learn about Christ, the more there is to marvel at. Never lose your wonder. This week, read one passage about him you think you know well, and ask what you have never noticed in it.

For worship. Christ is inexhaustible. Those who knew him best were still being astonished by him, and the saints in glory will be astonished for ever. There is no bottom to his riches and no edge to his glory. We will never come to the end of him, and that is our joy.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.

And Simeon blessed them. Simeon has blessed God. Now he blesses the parents. He does not bless Jesus; the child is the source of blessing.

And said to Mary his mother. Then he turns to Mary alone and says something that must have taken the warmth out of the morning. Not to Joseph, perhaps because Joseph would not live to see what follows.

This child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel. Now a darker note. The word is appointed: set, placed there on purpose. And note the order: fall first, then rising. Jesus will divide Israel. Some will fall because of him, stumbling over him; others will rise, be raised up, through faith in him. Simeon is echoing Isaiah, where the LORD of hosts says he will become a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling, and many shall stumble on it, and fall and be broken (Isaiah 8:14–15). He is the stone that some stumble over and others build on (Isaiah 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6–8; Luke 20:17–18). The child is a stone laid in the middle of Israel’s road, and it is not possible to walk past him without either tripping over him or standing on him. No one can be neutral toward him.

And for a sign that is opposed. A sign spoken against. Jesus will be rejected, opposed, contradicted, and finally killed. Simeon does not say the child will meet some opposition; he says that being contradicted is part of what the sign is. Anyone who has hoped that a sufficiently winsome presentation of Christ would stop people objecting to him has hoped for something Simeon ruled out in the temple courts before Jesus could speak.

And a sword will pierce through your own soul also. A personal prophecy for Mary, in brackets, for her alone. The word for sword is not the small blade a soldier carried at his belt. It is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, the word used in the Greek Old Testament for Goliath’s weapon. Simeon does not soften it. She will suffer deep grief. Her son will be rejected and misunderstood, even by his own family (8:19–21). And she will stand at the cross and watch him die: standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and others (John 19:25). She was there. She watched him die, and there was nothing whatever she could do, and one of the last things he did was arrange for somebody else to look after her. The joy of the angels’ song is not the whole story. The salvation of the world will cost her the agony of seeing her son crucified.

So that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed. That is the purpose clause, and it explains the rest. Jesus reveals what is in people’s hearts. How people respond to him exposes what they really are (5:22; 6:8; John 3:19–21). He does not merely divide people; he shows what was already there. Everybody who meets him ends up disclosing something about themselves that they might otherwise never have had to face. He is the great revealer. The reaction to Jesus is a reading of the person reacting.

For a parent watching a child suffer. This is a word spoken to a mother about her son, and it is worth handling as one. There are parents reading this who have watched a child suffer and could do nothing: an illness, an addiction, a court, a coffin. It is a particular kind of pain and it does not answer to the usual comforts, because the wound is not in you, and the helplessness is the whole of it. Two things stand in this verse for such a reader. The first is that Mary was told in advance, thirty-three years in advance, and it did not make it easier; God does not seem to think forewarning is the same as sparing. The second is heavier and better. The sword went through her because the nails went through him, and he was there by appointment, and what looked from the foot of that cross like the end of everything was the hour the whole world had been waiting for since Eden. The grief was real. It was not the last word about the grief.

Why do people react so strongly to Jesus? Because he does not allow neutrality. He claims to be Lord and Saviour, and that claim either draws a person to him or offends him. People can be polite about religion in general, but Jesus puts his finger on the heart: our pride, our self-righteousness, our love of sin. So do not be surprised when friends are hostile, and do not water down the gospel to avoid offence. Pray for them, love them, and remember that some who stumble over him today may rise through him tomorrow. Paul himself first opposed the sign.

In a sentence. Simeon prophesied that Jesus would cause many in Israel to fall and rise, would be opposed, would reveal people’s hearts, and that Mary’s own soul would be pierced as by a sword.

On a Tuesday. How you respond to Jesus reveals your heart. And following him may bring grief as well as joy. That is not a sign that God has failed. Ask yourself honestly where you have been stumbling over him rather than building on him, and come back to the stone.

For worship. The child in Simeon’s arms was appointed for a cross, and the sword that pierced his mother’s soul was the shadow of the spear that pierced his side. God did not spare his Son, nor the mother who loved him, because he was determined to spare us. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and all who rest their weight on him will never be put to shame.

parallels.desc: a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day. Coming up at that very hour, she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

A man and a woman. The law required two witnesses for a matter to be established (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides them: an old man, and now an old woman. Luke often pairs a man and a woman: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna, and many others in the Gospel.

A prophetess. Like Miriam, Deborah and Huldah in the Old Testament (Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14), and the daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9). God spoke through her. God gave prophecy to men and women at the dawn of the gospel, as Joel had promised (Acts 2:17).

Does Anna show that women should prophesy or preach today? Anna’s gift belongs to the time when God was making his new work known, before the Scriptures were complete; it is not a pattern for new revelation today, since the canon is closed and the foundational gifts have ceased. And her ministry was in the temple courts, speaking to those who came, not in leading the worship of Israel, which belonged to the priests. The New Testament reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while honouring women’s gifts in countless ways. What Anna does show is that a godly woman’s prayer and witness are precious to God, and that she may and should speak of Christ to everyone who will listen.

Anna, the daughter of Phanuel. Luke gives Anna a genealogy, which is unusual for a woman in an ancient text and is not decoration. Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, grace, the name of Samuel’s mother, whose prayer Mary echoed (1:46–55). Phanuel is the same name as Peniel, face of God, where Jacob wrestled with God (Genesis 32:30).

Of the tribe of Asher. One of the northern tribes of Israel, carried off by Assyria in 722 BC and popularly written off as lost. Some families had kept their genealogies. Here is a daughter of Asher, in the temple, at the presentation of the Messiah. The lost tribes were not lost to God. Whatever else the exile did, it did not lose anybody God intended to keep. The Messiah comes for all Israel.

Having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin. Married young, widowed young.

And then as a widow until she was eighty-four. Or, as the ESV footnote has it, a widow for eighty-four years, which with seven years of marriage from girlhood would make her over a hundred. Either way, a very long widowhood, and it is the picture that matters: a woman married in her teens, widowed after seven years, and never remarried, who then gave the whole remaining length of her life to God in that building. Widows were among the most vulnerable people in Israel. Anna did not remarry, but devoted herself to God: she who is truly a widow has set her hope on God and continues in prayers night and day (1 Timothy 5:5).

She did not depart from the temple. Perhaps she lived in one of the rooms in the temple courts, or was there at every service.

Worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. A life of prayer, for decades, waiting. Do the arithmetic on what that meant. Decades of turning up. Fasting and prayer, night and day, in a temple that had grown corrupt and would be a den of robbers by the time her Messiah cleared it. Nothing to show for any of it. No congregation, no title, no record, and, so far as anyone watching could tell, no answers. She kept praying anyway. That is the whole of Anna’s biography until this morning.

And coming up at that very hour. Again, God’s timing. Not that day. That hour. She walks into the right court at the right moment after roughly sixty years of showing up.

She began to give thanks to God. Literally to confess, acknowledge, praise.

And to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. “Redemption” (1:68): the liberation God had promised: the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem (Isaiah 52:9). There was a circle of faithful people waiting, and Anna told them all: he has come. She was one of the first to preach Christ. Which tells us something else about her. She knew who those people were. She had a list. Sixty years in that temple had shown her exactly which of the crowd were praying for the same thing she was, and when the answer came she knew where to take it.

For the one whose life looks like the sixty years. Something needs saying here for the reader whose life looks more like Anna’s sixty years than like Anna’s one hour. There are believers who have prayed for a marriage, a child, a church, a country, for decades, and have watched nothing move. It is very easy to conclude that the years were the waste and the answer would have been the point. Anna’s years were not the waiting room for her ministry. They were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer are what produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family’s arms when the priests around her saw a queue, and who had, ready to hand, the names of everyone in Jerusalem who needed to be told. The single hour was the harvest. The decades were the field.

Should Christians fast today? Jesus assumed that his disciples would fast after he was taken from them (5:35; Matthew 6:16–18), and the early church fasted when seeking God’s guidance (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). It is not commanded on fixed days, and it earns nothing. But it is a good discipline: going without food, or something else, for a time, in order to give that time and hunger to prayer and to say to God that you want him more than his gifts. Start small, a meal rather than days, and talk to your doctor if you have health concerns. Keep it between you and God.

In a sentence. Anna, an aged widow and prophetess who spent her life in the temple in prayer and fasting, arrived at that moment, thanked God, and told everyone waiting for redemption about the child.

On a Tuesday. A life of prayer is never wasted, however long and unseen. And older believers can be among the most effective witnesses of all. If you are older, alone or widowed, your prayers are not the leftovers of a life; they may be its centre. And if you are younger, find the Annas of your church and ask them to pray for you.

For worship. God remembered a widow from a lost tribe and brought her into the right court at the right hour, after sixty years of prayer. He wastes no tear and no petition. He gathers the scattered of Israel and the lonely of every nation, and gives them a reason to give thanks: the redemption of Jerusalem has come, and his name is Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Asher was one of the northern tribes. The ESV notes that verse 37 can also mean she had been a widow for eighty-four years.

parallels.desc: the widow who continues in prayers night and day

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.

And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord. Luke closes the infancy narrative the way he opened it, with obedience to the law. He stresses (vv. 22, 23, 24, 27, 39) that Jesus’ family kept the law carefully. The Saviour came from an obedient, devout Jewish home.

They returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. Luke does not record the visit of the wise men, the flight to Egypt and the massacre at Bethlehem (Matthew 2), which happened between the presentation and the return to Nazareth. Each Gospel writer selects.

Do Luke and Matthew contradict each other? This is the sharpest question in the two birth narratives, and it is better faced than stepped over. Matthew has the magi arriving, the flight into Egypt, Herod’s killing of the boys of Bethlehem, and only after Herod’s death the settling in Nazareth. Luke moves from the temple courts to Nazareth in a single sentence, as though nothing came between. But look at what Luke’s sentence actually claims. He says they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord: he is closing the temple business, not publishing the next morning’s itinerary. And Matthew leaves exactly the room Luke needs. The magi come to a house (Matthew 2:11), not to a stable; and Herod kills the boys two years old or under, reckoning by what the magi had told him (Matthew 2:16), which places their visit months and possibly more than a year after the night of the manger. So a sequence holds both accounts without strain: the birth, circumcision on the eighth day, presentation on the fortieth, a settled stay in Bethlehem, the magi, Egypt, Herod’s death, and the return north. And it is Matthew who supplies the reason for the very move Luke reports here without explaining it: they went to Nazareth rather than back to Bethlehem because Archelaus was now reigning in Judea and Joseph was afraid to go there (Matthew 2:22).

Two witnesses, not competitors. The two Gospels are two witnesses telling what each was given to tell. Matthew writes from Joseph’s side, with Judea’s danger in view; Luke writes from Mary’s side, with the temple’s faithfulness in view. Luke is not concealing Egypt. He told us at the outset that he had sifted his material and arranged it (1:3), and no witness who selects is thereby lying about what he leaves out.

And the child grew and became strong. Jesus grew as a normal child. His humanity was real. He learned to walk, to talk, to read. Luke uses very nearly the same words of John at 1:80, and he will use them again of Jesus at v. 52. A real boy, developing in a real body, in an ordinary Galilean village.

Filled with wisdom. Not born knowing everything, in his human mind, but filled with wisdom as he grew (v. 52).

And the favor of God was upon him. “Favor” (charis): grace. God’s delight rested on him, not as a reward earned, but as the settled delight of a Father in his Son.

The silent years. What Luke gives instead of the drama is the thing Matthew does not: a dozen silent years in a hill town, and one sentence to cover them. The Son of God spent the overwhelming majority of his earthly life doing nothing that anybody thought worth writing down.

Did Jesus do miracles as a child? No. The Gospels say nothing of it, and John tells us that the water made wine at Cana was the first of his signs (John 2:11). The stories of a wonder-working boy come from later legends, not from Scripture. That silence is itself a teaching: the eternal Son lived for thirty years as an ordinary village boy and working man, without display, pleasing his Father in hidden obedience. His ordinary years were not a delay before the real work; they were part of the perfect life he lived for us.

In a sentence. After fulfilling the law, the family returned to Nazareth, where Jesus grew strong and full of wisdom, with God’s favour on him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent nearly thirty years in an ordinary town, growing up. Faithfulness in ordinary life is God’s will for most of us, most of the time. If your days are made of school runs, spreadsheets and meals, you are walking a road the Son of God walked for longer than any other.

For worship. The favour of God rested on a boy in Nazareth whom nobody noticed, and the Father’s delight was full. Every hidden day of those years was holy, obedient and pleasing to God, and every one of them was lived for his people. He sanctified ordinary life by living it, and he is not ashamed to call us brothers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The only story from Jesus's childhood in any of the four Gospels is this one: Jesus at twelve, in the temple, sitting among the teachers, leaving the learned astonished. Luke includes it not as a charming anecdote but as a theological statement. Before the public ministry begins, Jesus is already defined by a relationship with his Father that supersedes every other claim on him — including the entirely legitimate claim of his parents.

It is worth noticing what the story is not. The apocryphal gospels of later centuries are full of tales of the boy Jesus working wonders and settling scores. In the one childhood story Scripture preserves, he performs no miracle at all. He asks questions, and then goes home and does as he is told.

The setting is Passover — the feast of Israel's redemption, commemorating the night the LORD passed over the houses marked with blood. Jesus is twelve, the year before a Jewish boy took on personal responsibility for the commandments, and this is the last Passover of his childhood. The irony Luke intends is deep: the Passover Lamb has come up to keep the Passover.

When Mary and Joseph discover him missing from the caravan and search three days, her question is entirely natural and entirely human: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.” Scripture lets her say it, and does not correct her tone.

Jesus's answer contains the first recorded words of his life, and they are a claim of identity: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” The word must (dei) is one of Luke's great theological words, marking the divine necessity that drives the whole redemptive plan. And the Father he names is not Joseph. He distinguishes — gently, but unmistakably — between the father who has been searching for him and the Father whose house he is in.

He had not run away, and he had broken no commandment; his surprise is genuine that after twelve years they had to be told where he would be. And then, having said it, he goes down with them to Nazareth and is subject to them for another eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word dei — “it is necessary,” “I must” — runs through Luke and Acts and marks the divine necessity driving the story forward: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22); he must rise on the third day (24:7); the Scripture must be fulfilled (22:37). Here, at twelve years old, Jesus uses it for the first time.

This is not a child defying his parents. It is the Son of God expressing the first law of his existence: he must be about his Father's business. The whole of Luke's two-volume work is the outworking of that single must, from the temple courts in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Jesus's submission after the episode — “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (v. 51) — is the answer to anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be exempt from ordinary human obligations. He is subject to his parents: not one act of compliance but a settled condition sustained for eighteen years.

And he genuinely grows (v. 52). The one who knows all things grows in knowledge; the one who is all-powerful grows in stature; the one in whom all wisdom is hidden grows in wisdom. This is the mystery of two natures in one person, and it means the incarnation was never a costume. It was real human life, lived fully from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary and Joseph “did not understand the saying that he spoke to them” (v. 50) — and Mary “treasured up all these things in her heart” (v. 51). For the second time in the chapter Luke shows her holding what she does not yet understand, refusing to let go of it, waiting for the understanding to arrive.

This is one of the most honest and most encouraging pictures of faith in the Gospel. The mother of the Son of God did not always understand what he was doing. But she did not discard what she could not explain. She kept it, turned it over, and waited — and she was still carrying this one twenty years later when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began to make sense.

The closing verse is the New Testament's summary of the hidden years: Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man. Eighteen years of silence before the public ministry begins — of growing, learning, working, and being formed in a village nobody wrote about.

The God who could have compressed everything into three years of public ministry chose instead to spend thirty in ordinariness. That is the pattern of divine formation: the long preparation, the hidden years, the slow work of wisdom and character before the public work begins. Anyone impatient to skip the hidden years has not yet understood how God shapes the people he uses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.

The only story of Jesus’ boyhood. The Bible tells us nothing of Jesus between infancy and about thirty, except this one episode. It is the only story from Jesus’ childhood in any of the four Gospels. Later legends, the so-called infancy gospels of the following centuries, are full of tales of the boy Jesus: making clay birds fly, striking a playmate dead and raising him again. The contrast is worth a moment. The canonical Gospels are restrained. They record one incident, and in it the boy does nothing miraculous at all. He asks questions in a temple and goes home and does as he is told. This story, probably from Mary, gives a single window into his growing self-awareness.

Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. The law required every Jewish man to go to the sanctuary for three feasts each year: Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:16). Those who lived far away often went only once, at Passover. Women were not required to go, but Mary did. A devout family, and a poor one: the journey is eighty miles each way, on foot, and it costs a working man the better part of two weeks every spring. Nothing in Luke’s account of Jesus’ upbringing suggests anything unusual about it except the thoroughness of its ordinary godliness. The boy learned the Scriptures in a village synagogue, worked in a builder’s shop, and walked to Jerusalem with his family every Passover for twelve years.

The Lamb at the Passover. And it is Passover, which Luke has not chosen at random. This is the feast of the lamb whose blood on the doorposts meant the destroyer passed over the house; the feast of Israel’s redemption out of Egypt; the meal that every year told a nation how it had been bought. The Lamb of God is twelve years old and has come up to keep it. He will come up to keep it again, and the last time he does, he will take the bread in his hands at that meal and say something no one had ever said about it before.

And when he was twelve years old. At thirteen, a Jewish boy became a son of the commandment, responsible to keep the law; the formal bar mitzvah ceremony came later in history, but the principle was long established. The year before, he would begin to be prepared, and perhaps taken to the feast to learn. So this is the last Passover of his childhood and the threshold of his responsible life, which is exactly the moment Luke chooses to show him, once, before drawing the curtain again for eighteen more years.

They went up according to custom. Families travelled together in large caravans, with relatives and neighbours from their towns, for safety and company. The journey from Nazareth took about four days.

How can a family make worship a habit today? Begin with the Lord’s Day: be in church with your children every week, not when it suits, so that gathering with God’s people is simply what your family does. Add something simple at home: a short Bible reading and prayer at a meal, a psalm or hymn, praying for one another by name. Let children see you read Scripture and pray on your own. Talk about the sermon on the way home. Jesus grew up in a household where the rhythm of worship was fixed and costly, and he learned it there. Children notice what their parents treat as non-negotiable.

In a sentence. Jesus’ parents went to Jerusalem every year for Passover, and when he was twelve, they took him as usual.

On a Tuesday. Regular worship with God’s people shaped Jesus’ childhood. Make worship a habit of your family’s life. Look at next month’s calendar and see what is competing with the Lord’s Day, and decide now which wins.

For worship. The Lamb of God walked to the Passover with his family, year after year, keeping the feast that pointed to himself. He lived inside the story of redemption before he finished it, and every Passover meal he ate was a step towards the one where he would say, this is my body, given for you. He is our Passover, sacrificed for us, and we keep the feast with joy.
verseByVerse.note: Every Jewish man was to go up to Jerusalem for the great feasts; families travelled together in large groups.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group, they went a day’s journey. Then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.

When the feast was ended. Passover and Unleavened Bread lasted eight days. Some pilgrims left after the first two days; Jesus’ parents stayed for the whole feast. Now the part every parent reads with a tightening in the chest.

The boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. Deliberately, as his answer shows (v. 49). Not disobedience: his parents had not told him to stay with them, and assumed he was with the group. A twelve-year-old in that culture had considerable independence.

Supposing him to be in the group. In a large caravan, children ran among relatives and friends. Pilgrim caravans travelled in extended family groups, often with the women and younger children setting out earlier and the men catching up, and a twelve-year-old on the threshold of adulthood could plausibly have been with either party. Each parent may have thought he was with the other. It was not neglect.

They went a day’s journey. About 20 miles (30 km). Then, at the evening camp, they discovered he was missing. They search among their relatives and acquaintances: the horrible widening circle, the same question asked of one face after another, each of whom says no and looks worried.

And when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him. Any parent can imagine the fear: a child lost in a city crowded with pilgrims. A day’s walk back, alone, in the dark of the mind, to a city of tens of thousands full of Passover crowds.

When God seems lost. There is a use for this passage that has comforted believers for centuries, and it is worth stating plainly because it is exactly the shape of an ordinary Christian trouble. There are seasons when a person who has known God for years cannot find him. Prayer goes flat. The Bible reads like a manual. Nothing has been consciously renounced, and nothing is there. Notice what Mary and Joseph did. They did not press on to Nazareth hoping he would turn up. They went back to the last place they had him, and they kept looking until they found him. And notice where he turned out to be: not lost at all, not hiding, not withdrawn in displeasure. He was in his Father’s house, exactly where he had always been, doing exactly what he had come to do, and it was they who had walked a day’s journey in the wrong direction while assuming he was somewhere in the group.

Going back, not going further on. That is very often the shape of it. The sense of absence is real and the distress is real. But the searching is a going back, not a going further on: back to the word, back to the place he said he would be, back to the last thing he actually said. He is not usually as far away as three days of walking would suggest.

Can a Christian lose Christ? Not in the sense of losing salvation. Those whom the Father has given him, no one will snatch out of his hand (John 10:28–29), and the Westminster Confession teaches that true believers can neither totally nor finally fall from grace (Westminster 17.1). But a believer can lose the sense of his presence, through sin, neglect or a trial God sends, and it can last a long time (Westminster 18.4). The remedy is the one in this passage: do not assume, go back. Return to his word, confess what you know is wrong, come to the Lord’s Table, keep company with his people, and keep seeking. He has not moved.

In a sentence. After the feast, Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem without his parents knowing; after a day’s travel they discovered he was missing and went back to search for him.

On a Tuesday. Even Jesus’ godly parents assumed too much. Don’t assume Christ is with you; seek him: you will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart (Jeremiah 29:13). Ask yourself honestly when you last had real communion with him, and go back there today.

For worship. The Son who was lost for three days was never lost at all; he was in his Father’s house. And the Son who would one day be lost for three days in a tomb was never lost either; he was finishing his Father’s work. He is never as far as our fear supposes. He is where he said he would be, and he waits there to be found.

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.

After three days. One day out, one day back, and a day searching. Three days in which the two people responsible for the safety of the Son of God did not know where he was. Luke uses that number deliberately. He is a careful writer and he knows what he is doing; he will use it again, and the next time it is Mary’s son who is lost for three days and then found, and the finding will be in the same city, at the same feast, and the grief of those three days will be immeasurably worse. Some see here a foreshadowing of the three days before his resurrection, after which he was again found, in a sense, about his Father’s business.

They found him in the temple. In the temple courts, probably in the colonnades where teachers met.

Sitting among the teachers. The teachers of the law sat with their pupils, teaching by question and answer, especially during and after the feasts. Jesus sat as a student among the rabbis. The picture is not a boy lecturing the professors, which is how the story is often told and is not what Luke says. He is sitting among them, the posture of a student.

Listening to them and asking them questions. Not lecturing them, as later legends imagined, but learning, as a good student did. That was exactly how rabbinic instruction worked: the teacher put a question, the pupils answered, the pupils asked in return, and understanding was reached by exchange. The boy is doing what a learner does, in the ordinary manner, in the appropriate place. And yet his questions showed remarkable insight.

And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers. “Understanding” (synesei): insight, intelligence. He was asked questions too, and his answers astonished the experts. He is holding his own with the finest theological minds in Israel, in the temple, at twelve. This is the season when the leading teachers sat in the temple courts and taught publicly, and some of them may have lived long enough to hear him again. Twenty years later, the teachers in this same temple would be astonished, and then furious, at his answers (20:26, 40).

Remarkable, and learning. Two things deserve saying about this scene, and they pull in opposite directions until they are held together. The first is that his understanding is genuinely remarkable, and Luke wants that noticed. The wisdom announced in verse 40 is now visible, and it is not a normal twelve-year-old’s grasp of Scripture. Something is here that the teachers cannot account for. The second is that he is learning. He listens; he asks. The eternal Son, who as God knows everything, is a boy in a real human mind that has to be taught, and he is being taught, by ordinary Jewish teachers, in the ordinary way, out of the Scriptures. The wisdom Luke reports is not information downloaded past his humanity. It is the wisdom of a boy who has been listening carefully to the word of God since he could speak, and has never once let any of it go.

No shortcut. That is the most quietly encouraging thing in the paragraph. There is no shortcut here that we are not offered. The way the boy Jesus came to know the Scriptures is the way anybody comes to know them: by sitting where they are taught, listening to them, asking about them, and turning them over. He did it perfectly, and he did it by the ordinary means.

Is it all right to ask questions in church? Yes, and Jesus did. Ask your pastor about the sermon, join a Bible study where questions are welcome, ask older believers how they understand a hard passage. Good questions come from humility, a desire to understand and obey, not from a wish to catch someone out or to show off. And when you are the one being asked, do not be afraid of saying, I do not know; let us look it up together. A church where nobody asks questions is usually a church where nobody is listening.

In a sentence. After three days of searching, they found Jesus in the temple among the teachers, listening and asking questions, and everyone was amazed at his understanding.

On a Tuesday. Jesus listened and asked questions. Learn God’s word humbly, by listening and asking. Take one question from your reading this week to someone who can help you with it.

For worship. The Wisdom of God sat among the teachers as a learner. He who gave the law to Moses listened to men explain it, and asked them questions about his own word. There is no humility like his. And in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), opened to everyone who comes to learn from him.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law sat with their pupils in the temple courts, teaching by question and answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his parents saw him, they were astonished. His mother said to him: son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress. He said to them: why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?

They were astonished. To find him there, calmly among the teachers.

Son, why have you treated us so? The natural reproach of a frightened, relieved mother. Mary speaks; mothers often do. That is not a serene woman. That is a mother at the end of three days, and Luke does not clean it up. She is not asking for information; she is asking the question every frightened parent asks the moment the fear turns to relief, which is how could you do this to us.

Honest before God. It is worth registering that Scripture lets her say it. The mother of the Lord speaks sharply to the Son of God, in the temple, in front of the teachers, and the Bible reports it without embarrassment and without correcting her tone. There is a whole permission in that for people who have been taught that honesty with God must first be made polite.

Your father and I. She calls Joseph your father.

In great distress. “Distress” (odynōmenoi): anguish, pain. A foretaste of the sword that would pierce her soul (v. 35).

Why were you looking for me? Then the first recorded words of Jesus in this Gospel, the first words of his that anybody wrote down, and they are a question answering a question. Not rudeness, but surprise. Why search everywhere? You should have known where I would be.

Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house? These are Jesus’ first recorded words, and they are full of meaning. “My Father”: Mary said your father, meaning Joseph; Jesus says my Father, meaning God. At twelve, he is aware of his unique relationship to God as his Father. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, the word Jesus will use of his destiny of suffering. Luke will use it again and again across his two volumes for the compulsion of God’s plan: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22), must rise on the third day (24:7), the Scripture must be fulfilled in him (22:37; 24:26). Here it appears for the first time, on the lips of a twelve-year-old, and everything that follows in Luke and Acts is the working out of it. Even as a boy, he knows he is under his Father’s purpose.

In my Father’s house, or about my Father’s business? Literally in the things of my Father, which can mean his Father’s house, the temple, or his Father’s affairs, his Father’s business, as the King James has it. If your Bible reads about my Father’s business, nothing is wrong. The Greek will carry either sense, and both meanings fit; the two are not rivals, since the house is where the business is done.

Did Jesus sin by worrying his parents? A careful reader is entitled to ask. He is under the fifth commandment like every other Jewish boy, and he has just caused his parents three days of anguish. If he broke that commandment, the whole gospel comes apart, because a Saviour who needs saving cannot save anybody. He did not, and the answer is in his own reply. He had not run away, and he had not been forbidden to stay. He had done nothing his parents told him not to do; he had assumed, and his words say he expected them to assume it too, that when the caravan left, everyone would know where the son of this family would be. His did you not know is not insolence. It is genuine surprise that after twelve years they had to be told. Causing someone distress is not always a sin; the sin would have been disobedience or disregard, and there was neither.

A prior claim. And there is the gentlest possible correction inside it. Mary said your father and I. He answers by naming a different Father, and by locating himself in that Father’s house. He is not disowning Joseph, whom he will go home and obey for another eighteen years. He is telling his mother, once, and then not again for a very long time, that there is a prior claim on him, and that she of all people had the means to know it.

In a sentence. When his distressed mother reproached him, Jesus answered, in his first recorded words, that they should have known he must be in his Father’s house.

On a Tuesday. Be honest with God about your distress; Mary was. And then listen for his answer, which may be a gentle question back: did you not know where I would be? Go to his house and his word this week expecting to find him there.

For worship. Jesus called God my Father from his youth, as no one had ever done before, because he was the eternal Son. And through him, we too may call God Father: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba! Father! (Galatians 4:6). The boy in the temple who said my Father now brings many sons to glory, and is not ashamed to call them his brothers.
verseByVerse.note: These are Jesus’ first recorded words.

verseByVerse.quote: And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.

They did not understand. And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them. Even Mary and Joseph, after the angels and the prophecies, did not understand. Luke could have left that out. It is not flattering to anybody, and a writer building a legend would have had the parents nod wisely and treasure the moment. Instead he records that the two people closest to Jesus on earth heard him explain himself and did not follow it. Luke is honest about it. Mary is not portrayed as all-knowing; she too had to learn.

Take the measure of what they knew. Mary had been visited by Gabriel and told this child would be called the Son of the Most High. She had sung a song about it. Joseph had been told in a dream who the boy was, and had taken his family to Egypt to keep him alive. They had heard shepherds, and Simeon, and Anna. If anyone on earth had the material to understand a sentence about the boy’s Father, it was these two. They did not understand it. The mystery of who Jesus was, and what his relationship to his Father meant, was too great to take in at once.

Understanding comes in instalments. That is one of the most quietly liberating verses in the Gospel, and it should be said plainly for the reader who suspects that a real Christian ought to find all this clear by now. The mother of Jesus did not always know what her son meant. She had more evidence than any of us will ever have, and there were things he said that went straight past her. Understanding, in Scripture, is not the entry fee for faith. It is one of the things faith is given, in instalments, over a long time, and usually later than we would like.

Two ways with what we do not understand. Mary’s response is not to demand that he explain himself again, and it is not to decide that the saying cannot have meant much. Luke tells us in the very next verse what she did with it, and it is the same thing she did at verse 19: she kept it. There is a way of handling what we do not understand that quietly disposes of it, filing it under things that are probably not important, or that scholars disagree about, or that will make sense one day, and then never returning to it. And there is Mary’s way, which is to put it somewhere safe and go on carrying it.

What should I do with a passage I cannot understand? Do not throw it away and do not force it. Read it in its context, compare it with clearer passages on the same subject, since Scripture interprets Scripture (Westminster 1.9), and ask for help from a good commentary or a pastor. If it still will not open, put it on the shelf with a note and keep reading. The things necessary for salvation are plain in Scripture (Westminster 1.7); harder things can wait. Many believers find that a passage that baffled them for years suddenly opens in a hard season, because they kept it.

In a sentence. Jesus’ parents did not understand what he meant.
