On a Tuesday. It is all right not to understand everything about God at once. Keep treasuring and pondering, as Mary did. Write down the saying of Jesus that puzzles you most, and carry it with you this month.

For worship. She was still carrying this one twenty years later, when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began, at last, to make sense. The God who gave her words she could not understand gave her, in time, the understanding. He is patient with slow disciples, and he finishes what he begins: what we do not know now, we shall know hereafter.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went down with them, came to Nazareth, and was submissive to them. His mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man.

And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. The Son of God, conscious of his unique relationship with his Father, went home and obeyed his parents. The boy who has just spoken of a Father greater than Joseph gets up, walks eighty miles home, and puts himself under the authority of a village builder and a poor woman for the next eighteen years. “Submissive” (hypotassomenos): continually subject, obedient. Not a single act of compliance but a settled condition, sustained through his teens and into his manhood, working as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). He kept the fifth commandment perfectly, for us. His awareness of his heavenly Father did not lead him to despise his earthly parents.

Higher calling, nearer duty. There is no contradiction between verse 49 and verse 51, and the pairing is the whole point. Being about his Father’s business, for a twelve-year-old in Nazareth, meant obeying his mother. Anyone who has ever used a sense of higher calling as a reason for neglecting a plain nearer duty has the shape of this passage exactly backwards.

And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. As in verse 19: the second time in this chapter, and the same verb. She still does not understand it. She still will not let it go. And probably she told Luke.

And Jesus increased in wisdom. Growth in understanding. In his human nature, Jesus really learned and developed: although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8). This does not deny his deity, but affirms the reality of his humanity. He was not a divine being pretending to be a child, but a real child, growing up.

How can God increase in wisdom? Sit with that phrase, because it is one of the sharpest windows in the New Testament onto who Jesus is, and a thoughtful reader is right to stop at it. How can the eternal Son, the one through whom all things were made and in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), increase in wisdom? Did he not already know everything? The answer is the mystery the church has confessed from the beginning: in the one person of the Son there are two whole natures, divine and human, and they are not blurred into a third thing (Westminster 8.2). According to his divine nature he knew all things and never learned anything. According to his human nature he really was a boy in Nazareth who had to learn his letters, memorise the Scriptures, listen to the rabbis, and grow, mind and body together, as every child grows. The verse is not loose language. It is the exact truth about him. He did not merely appear to be a developing child; he was one. This is the same reality met from the other side in his own confession that he did not know the day of his return (Mark 13:32): all-knowing as God, genuinely limited as man, in the one undivided person.

And in stature. Or in years, or in maturity. Physical growth.

And in favor with God and man. Words used of the boy Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26). Loved by God and by people. A balanced, whole development: intellectual, physical, spiritual and social. This is the model of godly growth. And it covers silently the hidden years in Nazareth, ordinary years of work, family, synagogue and prayer.

Why it matters. It matters for more than doctrine. It means the Lord his people follow was once twelve, and once seven, and once an infant who could not lift his own head; that he knows growing up from the inside, and what it is to learn slowly and not yet understand. Bring your child’s struggles, and your own memories of growing up, to one who has been there.

What if my parents are not godly or ask me to do wrong? Honour them still: speak respectfully, help them, care for them in age. But obedience to parents is always in the Lord (Ephesians 6:1), and God’s command comes first. If a parent tells you to sin, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and say so as gently as you can. If a parent is abusive, you are not required to submit to harm; tell a trusted adult, a pastor or the authorities, and get safe. Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph because they were godly and asked nothing against his Father’s will. Your obedience, like his, is first to the Father.

In a sentence. Jesus returned to Nazareth and obeyed his parents, while Mary treasured these things, and he grew in wisdom, in stature, and in favour with God and people.

On a Tuesday. If you are a child or a teenager, Jesus obeyed his parents; you can too. And at any age, aim to grow as he did: in wisdom, in body, and in favour with God and others. Ask which of the four is being neglected in your life this year, and take one step in it.

For worship. He did not play at being human. He became it, and grew into it, and lived it out through eighteen unrecorded years in a hill town, so that at last a fully human life could be offered to the Father, from beginning to end, with nothing missing. The humanity he took up in order to save ours was the real thing, all the way down. Every year of it was obedience, and every year of it was for us.

parallels.desc: the boy Samuel grew in favour with the LORD and with man

3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Chapter 3 marks the formal beginning of the story Luke has been preparing for since chapter 1. Thirty years have passed in a single verse (2:52). Now the word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and the ministry of preparation begins. Luke anchors the moment in history with a precision unmatched anywhere in the Gospels: the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the governorship of Pontius Pilate, the tetrarchies of Herod and Philip and Lysanias, the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. Seven named officials, layered like the rings of a tree, establishing exactly when the word of God broke in. Luke the historian is insisting: this happened. You can date it. You can place it. It is not legend.

John's ministry is introduced through Isaiah 40 — “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” — establishing that his role is not to be the destination but the signpost. He is the voice; another is the Word. His message is the message of the prophet: repent, be baptised, bear fruits worthy of repentance. The crowds who come to him receive not comfort but confrontation: “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” John is the great deflater of religious presumption — the man who tells Israel that Abrahamic descent is not a sufficient credential before the coming Judge. The axe is at the root of the trees. The one who comes after him will separate the wheat from the chaff with an unquenchable fire.

The chapter ends with two moments of quiet immensity: the baptism of Jesus, where the Trinity is revealed in a form no theologian could have anticipated — the Son in the water, the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice from heaven — and the genealogy, which traces Jesus's lineage back through David, through Abraham, through Adam, to God himself. Luke's genealogy runs in the opposite direction from Matthew's and reaches further back: not just to Abraham (the Father of Israel) but to Adam (the father of the human race). Jesus is not merely the King of the Jews; he is the son of Adam come to undo what Adam did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke opens the public ministry with a synchronism — a dating device borrowed from the great historians of the ancient world, who anchored their narratives in the reigns of known rulers. Seven officials are named: Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas.

This is the world into which the word of God intrudes: Roman imperial power, Jewish client kings, and a compromised religious leadership. And the word comes to none of them. It comes to John, in the wilderness, the son of a village priest. The contrast is pointed. All the power of the world is irrelevant to God's timing; the word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not trouble to look.

The names are also checkable, and they have been checked. Lysanias of Abilene was long cited as proof of Luke's carelessness until an inscription from the reign of Tiberius turned up near Damascus honouring exactly that man in exactly that office.

John's message has three parts. First, a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins — a rite John did not invent, but radically reapplied. Jewish practice may already have had a baptism for Gentile converts entering the covenant people; John baptised Jews, which said out loud that being born inside the covenant was not enough and that Israel itself needed converting. It was scandalous, and it was meant to be.

Second, a demolition of presumption: “Do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Ethnic heritage is no substitute for personal repentance, and the axe is already at the root.

Third, practical instruction to three specific groups who ask the same question — what shall we do? The crowds are told to share a spare tunic and their food. Tax collectors are told to collect no more than the authorised figure. Soldiers are told not to extort, not to lay false charges, and to be content with their pay. Notably, neither the tax collectors nor the soldiers are told to leave their work. Repentance in John's mouth has hands and feet, and all three answers land on money.

The climax is not John's own proclamation but his announcement of another: “He who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” The one who follows is not an improved John; he is of a different order altogether. And Luke calls the whole of this preaching — vipers, axe, unquenchable fire and all — good news (v. 18).

The section closes with Herod shutting John in prison for confronting him over his marriage to his brother's wife. The voice is silenced immediately before the Word begins to speak. The herald makes way for the King.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's declaration that God can raise up children to Abraham from stones is the most radical possible challenge to the theology of ethnic privilege. It disconnects the promise from the bloodline and reconnects it to faith and repentance.

This is not the abolition of the covenant with Abraham; it is the clarification of what that covenant always meant. Paul will develop the same argument in Galatians 3 and Romans 4: the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham's faith, not merely his biology. John stands at the hinge of the covenants and announces what the new covenant will make explicit — the community of God is defined by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire announces two aspects of the Coming One's work that belong together. The Spirit is the agent of new birth and renewal, the fulfilment of Ezekiel's new heart and Joel's outpouring. Fire is the agent of purification — the refiner's fire that burns away dross, and the thresher's fire that consumes chaff.

John does not separate these two; they are two sides of one coming. For those who receive him the fire purifies; for those who reject him it consumes. Everyone who meets Christ is touched by fire. The only question is which kind.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's instruction to the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers is one of the clearest demonstrations in the Gospels that repentance is not a feeling but a change of direction that shows. The crowd asks “what shall we do?” and the answer is not “attend synagogue more faithfully” or “pray more earnestly.” It is “share your tunic and your food.”

The tax collector's repentance looks like honest accounting; the soldier's looks like honest soldiering. Genuine repentance always takes the shape of the specific sin it is turning from — and in both those cases it meant staying in a compromised trade and doing it straight, at real financial cost, alongside colleagues who would not.

John's willingness to confront Herod Antipas over his adulterous marriage (v. 19) — knowing what it would cost him — is the model of prophetic courage before political power. He did not reserve his hard message for crowds who could do him no harm; he took it to the palace, where it was entirely unnecessary and entirely dangerous.

The man who tells the crowd hard truths and comfortable things to the powerful has not yet learned from John. And John's own end is worth facing honestly: he did everything he was sent to do, and finished in a cell. Faithfulness is not always repaid in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.

Meaning first. Luke 3 brings us from the hidden years to the public stage. After thirty years in the wilderness, John the son of Zechariah receives the word of God and begins to preach a baptism of repentance, preparing the way of the Lord as Isaiah foretold. He warns the crowds of the wrath to come, strips away their trust in descent from Abraham, tells ordinary people exactly what repentance looks like at the wardrobe, the tax table and the barracks, and points away from himself to one mightier, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire. Herod silences him. Then Jesus steps into the river among sinners, the heavens open, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks: You are my beloved Son. Luke closes with a genealogy that runs backwards past David and Abraham to Adam, the son of God, to show that this is the Saviour of the whole human race, the second Adam come to undo what the first Adam did.

Luke the historian. Luke dates John’s ministry the way ancient historians dated great events, with a list of rulers. Seven names, in strict order of precedence: one emperor, one governor, three tetrarchs, two high priests. The whole political and religious world of the day. And then the sentence turns and the word of God goes past every one of them, and lands on a man in a desert. The structure is the argument.

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Tiberius succeeded Augustus in AD 14. His fifteenth year was about AD 28–29 (depending on how the years were counted, and whether from his co-regency with Augustus, which began in AD 11–12). Jesus’ ministry began shortly after.

Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea. Prefect from AD 26 to 36, who would condemn Jesus (23:1–25).

Herod being tetrarch of Galilee. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. “Tetrarch” originally meant ruler of a quarter of a kingdom, then any minor ruler under Rome. He would imprison and behead John (v. 20; 9:9) and mock Jesus (23:6–12).

His brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis. Another son of Herod the Great, who ruled the territory north-east of Galilee from 4 BC to AD 34. He rebuilt Caesarea Philippi.

And Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene. A region north-west of Damascus. For a long time this name was used to convict Luke of carelessness. The only Lysanias the history books knew of was a king of Chalcis executed in 36 BC, some sixty years too early to be reigning here, and sceptics pointed to it as proof that Luke had muddled his facts. Then the ground gave up its witness. An inscription found near Damascus, from the reign of Tiberius, names a Lysanias as tetrarch: a later Lysanias, holding exactly the office Luke assigns him, in exactly the period Luke places him. Luke was right, and his critics had been working from an incomplete list.

Luke can be checked. This is not an isolated rescue. Again and again where Luke can be checked against stone and inscription, the politarchs of Thessalonica, the proconsul of Cyprus, the first man of Malta, the detail once called a blunder has turned out to be precise. So when he says the word of God came in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with these men in these offices, he has earned the right to be believed. He is not decorating a legend with borrowed dates. He is reporting something that happened, at a time that could have been marked on a Roman calendar.

During the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. There was officially one high priest. Annas held the office from AD 6 to 15, when the Romans deposed him. But he remained the power behind the office; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas (AD 18–36) held it after him. Jews may have regarded Annas as still the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life. Jesus was taken first to Annas (John 18:13).

The word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. The language of the Old Testament prophets, the standard formula for the call of a prophet: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:2), to Hosea, to Joel, to Jonah. Israel had not heard it in four hundred years, and it is being used again. Luke’s readers would have felt the shock of it: the line of the prophets, which everybody assumed had closed, has just been reopened. A prophet is called. Not in Rome, not in Jerusalem, not in the palace or the temple, but in the wilderness, to the son of a country priest.

Where God speaks. Luke is making a point about where God speaks. All the power in that list is irrelevant to God’s timing. The word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not bother to look. It was always so: Moses at the back of the wilderness, Elijah at a brook, Amos among the sycamore figs. And it is worth noticing that God had a temple, a priesthood and a high priest in that list, and did not use them. God’s word does not depend on the powerful.

Does God still speak like this today? Not by calling new prophets with new words to add to Scripture. John was the last prophet of the old order, and the word of God came to its fullness in Christ, who is God’s final word (Hebrews 1:1–2). That word is now written, complete and sufficient (Westminster 1.6). But God still speaks it, through the Scriptures read and preached, and he still bypasses the powerful to do it. The word that came to John in the wilderness comes to you when you open your Bible, and it has the same authority.

In a sentence. In about AD 28, under Tiberius, Pilate, the Herods and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, God’s word came to John in the wilderness.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is rooted in real history, with real dates and rulers. And God still bypasses the powerful to speak through the humble. Do not wait for the important people in your church, your town or your country to take notice before you take God’s word seriously. It has always come first to the wilderness.

For worship. Tiberius, Pilate, Herod, Annas and Caiaphas held the world’s power, and not one of them could command a single word from heaven. God spoke where he chose, to whom he chose, when he chose, and the names of the powerful are remembered now chiefly because they lived when he spoke. He is the King of history, and his word does not wait on anyone’s permission.
verseByVerse.note: Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian: Tiberius’s fifteenth year was about AD 28–29. Philip ruled lands north-east of the lake; Abilene lay north-west of Damascus. Annas had been deposed as high priest but still held great influence; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office.

parallels.desc: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in the days of…

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

Into all the region around the Jordan. The Jordan valley, north of the Dead Sea, a hot, low-lying region. A place of crossing: Israel had entered the promised land by crossing the Jordan under Joshua, out of forty years in the wilderness (Joshua 3). Elijah was taken up near there (2 Kings 2:6–11). And the geography preaches. John stands at that same river calling the nation to come out and start again, as if the whole history since had to be wound back and begun once more from the crossing. John comes out of thirty years of silence with one message and one river.

Proclaiming a baptism of repentance. A baptism that expressed repentance. “Repentance” (metanoia) means a change of mind leading to a change of life: turning from sin to God. The first thing to get clear is the one most often misunderstood. It is not primarily an emotion. A man can weep over his sin all night and repent of nothing; a man can turn round with a dry face and have repented completely. The test is not how sorry you felt but which way you are now facing.

Whom he baptised. Jews were used to ritual washings for purification, and Gentiles who converted to Judaism were probably baptised, the washing by which a pagan entered the covenant people. John did not invent the rite. The startling thing was not that John baptised. It was whom he baptised. John’s baptism was shocking because he called Jews, God’s own people, to be baptised like Gentiles. To ask a son of Abraham to be immersed like a Gentile convert was to say something scandalous out loud: that being born inside the covenant was not enough, that Israel itself needed converting. You too need to start again. That is precisely why, four verses later, the crowd reaches for the credential it assumes will settle the matter, we have Abraham as our father, and why John knocks it away so hard. He had already answered it by the water he was standing in.

For the forgiveness of sins. John promised forgiveness to those who truly repented. Not that the water itself forgave, but that it was the sign of a repentance God would honour. And John’s baptism pointed forward to the one who would actually win forgiveness, by his death (1:77; 24:47).

Did John’s baptism itself forgive sins? No. Forgiveness came from God to those who repented; the washing was the sign of their turning. John’s baptism prepared for the Christ, and those who had received it were later baptised in the name of Jesus (Acts 19:4–5). Christian baptism, too, does not forgive by the water; it is the sign of a forgiveness received by faith, which is why it belongs to those who have repented and believed (Acts 2:38, 41). The water is precious as a sign, and nothing in it saves.

As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet. Isaiah 40:3–5. Isaiah 40 begins the second half of Isaiah, the great prophecies of comfort and return from exile: Comfort, comfort my people (Isaiah 40:1).

The voice of one crying in the wilderness. John is the voice. Not the Word, but the voice that announces it.

Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. The image behind it is a road gang. When a king was to visit a region, men went ahead to make the road passable: filling holes, cutting through ridges, straightening the route so the royal party could come through. In Isaiah, it is the LORD God himself who is coming, to lead his people home. John prepares for Jesus, so Jesus is the Lord God who is coming. That is what John is. Not the king. The road crew. And what he is levelling is not a highway in the desert but the ground in front of a nation’s heart, so that when the King comes there is a way in. The preparation is moral and spiritual: repentance.

How do I know if I have really repented? Look at the direction, not the feelings. Have you come to see your sin as an offence against God, not merely as a mistake or an embarrassment? Have you turned to him for mercy in Christ, rather than trying to make up for it yourself? And are you, by his grace, setting yourself against that sin, even if you still stumble? Real repentance is not perfection; it is a changed direction that keeps turning back to God each time you fall. If you find you still love the sin and have no wish to leave it, ask God to grant you repentance (2 Timothy 2:25). He gives what he commands.

In a sentence. John preached throughout the Jordan valley a baptism expressing repentance for the forgiveness of sins, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of a voice preparing the way of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. What in your life needs straightening to make way for the Lord? Repentance is the road on which he comes. Name one specific thing, not your character in general but a particular habit, attitude or relationship, and turn it round this week.

For worship. The King is coming, and he sends a road crew ahead of him, not to keep sinners away but to make a way in. He does not wait for us to level our own hearts; he sends his word to do it, and then comes himself along the road. The LORD who led Israel through the Jordan leads his people home still, and the way is open to all who turn.

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.

Two more verses of Isaiah. Luke quotes two more verses of Isaiah 40 than Matthew and Mark do, and he does it for the sake of the last line.

Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. Road-building language. The picture is of a landscape being made passable, and it works in both directions at once, which is the point. Valleys come up. Mountains come down. The low places are raised and the high places are levelled, and the result is a road on which everybody is walking at the same height. It is also a picture of the reversal Mary sang of (1:52): the lowly lifted up, the proud brought down.

Nobody arrives on the level he was standing on. That is what the coming of Christ does to people, and it is worth being concrete about it. The person crushed flat by failure, by shame, by years of being nobody, is lifted; the person built up high on competence and reputation and being right is brought down. Both are uncomfortable. Both are necessary. Nobody arrives at Christ on the level they were standing on, and the ones who find it hardest are not usually the ones in the valley.

And the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways. The word for crooked is the word for twisted, bent out of true. Crooked lives made straight: the tax collectors and soldiers of verses 12–14. Every honest person knows something in themselves answering to it: the thing that will not come straight, the habit of self-protection, the small dishonesty that has been there so long it feels structural. Isaiah says the road crew has been sent for that too.

And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. Here is why Luke kept quoting. Matthew and Mark stop before this line; Luke, writing with the whole world in view, will not, because this is his great theme. “All flesh” means all humanity, Gentiles as well as Jews. It is the universal note that has already sounded twice in this Gospel, in the angel’s all the people (2:10) and in Simeon’s arms, when he saw God’s salvation in the baby (2:30–32). The whole world will see it. Luke’s Gospel ends with repentance and forgiveness of sins proclaimed to all nations (24:47), and Acts ends with Paul in Rome declaring that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:28).

What it does not mean. Read what it actually promises, because the sentence is sometimes stretched further than it goes. It does not say all flesh shall be saved. It says all flesh shall see the salvation of God. The salvation will be public, visible, put where nobody can claim it was hidden from them. That is a promise about the reach of the announcement, not about the response to it, and John spends the next three verses making brutally clear that seeing and receiving are not the same thing. It gives no ground for the idea that everyone will be saved in the end, or that people may be saved without hearing of Christ. Salvation is through conscious faith in him, and that is why the announcement must go to all flesh.

What about people who have never heard? They are not saved by their ignorance, and they are not condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of; they are condemned for their sin against the light they had (Romans 1:18–20; 2:12). That is exactly why this verse matters. God has determined that all flesh shall see his salvation, and he has given his church the task of showing it to them (Romans 10:13–15). The right response to the question is not speculation but prayer, giving and going. And we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do right.

In a sentence. Isaiah’s prophecy promised the levelling of every obstacle, the straightening of the crooked, and the revelation of God’s salvation to all humanity.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether you are in the valley or on the mountain: crushed by shame, or propped up by pride. Either way, bring it to Christ. And pray this week by name for one people group or country that has not yet seen the salvation of God.

For worship. Praise God that his salvation is for all flesh, for people of every nation, including us. There is no corner of the world too far off the road for this. Isaiah’s highway runs through every landscape there is, and the salvation of God has been set where all flesh will see it: lifted up on a cross outside Jerusalem, and proclaimed to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke continues the quotation to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

parallels.desc: my eyes have seen your salvation

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptised by him: you brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?

He said therefore to the crowds. Stop and take in who he is talking to. These are not his enemies. They are not the delegation from Jerusalem or the men who will later arrest him. Luke says it plainly: the crowds that came out to be baptised by him. These are the people who walked into the desert to repent, and this is how he greets them. Matthew says he addressed this to the Pharisees and Sadducees (Matthew 3:7); Luke applies it to the crowds in general. Many came out of curiosity or because it was the thing to do.

You brood of vipers. A shocking way to greet people who came to be baptised. A brood of vipers is a nest of poisonous snakes, and the picture behind it is one every farmer in that country knew. When a fire swept through the dry scrub of the wilderness, or stubble was burned off a field, the snakes would come racing out ahead of the flames. John looks at a crowd streaming down to the river and says: I know what you look like. You look like the wildlife leaving a fire. These people were fleeing the coming judgement like snakes running from a fire, without any change of nature. And brood of vipers recalls the serpent of Genesis 3: children of the devil, not of Abraham (John 8:44).

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? The question is not a compliment on their foresight. It is sarcastic: who told you that running for the water would be enough? Do you think a dip in the river is enough to escape? “The wrath to come”: God’s judgement, the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:1; Zephaniah 1:14–18; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). John was not ashamed to preach the wrath of God. Without it, the good news makes no sense.

Why so hard on people doing the right thing? Because he can see what they have come for. There is a way of pursuing religion which is entirely about damage limitation: getting into the water, getting the ritual done, getting the insurance in place, and changing nothing whatever. A man may be perfectly sincere in wanting to escape the consequences of his sin and have no interest at all in leaving it. John will not baptise that. The next verse is his terms.

What is the wrath of God? A modern reader may find it harder than the snakes, and it needs saying plainly, because it is regularly caricatured. The wrath of God is not divine temper. It is not God losing control, or taking offence, or reacting badly. It is the settled, holy, entirely just opposition of God to everything that ruins what he has made. And it is worth asking honestly what the alternative would be. A God who looked at cruelty and abuse and betrayal and felt nothing would not be a kinder God; he would be a moral vacancy. We do not admire that in people. We do not call a man good because he can watch a child harmed and remain unmoved. The wrath of God is the shadow cast by the love of God: it exists because he cares, infinitely, about what is being done to his world and to the people in it.

Should a Christian fear God’s wrath? Not as one still under it. If you are in Christ, the wrath your sins deserved fell on him; he propitiated it, turned it away by bearing it himself (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). So a believer fears God with reverence and awe, but not with the terror of a condemned man. If you are not in Christ, the fear is a mercy: it is God’s warning while there is still time to flee to the only shelter.

In a sentence. John confronted the crowds as snakes fleeing a fire, asking who had warned them to escape God’s coming wrath.

On a Tuesday. The wrath of God is real. Don’t treat religious ritual as fire insurance. Flee to Christ with a changed heart. Ask yourself whether your church-going, your baptism, your prayers are a way of keeping God at a safe distance, or of coming to him.

For worship. John announces the wrath as coming, which means it is not here yet, which means there is time. That is the only reason a man stands by a river shouting at people instead of standing back and letting it arrive. And the God whose wrath is coming is the God who sent his own Son to stand under it in our place. The fire that should have fallen on us fell on him, and those who flee to him are safe for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, we have Abraham as our father. For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

John’s terms. Now John’s terms, and there are two of them: bear the fruit, and drop the credential.

Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. The phrase is precise: fruits that match. He is not asking for a general improvement. Repentance is not only an inner feeling, or a ritual. True repentance shows itself in a changed life, as a healthy tree shows itself by its fruit (6:43–45). It produces something visible and appropriate to the thing repented of, and in two verses’ time John will give three worked examples so that nobody can pretend the demand was vague. Paul preached the same: that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (Acts 26:20).

Fruit is evidence, not payment. Notice the direction of the logic, because this is where an anxious believer can get badly hurt. Fruit is evidence of repentance; it is not the cause of it, and it is not what earns anything. A tree does not become an apple tree by producing apples. But the fruit is how you can tell.

What if I look at my life and see so little fruit? There is a kind of self-examination that is faithful and a kind that is corrosive, and the difference is where it looks for the answer. The corrosive kind stands under the tree counting, gets a number it does not like, and concludes it is not really a Christian. The faithful kind notices the shortage and goes back to the root. John’s whole ministry was about turning people to God, and a man frightened by his own lack of fruit is a man in the exact condition John was preaching for. So do not despair; go back to Christ, abide in him, and ask for his Spirit. Fruit grows from the vine, not from anxiety (John 15:5). And ask a trusted believer what they see; others often see fruit that we cannot.

And do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father. Luke’s do not begin is almost affectionate: he can see the words forming. This was the answer everybody had ready: descent from Abraham, circumcision, membership of the covenant people, the credential nobody had ever seriously questioned. Many Jews believed that being physical descendants of Abraham guaranteed God’s favour; some later rabbis taught that Abraham sat at the gate of hell to turn back any Israelite. John says: your ancestry will not save you.

For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. He is probably pointing. The Jordan valley is full of stones, and the argument is devastating in its simplicity. There may be a pun in Aramaic between children (banayya) and stones (abnayya). God does not need you. The God who made Isaac out of a dead womb can make a son of Abraham out of a rock. There is nothing so unpromising that he cannot make it a child of the promise, which means that the family tree that seemed to guarantee everything guarantees nothing at all. And he will: Gentiles, as dead to God as stones, will become Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7, 29). The true children of Abraham are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12).

The modern credentials. The modern versions of the credential are not hard to name. Christian parents. Baptism, whether as an infant or as a believer. Membership of a good church. Thirty years in the same pew. Every one of these is a genuine mercy, and not one of them is the thing itself. A man may be inside all of it and still have never once turned round. Neither your church background nor your parents’ faith will save you.

Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Not the branches: the root. This is not pruning. The axe is already in position, lying at the root, ready to strike. And even now means the blade is already resting against the wood: not a threat about the distant future but a description of the present moment, with the axeman standing there. Judgement is near. The fig tree has had its time (13:6–9).

Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Fruitless trees are firewood. The fire is God’s judgement.

Then is a Christian upbringing worthless? Far from it. It is one of the greatest privileges a person can have: hearing the gospel from childhood, seeing faith lived, being prayed for daily (2 Timothy 3:15). But privilege is not the same as possession. Every child of believing parents must personally repent and trust Christ, and every one may. If you grew up in the church, thank God for it, and make sure you have done more than inherit the vocabulary. If you are a parent, do not assume your children are saved because they are yours; pray for them, teach them, and call them to Christ.

In a sentence. John demanded that repentance be shown in changed lives, warned that descent from Abraham would not save them, and declared that God’s judgement was ready to fall on every fruitless tree.

On a Tuesday. What fruit of repentance can be seen in your life? Don’t rely on your background; rely on Christ, and bear fruit. Pick the area where your repentance has stayed in words, and find the fruit that matches it: the apology, the repayment, the changed habit.

For worship. God does not need any of us, and he chooses us anyway. He who can raise children for Abraham from the stones of the Jordan raised us, dead as stones, and made us his children by faith. The axe was laid at the root of every tree, and it fell on the one green tree, Christ, so that dead wood might be grafted into him and live.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds asked him: what then shall we do? He answered them: whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.

What then shall we do? It is the right question, and it is the one the preaching was for. The right response to preaching (Acts 2:37; 16:30). Notice that they do not argue with him. Nobody points out that he has just called them snakes. The crowd hears that the axe is at the root and asks the only sensible thing a man can ask in that position. Three groups ask the same question (vv. 10, 12, 14). Only Luke records this section.

The most surprising answer. John’s answer is the most surprising thing in the chapter. Here is the last of the prophets, the forerunner of the Messiah, standing in the wilderness with the crowds of Israel in front of him and the whole weight of the old covenant behind him, asked point-blank what repentance requires. He does not say: come to the temple. He does not say: fast, pray, keep the feasts, tithe, study. He says: share.

Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none. The tunic was the inner garment, the basic garment worn next to the skin. Most people had one; a person with two had a spare, a luxury for the poor. So the instruction is not sell everything and it is not give until you are destitute. It is startlingly modest and startlingly concrete: if you have two and somebody near you has none, that is what the second one is for. Repentance is practical: share what you have with those in need. The fruit of repentance includes generosity.

And whoever has food is to do likewise. The same with food. Love your neighbour as yourself: if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? (1 John 3:17–18; James 2:15–16).

Whose is the second coat? Which lands somewhere very specific for a modern reader, because the honest arithmetic is uncomfortable. Almost nobody reading this owns two tunics. We own thirty, in a wardrobe, several of which have not been worn in two years. And John’s test is not what percentage we give away; it is whether the surplus is understood to be ours or understood to be for somebody. That is the shift he is asking for, and it is a shift of ownership before it is a shift of behaviour. The person who thinks of the second coat as their property, from which generosity is an occasional deduction, will always give a little and feel good about it. The person who thinks of the second coat as already belonging to whoever has none will simply hand it over, and will not think of it as generosity at all.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by giving things away. Nor a political programme of enforced equality. Nor that it is wrong to own more than one of anything, or to save for the future (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). But a heart that has truly turned to God will turn toward the needy.

So how much should I give? Scripture gives no fixed percentage for the new covenant, but it gives principles. Give first to the Lord’s work through your local church, regularly and in proportion to what you have been given (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously and cheerfully, not reluctantly (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Many believers find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. And keep your eyes open, as John says, for the person near you who has none: the brother out of work, the neighbour with an empty fridge. Generosity starts with what is in front of you.

In a sentence. When the crowds asked what to do, John told them to share their spare clothing and food with those who had none.

On a Tuesday. Look in your wardrobe and your cupboard. What do you have two of, that someone else needs? Here is a test that takes a minute. Look at what is in the cupboard, the fridge, the account, and ask, of the part beyond what is actually needed: whose is that? The answer, said out loud, is usually more revealing than any amount of introspection about one’s spiritual state.

For worship. Repentance, in the last prophet’s definition, reaches the wardrobe before it reaches the vocabulary. And behind it stands the generosity of God himself, who did not keep his only Son as a spare but gave him for us, and clothes the naked in the robe of Christ’s righteousness. Those who have been given everything learn, slowly and gladly, to hand over the second coat.
verseByVerse.note: The tunic was the inner garment; a second one was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, 'Teacher, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Collect no more than you are authorized to do.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tax collectors also came to be baptised and said to him: Teacher, what shall we do? He said to them: collect no more than you are authorised to do.

Tax collectors also came to be baptized. Then the tax collectors come down to the water, and it is worth understanding what that meant. Tax collectors were among the most despised people in Jewish society. These were Jews working the Roman revenue system. Rome sold the right to collect taxes to the highest bidder, who paid in advance and then collected what he could, keeping the surplus. The system did not merely permit extortion; it ran on it. So a tax collector was two things at once in the eyes of his neighbours: a traitor, working for the occupying power, and a thief with legal protection, overcharging his own people. They were barred from synagogues, their testimony was not accepted, they were lumped in with prostitutes, and they were hated with a completeness that is hard to convey. Yet they came to John, and later to Jesus (5:27–32; 15:1; 19:1–10). The despised were often more ready to repent than the respectable.

Teacher. They recognised John’s authority. They call John Teacher, which is a courtesy the crowds did not bother with. And they ask the same question the crowd asked.

Collect no more than you are authorized to do. Now watch what John does not say. He does not tell them to quit. This is one of the most remarkable moments in the chapter and it is regularly read past. Here is a profession soaked in injustice, tied to a pagan empire, despised by every godly person in Israel, and the prophet’s instruction is not get out of it. It is: do the job. Do it honestly. Take the legal figure and not a penny more. John does not tell them to stop being tax collectors; the state has the right to taxes (20:25; Romans 13:6–7). He tells them to be honest in their work. Repentance does not usually mean leaving your calling, but living differently in it.

What it cost. For a tax collector, honesty would mean a dramatic loss of income. A tax collector who takes only the authorised amount earns very little; the profit was in the margin. John is telling these men to accept a permanent drop in income in exchange for a clear conscience, and to go on working alongside colleagues who will not do the same and will do better out of it. That is far harder than resigning. Resigning is over in a day. This is every day.

Should I leave a job in a compromised industry? There is a persistent instinct that real repentance ought to mean leaving: leaving the industry, the firm, the compromised environment, and that staying is a failure of nerve. Sometimes leaving is right, and Scripture knows of work that cannot be done honestly at all: if your job requires you to lie, cheat, or take part in what God forbids, you must obey God rather than men. But John’s answer to a room full of men in a corrupt trade was to send them back into it clean. Ask whether you can do this work without sinning. If you can, stay and be the honest one, at whatever cost. If you cannot, seek counsel, pray, and plan your way out.

In a sentence. When tax collectors asked what they should do, John told them to collect only what was required, nothing extra.

On a Tuesday. Repentance shows itself at work. Be scrupulously honest in your dealings, even when it costs you: the expenses claim, the timesheet, the invoice, the tax return. That is the shape of most Christian obedience. Not a dramatic exit, but the same desk, the same job, the same people, done straight, with less money and no applause, for years.

For worship. The God of John the Baptist is the God who welcomes tax collectors. He did not wait for them to become respectable before calling them; he called them in the middle of their corruption and made them honest. Jesus would eat at their tables and make one of them an apostle. There is no profession so despised that his grace cannot walk into it and make a man new.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors typically profited from whatever they could collect above the amount owed.

verseByVerse.quote: Soldiers also asked him, 'And we, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers also asked him: and we, what shall we do? He said to them: do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.

Soldiers also asked him. Soldiers next, and their question has a small word in it that changes the tone: and we, what shall we do? There is something almost anxious in it. They have heard him answer the crowd and answer the tax collectors, and they want to know whether there is anything for men like them. These are probably not Roman legionaries but Jewish soldiers in the service of Herod Antipas, or police who protected the tax collectors, the muscle standing behind the table; possibly some Gentiles. They had power, weapons and poor pay, and the temptations that go with them. Which explains why John’s instructions are the ones he gives.

Do not extort money from anyone by threats. “Extort by threats” (diaseisēte): literally shake down, intimidate, use violence to get money. It is what happens when a man with a weapon stands near a man with a purse.

Or by false accusation. Sykophantēsēte, from which comes sycophant: to accuse falsely, to blackmail. Threatening to report someone for a crime unless they paid. A soldier could report a man, and the report would be believed, and the man would pay to make it go away.

And be content with your wages. The root of their sins was discontent and greed. Contentment is the cure (Philippians 4:11–12; 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Hebrews 13:5). Again, John does not tell them to leave the army. A pagan uniform, an occupying power’s business, and John sends them back to the barracks, with two things to stop doing and one thing to start being. Soldiering is a legitimate calling (7:1–10; Acts 10). But do it justly.

Contentment turns rules into freedom. That third instruction is the one that turns the other two into something more than rules, and it is worth staying on. John has diagnosed the root. Why does a soldier lean on people? Because his pay is poor and there is money to be had. Deal with the extortion by prohibition alone and you have a man permanently resentful, permanently tempted, obeying with clenched teeth. Deal with it by contentment and the temptation loses its handle. Contentment is not the same as having enough. Paul learned it in prison and said so explicitly: he had learned to be content in plenty and in hunger, and the learning was the point (Philippians 4:11–13). It is not a temperament some people are born with. It is something acquired, slowly, by people who have found something they cannot lose and have begun to reckon everything else against it.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. John does not tell the soldiers to leave the army, but to be honest and content in it. Jesus commended a centurion’s faith without telling him to resign (7:9), and the first Gentile household to receive the Spirit was a centurion’s (Acts 10). The state bears the sword as God’s servant to restrain evil (Romans 13:4). Some Christians are pacifists and read Jesus’ teaching as forbidding all violence; they are brothers to be respected, and their consciences honoured. But this verse, and the state’s God-given sword, point the other way. The soldier, like everyone else, is held to justice: no abuse of power, no cruelty, no unjust orders obeyed.

Three answers, all at the wallet. And notice that all three of John’s answers, to the crowd, to the tax men, to the soldiers, are about money. The last prophet of the old covenant had one question in the desert about what repentance looks like, and three times he answered it at the wallet. Not because money is the worst of sins, but because it is the place where a man’s actual convictions are recorded, in figures, whether or not he agrees with them.

How do I learn contentment? Paul calls it a secret he learned (Philippians 4:12), so it can be learned. Start by giving thanks, specifically and daily, for what you have; gratitude starves discontent. Notice the comparisons that feed it, the adverts, the feeds, the friend’s new house, and starve them. Remember what you cannot lose: Christ has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you, and that is the reason Hebrews gives for being content (Hebrews 13:5). And give some away; generosity loosens money’s grip. Contentment does not mean you may never seek a better wage, but that your peace does not depend on getting it.

In a sentence. John told soldiers not to use their power to extort money by violence or blackmail, and to be content with their pay.

On a Tuesday. Whatever power you have, at work or at home, never use it to take from others. And be content with what God has given you. Think of the small powers you hold, over a child, an employee, a customer, a spouse, and ask whether any of them is being used to get what you want at someone else’s cost.

For worship. The soldiers of Herod came to the river asking whether there was anything for men like them, and there was. The God who sent John sent his Son, who had all power in heaven and earth and never once used it to take; he used it to give, and laid down his life. In him the anxious find rest and the grasping find enough, because he himself is our portion for ever.
verseByVerse.note: These were probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all: I baptise you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and fire.

As the people were in expectation. Messianic hope was intense. Many were waiting for the promised Messiah, and here was a prophet like Elijah. The crowds have reached the point of asking the question out loud, or nearly out loud: all were questioning in their hearts concerning John.

Whether he might be the Christ. It is not an unreasonable guess. He is the first prophetic voice in four hundred years; the whole country is going out to him; and Israel had been waiting a very long time. John could have claimed it. Many did. Here is a man who could have had it, not by seizing anything, merely by not correcting them. He needed only to be a little vague, to let the question hang, to accept what people were pressing on him. John answered them all. He does not let it hang for a sentence.

I baptize you with water. John’s baptism was only water, an outward sign. Water is external; it can wash a man’s skin and leave his heart untouched, and John knows it.

But he who is mightier than I is coming. John points away from himself. Throughout his ministry, he made himself small, to make Christ great: He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

The strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals and washing his feet was the job of the lowest slave. Later rabbis said a disciple should do anything for his teacher that a slave would do, except untie his sandals; that was too degrading, left to Gentile servants. John says: I am not even worthy to do the lowest slave’s task for him. The greatest of the prophets (7:28) considers himself unworthy to be the Messiah’s slave. What he says is not modesty; it is arithmetic. That is not a man with a poor self-image. That is a man who has seen accurately the difference between himself and the one coming.

He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. The great promise. The contrast is not between two grades of the same thing. John’s baptism was outward; the Messiah’s will be inward. What is coming is a drenching in God himself. The prophets had promised that God would pour out his Spirit in the last days: the promise of Ezekiel, a new heart and a new spirit put inside a man (Ezekiel 36:25–27), and of Joel, the Spirit poured out on all flesh (Joel 2:28–29). John can put a man under the water. Only one person can put the Spirit inside him. Jesus will do this, as God does. Fulfilled at Pentecost, when tongues of fire rested on the disciples (Acts 2:1–4; 1:5).

What does and fire mean? Some take it as the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), others as a refining of believers. “Fire” has a double meaning: purifying fire for those who repent (Malachi 3:2–3), and the fire of judgement for those who do not (v. 17). The more likely reading is that it is one baptism with two outcomes, as the next verse shows: the Spirit for those who repent, and fire, the fire of judgement, for the chaff. One baptism of Spirit and fire: purifying the wheat, burning the chaff. John announces a Messiah who will both save and judge.

Where Christians differ: the baptism of the Spirit. Pentecostal teaching holds that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues. They point to Acts, where the Samaritans and the Ephesian disciples received the Spirit after believing (Acts 8:14–17; 19:1–7), and to the disciples themselves at Pentecost. Sincere Christians differ here, and many who hold that view love Christ better than most of us. Verdict: in the New Testament, all believers are baptised by the Spirit into Christ at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13; Romans 8:9). Those moments in Acts were the special occasions on which the gospel crossed new frontiers, and Pentecost was the unique, once-for-all outpouring at the beginning of the new age. Peter, explaining to the Jerusalem church what happened at Cornelius’s house, applies John’s words to that household the moment they believed, saying God gave them the same gift as he gave to us when we believed (Acts 11:16–17). Paul says plainly that in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, and that anyone without the Spirit does not belong to Christ. Every Christian has it. Believers are commanded to be continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), but not to seek a second baptism. That is not a reason to want less of the Spirit’s work; it is the ground for asking for more of it, out of security rather than out of fear.

I have been told I lack the baptism of the Spirit. What now? If you trust in Christ, you have the Spirit; you could not call Jesus Lord without him (1 Corinthians 12:3). You are not a second-class Christian waiting for a missing experience. Many believers have spent years anxious about this, and the anxiety itself is not from God. Thank him that you are already joined to Christ by his Spirit. Then ask, as Jesus told us to ask (11:13), for more of the Spirit’s work: more love, more holiness, more boldness, more joy. Seek him through the means he has given, the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship, rather than through a particular sensation.

In a sentence. When people wondered if John was the Messiah, he said the coming one was far greater than he, and would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point away from yourself to Christ. When someone praises you this week, or gives you more credit than you deserve, correct it gladly and send the praise where it belongs. And thank God that if you belong to Christ, you have his Spirit.

For worship. The greatest man born of women was not worthy to untie his sandals, and this Lord knelt and washed his disciples’ feet. He who is mightier than all pours out the Spirit of God on dust, and makes sinners into temples. John could only wet the skin. Christ gives himself.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

verseByVerse.quote: His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. John’s last recorded image is a farmyard, and it is not a gentle one. After harvest, grain was threshed, beaten or trodden to loosen the husks, on a hard, flat threshing floor of packed earth or rock, often on a hilltop to catch the wind. Then it was tossed into the air with a winnowing fork, a broad wooden shovel. The heavy grain fell back onto the floor; the light chaff blew away, and was swept up and burned. The tool does not create the difference between wheat and chaff. It reveals it. And the fork is already in his hand: not fetched when needed, held. The separating is about to begin.

To clear his threshing floor. To clean it completely.

And to gather the wheat into his barn. The repentant, the true people of God, will be gathered safely. The Messiah will save. This is the first thing named, and it should not be hurried past on the way to the fire. The purpose of a harvest is the grain. The whole operation exists for the barn.

But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. There is no way to soften that and no honest reason to try. Chaff was burned; it was worth nothing and it was got rid of. The unrepentant will be judged, with fire that cannot be put out (Mark 9:43, 48). This is the doctrine of hell in a single image, and it comes from the mouth of the man Jesus called the greatest of the prophets, as it comes, more often and more plainly, from the mouth of Jesus himself. The Messiah is not only Saviour but Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). Notice: it is his threshing floor, his wheat, his barn. Everything belongs to him.

Where Christians differ: is hell conscious and eternal? Some evangelicals hold that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, pointing to the picture of chaff burned up and to words like destroy (Matthew 10:28). Verdict: the mainstream of the church has not read it that way, and the words of Christ are hard to bend in that direction. The fire here is unquenchable, and Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46); the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever (Revelation 14:11). The punishment is conscious and unending (Westminster 33.2). What is not in dispute among any who take the text seriously is the reality of the judgement and the finality of it.

How can this be good news? Here is what must be said next, because it is what Luke says next: in the very next verse he calls all of this good news. How can it be? Because the alternative to a God who separates is a God who does not care what happens to his world, who lets the cruelty and the abuse and the lies go into the barn along with everything else, for ever. A universe with no final sorting is a universe where nothing is ever put right. The fire is terrible; a harvest with no fire in it would be a harvest with no justice in it.

How can a loving God send anyone to hell? Because he is holy and just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious. Hell is not God losing his temper; it is God giving people, justly, what their sin deserves and what they have chosen: a life without him, for ever. But the same God has done everything needed to save: he sent his Son to bear that very judgement in the place of all who trust him. No one goes to hell who wanted Christ and was refused. If the doctrine troubles you, let it drive you to Christ, and to pray and speak for those who do not know him. It troubled the apostles too, and it made them preachers.

In a sentence. The coming one will separate humanity like a farmer winnowing, gathering the wheat into his barn and burning the chaff in unquenchable fire.

On a Tuesday. Everyone will be either wheat or chaff. There is no third category. Make sure you belong to Christ. And think of one person you love who is not yet his. Pray for them today by name, and look for the opening to speak.

For worship. And the winnower is announced before he arrives, by a man sent out ahead of him for that purpose, standing in a river, with the water still running. Nobody has to be chaff. That is why he is shouting. The Judge with the fork in his hand is the Saviour who went into the fire for his wheat, and he will not lose one grain of it. Gathered into his barn, his people will be safe for ever.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back and the chaff blew away.

verseByVerse.quote: So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.

With many other exhortations. One sentence, and it does something to the whole chapter that a reader ought not to miss. Luke gives us only a sample of John’s preaching. What we have is a summary; there were months of it, and Luke has given us the shape rather than the transcript.

He preached good news to the people. “Preached good news” (euēngelizeto): evangelised. Go back over what has just been recorded. He called the congregation a nest of snakes. He told them the wrath of God was coming and asked who had tipped them off. He demolished the one credential they were all relying on. He said the axe was already against the root. He finished with a fire that cannot be put out. After all the warnings of wrath, the axe and the fire, Luke calls it good news. He was evangelising them.

One thing, not two. That single word settles an argument that never quite goes away. There is a persistent assumption that the hard parts of Christian preaching are the price of admission for the good parts: the unpleasant preliminaries a preacher gets through in order to arrive at the comfort. Luke does not see two things there. He sees one, and he calls all of it gospel. Why? Because the warnings are part of the good news. The coming one is near. Escape is possible. Forgiveness is offered. The bad news makes the good news necessary and precious. A gospel without warning of judgement is not the gospel.

The doctor and the tumour. And on reflection it is obvious. If the axe really is at the root, then a man who tells you so is not being harsh; he is being kind at some personal cost, and the man who assures you the tree is fine is not being kind at all. Nobody thanks a doctor for a cheerful manner about a tumour he has decided not to mention. The news is only good if it is true, and if it is true, then the warning is part of the goodness.

To the people. It is also worth noticing who he preached it to: the people. Not a school of disciples, not an inner circle: the ordinary population of Judea, streaming out to a desert to be shouted at by a man in camel’s hair, and going home changed. Whatever else John was, he was not an acquired taste.

How do I warn someone without driving them away? Let them see that you are warning them because you love them, not because you enjoy it or want to win. Speak about sin and judgement as one who stands under the same need, never from above. Be honest and plain, but gentle and patient (2 Timothy 2:24–26). Do not stop at the warning: always point to Christ, the way of escape, in the same breath. Choose your moment and listen first. And remember that it is the Spirit who convicts; your part is to be faithful and kind.

In a sentence. With many other appeals, John proclaimed the good news to the people.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be afraid to warn people of judgement. It is part of the good news, because it makes Christ’s salvation precious. And when the sermon on Sunday is hard, receive it as good news too: someone cares enough about your soul to tell you the truth.

For worship. He had one job, and he did it for a short season, and then it was over. The God who sent him is the God of the warning and the welcome, whose kindness tells us the truth about the axe so that we may run to the One who was cut down in our place. The whole of his word is good news, because the whole of it leads to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by John for Herodias, his brother’s wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all: he locked up John in prison.

But Herod the tetrarch. Herod Antipas. Luke closes John’s story before Jesus’ begins, and he does it in two verses with a great deal held back.

Who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother’s wife. Herodias had been married to Herod’s half-brother (called Philip in Mark 6:17; not the tetrarch Philip of v. 1). She was also Herod’s own niece. Herod had visited his half-brother in Rome and come back with his brother’s wife. To marry her he divorced his own wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, an insult that would eventually cost him a war; and Herodias divorced her husband. The marriage broke God’s law: you shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John told Herod to his face that it was unlawful (Mark 6:18). A prophet confronting a king, like Nathan with David (2 Samuel 12) and Elijah with Ahab (1 Kings 21).

He did not have to. That is the whole of it, and it is worth pausing on how unnecessary it was. John’s ministry was at the Jordan, among crowds who came to him. Nobody required him to address the tetrarch’s marriage. He could have preached repentance to Judea for years without ever mentioning the palace, and he would have died an old man. He went to the one man in the country who could have him killed, and told him the truth about his private life.

And for all the evil things that Herod had done. His sins were many. Luke’s phrasing is careful. So it was not one sermon about one marriage. John kept at it, across the whole range of the man’s conduct, and Mark tells us something Luke leaves out, that Herod was greatly perplexed by him and yet heard him gladly (Mark 6:20). There was a strange, doomed relationship there: a king who liked hearing the preacher who condemned him, and killed him anyway.

Added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. Instead of repenting, he silenced the preacher. Not a martyrdom scene. Not a speech. A door shut, and a summary clause, and the voice is gone from the story. Josephus tells us John was imprisoned in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Herod later had him beheaded (9:9; Mark 6:17–29).

Faithfulness is not always repaid here. There is something here that has to be faced by anyone who thinks faithfulness is repaid in this life. John did exactly what he was sent to do. He did it without flinching, without ambition, without ever once diverting the crowd’s admiration onto himself. And he finished in a cell in a desert fortress, and was executed at a birthday party because a girl danced well and her mother held a grudge. His reward was not in this life, and Jesus would say of him that among those born of women none is greater (7:28).

Luke’s order. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, before Jesus’ baptism (v. 21), though it happened later. He rounds off John’s story before turning to Jesus, so that the stage is clear for him. John decreases; Jesus increases. Luke’s placing is deliberate. The forerunner ends in prison on the page immediately before the one he announced steps into the river. The voice is silenced just as the Word begins to speak.

Should Christians speak out about the sins of public figures? Sometimes, yes. John did, and so did Nathan and Elijah. Church leaders have a duty to declare God’s law plainly, including to the powerful, and Christians may rightly say that what a ruler does is wrong. But notice John’s manner: he spoke to Herod, not merely about him; he was moved by the law of God, not by party politics; and he paid for it himself. Speak truth about public sin without gossip, without glee, and without forgetting the sins nearer home. And pray for rulers, including the ones you must oppose (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

In a sentence. When John rebuked Herod for marrying his brother’s wife and for his other sins, Herod added to his evil by imprisoning him.

On a Tuesday. Faithful preaching may cost you dearly. And beware of silencing those who confront your sin; it only adds to the sin. Think of the person who last told you a hard truth about yourself. Did you thank them, or shut the door?

For worship. Silencing the herald does not stop what the herald announced. Herod could shut the door on John. He could do nothing whatever about the man standing in the water at verse 21. Kings lock up preachers, and the word of God is not bound. The Lord John announced would himself be silenced, mocked by this same Herod and killed, and would rise, and reign over every throne.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas. Herodias had been married to his half-brother. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, ahead of the story, to close his account of John.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The baptism of Jesus is narrated with remarkable brevity in Luke — briefer even than in Mark. Luke does not linger on the event; the baptism itself is a participle, almost an aside. What he focuses on is what happens while Jesus is praying afterwards.

This is characteristic. Luke consistently shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points of his ministry (3:21; 6:12; 9:18; 9:28; 11:1; 22:41). The baptism is not the centre of the scene; the prayer is. And what happens during it is the most explicit Trinitarian moment in the Synoptic Gospels: the Son in the water; the Spirit descending in bodily form like a dove; the Father's voice from heaven.

Why is Jesus baptised at all? John's baptism was for repentance and forgiveness, and Jesus has nothing to repent of. Matthew records John's protest and Jesus's answer: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

He is baptised not because he needs what the water signifies but because he is identifying himself with the people he came to save. He enters the water of repentance as the representative of those who need to repent; he will enter the waters of death as the representative of those who deserve to die. The Jordan is the first public act of the substitution that ends at Golgotha.

The Father's voice weaves two Old Testament texts together. “You are my Son” is Psalm 2:7, the royal psalm of the Davidic king. “With you I am well pleased” is Isaiah 42:1, the opening of the first Servant Song. Jesus is simultaneously the royal Son of David and the suffering Servant of Isaiah — the King who will reign and the Servant who will be crushed. Both identities are laid on him at the outset, and the whole ministry is the working out of what it costs to be both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
The descent of the Spirit “in bodily form, like a dove” is Luke's careful insistence that this was a visible, physical event — not a vision or an inward impression but something anyone standing on the bank could have seen.

The dove carries a layered background: the dove of Noah signalling that the judgment was over (Gen. 8:8-12); the dove of the poor person's offering (Lev. 5:7; and 2:24 in this Gospel); and, most significantly, the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Gen. 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again. A new creation is beginning.

The Father's declaration comes before Jesus has performed a single public miracle, preached a single sermon, or won a single crowd. The pleasure of the Father in the Son is not contingent on performance; it is the expression of the love that existed between them before the foundation of the world (John 17:24).

That is the theological foundation of grace: the beloved Son is beloved before he does anything. And the Christian who is in Christ shares the status — not earned but given, not provisional but settled.
verseByVerse.examples:
