Jesus praying at his baptism is the first instance of a pattern that runs through the whole Gospel. The implication is not that prayer is a mechanism that causes the Spirit to descend. It is that prayer is the posture of one who depends entirely on the Father rather than on his own resources.

The Son of God prays before every major act of his ministry — not because he lacks information or power, but because prayer is the expression of the relationship that defines him. The disciple who prays before decisions and transitions is not following a technique. He is following his Lord.

The Trinity is present at the Jordan in a way impossible to mistake and impossible to fully systematise. The three are distinct: the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The three are simultaneously present, simultaneously active, simultaneously directed towards one redemptive event.

The doctrine of the Trinity is not a philosophical puzzle invented by later councils. It is the description of what happened at the Jordan. The church was simply trying to find words adequate to what the evangelists reported.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all the people were baptised, and when Jesus also had been baptised and was praying, the heavens were opened.

Now when all the people were baptized. Two details in that sentence are Luke’s alone, and both are worth having. The first is when all the people were baptised. Jesus is baptised among the crowd, one of the people. Luke puts Jesus at the end of the queue, in among everybody else. He tells it briefly, without naming John. He does not describe the baptism itself at all; the verb is a participle, almost an aside, and Luke moves straight past it. What interests him is not the ceremony but where Jesus was standing while it happened: in the same river, on the same day, with the same crowd, receiving the same sign.

And when Jesus also had been baptized. Which raises the question the chapter has been building towards. John was preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (v. 3). What is the one man in history with nothing to repent of doing in that water? Why was the sinless Son of God baptised with a baptism of repentance? Matthew records John’s objection, and Jesus’ answer: let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:14–15). He is not there because he needs what the water means. He identified himself completely with the sinners he came to save, taking his place among them: standing in the sinners’ queue, at the sinners’ river, receiving the sinners’ sign, on the first day of his public life.

The opening move of the great exchange. It will be finished on a hill where he takes the sinners’ death. Everything he did between those two points he did in that position: numbered with the transgressors, from the Jordan to the cross (Isaiah 53:12; Luke 22:37). He began his ministry as he would end it: standing in the place of sinners.

And was praying. No other Gospel says it. Only Luke notes this, and it is the first appearance of something Luke will do all the way through. Prayer marks every turning point of Jesus’ life in Luke: here; before choosing the Twelve, when he prays all night (6:12); before Peter’s confession, praying alone (9:18); at the transfiguration, when he goes up to pray (9:28–29); in Gethsemane (22:41–44); on the cross (23:34, 46). The Son of God depended on his Father in prayer. Note what that means and what it does not. The prayer does not cause the heavens to open, as though it were a technique. It is the posture of a Son who does nothing out of his own resources.

The heavens were opened. As Isaiah prayed: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). The barrier between heaven and earth is opened. God is about to speak.

Does Jesus’ baptism mean I should be baptised? Yes, though for a different reason. He was baptised to identify with sinners; we are baptised as sinners who have been joined to him, to show that we have died and risen with Christ (Romans 6:3–4). He commanded his disciples to baptise those who become disciples (Matthew 28:19), and the New Testament pattern is that those who believe are baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12, 36–38). If you trust Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your pastor. It is not what saves you, but it is the obedience of the saved, and the Lord who stepped into the Jordan for you asks it of you.

In a sentence. After Jesus was baptised along with the people, while he was praying, heaven opened.

On a Tuesday. If the Son of God would not begin his ministry without praying, the question of whether prayer is a good use of time before a decision has been settled by somebody with far better reasons than ours to skip it. Before the big decision this week, the conversation, the interview, the purchase, stop and pray first.

For worship. Jesus took his place among sinners at the start of his ministry. Thank him that he stood where we stand, so that we could stand where he stands. The holy one waded into the water of repentance for a people who had everything to repent of, and he never stepped out of that place until he had carried their sins to the cross. Heaven opened over the head of the one who came down for us.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke notes that Jesus was praying.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.

The Trinity. The heavens open, and all three persons of the Godhead are present in one sentence. The Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends. One of the clearest revelations of the Trinity in Scripture: one God, three persons, each distinct and each active.

And the Holy Spirit descended on him. Anointing him for his ministry. He is now the Christ, the Anointed One, in the fullest sense: anointed with the Spirit (4:18; Acts 10:38). Isaiah had foretold it: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1).

In bodily form, like a dove. Only Luke says in bodily form, and he adds it on purpose: a visible appearance, not just a feeling or an inward impression or a private vision. Something happened in the air over the Jordan that could have been seen by anyone standing there. Why a dove? The image has several roots and they run together. A dove came back to Noah over a drowned world with a leaf in its beak, and the judgement was over (Genesis 8:8–12): a new beginning after judgement. Doves were the offering of the poor, the two birds Mary had carried into the temple (2:24). Doves are gentle (Matthew 10:16). And at the very beginning, the Spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters (Genesis 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again. Something is being made new: a new creation begins.

You are my beloved Son. Then the voice, and it is two Scriptures woven together, and the combination is the whole programme of the ministry that is about to start. You are my Son is Psalm 2:7, where God says it to his anointed king: the coronation psalm of the Davidic king, the one who is given the nations for his inheritance. Jesus is the messianic King and the eternal Son. “Beloved” may also echo Genesis 22:2, Isaac, Abraham’s beloved only son, who was to be sacrificed.

With you I am well pleased. Isaiah 42:1: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. The opening of the first Servant Song, about the one who will not break a bruised reed, and who will be despised and crushed for the sins of others. Jesus is the Servant of the Lord, who will suffer and die for the sins of many (Isaiah 53). In one sentence, the Father declares Jesus to be both the Son-King and the suffering Servant. King and Servant: the throne and the cross, laid on him in a single sentence.

Before he had done anything. And that last point is the one to hold. The Father is pleased with him before he has done any public ministry: before the first sermon, before the first healing, before a single disciple has been called. There is no ministry yet to be pleased with. The thirty years of hidden obedience in Nazareth pleased the Father. The delight is not a wage paid for work completed; it is the settled love of the Father for the Son, older than the world (John 17:24).

Did Jesus become the Son of God at his baptism? No. He was the Son from eternity, and Luke has already said that the child to be born would be called the Son of God (1:35). Some ancient manuscripts here read today I have begotten you, which some took to mean he was adopted as Son at the Jordan; the better text reads with you I am well pleased. The baptism was the public anointing of the Son for his work, not his becoming Son.

For believers. Because we are in Christ, the Father’s words to him are true of us: in him, we are God’s beloved children, and God is pleased with us, not because of our performance, but because of his (Ephesians 1:6). That is the ground under the feet of everybody who is in Christ. The verdict spoken over him at the Jordan is the verdict spoken over all who are joined to him: not earned, not provisional, not reviewed annually. You do not work in order to be loved. You are loved, and then you work.

How can God be pleased with me when I keep failing? Because his pleasure in you rests on Christ, not on your record. When God looks at a believer, he sees him clothed in the righteousness of his Son, and he delights in him as he delights in his Son. Your failures grieve him, as a father is grieved, and he will discipline you for your good. But they do not change his verdict, because it was never based on you. So when you fail, do not hide from him; run to him, confess, and hear again over your head what he said over his Son’s: beloved. That is not licence to sin; it is the only soil in which real obedience grows.

In a sentence. The Spirit descended visibly on Jesus like a dove, and the Father declared from heaven that Jesus is his beloved Son, in whom he delights.

On a Tuesday. Begin today by hearing the Father’s verdict before you do anything at all. Work, serve and obey this week as one already loved, not as one trying to earn it.

For worship. Here is the Son, standing in the water where sinners stand, having taken their place before he has taken a step. Here is the Spirit, coming down on him as gently as a bird, to rest and not to depart. And here is the Father, breaking a four-hundred-year silence to say what he thinks of him. Everything the world was made for, and everything it was ruined for, is standing in one river on one morning, and heaven is entirely delighted with him. Father, Son and Spirit are at work together for our salvation, and the triune God is worthy of all praise.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's genealogy is unlike Matthew's in three decisive ways: it runs backward, from Jesus to Adam rather than from Abraham to Jesus; it is placed after the baptism rather than before the birth narrative; and it extends past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God.

These are not inconsistencies but theological choices. Matthew writes for a Jewish readership and presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's covenant story, beginning with Abraham. Luke writes with the world in view and presents Jesus as the answer to the human story, beginning at the Jordan — where his identity has just been declared by the Father — and tracing his lineage to the first man.

The genealogy also differs from Matthew's in many of the names between David and Joseph. Some hold that Luke traces the line through Mary; others that one evangelist follows legal succession and the other physical descent; others appeal to the complexities of levirate marriage. No solution is free of difficulty, and the church has lived with the two lists for two thousand years without resolving every detail.

What is clear is that the difference does work. Matthew's line runs through Solomon and the kings — the line that carries the legal right to the throne, and also the line under the curse pronounced on Jeconiah, that none of his offspring would prosper sitting on David's seat (Jer. 22:30). Luke's runs through Nathan, a son of David who never reigned and whose descendants never came under that word. On one common reading, the crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child.

Most of the names between David and Joseph are otherwise unknown — dozens of men of whom Scripture records nothing except that the line ran through their houses. Further back the list passes through Ruth the Moabite, through Perez the son of Tamar, through Abraham who twice lied about his wife. God ran the promise straight through a family history containing foreignness, deception and disgrace, and did not clean it up first.

The placement after the baptism gives the list its frame. The Father has just said “You are my Son”; the genealogy answers the question whose son, exactly? He is the son of Joseph as registered; the son of David, which is his royal credential; the son of Abraham, which is his covenantal one; the son of Adam, which is his human solidarity. And at the end of the list — the son of God.

He is the Son of God who has become the son of Adam, so that the sons of Adam might become the sons of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The genealogy ending in “son of Adam, son of God” is Luke's most compact statement of the theology of the incarnation. Jesus traces his human lineage to the first human, establishing the full solidarity of his humanity with every person who has ever lived.

He did not merely appear in human form. He entered the long human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history — which is what Paul means by “born of woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Fully embedded in the situation he came to redeem.

The contrast between Adam and Jesus implicit here becomes explicit in Romans 5:12-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49. Adam brought death; the second Adam brings life. Adam's disobedience constituted many sinners; the second Adam's obedience constitutes many righteous.

Luke's genealogy does not spell out that typology — that is Paul's work — but it establishes the premise on which the typology stands: Jesus is the son of Adam, which means Adam's story is part of his story, and his story is the answer to Adam's.
verseByVerse.examples:
The genealogy is one of the portions of Scripture readers habitually skip — a long list of unfamiliar names that looks like a necessary but uninspiring prelude. But it is the gospel in miniature. It announces that the salvation of the world came not through power or privilege but through the long, winding, sometimes scandalous history of real families making real choices.

Every name in the list is a person whose life contributed to the moment when the Son of God stood in the Jordan, and almost none of them had any idea of it. Providence is not abstract. It is as specific as a name — including the many names in this list about whom history has kept nothing else at all.

The final phrase, “the son of Adam, the son of God,” is the summary of everything the Gospel will demonstrate. Jesus is fully human and fully divine, and the two cannot be separated without destroying the gospel.

A Jesus who is only divine cannot save us, because he cannot represent us. A Jesus who is only human cannot save us, because he has no righteousness to give. The Jesus of Luke's genealogy — rooted in human history all the way back to Eden, and named by the Father as his Son — is the only Jesus who can do what needs doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph.

Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age. Luke gives the age with an about, which is exactly the sort of thing a careful historian says when he has not got the day: an approximate figure. But thirty is not a random figure. Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Levites and priests entered the service of the sanctuary at thirty (Numbers 4:3); Joseph stood before Pharaoh at thirty (Genesis 41:46); David began to reign at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4). Whatever else it signalled, it was the age at which a man in Israel was considered fit to be given a life’s work. Eighteen years of that life had gone by since the last thing Luke recorded, and not one line of them survives.

Being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph. Luke guards the virgin birth. The parenthesis is doing careful work. Luke has spent two chapters establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father, and he will not now quietly contradict himself. People supposed he was Joseph’s son; he was legally Joseph’s son, but not biologically. Joseph’s son by law, by household, by trade and by every register in Galilee; not by blood.

Why the genealogy is here. Matthew puts his genealogy at the very beginning, tracing Jesus forward from Abraham, to show that he is the son of Abraham and of David, the Jewish Messiah (Matthew 1:1–17). Luke places his after the baptism, just before the temptation, and traces it backward all the way to Adam, the son of God (v. 38). The voice from heaven has just called Jesus my Son. The genealogy shows him as the true Son, the new Adam, who will succeed where Adam failed, as the temptation (4:1–13) immediately shows.

The son of Heli. Now the difficulty any reader with two Gospels open will run straight into. Set Luke’s list beside Matthew’s, and from David onwards they do not match. Matthew says Joseph’s father was Jacob (Matthew 1:16). Matthew comes down through Solomon and the kings of Judah; Luke comes down through Nathan, another of David’s sons (2 Samuel 5:14), through names that appear nowhere in the royal chronicles. Matthew has roughly twenty-seven generations between David and Jesus; Luke has about forty-two.

Why do the two genealogies differ? Christians have answered this in three main ways. One: Luke gives Mary’s line, and Heli was Mary’s father, Joseph being reckoned son of Heli as his son-in-law. That fits Luke’s careful as was supposed and his close interest in Mary through chapters 1 and 2, though it must be granted that Luke writes son of Heli and not father of Mary. Two: Matthew gives the royal, legal line of succession through Solomon, and Luke the physical descent of Joseph through Nathan. Three: levirate marriage, the law by which a man who died childless had offspring raised up to his name by his brother (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), so that one man could have a legal father and a biological father under two names. The ancient historian Julius Africanus (about AD 220) gave this explanation, saying it came from Jesus’ own family relatives. Each answer carries a difficulty. Genealogies in that world were kept to make a point, not to satisfy a modern registrar, and these two evangelists are making different points. The more likely answer is that Matthew traces Joseph’s legal line through Solomon, the royal line, while Luke traces the physical line through Nathan, probably Mary’s, with Heli as Joseph’s father-in-law. Any of these is possible, and both Gospels trace Jesus to David: legally through Joseph, and by blood through his mother. The difference does real work rather than real damage, as the next entries show.

In a sentence. Jesus began his ministry at about thirty, supposed to be Joseph’s son, and Luke traces his ancestry back from Joseph.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent thirty years in preparation for three years of ministry. God’s timing in your life may be slower than you would like. Trust it. The years that seem to count for nothing are not wasted in his hands.

For worship. The Son of God waited thirty years before he spoke in public, content to be thought the carpenter’s son. He did not hurry his Father’s timetable or grasp at recognition. He who is the eternal Son allowed himself to be supposed something less, and the God who knows every name in the line knew exactly who he was. The Father’s timing was perfect, and his Son kept it.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Luke’s genealogy runs backward and differs from Matthew’s after David; many think Luke traces Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum … the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel … the son of Nathan, the son of David.

Names we do not know. Seven verses, thirty-five names, and almost none of them is known. That is worth stating rather than skipping, because it is the most striking thing about this stretch of the list. From Joseph back to David, Luke names men who appear nowhere else in Scripture. Maath, Naggai, Esli, Josech, Joda, Elmadam, Cosam, Jorim, Melea, Menna: no stories, no deeds, no record of anything they said or did. Ordinary people, faithful or unfaithful, in whose line, generation after generation, God was working toward the birth of his Son. Whoever they were, they lived and died and left nothing behind them except that the line ran through their houses. God remembers every one of them.

The son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel. Only two names in the whole stretch surface elsewhere. Zerubbabel led the first return of the Jews from exile in Babylon, and laid the foundation of the second temple (Ezra 3; Haggai 1–2). Haggai prophesied that God would make him like a signet ring (Haggai 2:23). Both genealogies include him and his father Shealtiel, perhaps because the two lines crossed there. Everything either side of them is silence.

The son of Nathan, the son of David. Then, at verse 31, the list arrives at Nathan, and here is where the two genealogies do their different work. Luke’s line runs through Nathan, a son of David by Bathsheba (2 Samuel 5:14; 1 Chronicles 3:5), not through Solomon, as Matthew’s does. Matthew’s line runs from David through Solomon and the kings. That is the line that carries the legal right to the throne, and it is also the line that runs through King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), Solomon’s descendant, of whom the LORD said that none of his offspring would succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:30). A curse lies across the royal succession.

The crown and the blood. Luke’s line runs from David through a son who never reigned, whose descendants never sat on the throne, and who therefore never came under that word. Put the two lists together and, on one common reading, something remarkable appears: the crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child. Jesus, physically descended through Nathan (if Luke gives the physical line), escapes the curse, while inheriting the legal right to the throne through Joseph. However the details are explained, both lines meet in David, and the two lists agree on everything that matters.

God kept their names. And there is a quieter thing in these seven verses for anybody who feels that their life has not amounted to much. Men whose only recorded achievement is that they existed, married, and had a son. History has kept nothing else about them. God kept their names. They had no idea what they were part of. Not one of them lived to see the point of his own place in the list. They simply took their turn, and every one of them was necessary, and every one of them is written down in the book that will outlast every other book, because the Son of God came through their houses.

Does an ordinary, unremembered life matter to God? Yes, more than we can see. Most believers will leave no mark on history: no book, no building, no name on a plaque. But God records what the world forgets. He numbers the hairs of your head (12:7), writes the names of his people in the book of life (Philippians 4:3), and remembers a cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). A faithful marriage, children raised in the faith, honest work, prayers for a grandchild: these are the links through which he has always carried his purposes. You may never see what your place in the line was for. He does.

In a sentence. The genealogy continues back through the exile’s leader Zerubbabel to David’s son Nathan and to David himself.

On a Tuesday. You may never be remembered in the history books. But God is working through ordinary faithful generations. Your faithfulness matters. Take your turn today, in your home, your work and your church, as one of the links God is using.

For worship. The God who keeps the names of forgotten men kept every promise he made to David, through curses and exile and centuries of obscurity, until the Son of David came. Nothing in his purpose was lost, no generation was wasted, and no faithful life went unseen. He writes our names too, and he will not forget one of them.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s line runs through Nathan, David’s son, not Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor.

Now the names begin to be recognisable. With them the whole familiar story comes back up through the list.

The son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz. The line of the book of Ruth, its last page (Ruth 4:18–22), and it is worth remembering what stands behind it. Boaz married Ruth, a Moabite widow, a foreigner, from a people the law had barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Their son was Obed, Obed’s son was Jesse, and Jesse’s son was David. The line of the Messiah runs directly through a woman who by birth had no right to be anywhere near it. Matthew names her (Matthew 1:5); Luke does not, but she is there. God’s plan included Gentiles from the beginning.

The son of Nahshon. The leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7), the man who led out at the head of the column when Israel marched.

The son of Perez, the son of Judah. Here the list goes somewhere most family trees would rather not. Perez was born to Judah by Tamar, his widowed daughter-in-law, whom Judah failed to provide for and then took for a prostitute at a roadside without recognising her (Genesis 38). It is one of the ugliest chapters in Genesis, a shameful story. And that is where the line runs. God worked even through human sin. Jacob had prophesied that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10). Jesus is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5).

The son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham. The patriarchs, to whom God made the promises (Genesis 12:1–3; 22:18), and the whole of the patriarchal history in three names. Jacob the deceiver; Isaac the son who should never have been born; Abraham who twice passed his wife off as his sister to save his own skin, and who was given the promise anyway. Matthew begins here; Luke goes further back.

The son of Terah, the son of Nahor. Abraham’s father and grandfather, idol-worshippers in Ur: they lived beyond the Euphrates and served other gods (Joshua 24:2). God called Abraham out of a pagan family.

He did not clean it up first. What that stretch of the genealogy says, and says without a single word of commentary, is that God brought his Son into the world through a family history containing deception, prostitution, foreignness, cowardice, idolatry and long stretches of nothing at all. He did not clean it up first. He did not route around the shameful parts. He ran the line of the promise straight through Judah’s roadside and Ruth’s Moab, and then had it written down and read aloud in public for two thousand years.

What about my family history? There is a mercy in that which is easy to miss. A family history is one of the things people are least able to change and most often ashamed of: the divorce, the addiction, the prison sentence, the abuse, the generations who never knew God. Luke is quietly reporting that the Saviour of the world has one too, and that God is not embarrassed by it, and did not require it to be respectable before he would work through it. Your family’s past does not decide your future in Christ. Patterns can be broken by grace (Ezekiel 18:14–17). Grieve what was wrong, forgive what you can, seek help where you need it, and begin a new line of faithfulness. God has done it before.

In a sentence. The genealogy goes back through David’s family, including Boaz and Ruth, to Judah and the patriarchs, and to Abraham’s pagan ancestors.

On a Tuesday. God’s grace runs through families with foreigners, scandals and idolaters. No family history is beyond his redemption. Pray today for the hardest member of your family, and for the generations after you.

For worship. The promise given to Abraham, that in his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed, had been travelling down this line for two thousand years by the time Luke wrote it out. It never once depended on the quality of the people carrying it. God carried it himself, through sin and shame and silence, and brought it safely to a manger. He is not ashamed of us, because his Son was not ashamed to be born of such a family.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

Beyond Abraham. The last four verses take the line back past Abraham, past the flood, past the whole history of Israel, to the first man, and then one step further. Luke takes the line back past Israel’s father to the father of all humanity, following Genesis 11 and Genesis 5. Matthew’s genealogy stops at Abraham, because Matthew is establishing that Jesus is Israel’s Messiah. Luke keeps going, and the difference is the whole shape of his Gospel. He is writing for the world. Jesus is not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of the whole human race. This fits Luke’s great theme: all flesh shall see the salvation of God (v. 6).

The son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad. A note for the reader with a Bible open at Genesis, because there is a real puzzle here. This Cainan (v. 36) is not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, which runs Arphaxad, then Shelah, but appears in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), which Luke and his readers used. Some hold that the Greek preserves a name the Hebrew line dropped; others that a copyist’s eye slipped, since a Cainan appears a few names later in the list. It cannot be settled from where we stand. What is worth knowing is that ancient genealogies were not always complete; they could skip generations, since son of can mean descendant of. Matthew does so openly, and genealogies were never intended to function as a complete census of everyone who lived.

The son of Noah. Through whom the human race was preserved through the flood: the whole human race narrowed to one boat.

The son of Enoch. Who walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Genesis 5:24).

The son of Seth. Born after Abel was murdered and Cain went out from God’s presence. In Seth’s days people began to call upon the name of the LORD (Genesis 4:26).

The son of Adam, the son of God. The climax. Adam had no human father; he was created directly by God, and so called God’s son. Jesus also had no human father; he is the eternal Son of God made man. Luke has put the genealogy immediately after the baptism, and now the reason is plain. At verse 22 a voice from heaven said You are my beloved Son. At verse 38 the list arrives at the same title from the other end. The Son declared at the Jordan is traced back, through more than seventy generations of ordinary and disgraceful and forgotten people, to the son of Adam, and past Adam, who had no father, to God.

The son of Adam. He is the son of Adam. That is the point of every name in the list. He did not appear in human form as a visitor wearing the costume of our race; he entered the human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history, all the way back to the beginning. What Adam ruined, he is now inside, as one of us, from the same stock, subject to the same conditions, related by blood to every person who has ever lived.

The last Adam. And he is the Son of God. Adam, the first son of God, failed the test in a garden and plunged humanity into sin and death. Jesus, the true Son of God, is about to be tested in the wilderness (4:1–13), and will succeed. Where the first Adam was made and failed, the second Adam has come and will not. He is the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45–49). As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

Does it matter whether Adam was a real man? Yes. Luke places Adam in the same list as David and Abraham, as a real ancestor, and Paul’s whole argument in Romans 5 depends on one man’s sin bringing death and one man’s obedience bringing life. If there was no first Adam, the parallel with the last Adam loses its footing. Christians discuss many questions about Genesis and science, and should do so humbly. But the Bible’s teaching that all humanity descends from one man created by God, who fell, and that Christ came as the second head of a redeemed humanity, is part of the gospel itself.

In a sentence. Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry back through Noah and Seth to Adam, the son of God, presenting Jesus as the new Adam and Saviour of all humanity.

On a Tuesday. In Adam you were born into sin and death. In Christ, the last Adam, you can be born into new life. When you meet someone today, of any nation or background, remember that he is your relative through Adam, and that Christ came as his kinsman too.

For worship. Two men stand at the head of the human race, and the list that runs between them is a catalogue of what the first one’s failure cost. Every name is a man who was born and died. Every name is a link in a chain of dust returning to dust, stretching unbroken from a garden to a river in Judea, and at the end of it, standing in the water with the Spirit resting on him and his Father’s voice still in the air, is the one who came to break it. Thanks be to God for the second Adam.
verseByVerse.note: Luke traces the line back to Adam — Jesus belongs to all humanity. The Cainan of verse 36 appears in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11, not the Hebrew.

3.text: <sup>1</sup> In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, <sup>2</sup> during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. <sup>3</sup> And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>4</sup> As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. <sup>5</sup> Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, <sup>6</sup> and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’” <sup>7</sup> He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup> Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>9</sup> Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” <sup>10</sup> And the crowds asked him, “What then shall we do?” <sup>11</sup> And he answered them, “Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.” <sup>12</sup> Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” <sup>13</sup> And he said to them, “Collect no more than you are authorized to do.” <sup>14</sup> Soldiers also asked him, “And we, what shall we do?” And he said to them, “Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.” <sup>15</sup> As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, <sup>16</sup> John answered them all, saying, “I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>17</sup> His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>18</sup> So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people. <sup>19</sup> But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, <sup>20</sup> added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. <sup>21</sup> Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened, <sup>22</sup> and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>23</sup> Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, <sup>24</sup> the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph, <sup>25</sup> the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, <sup>26</sup> the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, <sup>27</sup> the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, <sup>28</sup> the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, <sup>29</sup> the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, <sup>30</sup> the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, <sup>31</sup> the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David, <sup>32</sup> the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, <sup>33</sup> the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, <sup>34</sup> the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor, <sup>35</sup> the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, <sup>36</sup> the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, <sup>37</sup> the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, <sup>38</sup> the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the chapter of beginnings and confrontations. It opens with the Spirit leading Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of testing — the place where Israel repeatedly failed, now entered by Israel's true representative who will not fail. It continues with the dramatic scene in the Nazareth synagogue where Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 and announces that the Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing — only to be driven out of the town by the same people who had initially marvelled at him. And it concludes with a succession of healings and exorcisms in Capernaum that demonstrate in action what the Isaiah text announced in words: the kingdom of God has come.

The temptation narrative (vv. 1–13) is the interpretive key to the whole of Jesus's ministry. The devil offers Jesus three things — bread, power, and supernatural protection — and each offer is a shortcut around the path of obedience and suffering that leads to the cross. Jesus refuses each offer with the word of Scripture, demonstrating that the weapons of his warfare are not the weapons of power but the word of God and trust in the Father. The one who overcomes the devil in the wilderness will face him again, in various guises, throughout the ministry — and will face him definitively in the garden of Gethsemane and on the cross. The wilderness is not the final battle; it is the first.

The Nazareth sermon (vv. 14–30) is Luke's programmatic statement of Jesus's mission — the equivalent of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew. Luke places it at the beginning of the public ministry as the manifesto of the kingdom: good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, the year of the Lord's favour. The question the sermon raises — who is included in the “year of the Lord's favour”? — is answered by two Old Testament examples that the congregation finds intolerable: Elijah went not to an Israelite widow but to a Sidonian one; Elisha healed not an Israelite leper but a Syrian one. The good news of the kingdom is for the excluded, the foreigner, the unexpected. This is the gospel Luke has been writing toward since chapter 1 — and the congregation's response is homicidal rage.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temptation follows immediately on the baptism: the Spirit who descended at the Jordan now leads Jesus into the wilderness for forty days. The sequence is deliberate. The Father's declaration of sonship — “You are my beloved Son” — is at once followed by the devil's challenge to it: “If you are the Son of God…”

The wilderness is where the identity given at the baptism is tested, and where the question of what kind of Son Jesus will be is answered. Will he use divine power for his own relief? Will he take the world's kingdoms by the world's methods? Will he force the Father to prove his care? The answer each time is no — and the no is spoken not by supernatural force but with the word of Scripture.

The three assaults correspond to Israel's three great wilderness failures. Israel hungered and grumbled (Exod. 16); Jesus is tempted to turn stone into bread. Israel worshipped the golden calf (Exod. 32); Jesus is offered the kingdoms for an act of worship. Israel tested God at Massah (Exod. 17:1-7); Jesus is urged to throw himself from the temple. At every point where Israel failed, Jesus stands — and he does it by the means available to every Israelite: the word of God, believed and obeyed. All three of his answers come from Deuteronomy, the book Moses gave Israel before they entered the land.

The final offer is the subtlest, because it comes with chapter and verse. The devil quotes Psalm 91 — accurately, so far as it goes. But he stops the quotation at “to guard you” and omits the psalm's own qualifier, “in all your ways.” The promise covers the paths of obedience; it does not cover a stunt. The temptation is not to misread a promise but to use one as leverage — to demand that the Father demonstrate his care by preventing the consequences of a chosen folly.

Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:16 and the memory of Massah. The difference between trust and testing is the difference between resting in God's faithfulness and requiring him to prove it on our terms. The person who says “I will believe God loves me if he does this specific thing” is not trusting God. He is testing him.

The section ends with a phrase Luke intends to be remembered: the devil departed “until an opportune time.” The wilderness was the opening exchange, not the war.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temptation establishes Jesus as the second Adam as well as the true Israel. Adam was tempted in a garden of abundance and failed; Jesus is tempted in a wilderness of deprivation and stands. Adam's failure brought sin and death into the human story; Jesus's obedience begins the reversal.

This is the logic Paul unpacks in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15: what the first Adam lost, the second Adam wins back. And the victory is not won by raw divine force but by the very means God made available to Adam — the word of God, and the decision to trust it rather than the alternative on offer.

The devil's departure “until an opportune time” (v. 13) signals that the conflict continues through the ministry — in the demons, in the religious leaders, in the crowd's wish for a political king. The appointed opportunity is the passion: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3); “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53).

And at the cross the wilderness temptations return almost verbatim — save yourself; if you are the Christ; if you are the King of the Jews. What looks there like Satan's victory is the moment of his defeat, because the Son who refused every shortcut in the desert walked the full cost of obedience to its end.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's weapon against every temptation is Scripture — received, remembered, and spoken with precision. He does not argue philosophically, does not marshal feelings, and does not reach for resources unavailable to ordinary disciples. He quotes the word of God.

That is not a pastoral cliché but a pattern with hard practical consequences. The Christian who has stored up Scripture has the weapon Jesus used. The Christian who has neglected it is left to improvise arguments in the moment, which is not a fair fight.

The devil quotes Psalm 91 accurately, and with a clause removed. The most dangerous misuse of Scripture is never the obviously wrong use; it is the superficially plausible one — a true promise lifted out of its context and used to license what the context forbids. Every cult and every proof-texted disaster has this shape.

Which is the argument for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. A man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. A man who knows what God is doing across the whole of Scripture can recognise a true verse being turned against its own purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were ended, he was hungry.

Meaning first. Luke 4 shows the Son of God beginning his work, and the whole chapter is about the power of his word. In the wilderness he is tempted by the devil for forty days and answers every attack with Scripture, standing where Adam and Israel fell. In the synagogue at Nazareth he reads Isaiah’s promise of the Spirit-anointed one who brings good news to the poor and release to the captives, and says that it is fulfilled today, in him. His own town admires him, then tries to throw him off a cliff when he reminds them that God’s grace went to a Gentile widow and a Syrian general. In Capernaum his word silences a demon, rebukes a fever, and heals a whole street at sunset, one person at a time. And when the town tries to keep him, he goes on, because he was sent to preach the kingdom of God everywhere. The chapter answers two questions at once: who is this man, and what has he come to do? He is the obedient Son and the anointed King, and he has come to set captives free.

The setting. The genealogy has just ended with Adam, the son of God (3:38). Now the new Son of God faces the test the first Adam failed. Adam was tested in a garden, with every tree to eat from but one, and fell. Jesus is tested in a wilderness, starving, and stands. He is also the true Israel: God called Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22), and that son was tested in the wilderness for forty years and failed. All three of Jesus’ answers come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses’ words about Israel’s wilderness testing. Luke wants us to see that the story of the human race and the story of Israel are being lived again, by one man, and this time to the end.

Full of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit who came down at the Jordan (3:22) now leads him into a desert, not away from God but deeper into the Father’s purpose. And Luke is precise about the direction of travel: he goes in full of the Holy Spirit, and he is led by the Spirit. Being full of the Spirit does not mean being spared temptation; it means being equipped for it. The Spirit does not shield him from the testing. The Spirit conducts him into it.

Led by the Spirit in the wilderness. Temptation was not an accident or a defeat; it was part of God’s plan. The wilderness of Judea is barren and rocky, falling away between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, home of wild animals (Mark 1:13). It is the landscape of Israel’s failure and of the scapegoat sent away carrying sin (Leviticus 16:10). The Son goes out into it of his own will, led by the Spirit, because that is where the battle has to be fought.

For forty days. The number is not decorative. Israel was forty years in the wilderness and failed there repeatedly (Deuteronomy 8:2); Moses was forty days on the mountain without bread or water (Exodus 34:28); Elijah walked forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). Jesus goes where Israel went, on Israel’s terms, and does what Israel could not do.

Being tempted by the devil. The tense suggests continuous temptation throughout the forty days, coming to a head at the end. The devil (diabolos, the slanderer, the accuser) is a real, personal being, the enemy of God and of man. The temptations were real. Jesus was really tempted, as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. Luke, the physician, understates it. Forty days without food takes a body to the edge of what it can survive, and the last sentence is almost comic in its restraint. Real hunger, from a real human body, near starvation. The attack comes at the point of greatest physical weakness, which is where such attacks generally come.

If God tempts no one, why does the Spirit lead Jesus into temptation? A difficulty sits in the very first line, and a thoughtful reader should not step over it. James says plainly that God himself tempts no one (James 1:13). The knot loosens once you see that one Greek word (peirasmos) covers two things English keeps apart. It can mean a test, a trial meant to prove and strengthen, the way God tested Abraham on the mountain (Genesis 22:1) and tested Israel forty years to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). And it can mean a temptation, an enticement whose whole aim is to make a person fall. The two can occupy the very same moment while pulling in opposite directions. From the Father’s side this is a test: the Spirit leads the Son into the wilderness to prove and display an obedience the world would need to see. From the devil’s side the identical event is a temptation: every word out of his mouth is designed to make Jesus fall. God ordains the testing; Satan supplies the enticing. They share the same forty days, and God never does the second.

Then what am I asking when I pray, lead us not into temptation? Not that God might otherwise tempt us. When God leads you into hard testing he is never trying to make you sin (James 1:13); he is proving a faith he fully intends to carry through, and he has bound himself to provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). The prayer is the prayer of people who know their own weakness and ask the Father to keep the test from ever becoming a fall: to spare them trials they could not bear, and to hold them in the ones he sends. The sinless Son did not need to pray it for himself. We do, every day.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some say that if he could not have sinned, the temptation was not real. Others say that as God, he could not sin. Verdict: the historic view is that Jesus, being God, could not sin (he was “impeccable”), yet the temptation was real and fully felt. A strong bridge cannot fall, but the weight on it is real. A wall that cannot be breached still takes the full force of the siege. Indeed, only the one who never gave way knew the full force of temptation, because the rest of us give way before it reaches its height.

Is being tempted a sin? No, and this settles a question that torments sensitive believers. Jesus was tempted, really tempted, by a real enemy, at real cost, and he was without sin. The pull itself is not the fall. If it were, the Lord who was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), could not be our Saviour. What becomes sin is welcoming the thought, entertaining it, turning it over with pleasure, and acting on it (James 1:14–15). So when an ugly thought arrives uninvited, do not conclude that you are a hypocrite. Turn from it, at once, to the one who faced the same and stood. Feeling the pull is the battlefield, not the defeat.

In a sentence. Full of the Spirit, Jesus was led into the wilderness, where he fasted forty days and was tempted by the devil throughout, and at the end he was hungry.

On a Tuesday. Being full of the Spirit does not mean you will not be tempted. Expect it, especially when you are weak: tired, hungry, lonely, ill, or just after a high point. Notice which hour of the day and which state of body your worst temptations usually choose, and prepare for that hour beforehand, with Scripture you have already put away in your memory, and with someone you can be honest with. And when the hard season comes, do not read it as a sign that God has left you. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness. He may lead you into one, and he will be there.

For worship. Here is the second Adam, walking out alone into the wasteland the first Adam made, carrying the name his ancestor lost. Adam had a garden and fell; Israel had manna and grumbled; this man has nothing but stones and an enemy, and he stands. He went in our place, into our desert, on our terms, at the point of our weakness, and he did not give way. Every temptation you will face this week has already been met, at its full height, by the one who now intercedes for you. He knows the weight of it from inside, and he never once put it down on the wrong side.

verseByVerse.quote: The devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil said to him: if you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread. Jesus answered him: it is written, man shall not live by bread alone.

If you are the Son of God. The devil is not doubting it; the Greek form suggests since you are. The Father has just said it over the Jordan (3:22). He is proposing that a Son with a Father like that ought not to be this hungry, and that if the Father is not going to do something about it, the Son should. The temptation is: use your sonship for yourself. Use your power to meet your own needs, independently of your Father. Why should the Son of God go hungry?

Command this stone to become bread. Two things are being attacked at once. The first is obvious: hunger. And there is nothing wrong with bread. He will make it for five thousand people before this Gospel is much older (9:10–17), and he will hand it to his friends on the last night of his life. The temptation is not to a bad thing. It is to a good thing, taken by the wrong hand at the wrong moment. To do it now, for himself, at Satan’s suggestion, would be to step out of dependence on his Father, who had led him into the wilderness to hunger. It would also be to refuse the path of humiliation and weakness he came to walk (Philippians 2:7). He would not use his divine power to avoid the human condition he came to share.

The shape of temptation. It is worth naming, because this is the shape it usually takes. Temptation rarely opens by suggesting that God does not exist. It opens by suggesting that God is not looking after you, and that you had better see to yourself. In the garden the serpent did the same: has God really said? He is keeping something good from you. The lie is always about the Father’s heart.

It is written. Jesus answers with Scripture, three times. The Son of God, full of the Spirit, does not argue with Satan or rely on his own wisdom. He does not analyse the temptation or explain why it is wrong. He answers from the written word, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and stops. And the Scripture he uses is not obscure; it is from a book any Jewish boy would have known. His weapon was available to every person in Israel and is available now. If Jesus needed Scripture to resist temptation, how much more do we.

Man shall not live by bread alone. Deuteronomy 8:3, and the context is the whole point. Moses reminded Israel that God let them hunger in the wilderness and fed them with manna, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. Israel was hungry, grumbled, and demanded. Jesus is hungrier, and quotes the lesson Israel refused to learn, in the same desert, about the same God. Physical bread matters, but life depends ultimately on God and his word. His food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34).

Does this mean physical needs do not matter? No. Jesus did not despise bread; he fed the hungry and taught us to pray for daily bread (11:3). The verse says not by bread alone. Bread keeps the body alive for a time; God keeps the whole person alive for ever, and it is God who gives the bread in the first place. The point is order and dependence. A real need is not to be met by stepping outside the Father’s will, because the Father who gives the command is also the one who gives the food. If a choice ever comes between obeying God and getting what you need, the need is safer in his hands than in yours.

In a sentence. The devil tempted the starving Jesus to use his power as Son of God to make bread for himself, but Jesus answered from Scripture that life depends on more than bread.

On a Tuesday. There will be a moment, perhaps this week, when a real need meets a wrong way of meeting it. Where it applies: money that could be had by a small dishonesty on an expense claim; comfort that could be had from a bottle or a screen at the end of a hard day; affection that could be had from someone else’s spouse who seems to understand you. The need is genuine. The hunger is not sinful. What is being offered is a way of feeding yourself that does not go through the Father’s hand. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to refuse ordinary provision, to stop working, or to neglect medicine and food in the name of trusting God. Jesus was led by the Spirit to fast; most of the time the Father feeds us through ordinary means, and we should take them with thanks. The question underneath is always the same one: is he actually going to look after me, or had I better see to it myself?

For worship. The Son of God went hungry so that hungry people could be fed with the bread that does not perish. He would not turn one stone into bread for himself, and on the last night he took bread and broke it and said, this is my body, given for you. The one who refused to feed himself in the desert makes himself the food of his people. Everything he would not take for himself, he gives to us.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him, 'To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him: to you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.

The order. Luke’s order of the temptations differs from Matthew’s, who has the temple second and the kingdoms last (Matthew 4:1–11). Neither writer is mistaken, because neither claims a stopwatch account. Matthew joins his scenes with then and again; Luke strings his with and, the loosest connective in the language. Matthew ends with the kingdoms, perhaps because his Gospel ends with Jesus given all authority on a mountain (Matthew 28:18). Luke ends with Jerusalem and the temple, because Jerusalem is the goal of his whole Gospel: it began in the temple and will end there (9:51; 24:47, 53). The order is a signpost, not a clock.

Showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. The second assault changes altitude. Luke does not say how; no mountain is mentioned, and the phrase in a moment of time suggests a vision rather than an ordinary view. Kingdoms of the oikoumenē: the inhabited world, the Roman Empire and beyond. Every empire, every capital, every throne, all the power and glory of human civilisation, laid out in an instant.

For it has been delivered to me. Is he lying? It matters, because if that sentence is simply false the temptation has no force at all, and Jesus does not treat it as false. He disputes the price, not the ownership. The New Testament will not let us dismiss the claim. Jesus himself calls Satan the ruler of this world, three times in John’s Gospel (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11). Paul calls him the god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4). John writes that the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). Since Adam’s fall, humanity has been under his dominion. Something real is being described.

Delivered by whom? Look at the word he uses: handed over. Not seized, not created, not owned outright, but held on licence from someone who can revoke it. The devil is a usurper administering territory that was never his, on a lease he did not write and cannot extend. Ultimately all authority belongs to God, who gives the kingdom of men to whom he will (Daniel 4:17), and Satan is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). His claim is true, and it is far smaller than it sounds.

If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours. Here is what makes this the subtlest of the three. What he offers is not something Jesus should not want. The kingdoms of the world are exactly what the Father has already promised him: ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Psalm 2:8). Every empire in that flash of vision is going to be his. The devil is offering him his own inheritance. What is being offered is a short cut: the nations without Gethsemane, the crown without the cross. Everything the Father promised, delivered this afternoon, at a price that looks small. It is the same temptation Peter would put to him, and Jesus would answer him as he answers Satan here (Mark 8:32–33).

In a sentence. In a vision of all the world’s kingdoms, the devil offered Jesus all their authority and glory, claiming they were his to give, if Jesus would worship him.

On a Tuesday. This temptation is rarely a straightforward invitation to do evil. It is the right thing by a wrong route. Where it applies: the church growth built on a manipulated figure or a softened gospel; the marriage entered by a compromise of faith; the promotion gained by the quiet betrayal of a colleague; the peace in a family bought by pretending an offence never happened. In each case the goal is good. The road is the problem, and the road is what Jesus was sent to walk. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this does not mean that every success is suspect or that ambition is sinful. To seek a promotion honestly, to want a church to grow, to work hard for influence that can be used well, is not bowing to Satan. The question is not whether you want the kingdom but what you are willing to bow to in order to get it.

Does Satan really control the world, so that Christians should withdraw from it? No. His power is real but borrowed, limited and already broken. The earth is the LORD’s, and everything in it (Psalm 24:1). Satan blinds minds and holds people captive (2 Corinthians 4:4; 2 Timothy 2:26), and Christians must not be naive about him. But Jesus came to bind the strong man and plunder his house (11:21–22), and after the resurrection he declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). So Christians do not retreat from the world as enemy territory; they go into it as the King’s ambassadors, doing their work, raising their families and serving their neighbours under a better Lord.

For worship. He was offered the world for one bow, and he would not bow. And so the world came to him another way: through nails, a borrowed tomb and an empty one. He refused the throne from the usurper’s hand and received it from his Father’s, and it will never be revoked. Every knee will bow to him, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11). He went the long way round, by the cross, because we were on that road, and he would not reach the kingdom without us.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s order of the temptations differs from Matthew’s; Luke ends at Jerusalem, the goal of his whole Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: it is written, you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.

It is written. Again, Scripture. And notice what he does with the devil’s claim. He does not dispute it. He does not argue about who owns the kingdoms or on what terms. He goes straight past the whole question to the one word that decides it: worship.

You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve. Deuteronomy 6:13, and again the setting matters. It comes from the passage just after the Shema (Hear, O Israel), where Moses warns Israel about what will happen when they enter the land and find themselves suddenly comfortable: cities they did not build, wells they did not dig, vineyards they did not plant (Deuteronomy 6:10–12). The danger is not persecution; it is prosperity. Israel repeatedly bowed to idols for the sake of prosperity and security; Jesus will not. The commandment given for that moment is the one Jesus reaches for now.

Only. The word only is not in the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:13, but it is in the Greek Old Testament, and it is implied by the whole passage, which goes straight on: you shall not go after other gods (Deuteronomy 6:14–15). There is no room for divided worship. And that little word is the one that shuts the door. The offer was never really about territory. Strip away the vision and the glory, and what remains is a transaction: a moment of bowing in exchange for everything. Worship is not divisible. A man who worships two things worships neither; he simply has one master he admits to and one he obeys. No servant can serve two masters (16:13).

Jesus, who is God, worships God. As a man, he gives the Father the worship due to him. He who is the eternal Son, equal with the Father, has taken the form of a servant, and as the true man he does what every man was made for. He will receive all the kingdoms, but from the Father’s hand, through obedience and the cross (Philippians 2:8–11).

The hinge of all three. The first was about bread, the third will be about proof, but underneath every one of them is the same question: who is God here? Every temptation comes down to that, however small the surface of it looks. Behind the second glass, the unopened message, the figure adjusted on the form, is a very quiet transfer of allegiance: a moment in which something other than God is trusted to deliver what only God can give. Which means the test is not usually taken in the moment of crisis. It is taken beforehand, in the settled question of what a person actually worships when nothing is happening. Jesus came into that wilderness with the answer already fixed, and the devil found nothing in him to negotiate with (John 14:30).

How do I know what I actually worship? Here is a test that can be run without much difficulty. Not, what do I say I believe? But: what is the thing whose loss would make life feel unliveable? What do I daydream about when my mind is free? What do I spend money on without thinking, and what makes me angry when it is threatened? Whatever answers those questions is being worshipped, whether or not it has ever been called by that name. The answer may be a good thing: a child, a marriage, health, a reputation, a career. Good things become idols not by being loved but by being loved in God’s place. The cure is not to love them less but to love God more, and to bring them to him with open hands.

In a sentence. Jesus refused, quoting the command to worship and serve God alone.

On a Tuesday. Take the thing that came out of that test, the one whose loss you could not bear, and name it to God this week. Where it applies: if your mood for the whole day depends on what the bank balance, the scales or your child’s exam results say, something has taken a place that belongs to him. Thank him for it as his gift, ask him to keep it if it is his will, and tell him that you will trust him if he does not. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to stop loving your family or caring about your work, as though indifference were holiness. God gave them to be enjoyed. It is a call to hold them under him, not instead of him.

For worship. He would not bow, so that we might be set free from bowing to everything else. Here is the only man who ever gave God the whole of his worship with nothing held back, and he did it for us, as our representative. Our worship is divided and cold; his was single and burning, and in him the Father counts it ours. Worship the Lord your God, and him only: Jesus kept that commandment in a desert, starving, with the world on offer, and it is because he kept it that we, who have broken it every day, can come and worship at all.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took him to Jerusalem, set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: if you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you, and, on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.

And he took him to Jerusalem. The third assault moves to the holy city, the place of the temple, and it comes with a Bible verse. Whether in a vision or physically, Luke does not say.

And set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The pinnacle (pterygion, little wing) was a high point of the temple complex, probably the south-eastern corner of the platform, where the ground falls away sharply into the Kidron valley, a drop of perhaps 450 feet (140 m), which the Jewish historian Josephus said made you dizzy to look down. Or it may be the roof of the royal colonnade. Below, the courts would have been full. This is not a private test. It is a proposal for a public one.

If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here. Prove your sonship; force God to act. A spectacular rescue in front of the temple crowds would also prove to everyone that he was the Messiah: a sign from heaven, the very thing his enemies would demand (11:16). And notice what the temptation actually is. Not to doubt the promise, but to use it: to manufacture a crisis that obliges God to act, and call the manufacturing faith. It is the most religious of the three, and the only one that comes with chapter and verse.

For it is written. Now Satan quotes Scripture too. Twice Jesus has answered, it is written. Very well: for it is written. The devil can quote the Bible, and he can quote it accurately.

He will command his angels concerning you. Psalm 91:11–12, a real psalm, a genuine promise about the protection God gives to the one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High. Nothing about the words is invented. Except that something has been left out, and it is the clause that would have ended the conversation. The psalm promises that he will command his angels to guard you in all your ways. In Luke’s account the devil quotes to guard you and lifts the promise out of its setting; Matthew’s version drops the guarding clause altogether (Matthew 4:6). Either way, in all your ways is the point he hides. God guards his people in the paths they walk in obedience to him. Jumping off a building to see whether he will catch you is not one of your ways. It is not a way at all. And the psalm goes on: you will tread on the lion and the adder (Psalm 91:13), the serpent Jesus is about to defeat. The devil quoted the verse just before his own sentence.

How Scripture is nearly always misused. Not by inventing a verse; anyone can check an invented verse. By quoting a true one with the qualifying clause removed, or the occasion changed, or the covenant context stripped off. Every cult, every ruinous proof text, every disastrous decision made on the strength of a verse lifted out of its paragraph has this shape. The words were accurate. The sentence they came from was not consulted. That is the strongest argument there is for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. The man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. The man who knows what God is doing in Scripture as a whole can hear a true verse being used against its own purpose and say so.

How do I read a promise in context? Ask four plain questions. Who is speaking, and to whom? What does the rest of the paragraph and chapter say? Is the promise for a particular person and occasion, or for all God’s people? And does my reading agree with the rest of Scripture, and with the way Jesus and the apostles used it? Psalm 91 promises real protection to those who trust God, and Christians may lean on it in danger. It does not promise that a believer will never suffer, since the same Bible shows faithful people imprisoned and killed (Hebrews 11:36–38). It promises that nothing will touch them outside their Father’s will, and that in the end no harm will undo them.

In a sentence. On the temple’s highest point, the devil tempted Jesus to throw himself down to prove he was God’s Son, quoting Psalm 91’s promise of angelic protection.

On a Tuesday. Scripture can be twisted, and the most dangerous twisting is the one that agrees with what we already want. Where it applies: when someone, including you, uses a verse to justify a decision that the rest of Scripture forbids, such as leaving a spouse because God wants you to be happy, or giving recklessly because God will multiply the gift. Read the verse in its chapter before you lean your weight on it. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a reason to distrust the promises or to read the Bible only with a commentary in hand. The promises are meant to be believed and claimed. Read them, rest on them, and let the whole Bible tell you what they mean.

For worship. He stood at the top of the temple and would not jump, and some years later he stood at the bottom of a hill outside the city and let them lift him up on a cross. He refused to throw himself down to make his Father prove his love; instead he gave himself up to prove his Father’s love to us. The angels who would have caught him at the temple were held back at Calvary, so that he could fall the whole way into death for our sake. There was no rescue for him, so that there would be rescue for us.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: it is said, you shall not put the Lord your God to the test.

It is said. Jesus answers Scripture with Scripture. Scripture interprets Scripture; one verse is not to be set against the rest. The devil had a text; Jesus has the Bible.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. Deuteronomy 6:16, and Moses finishes the sentence with the place name that explains it: as you tested him at Massah. Massah is the incident in Exodus 17. Israel is thirsty in the desert; there is no water; and instead of asking, they quarrel and demand. The question they put is recorded because it is the question underneath all such demands: is the LORD among us or not? (Exodus 17:7).

What testing God is. It is not asking him for something. Scripture is full of people asking, urgently and repeatedly, and God never once objects.
