It is making his response the condition of believing him. It is setting up a situation in which he must act in a specified way or be found wanting, and then calling the arrangement faith. The line between trust and testing is fine to look at and absolute in practice. Trust says: he is good, and I will do what he has told me to do, and leave the outcome with him. Testing says: I will construct a circumstance that forces his hand, and I will read the result as a verdict on whether he loves me.

How it happens without our noticing. Most people who do this have no idea that is what they are doing. It is the bargain made silently at two in the morning: if this scan comes back clear, I will know he is with me. It is the decision taken with no wisdom and no counsel, on the grounds that God will surely honour boldness. It is the resignation handed in without a plan, filed under stepping out in faith. And it is the terrible weight that settles when the scan is not clear, because a verdict was attached to it that God never agreed to. He does not owe us a demonstration. That is not coldness; it is the only arrangement under which a relationship is possible at all. A God who could be summoned by staging the right circumstance would not be God, and a faith that needed him summoned would not be faith.

But God says through Malachi, put me to the test, and Gideon asked for signs. Yes (Malachi 3:10; Judges 6:36–40). Testing God in the forbidden sense means demanding that he prove himself on our terms, as Israel did at Massah and as Satan urged Jesus to do. Malachi’s call is God inviting his people to trust a promise he has made. Gideon’s fleece was a weak man’s request that God graciously answered; it is not a pattern for seeking guidance, now that God has spoken in his word.

Then how do I seek guidance without laying a fleece? Begin with what God has already said: is the choice in front of you commanded, forbidden, or left free by Scripture? If it is left free, pray for wisdom, which God promises to give (James 1:5). Think it through honestly; ask the counsel of mature Christians who know you; weigh your gifts, your responsibilities and the open doors in front of you; and then decide, trusting that God rules even your mistakes. You do not need a sign in the sky. A Christian who has prayed, consulted Scripture and sought counsel, and then chooses between two good paths, is not out of God’s will whichever he takes.

In a sentence. Jesus refused, answering from Scripture that we must not put God to the test.

On a Tuesday. Do not take reckless risks and expect God to bail you out; trust him in the path of obedience. Where it applies: driving after drinking because God will protect you; refusing a treatment your doctor urges because you have decided God must heal you without it; spending money you do not have because God will provide. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: obedience sometimes looks risky to the world, and that is not testing God. A missionary going to a dangerous place because Christ has called him, a believer refusing to lie at work and losing her job, a family taking in a child in need: these are not presumption but faith. The difference is not the size of the risk. It is whether God asked you to do it.

For worship. He could have jumped. The angels would have come; the promise was real. He declined to make his Father prove himself, and the reason he declined is that he did not need proving. He had heard the voice at the Jordan. He knew whose Son he was in the wilderness, hungry, with nothing whatever to show for it. And on the cross, when they said to him, come down and we will believe, he stayed, and trusted his Father in the dark: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). Here is faith perfected, in a man who never once put God to the test, and who was tested in our place to the uttermost.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.

When the devil had ended every temptation. Every kind: the arsenal was emptied. Whatever else the devil had, he used it, and none of it worked. That is worth stating plainly, because the wilderness is sometimes read as a warm-up. It was not. It was everything he had, brought against a man weak with hunger and forty days alone, and it failed completely. The three temptations represent the whole range: appetite, power and possessions, pride and presumption. John sums them up as the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life (1 John 2:16). The same three Eve faced, when she saw that the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and to be desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Jesus faced them all, and did not give way. He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

He departed from him. Defeated. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

Until an opportune time. Not merely a later date but a suitable one, the right moment. The enemy withdraws, and he withdraws to wait. Luke means this as a signal, and he will pick it up again exactly where he intends. Satan will return through opposition, through Peter (Matthew 16:23), and above all in the passion. The next time Satan moves openly against Jesus in this Gospel is at the Supper: then Satan entered into Judas (22:3). And in the garden, when they come for him with torches, Jesus tells them what hour it is: this is your hour, and the power of darkness (22:53). The wilderness was the opening exchange. The opportune time was Gethsemane and the cross, and there the temptations came back in almost their original shapes: save yourself; if you are the Christ; if you are the King of the Jews (23:35–39).

The victory is real, and it is not yet final. That is a fact about the Christian life as well. There is a particular discouragement that belongs to the believer who genuinely settled something, who fought a thing through and prayed it through and thought it was dealt with, and then finds it standing in the doorway again eighteen months later, looking exactly as it did. The conclusion that suggests itself is that the earlier victory was not real, or that nothing has changed, or that this will simply go on for ever. The verse says something different. The enemy left because he had been beaten, and he came back because he had been beaten and had not stopped. A returning temptation is not evidence that the last resistance was fraudulent. It is evidence that the war is longer than the battle.

The opportune time is the hour of exhaustion. Notice the timing he chose, both then and later. Not while Jesus was strong, but at the end of forty days without food. Not in the middle of the ministry, but on the last night, in the dark, when his friends were asleep. The opportune time is a real category, and it is generally the hour of exhaustion. Which is a good reason to be more careful, not less, when you are tired, and no reason at all to conclude, when it comes, that you have gone backwards.

If Jesus defeated Satan here, why does the devil still trouble me? Because his defeat comes in stages. Here, in the wilderness, he was beaten in single combat. At the cross he was disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15). At Christ’s return he will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (Revelation 20:10). We live between the second and the third: the enemy is defeated and doomed but still active, like an army that has lost the decisive battle and fights on in the hills. He can tempt and accuse and harass you, but he cannot condemn you, and he cannot take you out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28).

In a sentence. Having tried every temptation and failed, the devil left Jesus until a more opportune time.

On a Tuesday. A victory over temptation today does not mean it will not return. Stay alert, especially when you are tired. If the old sin is back at the door this week, do not tell yourself that nothing ever changed; tell yourself that you are still in the war, and fight it with the same weapons. And take comfort: Jesus has already defeated your tempter.

For worship. The devil emptied his arsenal on the Son of God and went away with nothing. When he came back at the opportune time, in the garden and on the cross, he threw everything again, and again found nothing in him; and that time his defeat was total, because the death he arranged was the death that undid him. Our champion has met the enemy twice and won twice, once by refusing every temptation and once by bearing every sin. We fight a beaten foe, under a Captain who has never lost.

parallels.desc: your hour, and the power of darkness

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus returns from the wilderness “in the power of the Spirit” — the forty days have not depleted him but concentrated the anointing. He teaches through Galilee and is praised by everyone. Then he comes to Nazareth, where he grew up, and on the Sabbath stands to read.

He is handed the scroll of Isaiah and finds the place: Isaiah 61:1-2. “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” He reads it, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down. Every eye in the room is on him. And he says: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

The passage is a Jubilee text — the year of the Lord's favour is the fiftieth year of Leviticus 25, when debts were cancelled, slaves freed, and lost land returned. Jesus announces that the true Jubilee has arrived. And he stops mid-sentence: Isaiah goes on to “the day of vengeance of our God,” and Jesus does not read it. The favour has come; the reckoning waits for a coming still ahead.

The congregation's first response is admiration — they marvel at his gracious words and say “Is not this Joseph's son?” It is simultaneously flattering and dismissive: impressed by the local boy, unprepared for the claim. Jesus reads the room and pre-empts the demand he can see forming: “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, 'Physician, heal yourself.' What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here also.”

Then he does the thing that turns admiration into fury. He tells two stories from their own Scriptures: Elijah sent past every widow in Israel to a pagan widow in Sidon (1 Kings 17), and Elisha cleansing a Syrian general while Israel's lepers went uncleansed (2 Kings 5). In both, the prophet bypasses Israel and the blessing lands on an outsider.

The congregation hears it perfectly. The year of the Lord's favour is not automatically theirs; they could be the ones passed over. It is a challenge to every form of religious privilege, and the response of privilege threatened is exactly what one would expect. They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill, intending to throw him off. He passes through the midst of them and goes away — because the hour, and the place, and the manner of his death are not theirs to choose.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Isaiah text Jesus reads is a Jubilee text, and the Jubilee was Israel's built-in rehearsal of release: the trumpet, the cancelled debt, the freed slave, the restored land. Jesus announces that the ultimate Jubilee has arrived — not an economic reset but a cosmic one. The debt of sin cancelled, the captivity to Satan ended, the blind given sight, the oppressed set free.

This is why he can say “today.” Not soon, not when conditions improve, but today, in your hearing — and the “today” does not depend on the congregation's response. It depends on who has just sat down.

The rage at the Elijah and Elisha stories is the rage of religious privilege challenged. They wanted a Messiah for Israel who would bless Israel and defeat Israel's enemies, not one who would take the blessing to the enemies themselves.

Every generation of the church faces the same temptation: to want Jesus for itself, to treat the gospel as the property of those who already have it, and to be offended when grace reaches people who had been written off. The Nazareth synagogue is the permanent warning against a Christianity that has lost the scandal of grace.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” is the most decisive today in Luke's Gospel — and this Gospel is full of them: “unto you is born this day a Saviour” (2:11); “today salvation has come to this house” (19:9); “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43).

The gospel in Luke is always a present-tense announcement, never merely past-tense history or future-tense hope. The Scripture fulfilled in Jesus is not fulfilled in some spiritual realm remote from the present moment; it is fulfilled now, here, in the hearing of particular people in a particular room.

Jesus walking through the crowd that means to kill him (v. 30) is the first of several moments in Luke where he moves through danger untouched — not because violence is ineffective but because his hour has not come. His death must be the death he chooses, on the terms the Father has set.

And the scene is a warning about familiarity. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus and was the one town where he could do almost nothing. The people who received him in this Gospel were, almost without exception, those who met him with no prior file: a centurion, a Samaritan, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector, a dying criminal.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. He taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.

And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit. Full of the Spirit (v. 1), led by the Spirit (v. 1), now in the power of the Spirit. He went into the wilderness full; he comes out in power. Forty days of hunger and assault have not depleted him. Something has been concentrated. That is worth registering, because the usual assumption about hard seasons is that they take something out of a person and the best that can be hoped for is recovery. Luke reports the opposite. The testing did not drain the anointing; it proved it, and a proved thing carries weight that an untested thing does not. Luke stresses throughout that Jesus’ ministry is empowered by the Spirit (v. 18; Acts 10:38).

To Galilee. The northern region, where most of his ministry will take place (4:14–9:50). Luke compresses here. Between the wilderness and Nazareth there is a period of ministry he does not narrate. John’s Gospel fills in some of it, with the wedding at Cana and the first visit to Jerusalem (John 1–4), and Luke simply notes that word was spreading.

A report about him went out through all the surrounding country. His fame spread. This matters for reading what comes next, because Jesus will shortly refer to things he did at Capernaum that Luke has not yet described (v. 23). Luke told us at the outset that he was writing an orderly account (1:3), and that word means arranged in a followable sequence, not clocked to the day.

And he taught in their synagogues. Synagogues were local meeting places for prayer and for the reading and teaching of Scripture, in every Jewish town. They probably began during the exile, when the temple had been destroyed and the people were far from Jerusalem. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak, and Jesus, and later Paul, used them for preaching (Acts 13:15). The gospel began its journey in the ordinary weekly gatherings of ordinary people.

Being glorified by all. At first, universal acclaim. Hold that phrase against what happens fifteen verses later, when the congregation of his own village tries to throw him off a cliff (v. 29). Luke has set the two side by side deliberately. The universal early approval is real, and it is worth almost nothing, because it has not yet been tested by anything he actually came to say. A ministry, a message or a man can be widely admired right up to the first moment of genuine confrontation, and the admiration tells you nothing about what is underneath it. The crowds that praised him in Galilee were the same kind of crowds that would shout in Jerusalem three years later, and the second shout was not a change of mind. It was the first one, finally tested.

Is it wrong to want to be liked? No. Wanting the good opinion of others is natural, and Scripture commends a good name (Proverbs 22:1). Jesus himself grew in favour with God and man (2:52), and elders must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). What is dangerous is needing it: letting the crowd’s approval decide what you say, or measuring your faithfulness by your popularity. Be glad when people think well of you, and do not lean on it. The approval that will last is the one you will hear at the end: well done, good and faithful servant.

In a sentence. Jesus returned to Galilee in the Spirit’s power, and his fame spread as he taught in the synagogues to universal praise.

On a Tuesday. Popularity is fleeting. Jesus was praised by all, and within days they tried to kill him. If you are enjoying approval this season, at work, at church or in your family, enjoy it lightly and do not trim what you say to keep it. If you have lost it for doing right, you are in his company. Seek God’s approval, not the crowd’s. And if the Lord has brought you through a hard season, look for what it has strengthened in you, not only for what it has cost.

For worship. He came out of the desert stronger than he went in, carrying the Spirit without measure, and turned towards the villages of Galilee with good news. The crowd’s praise could not inflate him and their hatred would not deflect him. He was not working for their applause; he was working for their salvation. Here is a Saviour who cannot be flattered into silence or frightened into retreat, and who walked into every synagogue in Galilee knowing exactly what the cheering was worth, and loved them anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. As was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written:

The programme of the ministry. Luke places this scene at the start of the Galilean ministry as a kind of manifesto, setting out what Jesus came to do. Mark and Matthew record a similar rejection at Nazareth later (Mark 6:1–6; Matthew 13:53–58). Luke may have brought it forward for its meaning, or it may be a different visit. Verse 23 implies that Jesus had already worked in Capernaum.

He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. His home town, a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, where everyone knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3). He had grown up there, worked there, and been known there for nearly thirty years.

As was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day. Stay on that phrase, because four words are doing a great deal of work. This was his habit. Week after week, for something close to thirty years, the Son of God walked to a small building in an unremarkable village and sat through the service. Consider what was on offer there. A synagogue in Nazareth in the 20s meant a handful of families, the same faces, an attendant, a set of scrolls, prayers everyone knew by heart, and a teaching ministry that on any given week was probably very ordinary indeed. Whatever he received in that room, it was not instruction he needed. He had more of the Spirit than every teacher in Galilee combined. He went anyway, every week, including, on this particular Sabbath, to a congregation that would try to kill him before the morning was over. If the sinless Son of God worshipped with God’s people every week, so must we (Hebrews 10:25).

What if my church is weak, or the preaching is thin? That is a quiet rebuke to a very common piece of modern reasoning: that a person who is not being fed, or who finds the preaching thin, or who has outgrown the place, is thereby excused. Jesus had better grounds for that argument than anyone who has ever used it, and he did not use it. Go, and go as a giver as well as a receiver: to pray with others, to sing, to encourage the person next to you, to hear God’s word read even if the sermon is poor. If a church has abandoned the gospel itself, that is a different matter, and you may need to find one that preaches Christ. But dullness, weakness and ordinary faces are not reasons to stay at home. They are the setting in which Jesus worshipped for thirty years.

And he stood up to read. A synagogue service included the Shema, prayers, a reading from the Law, a reading from the Prophets, a sermon, and a blessing. Readers stood to read Scripture, out of respect, and sat to teach. Any competent adult man could be invited to read, and a visiting teacher or a respected member could be asked to read and preach.

And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. Books were scrolls, kept in a special cupboard. The attendant (v. 20) handed it to him. Isaiah alone would have made a long roll, and finding a place in it meant winding through columns of handwritten Hebrew.

He unrolled the scroll and found the place. Whether the passage was the appointed reading for that day or one he sought out, he handled the scroll like a man who knew where things were in it, which, given the eighteen unrecorded years, he did. He was handed the book he had inspired, in the village he had grown up in, and he found the sentence about himself.

In a sentence. At Nazareth, Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath, as was his custom, stood to read, and found a chosen place in the scroll of Isaiah.

On a Tuesday. Make weekly worship with God’s people your custom, as it was his, not something you decide afresh each Sunday morning according to how you feel. A custom carries you on the weeks when desire does not. Plan your Saturday night so that Sunday morning is possible; sit near someone who looks alone; and between Sundays, read the Scriptures yourself, so that like him you know where things are in the book.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath kept the Sabbath. The one to whom every synagogue prayer was addressed stood among the villagers and prayed it with them. He did not despise the small congregation, the plain building, or the ordinary readings, because he was faithful in small things for thirty years before he did a single miracle. And when he unrolled the scroll, he found himself in it, because the whole book is about him. The Word who spoke the prophets’ words stood up in Nazareth to read them aloud, and every line was a promise he had come to keep.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to read and speak.

parallels.desc: Paul invited to speak after the readings

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour.

The passage. Isaiah 61:1–2, with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6, to set at liberty those who are oppressed. Luke, following the Greek Old Testament, brings the two together, and the effect is to sharpen the note of release. In Isaiah, the speaker is the Lord’s anointed servant, announcing the good news of return from exile and restoration. Jesus claims it as his own job description. And it is a job description: every clause names something the following chapters will contain.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Luke has been building towards this since the Jordan. The Spirit descended at the baptism (3:22), led him into the wilderness, brought him back in power, and now the man on whom the Spirit rests reads out the passage about the man on whom the Spirit rests. Father, Son and Spirit are all in the first line: the Spirit of the Lord, upon me.

Because he has anointed me. Anointed (echrisen) is the verb behind Christ, and its Hebrew equivalent is behind Messiah. Prophets, priests and kings were anointed with oil; Jesus is the Anointed One, anointed not with oil but with the Spirit (Acts 10:38). He is reading his own title aloud.

To proclaim good news to the poor. The poor (ptōchois) are the destitute, the needy, and in the Old Testament especially the humble poor who depend on God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 66:2). The gospel comes first to those who know they have nothing (6:20; 7:22). Luke’s Gospel will be full of them: shepherds, a widow with two small coins, a beggar at a gate, a tax collector who could not lift his eyes. Both material and spiritual poverty are in view.

To proclaim liberty to the captives. Liberty (aphesis) is the same word Luke uses for forgiveness (1:77; 3:3; 24:47). Release from captivity and release from sin are the same word. Jesus sets free those bound by sin, by Satan and by disease (13:16).

And recovering of sight to the blind. From the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 61:1. Jesus will heal the physically blind (7:21; 18:35–43), and open the eyes of the spiritually blind (Acts 26:18).

To set at liberty those who are oppressed. Isaiah 58:6. The oppressed are the crushed, the broken, those bruised under a weight they cannot lift.

To proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour. This is not a figure of speech. It is the Jubilee of Leviticus 25:8–55: the fiftieth year, when the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, debts were cancelled, slaves walked free, and land sold off in hard times went back to the family that had lost it. Israel’s own calendar contained a rehearsal of release, and he stands up in a village synagogue and says the real one has arrived. The age of God’s favour, freedom and restoration has come.

Where he stopped. Isaiah’s sentence does not end where Jesus ends it. The prophet went on: and the day of vengeance of our God (Isaiah 61:2). Jesus reads the first half, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down, breaking off in the middle of a line. That is not carelessness. It is the most eloquent silence in the Gospel. His first coming is for salvation; the day of vengeance is still to come, at his return (21:22; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Everything in between, every year the world has had since that morning in Nazareth, including this one, is the unrolled length of that unread half sentence.

Are these promises literal or spiritual? The question is badly put, and Luke will not let it be answered either way alone. Actual blind men receive actual sight in this Gospel; actual poor people are actually fed. And the same Gospel says that the deepest poverty is a man who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich towards God (12:21), and that the worst blindness is in people whose eyes work perfectly. Both are meant. A Christianity that spiritualises every one of these clauses has stopped doing what Jesus did; a Christianity that keeps them all material has stopped saying what he said.

What it does not mean. Not merely a programme of social or political liberation, as some liberation theologians have read it. Nor merely spiritual, with no care for the poor and sick. Jesus’ ministry addressed both: he forgave sins and healed bodies, preached to the poor and fed the hungry. But the deepest captivity is to sin, and the greatest liberty is forgiveness. A man can be freed from prison and remain a slave; a man can stay in chains and be free (Acts 16:25).

So is the church meant to fight poverty or preach the gospel? Both, in their order. The church’s distinctive task, which no one else will do, is to proclaim Christ and the forgiveness of sins (24:47). But the people who hear that message are given new hearts, and new hearts love their neighbours with food, money, time and justice (1 John 3:17; James 2:15–16). Mercy to the poor is not a substitute for the gospel and not an optional extra to it; it is what the gospel produces. A congregation that preaches release and ignores the widow down the road has misheard the sermon at Nazareth.

In a sentence. Jesus read Isaiah’s words of the Spirit-anointed one sent to bring good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind, freedom to the oppressed, and the year of the Lord’s favour.

On a Tuesday. Think of yourself in the list before you think of anyone else: you were the poor man, the captive, the blind and the crushed, and he came for you. Then think of the people around you who are still there. Where it applies: the colleague trapped in a habit, the neighbour who is lonely and struggling, the family at church who cannot pay a bill. Bring them the news and bring them help. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a promise that every Christian will be lifted out of poverty or sickness in this life, nor a political manifesto for one party. The Jubilee has begun in Christ, and it will be complete only when he comes again.

For worship. Here is the trumpet of the true Jubilee, sounding in a village synagogue. The debts are cancelled, the slaves walk free, and the land comes home, because the anointed one has come to pay what was owed and break what held us. The prison doors are standing open, and the year of favour has not closed, and the one who stopped reading in the middle of the verse is the one holding it open. The day of vengeance is coming, and he will bear the sword; but first he came to bear the vengeance himself, so that for everyone who comes to him, the day of favour will never end.
verseByVerse.note: “The year of the Lord’s favour” recalls the Year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves set free. Jesus stops before Isaiah’s next words, “the day of vengeance of our God.”

parallels.desc: to let the oppressed go free

verseByVerse.quote: And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. He began to say to them: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant. The attendant was the hazzan, the synagogue official who looked after the scrolls. Luke slows the film down. Three ordinary actions, described one at a time, and then a silence.

And sat down. Sitting was the posture for teaching. So the room knows a sermon is coming, and they are waiting for it: the local boy, back from wherever he has been, about to expound the great Servant passage.

And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. Intense expectation, vividly told. There will have been a rustle, and then nothing.

Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing. One of the most astonishing sentences ever preached. There may have been more (Luke says he began to say), but this is the whole of it in one line, and there is nothing else like it. Prophets said, thus says the LORD. Scribes said, Rabbi so-and-so taught. This man reads a seven-hundred-year-old prophecy about a Spirit-anointed liberator and says: that is about me, and it is happening now, in this room, while you are listening. Not one day, but today. The prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus. The Jubilee has begun.

There are only three possible responses. Either the man is deluded, or he is lying, or the year of the Lord’s favour has just begun in a small village. Being impressed is not one of the options. The one thing that cannot be done with a sentence like that is to admire the delivery, which is precisely what the congregation is about to attempt.

Today. The word is sēmeron, and it is one of Luke’s. Unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour (2:11). Today salvation has come to this house (19:9). Today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). Something in Luke’s Gospel refuses to let salvation be filed under history or postponed to the future. It keeps arriving in the present tense, at a particular address, on a particular afternoon. And notice what has to be true for that word to work. He does not say the Scripture will be fulfilled when the nation repents, or when the conditions are right, or when enough people believe. He says it is fulfilled in the hearing of a room that is about to reject him. The today does not depend on the response. It depends on who has just sat down.

How is the whole Old Testament about Jesus? Not that every verse is a hidden prediction, but that the whole story is heading towards him. Its promises are fulfilled in him (2 Corinthians 1:20); its sacrifices, priests and temple are pictures of what he would do; its kings and prophets point to the King and Prophet who would come; and its failures show why he was needed. After his resurrection he took the disciples through Moses and all the prophets and showed them the things concerning himself (24:27, 44). So when you read the Old Testament, ask not only what it meant then but where it leads: what does this show me of the Christ who was coming?

In a sentence. Jesus sat down to teach and, with every eye on him, declared that Isaiah’s prophecy had been fulfilled that day as they listened.

On a Tuesday. All Scripture finds its fulfilment in Jesus. Read your Bible looking for him, and when you finish a passage, ask: what does this show me of Christ? And hear his today as addressed to you. Whatever burden you are carrying, the release he announced is not for some future day when you are better; it is offered now, in your hearing, this week.

For worship. Every eye in that room was fixed on him, and they were right to look. Seven hundred years of longing had come down to a carpenter sitting in a synagogue, saying, today. The promises are not a beautiful idea about some deliverer one day; they are fulfilled in a person, who sat down in a real room and said, this is me. The one the prophets saw from far off is here. Fix your eyes on him (Hebrews 12:2): in him every promise God ever made is yes.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

parallels.desc: everything written about me must be fulfilled

verseByVerse.quote: And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this Joseph's son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All spoke well of him and marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said: is not this Joseph’s son?

And all spoke well of him. Or bore witness to him. At first, admiration. They marvel, as the neighbours wondered after the shepherds came (2:18), and it means what it meant there. Wonder is not faith. It is what a person feels when something has been genuinely interesting and nothing has yet been decided.

And marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. Gracious words are literally words of grace. Both his eloquence and the content: grace, favour, release. Grace is poured upon your lips, sang the psalmist of the King (Psalm 45:2). But notice what they are doing. He has just announced that the Jubilee has arrived in their village, and the congregation is appraising the performance.

And they said, Is not this Joseph’s son? The turning point. The compliment and the problem arrive in the same breath, and the second sentence cancels the first. At first the question is not hostile. It is the sound of a small community being pleasantly astonished by one of its own. They knew him at nine. They knew the family, the trade, the house, the brothers and sisters. They have watched him buy timber. And that is exactly the difficulty. It is not open unbelief; it is a settled framework into which the claim will not fit. They do not disbelieve the sermon so much as find the preacher already accounted for. He has been categorised, filed under people we know, and there is no category above it. Familiarity made it impossible for them to accept that God was at work in someone so ordinary. They did not know, as Luke’s readers do (3:23), that he was not really Joseph’s son. And Matthew and Mark record that they took offence at him (Mark 6:3).

The particular danger of everyone who has grown up near the things of God. Familiarity does not usually produce hostility. It produces a mild, pleasant, entirely unthreatened appreciation. The person who has heard the Christmas story every year since infancy has an account of Jesus in place before he ever hears a sermon, and the account is not wrong so much as too small, and it has the enormous advantage of never requiring anything. There is a way of knowing about someone which is the biggest single obstacle to knowing them. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus Christ, and it was the one town in Galilee where he could do almost nothing. The people who received him in this Gospel were, almost without exception, people who met him with no prior file: a Roman officer, a Samaritan, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector up a tree, a criminal with six hours to live.

I grew up in church. How do I stop Jesus becoming familiar? Familiarity itself is not the enemy; it is a great privilege to have known the gospel from childhood. The danger is assuming you already know what a passage says before you have read it. So read the Gospels slowly, as if for the first time, and ask what surprises you. Read them in a different translation. Notice the reactions of people who met him for the first time, and ask why you do not react the same way. Above all, pray: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Only the Spirit can make the old story new, and he loves to do it.

In a sentence. The congregation admired his gracious words but then asked how this could be, since he was only Joseph’s son.

On a Tuesday. Do not let familiarity with Jesus blind you to who he really is. Take one Gospel scene you know well this week and read it aloud, slowly, asking at each verse: what does this show me about him that I have stopped noticing? And watch how you treat the ordinary Christian beside you. God often speaks through people we think we have already filed.

For worship. He grew up among them so quietly that they could not believe he was anything more than the carpenter. That is the glory of the incarnation: the eternal Son was so truly man that his neighbours mistook him for an ordinary one. He did not glow; he worked with wood and sawdust for years. And the words of grace that came from his mouth that morning are still coming, to people who think they know him already. He is more than our file on him. He is always larger, kinder and holier than we had thought.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.' And he said, 'Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, physician, heal yourself. What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your home town as well. And he said: truly, I tell you, no prophet is acceptable in his home town.

He reads the room. He answers the question they have not asked out loud, and Luke lets us watch him do it.

Physician, heal yourself. A proverb, found in Greek and Jewish writings: look after your own before you go looking further afield. Here it means: prove yourself. Do for your own people what you did elsewhere. If you claim to be the Messiah, show us. They wanted signs, not faith. On the cross they will throw the same taunt: he saved others; let him save himself (23:35).

What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well. A reader tracking the narrative will stop here, because Luke has not told us about anything at Capernaum. That comes eight verses later (vv. 31–41). This is the clearest signal in the Gospel that Luke’s orderly account (1:3) means arranged, not strictly chronological. He has lifted the Nazareth visit out of its place in the sequence and set it at the head of the ministry, because it explains everything that follows: why Jesus is based at Capernaum and not at home, why the message goes to outsiders, and how it will end.

Is this the same visit as Matthew 13 and Mark 6? Matthew and Mark record a rejection at Nazareth much later (Matthew 13:54–58; Mark 6:1–6). Whether that is this visit told in its chronological place, or a second visit to a town that had not changed its mind, cannot be settled from the evidence; the details differ enough to allow either. What is certain is that Luke knew what he was doing when he put it first, and that none of the Gospels claims to give a diary.

The demand underneath. They want a miracle, and they want it on grounds of local loyalty. Not, show us you are the Messiah, but, do for us what you did for them. The claim underneath is one of entitlement: we knew you first, so we have first call. That is the request Jesus consistently refuses, and it is worth seeing why. A miracle performed to satisfy a home town’s sense of ownership would establish nothing except that he could be leveraged. He has just come from forty days of refusing exactly this, do something spectacular to prove yourself, and the wilderness is still on his clothes.

No prophet is acceptable in his hometown. Acceptable (dektos) is the same word as favour in the year of the Lord’s favour (v. 19). A play on words: Jesus proclaims the acceptable year of the Lord, but he himself is not acceptable to his own. He is not complaining. He is placing himself in a line, and the line is not a comfortable one. Israel’s prophets were consistently rejected by their own people and killed by the people who had the Scriptures (Jeremiah 11:21; Acts 7:52). He knows what he is stepping into, says so at the start of his ministry, and goes on with it anyway.

Why would God not do a miracle for people who asked for one? Because they were not asking in faith; they were setting terms. Jesus never refused anyone who came to him in need and trust: the leper, the centurion, the blind beggar. What he refused was the demand for proof as a condition of believing, the very thing he had refused the devil (11:29). A sign given to people who have already decided what they will accept does not produce faith; it produces spectators. When God seems silent to your prayers, it is not because he is withholding favours from those who have not earned them, but sometimes because he is drawing you from wanting a display to wanting him.

In a sentence. Jesus anticipated their demand that he prove himself with miracles as he had elsewhere, and observed that no prophet is accepted in his home town.

On a Tuesday. If those closest to you are least willing to hear the gospel from you, you are in good company. Where it applies: the brother who still sees you as the teenager you were, the parents who smile at your faith as a phase, the old friends who know your faults too well. Keep faithful, keep loving, and let your life speak over years. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: their resistance is not always the prophet’s rejection. Sometimes they are rightly put off by our own pride, preachiness or inconsistency. Before you comfort yourself with this verse, ask honestly whether the offence is the gospel or you.

For worship. He was the one prophet who deserved to be received everywhere, and he was received least by those who had watched him grow up. He accepted that rejection without bitterness, because he had come to be rejected. He would be despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3), so that we, who had rejected him, might be accepted in the Beloved. The one who was not acceptable in his home town proclaims to us the acceptable year of the Lord, and in him we are welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.

Two examples from Israel’s history. Now the two stories that turn admiration into a lynch mob, and it is important to see that Jesus chose them. He could have made his point about prophets and home towns and stopped. Instead he reaches for two episodes from Israel’s own Scriptures, both about the great miracle-working prophets, Elijah and his successor Elisha, and both about God going somewhere nobody expected.

Many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah. During the famine God sent in Ahab’s time (1 Kings 17–18), Israelite widows were starving in every village. Jesus gives three years and six months, as James 5:17 does; 1 Kings 18:1 says the rain came in the third year, probably counting from a different point, such as Elijah’s stay at Zarephath.

Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. 1 Kings 17:8–24. Zarephath was a Gentile town on the coast near Sidon, the very region of Jezebel, Israel’s great enemy and the homeland of the Baal worship Elijah was fighting. God sent his prophet past all the widows of Israel to a foreign widow, fed her through the famine with a jar of flour that did not run out, and raised her son from death.

And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian. 2 Kings 5. Syria (Aram) was the enemy. Naaman commanded the army that raided Israel’s borders; the little servant girl who told him about the prophet was a captive his own troops had carried off. He was healed when he humbled himself and washed seven times in the Jordan, and Israel’s lepers were not.

The point. Both stories are in their Bible. Neither is disputed. And put together they say something the congregation understands perfectly: the fact that the blessing is near you does not mean it is for you, and God has a settled habit of taking it past his own people to somebody they despise. Two Gentiles, an enemy’s widow and an enemy’s general, received God’s blessing, while Israel, in unbelief, did not. God is free to show mercy to whom he will (Romans 9:15). His grace is not limited to Israel, or to Nazareth. If they reject their prophet, his blessings will go to others, to the Gentiles. This is the story of Luke and Acts in miniature (Acts 13:46; 28:28).

Grace is grace. Note what makes this so much worse than an insult. He is not saying they are unworthy and Gentiles are worthy. He is saying that grace is not owed to anyone, and therefore cannot be claimed by anyone, and therefore may land wherever God pleases. God’s grace is sovereign: not earned by birth or nationality or religious upbringing. The Nazareth congregation’s rage is the exact rage of the elder brother in Luke 15, and of the workers hired at dawn who grumbled that the latecomers were paid the same (Matthew 20:11–12). It is what religious people feel when they discover that the thing they thought they had earned is a gift.

Is it unfair of God to bless some and pass by others? Fairness would mean everyone receiving what they deserve, and none of us wants that, because all of us deserve condemnation (Romans 3:23; 6:23). No widow in Israel had a claim on Elijah, and no leper had a right to be healed. That God shows mercy to any is grace; that he chooses where to show it is his right as God (Romans 9:15–16). The question that should astonish us is not why he passed by some but why he came to anyone at all. And the stories prove the door is open to the most unlikely: if a Sidonian widow and an enemy general were welcomed, no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that in the days of Elijah and Elisha, God sent his prophets past many in Israel to bless Gentile outsiders, a widow from Sidon and a Syrian general.

On a Tuesday. The test this passage sets is not difficult to state and is uncomfortable to answer. There is some category of person you have quietly written off: a nationality, a lifestyle, a political tribe, an individual with a name. Ask whether you would find it hard to be glad if God saved them tomorrow and left you exactly where you are. Whoever came to mind is your Naaman, and Naaman is the one the story is about. Pray for that person by name this week. No one has a claim on God’s grace by birth or background. Thank God that his grace reaches outsiders, including you.

For worship. God sent his prophet to the wrong address on purpose, to a widow in Jezebel’s country and a general of the enemy’s army, so that the whole world would know that his mercy is not a family inheritance. And then he sent his Son farther still, past every claim and every merit, all the way down to us. We were the foreigners, the enemies, the lepers outside the camp, and grace came looking for us. Blessed be the God whose kindness crosses every border we draw, and who loves to be found by those who were not looking for him (Romans 10:20).
verseByVerse.note: Both of these beneficiaries were Gentiles. Zarephath lay on the coast near Sidon.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. They rose up, drove him out of the town, and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.

All in the synagogue were filled with wrath. All of them. Six verses ago the same room was speaking well of him. Nothing has happened in between except two Bible stories. From admiration (v. 22) to fury in minutes. Why? Because Jesus suggested that God favoured Gentiles over them. National and religious pride was wounded. The thing that turned a congregation into a mob was not a miracle withheld, or a political provocation. It was the suggestion that God’s grace is free: free enough to go to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general and past the people who had the Scriptures. The gospel had been preached in Nazareth for a few minutes and the response was attempted murder. The same reaction met Paul when he mentioned the Gentiles (Acts 22:21–22).

And they rose up and drove him out of the town. This is a Sabbath. These are worshippers. They have come from a service in which the Scriptures were read, and the congregation has become a lynch mob, marching a man to a precipice. The men doing the marching have known him since he was a boy. Somewhere in that crowd are people who taught him, sold to him, employed him, possibly his own relatives. Luke does not say they intended a trial. There was no trial. This is a village losing its temper at a level that ends in a killing.

And brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built. Nazareth is built on a hillside, with steep drops nearby.

So that they could throw him down the cliff. Stoning, the penalty for blasphemy or false prophecy, sometimes began by throwing the condemned down a drop. It is a foreshadowing of the cross: his own people would reject him and try to kill him. And it is worth noticing that the devil had just suggested he throw himself down from a height. He refused to do it for the devil, and he will not let them do it to him.

But passing through their midst, he went away. Eight words, and Luke offers no explanation whatever. Perhaps by his sheer authority, perhaps by a miracle; Luke does not say. He does not vanish, or strike anyone down, or call for angels, which, so soon after the temple pinnacle, is worth noticing. He simply walks through the middle of them and leaves. Whatever happened there, the reason it happened is the one the Gospels give again and again: his hour had not yet come (John 7:30; 8:59). No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord: that is John’s wording, but it is Luke’s conviction (John 10:18). He cannot be killed early, or in the wrong place, or by the wrong hands. He would die in Jerusalem, not Nazareth (13:33). His death is not something that will happen to him. It is something he has come to do, on a specified day, in a specified city.

The pattern of the whole Gospel. The rejection at Nazareth sets the pattern for everything that follows: grace offered, rejected by his own, and going on to others. So the first congregation Jesus preached to tried to murder him, and he walked away and kept preaching. That is the beginning of the ministry, and it is a fair warning to anyone who imagines that faithful preaching is chiefly a matter of being well received.

How can religious people become so violent? Because religion without grace makes people possessive of God. When a person’s standing rests on his heritage, his correctness or his good record, anything that suggests God might welcome outsiders on the same terms feels like theft. The more he has invested in his own goodness, the angrier he becomes. That is why the people who killed Jesus were not the irreligious but the devout. The cure is not less seriousness about God but a deeper knowledge of our own need. A person who knows he was saved by grace alone cannot be furious when grace saves somebody else.

In a sentence. Enraged that God’s grace had gone to Gentiles, the congregation drove Jesus out of town to throw him off a cliff, but he walked through the crowd and went away.

On a Tuesday. Grace offends those who think they deserve it. Receive God’s grace humbly, as an outsider. And if you find yourself irritated when someone with a worse past than yours is welcomed at church, or praised, or blessed, stop and recognise the voice of Nazareth in your own heart. Where it applies: the new believer with a messy history who is asked to give her testimony; the young man who came to faith last year and is already more zealous than you. Rejoice with them. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this does not mean that a church should never question anyone’s profession or should hurry a new believer into leadership (1 Timothy 3:6). Wisdom is not envy. The heart test is whether you are glad.

For worship. They took him to the edge of a cliff, and he walked through them untouched, because his life was in his own hands and his Father’s, and not in theirs. Three years later he walked out of Jerusalem carrying his own cross, and that time he did not pass through their midst. He let them do it, because the hour had come. The one who could not be thrown from a cliff in Galilee chose to be lifted on a cross in Judea, for the very people who were shouting at him. He was never the victim of the crowd. He was always its Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth is built on a hillside with steep drops nearby.

parallels.desc: Jesus hid himself and went out

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From Nazareth, which rejected him, Jesus goes to Capernaum, which will be the base of the Galilean ministry. Within what appears to be a single Sabbath he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law, and at sunset heals a multitude brought to his door.

The contrast with Nazareth is complete. The hometown that had him from childhood loses him; the town that receives him gets a cascade of kingdom power — teaching, healing, and liberation.

The exorcism in the synagogue is Luke's first, and it raises a question that runs through the Gospel: what is the relation between the kingdom of God and the realm of demons? The demon's cry — “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God” — is the first confession of Christ in his public ministry, and it comes from a demon. The powers of darkness identify him before anyone in Galilee does, and their knowledge saves them nothing. The demons believe and shudder (Jas. 2:19); they do not trust and rest.

Jesus silences it and casts it out with a single sentence. No ritual, no incantation, no procedure — which is exactly what a first-century reader would have found astonishing, since contemporary exorcists used elaborate techniques. Luke, the physician, adds that the man was left unharmed.

The healing of Simon's mother-in-law is narrated with the same economy: Jesus rebuked the fever, the same verb used of the demon, and it left her. The response is immediate — she rises and serves. That is the New Testament pattern: what is received is not kept. The restored woman becomes the one who provides.

The healings at sunset, when the Sabbath ended and the sick could lawfully be carried through the streets, are the kingdom in miniature: a whole town at one door, and Jesus laying his hands on every one of them, individually, into the night.

Then, at dawn, he leaves for a desolate place, and refuses the crowd's attempt to keep him: “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” The healings are real and they are not the mission. He was sent to announce a kingdom, and he goes to the next town.
verseByVerse.theology:
The demon's address, “the Holy One of God,” appears elsewhere in the New Testament, outside this scene and its parallel (Mark 1:24), only at John 6:69, on Peter's lips. The irony is severe: the demon confesses what the disciples will grasp only gradually and the religious leaders will refuse. The spiritual world sees what the natural eye misses.

But knowledge of who Jesus is, without submission to who he is, is not faith. The demons have impeccable Christology and it does them no good whatever. Right doctrine held in terror is still a lost condition.

Jesus's withdrawal at daybreak to a desolate place, and his answer to the crowd who would have kept him, establishes the missionary imperative of the ministry. The word “must” (dei) appears again — the same divine necessity that took him to the temple at twelve and will take him to Jerusalem.

And this is the first mention in Luke of the phrase that will dominate the rest of the Gospel: the kingdom of God. It is not a place or a programme but God's rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King — which is why its arrival looks like demons evicted, bodies mended, and the poor given news.
verseByVerse.examples:
The demon's terror — “Have you come to destroy us?” — is the correct reading of what the kingdom of God means for the powers of darkness. Wherever the kingdom comes, the dominion of darkness gives ground.

That is the cosmic dimension of every healing, every exorcism, every act of forgiveness in the Gospels. It is not merely a personal benefit to the recipient; it is territory changing hands. The church that prays for the sick, that names fear and guilt and lies for what they are, and that proclaims forgiveness in the name of Jesus, is doing in its own place what he did in Capernaum.

The crowds “would have kept him from leaving them” (v. 42). The wish to possess Jesus — to keep him local, to make him the property of one congregation or one tradition — is a permanent temptation of Christian communities, and it is always well meant. Jesus consistently refuses it.

He came not to be kept but to be followed. The congregation that asks how to keep Jesus to itself has asked very nearly the wrong question. The right one is how to follow him to the next town.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. He was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.

Following Mark. From here Luke follows Mark’s account closely (Mark 1:21–39), with his own touches. And the section that follows is one long day: a sermon, an exorcism, a healing in a house, a whole town at the door at sunset, and a departure at dawn.

And he went down to Capernaum. Down: from the hills of Nazareth to the lakeside, about 700 feet (200 m) below sea level. Rejected at home, he moves to a fishing town on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, on the trade road, considerably larger than Nazareth and a good deal more mixed, with a customs post, a Roman garrison and a synagogue. It became his base for the whole Galilean ministry (Matthew 4:13). The remains of a later synagogue, built on the foundations of an earlier one, and of a house thought to be Peter’s, can still be seen there. The town that received him got him; the town that had him from childhood lost him.

A city of Galilee. Luke explains for his non-Palestinian readers.

And they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. The word is exousia, and it is the key to everything that follows in this chapter. It means the right to act, backed by the power to do it. To feel the force of it you have to know what teaching normally sounded like there. A scribe taught by citation: Rabbi Hillel said this, Rabbi Shammai said that, and the weight of a teaching came from the chain of authorities behind it. Nobody expected originality; originality would have been a defect. The teacher’s whole business was to transmit accurately what had been handed down. Jesus does not do this. He quotes Scripture constantly (he has just quoted Deuteronomy three times in the desert) but he never props himself on a rabbi, and he will shortly be saying, I say to you, in a way no scribe on earth would have dared (Matthew 7:28–29). His word is not commentary on the tradition. It is the thing the tradition had been trying to transmit.

The same authority in the sermon and the exorcism. Notice what Luke does with the word next. In four verses the crowd will use it again about something else entirely: with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits (v. 36). The authority in the teaching and the authority over the demons are the same authority. Luke has deliberately put the sermon and the exorcism in the same paragraph so that nobody separates them. What went out of his mouth in that synagogue is not a different order of thing from what went out of his mouth to the demon. The word that breaks a demonic hold and the word that is read on a Sunday morning are one word, and the reason preaching is worth anything at all is that it carries it.

Does a sermon today carry that authority? Only as far as it faithfully says what Scripture says. A preacher has no authority of his own; his opinions, illustrations and jokes carry none. But when he opens the Bible and explains truly what God has said, the word he speaks is the word of God, and the hearer is dealing with Christ, not merely with a man (1 Thessalonians 2:13). That is why you should test every sermon by the Bible (Acts 17:11), and why, when it passes the test, you should receive it not as advice to consider but as the Lord’s word to obey.

In a sentence. In Capernaum, Jesus taught on the Sabbath, and people were astonished at the authority of his word.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word still carries authority. Read it as his word to you, not just interesting advice. When you open the Bible this week, before you read, ask: Lord, what are you saying to me? And when you read a command, notice whether your first instinct is to discuss it or to do it.

For worship. His word did not need footnotes. The Creator who said, let there be light, stood in a fishing town and taught, and the people heard in his voice something they had never heard from any rabbi: not a report about God but God speaking. The same word that made the world unmade a demon and healed a fever, and it is still speaking from every page of Scripture. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away (21:33).
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, 'Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice: ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.

A rescue in church. The first miracle Luke records in the public ministry is not a healing. It is a rescue, and it happens in the synagogue, on the Sabbath. A man has sat in that synagogue, presumably for years, with an unclean spirit, and nobody knew, until the presence of Jesus made it impossible to stay hidden. Whatever else that says, it says that a religious setting is no proof of a clean one, and that the arrival of Christ does not create trouble so much as reveal it.

A man who had the spirit of an unclean demon. Luke, writing for Gentiles, for whom demon could mean a neutral spirit, adds unclean: an evil spirit.

What is a demon, and does this still happen? A modern reader has no framework for any of this, so the plain question has to be faced. Scripture gives less than curiosity would like and enough to go on. Demons are personal, created, spiritual beings in rebellion against God, angels who fell (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). They are not equal and opposite to God; they are creatures, and Luke will shortly show one obeying a single command. They are not the explanation of ordinary sin, ordinary illness or ordinary sorrow: Luke, a physician, carefully distinguishes the demonised from the sick a few verses on (vv. 40–41). And they are real. The New Testament does not treat them as a first-century way of describing epilepsy. Does it happen now? Scripture never suggests the enemy has gone out of business, missionaries in many parts of the world report encounters they cannot explain any other way, and a person in the modern West is far likelier to be destroyed by respectable idolatry than by anything dramatic. Both errors are real: to see a demon behind every difficulty, and to have quietly stopped believing in the enemy at all. The second is much the commoner, and it suits him better.

Ha! A cry of surprise, anger or dismay. Or, leave us alone!

What have you to do with us. Literally, what to us and to you?, a Hebrew idiom meaning: what do we have in common? Why are you interfering with us? (1 Kings 17:18). Us: the demon speaks for all the demons. The kingdom of God has invaded Satan’s territory.

Have you come to destroy us? They know their end is coming (Matthew 8:29; Revelation 20:10). Jesus has come to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). The demon knows exactly what the arrival of this man means for him, and he is right.

I know who you are, the Holy One of God. That is the first confession of Christ in his public ministry, and it is made by a demon. Not by a disciple; the disciples have not been called yet. The powers of darkness identify him correctly before anybody in Galilee does, and their theology is impeccable. The Holy One of God: set apart by God, sinless, belonging to God (1:35). It may be an attempt to gain power over Jesus by naming him, as was believed in ancient magic. And it saves them nothing. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). Here is the proof in a sentence: right doctrine, held with terror, in a being that will be lost. Knowing who Jesus is and being willing to have him are two entirely different things, and this creature has the first and would die rather than have the second.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ, and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). The New Testament never describes a believer possessed, nor tells believers to cast demons out of one another. Christians can be tempted, deceived and attacked, and must resist the devil (James 4:7) with the armour God gives (Ephesians 6:10–18); but they cannot be owned by a demon.

Then what is the difference between my faith and the demon’s knowledge? The demon knows who Jesus is and hates him. Saving faith knows who he is and trusts him: it agrees that what God says about Christ is true, and it rests on him, personally, for forgiveness and life (Westminster 14.2). The demon says, have you come to destroy us? Faith says, you have come to save me. The test is not whether you can recite the creed, but whether you want him: whether you come to him, lean on him, and would rather have him than anything else. A frightened believer who clings to Christ has what this demon, for all its accurate theology, can never have.

In a sentence. In the synagogue, a man with an unclean spirit cried out, recognising Jesus as the Holy One of God who had come to destroy the demons.

On a Tuesday. Knowing correct facts about Jesus is not faith. Even demons know who he is. Trust him and follow him. And do not imagine that a church service is a safe place where nothing spiritual is at stake. When the word of Christ is preached, things are being revealed and battles are being fought. Pray before you go.

For worship. The demons know his name and tremble, and we know his name and sing. He is the Holy One of God, and hell recognised him the moment he walked into the room. What terrifies the powers of darkness is our comfort: he has come to destroy them, and he will. The one before whom unclean spirits shriek is the one who calls us his friends, and the holiness that is their doom is the holiness he shares with us.
verseByVerse.note: “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God — the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, 'Be silent and come out of him!' And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. And they were all amazed and said to one another, 'What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!' And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus rebuked him, saying: be silent and come out of him! When the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. They were all amazed and said to one another: what is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out! And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.

But Jesus rebuked him. Two commands follow, and the first is as striking as the second.

Be silent. Literally, be muzzled. The demon has said nothing false. It called him the Holy One of God, which is precisely what he is, and it said so out loud in a crowded synagogue where the truth had been in short supply. And he shuts it up. He will do it again six verses later, and repeatedly through this Gospel. He will not accept testimony from unclean spirits, however accurate. Partly because the messenger discredits the message; partly because a public identification at this stage would force the ministry into the wrong shape too early. His identity was to be revealed in God’s time and God’s way. But mostly because truth spoken by an enemy in terror is not witness. Witness comes from people who have been rescued and love him, and by the end of Luke’s second volume there will be thousands of them.

And come out of him! That is the whole exorcism. No ritual, no formula, no repetition, no objects, no appeals to other authorities, no contest. Jewish exorcists of the period used elaborate techniques and invoked greater powers; a first-century reader would have expected at minimum a lengthy procedure. Jesus uses one sentence, and it is finished.

Having done him no harm. A detail only Luke, the physician, records. The demon threw the man down on its way out, a last spiteful act by a creature that has lost, and Luke checks the man over and reports that he was unhurt. It is the note of someone who cared what happened to the person and not only to the story.

What is this word? Or, what is this message? Both his teaching and his command. The crowd’s reaction is exactly right. They do not ask what technique he used or where he trained. They ask about the word. They have grasped the connection Luke has been drawing since verse 32: the authority in the teaching and the authority over the spirits are one thing.

For with authority and power. Authority (exousia) is the right to command; power (dynamis) is the ability to enforce it. Jesus has both, and Luke often pairs them (9:1). Men may have authority without power, like a king in exile, or power without authority, like a thief with a gun. Jesus has the right and the might, perfectly joined.

He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out! The kingdom of God has come, and Satan’s power is being broken (11:20). Here is the beginning of the war, and here is how it goes. The strong man’s house is entered by someone stronger, and there is no struggle in the doorway (11:21–22).

Should Christians today try to cast out demons? The New Testament never gives believers a technique of exorcism, and Jesus’ authority here was his own. The apostles cast out demons in his name as signs of the kingdom, and what is now laid on every Christian is to resist the devil, firm in faith (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:9), to put on the armour of God, and to pray. Where someone seems genuinely oppressed by evil, the right response is not drama but the gospel: patient prayer, the word of God, the elders of the church, and wise care, including medical care where illness may be part of the picture. The power is in Christ’s name and word, not in a ritual.

In a sentence. Jesus silenced the demon and commanded it to come out, and it left the man unharmed, while the people marvelled at the authority and power of his word.

On a Tuesday. No power of evil can stand against Jesus’ word. If you belong to him, you need not fear the devil. When you feel attacked, by dark thoughts, by accusation, by fear in the night, do not argue with the enemy for hours; do what Jesus did in the wilderness, and answer with the word. Speak a promise of Scripture aloud, and run to Christ in prayer.

For worship. Everything that holds a human being, the powers of darkness and death itself, is under orders it did not choose to take, from a voice that made it. He speaks once, and what has held a man for years lets go and goes out, and the man sits up unharmed on the floor of a village synagogue. There has never been a rival. There has only ever been a King, and a rebellion that had not yet been told it was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He arose, left the synagogue and entered Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.

And entered Simon’s house. Out of the synagogue and straight into a house. The authority that silenced a demon in public now walks into somebody’s kitchen. Simon, later called Peter, has not yet been formally called in Luke (5:1–11). Luke assumes his readers know him. It is another mark of his arrangement rather than his chronology, and it fits, because Simon must already have known Jesus before the boat scene in chapter 5, or the story there makes no sense.

Simon’s mother-in-law. Simon Peter was married. Paul mentions it in passing years later, noting that Cephas took a believing wife with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). The leader of the apostles had a wife and a mother-in-law, which hardly fits later teaching about compulsory clerical celibacy.

Ill with a high fever. Luke, the doctor, grades the fever. Only he says high (megalō), a medical term used by Greek physicians who distinguished great and small fevers. Mark says she had a fever; Luke says how bad it was.

And they appealed to him on her behalf. She did not ask. Somebody else did: a household asking on behalf of a woman too ill to ask for herself. That is intercession, and it is worth having by anyone who has ever sat by a bed with nothing to offer but a request.

And he stood over her and rebuked the fever. The same verb as for the demon (v. 35) and the storm (8:24): he rebuked it. Luke is not suggesting the fever was demonic; he is describing the same sovereign word applied to a different enemy. Jesus confronts illness as an enemy, part of the disorder sin has brought into the world, and he has authority over every power that harms. Sickness gets spoken to in the imperative.

And it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. Immediately: complete healing, with no weakness or convalescence, which usually follows a high fever. She was well enough at once to serve the meal. And her first act with a restored body is to feed the people in her house. Serve (diēkonei) is the word for ministry. That is the shape of the thing all through Luke: what is received is not kept. She got up and put the meal on.

Why does God heal some people and not others? A chapter of instant healings will be read by somebody who has prayed for years and buried the person anyway. Luke is not describing the normal experience of God’s people, and he never says he is. Paul left a co-worker ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and had a thorn he asked three times to have removed, and it was not (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).
