What these days in Capernaum show is not a policy but a person: what he is like, what he will finally do, and what has already begun. Every fever he rebuked came back eventually and every person he healed later died. These are signs of the morning, not the noon. If your prayer was not answered with healing, it was not because you lacked faith or God lacked love. The full healing is still coming, at the resurrection (Revelation 21:4).

Does Christ still heal like this today? God still hears and answers prayer for the sick, sometimes with healing, often through ordinary means. But the healing miracles of Jesus and the apostles were signs that confirmed who he was and what they preached (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Many Christians believe the gift of healing continues; the more likely reading is that such sign gifts belonged to that foundational period. The church prays for the sick (James 5:14–15) and leaves the outcome to God.

In a sentence. At Simon’s house, Jesus rebuked the high fever of Simon’s mother-in-law, and she was instantly healed and got up to serve them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick, as Simon’s family asked for her: by name, specifically, and more than once. Visit them, and ask what would help. And when Jesus has blessed you, in recovery, in an answered prayer, in an ordinary week of health, serve. Ask whom you could feed, help or visit this week with the strength he has given you.

For worship. The Lord of glory went home from the synagogue to a fisherman’s house and stood by the bed of an old woman with a fever. He did not think a kitchen too small for his authority or a mother-in-law too unimportant for his care. The word that silenced hell in the morning cooled a fever at lunchtime. Nothing in our lives is beneath his notice, and no illness is beyond his command; and one day he will stand over all his people and rebuke the last enemy, and we will rise and serve him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, notes that it was a high fever. Simon (Peter) was married.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. And demons also came out of many, crying, 'You are the Son of God!' But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. Demons also came out of many, crying: you are the Son of God! But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.

Now when the sun was setting. Luke gives the hour because it explains the crowd. The Sabbath ended at sundown, and carrying a burden, a sick relative on a mat, counted as work under the rules about carrying burdens (Jeremiah 17:21). So the whole town has been waiting, watching the light go, and the moment the sun is down the doors open all along the street.

All those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him. Picture it. A single doorway in a fishing village, and a queue forming in the dark that stretches out of sight; families half-carrying people who have not been out of a house for years; the noise; and one man, who has already taught in the synagogue, fought a demon and healed a woman since dawn.

And he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. That is the sentence to stop at. Only Luke says every one. He could have done it from the doorway. One word had emptied a man of a demon that morning; a word over a crowd would have been well within his power and would have taken about four seconds. He touched them one at a time. All of them. Every single person in that queue got his hands, his eyes, his attention, and given the numbers, that means hours of it, going on into the night, with the next face and the next and the next. Not mass healing, but individual care. And he healed every one.

The untouched. Some of those he touched had not been touched by anybody for years. Chronic and disfiguring conditions, the long-term sick: the conditions in that street were the kind that left a person at the margins, and the ceremonial law was not a cruelty, but it did leave people alone. He put his hands on every one of them. That is not efficiency. It is not even, strictly, necessary. It is what he is like.

You are the Son of God! The demons know.

But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. Luke links Son of God and the Christ. It is not that they were wrong; it is that they knew, and he would not be announced by them. Testimony from demons would discredit him (11:15), and the popular understanding of Messiah was political and military. He would reveal his identity himself, in his own way, culminating in the cross.

Does Jesus still notice individuals, when millions pray to him? Yes, and this verse is the proof. He is not a crowd manager. He laid his hands on every one of them, and he has not changed (Hebrews 13:8). As the risen Lord he knows his sheep by name (John 10:3), and because he is God, his attention is not divided: he is not less present to you because he is also present to someone else. When you pray, you are not a number in a queue. You are one person, known completely, with his full attention.

In a sentence. At sunset the whole town brought their sick, and Jesus laid hands on each one and healed them, while silencing the demons who declared him the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cares for people one by one. Bring the people you love to him, individually, in prayer, by name. And imitate him: in a busy week, choose one person who is easy to overlook, the housebound neighbour, the elderly member who no longer comes, the colleague nobody eats with, and give them your full attention, unhurried, for an hour.

For worship. Here he is, then, at the end of the first day anyone recorded. The Son of God, who could have spoken once from a doorway and gone to bed, standing in a Galilean street after dark, putting his hands on one broken person after another until there was nobody left in the queue. He was not tired of them. He has never been tired of them. There is no one so far gone, so long untouched, or so far down the line that he works through the crowd and stops before he gets there.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown; only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them, 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. The people sought him, came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them: I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.

And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. After a night like that, the first thing he does is leave. Luke does not say here what he went to do; Mark, telling the same morning, says he went to pray (Mark 1:35). It is the pattern Luke has already established at the Jordan and will keep returning to: before the Twelve are chosen, before Peter’s confession, on the mountain, in the garden (6:12; 9:18, 28; 22:41). Note when it happens. Not after a failure, not in a crisis, but the morning after the most spectacularly successful day of his ministry so far. The town is at his feet. That is the moment he walks out into the wilderness alone, which suggests that the hour of greatest danger is not the one that feels like it.

And would have kept him from leaving them. They tried to hold on to him. This is not hostility. It is Capernaum at its best: a town that has seen what he can do and does not want to lose it, and there is nothing wicked in wanting him to stay. Yet notice the contrast: Nazareth drove him out; Capernaum tried to hold him in. Both wanted him on their own terms. He goes anyway.

I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God. There is the must again, dei, the divine necessity that first appeared on the lips of a twelve-year-old in the temple (2:49) and will drive him all the way to Jerusalem. And notice what it is attached to. Not to healing. To preaching. That is startling given the previous night, and it deserves saying plainly: the healings are real, and they are not the mission. He was sent to announce something, and the healings are the announcement made visible. Healing a body was good, but bodies die again. The word of the kingdom gives eternal life.

The kingdom of God. Here is the first mention in Luke of the phrase that will dominate the rest of the Gospel. It is not a place and it is not a programme. It is God’s reign, his rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King, to save and to judge. Which is why its arrival looks like this: demons evicted, bodies mended, the poor given news, debts cancelled. Wherever he goes, the territory changes hands.

To the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose. Sent by the Father. His mission was wider than one town. The desire to keep him is a permanent temptation of Christian communities, and it is always well meant. A church that asks how to hold on to what God is doing among them has asked a natural question and very nearly the wrong one. He was not sent to be kept. He was sent to be followed, to the next town.

Is it wrong to want our church to keep what God is doing? Not to be thankful and to want it to continue. What is wrong is to turn blessing inward, as though God’s work existed for us. A church blessed with gifted people, money and growth should ask not only how to keep them but where to send them: planting another congregation, supporting missionaries, releasing its best people to go. The church in Antioch, at the height of its blessing, sent away its two best teachers (Acts 13:1–3). Healthy churches give away what they have been given.

In a sentence. When the people tried to keep Jesus in Capernaum, he said he must preach the kingdom of God in other towns too, because that was what he was sent to do.

On a Tuesday. Jesus prioritised preaching the gospel. Do not let good things crowd out the main thing. And notice when he prayed: after success, not only before trouble. When a week goes well, take time alone with God before the next demand arrives. Where it applies: the Christian worker so busy meeting needs that the gospel is never spoken; the parent so busy with the children’s activities that they never hear about Christ at home. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this does not make practical help unimportant. Jesus healed all night before he left. Do the good works, and do not let them silence the good news.

For worship. He prayed alone at dawn, after the greatest night of healing Capernaum had ever seen, because he lived from his Father and not from the crowd. And then he turned from the town that loved him to the towns that had never heard, because there were more lost sheep than one village. That must is the reason the gospel reached you. He would not stay where he was wanted, because he had been sent for those who did not yet know him, and he has been coming to the next town ever since.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea. One sentence closes the chapter, and Luke uses it to widen the frame. The tense means he kept on preaching: a summary of an extended period of ministry.

Judea or Galilee? A reader with an older translation may find Galilee here instead, and the difference is a genuine textual one. The manuscripts divide, and the best manuscripts read Judea, which is also the harder reading. That is generally the stronger claim, since a copyist is far likelier to smooth a difficulty than to create one. Everything in this chapter has happened in Galilee, and Mark 1:39 has Galilee, so Judea looks like a slip and would have invited correction. But Luke uses Judea elsewhere for the whole land of the Jews, including Galilee, rather than the southern province alone (1:5; 6:17; 7:17; 23:5; Acts 10:37). On that usage there is no difficulty at all. He is saying that the preaching spread throughout the Jewish land.

Why put the sentence here. The chapter began with one man alone in a desert and ends with a preaching circuit across a nation. Between those two lines he has been offered the kingdoms of the world and refused them, been driven out of his own village, and emptied a street of its sick. And note what he is recorded as doing at the end of it: preaching. Not consolidating Capernaum. Not building on the momentum of a spectacular night. Moving on, synagogue by synagogue, saying the same thing in the next town, which is exactly what he said in verse 43 he had been sent for.

In the synagogues. The ordinary weekly gatherings of ordinary Jewish people, the same institution whose Nazareth branch had just tried to kill him. He did not abandon the synagogue because a synagogue rejected him. He went to the next one.

Does a textual difference like this mean we cannot trust the Bible? No. Differences between manuscripts are real, and honest translations tell you about them in footnotes. But the great majority are tiny matters of spelling or word order, and none of them changes a single doctrine of the faith. Here, whichever word Luke wrote, the meaning is the same: Jesus preached throughout the land. We have far more early copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and by comparing them scholars can recover what was written with remarkable confidence. God has kept his word.

In a sentence. Jesus went on preaching in the synagogues throughout the land of the Jews.

On a Tuesday. The good news must go to every town. Pray this week for a preacher you know by name, and for one place that has not yet heard; and give, if you can, towards the spreading of the gospel there. And if a door has closed on you somewhere, as Nazareth closed on him, do not conclude that God has finished with you. Go to the next one.

For worship. The trumpet of the Jubilee had sounded in one village and been shouted down. So he took it to the rest of them, and he has never yet stopped taking it to the next town, or run out of patience with congregations that will not have him, or decided that a place has heard enough. He came for the wilderness and the synagogue, the cliff edge and the kitchen, the queue at sunset and the empty place at dawn, and in all of them he was the same: the Son who would not bow, the King whose word cannot be resisted, the Saviour whose hands reached every one. Blessed be the Lord who keeps preaching good news to the poor, until every captive has heard.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Galilee. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews.

4.text: <sup>1</sup> And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness <sup>2</sup> for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup> The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.” <sup>4</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’” <sup>5</sup> And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, <sup>6</sup> and said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. <sup>7</sup> If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.” <sup>8</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>9</sup> And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, <sup>10</sup> for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ <sup>11</sup> and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>12</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>13</sup> And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time. <sup>14</sup> And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. <sup>15</sup> And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. <sup>16</sup> And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. <sup>17</sup> And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, <sup>18</sup> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, <sup>19</sup> to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.” <sup>20</sup> And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. <sup>21</sup> And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” <sup>22</sup> And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, “Is not this Joseph's son?” <sup>23</sup> And he said to them, “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.” <sup>24</sup> And he said, “Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. <sup>25</sup> But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, <sup>26</sup> and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. <sup>27</sup> And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.” <sup>28</sup> When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. <sup>29</sup> And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. <sup>30</sup> But passing through their midst, he went away. <sup>31</sup> And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, <sup>32</sup> and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. <sup>33</sup> And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, <sup>34</sup> “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>35</sup> But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. <sup>36</sup> And they were all amazed and said to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” <sup>37</sup> And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region. <sup>38</sup> And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. <sup>39</sup> And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. <sup>40</sup> Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. <sup>41</sup> And demons also came out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. <sup>42</sup> And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, <sup>43</sup> but he said to them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” <sup>44</sup> And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

5.title: Calling, Cleansing, and the New Wine
5.overview:
Chapter 5 gathers five scenes that together define what it means to encounter Jesus: a miraculous catch of fish that produces not pride but prostration; the cleansing of a man whose disease had made him untouchable; the healing of a paralytic whose friends refused to be stopped by a crowd; the call of a tax collector from his booth; and a dispute about fasting that opens into the deepest question of the chapter — whether the new thing Jesus is doing can be contained in the old structures of Judaism. The answer is no. New wine requires new wineskins. What Jesus brings is not a reform of the old system; it is something genuinely, radically new.

The call of the first disciples (vv. 1–11) is Luke's fullest account of how Peter, James, and John came to follow Jesus — fuller than the brief summaries in Matthew and Mark, because Luke wants to show not just the what but the why. They did not follow a charismatic teacher because he seemed promising. They followed because they had encountered something that simultaneously exposed their unworthiness and compelled their trust. Peter's “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” is the most honest response to the presence of holiness in the New Testament — the instinct that knows it cannot stand in the presence of what it has just encountered, and is answered not with departure but with the word: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.”

The chapter closes with a theological dispute about fasting (vv. 33–39) that turns out to be the interpretive key to everything that has come before. The Pharisees and John's disciples fast; Jesus's disciples do not. The question is not merely about religious practice; it is about eschatology. Jesus answers with the image of a wedding: the bridegroom is present. The time of mourning is over; the feast has begun. This is not the time for old wineskins; the new wine of the kingdom — the presence of the Son of God himself — cannot be contained in the structures designed for a world still waiting for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Jesus Calls the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The call of the first disciples is set on the shore of the Lake of Gennesaret, where Simon Peter and his partners James and John have fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus borrows Peter's boat as a floating pulpit, teaches the crowd from the water, and then tells Peter to put out into the deep and let down the nets.

The instruction is professionally absurd. Fishermen who have worked the prime hours of the night without result do not take advice on technique from a carpenter, in daylight, with the nets already cleaned. But Peter obeys — “at your word I will let down the nets” — and the catch is so large that both boats begin to sink.

The miracle is not primarily about fish. It is about the person who commanded them. Peter, who knows these waters better than almost anyone alive, has just watched something no expertise can produce, and his response is immediate: he falls at Jesus's knees and says “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”

That is the language of Isaiah's vision (“Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips,” Isa. 6:5), of Job before the whirlwind (Job 42:5-6), of John falling as dead at the feet of the risen Christ (Rev. 1:17). It is what happens when a creature with a conscience encounters holiness. Nothing had been said about sin; a boatload of fish had told him who was in the boat.

Jesus's answer to the confession of unworthiness is not agreement and not dismissal but a commission: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” The fear that holiness produces is not the end of the encounter; it is the beginning of the calling — because the calling was never going to rest on Peter's worthiness.

The verb is zōgreō, to take alive. Fishing is bad news for fish; this net means the opposite. The trade is the same and the direction is reversed.

“From now on” is one of Luke's phrases for a hinge. They bring the boats to land, leave everything — including the greatest catch of their lives, lying on the shingle — and follow him.

And this is not the first meeting. Jesus was in Simon's house a chapter earlier (4:38-39), and John records an earlier introduction at the Jordan (John 1:35-42). Matthew and Mark give the decisive moment; Luke shows what was behind it. Most people are called the way Simon was — not all at once, but finally.
verseByVerse.theology:
The miraculous catch authenticates the call. Jesus does not simply appear on the shore and invite Peter to follow; he first demonstrates, in the domain where Peter's competence is greatest, that Peter's competence is not the final authority over the natural world.

The one who commands the fish is the one who made them. Peter's professional knowledge is real and valuable, and it is relativised — not demeaned. In the presence of the maker of the sea, every human expertise finds its proper place, which is a genuine place and not the top one.

The commission “you will be catching men” describes a rescue rather than an occupation. The disciples are being called to pull people alive out of the water that was drowning them — which is why the calling that begins with a catch of fish reaches its first great haul at Pentecost, when three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41), and has not stopped since.

And the pattern of the encounter is the pattern of every conversion: an approach from Christ's side, a demonstration that leaves the man with nothing to stand on, an honest confession of unworthiness, and a calling that does not depend on the confession being answered with reassurance.
verseByVerse.examples:
“At your word I will let down the nets” — spoken after a night of futile effort, in the daylight hours when fishing is least productive, on the instruction of someone who is not a fisherman — is the model of obedient trust.

It is not blind obedience. Peter states the professional futility of the exercise plainly and is entirely right to state it. But he has heard something that overrides his own competence, and the reason he gives is the only one he has: not that the strategy makes sense, but that the one who commands can be trusted.

“They left everything and followed him” (v. 11) is the most radical vocational change in the New Testament. James and John leave their father in the boat — not just a career but a family business and a family obligation. The “everything” is genuinely everything: livelihood, security, plans, and the future they had imagined.

Not every disciple is told to leave a trade; Luke's own Gospel sends several people home. But everyone who follows has a moment when something must be left on the beach — and it is very often the thing that had only just started going well.

verseByVerse.quote: On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret. He saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.

Meaning first. Luke 5 shows the authority of Jesus reaching into ordinary lives and calling them to himself. A fisherman who has caught nothing all night lets down his nets at Jesus’ word, hauls in a catch that sinks two boats, falls on his knees confessing his sin, and is made a fisher of men. A man full of leprosy is touched and cleansed. A paralysed man lowered through a roof is told first that his sins are forgiven, and then, to prove that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, is told to get up and walk. A despised tax collector leaves his booth, throws a feast for his friends, and Jesus defends eating with sinners: a doctor goes to the sick. And when asked why his disciples do not fast, Jesus answers that the bridegroom is here, and that his new wine cannot be poured into old wineskins. The chapter shows who Jesus is, the Lord whose holiness makes sinners tremble and whose grace makes them follow, and it shows what he has come to bring: forgiveness, cleansing and a new life that the old forms cannot hold.

The setting. Only Luke tells the story of the great catch at the call of Peter. Matthew and Mark record the call of these same four men in a few brisk lines by the lakeside, with no sermon and no catch of fish: Jesus walks past, says follow me, and they go (Matthew 4:18–22; Mark 1:16–20). Luke gives a whole morning. Is this the same event told differently, or a different one? Luke has already put Jesus inside Simon’s house one chapter earlier, healing his mother-in-law (4:38–39), and here Jesus steps into Simon’s boat as a man borrowing from someone he knows. Luke plainly does not think this is their first meeting. John fills in the earlier stage: Andrew and another disciple met Jesus by the Jordan, and Andrew had already brought his brother to him (John 1:35–42). So the picture that holds all four together is not a single lightning-bolt summons but a deepening: an introduction at the Jordan, an acquaintance in Capernaum, and then this morning on the shore, when the acquaintance becomes a leaving of everything. Matthew and Mark give the decisive moment; Luke shows what was behind it. This is the moment of decisive commitment.

The crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God. Luke introduces the first disciples through a sermon, not a miracle. The crowd is pushing, physically crowding, and they came hungry for the word of God, Luke’s phrase for Jesus’ preaching. He needs a platform.

The lake of Gennesaret. Luke’s precise name for the Sea of Galilee, from the fertile plain of Gennesaret on its north-western shore. Luke, who had seen the Mediterranean, does not call a lake about 13 miles by 8 (21 by 13 km) a sea.

The fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. After a night’s fishing, nets had to be cleaned of weed and debris, mended and dried. It is the last job of a night shift, done by people who want to go home. Simon will say why in a moment: they caught nothing (v. 5). These are not prosperous boat owners at leisure. They are labourers at the end of a wasted night, cleaning weed out of nets that earned nothing, and a teacher climbs into the boat and asks for a favour.

Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s. Jesus chooses Simon’s boat. He borrows what belongs to Simon, as a first step in claiming Simon himself. The relationship that will become the central human relationship of this Gospel begins as a practical arrangement between a preacher who needs a pulpit and a fisherman who has one going spare. Jesus enters their exhaustion and their disappointment before he asks anything of them, and he asks for something small before he asks for everything.

And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. A natural pulpit. Water carries sound, and the shore sloped like an amphitheatre; a boat pushed out a few yards turns a beach into an auditorium. Simon sat in the boat listening, while he held it steady. Before he is called, he is made to hear.

How does God usually call people? Most people are called the way Simon was: not all at once, but finally. A few Christians can name the hour they first believed; many cannot, and came to Christ over months or years, through a Christian home, a friend, a church, a slow dawning, and then a moment when it became their own. Both are real conversions. What matters is not whether you can date it but whether you are now following him. If your story is gradual, do not doubt it for that reason. God was at work in every stage, as he was with Simon at the Jordan, in his house, and in his boat.

In a sentence. With the crowd pressing to hear God’s word, Jesus got into Simon’s boat, asked him to push out a little, and taught from it.

On a Tuesday. Jesus often begins by asking for the use of something ordinary of yours: your car for someone without one, your kitchen for a meal with a new neighbour, your spare hour for the child who needs reading help, your living room for a Bible study. Let him have it. You may not see at first that he is not only borrowing the boat but coming for the boatman.

For worship. The Lord of the sea climbed into a borrowed boat, sat down among wet nets, and preached from it. He came to tired men at the end of a fruitless night, and he did not wait for them to be fresh or successful before he came near. He borrows our small things to give us great ones. The one who would soon ask Simon for everything began by asking for a few yards of water, and he is still coming to people in the middle of their ordinary work, patiently, until they are his.
verseByVerse.note: The lake of Gennesaret is the Sea of Galilee. Nets were washed and mended after a night’s fishing.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, 'Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.' And Simon answered, 'Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon: put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch. Simon answered: Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.

Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch. Consider how that sounded. Simon has fished this lake all his working life. Fishing on the lake was done at night, when the fish came near the surface and could not see the nets, and he has just worked the whole of it for nothing. It is now morning, the worst time, and the gear has been cleaned and stowed. Daytime, in deep water, was the wrong time and the wrong place. And a carpenter from an inland village is telling a fisherman how to fish. Your nets is plural: the whole crew is to do it.

Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! Luke lets the objection stand, and the exclamation mark is right. This is not a pious man swallowing his doubts. He states the professional reality plainly, and he is entirely correct to state it: it makes no sense. Notice also what he calls him: Master (epistatēs), a word Luke alone uses, and only on the lips of disciples, meaning someone in charge, a commander or superintendent. It is a real title, and it is not yet Lord. Three verses from now it will be. He knows enough to obey; he does not yet know who he is obeying. That is where most obedience begins, and there is no other way to start.

But at your word I will let down the nets. That is one of the great sentences of the Gospel, and its greatness lies in what it does not claim. Simon does not say he now expects fish. He does not say he has received an inner assurance, or felt a stirring, or reconsidered the science of it. He gives the reason, and there is exactly one: at your word. This is faith: acting on Christ’s word when it contradicts what we think we know. Not blind faith, but faith in a word, from a person he had begun to trust. And it is what faith looks like from the inside far more often than the confident version people imagine. Faith is not the disappearance of the objection. It is the objection stated honestly, and then the obedience anyway, because of who is speaking.

The cost of obedience. It is easy to miss. The nets were clean. Letting them down again means hours more work at the end of a shift, in front of a crowd on the shore, at a time of day when everyone watching knows it will not work. Simon is not risking his life. He is risking looking a fool, which for most people is harder.

Does this mean I should obey any impression that comes to me? No. Simon obeyed a word spoken audibly by Jesus himself. For us, Christ’s word is Scripture, and that is where we must look for his commands (2 Timothy 3:16–17). A strong feeling or an inner voice is not the same thing, and should be tested by the Bible and by wise counsel, not obeyed as if it were the voice of Christ. But where Scripture does speak, to forgive, to give, to be honest, to keep a vow, to tell someone the gospel, Simon is our pattern: obey, even when experience says it will not work.

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon to go into deep water and let down the nets, and Simon, though they had caught nothing all night, obeyed because Jesus said so.

On a Tuesday. Where does Christ’s word tell you to do something that seems pointless by your own experience? Where it applies: forgiving the relative who has never changed; giving generously when the budget is tight; telling a friend about Christ when every past attempt fell flat; going on praying for a child who shows no sign of interest. Say with Simon: at your word, I will. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a licence for reckless schemes in the name of faith, such as quitting a job without a plan or ignoring a doctor because you feel God has told you something. Obey what he has actually said, and use the wisdom he has given you for everything else.

For worship. Here is the Lord whose word is worth more than a lifetime of experience. Simon knew the lake; Jesus made it. The man who had worked all night for nothing was about to learn that one word from this carpenter could do in a minute what all his skill could not do in a night. Blessed is the Master whose commands make no sense to us until we obey them, and who never once asks his people to let down their nets in vain.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night; daytime in deep water was the wrong time and place.

parallels.desc: a night of nothing, then a great catch

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signalled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.

They enclosed a large number of fish. Luke does not describe the fish arriving. He describes the equipment failing. Not a lucky shoal, but a miracle of the Lord of creation, under whose feet God put the fish of the sea (Psalm 8:8), who appointed a great fish for Jonah (Jonah 1:17).

And their nets were breaking. Literally, were beginning to break: overwhelming abundance. Torn nets, a shout across the water, two boats down to the waterline and going under. The miracle is reported from the point of view of men trying to cope with it.

They signalled to their partners in the other boat. James and John (v. 10): a small fishing business. Then a detail worth having: they could not manage it alone. The catch was so large that the men in the second boat had to be called, and even then both crews together barely coped. There is a picture in that of everything that follows in Luke’s second volume: a haul too big for one boat, and partners signalled for.

And filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. More than they could hold. God’s generosity overflows: after a night of empty nets, two boats full to sinking. That excess is the message. A moderate catch would have been a pleasant surprise and could have been put down to luck; a good fisherman has strange mornings. What happens here cannot be absorbed into anybody’s experience. The gear that was designed for this work cannot handle it, and neither can the boats. It is a picture of the harvest of people that the gospel would bring (v. 10; Acts 2:41).

In his own trade. It happens in the one arena where Simon is the expert, and that is not accidental. Jesus does not demonstrate his authority to these men in a synagogue, where they would have deferred to him anyway; he does it in their own trade, on their own water, at the exact point where their competence was greatest and had just failed. Simon’s professional knowledge is real, and it is not overturned so much as put in its place. In front of him is someone the fish obey.

The same lake at the end. This is the same lake, and very possibly the same men, on the morning after the resurrection in John’s Gospel, when a voice from the shore says, cast the net on the right side, and the net comes up full and unbroken (John 21:6, 11). Simon’s story begins and ends with a catch he did not earn, from a word he did not expect, in water he had already worked all night for nothing.

Will obeying Christ always bring visible success? No. Here obedience brought a spectacular catch, but Scripture is full of faithful people whose obedience brought prison, loss or apparent failure: Jeremiah preached for forty years and was largely ignored; Paul was beaten and imprisoned. The promise is not that obedience is always rewarded with results we can measure, but that it is never wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58). God sometimes gives the overflowing net to show what he can do; more often he asks us to keep letting down the nets and trust him with what comes up.

In a sentence. When they obeyed, they caught so many fish that their nets began to tear, and two boats were filled to sinking.

On a Tuesday. Obedience to Christ’s word may bring a blessing far beyond what you expected. Trust him with your empty nets: the ministry that has seen no fruit, the prayer that has had no answer, the work that has gone unnoticed. And when blessing comes, signal for the partners. Share it, and ask for help; the catches God gives are usually too big for one boat.

For worship. The God of the overflowing net does not deal in moderate measures. He fills boats until they sink, wine jars to the brim, baskets of leftovers after the crowds are fed, and cups until they run over. He gives a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over (6:38). The nets that broke on the lake of Gennesaret are a small picture of the grace that would break every container we have, and of a Lord who delights to give far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20).

parallels.desc: the net full of large fish

verseByVerse.quote: But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.' For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying: depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken.

Simon Peter. The only time Luke uses both names before 6:14, as if to mark the moment Simon became Peter.

He fell down at Jesus’ knees. In the boat, among the fish. Simon’s response is not the one anybody would predict. He does not shout. He does not count the fish. He does not thank Jesus, or ask how it was done, or invite him back tomorrow. He goes down on his knees in a sinking boat full of the largest catch of his life, in worship, and asks the man responsible to go away.

Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. A surprising response to a miracle of blessing. Not thank you, but go away. Nothing has been said about sin. There has been no sermon on repentance, no accusation, no exposure of anything Simon has done. There has only been a boatload of fish. And the fish have told him something about the man in the stern that his conscience cannot survive standing next to. Simon suddenly saw who Jesus was. In the presence of divine holiness and power, he saw his own sinfulness.

The oldest pattern in Scripture. Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up and the first word out of him is: woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts! (Isaiah 6:5). Job argues for chapter after chapter, meets God, and says, now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes (Job 42:5–6). John, who had leaned on Jesus’ chest at supper, sees him in glory and falls at his feet as though dead (Revelation 1:17). Not one of them is told to feel this way. It is simply what happens when a creature with a conscience gets close to holiness. The nearer we come to God, the more we see our sin. Conviction of sin is the beginning of true discipleship.

O Lord. Notice the title. Two verses ago he said Master. Now he says Lord, the title Israel’s Scriptures give to God himself. The fish have moved his vocabulary. He is a very long way from understanding, and he has understood the one thing that matters: the gap between himself and this man is not the ordinary gap between two men.

For he and all who were with him were astonished. Astonished (thambos): awe, amazement, fear. The whole crew felt it.

Depart from me: the shame that wants to be left alone. It is a sentence a great many people have felt without ever saying aloud. There is a kind of shame that does not want to be forgiven so much as to be left alone: that finds the nearness of God unbearable and would genuinely prefer distance to exposure. Simon is not being falsely modest. He means it. What is worth seeing is that he is right about himself and wrong about what to do with it. He is a sinful man. That is the accurate diagnosis, and it is the reason Jesus got into the boat.

I feel more sinful now than before I was a Christian. Is something wrong? Usually, something is right. Growing in grace means seeing God more clearly, and the clearer the light, the more dust you see in the room. Paul near the end of his life called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). A deepening sense of sin is not a sign that you are going backwards, provided it drives you to Christ and not away from him. The danger is not feeling your sin but concluding, as Simon did for a moment, that you must keep your distance. The right response to seeing your sin is the one Simon made next: to stay at Jesus’ knees and hear him say, do not be afraid.

In a sentence. Seeing the miraculous catch, Simon fell at Jesus’ knees and begged him to depart, because he was a sinful man in the presence of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. When God shows you something of yourself this week, through Scripture, a sermon, or a moment of his kindness that you did not deserve, do not run from it and do not hide from him. Say honestly what Simon said, I am a sinful man, and then stay where you are, on your knees and near him. Notice too that it was a blessing, not a rebuke, that broke Simon open. Let God’s goodness to you lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4).

For worship. Here is holiness so bright that a boatload of fish could make a fisherman fall on his face. The Lord in the stern of that boat is the Holy One before whom seraphim cover their faces. And yet the holiness that made Simon cry, depart from me, did not depart. The one who is too pure to look on evil climbed into a boat with a sinner and stayed there, and would one day go to a cross for him. Have you seen Christ’s holiness clearly enough to see your sin? That is not the end but the beginning. He does not depart.

parallels.desc: woe is me, for I am lost

verseByVerse.quote: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.' And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon: do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men. When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Business partners in the fishing trade. With Simon, they became the inner three, present at the raising of Jairus’ daughter and on the mountain of transfiguration (8:51; 9:28).

Do not be afraid. It is the fourth time in this Gospel. Gabriel said it to Zechariah, and to Mary; the angel said it to the shepherds; and now Jesus says it to a fisherman on his knees (1:13, 30; 2:10). The encounter with holiness always produces the fear, and the answer to the fear is always the same word. And note that he does not argue with the diagnosis. Simon says, I am a sinful man, and Jesus does not say, nonsense, or, you are being hard on yourself. He does not correct the self-assessment at all. He answers it with grace. A sinful man is exactly the kind of man he calls. He simply declines to leave, and gives the man a job.

From now on you will be catching men. From now on is a phrase Luke reserves for hinges. Everything before this morning was one kind of life; everything after it is another. And the word for catching is stronger than English lets on. Luke does not use the ordinary verb for fishing. He uses zōgreō, which means to take alive, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for sparing captives in battle rather than killing them (Numbers 31:18). Fishing, after all, is not good news for the fish; the net means death. This net means the opposite. Simon is not being told he will collect people the way he collected fish. He is being told he will pull them out alive, out of the water that was drowning them.

The same trade, reversed. Nothing of who he is gets discarded. The patience, the nerve, the long nights, the knowledge of when to move: all of it is taken up and turned round. Simon’s skills and hard work would be redirected to a new purpose. The first great haul comes on a morning in Jerusalem when about three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41).

They left everything and followed him. Only Luke says everything, and everything includes the fish. That is worth stopping on. They had just landed the catch of a lifetime, enough money to change a family’s year, the best night’s work of their lives, and they beached the boats and walked away from it: boats, nets, fish, business. They did not sell it first. The greatest professional success of Simon’s life lasted about ten minutes and was abandoned on the shingle. Jesus was worth more. This is what following him means (14:33; 18:28).

Must every Christian leave his job to follow Jesus? No. Not everyone is called to leave a trade; Luke’s own Gospel is full of people sent home (8:39). Most Christians follow Christ as fishermen, nurses, accountants and parents, and serve him in that calling (1 Corinthians 7:17, 20). What every follower must leave is the claim of anything else to be first. Everyone who follows Christ has a moment where something has to be left on the beach, and it is usually the thing that had just started going well. For some it is a job; for others an ambition, a relationship, a habit, a way of spending money, or the right to run their own life.

Is every Christian meant to be catching people? Yes, though not all in the same way. The Twelve were called to a unique apostolic office, and some are called to preach. But every believer is part of a church that is sent into the world with the gospel (Matthew 28:19–20), and every believer is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him (1 Peter 3:15). For most that means praying for people by name, living so that faith is visible, inviting friends to hear the gospel, and speaking of Christ when the door opens. You catch people alive by bringing them to the one who saves; you do not have to do the saving.

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon not to fear, for from then on he would catch people, and Simon, James and John left everything and followed him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus calls sinners to follow him and to fish for people. Ask honestly what is on the beach in your life: what you would find hardest to leave if he asked. Where it applies: the career ambition that has quietly become the centre; the evening hours that never have room for him; the savings you could not bear to share. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to neglect your family, walk out on your obligations, or despise ordinary work as second-class. Following Christ usually means serving him faithfully where you are. And this week, ask him for one person you might bring alive to him.

For worship. Do not be afraid: the first words Jesus spoke to the sinner at his knees were not a sentence but a calling. He took a man who wanted him to leave and made him a fisher of men and the first preacher of Pentecost. The Lord who could have sent Simon away instead sent him out. That is how grace works. It does not deny the sin; it outbids it. And the net Simon would cast at Pentecost had been woven first around Simon himself, by the Lord who catches men alive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man “full of leprosy” comes to Jesus. The description is Luke's medical precision: this is not an early skin complaint but an advanced case. Leprosy in the ancient world covered a range of chronic conditions, all of which rendered the sufferer ritually unclean (Lev. 13-14).

The consequences were total. He lived outside the settlement, was required to warn others of his approach — “Unclean! Unclean!” (Lev. 13:45-46) — and was excluded from worship. He was the ultimate social and religious exile, and not because of anything he had done. He simply had a condition, and the condition put him outside.

His approach is itself an act of desperation and faith: he is in a city he may not enter, on his face in public, saying “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” He does not doubt the power. He is uncertain only about the will — which is exactly the right question to bring, and the answer is the most intimate thing in the chapter.

Jesus reaches out his hand and touches him: “I will; be clean.” The touch is the miracle inside the miracle. Any rabbi could have spoken healing from a safe distance; a word would have done it. Instead the hand lands on the one body in Galilee nobody had been permitted to touch for years.

Under the law, contact ran one way: touching a leper made you unclean. Here the direction is reversed. The holiness of Jesus is not contaminated by the leper; the leper is cleansed by the holiness.

The instruction to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded (Lev. 14) is not legalism but pastoral wisdom. The priest's certificate was the man's ticket back into the community; without it, even a healed leper could not go home. Jesus heals the disease in a second, then walks the man through the process that heals everything else the disease had done to him — and the certificate stands in the temple records as “a proof to them.”

“Tell no one” is the recognition that a reputation as a healer will bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate. It does, immediately. And Jesus's answer to growing fame is the one Luke keeps recording: he withdraws to desolate places and prays.
verseByVerse.theology:
The touch of the leper is the incarnation in miniature. The Son of God who became flesh did not keep a hygienic distance from the contaminated human condition. He entered it, touched it, took on himself what should have made him unclean, and transferred his own wholeness to the sufferer.

This is what Paul means: “he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Cor. 5:21). The direction of the transaction never varies. He takes what is ours; we receive what is his. The leper's healing is a parable of salvation performed on a real body.

The willingness Jesus expresses — “I will” — is the answer to every theology that doubts the desire of God to save. The leper's “if you will” is the question of everyone who has been told, explicitly or by implication, that God may not want them, that their case may be outside the scope of his grace, that they may be too far gone.

The reply is not merely “I can.” The power was never in question. It is “I will” — the desire, the purpose, the determination to cleanse, as absolute as the power.
verseByVerse.examples:
The leper models the prayer of humility. He falls on his face; he presumes nothing about Jesus's willingness; he makes no claim on his own account — and he comes. The combination of complete certainty about the power (“you can make me clean”) with complete submission about the will (“if you will”) is the posture faith takes before sovereign grace.

It is not the prayer of someone with low expectations. He expects everything. It is the prayer of someone who knows exactly what he is asking and knows he cannot command the answer. He can only ask, and trust the character of the one he asks.

Jesus's withdrawal to desolate places in the middle of growing popularity (v. 16) is the model of spiritual formation under pressure — and it was a habit, not an episode. The more the ministry succeeded by external measures, the more he went away.

The pattern refuses the assumption that fruitfulness makes prayer less necessary. For Jesus, fruitfulness was the reason to pray more, because fruitfulness creates demands that only communion with the Father can carry. The minister who cuts prayer in order to meet ministry demands has confused the cause with the effect.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, 'Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.

A man full of leprosy. Only Luke, the physician, says full: an advanced case, covered with it. Not early, not doubtful. Leprosy in the Bible (Hebrew tsara‘at) covers a range of chronic, disfiguring skin diseases, not only what we now call leprosy (Hansen’s disease). Leviticus 13–14 gives the rules. A person with it was ceremonially unclean. He had to wear torn clothes, leave his hair unkempt, cover his upper lip, and cry out, unclean, unclean, to warn people away. He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46). No one could touch him without becoming unclean themselves. The rabbis considered curing leprosy as hard as raising the dead, as the king of Israel said when Naaman came: am I God, to kill and to make alive? (2 Kings 5:7).

A living death. Take in what that meant. No home. No synagogue. No temple. No work. Nobody has touched him in years: not a handshake, not a hand on the shoulder, not an embrace at a funeral. He has been required, by the law of God, to announce his own contamination to anyone who came near. And he was not necessarily being punished for anything. He simply had a condition, and the condition put him outside. And here he is in one of the cities, where he was not supposed to be, breaking every convention to get to Jesus.

He fell on his face. Desperate reverence, in front of a crowd.

Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. That is one of the most exactly worded prayers in the Gospels, and both halves matter. You can is not a request; it is a statement. He has no doubt whatever about the power. He is not asking Jesus to try. If you will is where the uncertainty is, and it is not doubt so much as the absence of any claim. He does not tell Jesus why he deserves this. He does not bargain, or promise, or point to how long he has suffered. He puts the whole thing in the other man’s hands and leaves it there. And clean means not just healed but restored: to God’s people, to worship, to his own family.

The shape of real petition. It is not the prayer of low expectations; he expects everything. It is the prayer of someone who knows exactly what he is asking for and knows he cannot command it. He can only ask, and trust the character of the one he is asking. And underneath it is a fear a good many people carry and few say out loud. Not, is God able? But, is God willing, for someone like me?

Should I add if it is your will to every prayer? It depends on what you are asking. Where God has plainly promised something, such as forgiveness to those who confess (1 John 1:9), wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), or the Spirit to his children (11:13), you need not pray if you will; he has told you he wills it. Where he has not promised, healing, a job, a spouse, a particular outcome, it is right to ask boldly and add, as Jesus did in Gethsemane, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). That is not weak faith. It is trust in a Father who knows better than we do.

In a sentence. A man covered in leprosy fell before Jesus, confident that Jesus could make him clean, if he was willing.

On a Tuesday. Never doubt Christ’s power. And bring your request humbly: if you will. If the thing that makes you feel unclean is sin, the shame you hide, the habit you hate, the history you would never tell, bring that too, and do not wait until you feel worthy to come. He is always willing to cleanse those who come to him.

For worship. The man came with his whole life summed up in one word, unclean, and laid it down in front of Jesus with nothing to offer but a question about his will. And the Lord of glory did not turn away. No disease is too advanced for him and no outcast too far outside the camp. He is the one who went outside the camp himself, bearing reproach (Hebrews 13:12–13), so that those who were outside could be brought in. The question the leper asked, is he willing?, has been answered for ever at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, 'I will; be clean.' And immediately the leprosy left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: I will; be clean. And immediately the leprosy left him.

And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him. Read that again slowly, because it is the miracle inside the miracle and the most shocking detail in the scene. He did not need to. A word would have been enough; he will heal a centurion’s servant from a different part of town without going near him (7:7). A word from three feet away would have cleansed this man perfectly. Instead the hand goes out, and lands on the one body in Galilee that nobody had been permitted to touch for years. This man may not have felt a human touch since the day the priest declared him unclean.

Holiness is contagious in him. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean. The contamination ran in one direction, and everyone knew which. What happens here reverses it. Jesus is not defiled by the leper; the leper is cleansed by Jesus. The uncleanness did not pass to Jesus; the cleanness passed to the leper. The holiness is the stronger thing, and it moves outward. That is the incarnation in a single gesture, and it is what Paul means: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The direction of the transaction never changes. He takes what is ours; we receive what is his.

I will; be clean. The answer to his question. Two words in Greek (thelō, katharisthēti), and they answer the exact thing the man was unsure of. He had not questioned the power; you can make me clean was said as settled fact. What he did not know was the will. And Jesus replies to precisely that, and to nothing else. Not, I can. The power was never in question. I will: the desire, the readiness, the glad determination to make this man clean. His will and his power are one.

And immediately the leprosy left him. Not gradually. Complete, instant cleansing: skin that had been rotting for years made whole in a moment. A sign that the Messiah had come: the lepers are cleansed (7:22).

A picture of salvation. Sin is like leprosy: it defiles, isolates, spreads and kills, and no human remedy can cure it. Christ alone can cleanse it, and he does so by touching us in our uncleanness, taking it on himself at the cross. A whole life of exclusion had taught this man to expect a no, or at best a reluctant and distant maybe. What he got was a hand on the skin nobody would touch, and a word with not a hair’s breadth of hesitation in it.

Does I will mean that God always wills to heal every sick person who asks in faith? No. This healing was a sign that the kingdom had come in Jesus. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and was told, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). Every prayer for healing is rightly prayed as the leper prayed, if you will.

What does it mean for me that Jesus touched the leper? It means there is nothing about you that makes him recoil. People who carry deep shame, from abuse suffered, from sin committed, from a body or a mind that does not work as it should, often feel untouchable, as if God would keep his distance if he really knew. This verse says otherwise. He comes nearest to what we hide. Bring him the thing you are most ashamed of, by name, in prayer; and if you can, tell a mature Christian, so that you hear his welcome spoken aloud. And then become his hand to others: notice who in your church or street is untouched, and go near.

In a sentence. Jesus reached out and touched the leper, saying he was willing, and commanded him to be clean, and the leprosy left him at once.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your circle whom others keep at a distance: the one with a contagious reputation, the awkward relative, the elderly neighbour who smells of neglect, the colleague everyone avoids after the scandal. Jesus could have healed from a distance and did not. Go near this week. A visit, a meal, a hand on the shoulder can say what words cannot.

For worship. Here is what he is like, and it has not altered since. He is not standing at a safe distance weighing whether a case qualifies. He is not reluctant, he does not have to be persuaded, and he has never once recoiled from anybody who came to him. The hand goes out first. The word is, I will. Come to him with your sin, however foul, and hear him say it to you: I will; be clean. And he who touched the leper was himself, at the end, despised and cast out and numbered with the transgressors, so that the unclean could be clean for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he charged him to tell no one, but 'go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He charged him to tell no one, but: go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.

Two instructions that seem to cancel each other. Tell no one, and go and show yourself to the priest. They do not cancel. The second is a legal procedure, not a publicity campaign, and it is the thing the man most needs.

He charged him to tell no one. It is a restraint Jesus imposes repeatedly in Galilee, and the next verse shows why it was needed. Jesus did not want to be known mainly as a miracle worker. A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate, which is exactly what happens anyway (v. 15). He came to announce a kingdom, and the miracles were the announcement made visible, not a service he had come to provide.

Go and show yourself to the priest. Leviticus 14 lays down the ritual by which a healed leper is examined, declared clean and restored: the priest inspects him outside the camp; two birds are taken, one killed and one released alive over running water; there is a week’s wait; and on the eighth day there are offerings, and the man is pronounced clean and may go home. Without that certificate, a healed man is still, in every practical sense, a leper. He cannot re-enter the town, or the synagogue, or his own family’s house. So Jesus heals the disease in a second and then sends the man through a week-long process to heal everything else the disease had done to him. He could have declared the man clean on the spot with more authority than any priest in Israel. He sends him to the priest anyway, because the man needs to be received back by his community, and there is an appointed way for that to happen. Jesus respects the law of Moses, and wants the man to be fully restored.

Grace does not despise process. There is a kind of spiritual enthusiasm that thinks anything procedural is beneath it. Jesus, who could have skipped every step, walks the man through all of them.

For a proof to them. That phrase carries an edge. It is a testimony to the priests, and to the people, that he was truly clean. And since leprosy was rarely if ever cured, it was a testimony that the Messiah had come. The priests will have to examine this man and certify him, which means that somewhere a priest examined a man who had been full of leprosy and declared him clean. The establishment that would shortly decide Jesus was a blasphemer had been handed, by its own procedure, a public proof of what he could do.

Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because the moment was different. Before the cross, a reputation as a wonder worker would have drawn crowds who wanted miracles and a political Messiah, and would have obscured what he came to do. After the resurrection, when his identity and his saving work were complete, the command was the opposite: go and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). The silences of the Gospels are temporary. Now the whole story can be told, and must be.

In a sentence. Jesus told the man not to spread the news, but to go to the priest and offer the sacrifice Moses commanded, as proof of his cleansing.

On a Tuesday. Jesus respected the proper process and authorities. Follow through on what God requires, even after a great blessing. Where it applies: a person converted from a life of fraud still needs to pay back what he took and face the consequences honestly; a believer restored after a fall still needs the patient process of rebuilding trust with the church and family. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to add human rituals to the gospel or to make people jump through hoops before they can be welcomed to Christ. The cleansing is his gift, complete; the process is for restoring the life around it.

For worship. The Lord who healed in a moment cared about the week that followed. He sent the man home by the proper road, so that his family could have him back and his town could receive him. There is no part of our restoration he forgets. He cleanses the heart in an instant, and then patiently walks us back into every relationship that sin had broken. And the priest who certified the leper clean had no idea that the true High Priest had already done it, with a touch.

verseByVerse.quote: But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.

Even more the report about him went abroad. The instruction to keep quiet has failed, as such instructions generally do. Mark tells us the man disobeyed and spread the news everywhere (Mark 1:45).

Great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. Note the order: to hear first. Both, in that order, and Luke does not sneer at them. They want the word and they want their bodies mended, which is a perfectly reasonable pair of things to want.

But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. Two sentences, set deliberately side by side, and the but between them is the whole point. Luke’s wording is worth having: he would withdraw. The tense means it was his habit: he kept on withdrawing. This was not a single retreat but a pattern. Again and again, the busier it got, the more he went away. Only Luke records this here. He goes back to the empty country on purpose. There is nothing there. That is what it is for.

It inverts the usual assumption. The natural reading of a growing ministry is that prayer becomes a luxury one can no longer afford. The demands are real, the people are genuinely needy, and the hours have to come from somewhere. Jesus does the opposite. As the crowds increase, so does the withdrawal. He treats fruitfulness as a reason to pray more, not less. Prayer was not a luxury for him but a necessity. If the Son of God needed to pray, how much more do we.

The danger of crowds. He understood something about crowds that is easy to miss. A large and admiring crowd is not a neutral thing to stand in front of. It is one of the most dangerous places a person can be, and the pressure it exerts, to be what they want, to keep producing, to believe their estimate of you, is not resisted by good intentions. He met it by leaving.

Why did the Son of God need to pray? Because he was truly man, living in dependence on his Father, and because prayer is the communion of the Son with the Father, not a sign of lack. Hebrews says he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7).

I am too busy to pray much. What do I do? Begin by being honest that busyness is the reason to pray more, not the excuse to pray less. Then be practical. Choose a fixed time, even fifteen minutes, before the day’s demands begin, and guard it as you would a meeting with your employer. Find a place, as he did: a room, a car parked before work, a walk. Use Scripture to guide your prayers, a psalm or the Lord’s Prayer, so that you are not left staring at a blank wall. And pray in the gaps, briefly and often, through the day (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Small, regular prayer will do more than occasional heroic efforts.

In a sentence. As his fame spread and crowds came to hear him and be healed, Jesus regularly withdrew to lonely places to pray.

On a Tuesday. There is a plain diagnostic here for anyone, and especially anyone in Christian work, and it is uncomfortable. If prayer is the thing that gets cut when the demands rise, the demands are being served and the life is being hollowed out, because what the crowds actually needed from Jesus came out of the desolate places, and he never once let them have it on any other terms. When life is busiest, you most need to pray. Look at this week’s diary and put the time for prayer in first.

For worship. The one through whom all things were made went out alone into the empty places to speak with his Father. He lived on prayer. And the Son who prayed in the desolate places then still prays now: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). When the crowds pressed him, he went to the Father; when the pressure of our lives presses us, he is already there before the Father for us, and he has never once grown too busy to pray for his own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the first confrontation between Jesus and the religious authorities in Luke, and it is carefully staged. Pharisees and teachers of the law have come from every village of Galilee, and from Judea, and from Jerusalem — a gathering with the shape of an inspection. They are seated. And Luke notes, before anything happens, that the power of the Lord was with Jesus to heal.

Meanwhile four men are carrying a paralysed friend, and the crowd has made the door impassable. So they go up on the roof, take it apart, and lower the man on his mat into the middle of the room, through the ceiling, in front of everyone. It is rude, destructive and entirely out of order — and Luke calls it faith.

The faith Jesus sees is not the paralysed man's alone. It is “their” faith: the faith of friends who refused to be stopped. The man himself says nothing in the entire passage. His only contribution is to lie there and be carried, and everything that follows happens because other people would not leave him outside.

What Jesus then says is not what anyone came for: “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” Not “rise and walk.” The physical healing is four verses away; forgiveness comes first.

The scribes and Pharisees recognise the claim at once: “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Their theology is entirely correct — only God can forgive sins against God. Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the premise right and the observation right, and instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy.

Jesus's challenge is pedagogical. “Which is easier, to say 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say 'Rise and walk'?” It is easier to say the first, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. The second is the dangerous sentence. So he does the checkable one — as the credential for the claim that cannot be checked: “that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.”

The miracles are never the message in this Gospel. They are the authentication of it.

And the man rises, picks up the mat he has spent his life lying on, walks out through the crowd, and goes home glorifying God — leaving a room full of people, dignitaries included, filled with awe and saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness before healing establishes the priority of Luke's whole Gospel: the deepest human need is not physical. The paralysis is real, the suffering is real, the exclusion from ordinary life is real — and Jesus removes all of it. But he deals first with something that would still have been wrong after the legs worked.

This is not a denigration of physical suffering, and it is emphatically not a suggestion that the paralysis was caused by the man's sin; Jesus explicitly rejects that reasoning elsewhere (John 9:3). It is a statement about what finally matters — the standing before God that sin destroys.

The scribes' objection is the most important theological sentence in the passage, and Jesus does not answer it by denial. He never says they are wrong about the exclusive divine prerogative. He acts on it, and offers the visible miracle as the proof.

“Son of Man” sounds modest in English and is not.
