It is Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples shall serve. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, that title while forgiving sins was the claim doubled — and “on earth” presses it further still. The authority is here, at ground level, exercised by a man they can see.
verseByVerse.examples:
The four friends are the model of intercessory persistence. They could not bring their friend by the normal route, so they found another. They could not get through the door, so they went through the roof. Their determination is not disrespect for the gathering; it is the overflow of confidence that Jesus can and will do what they believe he can.

This is what intercession looks like when it becomes serious: not eloquence, not technique, but the refusal to accept that the door is the only way, and a willingness to look foolish on somebody else's behalf.

“When he saw their faith” — the faith Jesus responds to is the faith of the group. That is a significant detail for understanding how the church actually works. The person who cannot bring themselves to pray, whose faith is exhausted or paralysed by their suffering, can be carried to Jesus by the faith of those around them.

People do get carried. There are seasons — grief, depression, shame, sheer exhaustion — when a believer will not get themselves into the room, and somebody else has to do the carrying. This passage says the carrying counts.

verseByVerse.quote: On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. The power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralysed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.

Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. The religious authorities appear in Luke’s narrative for the first time, and they are sitting down. Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes (v. 21), experts in the law of Moses. Luke is careful about who they are and where they have come from: from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. That is not a few curious locals. Word has reached the capital, and men have travelled to see for themselves. Whatever this gathering formally was, it has the shape of an inspection, perhaps an official investigation of this new teacher. And they are seated while everyone else is pressed in standing. They have been given the places of honour in the room, and they are watching. The conflict that will run through the Gospel begins here.

Who were the Pharisees? A movement of devout laymen, perhaps six thousand strong at this time, who were zealous to keep the law of Moses in every detail of daily life, and who added a large body of oral tradition to guard it. They tithed even their herbs, fasted twice a week, and kept strict rules about purity, food and the Sabbath. Ordinary people respected them as the most serious believers in Israel. Their fault was not that they cared about God’s law, which was good, but that they trusted in their own keeping of it and looked down on others (18:9). Paul had been one (Philippians 3:5), and some came to faith (Acts 15:5).

And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. Luke adds a sentence that has no obvious grammatical business being there. He states it before anything happens, like a stage direction. The Lord here means God. Jesus’ healing power was the power of God, by the Spirit (4:14). The room is full of the men who decide what may be believed in Israel, and the power that actually matters is already present, and it is not with them.

Some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralysed. Luke’s and behold is the narrator turning the reader’s head. Outside, while the inspection proceeds, men are carrying a friend on a mat; Mark says four (Mark 2:3). A man who could not come himself, carried by friends. Consider what that took before they reached the door. Somebody had to notice him. Somebody had to decide it was worth a day. Four men had to be found, and a route agreed, and a paralysed body carried through streets on a pallet, with all the awkwardness and slowness and public spectacle of it, and at the end of the journey, a house so full that there was no way in.

They were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus. They had one aim: to get him to Jesus. Luke says they were seeking: they kept trying. They did not arrive, see the crowd, and go home. They worked at it. The man on the mat has not said a word and will not say one in the whole passage. Everything that is about to happen to him happens because other people would not give up on getting him in front of Jesus.

How do I carry someone to Jesus today? First, in prayer: name them before God, regularly and specifically, for years if need be. Then in friendship: time, practical help, meals, lifts, honest conversation. Bring them where Jesus is spoken of, to church, to a Bible study, to a Christian friend who can answer their questions, and when the moment comes, tell them plainly about him yourself. Carry them together with others, as these four did; it is too heavy a load for one person. And remember that your task is to bring them, not to heal them. That is his part.

In a sentence. As Jesus taught, with Pharisees and teachers of the law from all over the land watching, some men tried to bring a paralysed friend to him on a mat.

On a Tuesday. Some people cannot come to Jesus on their own. Who can you carry to him in prayer and in friendship? Write down the names of two people this week, find one other Christian to pray for them with you, and do one practical kindness for each.

For worship. The power of the Lord was present to heal, and it was not in the honoured seats but in the one who sat among the crowd. The real authority in Israel was a carpenter from Nazareth, teaching in a borrowed house. He does not need the approval of the important to do his work, and he does not overlook the ones who must be carried. The great of the land came to inspect him; the helpless were brought to be healed by him; and he received them both into a room where God was at work.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes, experts in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst, before Jesus.

Finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd. The crowd was an obstacle, as crowds often are to those who need Jesus most (18:39; 19:3).

They went up on the roof. Houses in Palestine had flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase or ladder. Stop and picture the actual logistics, because familiarity has made this scene charming, and it was not charming. An outside stair, four men, and a stretcher with a grown man on it. Then a roof, over a room that is at that moment packed with people, including religious dignitaries from Galilee to Jerusalem. And they begin taking it apart.

And let him down with his bed through the tiles. Dust and debris coming down on the heads of the seated Pharisees. An interruption that cannot be politely absorbed. Somebody’s property being damaged, and no evidence that anybody asked the owner. It is rude, it is destructive, it is entirely out of order, and Luke, in the next verse, calls it faith. Persistent, creative, costly faith. The four men did not have better theology than the men in the room; they had a friend they refused to leave outside. They could not get to Jesus by the obvious route, so they made a new one. The obstacle sent them upward.

Tiles or clay? One small detail draws the charge that Luke did not know Palestine. Mark says the men dug through the roof (Mark 2:4), which fits an ordinary Galilean house of beams, branches and packed clay; Luke says through the tiles. But tiled roofs were the normal Greek and Roman construction and had appeared in the towns of the region, and in any case Luke is writing for readers across the empire, who would picture a roof the moment he named its material. He is translating the scene into terms they could picture. Two witnesses describing the same hole from different sides of the Mediterranean is not a contradiction. Either way, they made a hole in someone’s roof.

Into the midst before Jesus. Right in front of him. They got him there.

The man who could do nothing. The man they lowered could do nothing at all. He could not walk to Jesus, could not push through a crowd, could not climb a stair. His entire contribution was to lie there. Whatever faith he had, Luke does not mention it separately; he says Jesus saw their faith, and the man’s part in the sentence is as the thing being carried. There is a whole doctrine of the church in that. People do get carried. There are seasons when a believer cannot pray, cannot come, cannot generate any momentum whatever, through grief, depression, exhaustion or shame, and the honest truth is that they will not get themselves into the room. Somebody else has to do the carrying, and the carrying counts.

I am the one who cannot pray right now. Am I failing? No. There are seasons of illness, grief and darkness when a Christian can hardly pray at all, and Scripture does not condemn him for it. The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26), Christ intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34), and God gives brothers and sisters to carry us. Let them. Tell one or two trusted friends that you are struggling and ask them to pray for you. Keep coming to church if you can, even if you only sit there. You are not less a Christian because you are on the mat for now.

In a sentence. Unable to get through the crowd, they climbed onto the roof, removed the tiles and lowered the man on his mat right in front of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Do not let obstacles stop you bringing people to Jesus. Be persistent and creative in love. Where it applies: when the friend you invited to church says no for the third time, try a meal at home; when a relative will not talk about faith, keep praying and keep loving; when a sick church member cannot come, take the service to them. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: creative love is not a licence to manipulate people, to trick them into a meeting, or to pressure them until they give in. The men broke a roof, not a person’s will. Bring people to Jesus; do not drag them.

For worship. This is the kind of faith Jesus loves to see: faith that will tear up a roof to get someone to him. And it is a dim picture of his own love. He came down through more than tiles to reach us. He opened heaven itself, and came down into a crowded, hostile world, to lay himself where the helpless lie. We are the man on the mat, unable to move; and he is the friend who would not leave us outside.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks of tiles, the roofing his Greek readers knew; Mark describes digging through a roof of packed earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw their faith, he said, 'Man, your sins are forgiven you.' And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, 'Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw their faith, he said: man, your sins are forgiven you. And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying: who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?

And when he saw their faith. Faith he could see, because it acted: a hole in the roof is faith made visible. The faith of the friends, and presumably of the man too. Jesus honours faith that brings others to him. Our faith and prayers can matter for others.

Man, your sins are forgiven you. Nobody in that room expected that sentence, and it is worth registering how strange it is. Four men have gone to enormous trouble for one thing. The man on the mat wants one thing. The whole audience is waiting for one thing. And Jesus looks at a paralysed man lowered through a hole in somebody’s ceiling and deals with his sins. He will heal the paralysis; it is four verses away. But he does the other thing first, and the order is deliberate. Jesus deals first with the deeper problem. The perfect tense means: your sins have been forgiven, and stand forgiven.

Was the man’s paralysis caused by his sin? Not necessarily, and the passage must be handled carefully because it can be heard cruelly. Jesus is not saying the paralysis does not matter; he removes it. He is not suggesting it was caused by the man’s sin; he says nothing of the kind here. Some Jews believed sickness was always caused by sin. Sometimes it is (John 5:14), though not always, and Jesus explicitly denies that reasoning about the man born blind (John 9:2–3). What he is doing is treating the deeper condition first, in a man who had not come about it and may not have known he had it. If you are ill, do not assume God is punishing you for something. All sickness belongs to a fallen world; your particular illness may have no link to any particular sin at all.

The deeper need. That is a hard word and a merciful one. The thing wrong with all of us that will still be wrong after every other thing is put right is not physical. A man who is healed and unforgiven has been given a working body and a few more decades, and the account is still open. A man can be healed in body and still be lost; the greatest need of every person is forgiveness.

Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Blasphemy is speaking against God, or claiming what belongs to him alone. The penalty was death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). And notice where the charge is made: inwardly. They began to question, Luke says; they had not yet spoken it aloud (v. 22).

Who can forgive sins but God alone? Now this is important: their theology is correct. Entirely correct. All sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4). A person can forgive a wrong done to himself, but only God can forgive sins against God. That is not a Pharisaic invention; it is the plain teaching of the Old Testament: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isaiah 43:25). Any faithful Jew in that room would have said the same. Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the major premise right: only God forgives sins. They have the observation right: this man has just forgiven sins. And instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy. If Jesus is not God, he is a blasphemer. He is not a blasphemer, because he is God.

Those who reject him understand him. That is worth noticing about the whole of Luke’s Gospel. The people who reject Jesus are almost never the people who understand him least. They are usually the people who have grasped exactly what he is claiming.

Can someone else’s faith save a person? No. Luke does not say the paralysed man lacked faith, and the friends’ faith brought him to Jesus, which is what faith on behalf of others can do. We may carry others to Christ in prayer and witness, but each person must come to him in his own faith.

In a sentence. Seeing their faith, Jesus told the paralysed man his sins were forgiven, and the scribes and Pharisees thought this blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you most want from God this week. If it is all about circumstances, health, money, a relationship mended, bring it to him; he cares. But ask also whether you have come to him for the deeper thing. Hear the word Jesus spoke to that man as spoken to everyone who trusts him: your sins are forgiven. And if someone has asked you to forgive them, remember that forgiving is the most God-like thing a person can do.

For worship. Only God can forgive sins, and Jesus does. The scribes were right about God and wrong about the man in front of them: the God who blots out transgressions for his own sake had come to Capernaum in human flesh, and spoke his pardon to a paralysed man on a mat. He did not ask for sacrifices; he was about to become the sacrifice. Hear his word to you, as plainly as that man heard it: your sins are forgiven. No one else in the universe has the right to say it, and he says it gladly.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, 'Why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins'—he said to the man who was paralyzed—'I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them: why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, your sins are forgiven you, or to say, rise and walk? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (he said to the man who was paralysed), I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.

When Jesus perceived their thoughts. They had not spoken. Luke says they began to question, inwardly, and Jesus answers the argument going on inside their heads, which is itself a demonstration of something only God does. Only God knows the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). Another sign of who he is.

Which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Rise and walk? The question is sharper than it looks, and the answer is not the obvious one. Which is easier to say? Plainly the first. Anyone can announce that a man’s sins are forgiven, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. Saying rise and walk to a paralysed man is the dangerous sentence: in three seconds everyone in the room will know whether it worked. In another sense, forgiveness is far harder, because it is a divine act, and would cost Jesus his life. Jesus will now do the visible, harder-to-say thing, to prove the invisible one.

That you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. So Jesus does the checkable one, and he says exactly why. The healing is not the point. The healing is the evidence for the claim that cannot be verified: a visible miracle offered as the credential for an invisible one. That is the logic of miracle throughout the Gospels. The miracles are never the message. They are the authentication of the message. A Jesus who heals bodies and cannot deal with guilt would be a remarkable physician and no use at all at the end.

The Son of Man. This is Jesus’ favourite way of referring to himself, and the first time Luke uses it. It sounds modest in English; a son of man is just a human being. It was not modest. He is drawing on Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him, an everlasting dominion. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, choosing that title while forgiving sins was not a retreat from the claim. It was the claim, doubled.

On earth. Note the two small words in the middle. Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven, by God, at the appointed time and through the appointed sacrifices. Jesus says the authority is here, at ground level, in a crowded house in Capernaum, exercised by a man they can see. God forgives from heaven; Jesus forgives on earth, as God in human flesh. Which means that the thing the whole temple system existed to deal with has walked into a room and dealt with it, in one sentence, freely, for a man who did not ask.

Rise, pick up your bed and go home. Three commands, impossible for a paralysed man. The word of Jesus gives the power to obey. As Augustine prayed, give what you command, and command what you will.

How can I know my sins are really forgiven, when I cannot see it? By the same logic Jesus used here. You cannot see forgiveness, but you can see the one who grants it, and he has given you evidence enough: his miracles, his death, and above all his resurrection, by which God declared his sacrifice accepted (Romans 4:25). Your forgiveness does not rest on your feelings, which rise and fall, but on his word: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name (Acts 10:43). If you have come to him trusting him, you are forgiven, as surely as that man walked. Feelings of guilt may linger; take them to his promise, not his promise to your feelings.

In a sentence. Knowing their thoughts, Jesus healed the paralysed man before their eyes, so that they would know that he, the Son of Man, has authority on earth to forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ visible works prove his invisible authority. If he can heal, he can forgive. Trust him for both. When an old sin comes back to accuse you this week, answer it the way Jesus answered the scribes: point to what he has done. The risen Christ is the proof that the debt is paid.

For worship. The Son of Man from Daniel’s vision, the one who rides the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom, stood in a crowded room on earth and forgave a paralysed man. The King of all peoples bent down to a single mat. He read the hearts of his critics and answered their silent objections, and then he gave them proof they could see. And the forgiveness he spoke so easily that day was not cheap: it would be paid for at the cross. There is authority on earth to forgive sins, and it is in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, 'We have seen extraordinary things today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately he rose up before them, picked up what he had been lying on, and went home, glorifying God. Amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying: we have seen extraordinary things today.

And immediately he rose up before them. In front of everyone, including the sceptics.

And picked up what he had been lying on. Luke lingers on the bed. The phrasing draws attention to it. That mat was the whole visible history of his life: what he was carried on, what he lay on, the thing other people had to lift. He walks out with it under his arm. The bed that had carried him, he now carried. And he walks out through the crowd: through the doorway they could not get him in by, past the seated dignitaries, into a street where everyone knew him. Whatever else that town discussed that week, it discussed this.

And went home, glorifying God. Only Luke records his praise. Forgiven and healed. And the man went home. That is where Jesus sent him: not into the travelling company, not into public ministry. Go home. There was a house somewhere in Capernaum where a family had been carrying this man for years, and that evening he walked in on his own feet, carrying the mat.

And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God. Amazement (ekstasis) is being beside oneself. Luke says it of the man, and then immediately of the crowd: they glorified God and were filled with awe. Not with admiration of a technique. With awe. All of them, which in that room includes the delegation from Jerusalem.

We have seen extraordinary things today. Extraordinary (paradoxa), from which comes paradox: things contrary to expectation, things that overturn the settled order. They have no category for what they have watched, and they say so. Today: again, Luke’s word (4:21).

Amazed and unchanged. They are not converted. Luke does not say they believed; he says they were amazed and afraid, and by chapter 6 they will be watching him to accuse him (6:7). It is entirely possible to witness the undeniable, glorify God out loud, and go home unchanged. Amazement is not faith. The man who went home with the mat had been forgiven; the men who went home with an anecdote had only been impressed.

In a sentence. The man got up at once, carried his mat home praising God, and everyone was amazed and glorified God, saying they had seen incredible things.

On a Tuesday. Do not settle for being impressed by Jesus. Many people admire him, as the crowd did, and go home unchanged. Ask whether what you have seen of him has reached you: whether you are carrying your mat home as a forgiven sinner. And then tell your household, as that man surely did, what God has done.

For worship. Whatever the four friends had imagined when they started taking the roof apart, they got more than they had come for. They came for a pair of working legs. They went home with a man whose sins had been forgiven by someone with the authority to do it, and a Saviour they had not known they needed. Have you seen extraordinary things in Christ? A forgiven sinner is the greatest of them. The paradox of the gospel is that the holy God forgives the guilty and remains just, because the Son of Man would carry our sins as that man carried his mat, all the way out of the room.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From the crowded house Luke moves straight to one of the most understated calls in the Gospel. Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth and says “Follow me.” And Levi left everything and followed him.

The form is identical to the call of Peter, James and John (v. 11) — an encounter, a bare imperative, and complete abandonment. But Levi's “everything” carries a different weight. Tax collectors in the Roman system had purchased the franchise; leaving the booth meant writing off a substantial investment with no prospect of return, and no possibility of going back. The fishermen could have returned to fishing. Levi could not return to a tax booth.

He was also, by the reckoning of every devout person who walked past him, beyond the pale: a collaborator with Rome, a legally protected extortioner, ritually unclean, inadmissible as a witness. Jesus called him without an assessment, a probation, or an interview.

Levi's first act as a disciple is to throw a great banquet and fill it with the only people he knows — a large company of tax collectors and others. He has no theology and no method. He has a house and a contact list, and he puts Jesus in the middle of them.

The Pharisees and their scribes complain, and they complain to the disciples rather than to Jesus: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” The objection is not mere snobbery. Table fellowship in that world was a public declaration of acceptance and solidarity — closer to a signed statement than a meal — so this is a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God.

Jesus's answer is the programmatic statement of the whole ministry: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.”

The word “righteous” is ironic. Everyone in that house is sick; the difference between the two groups is entirely in what they know about themselves. A man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor, however available the doctor makes himself. And the last two words are not decoration — he called sinners to repentance. The table at Levi's house is a doctor's visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease.
verseByVerse.theology:
The call of Levi is Luke's announcement that the kingdom of God comes to the most unexpected people. Matthew's Gospel tells us this is Matthew himself (Matt. 9:9). The author of one of the four Gospels is a man whom the respectable religious society of his day considered beyond the reach of God's grace.

And of the four apostle lists in the New Testament, the only one that attaches “the tax collector” to his name is the one he wrote (Matt. 10:3). He never got over it.

“I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” is not a statement about two classes of people — the righteous who do not need Jesus and the sinners who do. Scripture is unambiguous that there are no righteous: “none is righteous, no, not one” (Rom. 3:10).

It is a statement about two self-perceptions. The “righteous” are the self-righteous, whose assessment of their own spiritual condition is so favourable that they see no need of a physician. The tragedy of the Pharisees is not their theology, most of which was sound. It is their self-knowledge. They could not be called to repentance because they did not believe they needed to repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Levi's banquet is the instinctive evangelism of someone who has just received grace and immediately wants the people he loves to meet the one who gave it. No training, no method, no strategy — he invites his friends to his house and invites Jesus to the same room.

The criticism this drew is the criticism grace-shaped evangelism has always drawn: it happens in the wrong places, with the wrong people, without sufficient concern for the reputation of those involved. Jesus's presence at that table is the answer to every objection of the kind.

“Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” is the perennial complaint of those who would like the church to be more selective in its welcome. The instinct to keep the table clean — to eat only with the already acceptable — is deeply human, and it rests on a real principle: that holiness is preserved by separation.

What it has not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round, which the same chapter has already shown at a leper's skin. Jesus's table is where the sick come for medicine, not where the well gather to congratulate each other on their health.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. He said to him: follow me. And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.

A tax collector named Levi. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew (Matthew 9:9); he had both names, as Simon was also Peter and Saul was also Paul. Two names for one man was entirely ordinary then. Tax collectors were despised (3:12). Levi probably collected tolls on goods passing along the trade route through Capernaum, for Herod Antipas.

Sitting at the tax booth. At work, in the place of his sin. What a tax booth was in Capernaum is worth spelling out, because it explains the shock. Capernaum sat on a trade route near a border; the booth taxed goods in transit. The man in it collected for whoever held the contract, and kept whatever else he could extract. That was not an incidental abuse of the job; it was how the job worked. So Levi is three things at once to everyone walking past: a collaborator with the hated regime, a thief with legal protection, and ritually unclean from constant contact with Gentiles. Tax collectors were not accepted as witnesses in Jewish courts. He would not have been received in a synagogue in any meaningful way. And he was very probably rich.

Follow me. Two words in Greek, and no preliminaries whatever. Jesus walks past his table and calls him with the same bare command he used on the fishermen: no assessment, no probation, no interview. Jesus calls a sinner, as he had just forgiven one. The Pharisees had complained about forgiveness; now Jesus makes a tax collector a disciple.

And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. Luke uses the same phrase he used at verse 11, and for Levi it costs differently. The fishermen left boats and nets; boats and nets are still there tomorrow, and a man can go back to fishing, which several of them eventually did for a night (John 21:3). Levi leaves a lucrative post. There is no going back to a tax booth once you have walked away from one; someone else will be sitting in it soon enough. He gave up a lucrative career for good. He is burning the only asset he has, and he does it standing up.

The man who wrote it down. Luke does not tell you this, and Matthew does. When the First Gospel reaches this same scene it names him Matthew (Matthew 9:9), and when it lists the twelve apostles it calls him Matthew the tax collector (Matthew 10:3), a description none of the other lists bothers to add. Which means the man rising from that booth is the man the church has always believed wrote the Gospel that opens the New Testament. And of the four lists of apostles in the New Testament, the only one that pins tax collector to that name is the one bearing his own name. He never got over it.

What did Levi do about the money he had taken? Luke does not tell us, but Zacchaeus, another tax collector, shows what repentance looked like for such a man: he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid anyone he had defrauded fourfold (19:8). Following Christ does not wipe out our obligations to people we have wronged. Grace forgives the sin before God freely and completely; it also makes us want to put right what we can. If you have cheated someone, the gospel does not ask you to earn forgiveness by repaying, but it will lead you, gladly, to repay.

In a sentence. Jesus called Levi, a despised tax collector, from his booth to follow him, and Levi left everything and followed.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond Christ’s call. He calls people from the middle of their sin, and he calls you to leave whatever holds you. Think of the person you consider least likely to become a Christian, the cynical colleague, the relative in a crooked business, the neighbour who mocks faith. Levi was that man in Capernaum. Pray for them this week as for a future disciple.

For worship. He walked past the most despised table in town and stopped. No one in Capernaum would have chosen Levi; Jesus did. Two words were enough, because the one who spoke them is the Word who calls the dead to life. And the man he called from counting coins was given a pen and the privilege of writing the first Gospel. Such is the grace of the Lord who chooses what is low and despised in the world (1 Corinthians 1:28), so that no one may boast, and every forgiven tax collector may sing.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew’s Gospel calls Levi “Matthew.” Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, 'Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying: why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?

And Levi made him a great feast in his house. Levi’s first recorded act as a disciple is to throw a party. He has no theology yet, no training, no idea what is coming. What he has is a house, a large one evidently, and a contact list. A rich man, he gave a banquet: a celebration.

A large company of tax collectors and others. Luke’s polite way of describing the social world a man in that trade moved in. Levi’s friends were tax collectors and other outcasts; respectable people would not associate with him. So he fills the room with the only people he knows, and he puts Jesus in the middle of it. That is the instinct of somebody who has just been given something and immediately wants the people he cares about to meet the one who gave it. It is not a strategy. It is a man who cannot think of anything better to do with his house. The natural evangelism of a new believer.

Reclining at table with them. Table fellowship in that world was not a casual matter. To recline at a man’s table was to declare peace with him, to accept him, to be publicly associated with him. It was closer to a signed statement than to a meal.

And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples. Grumbled (egongyzon) means murmured, the word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27). And notice who they complain to. Not to Jesus: they go round him to his disciples. It is the oldest form of religious criticism there is: raise it with the followers, where it will do most damage and cost least.

Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? The objection is worth understanding rather than dismissing. The Pharisees kept themselves separate from sinners: those who did not keep the law as they interpreted it, and the openly immoral. Eating with them would make you unclean. The Pharisees are not complaining about the menu; they are asking a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God, and by their own logic they are entirely right to ask it. Their premise is that holiness is preserved by separation: that you keep clean by keeping away. It is not a stupid premise. It is much of the book of Leviticus, and it had kept Israel identifiable through centuries of pressure. What they have not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round. Luke showed it two sections earlier, and they had no category for it: a hand stretched out to a leper, and the cleanness travelling from the toucher to the touched. To the Pharisees, holiness meant separation from sinners. For Jesus, it meant going to them. The charge will come again (7:34; 15:2; 19:7).

But does the Bible not tell us to avoid bad company? Yes: bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33), and we are not to walk in the counsel of the wicked (Psalm 1:1). The difference is the direction of influence and the purpose of the friendship. Jesus ate with sinners as their physician, and he was never drawn into their sin; they were drawn to him. Paul says Christians must not keep close company with someone who calls himself a brother and lives in open sin, but he does not mean the immoral of this world, or you would need to go out of the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). So be a friend to unbelievers, with open doors and real love; but if a friendship is pulling you into sin rather than you drawing them to Christ, step back.

In a sentence. Levi held a great feast for Jesus with many tax collectors and outcasts, and the Pharisees grumbled to the disciples about eating with sinners.

On a Tuesday. Introduce your non-Christian friends to Jesus. Levi’s method is open to anyone: a meal, a house, and the people you already know. Where it applies: invite a neighbour and a Christian friend to dinner together; ask the colleague who is going through a hard time to lunch; open your home at Christmas to someone who would otherwise be alone. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: welcoming sinners is not approving sin, and it is not joining in. Jesus ate with them as the one who called them to repentance (v. 32). And do not let fear of criticism keep you from friendship with outsiders.

For worship. The holy Son of God reclined at a table crowded with tax collectors and sinners and was glad to be there. He was not slumming or making a point; he was at home among the people he came to save. And he still keeps that table. One day, in the kingdom, he will sit down to the great feast with people from east and west and north and south (13:29), and the guest list will be full of Levis. He receives sinners and eats with them (15:2), and every one of us is at his table only because he does.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. A proverb, especially apt from Luke the physician, and its force is that nobody can disagree with it. A doctor goes to the sick. That is his job. A doctor found among the sick is not compromising his profession; he is doing it. His presence in the ward is not evidence that he approves of illness. It is evidence that he is a doctor. He does not catch their disease; he heals it. Jesus is the doctor; sinners are the sick. Where else should he be? So the question, why do you eat with sinners?, answers itself the moment you know what he came for.

I have not come to call the righteous. The word righteous here is ironic, and everyone at that table knew it. Jesus is not conceding that the Pharisees are righteous and therefore outside his remit. Scripture is unambiguous that there are none: none is righteous, no, not one (Romans 3:10, quoting the Psalms). He is using their own self-description back at them. The Pharisees thought they were righteous, and so did not think they needed him. Jesus cannot help those who think they are well.

Everyone in the house is sick. This is the thing to hold. The difference between the two groups at Levi’s dinner is not their condition. Everyone in that house is sick. The difference is entirely in what they know about themselves. The tax collectors are aware of it; the men in the doorway are not. And a man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor however available the doctor makes himself. That is the whole tragedy of the Pharisees, and it is not primarily a moral tragedy. They were not, by most measures, bad men. They were disciplined, serious, orthodox and self-denying, and they had a diagnosis of themselves that was wrong, and being wrong in that particular direction is the one condition Christ cannot treat, because it is a refusal of treatment.

But sinners to repentance. Note the last two words, because they are easily lost. Only Luke adds to repentance. He does not say he came to call sinners and leave them as they were. He came to call them to turn round. Jesus does not accept sinners to leave them as they are, but calls them to change. His welcome is not approval of sin, but the beginning of transformation. The table at Levi’s house is not an endorsement of anybody’s life. It is a doctor’s visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease. Grace receives sinners and changes them.

Does that mean Jesus accepts me as I am? Yes, and he will not leave you as you are. He receives anyone who comes to him, however sinful, without first requiring that he be cleaned up; the leper came full of leprosy, and Levi came straight from the booth. That is why you need not wait until you are better to come. But the same Jesus calls you to repentance, and his acceptance is the beginning of a new life, not a seal of approval on the old one. You come as you are; you do not stay as you are. Both halves are love.

In a sentence. Jesus replied that, like a doctor who goes to the sick, he came to call not those who think they are righteous but sinners to repentance.

On a Tuesday. You qualify for Jesus only by admitting you are sick. Come to him as a sinner, and he will heal you. And watch for the Pharisee in yourself: the sense, after years of church, that you are basically well and that the gospel is for people with worse problems. Name, in prayer this week, one specific way you still need the physician.

For worship. The Great Physician makes house calls, and he goes to the worst cases first. He sat down among the sick, not because he loved disease, but because he loved the diseased, and he came with the only cure there is. And his remedy is costly in a way no earthly doctor’s ever was: by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The doctor took the sickness into himself so that the patients could go free. Blessed be the Lord who came, not for the righteous, but for sinners like us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question about fasting is deceptively simple — why do Jesus's disciples not fast like John's disciples and the Pharisees? — and the answer, in two images and an observation, reframes the whole relationship between the old covenant and the new.

The bridegroom image is the most significant, because it is a claim about identity. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God: “Your Maker is your husband” (Isa. 54:5); “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hos. 2:19; cf. Jer. 2:2). Israel is the bride, and every apostasy is described as adultery. To explain his disciples' behaviour by saying the bridegroom is present is to say who has arrived — and John the Baptist had already made the same identification, placing himself in the wedding party rather than at its centre (John 3:29).

The disciples do not fast because this is not the season for it. Fasting at a wedding is not more serious; it is out of time.

Then the shadow: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” It is the first hint of the cross in Jesus's own teaching in Luke, dropped without warning into an argument about religious observance. Nobody at that table could have understood it.

The garment and the wineskin press the same point. A patch cut from a new coat ruins the new and does not match the old; new wine in a hardened skin bursts the skin and is lost. The kingdom Jesus inaugurates is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfilment — and fulfilment is not the same as continuation.

The new covenant is organically connected to the old; Jesus keeps the law, goes to the synagogue weekly, sends the leper to the priest. But what has arrived could not be contained by what preceded it, not because the old was worthless but because it was never designed to hold this.

And the last line is the sharpest: “no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good.'” It is not a compliment to the old wine. It is a description of a palate — and of the men in the doorway, who refused Jesus not because they had examined him and found him wanting but because they were comfortable, and he did not taste of what they were used to.
verseByVerse.theology:
The bridegroom language is one of the most significant implicit claims to deity in the Synoptic Gospels. In the prophets, the husband of Israel is the LORD himself, and the relationship between God and his people is consistently described in bridal terms.

Revelation carries the image to its conclusion — the marriage supper of the Lamb, the new Jerusalem coming down as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev. 19:7-9; 21:2-9). The fasting question in Luke 5 is a thread that runs all the way to the last page of the Bible.

The observation in v. 39 is not a sociological aside about wine preferences. It is a precise description of the spiritual condition of people who have grown comfortable in the old forms: they feel no need of new wine, because what they have is satisfying.

That is the condition of the Pharisees, and it was not a moral failure. The old wine of the law and the tradition was genuinely good — God gave it. This is the most dangerous spiritual position there is, because it requires a good thing to settle into: contentment with something genuinely good, in the presence of something better.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bridegroom's presence is the reason for the disciples' joy, and it remains the reason for Christian joy. The resurrection did not remove the bridegroom; it confirmed that he is alive and with his people until he returns.

So Christian fasting is not the fast of the men who asked the question. Jesus assumes his people will fast — “they will fast in those days,” and those days are these — but it is the fast of people who have known him, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God's attention. A body saying what the heart already knows: that the best thing is still ahead.

The new wineskins are a standing challenge to every Christian tradition, and the question has to be asked honestly. Not “is this old?” — age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown?

This is not a call to theological novelty. The wine is always the same wine, the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, and it is the oldest thing there is. But a wineskin's only job is to hold wine, and the moment it begins to be valued for itself it has started to fail at the one thing it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, 'The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.' And Jesus said to them, 'Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him: the disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink. Jesus said to them: can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.

The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers. The third complaint of the section, and it is about fasting. The observation is accurate. The law commanded only one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). But devout Jews fasted more. Pharisees fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (18:12). John’s followers, in particular, were an austere group, following his austere life, and their teacher was in prison.

But yours eat and drink. As they had just been doing at Levi’s feast. And here is Jesus at a tax collector’s banquet.

Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? He answers with a wedding. A Jewish wedding feast lasted up to a week and was a time of joy, and wedding guests were excused from certain religious duties, including fasting. Fasting expressed mourning, sorrow and longing. The point is not that fasting is wrong. It is that fasting at a wedding is absurd. It is not more serious; it is out of time. While Jesus is here, the time of longing is over.

The bridegroom. But the image is doing something much larger than settling a dispute about diet, and the men who asked would have felt it. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God. Your Maker is your husband (Isaiah 54:5); as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isaiah 62:5); I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19–20). Israel is the bride, and every failure of the nation is described as adultery. So when Jesus explains his disciples’ behaviour by saying that the bridegroom is present, he is not reaching for a pleasant metaphor about joy. He is saying who has arrived: another claim to be God. John the Baptist had already made the same identification and put himself in the wedding party rather than at its centre: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29). The messianic wedding feast has begun.

The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them. Then the shadow. Taken away (aparthē) means snatched, removed by force. This is the first hint of the cross in Luke’s record of Jesus’ own teaching, and it is dropped into an argument about religious observance without warning or explanation (Isaiah 53:8). Nobody at that table could have understood it. He knew already.

And then they will fast in those days. After his departure, his disciples will fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Fasting is right for Christians now, as we long for his return. But it is no longer a mark of mourning without hope, nor a means of earning favour.

Should Christians fast, and how? Jesus plainly assumes it: they will fast in those days, and those days are these. But it is not the fast of the men asking the question. It is the fast of people who have known the bridegroom, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God’s attention. A body saying what the heart already knows. In practice, fasting means going without food, or some meals, for a set time in order to give that time to prayer: before a big decision, in a time of repentance, in grief, or in longing for God’s work. Do it quietly, not for show (Matthew 6:16–18). Begin modestly, with one meal; take medical advice if you have a health condition; and never treat it as earning anything from God.

In a sentence. When asked why his disciples did not fast, Jesus answered that wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is present, but they will fast when he is taken away.

On a Tuesday. The Christian life has times of feasting and times of fasting. Rejoice in Christ’s presence, and long for his return. Where it applies: there are seasons to fast and pray, over a wayward child, a church decision, a besetting sin; and there are seasons to feast, at a wedding, a baptism, a birthday, with a clear conscience and a glad heart. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: do not make your own pattern of fasting a rule for others, or look down on Christians who do not fast as you do. That is exactly the error of the men who asked the question.

For worship. The bridegroom of Israel, the Maker who called himself her husband, came in person and sat down at a feast. And he knew, even as he spoke of the wedding, that he would be snatched away to a cross. He went to that cross for his bride, to wash her and present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Our fasting now is the longing of a bride whose bridegroom has gone ahead, and our feasting is the foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), when he will never be taken away again.
verseByVerse.note: The law commanded one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement. A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told them a parable: no one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.

He also told them a parable. Three short parables (vv. 36–39) explain why Jesus’ disciples do not follow the old patterns.

No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. Luke’s version of this saying is sharper than the others, and the sharpness is the point. Matthew and Mark speak of unshrunk cloth on an old garment (Mark 2:21); Luke has a man cutting up a new garment to patch an old one. So the loss is doubled. In Luke, you ruin the new garment by cutting a patch out of it, and the patch does not match the old one anyway. Both are spoiled.

The point. The question underneath is the one the whole section has been circling. Has Jesus come to repair Judaism? Is the kingdom of God a renovation of the existing arrangement: the same religion with better preaching, a bit of fresh material sewn over the worn places? The answer is no. What Jesus brings is not a patch to mend the old system. It is something entirely new: the new covenant, the kingdom of God. It cannot be stitched onto the old ways of fasting and rule-keeping without ruining both. The gospel is not a supplement to religion; it is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The old garment was not bad. The reason for the answer is not that the old garment was bad. God gave it. The law, the temple, the sacrifices and the priesthood were all his own design, and Jesus honours every one of them: he sends the leper to the priest, he goes to the synagogue weekly, he will keep the Passover. The old garment is not being criticised. It is being finished with, because what it was for has come.

How the saying is abused. This has to be held carefully in both directions, because the saying gets abused in both. It is abused by people who use it to junk everything old. New wine, they say, and away goes the creed, the confession, the twenty centuries of the church’s thinking, on the grounds that God is doing a new thing. But the newness in this parable is not new ideas. It is the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, which is the oldest thing there is. And it is abused by people who cannot distinguish between the fabric and the pattern: for whom every inherited practice is a doctrine, and any change is apostasy. That is the Pharisees’ error exactly, and Jesus is answering it here. What is genuinely new is not a programme. It is a person, and a covenant sealed in his blood, and a Spirit poured out on ordinary people. Nothing that existed before could hold it: not because the old was worthless, but because it was never designed to.

In a sentence. Jesus said that no one cuts a patch from a new garment to mend an old one, since that ruins the new and does not match the old.

On a Tuesday. Do not treat Jesus as a patch on your old life: a little religion sewn over a life that is otherwise run by the same desires and the same self. He makes all things new. Where it applies: the person who adds church to his week but keeps his business dishonest, or adds prayer to his marriage but keeps his temper unchecked. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: becoming new does not mean throwing away everything in your past, your family, your culture, your honest work and gifts. Christ does not discard those; he takes them up and makes them his.

For worship. Christ did not come to mend the old world but to make a new one. He is not a patch on the garment of religion; he is the robe of righteousness itself, given to clothe the naked (Isaiah 61:10). The law, the priests and the sacrifices were good, and they were a tailor’s pattern for what was to come; now the true garment has been woven, without seam, from top to bottom, and it is put on everyone who believes. Behold, he makes all things new (Revelation 21:5).

verseByVerse.quote: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.

Wineskins. The same point, with a better image. Wine was stored in goatskins, made from whole hides, sewn and sealed. New wine is still fermenting, giving off gas and expanding. A new skin was supple and stretched with it. But a skin that had already been through one fermentation was set hard: it had done its stretching, and it had nothing left. Pour actively fermenting wine into it and the pressure has nowhere to go. The skin splits, and you lose both.

Both are lost. Notice what Jesus says is lost: the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. Both. This is not a saying about how the old is expendable. It is a warning that forcing new life into hardened forms wastes the life and wrecks the form.

The point. The new wine is the life of the kingdom that Jesus brings: joy, grace, the Spirit, the new covenant. The old wineskins are the old forms of Judaism, the Pharisees’ traditions and rituals. They cannot contain the new life; they would burst. The new life needs new forms: the church, with its new covenant worship.

But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. Must (blēteon): it is necessary. And that is the whole prescription. Not: throw away the wine. Not: pretend the old skin is fine. Get the wine into something that can move with it. The point is not that novelty is good. It is that living things expand, and whatever contains them has to be able to give. That was true of the first Christian generation in the most literal way. Within thirty years of this conversation the gospel had gone to Gentiles who did not keep the food laws, met on the first day of the week, had no temple and no priesthood, and were being told that the whole apparatus had been a shadow of what had now come (Colossians 2:17). Not because the shadow was false, but because the substance had arrived.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is bad or useless. Jesus came to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). But the old covenant’s forms, the sacrifices, food laws, priesthood and temple, were shadows that pointed forward to Christ, and give way to the reality (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 8:13).

How do I tell a wineskin from the wine in my own church? Ask whether a thing is commanded in Scripture or chosen by people. The gospel, the preaching of the word, prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, the ordering of the church and the moral law are given by God; they are the wine and must not move. The time of the service, the style of music, the order of worship, the building, the translation used, are human choices, wineskins; they may be good and well loved, and they may be changed when they no longer carry the life. Not, is this old? Age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown?

In a sentence. Jesus said new wine must go into new wineskins, because old ones would burst, meaning the new life of his kingdom cannot be contained in the old forms.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith so tied to familiar forms that you resist anything new God is doing? Hold to the gospel; hold forms loosely. A wineskin’s only job is to hold wine. The moment it starts being valued for itself, it has begun to fail at the one thing it was for. What must never move is the wine. Everything else is leather.

For worship. The new wine of the kingdom is Christ’s own life, poured out in the Spirit, and nothing made by human hands can hold it. It burst the old skins of temple and ritual and ran out into the whole world, to Gentiles and slaves and children, in every language under heaven. At Cana he turned water into the best wine, kept until last (John 2:10); at the Supper he gave the cup of the new covenant in his blood (22:20). He is the wine, and he is the one who pours it, and he has never run dry.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says: the old is good.

Only Luke adds this saying. A wry, almost humorous comment on human nature, and the most quietly devastating sentence in the chapter. It is also frequently misread, because it sounds at first as though Jesus is conceding the point.

No one after drinking old wine desires new. Old wine is smooth and mellow; new wine is raw and harsh, still working. People who are used to the old prefer it, and will not even try the new. He is not commending old wine. He is describing a palate.

For he says, The old is good. Some manuscripts read better, but the best read good: the old is good enough. Why change? Jesus is not making a claim about the merits of the two covenants. He is stating a fact about human beings: having settled into something, we do not want the alternative, and we will always find a reason. The old is good. And so it is. And that is what makes it so hard to leave.

The point. Jesus explains why the Pharisees and many others reject him. It is not that they have tried the new and found it wanting. They are content with the old, comfortable in their religion, and do not want anything new. They do not feel the need for what Jesus brings. Self-satisfaction is a great obstacle to faith. This is the diagnosis of everyone in the doorway at Levi’s house, and it explains them better than anything else in the passage. Their problem was never that they had chosen something bad. Their problem was that they had something genuinely good, a real law given by God, a real tradition, hard won, real discipline, real reverence, real Scripture, and they were comfortable in it, and it had made the arrival of something better feel like a disturbance rather than a fulfilment.

The most dangerous spiritual position. It is not available to obvious sinners. It requires a good thing to settle into. Levi could be reached in two words at his tax booth; the men outside had spent thirty years acquiring a taste that made the new wine unpalatable. Nobody in this chapter refused Jesus because they had examined him and found him wanting. They refused him because they were comfortable, and he was not what they were used to.

Does this mean tradition is bad and new is always better? No. Jesus is not saying that whatever is new is from God; most novelties in the church’s history have been errors. The new wine is not a new idea but himself, the fulfilment of everything the old covenant promised. And Scripture tells us to hold fast to the traditions of the apostles (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The warning is against a heart so settled in its religion that it no longer needs Christ, or cannot hear him when he does not taste like what it is used to.

In a sentence. Jesus observed that those who are used to old wine do not want new, because they think the old is good enough, explaining why many rejected him.

On a Tuesday. Being content with your religion can keep you from Christ. Ask whether you are truly drinking his new wine, or just the old. Every long-standing Christian has an accumulated set of preferences, a way of worship, a style of preaching, a shape of church life, a period of hymnody, a translation, much of which is genuinely good and none of which is the gospel. The test is not whether we like the old. Of course we like the old. The test is what happens when God does something that does not taste of it.

For worship. He did not force his new wine on anyone. He set it out at Levi’s table and let the tax collectors drink, while the experts stood in the doorway saying the old was good enough. And the wine he offers is better than anything the old could give: forgiveness complete, the Spirit poured out, the Father’s welcome, life that never ends. O taste and see that the LORD is good (Psalm 34:8). Those who have drunk the wine of the bridegroom never want to go back.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke adds this saying — a wry comment on those content with the old ways.

5.text: <sup>1</sup> On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, <sup>2</sup> and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. <sup>3</sup> Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. <sup>4</sup> And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” <sup>5</sup> And Simon answered, “Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.” <sup>6</sup> And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. <sup>7</sup> They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. <sup>8</sup> But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” <sup>9</sup> For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken, <sup>10</sup> and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” <sup>11</sup> And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him. <sup>12</sup> While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>13</sup> And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately the leprosy left him. <sup>14</sup> And he charged him to tell no one, but “go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>15</sup> But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. <sup>16</sup> But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. <sup>17</sup> On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. <sup>18</sup> And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus, <sup>19</sup> but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. <sup>20</sup> And when he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” <sup>21</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, “Why do you question in your hearts? <sup>23</sup> Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>24</sup> But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the man who was paralyzed—“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>25</sup> And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. <sup>26</sup> And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.” <sup>27</sup> After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, “Follow me.” <sup>28</sup> And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. <sup>29</sup> And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. <sup>30</sup> And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>31</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>32</sup> I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” <sup>33</sup> And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? <sup>35</sup> The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” <sup>36</sup> He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. <sup>37</sup> And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. <sup>38</sup> But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. <sup>39</sup> And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

6.title: The Sermon on the Plain
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is Luke's equivalent of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount — shorter, sharper, and structurally parallel, though not identical. Before the sermon comes the choosing of the twelve and two Sabbath controversies that frame the sermon's radical ethics with a theological question: by what authority does Jesus define what is lawful, and what kind of community does that authority create? The Sermon on the Plain (vv. 20–49) is the charter of the kingdom community — the description of what it looks like to live under the reign of God when that reign runs against every instinct of the natural self.

The beatitudes and woes (vv. 20–26) are the most direct statement in the chapter: the kingdom reverses the world's value system. The poor are blessed; the rich are warned. The hungry are filled; the full are emptied. Those who weep now will laugh; those who laugh now will mourn. This is not a promise that poverty is virtuous or that comfort is sinful; it is a statement about the direction of the kingdom. God's attention, God's blessing, God's purposes consistently run toward those whom the world has left behind — and consistently challenge those who have arranged their lives to need nothing from anyone, including God.

The ethical core of the sermon (vv. 27–45) — love your enemies, do not judge, produce good fruit — is the most demanding teaching in Luke's Gospel, and it rests entirely on the character of God. Love your enemies because your Father is kind to the ungrateful and evil. Do not judge because you will be judged by the measure you use. Bear good fruit because the tree is known by its fruit. The final image — the house on the rock — is the sermon's warning: hearing these words is not enough. The one who hears and does not do is building on sand. The storm will come, and only the house that is built on hearing and doing will stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Jesus Is Lord of the Sabbath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two Sabbath controversies open the chapter, and together they establish the claim that makes everything in the sermon possible: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath.

The first is about disciples plucking grain as they walk through fields. Plucking ears from a neighbour's standing grain was expressly permitted (Deut. 23:25), so the objection is not theft; it is that plucking counts as reaping and rubbing as threshing, both forbidden on the Sabbath by the scribal fence built around the commandment.

That fence did not begin in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people whose nation had gone into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment. And it had become unbearable — a gift turned into an audit, a day given to relieve working people now governed by case law only the leisured could master.

Jesus's response reaches back to 1 Samuel 21:1-6. David, on the run and hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which the law reserved for priests, and shared it with his men — and Scripture records it without a word of censure. The point is not that rules do not matter. It is that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. Jesus is not appealing over the head of Scripture; he is appealing to Scripture against a reading of it.

The choice of precedent is not accidental either. Of all the cases available, he reaches for the one about God's anointed king, rejected and on the run, with his own small band of followers, doing what the authorities called unlawful.

Then the conclusion: “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” He does not argue that the Sabbath is unimportant. He claims that he is the one who determines its meaning — which, given that the Sabbath is rooted in creation, enshrined in the Ten Commandments, and named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel, is a claim about who he is.

The Pharisees are not wrong to take the Sabbath seriously. They are wrong to think their authority over it exceeds the authority of the one who instituted it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” is a divine claim in Jewish ears. The Sabbath is God's own institution — rooted in creation (Gen. 2:2-3), enshrined in the Ten Commandments (Exod. 20:8-11), and described as a sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever (Exod. 31:12-17).

To be Lord of the Sabbath is to exercise authority over the covenant sign of God himself. Jesus is not relativising the day; he is claiming to be its author. This is among the most compact and most decisive of the implicit claims to deity scattered through the Synoptic Gospels.

And the title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7:13-14 — the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. It sounds modest in English and was not.

What is worth adding is what this lordship is for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest, but to give it back. The day always pointed at a person, and the person has arrived.
verseByVerse.examples:
The complaint about grain-plucking is a case study in confusing the purpose of a law with the law itself. The Sabbath was given as a gift — a day of rest for those who worked, and a sign of trust that God would provide without their constant labour.

The Pharisees' elaborate hedge of regulations (the Mishnah tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters) had turned that gift into a burden. When a law loses contact with the grace and wisdom that gave it, it becomes oppression. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he liberates it from the accretion that had buried what it was for.

The sequence is worth watching for, because it is not confined to the first century and does not require bad motives: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule — and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of the point.

The test is simple enough to apply. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, which one does the rule-keeper find himself defending?

verseByVerse.quote: On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said, 'Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said: why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?

Meaning first. Luke 6 shows the Lord of the Sabbath forming a new people and teaching them how to live. It opens with two Sabbath conflicts: hungry disciples picking grain, and a man with a withered hand healed in the synagogue, and Jesus claims that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath, with authority over God’s own law. His enemies begin to plot. He answers by spending a whole night in prayer and then choosing twelve apostles, a new Israel gathered around himself.
