Then, on a level place, he preaches the Sermon on the Plain: blessings on the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the persecuted, and woes on the rich, the full and the popular; the command to love enemies, to give without expecting return, and to be merciful as the Father is merciful; warnings against judging, against blind guides and against hypocrisy; and the tree known by its fruit. He ends with two houses, one built on rock and one without a foundation. The chapter shows who Jesus is, the Lord whose word is law, and it shows the shape of life in his kingdom: mercy received from the Father, and mercy given to everyone else.

The Sabbath controversies. Two conflicts over the Sabbath (vv. 1–11) follow the conflicts of chapter 5. The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest (Exodus 20:8–11), was one of the great marks of Jewish identity, along with circumcision and the food laws. The Pharisees had built a vast fence of rules around it, defining 39 categories of forbidden work, including reaping, threshing, winnowing and preparing food.

His disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. Hungry men walking through a field, pulling heads of grain and rubbing the husks off between their palms as they go. It is the most ordinary thing in the chapter, and it starts a fight that ends at a cross. Only Luke mentions rubbing them in their hands, to remove the husks. Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field while walking through was explicitly allowed by the law: you may pluck the ears with your hand (Deuteronomy 23:25). Israel’s law had a built-in provision for the hungry traveller, and the disciples are within it. The disciples were hungry.

Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath? The objection was not theft but the day. By the Pharisees’ rules, plucking was reaping, and rubbing was threshing and winnowing. Which sounds absurd until you understand where the reasoning came from, and it is worth being fair to them, because caricature makes the passage useless. The fourth commandment forbids work on the Sabbath and does not define work. So the rabbis, trying to obey, drew up definitions: thirty-nine categories of labour, of which reaping and threshing are two. And around those definitions they built what they called a fence: additional restrictions, so that a man would stop well short of the actual line and never break the commandment by accident. The Mishnah’s tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters. None of that began in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people who had watched their nation go into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment (Jeremiah 17:27).

A gift turned into an audit. And it had become unbearable. They had turned a day of rest and delight (Isaiah 58:13) into a burden of regulations. The day God gave to relieve working people had acquired a body of case law that only the leisured could master, and the men enforcing it were now standing in a cornfield watching hungry men eat. That is the sequence worth watching for, because it is not confined to the first century and it does not require bad motives. It requires only this: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule, and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of what the thing was for.

Is it wrong to have church rules and customs that the Bible does not command? No. Every church needs some ordered customs: a time for the service, an order of worship, a way of receiving members. Wise guidelines can protect good things, such as a family deciding to keep Sunday free of sport so that they can worship together. The error comes when a human rule is treated as God’s law, binding other people’s consciences (Mark 7:8), or when the rule is kept at the expense of the very people it was meant to serve. Ask of any rule: does Scripture command this, or did we choose it? If we chose it, hold it gladly and lightly, and never let it stand between a hungry person and bread.

In a sentence. When Jesus’ disciples picked and rubbed some grain to eat as they walked through a field on the Sabbath, Pharisees accused them of breaking the Sabbath law.

On a Tuesday. Human rules can turn God’s good gifts into burdens. Make sure the rules you live by are God’s, not just tradition’s.

When a rule meets a hungry person. The test is simple enough to apply. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, which one does the rule-keeper find himself defending? Notice which rules you are quickest to enforce on others, and ask whether they are God’s or yours.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest walked through a grainfield with his hungry friends, and let them eat. The law he had given was full of provision for the hungry traveller, because he is a God who feeds. The Pharisees saw a violation; he saw his own kindness at work. His commandments are not burdensome (1 John 5:3), and his yoke is easy: he never made a rule to keep bread from the hungry, and he gave his own body as bread for the world.
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking and rubbing counted as harvesting and threshing, work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?

Have you not read. A pointed question to experts in Scripture. Jesus answers from the Bible, and the way he introduces it has an edge: have you not read? To men whose life’s work was reading.

What David did when he was hungry. The episode is 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David, fleeing from Saul, came with a handful of men and no food to the priest Ahimelech at Nob, where the tabernacle then stood, and asked for bread. The only bread was the holy bread.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out on a golden table in the Holy Place before the Lord each Sabbath, and then eaten by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9). Only priests could lawfully eat it. The priest gave it to David. David ate it, and shared it with his men.

The argument. Scripture records without criticism that David, God’s anointed king, and his men ate the holy bread in a time of need. The narrative records it without a word of censure, and the anointed king of Israel walks away fed. The ceremonial law gave way to human need. If David could do that, then the Son of David, the greater anointed king, and his followers can do much more. And if Scripture itself shows that ceremonial rules yield to need and mercy, the Pharisees’ rules certainly must. God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 12:7).

What Jesus is arguing. Not that rules do not matter, and not that hunger dissolves the law. Something more precise: that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and that the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. He is not appealing over the head of Scripture. He is appealing to Scripture, against a reading of it.

Why David? There is a further thing in the choice of story, and the men listening would have felt it. Of all the possible precedents he reaches for the one about God’s anointed king, on the run, rejected, with his own small band of followers, doing something the authorities would call unlawful. The parallel is not accidental and it is not subtle. Here is another anointed king, gathering another company, being told by the officials of the day that what he does is not lawful. If David’s men could eat, so can his. Which means the argument is not chiefly about corn at all. It is about who this is, and the next verse says so out loud.

Does this mean I may break God’s commands when I am in need? No. The holy bread was a ceremonial law, about the use of sacred objects, and it was always meant to serve life. God’s moral law, do not steal, do not lie, do not commit adultery, is never set aside for convenience or need; David did wrong when he lied to the priest in this same chapter (1 Samuel 21:2). The lesson is not that hunger excuses sin, but that God’s law is kind, and that its outward ceremonies were never meant to be used against the hungry and the suffering.

In a sentence. Jesus answered from Scripture that David and his men, when hungry, ate the holy bread that only priests could lawfully eat.

On a Tuesday. God’s law is for human good. Use it to show mercy, not to load burdens on others.

For worship. The Son of David came to his own people with his small band of followers, rejected by the officials as David had been by Saul. And he is greater than David: David ate the bread of the Presence, but Jesus is the bread of life, the true Presence of God among his people. The loaves on the golden table were a picture of God’s fellowship with the twelve tribes; now the Lord of that table walks through the fields with his twelve, and feeds them. Blessed be the King who keeps open house.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.

The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. An enormous claim, nine words in English, among the largest Jesus ever made. Consider what the Sabbath was. Not a custom, not a national tradition, not a piece of religious furniture that could be rearranged. God instituted it at creation: he rested on the seventh day and made it holy (Genesis 2:2–3). It stands in the Ten Commandments, spoken by God from the mountain in fire and thunder (Exodus 20:8–11). And it is named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever (Exodus 31:17). There is no institution in Judaism more directly and personally God’s than this one. And a Galilean carpenter says he is its lord.

No soft reading. To be lord of the Sabbath is to have authority over God’s own law, to determine its meaning and use. Only God could claim that. He does not say the Sabbath is unimportant. He does not say his disciples were within the rabbinic rules after all. He says that the authority to determine what this day is and how it works belongs to him, which is to say that he stands where the Lawgiver stands. A man may say the Sabbath has been misunderstood. Only its author can say he is its lord. Jesus is not breaking the Sabbath; he is its Lord, who gives its true interpretation. Mark adds: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

The Son of Man. The title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7 again: the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14). It sounds humble in English; it was not. So the confrontation that began over a handful of grain has arrived, in five verses, at the question the whole Gospel is about. Not, what may be done on the Sabbath? But, who is this? Every dispute in Luke ends there eventually, and the Pharisees are quite right to be alarmed. Somebody in that cornfield is either speaking blasphemy or telling the truth, and there is no third possibility on offer.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that Christians must keep Saturday. Many Reformed and Puritan Christians (following the Westminster Confession 21.7–8) hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday, the “Christian Sabbath”, to be kept by resting from work and recreation and devoting the day to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath was a sign of the old covenant fulfilled in Christ. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest it pointed to (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10); Christians are not bound to its ceremonial regulations (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5). Yet the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of resurrection, is the church’s day of gathering for worship (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). It is a privilege and a gift, not a burden, and the principle of a regular day of rest and worship remains wise and good. This is held charitably toward those who keep a stricter Sabbath.

Lord in order to give rest. What is worth adding is what this lordship turns out to be for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest. He is its lord in order to give it back, and elsewhere he says what he means: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The day always pointed at a person. The person has arrived, and he is not standing in the cornfield to take anything away.

So how should I spend Sunday? Begin with gathering: the Lord’s Day is first of all the day his people meet to hear his word, pray, sing and share the Lord’s Supper, and that should be the fixed point around which the day is arranged. Then rest: make room for what refreshes body and soul, family, a walk, a meal with others, visiting the lonely, reading. Christians who hold the stricter Sabbath view will set aside work and ordinary recreation for the whole day, and they are to be respected for it; others will use more freedom. Whichever conviction you hold, do not judge the brother who differs (Romans 14:5–6), and do not let the day become either a burden or just another day.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath, with authority over God’s own law.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, and he gives true rest. Use the Lord’s Day as a gift: rest in him, and worship with his people.

For worship. The one who rested on the seventh day after making the world stood in a Galilean field and called himself its Lord. He made the Sabbath, he kept it perfectly, and he fulfilled it, resting in the tomb on the seventh day and rising on the first, so that his people could enter the rest that remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9). We do not work towards our rest; we begin from it, because he has finished the work. Lord of the Sabbath, Lord of the law, Lord of all: the rest we were made for has a name, and it is his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Man with a Withered Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second Sabbath controversy involves a man with a withered right hand — which, in a manual economy, meant an inability to earn a living. Luke the physician notes which hand.

The scribes and Pharisees are watching to see whether Jesus will heal, “so that they might find a reason to accuse him.” The watching is calculated and hostile, and it is worth registering how ugly it is: they are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. His hand interests them only as evidence.

Jesus knows exactly what they are doing, and he does not avoid the confrontation — he creates it. He tells the man to stand up in the middle, where everyone can see, and puts a question to the room: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?”

That question is the interpretive key to his whole Sabbath theology, and it is why they cannot answer. They came prepared to argue that healing is work and that a hand withered for years can wait until sundown — a reasonable position on their own terms. Jesus refuses the terms. He removes the neutral square marked “wait until tomorrow”: to be able to relieve suffering and to decline is not inaction but a choice, and it belongs in the other column.

The Sabbath is not a day of inaction. It is a day defined by the character of its author — and the God who rested on the seventh day is the God who sustains life on every day. Their silence answers the question for them.

Then he heals without touching. The man is simply told to stretch out the hand he cannot stretch out, and the strength arrives inside the obedience. There is nothing to accuse.

And the response is fury — the first time in Luke that the religious leaders plot against him. It has taken six chapters, and the cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The hardness that sets in at this point — “they were filled with fury” — begins the trajectory that ends at the cross. The fury is not primarily moral; it is theological. Jesus has publicly claimed authority over the Sabbath, healed in defiance of their interpretation, and refused to be intimidated by their watching.

Every confrontation confirms what they most fear: this man is either a blasphemer or he is what he claims to be. They have decided he is a blasphemer, and from that decision every subsequent action follows with a terrible logic.

Their fury is a rage that has stopped thinking. It is what a framework does when it has been exposed in public and its owners are unwilling to revise it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were.

So these Sabbath controversies are not peripheral disputes about religious practice. They are the opening moves of the confrontation that will define history.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man with the withered hand is told to stand up and come out into the middle — to be visible, exposed, in front of everyone. He obeys, knowing his disability will be on display, and Luke records that he rose and stood there.

There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately. The person who keeps their need hidden, who manages a difficulty from the edge of the community, does not receive what the one standing in the middle receives. Jesus consistently calls his healings into the light.

And the command he gives is the one thing the man cannot do — stretching out that hand is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first so that obedience becomes possible. He is told to do the impossible thing, and discovers in the doing that it is possible.

That is very often the order in the Christian life. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience — which is why so much of following Christ feels like being told to move a hand that does not work.

verseByVerse.quote: On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, 'Come and stand here.' And he rose and stood there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On another Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. The scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand: come and stand here. And he rose and stood there.

On another Sabbath. A different day, a different setting, the same question, and this time the stakes are a man’s livelihood.

A man was there whose right hand was withered. Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand: the working hand. In a manual economy that is not an inconvenience; it is the end of a man’s ability to earn. Without it, a labourer could not earn a living. Withered means shrunken, paralysed. He is in the synagogue on the Sabbath, as he presumably is every week, with a hand that has not worked for years and no expectation that today will differ.

The scribes and the Pharisees watched him. Watched (paretērounto) means watched closely, spied on. They were there not to worship but to catch him out, and Luke tells us exactly why: so that they might find a reason to accuse him. Sit with that for a moment, because it is uglier than it first appears. They are in a house of God, on the day of God, and they are hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. The man’s hand is of no interest to them except as evidence. They are not asking whether healing is right; they have already decided, and they are waiting for their case to walk in. That is what religion becomes when it has stopped serving God and started defending itself. It can sit in a service, look at a suffering man, and see an opportunity.

To see whether he would heal on the Sabbath. By the rabbis’ rule, healing counted as work, and was allowed on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. A withered hand could wait until tomorrow.

But he knew their thoughts. As in 5:22. Luke says it flatly. Jesus is not walking into this unaware, and what he does next is therefore entirely deliberate.

Come and stand here. Literally, stand in the middle. Jesus does not avoid the confrontation. He makes the healing public, in full view of his critics. He could have healed the man where he sat, quietly, at the end of the service, and nobody could have proved anything. Instead he puts him in the centre of the room, in front of everyone, and makes the confrontation unavoidable.

And he rose and stood there. And the man goes. He has spent years managing a disability from the edge of the room, and he is now standing in the middle of it with his hand exposed and a row of officials staring. He does not know what is coming. He knows he has been called out. There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately. Some things have to be brought into the middle, in front of people, before anything can be done about them.

Should I deliberately provoke people who oppose me? No. Jesus did not seek conflict for its own sake; he sought the man’s good and the truth, and refused to let fear of critics hide either. Christians are to live peaceably with all, as far as it depends on them (Romans 12:18), and to answer opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). What this verse forbids is the opposite fault: doing good only when no critic is watching, or abandoning what is right because someone is waiting to accuse you. Be quiet where quietness serves; be open where hiding would mean failing someone.

In a sentence. In the synagogue on another Sabbath, with scribes and Pharisees watching to accuse him, Jesus, knowing their thoughts, called a man with a withered right hand to stand in front of everyone.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let fear of critics stop you doing good openly.

For worship. He saw the man at the edge of the room whom everyone else had stopped noticing, and the men in the front row who were watching only to accuse, and he knew the thoughts of both. He called the forgotten man into the middle, where mercy could be seen. That is what he does with us: he brings our withered places out of hiding, not to shame us but to heal us. No critic’s stare could stop him doing good, and no hiding place can keep us from his kindness.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand. By the rabbis’ rule, healing a condition that was not life-threatening should wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?' And after looking around at them all he said to him, 'Stretch out your hand.' And he did so, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it? After looking around at them all he said to him: stretch out your hand. And he did so, and his hand was restored.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm. The question is deadly, and it is worth seeing why they cannot answer it. They came prepared for a different argument. Their case was that healing is work, that this man’s condition is not life-threatening, and that a hand withered for years can perfectly well wait until sundown, which, on their own terms, is a reasonable position. Even their own tradition permitted saving a life on the Sabbath. Nobody’s life is at risk here. Jesus refuses the terms. He reframes the question: not, is healing work?, but, what is the Sabbath for? He asks whether it is lawful to do good, and by pairing it with its opposite he removes the middle ground they were standing on. There is no neutral square marked, wait until tomorrow. To fail to do good when you can is to do harm. There is no neutral option.

To save life or to destroy it? Life (psychē) can also mean soul. And the irony: Jesus is doing good on the Sabbath, while his critics are plotting to destroy him on the Sabbath (v. 11).

Stricter, not laxer. That is the principle behind the whole of his Sabbath teaching, and it is not lax. It is stricter than theirs. Their rule asked what may be avoided. His asks what may be done, and a day designed by a God who never stops sustaining his creation cannot be a day for withholding mercy.

And after looking around at them all. A long, searching look. Mark says with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). Luke pauses the scene. He waits. The look goes round the room, one face at a time, and nobody says anything, and in that silence they have already answered, and they know it.

Stretch out your hand. The very thing he could not do. Notice that he does not touch him. Jesus did no work that could be charged: no touch, no medicine. Just a word. A man is told to move, and moves, and even the strictest reckoning could not call that work by anybody. And notice what is asked. Stretch out your hand is the one thing this man cannot do; it is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first, so that he could then obey. He is told to do the impossible thing, and in the doing of it he discovers it is possible. The command brings the power to obey.

And his hand was restored. Made whole, as it had been.

The order of obedience. That is very often the order. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience, which is why so much of the Christian life feels like being told to move a hand that does not work. Forgive, he says, to a heart that cannot; love your enemy, to a will that refuses; and the one who commands is the one who gives (Philippians 2:12–13).

But I cannot obey. What do I do with a command I have no strength to keep? Do what the man did: try, in dependence on Christ. Do not wait until you feel able; you may never feel able. Ask him for help, and then take the first small step he commands: the first sentence of the apology, the first prayer for your enemy, the first refusal of the old habit. God works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13), and very often his strength is felt only in the moving. If you fail, confess it, receive his forgiveness, and stretch out your hand again tomorrow.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or harm, to save life or destroy it, and then told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored.

On a Tuesday. Failing to do good when you can is not neutral. Look for the good you can do today.

For worship. The God who never stops sustaining his creation, even on the day he rested, stood in a synagogue and did good on the Sabbath. With a single word he restored a hand that had hung useless for years, and he did it in the face of men who were already planning to destroy him. He saves life; they sought to destroy it; and in the end he gave his own life to save theirs and ours. His commands are never empty, because his word carries his power: what he tells us to do, he gives us strength to do.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.

But they were filled with fury. Fury (anoias) is literally mindlessness, a senseless rage, unreason, a rage that has stopped thinking. And it is the response to a man’s hand being made whole. Not joy that a man was healed, but anger that their rules had been broken. Nothing has been stolen. No law of Moses has been broken; Jesus was careful about that, and did not so much as touch him. A disabled man in their own congregation can work again. And the reaction of the religious leadership is not merely disagreement but the beginning of a plot. Their religion had made them blind to mercy.

And discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. The plotting begins. Mark says they began to plot with the Herodians how to destroy him (Mark 3:6). Luke’s wording is milder at this stage, but the direction is clear. This is the first time in Luke’s Gospel that the religious leaders plot against Jesus, and it should be registered as the turning point it is. From here the shadow does not lift. It has taken six chapters, and the cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.

Why such rage? Not because they were unusually wicked men. Because he had made their position untenable in public, and they were not willing to revise it. Fury is what a framework does when it has been exposed and its owners have decided to keep it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were. So the mind goes past the argument to the arguer. If the position cannot be defended, remove the man who exposed it.

An ordinary mechanism. It is worth being honest about how ordinary that is. It does not require a council. It happens in churches, in families, in any relationship where somebody has said something true that cannot be answered, and the response is not to weigh it but to look for a way of discrediting the person who said it. The fury feels like conviction from the inside. It is nearly always the sound of a defence that has run out. These men went home from a service in which God had healed a crippled hand in front of them, and began working out how to get rid of him.

How do I know whether my anger is righteous? Righteous anger is anger at what grieves God, for the sake of others, and it stays under control and seeks good. Jesus was angry in this very scene (Mark 3:5), grieved at hardness of heart, and he healed the man. Sinful anger is usually about me: my position, my pride, my being shown up, and it seeks to hurt. Ask: what exactly am I angry about? Would God be angry at it? Does my anger make me want to help someone, or to win? Be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26); and if you find you are furious with someone who has told you the truth, stop and listen before you speak.

In a sentence. The scribes and Pharisees were filled with senseless rage and discussed what they could do to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Religion without love can make people furious at the very goodness of God. Examine your reactions when God blesses people in ways you don’t expect.

For worship. They planned his destruction on the day he restored a man’s hand, and he knew it, and he went on doing good. The rage of men could not turn him aside, and their plot, when it ripened, became the means of our salvation. The wrath of man shall praise him (Psalm 76:10). What they meant for evil, God meant for good, and the hands they would nail to a cross are the hands that still restore the withered and the broken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before choosing the twelve, Jesus spends the whole night in prayer on the mountain. This is characteristic of Luke: the major decisions of the ministry are set in the context of prayer. And the placing is deliberate — Luke has just recorded the first plot against Jesus, and the next thing he records is a night on a hillside.

The choice of twelve from a larger body of disciples is not made lightly or impulsively. Luke gives the two stages precisely: he called the disciples, and from them he chose twelve.

The number is not convenient; it is theological. Israel had twelve tribes named for twelve sons, and no Jew could hear the number accidentally. Jesus is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people — and at the end of the Bible the wall of the city has twelve foundations bearing these men's names (Rev. 21:14).

They are called apostles here for the first time in Luke — apostoloi, sent ones. They remain disciples, learners; but a disciple who has been given an errand is something more.

The list itself is a study in unlikely combinations. Peter, who a chapter ago asked Jesus to leave because he was a sinful man. Matthew, the tax collector from the booth. And Simon the Zealot — a man whose title points to zeal for Israel and the law, and very possibly to sympathy with armed resistance to Rome. In ordinary life Matthew and Simon would not have shared a road. They shared a purse and a mission for three years.

Several of the twelve are almost unknown — James the son of Alphaeus above all, of whom the Gospels record no words and no deeds, nothing but a name in the lists.

And the list ends with Judas Iscariot, “who became a traitor.” Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached, and the wording matters: not who was a traitor but who became one. He was chosen after the night of prayer, with the others, and heard and saw everything they did.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apostles are distinguished from disciples by a specific function: they are sent ones, commissioned witnesses rather than merely learners. Their testimony to the life, death and resurrection of Jesus will be the foundation of the church's proclamation.

Paul will later say the church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20). The night of prayer before the choice establishes that this foundation is not a human selection but a divinely guided one, even though the divine guidance works through a human process.

Luke's parenthesis on Judas — chosen deliberately, after a night of communion with the Father, and yet becoming a traitor — is a weight the reader is not permitted to set down. Election to office is not the same as salvation, and proximity to Christ is no protection.

He handled the money, was sent out with power like the rest, and heard every word of the sermon that follows. The verb Luke chooses describes a process, not a category — which should sober anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time.
verseByVerse.examples:
The night of prayer before the choice models the principle that consequential decisions belong to God before they belong to us. Not every decision requires a night of prayer — but every decision that will shape the community of God's people belongs first to the Father.

The Jesus who spent a whole night praying before choosing twelve men puts a question to every leader, every elder board, every appointment committee: have we prayed as long and as seriously as this decision actually deserves?

And the composition of the twelve is a standing rebuke to congregations divided along political lines. Whatever holds a church together, it is not agreement about Rome, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be.

If a former agent of the Roman revenue and a man called the Zealot could eat from the same bag for three years, the divisions that currently make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

verseByVerse.quote: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles:
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. When day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles.

He went out to the mountain to pray. Luke has just recorded the first plot against him. The next thing he records is a night on a hillside. Only Luke records this night of prayer. At a time of growing opposition (v. 11), and before a crucial decision, Jesus prays.

And all night he continued in prayer to God. The whole night, from dark to first light, alone. This is not a phrase to skim. Luke has shown us Jesus praying at the Jordan (3:21) and withdrawing to desolate places (5:16). This is the longest, and it comes before the largest decision of his ministry so far. The only time the Gospels record this before Gethsemane. The choice of the Twelve was so important that Jesus spent the night seeking his Father’s will. It is worth asking what the Son of God was doing out there for eight or nine hours, and the honest answer is that we are not told, and it is better not to invent. What Luke gives us is the fact and the proportion: a whole night, for twelve men. Even Judas was chosen after a night of prayer (John 6:70).

He called his disciples and chose from them twelve. Two stages, and the wording matters. He called the disciples, a larger group of followers (Luke will mention seventy-two of them later, 10:1), and from them he chose twelve, an inner circle. This is selection, and it is his, and it comes out of the night. Twelve is not a convenient number. Israel had twelve tribes, named for twelve sons; a Jew could not hear it accidentally. Jesus is reconstituting the people of God around himself. He is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people, and a man does not lay the foundations of Israel unless he is entitled to. The Twelve will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (22:30), and at the end of the Bible, the wall of the city has twelve foundations, and on them the names of these men (Revelation 21:14).

Whom he named apostles. Apostle (apostolos) means one who is sent, an envoy, an authorised representative, from the verb to send. A disciple is a learner, and they remain that. An apostle has been given an errand. They would be sent with his authority to preach (9:1–2), and after his resurrection, to be his witnesses to the world (24:48; Acts 1:8). Luke uses the title more than the other Gospels.

The apostles’ unique role. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21–22), commissioned directly by him, and laid the foundation of the church through their teaching, which we have in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). There are no apostles in this sense today. Their teaching, in Scripture, is our foundation.

Two decisions. There is something quietly steadying in the sequence. The men who now decide he must be destroyed have made their decision in discussion, in fury, after a service. His decision was made alone, on a mountain, after a night of asking his Father, and it is the one that is still standing.

If Jesus prayed all night and still chose Judas, did his prayer fail? No. Jesus chose Judas knowingly: did I not choose you, the Twelve? And yet one of you is a devil (John 6:70). Prayer is not a way of getting a guarantee that everything will go smoothly; it is submitting our choices to the Father’s will, and the Father’s will included the betrayal, through which the Scriptures would be fulfilled and the world redeemed (Acts 2:23). So when you pray before a decision and it later brings pain, do not conclude that you missed God’s guidance. He may have led you exactly where he meant to, for purposes you cannot yet see.

In a sentence. After spending the whole night in prayer on a mountain, Jesus chose twelve of his disciples and named them apostles.

On a Tuesday. Pray before big decisions. If Jesus spent all night in prayer before choosing, how much more do you need to?

For worship. The Son of God climbed a mountain and spent a whole night with his Father before he named the men who would carry his gospel to the world. Every name was chosen in prayer, and every name was known. And the one who prayed over the Twelve prays still over all his people: I am praying for them, he said on the last night, for those whom you have given me, for they are yours (John 17:9). Before you ever chose him, he chose you, and he did it with his Father, in love.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

Four lists. The Twelve are listed four times in the New Testament (Matthew 10:2–4; Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). The order varies, but Peter is always first and Judas Iscariot always last. They fall into three groups of four, each headed by the same name (Peter, Philip, James son of Alphaeus). Luke sets the names down without comment. But look at who is in the list.

Simon, whom he named Peter. Peter (Petros, Aramaic Kēphas) means rock. Not what he was, but what he would become (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42). A fisherman who a chapter ago asked Jesus to go away because he was a sinful man, given a new name that he will spectacularly fail to live up to before he grows into it.

Andrew his brother. Who first brought Peter to Jesus (John 1:40–42).

James and John. Sons of Zebedee, fishermen (5:10). James was the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2); John wrote the Gospel, letters and Revelation.

Philip, and Bartholomew. Philip was from Bethsaida (John 1:44). Bartholomew (son of Tolmai) is probably the Nathanael of John 1:45–51, since he is paired with Philip.

Matthew. The tax collector Levi (5:27), from the booth in chapter 5. A man who took money from his own people on behalf of the ruling power.

Thomas. The twin (John 11:16), remembered for his doubt and his great confession: my Lord and my God! (John 20:28).

James the son of Alphaeus. Possibly James the younger (Mark 15:40). Of him the Gospels record no words and no deeds, nothing but a name in the lists. Several of the Twelve are almost unknown. They gave their lives to this, and history kept only that they were chosen.

Simon who was called the Zealot. Zealot may mean zealous for the law, or a member of the nationalist movement that wanted to overthrow Rome by force. If so, he and Matthew, the tax collector who worked for Rome’s client, were political enemies, now united in Christ. Whatever precise stage the movement had reached by this date, the label meant a man of fierce conviction.

Enemies at one table. So in one company of twelve, Jesus may have put a former agent of the revenue and a man who believed such agents were traitors. In ordinary life these two would not have shared a road, let alone a purse and a mission. They walked the same country together for three years. That is worth pausing on, because it is not resolved in the text and Luke does not tell us it was easy. He simply records that both names are there. Whatever holds a church together, it is not political agreement, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be. If Matthew and Simon could eat from the same bag, the divisions that make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

Judas the son of James. Probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark; the same man with two names. Also called Judas (not Iscariot) in John 14:22.

And Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. And then the last name, with Luke’s terrible parenthesis. Became: he was not chosen as a traitor, but became one. He is in the list. He was chosen after the night of prayer, with the same privileges as the others. He heard everything they heard, saw everything they saw, was sent out with power like the rest, and handled the money (John 12:6). Yet he betrayed his Lord. Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached. He does not say who was a traitor. He says who became one, which is a sentence about a process, and it should frighten anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time. A sobering warning that outward closeness to Jesus is no guarantee of a true heart.

Could I become a Judas? Can a true Christian fall away? A true believer cannot finally be lost; those whom Christ has given eternal life will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28–29). Judas was never a true believer, though he looked like one; Jesus says he was a devil from the start (John 6:70) and that he was lost so that Scripture might be fulfilled (John 17:12). So the warning is not meant to terrify true believers but to wake up false ones. If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is itself a good sign: Judas did not fear it. Examine yourself (2 Corinthians 13:5), and run to Christ; no one who comes to him is cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. The twelve apostles were Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

On a Tuesday. Jesus chose ordinary, very different, flawed men: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot. He can use you. And he unites people who would otherwise be enemies.

For worship. Look at the list and marvel at the Lord who chose it. A man who would deny him, two brothers who wanted to call down fire, a doubter, a tax collector, a zealot, and several men we know nothing about, and he made them the foundation stones of his church. He chose the weak to shame the strong, the unknown to carry his name to the ends of the earth. And he has not changed his method. Your name, if you are his, is written in a book far older than these lists (Revelation 21:27), by the same hand, in the same love.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s “Judas the son of James” is probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sermon on the Plain begins with a declaration that sounds like a mistake on first reading: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”

Luke's beatitudes are addressed directly to the disciples — “blessed are you” — unlike Matthew's more generalised forms. And they are paired with woes Matthew does not include. The poor are blessed and the rich are warned; the hungry are promised satisfaction and the full are warned of hunger; those who weep now will laugh, and those who laugh now will mourn.

The poverty is not romanticised. Luke does not say “poor in spirit” but simply “poor” — the destitute, those with nothing of their own who depend entirely on what others give. This is not a spiritualisation of poverty; it is the announcement that the kingdom belongs to those whose condition leaves no room for self-sufficiency. Not because poverty is virtuous, but because the poor have no resources to trust except God.

Set beside Matthew's “poor in spirit,” the two hold opposite ends of one truth, and neither is safe alone. Luke without Matthew makes an empty purse a ticket. Matthew without Luke lets “poor in spirit” be quietly spiritualised until it costs nothing. Matthew names the poverty God blesses; Luke names the room such people are usually standing in.

The woes are the other edge of the same blade. “Woe” (ouai) is the prophets' word, carrying grief as much as warning (Isa. 5:8-23; Amos 6:1-7). It is not a wish for harm but a declaration that those who have “received their consolation” have been paid already and have nothing further outstanding.

The last woe is the most searching: “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.” Israel's true prophets were consistently unwelcome; the popular ones were the ones who told the king what he wanted to hear.

And the final beatitude (vv. 22-23) is the only one about something the disciples bring on themselves. Four escalating forms of social death — hated, excluded, reviled, name thrown out as evil — and the command attached is not endurance but leaping.
verseByVerse.theology:
The beatitudes and woes together express the eschatological reversal — the biblical pattern in which the last days invert the present order. Mary sang it in the Magnificat: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted, the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty.

This is not a programme of economic analysis; it is a prophetic announcement about the direction of God's kingdom. Those whose present condition drives them to dependence on God are in the right position to receive what the kingdom gives; those who can be self-sufficient are in the wrong one.

Read through the whole gospel, these blessings and woes are far more than social reversal — they are anchored in Christ himself, who entered the very conditions he calls blessed. He became poor though he was rich (2 Cor. 8:9), hungered in the wilderness (4:2), wept real tears, and was hated, excluded and reviled for us.

The great reversal is therefore no abstract law of history but a sure thing purchased in him. We are not blessed for managing to be poor or hungry, but by being joined to the One who was made poor that we might be made rich, and who fills the empty out of his own fullness. And the woes are not cruelty but mercy raising its voice — a warning to the comfortable to loosen their grip on thin, passing riches before the day the tables turn.
verseByVerse.examples:
The beatitudes are often preached as comfort to those who suffer, and they are that. But they are also diagnosis and invitation. The question they put to every hearer is: in which column do you find yourself? The sermon does not allow a neutral answer; it creates a crisis of self-knowledge.

And the woes have to be applied honestly, because almost everyone reading them is, by any measure the world has ever used, among the rich. The question is not whether you enjoy good things but where your consolation actually comes from — what steadies you when the day has gone badly. A God who cannot be lost, or an arrangement that can?

“Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy” (v. 23) is the response Jesus commands to persecution — not stoic endurance, not grim determination, but leaping joy. The verb is the one used of the unborn John moving in Elizabeth's womb (1:41).

This is eschatological joy: the joy that knows how the story ends and can afford to leap because the future is secure. It is what Paul means in Romans 8:18 — the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed. The leap is only possible if the landing is sure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. Those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.

The Sermon on the Plain. What follows (vv. 20–49) is Luke’s version of Jesus’ great sermon, shorter than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), with much of the same material. Matthew’s is given on a mountain; Luke’s on a level place. Either they are two occasions (Jesus surely preached similar sermons many times), or Luke’s level place was a plateau on the mountain. Luke omits material about the Jewish law, which would interest his Gentile readers less, and adds the woes.

One sermon or two? Luke says Jesus came down and stood on a level place; Matthew says he went up on the mountain and sat down (Matthew 5:1). What follows in each has obvious overlap, beatitudes, love of enemies, judge not, the tree and its fruit, the two builders at the end, and equally obvious differences. Matthew runs to three chapters where Luke runs to thirty verses; Luke adds four woes Matthew does not have; Matthew includes long stretches on the law, prayer and fasting that Luke places elsewhere. Both answers have been held by careful readers, and neither damages anything. Some take them as the same occasion from different angles: the phrase Luke uses need not mean flat ground at the foot of a hill; it can as easily mean a plateau or a shelf on the hillside. Others take them as two occasions, which is simply what travelling preachers do. Jesus spent perhaps three years saying these things village by village, and no teacher says a thing once. Either way the words are his, and the differences are not contradictions but the ordinary shape of a real ministry. The same voice is speaking in both, and it is asking for the same life.

And he came down with them. Jesus comes down from the mountain with the newly chosen Twelve, like Moses coming down from the mountain with the law. But Jesus brings the law of the kingdom.

From all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon. The crowd is enormous, and it is deliberately described. Jews from the south, the religious heartland, and people from the Gentile coastal cities of the north, pagan cities on the Phoenician coast, the country Elijah was sent to (4:26). Luke’s map is already the map of Acts: a foretaste of the gospel to all nations.

Who came to hear him and to be healed. Again, hearing first. And both happen.

For power came out from him and healed them all. The power of God (5:17), flowing from him (8:46). The word is dynamis, and the phrase is striking: something goes out of him. Healing is not a technique he applies. And so the sermon that follows is not addressed to a neutral audience. Every person in earshot has just seen the demonised freed and the sick made well, and many have felt it in their own bodies. When he says, blessed are you who are poor, he is saying it to people who have already had evidence.

Is the Sermon on the Plain a way to be saved, or a way to live? A way to live, for those who are being saved. It is addressed to disciples (v. 20), people who have already come to him, and it begins not with commands but with blessings: the kingdom is given before anything is asked. Its demands are real and searching, and no one keeps them perfectly; they show us how far we fall short and drive us to Christ, who kept them for us. But they are also the actual shape of the new life he gives. We do not obey this sermon in order to be accepted; we obey it because we have been, and because the one who preached it lives in us by his Spirit.

In a sentence. Jesus came down with the Twelve to a level place, where crowds from Judea, Jerusalem and the Gentile coast came to hear him and be healed, and power went out from him and healed them all.

On a Tuesday. Come to Jesus to hear him, as well as to receive from him.

For worship. Before he said a word of the sermon, he healed them all. Jews and Gentiles, the city crowd and the coastal pagans, every one of them who touched him went away whole. That is the order of the kingdom: grace first, then the call. The one who would ask them to love their enemies had just poured out his power on people who would one day shout for his death. He came down from the mountain to the level place, to stand where we stand, and the power that came out of him then is the same power that has reached us now.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities to the north. Luke’s sermon is given on a “level place”; Matthew’s similar sermon on a mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.

And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples. The sermon is addressed to disciples, though the crowd hears it. It describes the life of those who follow him.

The Beatitudes. Luke gives four blessings (vv. 20–23) and four matching woes (vv. 24–26). Matthew gives nine blessings and no woes (Matthew 5:3–12). Luke’s are in the second person (you), direct and personal; Matthew’s in the third (those who). Not blessed are the poor but blessed are you, spoken while looking at them, to actual people whose actual circumstances everyone standing there could see.

Blessed. Makarioi: not happy in a shallow sense, but fortunate, in a good position before God, approved by him. The Hebrew equivalent opens the Psalms: blessed is the man (Psalm 1:1). It is God’s verdict, not a feeling.

Are you who are poor. Luke’s word is ptōchoi, which is not the word for someone of modest means. It means destitute: a beggar, a person with nothing of their own who depends entirely on what others give. Matthew says poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3). Luke speaks of the poor as they actually were. Many of Jesus’ disciples were literally poor, having left everything (5:11, 28). But in the Old Testament, the poor were also the humble, who had no one to depend on but God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2). Poverty is not itself a virtue, and not every poor person is blessed. But the poor are often more ready to receive the kingdom, because they know their need. The two readings come together: the blessed poor are those who come to God empty-handed.

Luke and Matthew together. A reader who knows Matthew will stop here, because Matthew’s blessed are the poor in spirit and Luke’s flat blessed are you who are poor sound like different sentences. Did one of them adjust the Lord’s words? Better to see that they hold two ends of one truth, and that neither end is safe alone. Take Luke without Matthew and you get the error that poverty itself saves, as though an empty purse were a ticket. That would make the gospel a matter of income, and would leave a poor man who trusts in nothing but his own grievance exactly where he was. Take Matthew without Luke and you get the opposite and far more respectable error: poor in spirit quietly spiritualised until it costs nothing, a humble feeling entertained by comfortable people whose actual lives stay precisely as they were. Put them together and it stands clear. Matthew names the poverty God blesses: the poverty of a man who knows he has nothing to bring. Luke names where such people are usually found, and it is not where the world looks. It is far easier to know you have nothing when you actually have nothing. Not because God prefers the poor as people, but because money is extraordinarily good at hiding from us the emptiness we all have before him. Matthew names the empty hands; Luke names the room they are usually standing in.

For yours is the kingdom of God. Present tense: it is yours now. Not a promise for later. They have no earthly security, but they have God’s kingdom, the greatest wealth of all (12:32). Heaven keeps a different ledger from the one the world keeps. This fulfils Jesus’ mission: to proclaim good news to the poor (4:18).

I am not poor. Is this beatitude for me? Yes, if you come the way the poor come. Before God every one of us is destitute: we have nothing to offer him that is not already his, and no righteousness of our own (Isaiah 64:6). The comfortable Christian must learn by grace what the poor man often knows by experience: that he lives entirely on what God gives. So hold your possessions as a steward, not an owner; receive salvation as a beggar, not a customer; and let your money flow towards the poor, so that it does not wall you off from them or from God. The kingdom is given to empty hands, whatever is in the bank.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that they who are poor are blessed, because the kingdom of God belongs to them.

On a Tuesday. Come to God as one who is poor, with nothing to offer. The kingdom belongs to such people.

Where it applies: An elderly widow in your church lives on very little, and trusts Christ. Do not pity her as one who has missed out. She is rich in the kingdom, and you may learn more from her than she from you.

Where it would be wrong: Someone thinks poverty in itself makes a person right with God, or uses this verse as a reason not to help the poor, since they are blessed already. The poor Jesus blesses are those who look to God (Matthew 5:3), and the same Lord commands us to open our hands to them (1 John 3:17).

For worship. He looked at a crowd of day labourers and widows and beggars and said, yours is the kingdom. And he could say it because he had made himself poor: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The King of heaven was born in a borrowed stable and buried in a borrowed grave, so that the destitute could inherit everything. Blessed be the Lord who fills empty hands with a kingdom.

parallels.desc: has not God chosen those who are poor?

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.

Blessed are you who are hungry now. Two more blessings, and both are stated in the plainest possible terms with a now attached. Now is important, and only Luke has it. Present hunger, future satisfaction. Luke means it as flatly as it sounds: people who did not eat enough yesterday. Real hunger, physical (the poor often went hungry), but also hunger for God and righteousness (Matthew 5:6). Mary sang: he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53). The kingdom does not romanticise an empty stomach. Hunger is not a virtue, and Jesus never says it is. What he says is that the condition which the world reads as God’s absence is, in his accounting, the condition of people who are about to be filled.

For you shall be satisfied. Future tense. At the messianic banquet (13:29; 14:15; Isaiah 25:6), and in a measure even now. Satisfied completely: the word is used of animals fed full. And the filling is not a metaphor. There is a table at the end of this book, and the guest list was drawn up from the streets and lanes (14:21).

Blessed are you who weep now. Those who grieve over suffering, over their own sin, and over the world’s rebellion against God. Those who mourn (Matthew 5:4). Notice that he does not tell them to stop. There is no instruction here to cheer up, no suggestion that the tears are a failure of faith, no advice about perspective. He lets the weeping stand and puts a date on it.

For you shall laugh. Joy will come. God will wipe away every tear (Isaiah 25:8; Revelation 21:4). And the promised end of it is not relief, or peace, or resignation. It is laughter, which is a startling word to use of the far side of grief, and he chose it. The psalmist had reached for the same thing: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy (Psalm 126:5). Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (Psalm 30:5). Not a quiet settling. Shouting.

The pattern. The present is not the whole story. The kingdom reverses present conditions. Those who suffer now with Christ will rejoice with him later. This is the logic of the cross and resurrection. Both blessings turn on that little word now, and it is the hinge of the whole sermon. The hunger is now. The weeping is now. Neither is denied, minimised or explained. What is denied is that now is the last word about them.

Who is speaking. This is not a technique for feeling better, and it will not work as one. It is a claim about how the story ends, made by the only person entitled to make it. The one who promises to fill the hungry had gone forty days without food in a desert (4:2). The one who promises laughter to the weeping wept himself at a friend’s grave (John 11:35) and over Jerusalem (19:41). He is not calling out advice from the dry ground. He has been in the water.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve? No. Jesus blesses those who weep; he does not rebuke them. Christians grieve, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love continuing after loss, and the psalms are full of honest lament. You do not have to pretend to be fine, or hurry yourself out of sorrow to prove your faith. Bring your tears to God; he keeps count of them (Psalm 56:8). The promise is not that you will stop feeling the loss tomorrow, but that the one who is with you in the weeping will one day turn it into laughter.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced blessed those who are hungry and weeping now, because they will be filled and will laugh.

On a Tuesday. If you are weeping now, take heart: Jesus promises you will laugh. Your present sorrow is not the end.

Where it applies: A friend has lost her husband, and three months on she is still crying in church. Do not tell her it is time to move on, or that a strong Christian would be rejoicing by now. Sit with her, let her weep, and remind her gently that Jesus calls her blessed, and that the morning is coming.

Where it would be wrong: A neighbour has no food in the house, and you tell him he is blessed and will be satisfied in the kingdom, and leave it there. This beatitude is never a reason to leave the hungry hungry. If a brother or sister is without daily food and you say, be warmed and filled, without giving them what they need, what good is that? (James 2:15–16). Bring the promise and the groceries.

For worship. The one who promises to fill the hungry is the bread of life, and the one who promises laughter to the weeping is the man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. He took our hunger into the desert and our tears to the grave of Lazarus and the garden of Gethsemane, and he came out the other side alive. On the third day the women came weeping to his tomb and went away with fear and great joy. Every tear his people shed now is an IOU of laughter, signed by the risen Christ.

parallels.desc: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.

When people hate you and when they exclude you. The fourth beatitude is the longest, the most specific, and the only one about something the disciples will bring on themselves. Four verbs, and they escalate. Hatred: the inward turn. Exclusion: being cut off from the synagogue, from family, from community, the social world that was your whole life (John 9:22; 16:2). Reviling: verbal abuse, insult to the face. Spurning your name as evil: your name, or the name Christian, treated as a curse (Acts 11:26; 1 Peter 4:14–16). That is a complete social death, staged in four moves, and Jesus describes it to men who have followed him for perhaps a few weeks.

On account of the Son of Man! Not for being obnoxious, but for Christ’s sake. The qualifier is essential. This is not a blessing on being disliked. There is no promise here for the Christian who is excluded for being rude, or reviled for being a fool, or hated for opinions that have nothing to do with Christ. The clause is narrow on purpose. Persecution counts when it is about him. Suffering for wrongdoing has no blessing (1 Peter 4:15).

Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy. Not just endure it, but rejoice, even leap, like a lamb in spring, or like John in the womb (1:41, the same word). An astonishing command. Not endure; not bear it patiently. Leap. Jesus tells people who are about to lose their standing, their livelihood and their families to jump for joy on the day it happens. The apostles did exactly this: they left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

For behold, your reward is great in heaven. The reason for joy: God sees, and will reward. Not that we earn heaven by suffering, but that God honours faithfulness. The joy is not about the circumstance; it is about the accounting. Something is being stored where none of this can reach it.

For so their fathers did to the prophets. Persecution puts you in the company of the prophets. It is a mark of belonging to God’s true servants (11:47–51; 13:34). The second reason is stranger and more comforting: exclusion is company. If you are being treated like this, look at who else was, and every one of them turned out to have been right, and every one of them is now honoured by the descendants of the men who threw them out.

The landing is certain. The leap is only possible if the landing is certain. Nobody jumps in the dark. What makes this command sane rather than cruel is that the man giving it knows exactly how the story ends, and is himself, within three years, going to be hated, excluded, reviled, and have his name thrown out as evil.

How can I rejoice when it hurts? Rejoicing here does not mean pretending it does not hurt, or enjoying pain. It means looking past the hurt to what it means and where it leads. It means you belong to Christ; it means you stand with the prophets; it means a reward is being kept for you that no one can take. Paul could be sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). Begin by thanking God, honestly, even through tears, that you were counted worthy to share a little of his Son’s rejection. Then pray for those who wronged you (v. 28). Joy usually follows the thanks rather than coming before it.

In a sentence. Jesus called his disciples blessed when they are hated, excluded and insulted for his sake, and told them to leap for joy, because their reward in heaven is great, as the prophets’ was.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked or excluded for following Christ, rejoice. You are in the company of the prophets, and God will reward you.

Where it applies: You are left out of a family group chat because you became a Christian. Do not answer with bitterness. Rejoice: you are in the company of the prophets.

Where it would be wrong: You are left out because you lecture everyone at family meals. That is not being hated for the Son of Man’s sake. Ask first whether the offence is Christ or your manner (1 Peter 3:15–16).

For worship. He was hated without a cause, excluded from his own town, reviled on the cross, and his name was spat out as the name of a deceiver. He went first down the road he describes, and he did it for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Now the name men spurned is the name above every name. Those who share his rejection will share his glory, and on that day the leaping will be for ever.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. 'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. 'Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.

Woe. Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings. Woe (ouai) is a cry of grief and warning, used by the prophets: Isaiah’s woe to those who join house to house (Isaiah 5:8–23), Amos’s woe to those who are at ease in Zion (Amos 6:1). Not a curse, and not a wish for harm, but a lament: how terrible for you. It carries grief in it as much as warning. It is the sound a man makes looking at people walking towards a cliff.

Woe to you who are rich. Not that wealth is sinful in itself; Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich. But wealth tends to make people self-sufficient, satisfied with this world, and blind to their need of God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25). It is a great danger.

For you have received your consolation. Received (apechete) is a business word, used on receipts: paid in full. That is the whole argument in one verb. It is not that the rich are excluded. It is that they have already collected. You have had your comfort already. The account has been settled, the comfort has been drawn, and there is nothing further outstanding. Abraham said the same to the rich man: you in your lifetime received your good things (16:25).

Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Those who are satisfied with this world’s goods, and feel no spiritual hunger. Each woe is the exact mirror of a blessing, and each turns on the same now.

Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Not innocent laughter, but the careless laughter of those who do not take God or sin or suffering seriously (James 4:9).

Almost everyone reading this is rich. This has to be applied honestly, because almost everyone reading it is, by any measure the world has ever used, among the rich. It will not do to hurry past into a general observation about the dangers of materialism. So let it be put as a question rather than an accusation, since that is how Jesus put it. Where is your consolation actually coming from? Not what you would say in church, but what actually steadies you when the day has gone badly. A God who cannot be lost, or an arrangement that can? Because the danger these verses describe is not enjoying good things. It is being consoled by them: reaching a level of comfort at which the kingdom stops sounding like news and starts sounding like an optional extra for people whose lives are not working. Which is why the rich, in Luke’s Gospel, are so consistently in trouble. Not because God dislikes them. Because a man who has been paid already does not come to collect.

How rich is too rich? Scripture sets no figure, and the question usually hides a hope of being just under the line. The better questions are these. Am I trusting my money for security instead of God (1 Timothy 6:17)? Could I give a large part of it away without feeling that my life was gone? Is my giving generous, regular and costly, or the leftovers? Do I know any poor people by name? Is my spending shaped by love for others or by keeping up with those around me? If those answers trouble you, the remedy is not guilt but generosity: begin giving more, and more joyfully, and let money become a servant again.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that the rich, the full and those who laugh now have had their comfort already, and will hunger and weep.

On a Tuesday. If you are rich, full and laughing, examine yourself. Is your comfort in this world, or in God? Hold your blessings with humility and generosity.

Where it applies: You have plenty. Give generously this month to someone who has little, and give thanks for what you have, holding it loosely.

Where it would be wrong: You look down on wealthy Christians, or feel guilty over every good meal. The woe is on those whose comfort is in their riches instead of God. Abraham, Joseph of Arimathea and Lydia were wealthy and faithful (Genesis 13:2; Matthew 27:57; Acts 16:14–15). Paul tells the rich not to hope in riches but to be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

For worship. The woes are spoken with tears, by the Lord who did not want anyone to be paid off with this world. He offers a consolation that is not a receipt but a river: the consolation of Israel that old Simeon waited for (2:25), the God of all comfort (2 Corinthians 1:3). Every good thing we have is a gift from his hand, and he gives them so that we would love the Giver. His warnings are mercy too: he tells us where the cliff is because he would rather we came home.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings.

parallels.desc: woe to those at ease in Zion

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.

When all people speak well of you. This is the most searching sentence in the sermon, and it is aimed squarely at anyone who speaks for God. Universal popularity is a danger sign. A faithful witness to Christ will always offend some (v. 22). If no one ever objects to what you say, perhaps you are saying only what people want to hear.

For so their fathers did to the false prophets. The logic is exact. Israel had true prophets and false ones, and there was a reliable way to tell them apart from the outside: not their doctrine, which took discernment, but their popularity. The true prophets were nearly always unwelcome. Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern. Micaiah was hated because he never prophesied good concerning the king (1 Kings 22:8), and was kept in prison on bread and water. Amos was told to go and prophesy somewhere else (Amos 7:12). Elijah was the most wanted man in the kingdom. The false prophets, meanwhile, were doing very well. They had access, standing and a hearing at court, and the reason is not mysterious: they told people what they wanted. Peace, peace, when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 1 Kings 22:13; Isaiah 30:10). The true prophets were persecuted; the false ones were praised.

A diagnostic that cannot be faked. So Jesus offers his hearers a test, and it is uncomfortable in exactly the direction nobody wants. If everyone is speaking well of you, something has gone wrong. Either you have said nothing worth opposing, or you have said what people wanted to hear.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should try to be unpopular, or that being well thought of is always wrong (Acts 2:47; 1 Timothy 3:7). But seeking everyone’s approval will lead to compromising the truth. It is not a licence for being obnoxious. Some people are disliked for reasons that have nothing to do with Christ, and a man who has made himself unpleasant may console himself that he is being persecuted when he is only being avoided. The beatitude four verses earlier was carefully limited, on account of the Son of Man, and this woe carries the same limit. And Luke will shortly commend a centurion whom the whole town liked (7:4–5).

The temptation to shave the corners off. What the verse forbids is the pursuit of universal approval by someone who is meant to be carrying a message. There is a particular temptation, in preaching and in ordinary Christian conversation, to shave the corners off: to find the version of the truth that will not cost anything with this person, in this room. It works. Everyone speaks well of you. And that is precisely what the false prophets did, and every one of them was well liked, and every one of them was wrong.
