How do I speak the truth without being needlessly offensive? Separate the offence of the message from the offence of the messenger. The cross will offend some people whatever you do (1 Corinthians 1:23); your tone, timing and manner should offend no one. So speak when asked, or when love requires it, rather than at every opportunity. Listen first, and understand the person. Say the hard thing kindly, briefly and without contempt, and be honest about your own need of grace. Let your speech be gracious, seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6). If people still object, let it be to Christ, not to you.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that being praised by everyone is a danger, because that is how people treated the false prophets.

On a Tuesday. Are you more concerned about pleasing people than pleasing God (Galatians 1:10)? Speak the truth in love, even when it is unpopular.

Where it applies: Your friends all approve of something Scripture calls sin, and expect you to cheer. Gently say what you believe, even if it costs you their good opinion.

Where it would be wrong: You take being disliked as proof that you are faithful, and do not care what outsiders think of you. Unpopularity proves nothing on its own. An elder must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and Christians are to commend the gospel by honest, kind lives (1 Peter 2:12).

For worship. Here is the one true Prophet who never once shaved the corners off the truth, and who was never once unkind. He spoke with grace and he spoke the whole counsel of God, and for it they spoke evil of him to the end. He did not seek the praise of men; he sought the glory of his Father and the salvation of the very people who despised him. And the Father spoke well of him, from heaven, which is the only approval that lasts: this is my beloved Son, listen to him.

parallels.desc: the prophets prophesy falsely, and my people love to have it so

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.” This is probably the most demanding ethical command in the New Testament, and it is not an aspiration but an imperative, repeated in four parallel forms.

All four are verbs of action, and none is a verb of feeling — which matters enormously for anyone who has read this and concluded they cannot do it. He does not command warm feelings; he commands treatment. And the four escalate in cost: do good can be done at a distance; bless requires words; pray for is hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long.

The natural instinct is reciprocity — love those who love you, do good to those who do good to you. Jesus points out that reciprocal love proves nothing: “even sinners love those who love them.” It requires no faith and no change of heart; self-interest produces it unaided. The question the passage forces is whether anything in a Christian's life could not have been produced by ordinary human decency.

The ground of the command is not the worthiness of the enemy. There is no suggestion that the enemy deserves love. The ground is the character of God, “for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.” The disciple who loves enemies is not performing an act of heroic willpower; he is showing a family resemblance.

The concrete instructions in vv. 29-30 — the cheek, the cloak, the beggar, the goods taken — have been read both as absolute commands and as radical illustrations of a disposition. What is certain is their subject: a backhanded blow was an insult to honour, and the cloak is taken by force. These are about personal affront and personal loss, and what is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of one's own dignity.

They are not, and have never been, a command to remain within reach of violence. Jesus walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29-30); Paul invoked his citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37).

“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (v. 36) is the summary — and mercy presupposes a real debt and then declines to collect it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The command to love enemies is the most radical expression of grace in the New Testament — and it is exactly what God has done towards his own. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us… while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:8, 10).

The cross is the supreme act of love towards enemies. The disciple who loves an enemy is not doing something beyond what God has done; he is doing what has already been done to him, and doing it because he received it. The ethics of the sermon flow from its gospel: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Luke's “be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” is a different formulation from Matthew's “be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), and the difference is instructive. Matthew names the standard; Luke names the specific attribute this whole section reflects. In a passage about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

And the order can never be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all — which is also why the sentence begins “your Father,” addressed to people who already hold the position they are being asked to display.
verseByVerse.examples:
The command to love enemies has been the most transformative teaching in Christian history — the basis of martyrdom (Stephen dying while forgiving, Acts 7:60), of peacemaking, of every real reconciliation in the church's story.

It has also been the teaching most frequently domesticated into something manageable: being pleasant to people who are slightly difficult, or to former enemies who are now friends. The test is not whether we are kind to the kind. It is what we do with the person who is actively hostile, who has genuinely wronged us, and who continues to wish us harm.

The Golden Rule (v. 31) has parallels in nearly every ethical tradition — and almost all of them state it negatively: do not do to others what you would not want done to you. A man can keep that rule perfectly by doing nothing at all.

Jesus states it positively, which cannot be kept by inaction. It requires initiative, imagination, and going towards somebody at your own cost without being asked. And there is a mercy in how he frames it: he does not ask for an abstract theory of the good but for the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks — how you would want to be treated — applied in the other direction.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say to you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.

But I say to you who hear. Those who are really listening. The woes were to outsiders; now Jesus turns back to his disciples. The qualifier is not decoration. Jesus is about to say the hardest thing in the sermon, and he marks off in advance the people who are actually listening.

Love your enemies. The heart of the sermon. Not just your neighbour, but your enemy. The love Jesus means (agapē) is not a feeling of liking, but a commitment to seek someone’s good, whatever they deserve. No ancient religion or philosophy taught this so radically. And it is exactly how God loved us: while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10).

Four commands. Love is shown in action, in four rising steps. Love (attitude). Do good (deeds). Bless (words): speak well of them, wish them well, even when they curse you. Pray for them (prayer): bring them before God. Jesus did all four on the cross: Father, forgive them (23:34). So did Stephen (Acts 7:60).

Verbs of action, not feeling. All four are verbs of action, and none is a verb of feeling. That matters enormously for anyone who has read this and concluded they cannot do it. He does not command warm feelings towards a person who has wronged you; he commands treatment. You do not have to like your enemy to do good to him, and the command does not wait for the emotion to arrive.

The enemy is real. Luke gives three words for what this person is doing, hating, cursing, abusing, and none of them describes a mild difficulty. Jesus is not talking about a colleague who irritates you. He is talking about somebody who wishes you harm and is acting on it.

Those who abuse you. Abuse (epēreazontōn) means mistreat, insult, harass.

The commands escalate in cost. Do good is an action, which can be done at a distance and without much of yourself. Bless requires words, and words about a person come out of somewhere. Pray for is the hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long. It is very difficult to keep asking God to be good to somebody and go on hating them; one or the other will give way, which is presumably the point. There is a practical order in that worth using. Nobody arrives at loving an enemy by working on their feelings. It generally goes the other way round: an act, then a word, then a prayer, and somewhere in the third the heart begins to move.

Does this forbid self-defence, military service or the state’s use of force? Jesus is speaking of personal retaliation and the way his disciples treat those who wrong them. The state’s sword is a different matter, given by God to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), and a Christian may serve in it (3:14). Protecting the weak from harm is not hating an enemy.

What it does not mean. This is not a command to pretend nothing happened; forgiveness in Scripture never requires the pretence that the wrong was not a wrong. Nor is it a command to remain within reach of harm; the next verses deal with that directly. What is forbidden is the natural, satisfying, entirely human project of returning what was given.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded his followers to love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, bless those who curse them, and pray for those who mistreat them.

On a Tuesday. Who is your enemy, the person who has hurt or opposed you? Do one good thing for them today, speak well of them, and pray for them by name.

Where it applies: A former friend is spreading unkind things about you online. Do not reply in kind. Pray for him by name, and do him good when you have the chance.

Where it would be wrong: The lie is serious: it accuses you of a crime, or it will lose you your job and hurt your family. Loving an enemy does not mean letting a damaging falsehood stand. Correct it calmly and truthfully, and if need be ask the platform or the law to deal with it. Paul defended himself against false charges more than once (Acts 24:10–21; 25:8–11).

For worship. Love your enemies: the command is a portrait of the one who gave it. We were his enemies, hostile in mind and doing evil deeds (Colossians 1:21), and he loved us. He did good to those who hated him, healing the ear of the man who came to arrest him (22:51). He blessed those who cursed him, and from the cross he prayed for the men driving the nails. Every word of this command he kept, at its full height, for us. There is no enemy of yours so hard to love as you were to him.

verseByVerse.quote: To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.

Four illustrations. They are meant to shock. A blow to the face, a coat taken, a beggar’s hand, goods carried off, and in each case the response is the opposite of the reflex.

To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also. The first needs its background. A slap on the cheek was more an insult than an injury, a calculated humiliation. In that culture it was normally a contemptuous blow, the way a superior humiliated an inferior, the way an argument was ended by putting a man in his place. Jewish law treated it under fines for damaged honour rather than damaged bodies. So to offer the other cheek is not to invite a beating. It is to refuse the humiliation on its own terms: to decline to be drawn into the exchange the insult was designed to start. Do not retaliate. Do not return insult for insult (1 Peter 2:23; 3:9). Absorb the wrong, rather than escalate it.

From one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one. If someone takes your coat, do not fight to get it back; let him have your shirt as well. Put people before possessions.

Give to everyone who begs from you. Generosity without discrimination.

And from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back. Hold possessions loosely. Do not live for revenge or recompense.

What this verse does not say to the abused. Something must be said plainly here, because few verses in the Bible have been so cruelly misused. Turn the other cheek has been quoted to battered wives, to abused children, to the bullied and the trafficked, to tell them Christ requires them to stay and keep absorbing the blows. He requires no such thing, and it is a wickedness to say he does. Look again at what he is describing: an insult to a man’s honour, and a coat taken by force. This is about personal affront and personal loss, the wound to pride and pocket that makes us itch to hit back and stand on our rights. What is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of our own dignity. He is not handing a violent man a licence, and he is not telling his victim to hold still. Jesus himself walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29–30). Paul invoked his Roman citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37; 22:25) and let the believers lower him over a wall in a basket rather than be murdered (Acts 9:25). And the same love that will not retaliate for itself is fiercely bound to protect the weak, sometimes from the very person harming them.

If you are being harmed, hear this clearly. Getting to safety is not a failure of this verse. Removing yourself or a child from a violent home, calling for help, telling your pastor or elders, insisting that the law do its work: none of that is retaliation, and none of it is forbidden here. A church that tells an abused person to go back and submit to the abuse has disobeyed Christ, not obeyed him. What dies in these verses is the right to hit back for your own honour. Not the duty to keep the defenceless, including yourself, out of the reach of evil.

Where Christians differ: non-resistance. Some (Anabaptists, Quakers, Tolstoy) take these words literally and absolutely: Christians may never use force, serve in the army or police, go to court, or defend themselves. Verdict: these commands govern personal relationships and the disciple’s heart: no personal revenge, no retaliation for insult, generosity rather than grasping. They do not abolish the God-given role of the state to punish evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), nor the duty to protect others, nor all legal redress (Paul appealed to Caesar, Acts 25:11). Jesus himself, when struck, did not offer the other cheek literally but protested the injustice (John 18:22–23). The principle is: never repay evil for evil; overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17–21). Giving to everyone who asks is to be exercised with wisdom, for their real good (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

Must I give to every beggar, even if the money will be misused? Jesus commands an open hand, a readiness to give rather than an instinct to refuse. He does not forbid discernment. Paul says that if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10), and the church cared carefully for genuine need (1 Timothy 5:3–16). Sometimes the most loving gift is food rather than cash, or time rather than money. What this verse rules out is the closed hand.

In a sentence. Jesus called his followers not to retaliate when insulted, not to cling to their possessions when wronged, and to give freely to those who ask.

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you today, resist the urge to hit back. Overcome evil with good.

Better to let it go: A friend borrowed your drill years ago and never gave it back. Let it go. You do not need to demand it back, or let it sour the friendship.

Wrong to let it go: Your house is burgled, or your employer stops paying your wages. Jesus forbids personal revenge and a grasping heart, not justice through proper means. Report the burglary to the police; pursue your wages, for withholding a worker’s pay is a sin God hears (James 5:4). And if others depend on you, you owe it to them.

For worship. He gave his back to those who struck him and his cheeks to those who pulled out the beard (Isaiah 50:6). They took his cloak and gambled for his tunic at the foot of the cross (John 19:23–24), and he did not demand them back. He let everything be taken, not because he was weak, but because he was paying for our sins, and he had set his face to finish it. The one who could have called twelve legions of angels absorbed the insult of the whole world, and overcame evil with good.
verseByVerse.note: The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.

The Golden Rule. One of the most famous sayings of Jesus, and it sits here for a reason: it is the engine of everything around it. The commands on either side are extraordinary and difficult; this is the principle that makes them intelligible rather than arbitrary. Others had stated it negatively: Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Confucius and others said similar things. It is one of the few moral instincts that turns up everywhere. Jesus states it positively, which is much more demanding. Not just, do not harm others, but, do for others all the good you would want done for you. It requires active, imaginative love.

Why positive matters. The difference is not cosmetic. The negative form can be satisfied by a man who does nothing at all. Sit still, harm nobody, and you have kept it perfectly, which is why it is such a comfortable rule and why it has been so widely admired. The positive form cannot be kept by inaction. It requires initiative. It requires imagining what you would want if you were in that person’s position, and then going and doing it, at your own cost, without being asked. Consider what that means for the man on the other side of these verses: the enemy, the one who struck you, the one who took your coat. The negative rule permits you to leave him alone, which is very nearly what you wanted to do anyway. The positive rule asks what you would want if you were him, and sends you towards him.

As you wish. We know what we want: to be treated with kindness, patience, respect, generosity and forgiveness. That is the measure of how we should treat others. Matthew adds: for this is the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 7:12). And there is a hidden mercy in the way it is framed. Jesus does not ask you to work out an abstract theory of the good. He tells you to use the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks: the vivid, detailed, entirely reliable understanding of how you would like to be treated. Every person alive is an expert in that. He simply says: apply it in the other direction.

What it does not mean. Not, treat others well so that they will treat you well, as a self-interested bargain. The motive is love, not return (v. 35).

A test that is uncomfortably easy to run. Take the person you are currently having difficulty with, and ask what you would want from them if the positions were exactly reversed. The answer arrives immediately. It always does. That is the whole trouble with this verse.

What if what I would want is not good for me? The rule assumes a sensible, honest wish, not every passing desire. A man who wishes others would let him drink himself to death has not found a licence to supply someone else’s addiction. The rule is about the kind of treatment any reasonable person wants: honesty, fairness, patience, help in need, the benefit of the doubt, forgiveness, respect. Under all our particular wishes is the deeper wish to be truly loved, and true love sometimes says no. Ask, therefore, not only what you would like but what you would be grateful for in ten years’ time.

In a sentence. Treat others in every way as you would want them to treat you.

On a Tuesday. In every conversation today, ask: how would I want to be treated if I were them? Then do it.

Where it applies: You would want your manager to tell you plainly, but kindly, where your work falls short. Do that in your next review of someone else.

Where it would be wrong: A friend asks you for a glowing reference that you know is not true. The golden rule does not mean giving people what they ask for. The employer who will read the reference is also someone you must treat as you would want to be treated. Write honestly and kindly.

For worship. Only one man has ever kept this rule perfectly, and he kept it towards us. He did for us everything he would have wanted done if he were in our place, and then he went further: he put himself in our place. He who had no need of mercy came to give it; he who deserved honour took our shame. The Law and the Prophets are summed up in this one sentence, and they are fulfilled in one life. Blessed be the Christ who treated his enemies as he would wish to be treated, and then let himself be treated as his enemies deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: 'If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.

What benefit is that to you? Three questions, all the same shape, and each one dismantles a way of feeling good about yourself. Benefit (charis) is the word for grace, credit, thanks. What is there about that which deserves God’s thanks? What is gracious about it? What Jesus is asking, quite literally, is: what grace is there in that? And the answer is none, because grace by definition is unearned, and love returned for love is a transaction that has been earned.

For even sinners love those who love them. Love that is returned is just an exchange. Everyone does it. It shows nothing distinctively Christian. The same move comes twice more, covering the three main forms of human exchange: affection, kindness, money. Do good to those who do good to you: a favour repaid.

Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount. Lending that expects repayment is business, not grace: credit extended against security. Each is perfectly respectable, and each is done by everyone.

The sting. Jesus’ comparison is not with wicked people but with ordinary people. Even sinners: a word that in this Gospel means the openly disreputable, the ones the Pharisees would not eat with. Even they manage reciprocal love. It requires no faith, no Spirit, no change of heart whatever. Self-interest produces it unaided. So the question the passage forces is not, am I a decent person? Most people are, in this sense, and it proves nothing. The question is whether there is anything in your life that self-interest could not have produced.

A harder audit than it sounds. Reciprocity is very good at looking like generosity. The friendships that are mutually enjoyable. The kindnesses to people who will be pleased and will say so. The giving that goes where thanks will come back. None of it is wrong. All of it would happen anyway. Jesus is not condemning any of these things. He is saying they establish nothing about who you belong to, and that if the whole of a Christian’s love could be accounted for by ordinary human decency, then something is missing that the gospel was supposed to have put there. The test is not the warmth of your affections. It is whether anything you do costs you something that will never be returned.

The point. Disciples are to be different. Their love goes beyond what is natural and expected. It loves the unlovable, gives without expecting return, and does good to those who cannot or will not repay. That is grace. And it is the kind of love that shows the family likeness of God (v. 35).

Is it wrong to enjoy friendships where love is returned? Not at all. Mutual love is one of God’s best gifts, and Jesus had close friends himself (John 11:5; 15:15). Marriage, family and Christian fellowship are meant to be full of love given and received. The point is not to despise reciprocal love but to refuse to stop there. Enjoy your friends with thanks; and then look beyond them, to the person who will never return your kindness, and love them as well.

In a sentence. Loving, doing good to and lending to those who will repay you is nothing special, since even sinners do it.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything about your love that could not be explained by self-interest? Do something today for someone who cannot repay you.

Where it applies: A single mother in your church cannot cover this month’s bills. Lend her what she needs, without setting a date, and be ready never to see it again.

Where it would be wrong: A relative wants you to co-sign a loan you could not repay, or keeps borrowing to cover gambling. Lending that feeds a destructive habit, or that puts your own family at risk, is not love (Proverbs 22:26–27; 1 Timothy 5:8). Give what you can afford to lose, and help in ways that actually help.

For worship. What grace is there in loving those who love you? None; and that is why God’s love for us is grace. He did not love us because we loved him; we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). He gave to people who had nothing to give back and lent to debtors who could never repay, and then he wrote off the whole debt at his own cost. Every Christian is living on a loan that was never called in, from the God whose love is pure charis.

verseByVerse.quote: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.

But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return. The opposite of verses 32–34. The three questions are answered by repeating the three commands with the reciprocity stripped out. Love, do good and lend, without hope of return. And that last phrase is the one that bites. Not lending at generous rates. Not lending patiently. Lending with the expectation of repayment removed from the transaction, which, in plain terms, is giving with paperwork. In a society without banks, lending to the poor was a major act of charity, and the law forbade charging interest to fellow Israelites (Exodus 22:25).

Does this forbid charging interest or expecting repayment? The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11), and Jesus goes further: when lending to someone in need, be ready to lose it. That is different from ordinary business lending and investment, which the Bible does not condemn. The heart of the command is generosity to the needy, even the ungrateful.

And your reward will be great. You will not lose by it. God will repay (14:14). Notice that Jesus has no embarrassment about reward. He does not say the disciple should want nothing; he says the disciple should stop expecting it from the debtor and start expecting it from God. The money is not written off. It is transferred to a different account.

And you will be sons of the Most High. This is the real payment, and it needs unpacking. You will show that you are God’s children by acting like him. A son resembles his father. In Hebrew idiom, to be called the son of something is to bear its character: sons of thunder, son of encouragement, sons of disobedience. To be a son of the Most High is to be recognisably like him. Not that loving enemies makes you a child of God (that comes by grace through faith), but that it shows it.

For he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. The whole theology of the sermon in ten words. Common grace. Not kind to the deserving. Not kind to those who respond well. Kind to the ungrateful, people who take what he gives and never once acknowledge where it came from. Kind to the evil, people actively opposed to him. God sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). He gives life, food and countless blessings to people who never thank him and who hate him. Every meal an atheist eats came out of the ground God keeps making fruitful. And supremely, he gave his Son for enemies (Romans 5:8). His children must be like him.

The family resemblance. So the command to love enemies is not an arbitrary height set for spiritual athletes. It is a description of the family likeness. God has been doing this since the world began, and he did the ultimate version of it at a cost nobody had guessed: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). That is the order, and it cannot be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all.

Is it wrong to want a reward from God? No. Jesus offers it here as a motive, and Hebrews says that whoever would draw near to God must believe that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6). What is wrong is wanting the wrong reward, or wanting it from the wrong person: doing good to be admired, or to put others in our debt. The reward Jesus promises is God himself, his approval, and the joy of being like him, and these are rewards only a child would want. It is like a son who wants to please his father, not a hired hand bargaining for wages.

In a sentence. Love your enemies, do good and lend without expecting return, and you will be rewarded and will show yourselves children of God, who is kind to the ungrateful and evil.

On a Tuesday. God has been kind to you when you were ungrateful and evil. Thank him, and be like him toward others.

Where it applies: A neighbour who has complained about your children for years, and never said thank you for anything, has a burst pipe while his family is away. Turn off his water, let him know, and clear up what you can, and do not mention it again.

Where it would be wrong: A colleague who has repeatedly lied about you asks for access to your passwords or your accounts, promising to repay a favour. Kindness to the ungrateful does not mean handing a dishonest person the means to do more harm. Be shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16). Do him good in ways that are good for him and safe for others.

For worship. He is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. Every sunrise is proof of it, and every harvest, and every breath drawn by a man who curses God. And the cross is proof beyond all others: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). We were the ungrateful, the evil, the debtors who never paid, and he called us sons. Our Father is the Most High, and his kindness has no bottom.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.

Be merciful. The summary of everything Jesus has said about love, from verse 27 onwards. Merciful (oiktirmones) means compassionate, full of pity, feeling for others in their need and acting to help. Matthew has: you therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). Luke shows that the perfection of God is seen above all in his mercy. Matthew names the standard; Luke names the specific divine attribute the whole passage has been describing. In a section about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

What mercy is. Mercy needs defining, because it is a word people use warmly without knowing what it means. Mercy is not being nice. It is not tolerance, and it is not the belief that the offence was minor. Mercy is what happens when someone deserves one thing and is given another; it presupposes a real debt, and then declines to collect it. Which means mercy can only exist where there is a genuine wrong. You cannot be merciful to someone who has not injured you; you can only be pleasant to them. The command therefore requires that the injury be taken seriously, named, understood as an injury, and then not paid back. Any account of forgiveness that begins by minimising what happened has skipped the only step that makes mercy possible.

Even as your Father is merciful. God is the Father of mercies (2 Corinthians 1:3), merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). The standard is not other people, but God himself. Not as much as you can manage. Not proportionate to the offence. The measure given is God’s own conduct, which is the reason this command can never be marked complete. And the motive: you have received mercy; show it (Matthew 18:33). This verse introduces the next section about judging.

Why it is not crushing. The sentence begins with your Father. It is addressed to people who are already in the family, who have already received exactly the treatment they are being told to give, and who are not being asked to earn a position they already hold. That is the whole logic of the sermon in miniature. The mercy comes first, from him, at the cross, unearned and unasked. The command comes second, and it is not, be merciful in order to become his. It is: you have seen how your Father behaves. Do it like that. Nothing in this section is possible for someone who has not been on the receiving end of it. Everything in it becomes possible, slowly, for someone who has.

Does being merciful mean there should be no consequences? No. Mercy gives up the right to personal revenge and the desire to see someone suffer; it does not abolish justice or wise protection. A parent can forgive a child and still apply a consequence; a church can forgive a man who stole from it and still not give him the accounts; a victim can forgive an abuser and still give evidence in court. God himself is merciful and just. What mercy refuses is the grudge, the gloating, the long memory kept like a weapon, and it always leaves room for the person to be restored.

In a sentence. Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.

On a Tuesday. Reflect today on the mercy God has shown you. Let it overflow in mercy to others.

Where it applies: Your teenage son crashes the car after you told him to be careful. He is shaken and ashamed. Before you list the cost, put your arm round him; then, together, work out how he will help put it right.

Where it would be wrong: A church treasurer is found to have taken money for years. Being merciful does not mean hushing it up or leaving him in charge of the accounts because he says sorry. Forgive him, care for him and his family, and still remove him from that role and make the matter right (1 Corinthians 4:2). Mercy and wisdom walk together.

For worship. Our Father is the Father of mercies, and he has never once dealt with us according to our sins. He took the real debt seriously, so seriously that it cost him his Son, and then he declined to collect it from us. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Psalm 103:13). Every mercy we show is a small reflection of that, and every mercy we have received is a drop from an ocean that will never run dry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–45 — Judging Others and the Tree and Its Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The teaching on judging (vv. 37-42) and on fruit (vv. 43-45) form one unit held together by the theme of discernment: how we assess others and ourselves.

“Judge not” is one of the most misquoted sentences in the Bible, taken to mean that no moral assessment of anyone is ever permitted. It cannot mean that. Four verses later Jesus tells his hearers to remove the log from their own eye so that they will see clearly to remove a brother's speck — an instruction to make a judgement, having first qualified oneself to make it. Two verses after that he explains how to tell a good tree from a bad one.

What is forbidden is not discernment about conduct but condemnation — pronouncing a verdict on a person, assigning their final worth and destiny. That work belongs to a court, and there is only one. The difference is felt easily enough: “that was a lie” assesses an act; “he is a liar” delivers a summary of a life, and requires access to motives and history that no human being has.

The image of the measure in v. 38 is from a grain market: filled, pressed down to compact it, shaken so the grains settle, then heaped until it spills over into the fold of a man's garment. It is not a level measure. It is a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous.

The blind guide and the log-and-speck follow, and the comedy is deliberate. A man with a plank in his eye leaning in to extract a splinter is an optical impossibility, and the audience can see it. Note that Jesus does not say “leave the speck alone.” The brother is still to be helped; what is corrected is the order. “First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly.”

The tree-and-fruit teaching is the positive counterpart: character produces conduct. This is not moralism — it does not say “try harder to produce good fruit.” It is a statement about the direction of causation. The fruit reveals the tree; what a person does consistently reveals what they are.

And the source is the treasury of the heart: “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” — out of the overflow. Speech is not what a person decides to say; it is what spills when the container is full and nobody is watching.
verseByVerse.theology:
The measure-for-measure principle of v. 38 recurs across both testaments (Matt. 7:2; Rom. 2:1; Jas. 2:13). It is not mechanical karma but a reflection of God's character — the God who shows himself merciful to the merciful and severe to the severe (Ps. 18:25-26).

The warning is not that God will be unkind to those who judge. It is that a person who approaches God without mercy will meet his justice applied with the rigour they themselves used. Someone who has received grace and then withholds mercy has fundamentally misunderstood what grace is.

The word “hypocrite” at v. 42 needs care. In ordinary English it means a conscious fraud. But the man Jesus describes genuinely does not see the log — it is stated twice. The hypocrisy is not deliberate pretence but a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere.

Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best — and the blind guide of v. 39 is in the same condition, sincerely certain he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain.
verseByVerse.examples:
The log-and-speck has a sharp application for every relationship involving authority: parents with children, leaders with congregations, employers with employees, elders with members. The right to speak into another person's life is not conferred by position; it is earned or forfeited by the quality of one's own self-examination.

The mentor who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it can be trusted with somebody else's failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better about himself. There is a practical test before speaking: ask what this conversation will cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

“Everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (v. 40) is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone choosing whom to learn from. Formation works. The ceiling of what you become is set by the person you follow, whether or not you intend it.

And “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” (v. 45) is the most usable diagnostic Jesus gave. Not what a person says when trying to impress, but what comes out when they are tired, unobserved, or talking about people who are not in the room. That is the overflow, and it is a straight readout of the treasury. Nor can it be fixed by monitoring speech — that produces a careful hypocrite. What must change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.

Judge not, and you will not be judged. Four commands in a row, two negative and two positive, each with a consequence attached. These are probably the two most quoted words of Jesus in the modern world, and they are quoted almost entirely wrongly, usually to mean that no one may ever assess anyone’s conduct, which would make the sentence unusable and its speaker inconsistent. Not a ban on all judgement. Jesus will tell us to recognise trees by their fruit (vv. 43–44), and to rebuke a brother who sins (17:3). Four verses later he tells his hearers to take the log out of their own eye so that they will see clearly to take out the speck from a brother’s, which is an instruction to make a judgement, having first qualified yourself to make it. Christians must discern right and wrong, and the church must exercise discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What Jesus forbids is a censorious, fault-finding, self-righteous spirit, that judges others harshly while excusing oneself, assumes the worst, and takes God’s place as judge (Romans 2:1; 14:4, 10–13; James 4:11–12).

The judge’s seat. The distinction is practical and it is not hard to feel. There is a difference between, that was a lie, and, he is a liar; between assessing what a person did and delivering a summary of what they are. The first is often required of us. The second requires access to information, motives, history, what a person was given to work with, what they have resisted, that no human being has. To pronounce a final verdict on a person is a work that belongs to a court, and there is only one.

Condemn not, and you will not be condemned. Do not pronounce the final verdict on others. That belongs to God.

Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Forgive (apolyete) means release, let go. A forgiving spirit is the mark of those God has forgiven (11:4; Matthew 6:14–15).

Give, and it will be given to you. Generosity is repaid by God’s generosity.

Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. A picture from the grain market. Grain was measured into a container, or into a fold of the robe used like an apron, the lap, which a man held out as a bag. A generous seller filled the measure, pressed it down to compact it, shook it to settle the grain, and heaped it until it overflowed. This is not a level measure. It is a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous. God gives like that: generously, more than we could hold.

For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you. A principle of God’s dealings. The way you treat others is the way God will treat you. Harsh judgement brings harsh judgement; generous mercy brings generous mercy (James 2:13). That is not a transaction, and it is not karma. It is a description of how the same person meets God at both ends: the one who has understood mercy well enough to give it is the one who will know what to do with it when it comes.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by forgiving or giving, nor a prosperity gospel promise that giving money guarantees getting more money back. But God is no one’s debtor, and he repays generosity in his own way and time.

Is this a promise that giving money will bring financial return? No. The context is mercy, not judging, forgiving and generosity, and the measure returned is God’s generosity in kind. Paul says that whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Corinthians 9:6), but the harvest he means is righteousness and thanksgiving, not wealth (2 Corinthians 9:10–11).

If I struggle to forgive, does that mean God will not forgive me? No, not if you are struggling. The verse describes the settled heart of a forgiven person, not a test that a single hard battle can fail. Forgiveness of a deep wound is often a long road, chosen again and again, and God is patient with those who are walking it. What Jesus warns against is the heart that refuses to forgive at all, that holds the grudge and wants it held, because such a heart shows it has never understood its own forgiveness (Matthew 18:32–35). If you want to forgive but cannot yet feel it, ask God for help, decide not to take revenge, pray for the person, and keep going.

In a sentence. Don’t judge, condemn, or withhold forgiveness, but forgive and give, and God will treat you with the same measure, generously, overflowing.

On a Tuesday. Are you quick to judge others? Choose today to assume the best, to forgive and to give, and trust God to repay.

Where it applies: A family leaves your church, and rumours begin about why. Refuse to assume the worst. Think the best of them, and if you have reason to, ask them kindly.

Where it would be wrong: An employer must evaluate staff, a parent must decide which friends are safe, and a church must deal with open sin (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). Jesus forbids condemning and harsh judgement, not discernment or right decisions. And give, and it will be given to you is not a promise of money in return for giving: God repays in his own measure and his own way.

For worship. Our God is the merchant who heaps the measure until it spills into our laps. He gave his Son, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32). He has not judged us as we deserve; he has forgiven us beyond all reckoning, pressed down, shaken together, running over. The one Judge who has every right to condemn took the condemnation himself, so that for those in Christ there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Blessed be the God whose measure has no level brim.
verseByVerse.note: Grain was measured into a fold of the robe used like an apron; a generous seller pressed and shook it down so it held more.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told them a parable: can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.

Can a blind man lead a blind man? Two short sayings, and Luke has placed them exactly where they explain the one before. It is a joke with a knife in it. The picture is obviously absurd, and the audience would have laughed, and then stopped laughing, because they knew who it was aimed at. A judgemental person is blind to his own faults (vv. 41–42), and cannot guide others. Jesus applied this especially to the Pharisees (Matthew 15:14), who claimed to be guides of the blind (Romans 2:19). The men who had been watching him in the synagogue, hoping to build a charge out of a withered hand, were the recognised guides of Israel.

Will they not both fall into a pit? Teacher and follower alike come to ruin. Note that the blind guide is sincere. Nobody in the parable is lying. He genuinely believes he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain. A guide who knew he was blind would stop. Choose your teachers carefully. And if you teach, make sure you can see.

A disciple is not above his teacher. Students cannot rise higher than their teachers. Follow a blind guide, and you will be blind.

But everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. Fully trained (katērtismenos) means equipped, completed, mended: the word for mending nets (Mark 1:19). This is the sober half, and it is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone choosing whom to learn from. The claim is simply that formation works. A trained disciple ends up resembling the one who trained him, not partly, not in some respects, but characteristically. Which means the ceiling of what you will become is set by the person you are following, and it is set whether or not you intend it.

Whose voice is forming you? The first practical question is about intake. Not whose books are on the shelf, but whose sentences come out of your mouth when you are tired: the preacher you always listen to, the writer whose tone you have absorbed, the friend whose judgement you find yourself repeating, the voices on your phone every evening. You are going to end up like them. That is not a warning against having teachers; it is an argument for choosing them deliberately.

A warning to anyone who teaches. You are not merely passing on content. You are reproducing yourself, including the parts you would rather not pass on, and the reproduction will be more thorough than the instruction. Parents, Sunday school teachers, pastors and mentors teach most by what they are.

The one teacher worth becoming like. Which is why the sermon’s own answer to the whole problem is a person rather than a syllabus. Follow the right teacher, Jesus, and you will become like him: merciful, non-judgemental, loving even enemies. God has predestined his people to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29). There is one teacher whose disciples, fully trained, will be like him, and that is not a disaster.

How do I tell whether a teacher can see? Test what he teaches by Scripture (Acts 17:11): does he say what the Bible says, all of it, including the parts that are unwelcome? Look at what he says about Christ, whether he exalts him as Lord and Saviour or uses him for something else. Look at his life, his humility, his honesty about money and power, his treatment of people who cannot help him (1 Timothy 3:1–7). And look at his followers: do they become more like Christ, more loving, more holy, more humble, or more like the teacher, proud and quarrelsome? A teacher who can see will point away from himself.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that a blind guide leads his followers into a pit, and that disciples become like their teachers.

On a Tuesday. Who are you learning from? You will become like them. Make sure your teachers lead you to Christ.

Where it applies: You spend an hour every evening listening to a popular online preacher whose sermons are mostly about success and self-esteem, and you notice you have become impatient with your ordinary church. Turn him off for a month, and spend that hour in one of the Gospels instead.

Where it would be wrong: You decide no human teacher can be trusted, stop listening to anyone, and read the Bible only on your own terms. Christ gave pastors and teachers to his church for our good (Ephesians 4:11–13). The answer to blind guides is not no guides but faithful ones, tested by Scripture.

For worship. Here is the one Teacher who sees perfectly, who never led anyone into a pit, and whose every disciple, fully trained, will be like him. When he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). He mends us as a fisherman mends a torn net, patiently, knot by knot, until we are whole. Blessed be the Master whose school ends in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye, when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother’s eye.

The speck and the log. A comic exaggeration, perhaps from the carpenter’s workshop. A tiny speck of sawdust, against a beam of timber. A man with a beam sticking out of his eye socket leans in with great concern to remove a speck from his friend’s eye. Jesus is not describing a moral failing so much as an optical impossibility, and everyone listening can see it.

The point. We are very good at seeing small faults in others and very bad at seeing large faults in ourselves. The critic is often guilty of a greater sin than the one he criticises, often the sin of judging itself. Our moral vision has astonishing resolution at range and is useless up close. We can detect a small fault in another person, an evasion in their tone, a self-serving detail in their account, an inconsistency between what they said last week and this, with real precision. And we walk about with structural failures of our own that everybody else can see from across a room.

You hypocrite. An actor, pretending to a righteousness he does not have. But it is worth being exact. In ordinary English a hypocrite is a conscious fraud, a man who knows he is play-acting. The picture Jesus draws is of somebody who genuinely does not see the log; that is stated twice. The hypocrisy here is not only deliberate pretence. It is a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere. Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best.

First take the log out of your own eye. Deal with your own sin first. Self-examination comes before correction of others.

And then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother’s eye. Notice: Jesus does not say leave your brother’s speck alone. The speck is still to come out. The brother is still to be helped. What is being corrected is the order. Once you have dealt with your own sin, you are able, and responsible, to help your brother, gently and humbly (Galatians 6:1). Removing a speck from an eye requires great care and gentleness. This passage is used almost as often to avoid responsibility as to practise it, quoted to mean that nobody may ever say anything to anybody. Jesus assumes the opposite. Christians are meant to help each other see. He is telling you what qualifies you to do it.

The qualification is honest sight. Not moral superiority. A man who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it is precisely the man who can be trusted with somebody else’s failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better. There is a practical test in it. Before speaking, ask what this conversation would cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

How do I find the log, if I cannot see it? Ask for help from outside, because the log is by definition in the eye you are using. Ask God: search me, O God, and know my heart, and see if there be any grievous way in me (Psalm 139:23–24). Read Scripture slowly and let it read you. Ask a spouse or close friend, and mean it: what do you see in me that I do not? Notice what irritates you most in others, because it is often a reflection of your own. And when you find the log, do not merely regret it; confess it, and ask the person you have wronged to forgive you.

In a sentence. Jesus warned against criticising others’ small faults while ignoring our own great ones, telling us to deal with our own sin first, so we can then help others clearly.

On a Tuesday. Before you correct someone today, ask God to show you the log in your own eye.

Where it applies: Before you speak to your teenager about time on the phone, look honestly at your own.

Where it would be wrong: You never correct anyone, because you are not perfect either. Jesus does not say leave the speck; he says take out the log first, then you will see clearly to take out the speck (v. 42). Humility makes correction gentle; it does not make it silent.

For worship. The carpenter who joked about the beam in the eye was himself the only man with clear sight, and he was gentle with our specks and patient with our logs. He saw everything wrong in us and did not stand over us with a pointing finger. He came down to us, took our sin on himself, and gave us his own eyes to see. The one perfectly qualified to judge became the one who heals, and he still handles the eyes of his people with infinite care.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.

For no good tree bears bad fruit. The sermon now shifts from conduct to cause, and the image is agricultural and inarguable. Nobody disputes this. You do not get figs off a thornbush. The nature of the tree determines the fruit. What a person does flows from what he is. The fruit does not determine the tree; it reveals it.

The direction of the passage. It is worth getting right, because this could be read as a demand to try harder, produce better fruit or else, and it is the opposite. A tree does not decide what fruit to bear. It bears according to what it is. Which means the question this raises is not, what should I be producing? But, what am I?

For each tree is known by its own fruit. You can tell a tree by its fruit. And you can tell a person, and a teacher, by the fruit of their life (Matthew 7:15–20). This is right judgement, the discernment Jesus approves.

Figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. Common plants of Palestine. You cannot get good fruit from a bad plant.

The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good. The heart is a storehouse, a treasury, the accumulated deposit. Whatever has been put in over the years is what comes out.

For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. Out of the overflow. Words especially reveal the heart. What overflows from your mouth shows what fills your heart (James 3:10–12). Speech is not only what a person decides to say. It is what spills over when the container is full and no longer being watched.

The most usable diagnostic. It can be run on yourself this afternoon. Not: what do I say when I am trying to make an impression? Anyone can manage that. But: what comes out when I am tired, when I am driving, when the phone call has gone badly, when I am among people I do not need to impress? What do I return to in conversation without meaning to? What is the tone of my speech about people who are not in the room? That is the overflow, and Jesus says it is a straight readout of the treasury.

The implication. To change the fruit, the tree must be changed. Outward reform cannot produce good fruit from a bad heart. A person needs a new heart, which only God can give (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 5:17). Then good fruit follows. You cannot improve the fruit by working on the fruit, and you cannot change your speech merely by monitoring your speech; that produces a careful hypocrite, which is where this sermon started. What has to change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

One bad word does not prove a bad heart. He is not saying that a single bad word proves a bad heart; the language is about what a tree bears, which is a pattern over seasons, not one morning’s crop. Every Christian says things they hate having said.

Then how is the treasury restocked? By God, through ordinary means he has given. The Spirit gives the new heart in the new birth, and then fills it over a lifetime as we take in his word: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (Colossians 3:16). So fill your mind with Scripture, read and memorised; with prayer; with the worship and teaching of the church; with good books and good friends; and starve what feeds the old heart, the gossip, the bitterness, the screen that leaves you worse. Whatever you think about, dwell on what is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely (Philippians 4:8). Slowly, the overflow changes.

In a sentence. As a tree is known by its fruit, so a person’s words and deeds show what is stored in their heart.

On a Tuesday. Listen to what comes out of your mouth today. What does it reveal about your heart? Ask God to fill it with good.

Where it applies: You notice that whenever a certain colleague’s name comes up, you make a cutting remark. That is fruit, and it is telling you something about the root. Confess the resentment to God, pray for her by name, and say one good thing about her this week.

Where it would be wrong: You conclude that a Christian friend cannot be a believer because he lost his temper badly once at a football match. A tree is known by its fruit over seasons, not by one bad apple. Speak to him gently if need be, but do not pronounce on his soul from a single morning’s crop.

For worship. Only one tree has ever borne nothing but good fruit, and it was cut down for us. The good man out of whose heart came nothing but grace and truth hung on a tree, so that bad trees like us could be grafted into him and bear fruit. I am the vine; you are the branches, he said (John 15:5). The new heart is his gift, the good treasure is his own life in us, and every good word that comes out of a Christian’s mouth is overflow from him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — Build Your House on the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon ends with two builders, two houses, and one storm — and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen.

It is preceded by the question that makes the parable necessary: “Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you?” Jesus does not doubt that they call him Lord, or suggest they are insincere; the doubled address is the language of warmth. The problem is that the word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter — and to call a man Lord while deciding independently what to do with his instructions is a contradiction in terms.

The parable is not a contrast between a man who heard and a man who did not. Both come to Jesus. Both hear his words. Both build. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them.

The difference is entirely underground. The wise builder “dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock” — two verbs describing the least rewarding work in construction. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

Then the flood, and Luke is precise: the same stream breaks against both houses. The storm is not sent to test one and spare the other. It is weather, and it comes to everyone — which rules out the reading in which the obedient are protected from trouble. Both are hit equally. What differs is what happens next.

“Immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.” There is no gradual subsidence and no chance to shore it up. A life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

The storm is unspecified, and the vagueness is the point: bereavement, illness, betrayal, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, and finally the judgement. Something always comes.

And the rock is not a set of principles. Jesus has spent thirty verses saying things no one can live out by admiration, and he ends by describing a man who hears my words and does them. The digging is obedience, and what it reaches is him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The eschatological note — the house that falls, and “the ruin of that house was great” — places the sermon's ethics in the context of final judgement. This is not moralism; it is eschatology.

The commands of the sermon are not useful guidelines for a better life. They are the description of the life that will stand on the day when every life is tested — which is why the sermon cannot be domesticated into a programme of self-improvement. It describes a life that is only possible through the transformed heart the kingdom produces, which is exactly what the tree-and-fruit teaching has just said.

And it is why the question at v. 46 is not an attack on assurance. It is a question about the relationship between what a person says about Christ and what they do about what Christ says. Every command in this chapter is checkable, and not one of them can be kept by admiring it.

The rock, finally, is not the sermon. It is the one who preached it. To hear these words and do them is to build on Jesus himself, and he is what the digging reaches.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable of the two builders has been used in Christian preaching from the earliest centuries as the description of the difference between nominal and genuine faith. Both builders heard Jesus; both began to build; both appeared to be doing the same thing. The difference was invisible until the storm came.

This is Jesus's own warning against the self-deception that hears the word, feels its power, admires its truth, and then returns to a life built on other foundations. The church in every generation has members who have heard much and built little.

The wise builder “dug deep” — the effort of foundation-laying is not passive. It requires excavation, the removal of everything covering the rock, the work of getting down to what will hold. That is spiritual formation: not merely hearing but digging, through prayer and Scripture, through accountability, through obedience in small things, until the foundation is no longer mood and circumstance and social approval.

The digging is unglamorous and nobody sees it. The house is what people see. But the digging is what determines whether the house stands — and the way to start is not in general. Take one command from this chapter, with an actual name attached, and ask what it means this week.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?

Why do you call me Lord, Lord. Fourteen words, and there is nowhere to stand while reading them. The repetition shows fervour, perhaps in worship. Notice first what is not being questioned. He does not doubt that they call him Lord, and he does not suggest they are insincere in saying it. The doubling, Lord, Lord, is the language of warmth, even fervour; it is how you address someone you mean it about. The problem is not coldness. To call Jesus Lord is to acknowledge his authority, and in the full sense, his deity.

And not do what I tell you? A contradiction. A lord is someone you obey. The word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter. To call a man Lord and then decide independently what to do with his instructions is not merely a moral failure but a contradiction in terms. It is like calling someone your employer and never coming in. To call Jesus Lord and ignore his commands is hypocrisy. Words of worship without obedience are empty (Matthew 7:21–23; James 1:22). The test of whether Jesus is really your Lord is whether you do what he says, including everything in this sermon: love your enemies, don’t judge, give.

He asks why. The question is put as a genuine question. There is an answer, and every honest Christian knows roughly what it is: because the saying is warm and the doing is expensive; because the language of discipleship costs nothing and its substance costs everything; because it is entirely possible to love the person of Jesus in a general way and to have quietly arranged one’s life so that nothing he said in this chapter applies.

Why it comes exactly here. Read back over what he has just said. Love your enemies. Do good to those who hate you. Bless the man who curses you. Give and expect nothing back. Do not condemn. Take the log out of your own eye. Every one of those is checkable, and none of them can be done by admiring it.

Does this mean I am not saved if I fail to obey? No. The verse is not an attack on assurance and it is not a demand for perfection. Every Christian fails to do all that Jesus says, every day, and the same Lord taught us to pray, forgive us our debts. The question is the direction of a life: whether you call him Lord and are trying, however falteringly, to do what he says, grieving when you fail and getting up again; or whether you call him Lord and have no intention of letting it change anything. The first is a weak disciple. The second is not a disciple at all. If you are troubled by your failures, that trouble is itself a sign that he is your Lord.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why people called him Lord but did not do what he said.

On a Tuesday. Which of Jesus’ commands in this sermon are you not doing? Don’t just call him Lord; obey him.

Take one. It is worth answering slowly, with one specific instruction in mind, rather than in general. Take one, any one of them from this chapter, and ask what it would mean this week, with an actual name attached. That is the whole of what the next three verses are about, and it is the difference between two houses that look exactly alike.

Where it applies: You sing with real feeling on Sunday that Jesus is Lord of all, and on Monday you are still refusing to speak to your brother over an inheritance. This week, ring him, and begin the conversation Jesus told you to have.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of being a Lord, Lord hypocrite that you stop singing, praying aloud or calling him Lord at all until your obedience is better. Jesus does not tell you to stop confessing him; he tells you to obey the one you confess. Keep calling him Lord, and let him make the words true.

For worship. He is Lord, and he is worthy of every word of worship we give him and of every act of obedience we owe him. The one who asks why we call him Lord and do not obey is the one who, being Lord, became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). He did all his Father told him, so that disobedient people who have called him Lord with empty words could be forgiven and made new. And one day every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, and every knee will bow, and none of it will be empty.

parallels.desc: if I am a master, where is my fear?

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.

Two builders. The sermon ends with two builders, and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen. Read the description carefully, because the usual telling gets it wrong. This is not a contrast between a man who heard Jesus and a man who did not. Both come to him. Both hear his words. Both build houses. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them.

Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them. Three steps: come, hear, do. Not hearing alone; doing.

He is like a man building a house, who dug deep. Only Luke says dug deep. Hard work, below the surface, where no one sees, through the soil to the bedrock. It describes the least rewarding work in construction. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, costs real effort, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first and has more of a house to show for the same season’s work.

And laid the foundation on the rock. In the parable, the rock is hearing Jesus’ words and doing them (v. 47). Since they are the words of the Lord (v. 46), building on them means building on him: trusting and following him (see the note on Matthew 7:24–27). The foundation is invisible once the house is built, but it determines everything.

The rock in the rest of Scripture. The text itself defines the rock as Jesus’ words heard and done, and then later Scripture shows why that is not a gospel of self-effort. Long before, God was the rock of his people: the Rock, his work is perfect (Deuteronomy 32:4); the LORD is my rock and my fortress (Psalm 18:2). Isaiah promised a tested stone laid in Zion, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation, and whoever believes will not be in haste (Isaiah 28:16). The apostles tell us who that stone is. Peter quotes Isaiah of Christ, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen by God (1 Peter 2:4–6). Paul says no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), and that the church is built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). So the reader should understand the parable rightly: the rock is not our obedience considered on its own, as if we built our own foundation. It is Christ himself, the Lord whose words these are. To dig deep is to come to him, hear him and do what he says; obedience is how a life rests its whole weight on him, and it is that resting, not the effort, that holds the house up.

And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it. In Palestine, wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season, with devastating force. Notice how Luke describes it: the stream broke against that house, and the same stream broke against the other. The storm is not sent to test one and spare the other. It is simply weather, and it comes to everyone. This parable is sometimes read as though the obedient are protected from trouble. They are not. Both houses are hit, equally, by the same water. What differs is what happens next. The flood is any crisis: suffering, temptation, persecution, death, and finally the judgement of God.

Could not shake it, because it had been well built. The storm can be almost anything: bereavement, a diagnosis, a betrayal, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, and finally the judgement. Jesus does not specify, and the vagueness is the point. Something always comes.

But the one who hears and does not do them. He has heard the same sermon. The difference is not in hearing but in doing.

Is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. Easier, quicker, and in fair weather it looks just the same.

When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great. The end of the sermon is a warning. Hearing Jesus without obeying him leads to ruin. The difference between the two houses is only revealed when the storm comes. Luke’s immediately is grim. There is no gradual subsidence, no chance to shore it up. The first serious pressure and it is over, and the wreckage is described as great, because a life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by works. Jesus’ words begin with blessing for the poor and with the Father’s mercy (vv. 20, 36), so doing them starts with receiving mercy, not earning it. But true faith in Christ shows itself in obedience. Faith that does not obey is not saving faith (James 2:17).

How do I know whether I have dug deep? Look not at the outside of the house but at what you lean on when the water rises. When trouble comes, do you go to Christ, pray, open his word, and keep doing what he says, even through tears? Or does faith evaporate, and you reach for something else to hold you up? Look too at the ordinary weeks: is there a pattern, however imperfect, of hearing his words and doing them, in forgiveness, honesty, generosity, love for enemies? If you find you have built on sand, it is not too late while the sun is shining. Come to him now, hear him, and begin to dig.

In a sentence. Jesus ended by comparing those who hear and obey him to a man who built on rock and survived the flood, and those who hear and do not obey to a man whose house without foundations was swept away.

On a Tuesday. Storms are coming. Dig deep today: hear Jesus’ words and put one of them into practice.

Where it applies: You have heard this sermon many times, and you know you have been carrying a grudge against your former business partner for years. Dig today: tell God you forgive him, write the letter, and stop rehearsing the wrong. Do it now, in the dry season, before the flood comes.

Where it would be wrong: You treat digging deep as a programme of self-improvement, and measure how safe you are by how hard you are working at it. The rock is Christ, not your effort (1 Corinthians 3:11). Obey him, and rest your weight on him, not on your obedience.

For worship. Both men heard the sermon. One of them built his life on the man who preached it. He is the Rock of Ages, the tested stone, the sure foundation, and no flood has ever shaken him.
