Soon afterwards he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.

Meaning first. Luke 8 is about hearing, and about the one whose word must be heard. It opens with the company that travelled with Jesus: the Twelve, and women he had set free, who paid for the mission out of their own money. Then comes the parable of the sower: the same seed, the word of God, falls on four kinds of ground, and only the honest heart that holds it fast and waits bears fruit. A lamp is lit to be seen, everything hidden will come to light, and so we must take care how we hear; Jesus’ true family are those who hear God’s word and do it. Then Luke shows why his word deserves such hearing. In four scenes Jesus rules over the storm, a legion of demons, a disease no doctor could cure, and death itself. The sea lies down at his rebuke, the man who lived among the tombs sits clothed at his feet, a woman unclean for twelve years is called daughter, and a dead girl gets up and is given something to eat. The question the disciples ask in the boat hangs over the whole chapter: who then is this? The answer is that the Lord of Psalm 107 is in the boat.

Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages. Luke gives the shape of the ministry in a sentence: town after town, on foot, saying the same thing. This was his main work, as he had said (4:43): I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.

Proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. Two verbs. Proclaiming (kēryssōn) is the word for a herald making a public announcement in the king’s name. Bringing the good news (euangelizomenos) is the verb behind our word gospel. He is not lecturing. He is announcing something that has happened: the King has come, and his reign has begun.

And the twelve were with him. Learning by being with him (Mark 3:14). The Twelve were trained less by lectures than by company: they watched him, walked with him, and heard the same message preached in a hundred villages until it was in their bones.

And also some women. Stop there, because a first-century reader would have. Only Luke records this, and it was remarkable in its culture. Rabbis had disciples, and disciples were men. Some rabbis said it was better to burn the words of the law than to teach them to a woman. A teacher travelling from village to village with a company that included women was not merely unusual; it was the kind of arrangement that generated exactly the accusation his enemies had already made in the previous chapter, that he was a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence. Jesus welcomed women as followers, who travelled with him and learned from him, and Luke gives special attention to women throughout his Gospel.

Who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Notice how they are identified. Every one of them is described by what was done for her, not by what she brought. Their discipleship was a response to what Jesus had done for them, like the woman of 7:36–50. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising. It is a collection of the rescued.

Mary, called Magdalene. Then a name, and it needs rescuing from fourteen centuries of misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the western shore of the lake, south of Capernaum, and the surname simply says where she was from. She stood at the cross when the men had gone (23:49; Mark 15:40), saw the burial (23:55), was at the tomb on the third morning (24:10), and was the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:11–18).

From whom seven demons had gone out. What Luke tells us about her is that seven demons came out of her: a severe case of possession, perhaps over a long time. Seven speaks of complete bondage, and of complete deliverance. It is affliction, not scandal, and it is the only thing Scripture ever says about her past. She was a woman under an oppression so total that Luke has to use a number for it, and she got free.

What it does not mean. Nothing in Scripture says Mary Magdalene was a prostitute. She is not the woman who wept at Jesus’ feet in the previous chapter. That woman is deliberately left unnamed, a few verses earlier; the accident of neighbouring paragraphs is what first invited the merger, and a sermon of Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century, identifying her with the sinful woman of 7:37 and with Mary of Bethany, fixed it in the Western imagination for a thousand years. There is no basis for it anywhere in the text. Luke introduces her here as a new character, freed from demons, not from immorality. She was a woman of means and devotion, and a witness of the resurrection.

Why does it matter who Mary Magdalene was? Because the truth honours both Christ and her. The legend turned her into a symbol of sexual sin repented, and in doing so it obscured what the Gospels actually say: that she was set free from a terrible bondage, that she gave her money and her life to Jesus, that she stayed at the cross, and that the risen Lord appeared first to her and sent her to tell the apostles. That is a greater story than the legend. And it is a warning to all of us: tradition, however old and beautiful, must always be tested by Scripture.

In a sentence. Jesus travelled through towns and villages preaching the kingdom, with the Twelve and with women he had healed, including Mary Magdalene, freed from seven demons.

On a Tuesday. Jesus welcomes all who have been freed by him to follow him. What has he freed you from? Name it, and let it lead to devotion. And look at the company you keep at church: if you find you are drawn only to the promising, remember that his company was made up of the rescued.

For worship. The King of heaven walked the roads of Galilee proclaiming his own kingdom, and the people he gathered round him were the ones he had set free. He does not recruit the impressive; he rescues the bound, and then lets them walk with him. Mary Magdalene, once possessed by seven demons, became the first witness of his resurrection. That is what his grace does with a ruined life.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake. Nothing in Scripture says she was the sinful woman of chapter 7.

parallels.desc: from whom he had cast out seven demons

verseByVerse.quote: and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.

Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager. Two more names, and then the sentence that explains how any of this was possible. Herod is Herod Antipas. Chuza was his steward (epitropos), a high official managing the royal household or estates. Take in what that means. Chuza managed the estate and finances of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell and would eventually have his head brought in on a platter. Joanna is a court wife. She has status, money, and a husband employed by the enemy. And she is walking around Galilee with an itinerant preacher from Nazareth. Whatever conversations that produced in her household, Luke does not tell us, and they cannot have been comfortable.

The gospel in Herod’s house. The gospel reached even into Herod’s household. Acts 13:1 mentions Manaen, brought up with Herod, among the leaders at Antioch; and Paul sends greetings from the saints of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22). Joanna is named again at the empty tomb (24:10), so whatever it cost her, she was still there at the end. Perhaps she was one of Luke’s sources for the inside story of Herod (9:7–9; 23:8–12).

And Susanna, and many others. A name with no story at all, and then a crowd of women whose names nobody wrote down. Susanna is otherwise unknown. But she was known to Jesus, and her name is in Scripture for ever.

Who provided for them out of their means. Here is the detail that changes how the whole ministry looks. Provided (diēkonoun) means served, ministered: the root behind our word deacon. And it is in the continuous tense: they kept on providing. Out of their means is plain: it was their own money. So the Galilean ministry of Jesus Christ was funded by women. Thirteen men walking from village to village, eating every day, sleeping somewhere every night, for the better part of three years, with no visible income, and Luke tells us in half a verse where the money came from.

Somebody bought the bread. That is worth saying plainly, because it is easy to romanticise the finances of the gospel and pretend they were not there. They were. Somebody bought the bread. And the people who bought it are named here, once, and then never mentioned again in connection with it. Jesus, who would feed five thousand, allowed himself to be supported by the gifts of these women. Their giving was ministry. Women of means were the patrons of Jesus’ ministry, as Lydia and others would be of Paul’s (Acts 16:14–15).

A doctrine of giving. There is a whole doctrine of Christian giving in that half-verse, and it long predates Paul’s collection for Jerusalem. These women did not preach in the synagogues. What they had was resources, and they put them under the mission, quietly, for years, and the four Gospels exist partly because they did.

Is giving money really ministry, or just a lesser support role? It is ministry, in the full sense of the word. Luke uses the same verb for these women that the New Testament uses for the service of deacons and for Christ’s own service (22:27). Paul calls the Philippians’ gift to him a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Philippians 4:18). Not everyone is called to preach, but everyone who belongs to Christ is called to serve, and putting your money under the gospel is one of the plainest ways to do it. The preacher in the pulpit and the giver in the pew are partners in the same work (Philippians 1:5).

How much should I give? The New Testament does not set a fixed percentage, but it gives clear principles. Give regularly and in proportion to what God has given you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously, because whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly (2 Corinthians 9:6). Give cheerfully, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the work of the gospel in your own church, which supports those who teach you (Galatians 6:6), and then beyond it. Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. The real question is not what is the least I can give, but what does this gift say about where my treasure is (12:34)?

In a sentence. Joanna, from Herod’s court, Susanna and many other women supported Jesus and the Twelve from their own resources.

On a Tuesday. Giving your money to support gospel ministry is serving Christ. Do it gladly, as these women did. Look at your bank statement for last month and ask what it says about the kingdom of God. And thank God this week for the quiet givers in your church, whose names no one mentions, who keep the bread on the table.

For worship. The Lord of all the earth, who owns the cattle on a thousand hills, chose to be fed by the gifts of a handful of women. He who was rich became poor, so that through his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and he lets his people share in his work by sharing what he has first given them. Nothing given to him in love is forgotten. Joanna and Susanna are in his book.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas; Joanna came from his court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is Jesus's own explanation of why his ministry produces such varied responses — and why his disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. He tells it publicly (vv. 4-8), then explains it privately (vv. 9-15), with a hard word about the purpose of parables in between.

Note when he tells it. Not to a disappointing turnout, but to a great crowd — and what he says is a story in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing. He is telling the truth about crowds.

The picture was entirely ordinary. In that agriculture, sowing came before ploughing: a man walked the field broadcasting seed by the handful, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed genuinely did fall everywhere. The sower is not careless; that is simply how the job was done, and it matters — the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground.

The disciples ask what it means, and Jesus's answer is one of the most important passages in the Gospels on parabolic teaching: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'” The quotation is Isaiah 6:9-10, the commission given after the vision of the throne — the hardening that follows persistent rejection of revelation.

This should not be softened, and three things hold it together. It is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given; Luke has shown a Nazareth that tried to kill him and a delegation plotting his death. A parable is also a door held ajar, hiding the thing from the casual and rewarding the man who comes back and asks — which is exactly what has just happened in verse 9. And it is mercy as well as judgement: to be told plainly and reject it plainly is a far more terrible position.

The explanation identifies the seed as the word of God, which settles a great deal. The variable in this parable is never the seed; it is the ground. The path is hardened by ordinary traffic. The rock is shallow soil over limestone, where the fastest growth in the field is the first to die. The thorns are already rooted and simply grow at the same time, for the same water and light. And the good soil holds the word fast in an honest heart and bears fruit with patience.

It is not a rigid psychological classification. It is a mirror, and every hearer is invited to hold it up.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the sower is the foundational parable — Mark records Jesus saying, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” (Mark 4:13). It establishes the principle governing all his teaching: the response to the word determines everything.

The seed does not change. It is the same word in all four soils, and the same generous hand scattering it. What varies is the condition of the heart it lands in — which is the basis of the New Testament's consistent call to prepare the heart through humility, through the removal of competing loves, through the patient reception of what has been given.

The description of the good soil — “an honest and good heart” — describes a heart that is not simply admirable. The heart he commends is not the morally superior one but the honest one: the heart that will let the word say what it says without negotiating, and does not flinch when the diagnosis is unflattering.

And the last word is patience, patient endurance. The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is the slowest. Fruit takes a season, and there is no arrangement by which it can be brought forward.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable is a diagnostic tool. The question it puts to every hearer is not “have you heard the gospel?” but “what has happened to the word in you?”

Has it been taken away before it could go in — by distraction, by noise, by a life with no quiet in it? A footpath is not naturally hard ground; it is ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get into it, and the traffic that packed it down was perfectly innocent.

The rock soil frightens sincere believers, and it should be handled carefully. It describes someone who fell away — who is no longer there — not someone who is struggling and worried about it. Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes (Phil. 1:6; John 10:28), and John's own comment on those who left is that “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The remedy is never introspection; a plant cannot inspect its own roots. It is to go deeper, in the unspectacular disciplines nobody sees, before the drought arrives — because the sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

The thorns are the most dangerous soil, because nothing appears to be wrong. And not one of the three Jesus names is a sin: cares, riches, and the ordinary pleasures of life. The choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things — which is exactly why it is so hard to see, and why the outcome is stated so precisely: their fruit does not mature. Not nothing at all. Perpetually promising, and never actually there.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: a sower went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.

And when a great crowd was gathering. A great crowd is gathering, people coming from town after town, and this is the moment Jesus chooses to tell a story about how most seed fails. That is worth noticing before anything else. He is not looking at a discouraging turnout. He is looking at a great crowd, and what he says to them is a parable in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing. He is not being pessimistic. He is telling the truth about crowds, and preparing his disciples for the next three years, and for every century since. The crowds were large, but how many truly heard? The parable answers.

He said in a parable. A parable is a story from everyday life that carries a spiritual meaning. It reveals truth to those who want to hear, and conceals it from those who do not (v. 10).

A sower went out to sow his seed. The picture is entirely ordinary and every person listening had watched it done. Seed was scattered by hand, broadcast over the field as the sower walked. In that farming, it seems, sowing often came before ploughing: a man walked across the field with a bag at his hip, broadcasting seed by the handful in wide arcs, and afterwards the ground was turned over. Which means the seed genuinely did fall everywhere: on the path worn across the field by villagers, on the thin soil over the limestone shelf, into the corners where last year’s thorns were still rooted. The sower is not careless. That is simply how the job was done, and it matters for reading the parable: the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground. Only Luke says his seed.

Some fell along the path. Hard footpaths ran through and around the fields, packed hard by generations of feet. The seed could not sink in. It lies on the surface, gets walked on, and the birds have it before the ploughing. Nothing has gone wrong with the seed. It simply never got below the surface, because the surface would not let it.

And was trampled underfoot. Only Luke adds this, and it is the detail of a careful reporter. Before the birds even arrive, the ordinary traffic of ordinary life has walked over it.

And the birds of the air devoured it. Lying on the surface, it was easy picking.

The sower is not named. One more thing before the other soils, and it governs how the whole parable is heard. Jesus never identifies the sower. He identifies the seed (v. 11) and he identifies all four soils, and about the man with the bag he says nothing at all. That silence is deliberate, and it is a mercy to everyone who has ever tried to sow anything. The parable is not about the skill of the preacher. It is not a study in technique, or timing, or how the message was framed. The sower does one thing: he walks the field and scatters, generously, over ground he cannot control and mostly cannot even see.

So does it not matter how we share the gospel? It matters, but not in the way we fear. We should speak clearly, kindly and wisely (Colossians 4:5–6), and Paul worked hard to remove needless obstacles (1 Corinthians 9:19–23). But the parable lifts from us the burden of thinking the harvest depends on our skill. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). Your job is to scatter the seed faithfully and widely; the soil is in God’s hands. That frees you to share Christ without manipulation, and without despair when most people do not respond.

In a sentence. To a great crowd, Jesus told a parable of a sower whose seed partly fell on the path, where it was trampled and eaten by birds.

On a Tuesday. Being in the crowd around Jesus is not the same as truly hearing him. How are you hearing today? And if you are a parent, a Sunday school teacher, or a friend who has spoken of Christ and seen nothing, take heart: your task was to sow. Keep scattering.

For worship. The God who sows is extravagant. He does not measure out his word only to the ground that looks promising; he flings it across the whole field, path and rock and thorns alike. His generosity in the gospel is wider than our calculations, and the seed he scatters is living and abiding (1 Peter 1:23). Wherever it takes root, the harvest is his.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold. As he said these things, he called out: he who has ears to hear, let him hear.

And some fell on the rock. Three more soils, and each fails at a different depth. This is not bare stone. Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil, and to a man walking the field it looks like the rest. Seed goes in, germinates fast, precisely because the shallow soil warms quickly, and comes up before anything else in the field. Then the sun comes, and the roots find rock instead of water.

It withered away, because it had no moisture. Only Luke mentions moisture: no depth, no water, no life. The fastest growth in the field is the first to die.

And some fell among thorns. Here nothing appears to be wrong at all. The soil is good, the seed goes in, the plant grows, and so does everything else. The thorns are not planted; they are already there, roots left in the ground from last year, though not visible. They do not attack the wheat. They simply grow at the same time, for the same water and the same light, and they grow faster and stronger than the grain. Note the verb: choked. Strangled. It is a slow death by competition, and the crop is still standing when it happens.

And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold. Deep, clean, prepared ground. A hundred grains for one is an enormous return, an extraordinary harvest, far beyond what a farmer in that country would normally expect (compare Genesis 26:12, where Isaac reaped a hundredfold because the LORD blessed him). The figure is deliberately extravagant. Whatever the failures, the yield of the fourth soil is not merely adequate. It more than covers everything lost on the other three. The word of God bears abundant fruit in a good heart.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Luke says he called out: he raised his voice, at the end, over a crowd. A summons to pay attention. Everyone has ears; not everyone truly hears. Hearing in the Bible means listening, understanding and obeying. And the sentence is itself a test. Anyone can hear a story about farming; what he is asking for is the kind of hearing that goes past the surface and lets the thing in. Which is exactly what the parable is about. A man who listens to the parable of the soils and does not ask which soil he is has just demonstrated the answer.

Can a person change from one soil to another? Yes, by the grace of God. The parable describes how people respond to the word at a given time, not a fixed caste they are born into. Hard ground can be broken up; God promises to take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). Many Christians can look back on years when the word bounced off them, or sprang up and died, before God finally made the soil good. That is why we keep sowing, and why we keep praying for those who have heard and not yet believed.

In a sentence. Other seed fell on rock and withered, among thorns and was choked, and on good soil, where it yielded a hundredfold, and Jesus called out to those with ears to hear.

On a Tuesday. You have ears. Use them. Listen to Jesus’ word with your whole attention. Before you next hear a sermon, ask God to make your heart good soil, and afterwards ask yourself one honest question: what did that word ask me to do, and have I done it?

For worship. The harvest belongs to God, and it is glorious. Whatever is lost on the path, the rock and the thorns, the good soil yields a hundredfold, and the Lord of the harvest will not be disappointed in the end. A great multitude that no one can number will stand before his throne (Revelation 7:9), the fruit of seed scattered by hand across ordinary fields.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil. A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said: to you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant. Notice what the disciples do, because it is the whole point of what follows. They do not assume they have understood. They come back and ask. Disciples ask; the desire to understand marks those who truly hear. That asking is itself the parable being enacted. The crowd heard a story about farming and went home; these men heard the same story and pressed for more. What separates them at this stage is not superior insight. Mark records Jesus telling them plainly that they had not understood it either (Mark 4:13). What separates them is that they came back.

To you it has been given. A gift, by God’s grace. Note the passive: it has been given. Their understanding is not an achievement. Somebody handed it to them. Understanding the kingdom is not achieved by intelligence but given by God (10:21; Matthew 16:17).

To know the secrets of the kingdom of God. Secrets (mystēria) are mysteries: not puzzles, but truths once hidden and now revealed by God. Above all, the secret is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, in an unexpected form, like a seed, and not yet like a harvest (Ephesians 3:3–6).

But for others they are in parables. To outsiders who do not believe, the parables remain riddles.

So that seeing they may not see. This is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and it should not be softened. Jesus is quoting Isaiah 6:9–10: the commission God gave Isaiah after the vision of the throne, sending him to a rebellious people who would hear and not understand, and telling him in advance that his preaching would harden them. Luke, unlike Mark, leaves out the end of the quotation (lest they turn and be forgiven), perhaps because he holds it back for the end of Acts (Acts 28:26–27).

Does God then deliberately blind people? Three things have to be held together. First, this is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given. Isaiah’s commission comes after generations of ignored prophets, and Luke has already shown us a Nazareth that tried to kill Jesus and experts plotting against him. The parables are a form of judgement on those who have already rejected the truth. They hear the stories without understanding, because they do not want to. To those who reject the light, more light is withheld (v. 18). Second, a parable is not merely a veil. It is also a door held ajar. It hides the thing from the casual and rewards the man who comes back and asks, which is precisely what has just happened in verse 9. The same story that closed the crowd’s ears opened these men’s, and the difference was whether they returned. Third, this is mercy as well as judgement. To be told plainly and to reject it plainly is a far more terrible position than to be told in a story you did not follow. A parable leaves the door open longer than a sermon does.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was trying to keep people from salvation. He taught in parables also to draw people in, to provoke thought, and to make truth memorable. But for the hard-hearted, they confirm their blindness. The same sun melts wax and hardens clay. And what cannot be done with this verse is to use it to explain away one’s own dullness. The remedy is in verse 9, and it is not complicated. They asked.

If understanding is given, why do some get it and others not? Scripture answers with two truths and does not let us drop either. Understanding is God’s gift, given freely to whom he wills, so that no one may boast (Matthew 11:25–27; 1 Corinthians 4:7). And those who do not understand are not innocent victims; they are people who love the darkness and will not come to the light (John 3:19). God never blinds a willing seeker. If you want to understand, that wanting is itself the beginning of the gift, and the promise stands: ask, and it will be given; seek, and you will find (11:9).

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that God had given them to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but for others they remain in parables, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about seeing without seeing.

On a Tuesday. When you read a passage you do not understand, do what the disciples did: come back and ask. Pray over it, read it again, look it up, ask your pastor or a mature friend. Do not let it slide off because it is hard. And pray by name for those you love who hear and do not see.

For worship. If you understand the gospel, it is God’s gift. Thank him, and ask him to give the same gift to those you love. The God who said, let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). We did not find the secret; he told it to us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the parable is this: the seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.

The seed is the word of God. Now the parable is this. Before anything else, that identification settles a great deal. The seed is the gospel message. It is not the preacher, not the technique, not the atmosphere of the meeting, not the personality of the man scattering it. It is the word of God, and it is exactly the same seed in all four soils. Its power is not in the sower but in the seed (Isaiah 55:10–11; 1 Peter 1:23). The sower is first Jesus, and then everyone who spreads his word.

The variable is the ground. Which means the variable in this parable is never the seed. It is the ground. That is a hard word for anyone who preaches and a liberating one. Hard, because it removes the excuse that a poor response means the wrong method was used. Liberating, because it removes the burden of believing that a better performance would have produced a better harvest. The sower’s job is to scatter the seed. He cannot manufacture soil.

The ones along the path are those who have heard. The hard-hearted: the word does not get in. They hear it, but it makes no impression.

Then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts. The birds are the devil. Two things in that sentence deserve attention. The first is that there is an enemy, and Jesus names him. This is not a psychological account of inattention. Something intelligent and hostile is at work in the moment between hearing and believing, and its whole strategy here is remarkably modest. It does not need to refute the word. It does not need to produce an argument. It only needs to remove it before it goes in: by distraction, by doubt, by forgetfulness, by the next thing that comes along. The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4).

So that they may not believe and be saved. Only Luke adds this. That is what is actually at stake in a distracted hour. Jesus states plainly that Satan’s aim in taking the word away is to prevent faith and salvation. Faith comes from hearing the word (Romans 10:17); Satan’s strategy is to stop the hearing from taking root.

What a footpath is. Now think about what a footpath actually is. It is not naturally hard ground. It is ordinary soil that has been walked over so many times that nothing can get into it, and the traffic that packed it down was perfectly innocent. Nobody hardened it on purpose. Which is the exact danger of a life with no quiet in it. The word arrives on Sunday, and by the time the car is out of the car park there has been a conversation, a screen, a plan for the afternoon, and it is gone, and nobody did anything wrong.

Can the devil take the word from a Christian? He can steal a particular sermon from a believer’s attention, and he often does. But he cannot snatch a true believer out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28), because the word that saves has been planted by the Spirit, who keeps what he has begun. The path in this parable describes those in whom the word never went in at all. For the Christian, the warning is practical: guard the moment after hearing. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

In a sentence. The seed is God’s word, and the path represents those whose hard hearts let the devil snatch away the word before they can believe and be saved.

On a Tuesday. When you hear God’s word, do not let it lie on the surface. Think about it, pray over it, and let it sink in before the devil can take it. Try this next Sunday: before you speak to anyone after the sermon, take two minutes to name to God the one thing he said to you. On the drive home, talk about it instead of the weather. Protect the quiet.

For worship. The word of God is living and active (Hebrews 4:12), and the devil fears it. That is why he works so hard to take it away. The same word that called light out of darkness and Lazarus out of the tomb has been sown in our hearts. Blessed be the God whose word is stronger than every bird that comes for it, and who has caused it to take root in us.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.

And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. This is the soil that frightens people, and it should be handled carefully, because it has done real damage to sensitive consciences. Start with what is genuinely there. It is an enthusiastic response, and the response is real as far as it goes: they receive it with joy, and the joy is not called false. They seem to be converted. Something happened, and it was visible, and it may have been more visible than what happened in the good soil. But joy alone is not proof of genuine faith.

But these have no root. No depth: the word has not gone down into their heart and will. And root is precisely the part nobody can see, the underground work that nobody applauds and that only shows up in a drought.

They believe for a while. Only Luke says believe. A real but temporary belief: intellectual and emotional, but not a heart transformed by God.

And in time of testing fall away. Testing (peirasmos) is the same word as at 4:13: trial, or temptation, the two senses English keeps apart and Greek does not. Matthew says, when tribulation or persecution arises (Matthew 13:21). When following Jesus becomes costly, they give up. Fall away (aphistantai) means depart, apostatise. The plant does not die because a wind blew it over. It dies because the sun came out and there was nothing beneath it to reach for water.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall away? Arminians take this as a believer who loses salvation. Verdict: the parable describes a faith that was never rooted, never the saving faith of the good soil. Its fruit never came. Scripture teaches that those whom God truly saves he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and that those who fall away permanently show they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). This is the perseverance of the saints. But the warning is real, and it is one of the means God uses to keep his people: examine yourselves.

Is this me? Have I lost my salvation? The question presses on any believer who has ever gone through a bad season, and three things need saying, in this order. First, the passage is not describing someone who is struggling. It describes someone who fell away, who is no longer there. A person worried about this verse is by definition still asking the question, which is not what the rock soil does. Second, Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). John’s own comment on those who left is not that they lost something but that they went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The rock soil is not a Christian who was lost; it is a plant that never had root. Third, and this is the pastoral point, the remedy is never endless introspection. Staring at your own root system is exactly what a plant cannot do. What can be done is to go deeper: to put the word somewhere it can reach water, in the unspectacular disciplines that nobody sees, before the drought arrives. Because it will. The sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

How do I put down roots? Roots grow in hidden places and over time. Read the Bible daily, not for information only but to meet God. Pray, especially when you do not feel like it. Sit under faithful preaching week by week, and come to the Lord’s Table. Join yourself to a church where people know you well enough to notice if you wither. Learn the great truths of the faith, so that when trouble comes you know what God has promised. And obey what you already know, because obedience is how the word goes down from the head into the will. None of it is dramatic. All of it is how God keeps his people.

In a sentence. The rocky ground represents those who receive the word with joy and believe for a while, but having no root, fall away when testing comes.

On a Tuesday. Enthusiasm is not enough. Let God’s word go deep. When testing comes, it will show whether you have roots. If you are a new Christian full of joy, thank God for the joy and give your attention to the roots. If you are leading others, do not measure a conversion by its excitement; walk with new believers through their first drought.

For worship. The Lord who calls is the Lord who keeps. Those whom he justified he also glorified (Romans 8:30), and not one of his sheep will be lost. He does not plant his people in shallow ground and leave them to the sun. He sends his Spirit as the deep water, and he himself is the root of their life, so that they are like a tree planted by streams of water, whose leaf does not wither (Psalm 1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.

And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear. This is the most dangerous soil in the parable, because it is the only one where nothing appears to be wrong. They hear, and the word grows. But it shares the soil with other things. There is no bird here and no drought. The seed went in properly and the plant is growing. The man is still in the field, still green, still where he was. What is happening is entirely gradual and entirely invisible until harvest, when it turns out there is nothing on the stalk.

But as they go on their way. Gradually, over time, not in a sudden crisis. It does not happen at a moment. There is no decision, no crisis, no turning point. It happens over a decade, in the course of getting on with life.

They are choked. Strangled slowly.

By the cares and riches and pleasures of life. Look at the three thorns Jesus names, because not one of them is in itself a sin. Cares: anxieties, worries about daily life, the future, money, health, a difficult child, an ageing parent, a job that may not last (12:22–31; 21:34). Riches: not theft, simply having things and the work of keeping them, and the love of money and possessions that so easily grows from it (12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). Pleasures of life: only Luke adds this. Not vice, but the ordinary enjoyments; the word covers the perfectly innocent pleasures of an ordinary existence, good things that crowd out God.

The thorns are legitimate things. These are the thorns. Which means the choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things, and that is precisely why it is so hard to see. A man being strangled by an obvious sin usually knows it. A man being strangled by his mortgage, his hobbies and his family’s diary has nothing to repent of that he can name.

And their fruit does not mature. The outcome is stated with exact precision. Not, they bear no fruit at all. There is growth, perhaps even the beginning of fruit, but it never ripens. Perpetually promising and never actually there. A divided heart cannot bear the fruit of the kingdom. No one can serve two masters (16:13).

Are the thorn-soil hearers saved? The seed is choked and brings no fruit to maturity, and in the parable only the good soil bears a crop. The more likely reading is that they never truly believed: a faith that bears no fruit at all is not saving faith (compare John 15:2, 6). Some Christians read them as believers who are saved but fruitless. But a true believer may struggle with worries and riches and still bear fruit; the warning is not to let them choke the word.

Is it wrong to enjoy the good things of life? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and food, friendship, marriage, work and rest are his gifts. The thorns are not the pleasures themselves but the place they take. A pleasure becomes a thorn when it takes the time, the attention and the love that belong to God, when it becomes the thing you cannot give up. The test is not whether you enjoy things, but whether you could enjoy them less for Christ’s sake, and whether they lead you to thank him or to forget him.

In a sentence. The thorny ground represents those who hear, but whose faith is gradually choked by worries, wealth and pleasures, so that it never bears mature fruit.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that takes a minute and is uncomfortable. Not, what sins am I fighting? But: what has quietly become non-negotiable in my week, and when did I last examine it? Thorns are not planted. They are simply left, and they were there before the seed was. What thorns are growing in your heart: worries, money, or pleasures? Pull one out this week, before it chokes the word: cancel the thing that always crowds out prayer, give away what has begun to own you, hand the worry to God by name.

For worship. Christ is better than all the good things that compete with him. In his presence there is fullness of joy, and at his right hand are pleasures for evermore (Psalm 16:11). The cares he tells us to cast on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). The riches he offers are the unsearchable riches of Christ. The thorns promise life and deliver strangling; he promises his cross and delivers life. He wore the thorns himself, as a crown, so that the curse of the ground could be lifted.

verseByVerse.quote: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.

As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast. Four things, and every one of them is unspectacular. Hearing the word: the same word, from the same sower, that fell on all the other ground. Nothing different has been offered here. Hold it fast (katechousin): keep it, retain it, grip it, not letting it go. It is active. This is not passive reception; it is a man who has taken hold of something and does not let go of it, and the reason the word is needed is that things get taken. The bird came for the path soil. Nobody grips what nothing is trying to remove. Mary treasured the word (2:19). The good hearer hangs on to it.

In an honest and good heart. Only Luke has this phrase (kalē kai agathē), which in Greek described a person of fine and noble character. And Jesus fills it with entirely different content. The heart he commends is not the morally superior one. It is the honest one: the heart that is genuine and open to God, that is not managing an impression, that will let the word say what it says without negotiating, that does not flinch when the diagnosis is unflattering. That is the one qualification for good soil that anybody can identify in themselves. Not, am I fruitful? That is not visible yet. But: when the word says something I do not like, do I let it stand?

Where does a good heart come from? Such a heart is itself God’s gift; he prepares the soil. The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to what Paul said (Acts 16:14). No one is good soil by nature. Since the fall, every human heart is path, rock or thorns until God breaks it up and makes it new (Jeremiah 17:9; Ezekiel 36:26). If your heart has received the word and held it fast, give God the glory. And if you long for a better heart, ask him for it. That longing is already his work.

And bear fruit with patience. The last word is patience (hypomonē): endurance, perseverance, steadfastness under pressure. It is the opposite of the rocky ground (v. 13), and it is the note the whole parable ends on. Genuine faith keeps going. Fruit takes time; it does not appear overnight. That deserves emphasis in a hurried Christianity that measures everything by immediate visible outcome. The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is the slowest. Fruit takes a season, and it takes the same season whether or not anybody is watching, and there is no arrangement by which it can be brought forward.

What is the fruit? The fruit is a changed life: the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience and good works (Colossians 1:10); and, in God’s time, others brought to faith. It is not measured by size or fame. A hundredfold in the parable is the same seed reproduced, and the fruit of the word in you is Christlikeness. Do not compare your harvest with someone else’s; Jesus speaks elsewhere of a hundredfold, sixty and thirty, and all of it is good soil (Matthew 13:23).

The marks of good soil. So the marks of the only soil that works are these: an honest heart, a firm grip, and time. Nothing here is dramatic. Nothing here is beyond an ordinary believer. And it is the only one of the four that ends with a harvest.

In a sentence. The good soil represents those who hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and patiently bear fruit.

On a Tuesday. Hear, hold fast, and persevere. Fruit comes with patience. Do not give up. Choose one verse from Sunday’s sermon and carry it with you all week: write it down, repeat it, pray it. That is what holding fast looks like in an ordinary week. And when you see little fruit in yourself, remember that the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it (James 5:7).

For worship. The Lord of the harvest is patient. He waits through the long seasons, and he does not give up on the soil he has prepared. He who began a good work will complete it, and the harvest of his word in his people will be a hundredfold, to the praise of his glorious grace. Every bit of fruit in us is his, and every bit of patience is his gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two brief teachings follow the parable, and both apply it.

The lamp saying comes first, and its placing is deliberate. Jesus has just explained a parable privately, to a small group, after saying that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not others. A disciple could easily draw the wrong conclusion: we have been let into something, and it is ours.

“No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.” Both absurdities are exact: a jar smothers the flame for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed burns the house down. Neither preserves light; both destroy it while pretending to keep it.

And note the purpose clause — so that those who enter may see. Not so the lamp may be admired, and not for the household's benefit. The secrets of the kingdom were given to be put where strangers can see by them.

“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest” cuts both ways. Forward, it is a promise: the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house, and Luke is writing the second volume that proves it. But everything concealed also comes out eventually — which is terrifying for anyone hiding something, and one of the great comforts of Scripture for anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off.

“Take care then how you hear” is the imperative that gathers up the whole chapter. And the principle attached to it — to the one who has, more will be given — is not a cruelty but a description of how understanding actually behaves. Capacity grows by use, and atrophies without it. Luke alone adds the sharpest phrase: “even what he thinks that he has.” The man's holdings were never what he supposed.

Then Jesus's mother and brothers arrive, and he redefines family: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” It is not a rejection of Mary. It is the good soil of verse 15, six verses on, given a family name — and it is the same hearing-and-doing that ended the sermon at 6:47-49.
verseByVerse.theology:
The lamp saying and the redefinition of family are the application of the parable to the disciples' own vocation. They have been given the secrets of the kingdom (v. 10) — not for private illumination but for public proclamation. The word they received is the lamp; the world they are being sent into is the stand.

The parable of the sower describes what happens when the word meets different soils. The lamp saying describes what those in whom it took root are to do with it.

And the family saying should be read alongside what Luke has already established about Mary. She is not being demoted; she is the founding member of the category. The woman who said “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38) heard the word of God and did it, and Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the one she walked through.

Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing — which is why the brothers standing outside at this point in the story, who did not yet believe in him (John 7:5), are outside in more senses than one.
verseByVerse.examples:
The redefinition of family as those who “hear the word of God and do it” is the basis of the extraordinary community the church creates across every natural human division. People who share nothing by blood, culture, language or class are family because they share the same word and the same response to it.

This is the sociological miracle of the first-century church, which drew together Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, into a community the ancient world had no category for. It remains the miracle of every congregation that takes hearing-and-doing as its defining identity rather than any natural affinity.

“Take care then how you hear” is worth turning into a practical question, because the parable has just made hearing the decisive variable. Not what was preached, but what was done with it between the car park and Tuesday.

And “even what he thinks that he has” is aimed precisely at the person who is quite sure they are fine. Both the rock soil and the thorn soil had something, and both would have described themselves as having it, and neither had what they supposed — and each found out at the worst possible moment. There is a mercy in being told now, in a season of quiet, rather than in a season of testing.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.

No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar. A lamp, and the saying is placed here on purpose. Jesus has just explained a parable privately, to a small group, after telling the crowd that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not to others. A disciple could very easily draw the wrong conclusion from that: we have been let into something, and it is ours. The lamp saying shuts that down immediately. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick, holding perhaps an hour or two of light. You light it to give light, not to hide it.

Or puts it under a bed. The two absurdities are exact. A jar over it would smother it for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed would set the house on fire. Neither is a way of preserving light. Both are ways of destroying it while pretending to keep it.

But puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Note the purpose clause. Not so that the lamp may be admired, and not so that the household may enjoy it. So that those who enter, people coming in from outside, who do not live there, can see. The word of God, the light of the gospel, is meant to be seen. Those who have received it must let it shine (11:33; Matthew 5:14–16). The secrets of the kingdom were given to the disciples (v. 10) not for their private illumination, and not to be kept secret, but to be put where strangers can see by them.

For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest. This cuts two ways, and both are in the passage. Forward, it is a promise. The truth of the kingdom, now partly hidden in parables, will be fully revealed. What God has revealed is going somewhere; the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house. Luke is writing the second volume that proves it.

Nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. But the sentence has a second edge, and Scripture uses it that way elsewhere. Everything hidden in human hearts will be exposed at the judgement (12:2–3; 1 Corinthians 4:5). There is no permanently private life, no version of a man that stays behind the door for ever, and the day is coming when the lighting is universal. For anyone hiding something, that is terrifying. For anyone who has been misrepresented, slandered, or quietly written off, it is one of the great comforts of Scripture. Nothing stays hidden. Including the truth about you.

What if I have something hidden? Bring it into the light now, before God, and where needed before those you have wronged. The light that will one day expose everything is the same light in which there is forgiveness: if we walk in the light, the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). What is confessed to God is covered by Christ, and it will not be held against you on that day. The secrets that destroy are the ones we keep. A Christian has nothing to fear from the final light, because everything shameful in his life has already been dealt with at the cross.

In a sentence. As a lamp is lit to give light, not hidden, so the word must be made known, for everything hidden will be revealed.

On a Tuesday. Do not hide your faith. Let the light of the gospel be seen in what you say and how you live. Think of the one place in your week where no one knows you are a Christian, at work, at the gym, among a set of friends, and ask what it would look like this week to take the jar off.

For worship. Christ is the light of the world, and he has made his people lamps. The God who dwells in unapproachable light has not hidden himself from us; he has shone into our darkness and set us on a stand. And on the last day, when all things are brought to light, the light will be his glory, and the Lamb will be its lamp (Revelation 21:23).
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.

Take care then how you hear. The conclusion of the parable section. Not what you hear (Jesus has said that elsewhere, and it matters) but how: with an honest heart, holding it fast, obeying it. The whole chapter so far has been about the manner of reception, and this is the command that gathers it up: pay attention to the way you are listening, because the four soils were not four kinds of seed. Hearing is a moral act, with consequences.

For to the one who has, more will be given. Read at speed, the principle sounds like a cruelty: the rich get richer. It is nothing of the kind. It is a description of how understanding actually behaves, and everyone who has ever learned anything knows it is true. Capacity grows by use. To the one who receives the word and responds, more understanding and blessing will be given. A man who acts on what he has understood finds that more is opened to him; the next thing is intelligible because the last one was obeyed. Truth received leads to more truth.

And from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away. A man who receives and does nothing loses even the ability to receive, not by an arbitrary penalty but by atrophy. Nothing is confiscated. It simply wastes. The one who does not respond loses even what he seems to have: his superficial knowledge, his religious privilege. Neglected truth is lost. This is a principle of the spiritual life.

Even what he thinks that he has. Now the phrase that is easy to skim, and it is the sharpest in the sentence. Luke alone has these words. The parallel in Mark says simply what he has. Luke’s version says something more disturbing: the man’s holdings were never what he supposed. He has been carrying a receipt for something that is not in the vault. That is precisely the position of the rock soil and the thorn soil. Both had something. Both would have described themselves as having it. Neither had what they thought they had, and the discovery came at the worst possible moment: the drought, and the harvest. So the warning is not aimed at the person who knows they are empty. It is aimed at the person who is quite sure they are fine.

A mercy in being told now. And there is a mercy in being told now. A man can find out in a season of quiet self-examination what he would otherwise find out in a season of testing. The invitation is still open, and the remedy has not changed since verse 9: he can ask.

What does good listening look like on a Sunday? Come prepared: pray before the service that God would speak, and come rested enough to listen. Listen expecting God, not merely a speaker, to address you (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Have your Bible open and test what you hear by it (Acts 17:11). Listen for yourself before you listen for others: what is this saying to me? Afterwards, talk about it, and decide on one thing to do. And keep listening when the preacher is not gifted; the seed is the word, not the sower.

In a sentence. Be careful how you listen, because those who receive and respond will be given more, while those who do not will lose even what they think they have.

On a Tuesday. Respond to what God shows you today, and he will show you more. Ignore it, and you will lose even that. Is there one thing God made clear to you months ago that you have still not acted on? Do it this week. The next door will not open until you walk through that one.

For worship. God is not stingy with light. To those who receive his word he gives more, and then more again, grace upon grace (John 1:16). He delights to open the Scriptures to those who come back and ask, as the risen Lord opened them to the two on the road until their hearts burned (24:32). Blessed be the Teacher who never tires of teaching those who want to learn.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. He was told: your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you. But he answered them: my mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.

Then his mother and his brothers came to him. Two things are worth registering before the saying itself. The first is his brothers. Luke mentions them without explanation; Mark names four of them, James, Joses (Joseph), Judas and Simon, and mentions sisters as well (Mark 6:3). The plainest reading of the text is the one it invites: Mary and Joseph went on to have a family, and Jesus grew up the eldest of several children. And John tells us plainly what the brothers thought of him at this stage: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). They came to faith only after the resurrection (Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:7).

Why had they come? Luke is discreet; Mark is not, and records that his family set out to seize him, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31–35). Whatever exactly is happening at the edge of this crowd, it is not a social visit.

But they could not reach him because of the crowd. Even his family had to wait.

My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it. And then the answer, which has troubled readers for centuries. Read as a snub, it is shocking. Read carefully, it is not a snub at all. He does not say, I have no mother and brothers, and he does not refuse to see them. He loved his mother, and from the cross he provided for her (John 19:26–27). What he does is redefine the family, in public, in front of a crowd, at exactly the moment the claim of blood was being pressed on him. A new family has come into being, bound not by blood but by obedience to God’s word, and this relationship is closer, and more important, than the natural family.

The good soil with a family name. Notice what the definition is: those who hear the word of God and do it. That is the good soil of verse 15, six verses on, given a family name. It is the conclusion of the parables about hearing. It is also, almost word for word, the two builders at the end of the sermon (6:47–49). Luke has been circling this since chapter 6, and here he lands it.

Not a rejection of Mary. Which means the answer is not a rejection of Mary. It is an inclusion of everybody else on the terms Mary herself met first. The woman who said, let it be to me according to your word (1:38), is the founding member of the family. Even Mary’s blessedness lies chiefly in hearing and keeping God’s word (11:27–28). And Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the same one she walked through. Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing.

Who were these brothers? The natural reading is that they were Mary’s later children, Jesus’ half-brothers (compare 2:7, where Jesus is her firstborn son; Mark 6:3). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, read them as cousins, since the Hebrew word for brother can be broad, or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. But Scripture never suggests either, and the plain reading is the more likely.

Does following Jesus mean neglecting my family? No. Scripture commands us to honour father and mother (Ephesians 6:2) and says that anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus himself cared for his mother to the end. What this passage teaches is priority, not neglect: when family claims and Christ’s claims collide, Christ comes first (14:26). For many believers, especially converts from other faiths, that collision is painful and real. For them the promise is precious: they gain, in the church, mothers and brothers and sisters a hundredfold (Mark 10:29–30).

In a sentence. When told his mother and brothers wanted to see him, Jesus said that his true mother and brothers are those who hear God’s word and do it.

On a Tuesday. If you hear and do God’s word, you belong to Jesus’ family. Treat other believers as your family. Who in your church has no family nearby, or a family that has rejected them for Christ? Invite them to your table this month. And if your own relatives do not yet believe, keep loving them as Jesus loved his brothers: patiently, until the day they too may come in.

For worship. The eternal Son of God is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He has opened the family of God to people with no claim of blood, and adopted them through his own blood. Strangers in a crowd, Gentiles from the ends of the earth, sinners like us: all who hear the word of God and do it are his mother and brothers and sisters. What a family, and what an elder Brother.

parallels.desc: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus and the disciples set out across the lake at his own initiative — “Let us go across to the other side.” They are in that boat, in that weather, because he told them to get in. The storm is not a consequence of any failure; obedience put them there.

He falls asleep. It is the only place in the Gospels where he is described as sleeping, and it is one of the plainest windows into his humanity: he had been preaching all day, and the moment the boat was under way he was unconscious in the stern.

Then a windstorm comes down on the lake. The geography explains it — the lake sits some two hundred metres below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling cold air off the heights into the warm basin without warning. A small, shallow lake goes from flat to lethal in minutes. It still does.

And these are professional fishermen who have worked this water all their lives. When they wake him with “Master, Master, we are perishing!” it is not landsmen panicking. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown — which is worth saying to anyone taught that fear is always a failure of faith. Sometimes fear is an accurate reading of the instruments.

He “rebuked the wind and the raging waves” — the same verb Luke used of the demon in the synagogue (4:35) and of a fever (4:39). There is no prayer. He speaks to the weather in the imperative.

“And they ceased, and there was a calm.” Luke's word is calm, a dead flat calm — and anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When wind drops, the swell runs on. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant.

“Where is your faith?” is gentler than it looks. He does not ask why they have none; he asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some and mislaid it. What was missing was not courage but the conclusion they should have drawn from everything they had already seen.

And they were more frightened afterwards than during. The wind had threatened their lives; what came next threatened their categories. “Who then is this?”
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is the New Testament's most direct claim that Jesus exercises the prerogatives of the Creator over the natural world.

In the Old Testament only the LORD commands the wind and the sea. “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Ps. 107:29). “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them” (Ps. 89:9). “Who shut in the sea with doors… and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther?” (Job 38:8-11).

The disciples' question — “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” — has only one available answer, and every man in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood. Luke leaves the question hanging; it will not be answered aloud until Peter's confession (9:20).

The sleeping is theologically as significant as the stilling. He is not asleep because he is unconcerned but because he is at peace — the one who will say “do not be anxious” (12:22) practising it in a sinking boat. And it is the fullest possible statement of the incarnation: the Lord of the storm, too tired to stay awake, four feet from men who thought they were dying.
verseByVerse.examples:
The disciples have Jesus in the boat and they are terrified. They have heard the sermon, seen the healings, received the explanation of the parables — and when the storm comes they are afraid and amazed.

That is the honest portrait of early discipleship, and of most later discipleship too. Knowing who Jesus is in the abstract is not the same as trusting him in the specific, wet, embodied crisis. Faith is very seldom lost in a crisis; it is mislaid — and “where is your faith?” is a search rather than an accusation.

The passage is not primarily about the disciples' failure. It is about the one who was in the boat with them. He did not abandon them in the storm and he did not scold them for waking him. He stilled it, and then invited them to examine where their faith had been — not to condemn but to grow.

And the sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these. It heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them: let us go across to the other side of the lake. So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. A windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.

Four miracles. Luke now records four great miracles (8:22–56): over nature, demons, disease and death. They show the authority of the one whose word the disciples are to hear. Having taught them how to hear, he now shows them who it is they are hearing.

Let us go across to the other side of the lake. Hold on to who said that, because it matters for everything that follows. The trip was not the disciples’ idea and it was not a detour. They are in that boat, in that weather, because Jesus told them to get in and where to go. He intended them to reach the other side. That disposes at the outset of a reading this story often gets: that the storm was a consequence of some failure. It was not. Obedience put them there.

As they sailed he fell asleep. It is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus is described as sleeping, and it is one of the plainest windows into his humanity. He is a real man, exhausted after a day of ministry. He has been preaching to crowds all day, and the moment the boat is under way he is unconscious in the stern; Mark adds the detail that he was on the cushion (Mark 4:38). The Son of God, asleep, in a fishing boat, because he was too tired to stay awake. That is not a lapse in the narrative. It is the incarnation, doing what a body does. And he is at peace, trusting his Father: in peace I will both lie down and sleep (Psalm 4:8).

And a windstorm came down on the lake. Came down: the geography explains it. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet (210 m) below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling down to the water from the heights to the east. Cold air off the heights drops into the warm basin without warning, and the lake, which is small and shallow, goes from flat to dangerous in minutes. It still does.

And they were filling with water and were in danger. Luke states the professional verdict plainly: they were in danger. And the men making that assessment include four commercial fishermen who had worked this water their whole lives. This is not landsmen panicking. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown. Which is worth saying to anyone who has been told that fear is always a failure of faith. Sometimes fear is simply an accurate reading of the instruments.

If I am obeying God, why am I in a storm? Because obedience does not exempt us from storms; sometimes it leads us into them. The disciples were exactly where Jesus told them to be. Paul was shipwrecked on a voyage God had appointed (Acts 27). A storm is not proof that you have taken a wrong turn. It may be the very path on which Christ means to show you who he is. The question is not whether storms will come, but who is in the boat with you.

In a sentence. As Jesus and the disciples crossed the lake, he fell asleep, and a violent storm struck, swamping the boat and endangering their lives.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus does not keep you out of storms. He sent them into this one. If you are in one now, at work, in your health, in your family, do not conclude you are outside his will. And be honest about your fear; it may be an accurate reading of the instruments. Then read the next verse.

For worship. He slept in the storm because he was truly man; he stilled it because he was truly God. The Word made flesh grew tired, laid his head on a cushion, and slept in a fishing boat, sharing our weakness so that he could be our Saviour. He knows what exhaustion is. And the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4); even asleep in the stern, the Son of God had never stopped holding the sea.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went and woke him, saying: Master, Master, we are perishing! He awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.

Master, Master, we are perishing! The doubled address is the sound of men shaking somebody awake. Luke’s version is gentler than Mark’s, where they say: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). And their verdict is in the present tense: not, we are going to drown, but we are perishing; it is happening.

They wake him. Notice what they do, though, underneath the panic. They wake him. Whatever they expected of a carpenter in a storm, some instinct sent them to the back of the boat rather than only to the oars. It is not much of a faith, and it is pointed in exactly the right direction, which is very often what faith looks like at three in the morning.

And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves. The verb is rebuked, and Luke has used it before in this Gospel: of the demon in the synagogue (4:35), and of Peter’s mother-in-law’s fever (4:39). It is the word for a sharp word of command to something that has no business behaving as it is. Jesus speaks to the storm as a master to a disobedient servant. And here is the thing to sit with. There is no prayer. He does not ask his Father to still the storm, as a prophet would have. He speaks to the weather, in the imperative.

And they ceased, and there was a calm. Instantly. What followed was a dead flat calm. Anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When a wind drops, the sea does not; the swell runs on for hours afterwards. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant, and the boat is suddenly sitting still on a mirror with twelve soaked men in it. This calm was immediate and complete. What they had asked for was rescue. What they got was a demonstration.

Jesus does what God does. Because in the Scriptures they had learned as boys, there is exactly one person who does this. In the Old Testament, only God controls the sea. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Psalm 89:9; also 65:7). He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Psalm 107:29). God shut in the sea with doors and said, thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:8–11). The one who does that is asleep in the stern of their boat, and they had just woken him up.

Will Jesus always calm my storm? Not always in the way we ask.
