Sometimes he stills the storm; sometimes he stills his child in the storm, and carries him through it; sometimes he brings him home through it. Paul’s thorn was not removed, and many martyrs were not rescued. But this story shows what is always true: nothing in your storm is beyond his command, and you are never in the boat alone. Cry out to him, as the disciples did. He hears, and whatever he does, he will bring you to the other side he promised.

In a sentence. The terrified disciples woke Jesus, and he rebuked the wind and waves, and there was an instant calm.

On a Tuesday. When panic rises, do what the disciples did right: go to the back of the boat. Before you reach for the oars of your own solutions, cry out to him, honestly, even in a sentence. Then do the next sensible thing, trusting that the wind and the waves are under his command.

For worship. The one who sleeps in your boat is Lord of the wind and waves. Cry out to him in your storms. He spoke to the sea that he made, and it lay down like a dog at its master’s word. The God of Psalm 89 and Psalm 107 sat up in a fishing boat, wet and tired, and rebuked the storm. There is no chaos in your life, and no darkness in the world, that does not hear his voice.

parallels.desc: he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: where is your faith? They were afraid, and they marvelled, saying to one another: who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?

Where is your faith? The question is gentler than it looks in English, and it repays attention. He does not say, why have you no faith? He asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some, and that it was mislaid rather than absent. They had faith, but where was it in the storm? It had gone missing when they needed it.

What he is not rebuking. And it is worth being clear about what he is not rebuking. Not their fear of the storm; that was an accurate assessment by professionals. Not their waking him; that was the right instinct. What has gone missing is the conclusion they should have drawn from everything they had already seen: that the person in the boat with them was not in the same category as the weather. Jesus’ word, let us go to the other side, should have been enough. And he was in the boat. They had watched him command a demon and a fever with a word. They had watched a dead man sit up at a town gate. The storm did not find them ignorant; it found them not applying what they knew.

Mislaid, not lost. That is the ordinary condition of most believers in most crises, and there is comfort in seeing it named without contempt. Faith is very seldom lost in a crisis. It is mislaid, and the question is not an accusation but a search: where did you put it?

And they were afraid, and they marveled. Luke is precise and slightly startling here. They were more frightened after the storm stopped than during it. A new fear: not of the storm, but of him. The wind had merely threatened their lives. What came next threatened their categories. The fear of the storm was replaced by awe at the one who controls it.

Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him? There it is: the question this whole Gospel exists to answer, asked out loud for the first time by the men closest to him, sitting in a wet boat on a flat sea. They do not answer it. Luke leaves it hanging, and he will leave it hanging until the next chapter, when Peter finally says it (9:20). But everyone in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood: then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress; he made the storm be still (Psalm 107:28–29). They are with the Lord himself.

Is fear always wrong for a Christian? No. There is a fear that is simply realism, and a fear that is reverence. The disciples’ first fear (of drowning) was natural; their second fear (of him) was the beginning of wisdom. What Jesus questions is not the feeling of fear but faith gone missing: forgetting who is in the boat. The answer to sinful fear is not to stop feeling, but to fear God more. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). The psalmist is afraid and trusting in the same breath.

In a sentence. Jesus asked where their faith was, and the disciples, filled with fear and wonder, asked who he could be, that wind and water obey him.

On a Tuesday. Where is your faith today? Put it in the one who commands the wind and water. When the next crisis comes, ask yourself his question: where did I put my faith? Then go and find it in what you already know: what he has said, what he has done, who he is.

For worship. The sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these and will again. And it heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down. There is only one who has ever been obeyed like that, and he had been asleep a few feet away from them the whole time. Who then is this? He is the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth and the sea, and he is in the boat with his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the far shore — Gentile territory, east of the lake, with pigs on the hillsides — a man possessed by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet.

The description is harrowing and deliberate. He wore no clothes; he did not live in a house but among the tombs; he had repeatedly broken the chains put on him and been driven into the desert. Stripped of clothing, of community and of self-determination, he is not described as a man with a problem but as a site.

Two puzzles meet a careful reader here. Gerasa lay thirty miles inland, and Gadara six miles off; neither is on the shore. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, modern Kursi, was the spot — a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water — while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached that coast. And Matthew names two men where Mark and Luke name one: Matthew adds a second, he does not subtract one, and the other two follow the man who spoke and who was left with a story to tell.

The demons recognise Jesus at once and their theology is impeccable: “Son of the Most High God” — a title Jews and Gentiles alike used of Israel's God, fitting on this side of the lake. But look at the verb. They beg. Three times in this scene the powers of darkness plead, which is Luke's way of showing how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore.

“Legion” was nominally six thousand men, and a legion is not a crowd but an occupying force. The word would have had an edge in the Decapolis, where people had watched real ones march. And the answer comes from the occupation rather than the man: asked his own name, there is no I left to reply.

They beg not to be sent to the abyss — the sealed prison of rebel spirits (Rev. 20:1-3) — but into the pigs. Jesus permits it, and it is the demons who stampede the herd, doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had done to one man for years. The lake full of drowned swine is the plainest possible evidence of what he had been living under.

The townspeople find him clothed, in his right mind, and sitting at the feet of Jesus — the posture of a disciple. And they ask Jesus to leave. The man himself begs to come along; that is the one request in the chapter that is refused. “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.”
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the most comprehensive exorcism narrative in the Gospels, and it is performed in Gentile territory, on a Gentile man, before an audience of Gentile herdsmen. The geography is the theology: the kingdom of God does not stop at the borders of Israel.

The Gerasene man is the Gentile counterpart to the demonised man in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33) — both liberated by the same word, with the same authority, and neither able to put up the slightest resistance.

The restored man is “in his right mind” — sober, self-possessed — and he is sitting at Jesus's feet, where a disciple sits (cf. 10:39; Acts 22:3). The demonic occupation has not merely been evicted; the ground has been given to somebody else.

That distinction matters, because a deliverance that only removes does not hold. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24-26). The sitting at the feet is not incidental colour. It is the theological point of the healing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople who ask Jesus to leave are the cautionary portrait of a community that values what it can calculate over what it cannot control. The pigs are gone; the man is well. The arithmetic should be straightforward.

But the fear is real, and Luke names it: something has happened here that they do not control. A lunatic in the tombs can at least be chained. Every generation of the church has had to decide whether to welcome the disruptive grace of God or manage it into something more comfortable — and Jesus does not argue with them. He gets into the boat and goes. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

The man's desire to follow, and Jesus's refusal, is the missionary call in its most particular form: go to the people who already know you. That is a harder road than the boat. Everyone who has been converted where their old life is public knowledge understands it.

And he is sent to declare not a doctrine but a testimony — the one subject on which he is the world's leading authority. Then Luke does something quietly enormous and leaves it without comment: Jesus said “declare how much God has done for you,” and the man went and proclaimed “how much Jesus had done for him.” The two sentences sit side by side, and Luke sees nothing to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.

The country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. They land on the far shore, and everything about the place is foreign. This is Gentile territory: the region of the Decapolis, east of the lake, Greek-speaking, with pigs on the hillsides, which tells you at once that no Jewish community is farming here. Luke explains opposite Galilee for readers who did not know the geography.

Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? Two things about this crossing will stop a reader with a map, and both are worth settling. The first is the place. Some manuscripts read Gadarenes or Gergesenes. Gerasa lay some thirty miles inland; no herd could run from there down a bank into the lake. Matthew names the Gadarenes, and Gadara is about six miles off, still not on the shore. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, perhaps modern Kursi, was the actual spot, a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water, exactly as the story requires, while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to that coast. Each writer named the region by the city his own readers would recognise, much as one might place a village in greater London. The steep bank is still there.

One man or two? The second is the number. Luke describes one man, and so does Mark; Matthew says there were two (Matthew 8:28). Neither denies the other. Matthew adds a second man; he does not subtract one. Where a pair is involved and only one does the talking and only one is left with a story to tell, a writer naturally follows him. Mark and Luke keep the camera on the man who spoke, who was called Legion, who begged to come along and was sent home instead. The same thing happens at Jericho, where Matthew has two blind men and Mark names only Bartimaeus.

There met him a man from the city who had demons. Then Luke sets out what was left of him, in three strokes.

For a long time he had worn no clothes. Only Luke mentions this. It is not an eccentricity but the loss of the most basic mark of human dignity: shame and degradation. And Luke’s for a long time says this was his settled condition, not a crisis.

And he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. No house: no address, no household, no place at anybody’s table. Among the tombs: tombs were caves cut into the hillside, unclean places, which in a Jewish frame is the last word in uncleanness, and in any frame is a man living among the dead because the living will not have him. He lived among the dead, unclean, cut off. Here is Satan’s work: degradation, isolation, uncleanness, death. He has been stripped of clothing, community and personhood. He is not described as a man with a problem. He is described as a site.

Was this man demon-possessed, or mentally ill? Luke, a physician, distinguishes healings from exorcisms (4:40–41), and this man’s condition had a demonic cause: the demons speak and are cast out into the pigs. Possession is real, and the New Testament does not say it has ceased. But most mental illness has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Christians should neither see demons behind every illness nor deny that the devil works.

Can a Christian be possessed? No. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), sealed by him (Ephesians 1:13), and has been delivered from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). A house cannot have two owners. Christians can be tempted, attacked and deceived, and they are told to resist the devil (1 Peter 5:8–9), but never to fear being taken over by him. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In a sentence. On the eastern shore, in Gentile territory, Jesus was met by a demon-possessed man who had gone naked for a long time and lived among the tombs.

On a Tuesday. No one is too far gone, too degraded, too unclean for Jesus to reach. Think of the person in your town everyone has given up on: the addict, the man who sleeps rough, the relative no one mentions. Jesus crossed a stormy lake for a man like that. Pray for them by name, and ask what step of love you could take.

For worship. The Lord of glory crossed a storm and stepped onto a Gentile shore for a naked man living in a graveyard. He came to seek and to save the lost (19:10), and there is no one so lost that he will not cross the sea for them. Satan strips, isolates and destroys; Christ clothes, restores and brings home.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gadarenes, some Gergesenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice: what have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me. For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)

When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him. He gets there first. Jesus has just stepped off the boat; the man comes at a run, screaming, and goes down at his feet. The demon recognises its master and submits. Whatever else is happening inside him, it is the posture of worship, forced out of an enemy.

What have you to do with me? The opening phrase is a stock formula of confrontation, literally what to me and to you?, the ancient equivalent of what do you want with me? The same words came out of the demon in the Capernaum synagogue (4:34).

Jesus, Son of the Most High God. And once again the theology is impeccable. Son of the Most High is the title Gabriel used to Mary (1:32). Most High God is a title often used by or to Gentiles for the God of Israel (Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 3:26; Acts 16:17), a natural way for outsiders to name him. The demons know exactly who Jesus is.

I beg you, do not torment me. Look at the verb: I beg you. This is the first of four times in this scene that begging happens, and three of them come from the demons. The powers of darkness spend this entire passage pleading, which is Luke’s way of telling you exactly how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore. And do not torment me: they are not asking to be left alone. They are asking about timing, and they know there is a schedule. The demons know they face judgement. Matthew records the same demons saying it outright: have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29). They fear Jesus, and they have better eschatology than most of the people in this Gospel.

For many a time it had seized him. Then Luke’s parenthesis, and it is a detail easily skipped. Luke explains the background, as a doctor would describe a case history.

He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles. Two facts about the town are buried in that. They had tried. Somebody bought chains, and posted guards, and did it repeatedly: this was a community attempting, in the only way it knew, to manage a man it could not help. The townspeople tried to control him by force. Human methods failed.

And be driven by the demon into the desert. The demon drove him, as a herdsman drives cattle: bondage, not freedom. And every attempt at restraint failed, and each failure sent him further out into the desert. That is what human management of a spiritual bondage looks like. Restraint is not deliverance. Chains can stop a man harming anybody; they cannot give him back his mind.

Should Christians fear demons? No. This passage is written to cure that fear. The demons are the ones who are terrified; they fall down, beg, and know their doom. Christ has disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Christians should take the devil seriously, be watchful and resist him, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:8–9). But they should never be fascinated by him or afraid of him. The right response to the dark powers is not fear of them, but trust in the one before whom they tremble.

In a sentence. The man fell before Jesus, and the demon in him cried out, recognising him as Son of the Most High God and begging not to be tormented, for it had long controlled the man, defying every chain.

On a Tuesday. No human chain could hold this man. Only Christ could free him. Trust him with the bondages that human methods cannot break: the addiction that has beaten every programme, the anger that has outlasted every resolution. Use the help God gives through doctors and counsellors and friends, and bring it all to the one before whom every bondage must give way.

For worship. Even the demons confess him. Every knee will bow at the name of Jesus, in heaven and on earth and under the earth (Philippians 2:10), and on that Gentile shore a legion of demons bowed already. The Son of the Most High God is not one power among many; he is the Lord before whom all darkness trembles, and he has come to set the captives free.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then asked him: what is your name? And he said: Legion, for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.

Jesus then asked him, What is your name? It is the only question Jesus asks in the whole encounter, and it is worth asking why he asks it. Not for information. Perhaps to bring the man to awareness of his condition, or to expose the extent of the possession. But the likeliest reason is the simplest: a name is what a person has, and this man has not been addressed as a person in years. The town called him a danger; the tombs were his address. Jesus asks him who he is.

Legion. The answer is horrifying on two counts. First, what it means. A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers (about 5,000 to 6,000). Whether the number is literal or a way of saying an army, the sense is the same: a legion is not a crowd. It is an occupying force: organised, disciplined, under orders, and in possession of ground. And there is an edge in the word that a man in the Decapolis would have felt. In a land under Roman occupation, the people knew what a legion was; they had watched them march. The word for what has destroyed this man is the word for what occupied his country.

For many demons had entered him. Luke’s explanation. And the second horror is who answers. The question was put to the man, and what comes out is the occupation speaking. He has been so comprehensively taken over that when asked for his own name he gives theirs. There is no I left to reply.

And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. Only Luke mentions the abyss. The abyss (abyssos) is the deep: in the Greek Old Testament it renders the waters of the deep in Genesis 1, and in later Jewish writing and in Revelation it is the bottomless pit, the prison of rebel spirits before their final judgement (Romans 10:7; Revelation 9:1–2; 20:1–3). So they know where they are going, and they know he can send them there, and they know they cannot stop him. Everything in this exchange is negotiation from a position of total defeat. The one thing they never attempt is resistance. Between the arrival at verse 27 and the request at verse 31, there has not been a struggle. There has only been begging.

Why did Jesus not send them to the abyss at once? Because the time of their final judgement had not yet come (Matthew 8:29). Christ has defeated Satan decisively at the cross, but the final sentence will be carried out at his return, when the devil and his angels are thrown into the lake of fire (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10). Until then, evil is real but bound and limited, able to do only what God permits (Job 1:12). We live between the victory and the final execution of judgement, which is why we must still resist the devil, and why we can do so with confidence.

In a sentence. Asked his name, the man said Legion, because many demons possessed him, and they begged Jesus not to send them to the abyss.

On a Tuesday. However many and powerful the forces of evil, they tremble before Jesus. Take courage. And remember that you have a name, given by him. Whatever has defined you, the addiction, the diagnosis, the failure, the label others have put on you, it is not who you are in Christ. He calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3).

For worship. A legion could not stand before one man from Nazareth. The army that had occupied a human soul for years begged for terms the moment he set foot on the beach. The Lord who will shut Satan in the abyss gave a ruined man back his own name. Mighty and merciful, he is the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (11:21–22).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers. The abyss is the place where evil spirits are confined.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside. Pigs were unclean animals under the law (Leviticus 11:7). This was Gentile territory, where pigs were raised. Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13).

And they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Even demons need Jesus’ permission. They are completely under his authority. Two questions press on any thoughtful reader here, and both deserve straight answers rather than being hurried past. Why did Jesus permit it? And what is the drowning meant to say?

Who does the drowning. Start with who does the drowning. Jesus does not command the pigs into the lake. He grants a request, and it is the demons who stampede the herd to its death, doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had been doing to one man for years. The destruction is theirs, and it unmasks them.

And the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. Several reasons may be seen. It demonstrated visibly that the demons had left the man, and how many there were. It showed the destructive purpose of the demons: what they did to the pigs, they wanted to do to the man. The town had been looking at a naked man in the tombs and calling it madness. Now they have a hillside of evidence about what had actually been living in him, and it is impossible to misread. It showed that a human being is worth more than a whole herd of pigs (12:7). And unclean spirits went with unclean animals into the deep.

The arithmetic. The objection has to be met honestly: sceptics have long pointed to the drowned herd as proof that Jesus was careless of property and cruel to animals. Weigh the exchange as it stands. One human being, made in the image of God, somebody’s son, is pulled out of a living death. A herd of pigs is lost. Jesus refuses the calculation that counts the livestock and forgets the man. Of how much more value is a man than a sheep, he says elsewhere (Matthew 12:12), and the scale holds here. A Saviour who would leave a man among the tombs to protect a herd would be no Saviour at all. There is a third thing, and the next verses will show it. The ruined herd forced the district to a decision it could no longer avoid. It put a price on the table.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless about property or animals. A righteous man has regard for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10), and God feeds the sparrows. He judged that the deliverance of one man was worth the loss. The townspeople judged otherwise (v. 37). Scripture does not linger over the owners’ loss, not because the loss did not happen, but because the point of the story is about to be standing there clothed and in his right mind. The pigs are the price tag the town could see. The man is the treasure it could not.

In a sentence. Jesus permitted the demons to enter a large herd of pigs, which rushed down the bank into the lake and drowned.

On a Tuesday. One person is worth more than great wealth. Value people as Jesus does. Ask where your own spending of time and money shows that you value things more than people: the evening given to the project rather than the friend in trouble, the budget that has room for everything except mercy.

For worship. The Lord counts one human soul worth more than all the herds on all the hills. He paid an infinitely higher price for us than a herd of pigs: he gave his own life. What is man, that you are mindful of him? (Psalm 8:4). We are the treasure for which the Son of God sold all that he had.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. People went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. Those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.

Then people went out to see what had happened. Luke sets the restoration against the ruin, item by item, and every term answers something in verse 27. He had worn no clothes: he is clothed. He had lived among the tombs, driven into the desert: he is sitting. He had been out of his mind: he is in his right mind.

Sitting at the feet of Jesus. And the fourth item is the one that is not merely a reversal: at the feet of Jesus. Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple. It is where Mary of Bethany will sit (10:39), and where Paul says he sat under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). The wild man who roamed the tombs now sits quietly as a learner. He has not simply been emptied. He has been re-seated. That distinction matters, because deliverance that only removes is not deliverance for long. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24–26). What happened here is that the ground was taken back and then given to somebody.

Clothed. No longer naked (v. 27). Someone had given him clothes, perhaps from among the disciples.

And in his right mind. The word is sōphronounta: sober, self-possessed, sane, at peace. A complete transformation. This is what Jesus does.

And they were afraid. Not glad, but afraid. The power of God at work frightened them.

How the demon-possessed man had been healed. Healed (esōthē) is literally saved. Physical, mental and spiritual salvation. Luke uses the word that will run through the rest of the chapter.

Then all the people asked him to depart from them. The sentence that is the real indictment of the passage. Look at what they are looking at. The man everyone in that district had given up on, the one they had chained, and guarded, and finally left in the graveyard, is sitting quietly in his right mind, dressed, listening. It is the best thing that has happened in that region in years. And they want the man who did it to leave. Two things are moving in them, and Luke names one and implies the other. The stated reason is fear, for they were seized with great fear, and it is the same fear that fell on the fishermen when the sea went flat. Something has come into their district that they cannot manage, and that is genuinely more unsettling than a madman in the tombs, because a madman can at least be chained. The unstated one is the hillside. There is a herd in the lake and somebody has to account for it. It is a tragic response. They preferred their pigs, their peace, and their way of life to the presence of Jesus. The power of God was too disturbing and too costly. Many still ask Jesus to leave, for the same reasons.

So he got into the boat and returned. Notice what Jesus does with the request. He does not argue, or press, or stay to reason with them. He does not force himself on people. He came a long way across a dangerous lake for one man, and when the district asked him to go, he went. That is a sobering mercy. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

Can someone ask Jesus to leave for good? Jesus is patient, and he came back to the Decapolis later, where crowds received him (Mark 7:31–37). But this passage is a warning not to presume. The Gerasenes had one visit and sent him away. Scripture warns against hardening your heart today (Hebrews 3:15), because the day of opportunity does not last for ever. If you sense Christ calling you and you are inclined to send him off because he is disturbing or costly, do not wait. He may not cross the lake again on your timetable.

In a sentence. The townspeople came and found the man sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and sane, and seized with fear, they asked Jesus to leave, and he did.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you value more than Jesus’ presence, and would ask him to leave rather than lose? It may be a habit, a relationship, a way of making money, or simply a comfortable life he keeps disturbing. Name it before God. And when someone in your circle is changed by Christ in a way that unsettles everyone, be the one who rejoices.

For worship. Look at the man at his feet: clothed, quiet, in his right mind. That is what Christ does with a ruined life. He does not tidy up the surface; he gives a man back himself, and then gives him a place at his feet. And he does all this for people who may ask him to leave. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11), and still he came, and still he saves.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple.

parallels.desc: Mary sat at the Lord’s feet

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying: return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you. And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.

The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him. This is the fourth begging in the passage, and the first that comes from a human being. The demons begged not to be tormented, begged not to go to the abyss, and begged to enter the pigs. The people begged Jesus to leave. Now the man begs to go with him. The natural desire of the redeemed is to be with their Redeemer. And it is the only request in the scene from a human being that is refused.

A reasonable request. Consider what he was asking for and why it was reasonable. His neighbours had just told Jesus to leave. Every person in that district knew what he had been; there is no starting again in a place like that. The boat was leaving, and on it were twelve men who had also left their trades to follow, and he wanted a place among them. Given what he had come out of, it is difficult to imagine a more understandable request.

But Jesus sent him away. Jesus had another plan for him. Not everyone is called to leave home. Some are called to stay and witness where they are.

Return to your home. Two commands, and both cost him something. Return to your home: back to the house he had not lived in, to relatives who had watched him deteriorate, to a town that had chained him and then given up. That is a harder road than the boat, and everyone who has ever been converted in a place where their old life is public knowledge knows it.

And declare how much God has done for you. He is not sent to argue, or to teach, or to explain the kingdom of God; he has had perhaps an hour’s instruction. He is sent to tell people what happened to him, which is the one subject on which he is the world’s leading authority. He becomes the first missionary to the Gentiles of the Decapolis. In Jewish territory Jesus often told people to keep quiet (8:56); here, in Gentile territory, where messianic excitement was less of a danger and where Jesus himself was not staying, he sends the man to tell. His testimony was simple: what God had done for him. Everyone knew what he had been; now they could see what he was. That is worth holding on to by anybody who has ever felt disqualified from saying anything. The first missionary to Gentile territory had no training, no theology, and no time with Jesus to speak of, and he had a before and an after that an entire district had witnessed.

Proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. And then Luke does something quietly enormous, and leaves it without comment. Jesus said: declare how much God has done for you. And the man went away proclaiming how much Jesus had done for him. He was told to speak about God. He spoke about Jesus. Luke sets the two sentences side by side and does not explain, because as far as he is concerned there is nothing to explain. What Jesus did, God did. Without saying so, Luke equates Jesus with God. He is the one the demons called Son of the Most High God (v. 28). And the testimony bore fruit: when Jesus returned to the Decapolis later, crowds came (Mark 7:31–37).

How do I know whether to stay or go? Most Christians are called, like this man, to serve Christ where they already are: in their family, their street, their workplace. Some are called to leave for the gospel, and the church should test and send them gladly (Acts 13:1–3). Wanting to be with Jesus is right; but being with Jesus is not only a matter of geography. He goes with those he sends. If you are unsure, ask what doors God has opened, seek the counsel of your church, and remember that home is often the hardest and most fruitful mission field there is.

What should I say when I tell people about Jesus? Start where this man started: with what the Lord has done for you. You do not need to win every argument. Tell honestly what you were, what Christ did, and what he is to you now (1 Peter 3:15). Then point beyond yourself to him: who he is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he receives all who come to him. Your story opens the door; his story is the message.

In a sentence. The healed man begged to follow Jesus, but Jesus sent him home to tell what God had done for him, and he proclaimed throughout the city what Jesus had done.

On a Tuesday. You are called to tell those around you what Jesus has done for you. Start at home. Write down, in three or four sentences, your own before and after, and pray for one person this month with whom you could share it.

For worship. Jesus is God, and what he does is the work of God. The man from the tombs could not tell the difference between how much God had done and how much Jesus had done, because there is none. He who was sent home with an hour’s teaching filled a city with the name of Jesus. Great is the Lord who saves the worst, and then sends them back to the places that knew them worst, to tell of his mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section is Luke's most carefully interlaced double narrative — a healing folded inside a raising, with each story interpreting the other.

Jairus is a ruler of the synagogue: a lay official who organised the services and carried the community's respect, and a member of the class that had been watching Jesus with hostility since chapter 5. He falls at Jesus's feet in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is. His only daughter, about twelve, is dying, and every consideration of position has gone.

Jesus goes with him. The crowd presses. And a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years — exactly as long as the girl has been alive — reaches through the crowd and touches the tassel on the corner of his garment.

Her twelve years had cost far more than health. Leviticus 15:25-27 put a woman in her condition under continuing ritual uncleanness, and not only her: anything she sat on, anyone who touched her. Twelve years without the synagogue, without normal contact, very likely without a husband — and none of it her fault. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching: she had spent everything and was no better.

Her approach is furtive because it had to be; by the law she understood, her touch would defile him. And once again the traffic runs the wrong way. The bleeding stops.

Jesus stops the whole procession to ask who touched him — a question he already knows the answer to. Peter's exasperation is reasonable and Luke lets it stand. But he will not take a transaction where a person is available: she had tried to take the gift and stay invisible, and that would have left her physically healed and socially exactly as she was. He makes her say it out loud, in public — which puts her restoration on the record where her whole town can hear it — and then calls her “Daughter,” the only time in the Gospels he uses that word to a woman.

And while he is still speaking, the message comes: “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” From where Jairus stands, the delay killed her. Somebody else's twelve-year problem was attended to first, and his child ran out of time.

“Do not fear; only believe.” Then the mourners are put out, the girl is taken by the hand — “Child, arise” — and her spirit returns. And the first thing Jesus says afterwards is that somebody should get her something to eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The interlacing of the two stories is a masterpiece of narrative theology. The woman healed on the way to Jairus's house teaches Jairus — and the reader — that the delay did not diminish Jesus's power or exhaust his compassion. The one who felt power go out of him for her has more than enough for a dead girl.

Jairus is being taught, at his own cost and in real time, to resist the word that says “it is too late.” The “too late” of the messengers is not too late for the Lord of life, and Jairus had just watched, at close range, what this man does for somebody who ran out of options twelve years ago.

“She is not dead but sleeping” is not a correction of the diagnosis, and Luke — a physician — gives three signals that she was genuinely dead: the professional mourners had arrived, the crowd knew, and “her spirit returned.” Jesus is changing a category, not disputing a fact. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and that is now what death is for those who belong to him (1 Thess. 4:13-15; John 11:11).

The woman's touch of the “fringe” may point to the tassels of Numbers 15:38-40, worn as a reminder of the commandments. Malachi 4:2 had promised that the sun of righteousness would rise “with healing in its wings,” and the Hebrew for wings is the word for the corners of a garment. She may have been reaching, knowingly or not, for exactly that.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's twelve years, her exhausted resources, her uncleanness and her invisibility are the conditions in which she finally comes. She did not come while she still had options; she came when she had nothing left.

And Jesus's response — stopping in the middle of a crowd, insisting on finding her, calling her “daughter,” declaring her faith in front of everyone — is the public vindication of a person who arrived at the bottom of her resources. Her faith was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it aloud.

Jairus's journey is faith pushed to its absolute limit. He did everything right: he found Jesus, he fell at his feet, he asked in time. Then the delay, and then the word that it was over. This has to be said plainly, because it is what a great many lives feel like and pious hurry past it is worthless.

“Only believe” is not a technique, and it is not an instruction to generate a quantity of faith sufficient to raise the dead — that reading crushes bereaved people. It is a word to a man who has just been told it is finished, asking him to keep hold of the person beside him for another ten minutes.

And the last instruction in the house is the one that could not have been invented. A girl has been raised from the dead, the room is beyond speech, and the Son of God says: get her something to eat. She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. Falling at Jesus’ feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.

Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him. The contrast with the last verse is deliberate and painful. One shore asked him to leave; the other has been standing about waiting for the boat to come back, for they were all waiting for him.

And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. Luke gives us his name and his office, and both matter. A ruler of the synagogue was not a priest but a lay official: the man who organised the services, invited readers and preachers, cared for the building, and carried a good deal of the community’s respect. In a Galilean town he was somebody. He is also, by position, a member of the class that has been watching Jesus with increasing hostility since chapter 5. The Pharisees and teachers of the law who came from every village of Galilee and Judea to sit and observe (5:17) were his colleagues. Many synagogue officials were opposed to Jesus. Jairus set aside his dignity and his reputation.

And falling at Jesus’ feet, he implored him. He goes down in the road, in front of a crowd of people who know exactly who he is. Humbled by need. Whatever position he held in that town, and whatever the synagogue authorities had been saying about this preacher, it is all gone in a second. He is not managing his reputation. He has a dying child.

What suffering does. That is one of the things suffering does, and it is not always a cruelty. It strips away the calculations we cannot ordinarily get past. There are people who have arrived at Christ by roads they would never have chosen, and Jairus is one of them. He did not come because his theology changed. He came because his daughter was dying and there was nowhere else.

For he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age. Luke’s detail is a physician’s and a storyteller’s at once. Only Luke says only, as with the widow’s son at Nain (7:12) and the boy of 9:38, and it does the same work. Luke notices the depth of grief when an only child is lost. About twelve, which in that culture is the edge of womanhood, the age when a girl might soon be betrothed. She has had exactly one childhood, and it is ending. And twelve links her with the woman who had been ill for twelve years (v. 43): the girl had lived as long as the woman had suffered. The number will matter again in the very next verse.

And she was dying. Urgent.

As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. Pressed (synepnigon) means crushed, nearly suffocated. It is the same word as the thorns that choked the seed (v. 14). The crowd that presses on him can be as much an obstacle as a help.

What if I only come to Jesus because I am desperate? Then you are in good company. Jairus came because his daughter was dying; the woman in the next verses came because every doctor had failed; the prodigal came home because he was starving. Jesus never once asked anyone whether their motives were pure enough before he helped them. Need is not a bad reason to come to Christ; it is the usual one. What matters is not why you first came, but that you came to him, and that you stay. Many who came to him for a healing found the Healer.

In a sentence. On his return, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, fell at Jesus’ feet begging him to come to his dying only daughter, aged about twelve, and Jesus went, with the crowd crushing around him.

On a Tuesday. Desperate need levels everyone. Whatever your position, fall at Jesus’ feet. Is pride, or the fear of what others will think, keeping you from asking for help, from God or from his people? Jairus let it go in a second. And if you are a leader in a church, remember that you will never be more useful than when you are on your knees.

For worship. The crowd welcomed him, and well they might. He is the Lord who comes back across the lake for those who are waiting, and who never says no to a father on his knees. The proud he knows from afar, but the lowly he regards (Psalm 138:6). Blessed be the Saviour who meets us at the end of our resources.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.

And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years. Luke interrupts himself. Jesus is on his way to a dying child, the crowd is pressing, and the narrative stops for a woman nobody has noticed. Twelve: Jairus’s daughter has been alive for twelve years; this woman has been bleeding for exactly as long. Luke has set the two side by side on purpose: one has had a life, and the other has been losing hers, over the same span. It was probably continuous menstrual bleeding.

What those twelve years cost. Take in what they had cost her, because it is far more than a medical condition. Under the law, a woman with a chronic discharge was in continuing ritual uncleanness, and not only her. Anything she lay or sat on was unclean. Anyone who touched those things was unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:25–27). Which means twelve years unable to worship at the temple, twelve years cut off from normal contact, twelve years in which every human touch carried a consequence for the other person. If she was married when it began, she may well not be married now. She was physically ill, weak and probably anaemic, socially isolated, religiously excluded. And it is not her fault. She has done nothing.

And though she had spent all her living on physicians. Some manuscripts omit these words. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching, but he is gentler than Mark, who adds that she had suffered much under many physicians and had only grown worse (Mark 5:26). Luke says simply that she could not be healed by anyone. Twelve years of treatments, each one costing money and hope, and at the end of it she is bankrupt and no better.

She came up behind him. Secretly. Everything about this is furtive, and it had to be. She is ceremonially unclean in a dense crowd, touching a rabbi, and by the law as she understood it, her touch would defile him. She was not supposed to be in a crowd touching people. She has no right to be there at all.

And touched the fringe of his garment. The fringe is the tassel (kraspedon) that devout Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment, as the law commanded, to remind them of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). It is the furthest edge of him that a person crouching in a crowd could reach. Some believed the tassels of a holy man had power (Matthew 14:36). Her faith was mixed with superstition, but it was faith in Jesus.

And immediately her discharge of blood ceased. Luke uses the medical term for a flow stopping. After twelve years, in a moment. And once again the traffic runs the other way: instead of her uncleanness passing to Jesus, his healing passed to her. Wholeness travels from him to her.

Does Jesus accept a faith that is mixed with superstition? Yes, if it is reaching for him. Her understanding was confused; she thought the power was in the tassel. But Jesus did not wait for her theology to be corrected before he healed her. He honoured the faith, and then, as the next verses show, he corrected the theology: it was not the cloth but your faith in me. That is how he still deals with new and weak believers. A trembling, half-informed faith in Christ saves; a well-informed faith in anything else does not. And he will not leave a weak faith where he found it.

In a sentence. A woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years, incurable by any doctor, secretly touched the tassel of Jesus’ cloak and was instantly healed.

On a Tuesday. Even a weak and imperfect faith, if it reaches out to Jesus, finds his power. Reach out to him. If you have exhausted every other remedy, and spent all you had, come to him now, even if all you can manage is the edge of the garment. And think of the person in your church who has been sick or isolated for years. Twelve years is a long time to be forgotten.

For worship. Here is a holiness that is not threatened by our uncleanness but overcomes it. Under the law, the unclean defiled the clean; in Christ, the clean cleanses the unclean. He took our uncleanness upon himself at the cross, bearing our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), so that power and wholeness could flow out from him to all who reach for him. No uncleanness is too great and no case too long for him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the words about the physicians. Her condition made her ritually unclean. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: who was it that touched me? When all denied it, Peter said: Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you! But Jesus said: someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.

And Jesus said, Who was it that touched me? He is on his way to a dying child and he stops the whole procession to ask a question he already knows the answer to. Jesus knew. He wanted her to come forward, for her own sake.

When all denied it. Including, at first, her.

Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you! Peter’s exasperation is entirely reasonable and Luke lets it stand. There are hundreds of people jammed against him; the question is, on the face of it, absurd. Everyone is touching you.

Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me. He distinguishes between the crowd’s pressing and this touch, and the distinction is the point. Hundreds were in physical contact with him. One person took something. Many touched him; one touched him in faith. There is a difference between jostling Jesus in a crowd and reaching out to him in faith. Many are near Jesus; few touch him. Power (dynamis) is the power of God, flowing from him, and Luke has used it before of the healing that flowed from him (5:17; 6:19). Whatever exactly it means, it was not automatic and it was not without cost. Something went out of him, and he felt it go.

Why stop? Now the real question. He knows what happened. She has what she came for. The child is dying up the road and every second matters. He stops because a healing is not the same as a person, and he has not come for transactions. She had tried to take the gift and remain invisible, which is entirely understandable for a woman in her position, and it would have left her exactly as she was in every way except the physical. Still unspoken of. Still, as far as her town was concerned, unclean. Still nobody’s daughter. He will not let her have it that way. He is going to bring her to say it out loud, in front of everyone, and then he is going to say something to her that she can carry for the rest of her life, and he holds up a dying child’s father in the road while he does it.

Does power going out of him mean Jesus has limited power? No. Jesus is fully God, and his divine power is infinite. The phrase tells us that the healing was a real act of his, consciously given, not a magic that leaked from his clothes without his knowledge. He perceived it because he is the source of it. It also reminds us that his healing was personal and costly: he did not dispense blessings like a machine. Every mercy we receive from Christ is given by him, knowingly, to us.

In a sentence. Jesus asked who had touched him, and when Peter protested that the whole crowd was pressing on him, Jesus said someone had touched him, for he had felt power go out from him.

On a Tuesday. Being in church, near Jesus, is not the same as touching him in faith. Reach out to him personally. On Sunday, in the crowd of familiar words and songs, ask yourself whether you are jostling him or touching him. And if you have received something from him in secret, an answered prayer, a burden lifted, do not be afraid to let him bring you into the open. He asks the question because he wants you, not only your need met.

For worship. In a crushing crowd he knew the one touch of faith. He knows yours too. The Lord who is surrounded by the worship of heaven and the noise of the whole earth notices the faintest reaching out of a frightened believer. He knows his sheep (John 10:14), one by one, and nothing that is done towards him in faith goes unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her: daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.

And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling. Luke’s phrasing is exact. She did not come forward; she came when she saw that hiding had failed. She could not escape. And she is shaking. Why? Not, presumably, because she doubted the healing; she could feel it. She is frightened because of what she has just done. She was afraid of being rebuked for touching him while unclean: an unclean woman has touched a rabbi in public and taken something without asking. In front of a crowd, and a synagogue ruler, she is about to be exposed as both ceremonially defiling and presumptuous.

And falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people. Only Luke says in the presence of all the people. She tells the whole thing: why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. Twelve years of it, out loud, to a street full of strangers: the condition she has never been able to name in public, the money spent, the doctors, and what happened when she reached the tassel.

Why did Jesus make her do this? So that everyone would know she was clean. That is the confession he stopped the procession to get, and it is worth seeing why it was worth the delay. Her healing had been secret; her restoration had to be public. Her testimony is now on the public record. Everyone in that crowd has heard, from her own mouth, that she is well, which means she can go back to worship, and into her family’s kitchen, and into ordinary human contact, and nobody can say otherwise. After twelve years of exclusion, the whole town could now accept her. And so she would know that she had been healed not by magic but by Jesus, through faith. He did not merely stop the bleeding. He put her back into the community, and he did it by bringing her to speak.

Daughter. It is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus addresses a woman by that word. She has been nobody’s for twelve years, untouchable, unmentionable, perhaps alone, and the first word out of his mouth gives her a family. An outcast for twelve years, she is welcomed into the family.

Your faith has made you well. Made you well (sesōken) means has saved you. Not the tassel, but faith in Jesus. Body and soul. And notice what he says her faith did, and what it did not. It did not manufacture the power; that came out of him. Her faith was simply the hand that reached. It was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method, and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it in public.

Go in peace. As to the sinful woman (7:50). Peace is shalom: wholeness, everything put back in its right place. Not merely, you are cured. She came for one thing and he gave her the lot: her body, her standing, her place among people, and a name to be called by.

Do I have to tell people what Jesus has done for me? Not necessarily in a crowded street, but Christ does call his people to confess him openly. With the heart one believes, and with the mouth one confesses (Romans 10:10). For a believer, that confession is made in baptism, which is the public declaration that you belong to Christ, and then in a life of speaking of him. It is not a test you must pass to be saved; it is what Christ draws out of those he has saved, for their own good and for others. Like this woman, you may tremble. He will meet you there with peace.

In a sentence. Seeing she could not hide, the woman came trembling and told everyone what had happened, and Jesus called her daughter, said her faith had saved her, and sent her away in peace.

On a Tuesday. Jesus wants a personal relationship, not just a secret cure. Come to him openly and hear him call you son or daughter. If you have been a secret believer, consider what step of open confession he may be calling you to: baptism, church membership, a word to a friend. And when a trembling person tells their story in your church, receive it as the town should have received hers.

For worship. Daughter. The Lord of glory looked at a woman unclean for twelve years and called her his own. That is what he does for all who come to him: we who were far off are brought near, and the God of heaven calls us sons and daughters (2 Corinthians 6:18). He does not only heal; he adopts. Go in peace, for he is our peace.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler’s house came and said: your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more. But Jesus on hearing this answered him: do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.

While he was still speaking. The timing is unbearable, and Luke means it to be. Jesus is in the middle of the sentence that gives the woman her peace, and the messenger arrives. Consider what that means for Jairus, who has been standing there through all of it. He came running with minutes to spare. Then the crowd slowed them. Then a woman touched a tassel, and Jesus stopped, and would not move on until she had told her entire story in public, and while she was telling it, his daughter died. Imagine Jairus’s agony.

From where Jairus was standing. From where he was standing, the delay killed her. Somebody else’s twelve-year problem, which had waited twelve years and could surely have waited another hour, was attended to first, and his child ran out of time. That has to be said plainly, because it is what a great many people’s lives feel like, and a pious hurry past it is worthless. Jairus is the man who did everything right, asked in time, and watched the answer arrive too late. Jesus’ delays can seem cruel. But he had a greater purpose.

Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more. Hope is over. A teacher can heal the sick, but not raise the dead. And notice the messenger’s advice, which is kindly meant and entirely rational. There is nothing more to be done. The category has changed from illness to death, and everybody knows the difference. The word for trouble means to bother, to put to inconvenience: the man is being gently told to let the poor rabbi get on.

But Jesus on hearing this answered him. He intercepts it. Luke’s construction has Jesus overhearing the message and answering at once, cutting in before the sentence can land and take root.

Do not fear; only believe. Fear and faith are opposites. Only believe: keep on believing. Two words, and they are not a technique. Jesus is not telling him to generate a quantity of faith sufficient to raise the dead; that is the reading which crushes bereaved people, and it is not what the sentence says. He is telling a man who has just been informed that it is over to keep holding on to the person standing next to him for another ten minutes. And this is where the woman’s healing was for Jairus as much as for her. He had seen the woman healed through faith; now he must believe for something greater. He has just watched, at close range and at his own cost, what this man does for somebody who had run out of options twelve years ago.

And she will be well. Only Luke adds this. Well (sōthēsetai) means saved, the same word as verse 48. It is the promise of Jesus, given after the worst news, not before it.

Why does God seem to delay when I pray? Scripture never pretends that God’s delays are easy; the psalms cry, how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1). But the story of Jairus, like that of Lazarus (John 11:6, 15), shows that his delays are never neglect. He was not too late for Jairus; he was exactly on time for a greater miracle. Your waiting may be for something God means to do that is greater than what you asked. That does not mean every prayer is answered as Jairus’s was. It means the one who makes you wait is the same one who loves you, and he has never once been late for his own purposes.

In a sentence. Word came that Jairus’s daughter had died, but Jesus told him not to fear but only to believe, and she would be saved.

On a Tuesday. When the worst news comes, the diagnosis, the phone call, the letter, there will be voices, often kindly, telling you not to trouble the Teacher any more. Do not listen to them. Hold on to Jesus for the next ten minutes, and then the next. And when you are the one bringing bad news to someone, bring Christ’s word with it.

For worship. When the worst news comes, hear Jesus’ word: do not fear; only believe. He speaks into the very moment of despair, and his word is stronger than the news. The Lord who keeps his promises is never too late; even death is not the end of what he can do. Blessed be the Saviour who answers the messenger of death before the message can take root.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. All were weeping and mourning for her, but he said: do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.

And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James. Five people, and the composition is worth noticing. The inner three, who will also be on the mountain at the transfiguration (9:28) and, in Mark’s account, in the garden at Gethsemane (Mark 14:33): the three who see him raise the dead, see him in glory, and see him on his face in the dirt. They are witnesses.

And the father and mother of the child. Tender: the parents are included, because this is their daughter and not a demonstration. Everybody else is put out.

And all were weeping and mourning for her. The house is full of noise. Professional mourners, as well as family. Mourning (ekoptonto) means beating their breasts. In that culture the mourning began immediately and it was loud; even a poor family was expected to provide flute players and at least one wailing woman, and the wailing was a formal, public performance of grief. It had started within the hour.

Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping. Now, what does that mean? Because it is regularly used to argue that she was never dead: that this was a coma, and Jesus was correcting a medical error. That cannot be what Luke means, and Luke is a doctor. The messenger reported a death. The professional mourners had arrived, and they did not come for the unconscious. Luke’s own next sentence says the crowd knew she was dead. And when she revives, Luke writes that her spirit returned (v. 55), which is not the language of waking from a faint. Jesus does not deny that she is dead. He is not correcting a diagnosis. He is changing a category. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and in his vocabulary that is now what death is: temporary, from which he can wake her. That is exactly how the New Testament will go on to speak of believers who die: those who have fallen asleep (John 11:11–14; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). Death is not the end for those Christ will raise. The word is not a denial of death. It is a claim about who is standing in the room.

And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. Scornful laughter. Luke’s phrasing is careful and it is not kind to them: they laughed, knowing. This is not a misunderstanding; it is derision from people who were right about the facts. They knew she was dead. Luke makes it clear that this was a real raising from the dead, not a revival from a coma. They are the only people in this Gospel who are said to laugh at Jesus, and they had every reason. He said something absurd. And within minutes, the girl they had been paid to mourn got up and walked.

Does sleeping mean that the dead are unconscious? No. Jesus means that her death is not final; she will wake. The word describes the body awaiting resurrection, not the soul. Those who die in the Lord are with him at once, conscious and at rest (23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory: the believer’s soul goes immediately into the presence of Christ, and the body sleeps in the grave until he raises it on the last day (Westminster 32.1).

In a sentence. At the house, Jesus took only the three disciples and the parents in, and told the mourners she was not dead but sleeping, and they laughed at him, knowing she was dead.

On a Tuesday. For those who belong to Christ, death is sleep, from which he will wake them. Grieve, but with hope. When you stand at the grave of a believer, use his word: she is not dead but sleeping. It is not a euphemism; it is a promise. And if people laugh at your hope, do not be surprised. They laughed at him.

For worship. To the Lord Jesus, death is a sleep from which he can wake anyone, as easily as a parent wakes a child. The last enemy has become, for his people, a bed. He went down into death himself, lay three days in the tomb, and rose, so that every believer’s grave is now a resting place to be left on the morning of resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking her by the hand he called, saying: child, arise. Her spirit returned, and she got up at once. He directed that something should be given her to eat. Her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

But taking her by the hand. He takes her hand. Again, as with the leper, as with the bier at Nain, he touches what the law says will defile him. Touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), and he reaches out and takes hold of a dead twelve-year-old. But Jesus touches the dead, and death gives way.

He called, saying, Child, arise. And the word he uses is a family word. Mark preserves it in the original Aramaic, Talitha cumi (Mark 5:41), and it is the ordinary domestic phrase a mother uses in the morning: little girl, get up. A tender word, like waking a child in the morning. The greatest power in the universe is exercised in the tone of voice used to wake a child for school.

And her spirit returned. Only Luke says this. Her spirit had left her body at death (23:46; Acts 7:59), and came back. She had gone, and she came back. It is a clear statement that she had been dead, and that the human spirit lives on after death.

And she got up at once. Instantly, completely. No process, no recovery, no gradual return of colour: she stood up.

And he directed that something should be given her to eat. This is the sentence that gives the passage away, and it is the reason no one could have invented it. A twelve-year-old has just been raised from the dead in front of her parents and three grown men. The room must be beyond speech. And the first thing the Son of God says, having conquered death in a bedroom in Galilee, is: get her something to eat. She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry. It is a practical, caring detail. She was really alive, in a real body, and hungry. After the resurrection Jesus himself would eat to show he was not a ghost (24:41–43). There is more of what he is like in that instruction than in the miracle before it. The one who commands the wind and the abyss and the grave, and who has just called a girl’s spirit back into her body, is also the one who notices that nobody has thought about her supper.

And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened. Which is, on the face of it, impossible: a houseful of mourners is outside, and they had watched her die. Of course, everyone would know she was alive. But they were not to spread the story. He is not asking them to keep a secret so much as refusing to be turned into a spectacle, and Luke has recorded the same instruction before (5:14). Jesus did not want to be known as a wonder-worker, attracting crowds for the wrong reasons.

Why tell these parents to tell no one, when he told the Gerasene to declare it? The Gerasene lived in Gentile territory, where Jesus was not staying and where no crowd was waiting for a Jewish king. Here in Galilee, news of a girl raised from the dead would bring crowds wanting a wonder-worker or a political Messiah, and Jesus’ hour had not yet come. He was not hiding his glory; he was guarding his mission. The full truth of who he is could only be told rightly after the cross and resurrection, and then it was to be told to the ends of the earth.

Will Jesus raise my loved one who has died in him? Yes. This girl was raised to die again; what Christ promises his people is far greater. On the last day, all who are in the tombs will hear his voice (John 5:28–29), and those who belong to him will be raised imperishable, in bodies like his glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). The same hand that took this girl’s will take theirs. Meanwhile, their spirits are with him. Grieve for them, but grieve as one who knows that the Lord who says arise has never yet been disobeyed.

In a sentence. Jesus took the girl by the hand and told her to rise, and her spirit returned and she got up at once, and he told them to feed her and to tell no one.

On a Tuesday. Let the tenderness of this scene shape how you care for people. After the great moments, prayer answered, crisis over, someone has to think about the meal. Be the one who notices. And whenever you hear of a death, remember the girl standing up in her parents’ house: that is a picture of the morning that is coming.

For worship. Jesus has power over death. He will one day take every believer by the hand and say: arise. He came across a lake through a storm, was asked to leave by one district, stopped for a woman nobody could see, and walked out of that house leaving a family with their daughter and a strict instruction to say nothing about it. He was not building a reputation. He was going to a cross, and on the way he was raising the dead and asking whether anyone had fed the child. That is our Lord: almighty over death, and gentle enough to think of a child’s hunger.

parallels.desc: the child’s life came into him again

8.text: <sup>1</sup> Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, <sup>2</sup> and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, <sup>3</sup> and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. <sup>4</sup> And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, <sup>5</sup> “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. <sup>6</sup> And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. <sup>7</sup> And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. <sup>8</sup> And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>9</sup> And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, <sup>10</sup> he said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ <sup>11</sup> Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. <sup>12</sup> The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. <sup>13</sup> And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy.
