But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away. <sup>14</sup> And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. <sup>15</sup> As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. <sup>16</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>17</sup> For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. <sup>18</sup> Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.” <sup>19</sup> Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. <sup>20</sup> And he was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.” <sup>21</sup> But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” <sup>22</sup> One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” So they set out, <sup>23</sup> and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. <sup>24</sup> And they went and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Where is your faith?” And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” <sup>26</sup> Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. <sup>27</sup> When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. <sup>28</sup> When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” <sup>29</sup> For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.) <sup>30</sup> Jesus then asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered him. <sup>31</sup> And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. <sup>32</sup> Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. <sup>33</sup> Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. <sup>34</sup> When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. <sup>35</sup> Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>36</sup> And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. <sup>37</sup> Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. <sup>38</sup> The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, <sup>39</sup> “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. <sup>40</sup> Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. <sup>41</sup> And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, <sup>42</sup> for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. <sup>43</sup> And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. <sup>44</sup> She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. <sup>45</sup> And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!” <sup>46</sup> But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” <sup>47</sup> And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” <sup>49</sup> While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” <sup>51</sup> And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. <sup>52</sup> And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>53</sup> And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. <sup>54</sup> But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” <sup>55</sup> And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. <sup>56</sup> And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the pivot of Luke's Gospel — the hinge on which the whole narrative turns. Everything before it is the Galilean ministry of proclamation, healing, and gathering; everything after it (from 9:51 onward) is the great journey to Jerusalem, the road that leads to the cross. Within this single chapter, the Galilean ministry reaches its theological summit and its geographical end. The chapter contains the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the first and second passion predictions, the transfiguration, the healing of the epileptic boy, and the setting of the face toward Jerusalem. It is the most theologically dense chapter in Luke's Gospel.

The pivot on which chapter 9 turns is v. 51: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” The phrase “set his face” is the language of prophetic determination — Isaiah uses it of the Servant who “set his face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7) in the face of suffering and shame. From this moment, every step Jesus takes in Luke is a step toward the cross. The transfiguration (vv. 28–36), which precedes this turning point, is the divine confirmation of the way that is being chosen — Moses and Elijah appear and speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word translated “departure” is exodos. The cross is not a defeat; it is the Exodus, the supreme act of divine liberation toward which all of Israel's history has been moving.

The chapter's central theological contribution is the collision between two kinds of glory. The crowds see a miracle-worker; Herod is perplexed by a rumoured prophet; the disciples feed five thousand from five loaves; Peter confesses the Christ of God — and immediately Jesus reframes everything. The Son of Man must suffer. Anyone who wants to follow must take up their cross daily. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it. The glory of the transfiguration is flanked on both sides by the shadow of the cross — and that is exactly the point. The glory and the cross are not opposites; they belong together. The cross is the path to the glory; the glory is the validation of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus calls the twelve together, gives them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. Two words, and not synonyms: power (dynamis) is the capacity, authority (exousia) is the right. Both are given, and neither is earned.

The instructions are deliberately spartan — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. Between them those five items cover security, supply and comfort, and he takes all five away. The messengers are to depend entirely on the hospitality of those they visit, staying in whatever house first receives them and not moving on to a better one.

A reader comparing Gospels will find a difficulty: Mark records that they were to take nothing except a staff (Mark 6:8). Several explanations have been offered, and none is certain; what is plain is that both accounts fit the point of the list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Where they are not received, they are to shake the dust from their feet — the gesture a Jew used at the border when returning from Gentile territory, here applied to Jewish villages that refuse the kingdom's messengers. The old boundary has moved. It now runs not around the nation but around the message.

Luke reports the whole mission in one verse: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere. What is absent is as striking as what is there — no account of the first house, the first refusal, the first demon. The instructions were not an ideal held up for admiration; they were the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Herod's perplexity closes the section. He has killed the greatest of the prophets and is now hearing that something greater is happening. The three theories on offer — John raised, Elijah appeared, one of the old prophets risen — are all respectful and all too small. His question, “who is this about whom I hear such things?”, is exactly the right question. And “he sought to see him” is the tragedy: he gets his wish at the trial (23:8), and Jesus does not answer him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sending of the twelve is the first instance of the apostolic mission. The word apostle means simply one who is sent; it says nothing about the man's qualities and everything about his commission.

The authority they receive is delegated — the same authority Jesus has been exercising since chapter 4, now given to them to exercise in his name. This is the pattern that will run through Acts: the Spirit-empowered community carrying the same authority of the same word into the same world.

Note who receives it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), propose incinerating a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready.

And the errand has two halves held together: to proclaim and to heal. Luke will not let them come apart. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The instructions to take nothing are not a travel policy but a structural embodiment of dependence. The messengers carry no resources that would make them independent of those they are sent to, which creates a bond of mutual vulnerability: the messenger depends on the receiver, and the receiver depends on the message.

The rule about staying in the first house is more pointed than it looks. A travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on. A messenger who upgrades has begun to be paid — and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale.

The shaking of the dust takes a refusal seriously enough to mark it, without bitterness and without a backward argument. Two instincts are common and both are wrong: to keep pressing until the gospel becomes an irritation attached to a person, or to shrug it off and privately conclude they were never going to anyway. The dust does neither.

And Herod is the standing warning that the right question is not enough. A man can be genuinely interested in Jesus Christ for years, ask exactly the correct question, and go to his grave having done nothing about the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.

Meaning first. Luke 9 is the hinge of the Gospel. Jesus sends the Twelve out with his own power and authority, and the news of what they do reaches Herod, who asks the question the whole chapter answers: who is this? In a desolate place Jesus feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, taking, blessing, breaking and giving, as he will at the Last Supper and at Emmaus. Then, after prayer, he asks his disciples who they say he is, and Peter answers: the Christ of God. At once Jesus tells them what kind of Christ he is: one who must suffer, be rejected, be killed and be raised, and whose followers must deny themselves and take up their cross daily. On a mountain three of them see his glory, and Moses and Elijah speak with him about the exodus he will accomplish at Jerusalem; the Father’s voice says, this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him. Down in the valley the disciples fail, argue about who is greatest, and want to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and Jesus heals, sets a child beside him, and rebukes them. The chapter ends with Jesus setting his face to go to Jerusalem, and with three would-be followers learning that nothing may come first before him.

The setting. Chapter 9 is the climax of the Galilean ministry. It moves from the mission of the Twelve, through the question of who Jesus is (vv. 7–9, 18–20), to the first prediction of the cross and the transfiguration, and ends with Jesus setting his face toward Jerusalem (v. 51). From there, the great journey to the cross begins.

And he called the twelve together. They have been watching for four chapters. Now he hands them the equipment and sends them out. Chosen in 6:13, trained by being with him through chapters 6–8, they are now sent.

And gave them power and authority. Two words, and they are not the same. Power (dynamis) is the capacity, the ability to do the thing. Authority (exousia) is the right to do it. A man may have one without the other: a burglar has the power to open your door and no authority; a magistrate has the authority to arrest and may not have the strength. The Twelve are given both, and they are given them. Nobody in this sentence earned anything. Both are delegated from Jesus. They have no power of their own.

Over all demons and to cure diseases. Notice the scope. That is exactly what Luke has shown Jesus doing since chapter 4 (4:31–41): the same two categories, kept carefully distinct, as a physician would keep them distinct. What has been his alone is now delegated. And it is worth pausing over who is receiving it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), want to burn a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready. He never has.

And he sent them out. The verb is apesteilen, the root of our word apostle: one who is sent. They were his envoys. That is the whole meaning of the title. It says nothing about the man’s qualities and everything about his commission; an apostle is not a rank but an errand.

To proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. And the errand has two halves, held together: word and work, announcement and demonstration. Preaching first, then healing. The healings confirmed the message that the kingdom had come. Luke will not let them come apart. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.

Does this authority belong to the church today? It was given to the Twelve for their mission, and its signs confirmed their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many Christians believe it continues. The more likely reading is that the sign gifts belonged to the apostolic age, while the commission to proclaim the kingdom goes on for every generation. The church still prays for the sick and resists the devil, but does not claim the apostles’ authority.

So does God still heal? Yes. God heals today, often through medicine and sometimes beyond it, in answer to the prayers of his people (James 5:14–15). What has ceased, on the reading this commentary takes, is not God’s power or his willingness to answer prayer, but the gift given to particular people to heal at will as a sign authenticating new revelation. Christians who see it differently are brothers to be loved, not opponents. Either way, pray for the sick in faith, use the doctors God has given, and leave the outcome in his hands.

In a sentence. Jesus gave the Twelve his power and authority over demons and diseases, and sent them out to preach the kingdom of God and to heal.

On a Tuesday. Christ sends his people out with his authority, not their own. Whatever he calls you to, he equips you for. If you have felt unqualified to do anything for God, notice that the Twelve were unqualified too. Take the task in front of you this week, the conversation, the class, the visit, and go, depending on him.

For worship. There is something here for anyone who has ever felt unqualified to do anything for God, and it is not a compliment about hidden potential. It is better than that. What the Twelve took into those villages was not theirs. They had it because it was put into their hands that morning by somebody who had it to give, which is still the only way anyone has ever had anything worth carrying. All authority in heaven and on earth belongs to him (Matthew 28:18), and he shares his errand with weak men.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.

Take nothing for your journey. Five items, and the list is not random. The staff is for the road and for defence; the bag is the beggar’s or traveller’s satchel; the bread is the day’s food; the money is the reserve; the second tunic is the change of clothes and the blanket for a cold night. Between them they cover security, supply and comfort. He takes all five away. They are to travel light, depending entirely on God’s provision through the hospitality of those who receive them.

No staff. Mark says take only a staff (Mark 6:8). Perhaps Mark means take the one you have, while Luke and Matthew mean do not acquire another. The point is the same: no extra provisions. Several explanations have been offered, and none is certain. What is plain is that both accounts fit the point of the whole list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Nor bag. A traveller’s pack for supplies, or a beggar’s bag. They were not to beg, but to receive what God provided.

Nor bread, nor money. No food, no cash. And notice how far that goes. They are sent to preach the kingdom of God with no food and no money, which means that within a day of setting out, every one of them will be hungry and dependent on somebody who has not yet heard the message.

And do not have two tunics. No spare clothes.

Whatever house you enter, stay there. This is more pointed than it looks. In that culture, a travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on: a larger house, a wealthier host, a more comfortable room. The rule forbids it. Do not move from house to house looking for better hospitality. Be content with what is offered, and do not insult your host. The reason is not hard to see. A messenger who trades up has begun to be paid, and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale. It is also simply a matter of not humiliating the first family who took him in.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. Later Jesus told them to take a moneybag and knapsack (22:35–36). The instructions fit this short, urgent mission in Galilee. But the principles remain: urgency, simplicity, contentment, and dependence on God. None of this is a dress code for modern missionaries, and turning it into one misses it. What it is, permanently, is a description of the posture: go without the equipment that would let you pretend you are not dependent, and do not let your accommodation start deciding your message.

Should churches pay their ministers and missionaries? Yes. Jesus’ instruction assumes that those who receive the message will provide for the messenger, and he says elsewhere that the labourer deserves his wages (10:7). Paul argues the same at length (1 Corinthians 9:3–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18). What this passage guards against is the minister whose comfort shapes his message. A church should pay its pastor and support its missionaries generously, so that they are free from anxiety; and those who serve should be content, and never preach for gain (1 Peter 5:2).

In a sentence. Jesus told the Twelve to take no supplies or spare clothes, depending on God, and to stay in whatever house welcomed them.

On a Tuesday. Travel light in serving Christ. The more you depend on him, the more you will see his provision. Ask what in your life is extra equipment against the possibility that God will not come through: the savings you trust more than him, the back-up plan that makes obedience unnecessary. And if someone shows you hospitality this week, receive it graciously and do not compare it with what others might have given.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest provides for his workers. He sent them out with nothing, and when he asked them later, did you lack anything?, they said, nothing (22:35). He feeds the birds of the air, and he has never yet let a servant on his errand go hungry beyond what was good for him. He who did not spare his own Son will graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32).
verseByVerse.note: The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies; a second tunic was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.

Wherever they do not receive you. He tells them in advance that some places will refuse. That is worth registering before anything else: rejection is not treated as a possibility to be prayed against but as a certainty to be prepared for. The men going out with power over demons are told, in the same breath, that some towns will simply not have them.

Shake off the dust from your feet. The gesture itself was a familiar one. Jews returning to Israel from Gentile lands would shake the dust of the pagan road off their feet, so as not to bring unclean soil into the holy land. It said: that place and this place are not the same, and I am bringing none of it home. Which makes its use here extraordinary. These are Jewish villages. To do this to a Jewish town was a dramatic act: you are acting like Gentiles, outside God’s people. It says that a town of Israelites which has refused the kingdom of God has put itself, by that refusal, outside; that the old boundary has moved, and it now runs not around the nation but around the message. It was a sign that the town was being left to God’s judgement. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

As a testimony against them. A warning, and a witness at the judgement (10:10–16). Their responsibility has been discharged; the town is accountable. The last thing that town gets is a picture of what it has just done.

What it does not mean. Not a gesture of personal contempt or revenge. It is not a curse; the disciples call down nothing. There is no argument, no denunciation in the street. It is a solemn warning, which might still bring them to repentance.

Two wrong instincts. And there is something in this for the ordinary business of speaking about Christ to people who do not want to hear. Two instincts are common and both are wrong. The first is to keep pressing: to treat a refusal as a problem of technique, and to go back with a better argument, and again, until the relationship is ruined and the gospel has become an irritation attached to a person. The second is to shrug it off, decide it never mattered, and privately conclude that they were never going to anyway. The dust does neither. It takes the refusal with complete seriousness (this was not nothing, and something real has been declined) and then it leaves, without bitterness and without a backward argument, and walks to the next village. Which means there is a point at which a faithful messenger stops. Not because he has given up on the people, and not because the message has lost its power, but because the responsibility has changed hands.

So should I stop talking to my unbelieving friend about Christ? Not necessarily, and almost never from the relationship. The disciples were passing through towns on a short mission; most of us live alongside the same people for years. What changes, after a clear refusal, is usually the method, not the love. Stop pressing an argument he has heard and declined. Keep being his friend, keep praying for him, live the gospel in front of him, and be ready to speak again when he asks or when God opens a door (Colossians 4:5–6; 1 Peter 3:15). And remember that a refusal today is not a verdict for ever. Many who once shut the door have later opened it.

In a sentence. Where a town rejected them, the Twelve were to shake its dust off their feet as a testimony that it stood under God’s judgement.

On a Tuesday. You are responsible to tell the gospel faithfully, not to make people accept it. Leave the results with God. If you have been carrying guilt for someone who has heard and refused, hand the weight back to him. Your part was to tell them; his part is the heart.

For worship. God is patient, and he is just. He sends his messengers to town after town, and he does not force anyone through the door. But he takes his own gospel seriously: to refuse it is not nothing. The same Lord who told his servants to shake off the dust stretched out his hands all day long to a disobedient people (Romans 10:21), and his mercy waits at the edge of every town until the last moment.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

And they departed. They obeyed. One verse for the whole mission, and Luke tells us four things: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere.

What is not here. What is not here is as striking as what is. No account of how it felt to set out with no money. No record of a debate about the instructions. No description of the first house, or the first refusal, or the first demon. Luke, who is perfectly capable of narrating a mission in detail and does so at length in his second volume, gives this one a single sentence. The effect is to make the instructions of the previous verses land differently. They were not an ideal held up for admiration. They were the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men actually walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Preaching the gospel. Evangelising (euangelizomenoi), Luke’s favourite word. Notice the order, because Luke keeps it consistent: preaching the gospel and healing. The proclamation is named first here, as it was in verse 2 and as it was at 4:43, where Jesus said preaching was what he was sent for. The healings authenticate the announcement; they are not a substitute for it.

And healing everywhere. Everywhere: Luke’s word is emphatic and it sits at the end of the sentence. Twelve men, on foot, in an unbroken circuit of villages that had never had anything like this. They did not concentrate on the promising places. They went through. The kingdom’s power was at work through them. Jesus’ ministry is multiplied through his disciples, as it will be through the church in Acts.

Most obedience is like that. And there is a plain encouragement in the compression itself. The mission that Luke can summarise in a sentence was, for the men doing it, weeks of dust, strange houses, meals they had not paid for, and conversations they had no way of preparing. It looked, from the inside, like ordinary hard work with no guarantee. It was, from the outside, the kingdom of God arriving in villages that had waited centuries. Most obedience is like that. It is only ever visible as a summary afterwards.

What if my service for God feels ordinary and unseen? Then you are in exactly the place the Twelve were. Most of what God does through his people is never written up. Paul says that each one’s work will be revealed on the day (1 Corinthians 3:13), and Jesus promises that even a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). God sees the ordinary faithfulness: the Sunday school class taught for twenty years, the elderly neighbour visited weekly, the prayer list kept. The summary will come later, written by him.

In a sentence. The Twelve went out through the villages preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ work continues through his people. Where are you taking the gospel this week? Name one village, one place in your ordinary week (an office, a school gate, a ward), and pray before you go into it.

For worship. The risen Lord is still sending, and the kingdom is still arriving in places that have waited centuries. What he began in Galilee through twelve men he continues through his whole church, to the ends of the earth. Blessed be the King whose ordinary servants carry his extraordinary kingdom on foot.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said, 'John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?' And he sought to see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because some said that John had been raised from the dead, some that Elijah had appeared, and others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said: John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things? And he sought to see him.

Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening. The mission has been so effective that the news reaches the palace, and Luke turns the camera on a man who will not appear in person again until the trial. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea (3:1). Tetrarch is a lesser title; he wanted to be called king and Rome never allowed it. The mission of the Twelve had spread Jesus’ fame even into the palace.

And he was perplexed. Perplexed (diēporei) means thoroughly at a loss, unable to make sense of it, unable to find a way through.

John had been raised from the dead. The three theories he is hearing are all serious ones. John raised. Elijah appeared, the forerunner Malachi promised. One of the old prophets risen. These are popular opinions about Jesus, which the disciples will report again (v. 19). All of them high, none of them right. Every explanation on offer puts Jesus somewhere in the prophetic tradition, and every one of them is too small, which is precisely the trouble: the categories available to that court cannot hold what is happening in the villages.

John I beheaded. Luke does not tell the story of John’s death, which Mark tells at length (Mark 6:17–29). He records only Herod’s own confession. Herod is haunted by it. Luke gives Herod three words of autobiography and they are the three he would least want quoted. Notice the grammar: the verb is his own. Not, John was executed; not, there was an unfortunate business at a banquet. John I beheaded. Whatever else this man is, he is not lying to himself about what he did.

But who is this about whom I hear such things? It is the right question, the great question of the chapter and of the Gospel. It is the question the disciples asked in the boat (8:25), and it has just been asked, correctly and urgently, by a murderer in a palace. Herod asks it; the disciples will answer it (v. 20); the Father will declare it (v. 35).

And he sought to see him. There is the tragedy, and Luke will pay it off. Herod wanted to see Jesus out of curiosity, not faith. He wanted to see a sign. And he keeps wanting it, and eventually he gets exactly what he asked for. At the trial, Pilate sends Jesus to him, and Luke tells us Herod was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him (23:8). He questions him at some length. And Jesus does not answer him a word (23:9). Herod is the only person in Luke’s account of the trials to whom Jesus says nothing at all.

Why did Jesus not answer Herod? Because Herod had already had his answer and refused it. He had heard John preach, and liked to listen to him (Mark 6:20), and then killed him rather than lose face. He had heard about Jesus for years and never come to him. What he wanted at the trial was a show, not a Saviour. Jesus’ silence was a judgement: there comes a point where more words would only be entertainment. That is a solemn warning to anyone who treats Christ as a subject of interest rather than a Lord to be obeyed. Seek him while he may be found (Isaiah 55:6).

In a sentence. Herod, perplexed by reports about Jesus, and haunted by having beheaded John, asked who this could be, and wanted to see him.

On a Tuesday. Curiosity about Jesus is not enough. Herod wanted to see him, but never knew him. Seek him in faith. If you have been interested in Christ for a long time, reading, listening, asking good questions, ask yourself the harder question: what am I going to do about the answer? A man can be genuinely interested in Jesus Christ for years, ask the correct question, and go to his grave having done nothing about it.

For worship. The question that haunted a king in his palace has an answer, and the answer is glorious: this is the Son of God, the Christ, the one whom the Father loves. Herod wanted to see a sign; we have been shown the Saviour. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29).
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Luke records that he later saw Jesus at his trial.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The twelve return from their mission and Jesus withdraws with them to Bethsaida for rest. Mark gives his reason in his own words: “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” The crowds find out where the boat is going and get there first.

So the rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out the destination — and Luke records that “he welcomed them.” The verb means received gladly. He met the people who had wrecked his only plan for the week as though they had been invited, and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and cured those who had need of healing, until the day was nearly over.

The disciples' suggestion is sensible and they are right about almost everything: it is late, the place is desolate, thousands need food and lodging, and the villages are the only source of either. Sending away is not wickedness; it is arithmetic, done honestly, by tired men. What the arithmetic never includes is the person standing next to them.

“You give them something to eat” is emphatic in the Greek — you give them — and there is no reading on which the twelve can obey it. Their answer is what an honest man says when handed an impossible order: here is the inventory. Five barley loaves and two fish, which John tells us belonged to a boy. They have even costed the alternative: Mark records two hundred denarii, two-thirds of a year's wage, and even that would not be enough.

They are right. Five loaves and two fish do not feed five thousand men — and Luke's andres means adult males specifically, so with women and children (Matt. 14:21) the real number is far higher. No amount of faith changes that arithmetic and Jesus never suggests otherwise. What he does is ask for the loaves. Nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over.

The four verbs over the bread — took, blessed, broke, gave — are the ordinary actions of a Jewish householder, and Luke fixes them in the reader's memory because they return twice: at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus, where “their eyes were opened, and they recognized him” (24:30-31).

All ate and were satisfied — the satisfaction the Psalms say God gives (Ps. 107:9; 132:15). And twelve baskets of fragments were gathered: one for each man who had done the arithmetic.
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle besides the resurrection recorded in all four Gospels, which signals its weight. The typology is dense: a multitude fed in a desolate place, as Israel was fed in the wilderness; the crowd seated in ordered companies of fifty, as Moses set the people in fifties (Exod. 18:25); the one greater than Moses giving bread not prayed down from heaven but broken from his own hands.

It is the New Testament's great sign of the messianic banquet — the feast Isaiah promised (Isa. 25:6-9) and Revelation describes as the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9). Every time the church gathers at the Lord's table it is taking a foretaste of that feast.

And the eucharistic action defines the church's life: receiving grace, returning it in blessing, breaking it in service, giving it away. He could have distributed the bread himself. Instead it goes from his hands into the disciples' and from theirs to the people — so that the men who said “send them away” spent the next hour giving away food they did not have.

The twelve baskets left over say what the whole scene says: the kingdom of God does not issue minimum rations. There was more at the end than at the beginning, and it was not close.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Send the crowd away” is the reasonable option in far more situations than this one — the pastoral problem genuinely beyond a church's capacity, the person whose needs are more than anyone in the congregation can carry, the ministry that cannot be staffed.

And notice what had just happened to these men. They had come back that same week from a mission in which they healed the sick with nothing in their pockets, and were still telling him about it two verses earlier. Experience of God's provision has a remarkably short half-life, and it is almost never available in the moment it would be most use.

“Bring what you have” can be preached as though the trick were to be optimistic about the loaves. It is not. The loaves are genuinely insufficient and everyone in the story knows it. The command is to put them in his hands anyway, in full knowledge that they will not do, and see what he does with them.

The rhythm of withdrawal and interruption is worth having by anyone who works with people and has learned, rightly, to guard their time. The guarding is not unspiritual — Jesus withdrew constantly. But the plan is not the master. There will be a day when what was properly and prayerfully arranged is taken by people who need something, and the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests.

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. He took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.

On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. They come back full of it, and he listens. They report back. Ministry is accountable to Christ.

And he took them and withdrew apart. For rest, and private teaching. Mark records the reason in Jesus’ own words: come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while (Mark 6:31). The men have been working, and he is taking them away to recover.

To a town called Bethsaida. A fishing town at the north end of the lake, just east of where the Jordan flows in, in Philip’s territory, out of Herod’s reach. The feeding took place in a deserted place near it (v. 12).

When the crowds learned it, they followed him. So the rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out where the boat is going. Mark says they ran round the shore on foot and got there first. Here is the moment, and everything about the reaction is worth watching. Jesus has just brought twelve exhausted men to a quiet place for the express purpose of resting, and several thousand people have arrived and taken it.

And he welcomed them. Only Luke says this. Welcomed means received gladly, made welcome. Not tolerated, not endured. He met the people who had wrecked his only plan for the week as though they had been invited. His rest was interrupted, and he welcomed them anyway. No irritation. His compassion was greater than his need for rest.

And spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. Word and deed again. He does both, and he keeps doing them until the day is nearly over (v. 12). Luke’s phrase for the sick is careful: those who had need of healing. Not everyone in the crowd, but those who had come with a need. He attended to the ones who required attention.

The rhythm and the need. This pattern runs right through Luke, and it should not be flattened into a lesson about being available at all times, because that is not what Jesus does. He withdraws constantly. He gets into boats to get away. He goes up mountains alone at night (5:16; 6:12). The rhythm is real and he defends it, right up to the moment when the need is standing in front of him, and then the rhythm gives way, every time.

So should I never protect my rest? You should protect it; Jesus did. Rest is God’s gift and command, and a worker who never stops will soon have nothing to give. But the plan is not the master. There will be a day when the thing you had properly and prayerfully arranged is taken from you by people who need something, and the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests. Guard your time in the ordinary run of things. When the need is genuine and in front of you, let love decide, and trust God to give you the rest you missed another way.

In a sentence. When the apostles returned and reported, Jesus took them away to rest near Bethsaida, but the crowds followed, and he welcomed them, taught about the kingdom and healed them.

On a Tuesday. When interruptions come, welcome people as Jesus did. Watch your face the next time someone knocks on your door, rings at the wrong moment, or stops you in the corridor. It will tell you whether they are a guest or an intrusion. And if you are worn out, take Christ’s invitation seriously and plan a real rest.

For worship. The Lord who invites the weary to come to him and find rest (Matthew 11:28) was himself weary, and gave up his rest to welcome a crowd. He has never once treated a needy person as an interruption. Every one of us who has come to him has come uninvited, at an inconvenient time, and been received gladly. His welcome is the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day began to wear away, and the Twelve came and said to him: send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (Matthew 14; Mark 6; John 6). It was clearly of great importance to the early church.

Now the day began to wear away. Luke’s phrase is almost elegiac: the day was declining, the light going. And with the light goes the margin: a crowd of thousands, in open country, several hours from anywhere, with night coming.

Send the crowd away. A reasonable suggestion. The disciples saw the problem, and the solution: let them fend for themselves. And before this is criticised, it should be admitted that they are right about everything except one thing. They are right that it is late. They are right that the place is desolate. They are right that thousands of people need lodging and food and that neither is available where they are standing. They are right that the surrounding villages are the only realistic source of either. And they are right that somebody has to say something, because Jesus has been teaching and healing all day and the sun is going down. This is not laziness or hard-heartedness. It is twelve men who have taken responsibility for a practical problem their teacher appears not to have noticed, and their solution is the only sensible one available: send them off now, while there is still enough light for them to walk.

For we are here in a desolate place. A wilderness. As Israel was in the wilderness, needing bread, and God fed them with manna (Exodus 16). Anyone who knew the story of the exodus would feel the echo.

Experience has a short half-life. Notice too what has just happened to these men. They have come back this same week from a mission in which they cast out demons and healed the sick with nothing in their pockets. Two verses ago they were telling him all about it. And now, facing a crowd with no food, their instinct is to calculate the resources and organise a dispersal. That is not a special failing of theirs. Experience of God’s provision fades remarkably quickly in all of us, and it is almost never available in the moment it would be most use.

The reasonable option. It is worth hearing the phrase on its own, because it is the reasonable option in more situations than this one: the pastoral problem that is genuinely beyond the church’s capacity; the person whose needs are more than anyone in the congregation can carry; the ministry that cannot be staffed. Sending away is not wickedness. It is arithmetic, done honestly, by people who are tired. What the arithmetic never includes is the person standing next to them.

Is it ever right to say no to a need? Yes. No church and no Christian can meet every need, and Jesus himself sometimes moved on when crowds wanted more (4:42–43). Wisdom, limits, and referring people to others better placed to help are not unbelief. The question this passage puts is whether we have brought the need to Jesus before we decided. Sometimes, after prayer, the answer is that this is not ours to carry. Sometimes he hands it back to us and says, you give them something. The sin is not in saying no, but in leaving him out of the arithmetic.

In a sentence. As evening came, the Twelve urged Jesus to send the crowd away to find food and lodging, since they were in a remote place.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to see a problem and send people away. Bring the need to Jesus instead. Before your church committee, your family or you yourself decide that something is impossible, stop and pray about it by name. Then decide.

For worship. The God who fed Israel in the wilderness for forty years has not lost his power to spread a table in the desert (Psalm 78:19). The disciples counted the hours of daylight and the distance to the villages. They had not yet counted on him. He is the Lord who provides, and our arithmetic has never once included all of him.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to them: you give them something to eat. They said: we have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.

You give them something to eat. You is emphatic. He does not dispute their assessment of the situation. He hands it back. It is a shocking instruction, and it is meant to be. There is no possible reading on which the Twelve can obey it in their own strength. He is telling twelve men with nothing to feed a crowd they have just correctly judged to be unfeedable. Jesus puts the responsibility on them. They had just been out preaching and healing in his power; could they not trust him for this?

We have no more than five loaves and two fish. Their answer is exactly what an honest man says when handed an impossible order: here is the inventory. John tells us they came from a boy, and were barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9): small, flat loaves, and small dried or pickled fish, the ordinary relish that went with bread. A meal for one person. It is one packed lunch.

Unless we are to go and buy food for all these people. Impossible. There is a note of something in that clause, and it is not quite sarcasm but it is close. Mark supplies the figure they were working with: two hundred denarii, about two-thirds of a labourer’s annual wage (Mark 6:37), and John adds that even that would not give each of them a little (John 6:7). They have costed it. It cannot be done.

They are right. That has to be said plainly, because the disciples in this story are usually treated as slow, and here they are simply accurate. Five loaves and two fish do not feed five thousand men. No amount of faith changes that arithmetic, and Jesus never suggests otherwise. What he does is ask for the loaves.

The lesson. Which is the shape of the thing, and it is worth getting right, because bring what you have can be preached as though the trick were to be optimistic about the loaves. It is not. The loaves are genuinely insufficient and everyone in the story knows it. The command is not to believe in the bread. It is to put the bread in his hands anyway, in full knowledge that it will not do, and see what he does with it. The disciples look at their resources, and despair. Jesus wants them to look at him. Our inadequacy is the starting point for his sufficiency. Nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over. That is the whole point of the order of events.

What if what I have really is too little? It is too little, and that is not the problem. Whatever you bring to Christ, gifts, time, money, energy, a weak faith, is always too little for what he asks. Moses had a staff, David a sling, the widow a handful of flour, and the boy five loaves. The question is never whether it is enough, but whether you will put it into his hands. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).

In a sentence. Jesus told the disciples to feed the crowd themselves, and they replied that they had only five loaves and two fish.

On a Tuesday. What little do you have? Bring it to Jesus. He does not ask you to supply the need, but to give him what you have. Name the need in front of you that feels impossible, a ministry, a family situation, a neighbour, and the five loaves you have towards it. Then give them to him in prayer, and do the next thing.

For worship. Christ does not need our loaves, and he asks for them anyway. He delights to do great things with small offerings, so that the glory may be his. The Lord who made every barley field in Galilee asked a boy for his lunch, and with it fed a multitude. He is not limited by what we bring, and he is not ashamed of it either.

verseByVerse.quote: For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, 'Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.' And they did so, and had them all sit down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples: have them sit down in groups of about fifty each. And they did so, and had them all sit down.

For there were about five thousand men. Men (andres); Matthew adds, besides women and children (Matthew 14:21). The real number in that field was perhaps fifteen or twenty thousand people in all.

Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each. Consider what that instruction commits the Twelve to. They have just told him it cannot be done. He now sends them out into a crowd of thousands, in failing light, to organise it into roughly a hundred separate companies of fifty, which is an hour’s work at least, in front of hungry and increasingly irritable people, with five loaves in a bag and no explanation of what is about to happen. They have to seat the whole crowd before they know there is anything to serve. The word is literally reclining, as at a banquet.

And they did so. The disciples obeyed, before they saw how it would work. That is obedience with no visible warrant, and Luke records it in four words. Seating thousands for a meal with only five loaves required faith. Whatever else may be said about these men, they went out into that field and did it.

Why groups of fifty? Two reasons suggest themselves, and both are in the text. The practical one is distribution. A crowd of thousands cannot be fed by twelve men passing baskets through a mob; it can be fed by twelve men working a hundred defined companies, each one a manageable size, in order, with nobody missed. The other is older. When Israel came out of Egypt and was fed in the wilderness, Moses set them in ordered companies, with chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens (Exodus 18:21, 25). A crowd in a desolate place, arranged in fifties, about to be fed by God, is not an image any Jew would fail to recognise. Jesus is the new Moses, feeding the new Israel in the wilderness, and he is greater than Moses, because Moses did not make the manna.

The first picture of the church. And there is something in the shape of it worth keeping. He did not feed a mass. He fed people in groups small enough to see each other’s faces, seated on the grass, sharing out of the same basket, which is a good deal closer to a hundred suppers than to one enormous distribution. It is an early picture in this Gospel of what the church would turn out to look like.

Why does God ask me to obey before I see how it will work? Because that is what faith is. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen (Hebrews 11:1). Abraham went out not knowing where he was going (Hebrews 11:8). If God always showed us the outcome first, we would be trusting the outcome, not him. He gives enough light for the next step, and the next step is usually something ordinary: seating people on the grass. Do that, and leave the bread to him.

In a sentence. There were about five thousand men, and Jesus had the disciples seat them in groups of about fifty.

On a Tuesday. Obey Jesus even before you see how it will work out. Is there an instruction in his word you have been postponing until you can see the result: forgiving, giving, speaking, resting? Do the seating, and trust him for the bread.

For worship. The God of order is the God of abundance. He arranged a hungry crowd in ranks on the green grass, as a shepherd makes his flock lie down in green pastures (Psalm 23:2), and spread a table before them in the wilderness. The Good Shepherd counts his sheep in fifties and does not miss one.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.

And taking the five loaves and the two fish. Four verbs follow, and Luke has chosen them with great care: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave.

He looked up to heaven. To his Father, the source of every gift.

And said a blessing over them. Every Jewish household head did exactly this at the start of a meal. He lifted the bread, looked up, said the blessing: Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. He broke it, and handed it round. There is nothing strange in the actions. Jesus is the host of this meal, and Luke is fixing the actions in the reader’s memory.

Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples. Took, blessed, broke, gave: the same four actions come back twice more, and both times they matter enormously. On the last night: he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them (22:19). And at Emmaus, in the house, with two men who have walked seven miles with a stranger: he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened, and they recognised him (24:30–31). Take, bless, break, give. It is how five thousand were fed on the grass; it is how the Lord’s Supper was instituted; it is how the risen Christ was recognised. Luke has laid a thread through his Gospel, and this is where he ties the first end of it. Luke’s readers would recognise the shape of the Lord’s Supper.

No moment of multiplying. Notice also the sequence in this verse. He does not multiply the bread and then break it. He gives thanks over five loaves, the actual, insufficient five, and it is in the breaking and the giving that there turns out to be more. Luke does not describe the miracle happening. There is no moment at which the pile visibly grows. There is a man breaking bread and handing it to twelve others, and it does not run out.

To set before the crowd. He could have handed it out himself. Instead the bread goes from his hands into theirs, and from theirs to the people, so that the men who had said send them away spend the next hour walking up and down a hillside giving away food they did not have. The disciples become the servers, distributing what comes from Jesus’ hands. This is the pattern of ministry: we receive from Christ and give to others. We do not make the bread; we hand it out.

Is the feeding the Lord’s Supper? No, but it points towards it. The feeding was a meal in the wilderness for a crowd; the Supper is the ordinance Christ gave his church, a remembrance of his death and a means of grace in which, by faith, believers feed on him spiritually (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23–26). Luke uses the same four actions so that we see the connection: the one who fed the five thousand is the one who gives himself as the bread of life (John 6:35). When you come to his Table, you come to the same host, and he still takes, blesses, breaks and gives.

In a sentence. Jesus took the loaves and fish, looked up to heaven and blessed them, broke them and gave them to the disciples to distribute.

On a Tuesday. Give thanks before it is enough. Before your next meal, before your next week of work, before you face a need too big for you, take what you have, look up, and thank God for it. Then hand it on. Everything you have to give others has come first from his hands.

For worship. Jesus is the host who feeds his people. Receive from his hands, and pass it on. He took what was offered him, and he gave thanks for it before it was anything like enough. That is the sentence to sit with. Five small loaves, held up in two hands in front of a hungry multitude, and a blessing spoken over them by the one through whom every field of barley in Galilee had been made. And the hands that broke the bread would themselves be broken, so that the bread of life could be given to the world.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.

And they all ate and were satisfied. All: every one of the thousands, women and children included, down to the last group of fifty at the far edge of the field. Nobody was missed and nobody got the end of the supply. Everyone, fully. Were satisfied (echortasthēsan) is a strong word. It was used of animals grazed to the full, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the satisfaction God gives: I will satisfy her poor with bread (Psalm 132:15); he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things (Psalm 107:9). They were not given enough to take the edge off. They were fed until they had had enough, in a wilderness, at the end of a long day, by a man with five loaves. The Messiah gives abundantly, as God did with the manna.

Twelve baskets of broken pieces. And what was left over was picked up. Twelve baskets: not twelve crumbs, but kophinoi, the stiff wicker baskets a traveller carried. There was more at the end than at the beginning, and it was not close. God’s provision is not just enough, but overflowing. The number is unlikely to be accidental. Twelve is the number of the tribes: enough for all Israel. And it is the number of the men who had said it could not be done: one basket each, carried back by the very people who had done the arithmetic. Whatever else they were going to remember about that afternoon, each of them walked off the field holding the evidence.

Nothing wasted. And note the instruction implied in picked up. The one who had just produced a meal for thousands out of a boy’s lunch had the leftovers gathered. Nothing was wasted (John 6:12). Extravagance and carefulness sit in the same paragraph without the slightest tension.

Was it really a miracle? Some explain the feeding as a sharing miracle, the crowd moved by the boy’s example to bring out food they had hidden. But all four Gospels record it as a miracle; the disciples distributed food from five loaves and two fish; and twelve baskets of fragments were left over. Jesus himself later recalled it as something he had done (Mark 8:19). The point is that he is the one who feeds his people in the wilderness.

The meaning. John tells us that the next day Jesus explained: I am the bread of life (John 6:35). The miracle points to Jesus himself, who gives himself to satisfy the deepest hunger of the soul. And it is a foretaste of the messianic banquet, when people will come from east and west and recline at table in the kingdom of God (13:29; 14:15).

Why am I not satisfied, if Christ satisfies? Many Christians feel a restlessness that seems to contradict this verse. Part of the answer is that we often try to feed on other things while hungry for him, and they do not fill. Part is that our satisfaction in Christ is real now but not yet complete; we taste, and long for more (1 Peter 2:3). Even the hunger is a gift, a sign that we were made for him. Come back to him: in his word, in prayer, at his Table, among his people. And wait for the day when we shall hunger no more (Revelation 7:16).

In a sentence. Everyone ate their fill, and twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you go when you feel empty: food, screens, shopping, approval. None of it is wrong in its place, but none of it is bread for the soul. This week, when the hunger comes, take it to Christ first, even for five minutes. And waste nothing he gives you, whether money, time or grace.

For worship. Jesus is the bread of life, and he satisfies completely. Come to him hungry. What was brought to him was five loaves and two fish, and it was not enough, and everyone knew it, and the men who brought it said so out loud. And there was food on that hillside until thousands had eaten all they could hold, and then there was more left over than had been there to start with. He has never yet been handed something too small to work with. He has never yet run short at the far end of the field. And whatever is put into his hands comes back multiplied, in baskets, with the ones who said it was impossible carrying them home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying — Luke alone tells us so, as he does at every hinge of this Gospel — and out of that prayer comes the question the whole book exists to answer.

“Who do the crowds say that I am?” The answers are the same three that reached Herod's court: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. Every one is respectful; every one is wrong in the same way, placing him within the prophetic tradition rather than beyond it.

“But who do you say that I am?” It is a question no survey can answer. Peter says: “The Christ of God.”

And immediately, without celebration, Jesus charges them to tell no one — and begins to teach what the title actually means. “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”

The silence is not modesty. In Galilee in that decade Messiah meant a son of David who would raise an army and break Rome; John records a crowd trying to make him king by force (John 6:15). The word is embargoed until it can carry the meaning he is about to give it. And the rejection is specified by office — the Sanhedrin, which is to say the entire official religious leadership of the people of God. Not Rome. The men who had the Scriptures.

The call to discipleship follows on the same terms, and Luke marks the audience: “he said to all.” This is not advanced material for the twelve. “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”

To deny the self is not to deny oneself things. The verb is the one Luke will use of Peter's denials in the courtyard (22:34, 61). And “take up his cross” was not a metaphor to anyone hearing it: crucifixion was a live Roman practice, and the phrase described a condemned man carrying the beam of his own execution to the place where he would be nailed to it.

Then “daily,” which is Luke's addition — Matthew and Mark do not have it. It takes the most final image available and makes it a routine, which means it is not chiefly about martyrdom and not reserved for the exceptional.

The section closes with a promise that has troubled readers ever since: “there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” Luke answers it in the very next sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's confession is correct, and Luke records no commendation of it — Matthew's account has the blessing on Peter; Luke, writing for a Gentile church, moves straight to the reframing. The Christ of God is the suffering, dying, rising Son of Man.

“Son of Man” is not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying “a human being.” It comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion and a kingdom that shall not pass away. It is a claim of enormous weight wrapped in a phrase that sounds humble — which is exactly why he could use it in public.

The word must (dei) is the divine-necessity word Luke uses at every turning point. The cross is not an accident, a miscalculation, or the defeat of the mission. It is the appointment. And he never once announces the death without the rising in the same breath.

On “will not taste death,” three answers are given and they are not equally strong. The weakest strains the words. The second, and much better, takes the kingdom in Luke's usual sense — God's reign breaking in — and points to the resurrection, Pentecost, and the spread Luke describes in his second volume, all within the lifetime of the hearers. But the strongest is the one Luke himself supplies: eight days later, three of them went up a mountain and saw the Son of Man in glory.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Daily” is the word that brings the cross within reach of an ordinary believer. It is not the dramatic act of martyrdom reserved for the exceptional disciple; it is the ordinary Tuesday in which the self is again told it does not rule here.

And self-denial needs guarding, because it can be twisted into something poisonous. It is not self-hatred, and it is not the erasure of a personality God made. It is the dethroning of the self as the thing every decision is finally referred back to.

“What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself?” is put at the extreme deliberately: if the trade fails at the maximum price it fails at every price below it. Nobody reading this will gain the whole world. The prices most people actually pay are small — a working life arranged around security, a set of decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

And shame is the right word, chosen over “deny” or “reject.” Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ; a great many are embarrassed by him, and by his words particularly. What is actually being weighed, in the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, is the estimate of a roomful of people against the estimate of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, 'Who do the crowds say that I am?' And they answered, 'John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.' Then he said to them, 'But who do you say that I am?' And Peter answered, 'The Christ of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. He asked them: who do the crowds say that I am? They answered: John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen. Then he said to them: but who do you say that I am? And Peter answered: the Christ of God.

The great omission. Luke moves directly from the feeding to Peter’s confession, omitting a long section of Mark (Mark 6:45–8:26). This places the question who is he? immediately after Herod’s question (v. 9) and the feeding.

Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. Luke’s sentence is slightly odd in English and deliberately so: praying alone, with the disciples there. It is his way of saying that Jesus was in prayer and they were nearby. Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi, Mark 8:27) but notes that Jesus was praying, and Luke alone tells us this. That is worth noticing, because it is a habit of this Gospel. The baptism, the choosing of the Twelve, the transfiguration, Gethsemane, the cross: Luke puts Jesus at prayer before every turning point in the story (3:21; 6:12). The most important question in the book comes up out of a conversation with the Father.

Who do the crowds say that I am? The answers are the same three that reached Herod’s court a few verses earlier (vv. 7–8): John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. The crowds are not hostile and they are not stupid. Every one of those answers is respectful, and every one puts him in the prophetic line: a great man in a great tradition. And every one is wrong in the same way. They are all attempts to fit him into a category that already exists.

But who do you say that I am? You is emphatic. The Greek puts the pronoun first and hard: you, what do you say? It is the pivot of the Gospel, and it cannot be answered by a survey. Everything up to this point has been evidence; the question is what has been made of it. It is the question every person must answer.

The Christ of God. Four words in Greek, and they are the right ones. Christos is the Greek for Messiah, the Anointed: the one Israel had been promised since David, the king who would come. Of God: God’s Messiah, the one God has anointed and sent (2:26; 23:35). Peter has stopped putting him in the line of the prophets and named him as the one the whole line was pointing at. Peter sees what the crowds do not. Matthew records the fuller confession and Jesus’ blessing (Matthew 16:16–19).

Right word, wrong picture. Two things follow, and they will occupy the rest of the chapter. The first is that the confession is correct and Luke records no commendation of it; he moves straight past it to what comes next. The second is that being right about the title is not the same as understanding it. Peter has the correct word and, as the other Gospels show, the wrong picture. He is about to hear what the Christ of God actually involves, and in Mark’s account, within moments of getting it right he is arguing with it (Mark 8:32). Which is a fair description of most people’s first real confession. The word is true. The content arrives later, and usually costs something.

How did Peter know? Matthew tells us Jesus’ answer: flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matthew 16:17). Peter did not reason his way to the confession by being cleverer than the crowds. He had seen the same evidence, and God opened his eyes. That is still how anyone comes to say Jesus is Lord: only by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). If you can say it from the heart, it is the gift of God, and you have reason to give thanks rather than to be proud.

What if I am not sure what I believe about Jesus? Then do what Peter did: stay close to him and look at the evidence. Read one of the Gospels through, asking at every page who this is. Pray honestly, even if your prayer is, if you are there, show me. Speak to a Christian you trust. Jesus did not ask the question to shame his disciples but to bring them to the answer, and he has not stopped asking it. The crowds had opinions; Peter had a confession. The difference is not cleverness but coming close.

In a sentence. After praying, Jesus asked who the crowds said he was, and then who the disciples said he was, and Peter answered: the Christ of God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus asks you the same question. Who do you say that he is? Not what your church says, or your parents, or the culture. Say it, aloud if you can, to him in prayer this week. And then ask what that confession requires of you by Friday.

For worship. He is the Christ of God: the anointed King, the Son of David, the one every prophet pointed to and every promise was waiting for. The crowds called him a prophet; heaven calls him Lord. Blessed be the Father, who has revealed his Son to babes, and has given us the words to confess him.
verseByVerse.note: Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi) but notes that Jesus was praying. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying: the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.

And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one. Two verbs, both forceful, stacked one on the other. Peter has just said the right thing and Jesus immediately puts a lid on it. Why silence a true confession? Because in Galilee in that decade, Messiah meant something specific and largely political: a son of David who would raise an army, break Rome, and restore the kingdom. Popular ideas of the Messiah were political and military. John’s Gospel records a crowd trying to make him king by force after the feeding (John 6:15). A public messianic claim would have started a movement he had not come to lead, and finished with soldiers. Announcing him now would provoke the wrong response. They themselves did not yet understand what kind of Messiah he was. So the word is held back until it can carry the meaning he is about to give it, which he does in the very next sentence.

The Son of Man. Take the title first. Having accepted the name Christ, he immediately calls himself the Son of Man, which is his own preferred title and is not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying a human being. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not be destroyed. It is a claim of enormous weight, wrapped in a phrase that sounds humble, which is exactly why he could use it in public.

Must suffer many things. This is the first passion prediction, immediately after the confession. Yes, I am the Christ, but the Christ must suffer. Must (dei) is divine necessity, the plan of God written in Scripture (24:26, 44–46). Luke uses it at every hinge of this Gospel: a boy in the temple who must be in his Father’s house (2:49), a preacher who must go to the next town (4:43), and now this. The cross is not a miscalculation, a tragedy, or a plan that went wrong. It is the appointment.

And be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin. The rejection is specified by office, which is to say the entire official religious leadership of the people of God. Not Rome. Not the pagans. The men who had the Scriptures.

And be killed, and on the third day be raised. Death and resurrection together, always. Note where he puts the resurrection: in the same sentence, the first time of telling. He never once announces the death without the rising. The disciples will still be devastated, and Luke will tell us why: they did not understand it (v. 45), and they were afraid to ask.

Luke’s omission. Luke does not record Peter’s rebuke and Jesus’ get behind me, Satan (Mark 8:32–33). Perhaps to spare Peter, or to keep the focus on the teaching.

Why must the Christ suffer? Because there was no other way to save sinners.
