God’s justice required that sin be punished, and his love purposed to save; at the cross both were satisfied, when the Son of Man bore in his own body the penalty his people deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:25–26; 1 Peter 2:24). The must is not fate imposed on Jesus from outside. It is the eternal plan of the Father, Son and Spirit, written in Scripture, which the Son freely embraced: no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

What Peter confessed and what Jesus described. What Peter has confessed and what Jesus has just described are the same person. That is the hardest thing in the chapter, and everything after it is the working out.

In a sentence. Jesus ordered them to tell no one, and explained that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and be raised on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Check the picture of Jesus you carry around. Is it a Christ who exists to make your life go well, or the Christ of God who must suffer and calls you to follow? When suffering comes, it is not proof that he has failed you. It is the road he walked first.

For worship. The Christ of God had to suffer for you. Worship the crucified and risen Messiah. The Son of Man to whom all dominion has been given went down into rejection and death of his own will, because it was the only way to bring us home. And on the third day he was raised. The must of the cross is the measure of his love.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to all, 'If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to all: if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.

And he said to all. Luke marks the audience deliberately. What follows is not advanced material for the Twelve. Not only the Twelve: every disciple. It is the terms of entry, said to everyone standing there.

If anyone would come after me. Would: wants to, wills to. A choice. Three clauses follow, and the middle one has a word in it that is Luke’s alone.

Let him deny himself. This is the first thing, and it is regularly misheard. It is not deny himself things, which is self-denial in the ordinary sense, giving up sugar or television, and it is not what the word says. It is to deny himself: say no to self as the centre and master of life. The verb is aparneomai, and Luke uses it again of Peter in the courtyard, in the warning that he would deny Jesus and in his remembering it (22:34, 61). To deny the self is to say about your own claims what Peter said about Jesus: I do not know him; he has no standing here. And this can be twisted into something poisonous, so it must be guarded. It is not self-hatred, and it is not the erasure of a personality God made. It is the dethroning of the self as the thing every decision is finally referred back to.

And take up his cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. Everyone knew the sight. The picture was not a metaphor to anyone hearing it. Crucifixion was a live and public Roman practice, and the phrase described one thing: a condemned man carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets to the place where he would be nailed to it. It meant a man going to his death, having lost everything. So the image is not merely bear your hardships. A difficult marriage, a chronic illness, a hard employer are real, and Scripture has a great deal to say about them, but they are not this. The cross is what a man picks up when he has already been sentenced and is on his way out of the city. To take up your cross is to accept rejection, shame and even death for Jesus’ sake.

Daily. Only Luke adds daily. Matthew and Mark record the saying without it (Matthew 16:24; Mark 8:34), and it changes the shape of the whole thing. A cross is carried once. Luke’s addition takes the most final image available and makes it a routine, which means it is not chiefly about martyrdom, and not reserved for the exceptional. Not only in moments of martyrdom, but every day. The cross is a way of life: dying to self in a thousand daily choices, for Christ. It is the ordinary Tuesday of an ordinary believer, in which the self is again told it does not rule here. For what dying to self does and does not mean, see the note on Philippians 3:10.

And follow me. To Jerusalem, to the cross, and beyond. Self-denial and the cross are not the goal; he is. The point of putting the self down is to walk after him.

For whoever would save his life will lose it. Life here is the self, the whole person. Cling to your life, protect it from the cost of following Jesus, and you lose it eternally. And the sentence is not a moral exhortation but a statement about how reality is built. A life organised around its own preservation is being lost in the act of being protected.

But whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. Give it up for Jesus, and you find it. There is no third option on offer, and the man who declines to choose has chosen.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by self-denial; only Christ’s cross atones. And not seeking suffering for its own sake. But the life that belongs to Christ takes the shape of his cross.

Does this mean I cannot enjoy anything? No. Self-denial in this sense is not the rejection of God’s good gifts; God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). It is the refusal to let the self be king over them. A Christian may enjoy a meal, a holiday, a career, a marriage, and enjoy them more than others, because he receives them from God’s hand and is ready to give them up if Christ asks. What he may not do is make any of them his master. The question is not, do I have good things? but, who rules over them?

In a sentence. Jesus told all who would follow him to deny themselves, take up their cross every day and follow him, because to cling to your life is to lose it, and to lose it for him is to save it.

On a Tuesday. What does taking up your cross today look like? Name one way you can say no to yourself for Christ’s sake. It may be telling the truth when a lie would protect you; serving someone who will not thank you; giving up the evening you had planned to help; keeping quiet about yourself so that Christ can be spoken of. Small crosses, carried daily, are how the self is dethroned.

For worship. He did not ask us to carry anything he did not carry first. The Son of God took up the real cross, the one with nails, and walked out of the city to die, so that our crosses would never have to bear the weight of our sin. Because he lost his life, we save ours. Every daily dying is a following of the one who has already conquered death, and the road we walk behind him ends in resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. Only Luke adds “daily.”

verseByVerse.quote: For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.

For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world. It is a commercial question, and the vocabulary is commercial: profit, gains, forfeits. He is asking about a transaction, and inviting the hearer to check the arithmetic. And he sets the exchange rate at the most extreme point available. Not a good salary, not a comfortable life: the whole world. Everything. Every currency, every pleasure, every honour, every acre. The greatest possible gain. Put all of it on one side of the scale.

And loses or forfeits himself? Against it he sets one item: himself. Luke says himself, where Mark says his soul. The self, the whole person: not the soul as some detachable religious component, but the man, the self who was going to enjoy all that. Nothing in the world is worth losing yourself for. And the point is that the trade is not merely bad; it is incoherent. The buyer has purchased everything and disposed of the only person who could have had it.

The prices people actually pay. Nobody in that crowd would ever gain the whole world, and nobody reading this will either. That is why the question is put at the extreme: if the trade fails at the maximum price, it fails at every price below it. And the prices most people actually pay are small: a working life arranged around security, a set of decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words. Shame is the right word for what usually happens, and he chose it rather than denies or rejects. The pressure on disciples was often not violence but scorn. To follow a crucified Messiah was shameful. Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ. A great many are embarrassed by him, and by the words particularly, which is what he specifies: me and my words. It is one thing to hold a private faith and quite another to be the person at the table who believes what he said about sin, or judgement, or himself.

Of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory. Measure for measure. At the judgement, Jesus will disown those who disowned him (12:8–9). The warning is exact and it is symmetrical: what is done to him now is what will be done then.

And the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. A threefold glory: his own, his Father’s, and the angels’. Jesus claims to share the Father’s glory. The one about to be rejected and killed will return as the glorious Judge. And the then is described in a way designed to reframe the now. The man whose association is currently a social liability is going to arrive in a company like that.

If I have sometimes been ashamed of Jesus, will he disown me? This verse describes a settled refusal to own him, not a moment of weakness. Peter denied him three times and was restored (22:61–62; John 21:15–19). Paul says if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful (2 Timothy 2:12–13). The answer to shame is not despair but to turn back to him, as Peter did.

In a sentence. Nothing gained in the world is worth losing yourself, and whoever is ashamed of Jesus will be disowned by him when he comes in glory.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to be ashamed of Jesus? Remember the day of his glory. Which puts the embarrassment in proportion. What is actually being weighed, in the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, is the estimate of a roomful of people against the estimate of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father. Next time the conversation turns, ask God for courage to say one true sentence about him.

For worship. The one we are tempted to be ashamed of was not ashamed of us. He was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11); he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and bore our disgrace outside the camp. And he is coming in the glory of the Father with the holy angels. On that day, all who belong to him will be owned before heaven, and the whole world will see that he was worth everything.

verseByVerse.quote: But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.

But I tell you truly, there are some standing here. Some standing here: not all. This is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and it should not be hurried, because sceptics have built a case on it and honest readers stumble over it. The charge is simple. Jesus told the people in front of him that some of them would still be alive when the kingdom of God arrived. They all died. Therefore he was mistaken, and the church has been explaining away a failed prediction ever since.

Who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God. Luke leaves out Mark’s come with power (Mark 9:1), making it simpler: they will see the kingdom. Three answers are given, and they are not equally strong. The weakest treats see the kingdom of God as the second coming and then argues about what taste death means. That does not work; the words are plain, and straining them does the text no favours. The second, and much better, takes the kingdom to mean what Luke consistently means by it: not the end of the world but the reign of God breaking in. On that reading the promise was kept within the lifetime of the hearers, and spectacularly: in the resurrection, when the King came out of a tomb; at Pentecost, when the Spirit fell and three thousand entered the kingdom in a morning; and in the years Luke describes in his second volume, when the gospel spread from Jerusalem to Rome. Men standing on that hillside saw all of it.

The answer in the next sentence. But the strongest answer is the one Luke himself supplies, and he supplies it in the very next sentence. Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain (v. 28). All three of the first Gospels put the transfiguration immediately after this promise, and none of them does it by accident. Some standing here, and eight days later exactly three of them are taken up a mountain and shown the Son of Man in his glory, with Moses and Elijah beside him and the voice of the Father over him. He said some of them would see the kingdom before they died. Eight days later, three of them did. The fulfilment begins there, a preview of the kingdom, and it continues in the resurrection, the ascension and Pentecost, when the kingdom comes in power, all within their lifetime.

A mercy as well as a fulfilment. And the placing is a mercy. He has just told them he is going to be rejected, killed and raised, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. Which is more or less how it still works. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

Is the kingdom here now, or still to come? Both. The kingdom of God came with Jesus: in his works, his death and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit, God’s reign broke into the world, and every believer has been transferred into it (Colossians 1:13). But it has not yet come in its fullness; that awaits Christ’s return in glory, when every enemy will be put under his feet and the dead raised (1 Corinthians 15:24–26). We live between the two: citizens of a kingdom that is real now and will be visible then. That is why Christians can be joyful and longing at the same time.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that some standing there would see the kingdom of God before they died.

On a Tuesday. The cross is not the end. The kingdom is coming, and in Christ you already belong to it. When the cost of following feels heavy, remember the mountain: God gives his people glimpses, in his word, in answered prayer, in the fellowship of his people, to strengthen them for the road. Thank him for the glimpses you have had.

For worship. The kingdom of God is not a failed prediction but an unstoppable reign. It came in power at the empty tomb and on the day of Pentecost, it has been spreading across the earth ever since, and it will come in glory when the King returns. Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end (Isaiah 9:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
About eight days after the confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray — and Luke alone tells us that is why he went. It happened while he was praying.

Luke is careful with his words. Mark and Matthew say he was transfigured; Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, describes what was seen: his face became different, his clothing turned a white that flashed. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus becoming something more than he was; it is the covering coming off something always there.

Moses and Elijah appear in glory — the Law and the Prophets. Both had met God on the same mountain, Sinai and Horeb; both had asked in their way to see him and been given a back and a whisper. Now they stand in the light, talking with him.

And Luke alone tells us the subject. They “spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word is exodos. The man who led the first one — out of Egypt, through the blood of a lamb, through the sea — is standing there while the word is applied to a death in Jerusalem. It is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven, before it happens: not a defeat but a deliverance, accomplished by a lamb, on a fixed date, by a leader who goes ahead of his people. And the verb is accomplish, not suffer.

The three were heavy with sleep and nearly missed it — and Luke will find the disciples asleep again in Gethsemane (22:45). Peter's proposal to build three tents comes as Moses and Elijah are leaving: a man trying to stop something ending, and Luke's aside is candid and gentle, “not knowing what he said.” The proposal is wrong in a specific way: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, three equals.

The cloud interrupts him mid-sentence. It is the shekinah — the cloud of Sinai, of the tabernacle, of Solomon's temple, unseen in Israel for centuries — and the verb “overshadowed” is the one Gabriel used to Mary (1:35).

“This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” Then the cloud lifts, and Moses is gone, and Elijah is gone, and there are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents.
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration is at once christological and eschatological — revealing who Jesus is, and what the coming kingdom will look like. What the disciples see is not a separate divine form he can put on and take off; it is the radiance belonging to who he always is, momentarily unrestrained. The humanity that veiled the glory at Bethlehem is for a few minutes transparent to it. This is what John means by “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14).

Moses and Elijah's conversation is the most extraordinary discussion never recorded — two of the greatest figures of the Old Testament speaking with the Son of God about the cross that will accomplish the ultimate Exodus. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it.

Some Bibles read “my Beloved” at v.35 rather than “my Chosen One,” and the manuscripts do differ. “Chosen One” is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading — a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the baptism and the parallel in Matthew. And the phrase is deliberate: “my chosen” is Isaiah's word for the Servant (Isa. 42:1). On a mountain where they have just discussed his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant's title.

“Listen to him” is the only imperative in the scene, and it is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one particular thing he said.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's desire to build three tents is the perennial temptation to institutionalise a moment of glory — to capture the experience, preserve it, replicate it. Every significant encounter with the living God carries it. The glory was never given to be housed; it was given for the road down.

And the road down is where nearly all Christian work is actually done. Jesus comes off that mountain the next morning into a crowd, a boy in convulsions, and a ministry that has failed. Moses came down Sinai carrying the tablets of God and found a golden calf.

“Listen to him” is the transfiguration's practical legacy. The disciples have been given an extraordinary visual confirmation, and are told the appropriate response is not to build but to listen. The Christian life is not primarily about spectacular experiences of divine glory, though God gives those in his mercy. It is about listening to the voice of the Son, in Scripture, in prayer, in the community of faith.

And the placing of it is a mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them he will be rejected and killed, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.

Now about eight days after these sayings. Luke ties it to what came before. Eight days ago Peter said the Christ of God, and Jesus said the Son of Man must suffer, and everyone was told to take up a cross. Now three of them are going up a mountain. About eight days counts inclusively, and Luke says about; Matthew and Mark say after six days. There is no contradiction. Luke’s about is doing exactly the work it appears to do, and the two are the same span counted in the ordinary way people speak.

He took with him Peter and John and James. The inner three (8:51): the same three who were in the room when Jairus’s daughter was raised, and the same three who, in Mark’s account, are taken deeper into the garden at Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). They see a dead girl stand up, they see him in glory, and they see him on the ground with his sweat like drops of blood, and the third scene is unintelligible without the second.

And went up on the mountain to pray. There it is again, and Luke is the only one who says it. Matthew and Mark have him take them up the mountain; Luke says why he went. He did not go up to be transfigured. He went up to pray, and it happened while he was praying, as the voice at the baptism came while he was praying (3:21–22).

The appearance of his face was altered. Luke is careful with his verbs, and there is a reason. Mark and Matthew use metemorphōthē: he was transfigured, the word behind metamorphosis. Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, avoids it, perhaps because Greek readers would think of pagan myths. He describes what was seen: his face became different. But the meaning is the same. Matthew says his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). As Moses’ face shone after being with God (Exodus 34:29–35); but Moses reflected a borrowed glory, and Jesus’ glory was his own, shining from within.

And his clothing became dazzling white. Dazzling (exastraptōn) means flashing like lightning: the glory of heaven.

Not added, but uncovered. And altered is the right sense. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus temporarily becoming something more than he had been; it is the covering coming off something that was there all along. The glory that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35) was, that evening, standing on a hillside in a human body, praying, and for a few minutes the body did not hide it. Which is why the detail about prayer matters so much. Whatever passed between the Son and the Father on that mountain, the glory of God broke through the surface of it.

Where did the glory come from? From who he is. Jesus is the eternal Son, the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature (Hebrews 1:3). In becoming man he did not stop being God; he veiled his glory in our flesh (Philippians 2:6–7; John 1:14). On the mountain the veil was drawn back for a moment. It is also a preview of the glory he would enter after his suffering (24:26), and of the glorified body that believers will one day share, when he transforms our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

In a sentence. About eight days later, Jesus took Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray, and as he prayed his face changed and his clothes became dazzling white.

On a Tuesday. Pray. The transfiguration happened while Jesus prayed, and the great moments of his life all came out of prayer. You will not shine like the sun, but prayer is where the Christian is changed. Set aside a time this week longer than usual, and simply behold him in his word.

For worship. The Jesus you pray to is this glorious Lord. And as you pray, you are being changed into his likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18). The carpenter from Nazareth, tired and dusty from the roads, is the Lord of glory, whose face outshines the sun. Behold your God: veiled in flesh for our sake, and unveiled for a moment on a mountain so that we might know who walks beside us down the hill.
verseByVerse.note: “About eight days” counts inclusively; Matthew and Mark say “after six days.” Only Luke says Jesus went up to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.

And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah. Of all the figures in Israel’s history, these two. Moses, who gave the law; Elijah, the greatest of the prophets. Between them they are the Law and the Prophets: the whole Old Testament, standing on a hillside, in conversation. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus (24:27, 44). Both were expected before the end (Malachi 4:4–5).

Both met God on a mountain. There is a second thing they share, and it is not usually noticed. Both of them had met God on a mountain: Moses at Sinai, Elijah at Horeb, which is the same mountain, and each was hidden in a cleft or a cave while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22; 1 Kings 19:9–13). Both had unusual ends. Moses died on a mountain in Moab and God buried him, and no one knows the place (Deuteronomy 34:5–6). Elijah did not die at all; he was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Each of them once asked, in his own way, to see God, and was allowed a glimpse of his back and a low whisper. Now they are standing in the light, talking with him.

Who appeared in glory. They share in the glory of the heavenly world.

And spoke of his departure. Only Luke tells us what they talked about, and the word he uses for it is startling. The word for departure is exodos: exodus. They are talking about his exodus. Consider who is standing there while that word is used. Moses led the first exodus from slavery in Egypt: through the blood of a lamb on a doorpost, through the Red Sea, toward the promised land. And the word for what he did is now being applied, in his hearing, to a death in Jerusalem. Jesus will lead a new and greater exodus, through his death, resurrection and ascension, freeing his people from slavery to sin and death and bringing them home to God. That is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven, before it happens. It is not a defeat, not an accident, not a tragedy to be redeemed afterwards. It is an exodus: a deliverance of a people out of a slavery deeper than Egypt’s, accomplished by a lamb, through blood, by a leader who goes ahead of them. The word also means death, departure from life (2 Peter 1:15).

Which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. And note the verb. Accomplish (plēroun) means to fulfil, complete. Not suffer. Not undergo. His death is not something that will happen to him, but something he will achieve. The cross is spoken of on that mountain the way a man speaks of a work he is going to finish. Jerusalem is the goal of the whole Gospel (v. 51; 13:33).

How did the disciples know who Moses and Elijah were? The text does not say; most likely it was given with the vision itself, or by what they heard them say. This is not a precedent for contact with the dead (compare 16:27–31). It was a unique revelation of the glorified state of God’s people and of the Law and the Prophets bearing witness to Christ’s departure.

Does this show the dead are conscious? It shows that Moses and Elijah were alive with God, centuries after they left the earth, and that they knew and cared about the work of Christ. That fits the rest of Scripture: God is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him (20:38), and those who die in the Lord are with him at once (23:43; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep. But Scripture forbids us to seek contact with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). This was God’s doing, once, on a holy mountain, for his Son’s sake.

In a sentence. Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke with Jesus about his exodus, which he would accomplish in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. The whole Old Testament points to the cross. Read it that way. When you read the Passover, the Red Sea, the wilderness, the prophets, ask how they lead to Calvary. And when you think of your own death, think of it as Luke does: for a believer, an exodus, a departure out of bondage into the presence of God.

For worship. Moses and Elijah are in glory, and they are not talking about glory. They have the attention of the Son of God on a mountaintop with the light of heaven on them, and what they discuss is Calvary. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it, and now the road runs downhill from here to Jerusalem. The greatest of the saints in heaven are absorbed in the cross. So shall we be, for ever: worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:12).
verseByVerse.note: The word for “departure” is exodus — his death, resurrection and ascension as a new rescue of God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah'—not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. As the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus: Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, not knowing what he said.

Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep. They almost missed it. Luke alone records this, and it is not a flattering detail to preserve. Perhaps it was night. The three of them are on a mountain where the Son of God is shining and two of the greatest figures in the history of redemption have arrived to discuss the salvation of the world, and the disciples are struggling to stay awake. It is worth noting where else Luke tells us this. In Gethsemane he finds the disciples sleeping for sorrow (22:45), and Mark names the same three (Mark 14:33–37). Twice, on the mountain of glory and in the garden of agony, at the two most significant nights of their lives, they cannot keep their eyes open. There is no rebuke attached to it here. They are tired, it is presumably late, and they have climbed a mountain. It is simply what men are like.

But when they became fully awake they saw his glory. They did see it. Luke is careful to say so, because the testimony for this scene depends on these men and he wants it clear that they were awake for it. Peter himself would later write: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, and we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:16–18). John wrote: we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

And as the men were parting from him. Notice the timing. Peter speaks as Moses and Elijah are leaving, which suggests a man trying to stop something ending. Peter wanted to keep them there.

Let us make three tents. Booths, shelters, almost certainly an echo of the Feast of Booths, when Israel lived in shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, and which looked forward to God dwelling with his people in the age to come. Peter has grasped that this is a foretaste of the kingdom. His instinct is to set up camp. And the proposal is wrong in a specific way: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah. Three tents, three equals. He puts Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah, and he wants to stay on the mountain when Jesus has just told him the way lies through Jerusalem and the cross. The next verse will correct that from the cloud, and the correction will leave Jesus standing alone.

Not knowing what he said. Luke’s comment is candid and gentle. Peter spoke from awe and confusion. He is not being wicked; he is doing what people do in the presence of something overwhelming, which is to talk, and to propose a project.

Why can we not stay on the mountain? Because the glory was given for the road, not instead of it. Christians have high moments: a conference, a season of revival, a time of deep closeness to God in prayer. They are real gifts. But they are not meant to be housed and preserved, and trying to recreate them leads to disappointment or worse. The way to the final glory runs through Jerusalem: through faithful ordinary obedience, through suffering, through the cross. The mountain strengthens you for that; it does not excuse you from it. And one day there will be a dwelling that does not end, when God himself makes his home with his people (Revelation 21:3).

In a sentence. The drowsy disciples woke to see Jesus’ glory, and as Moses and Elijah were leaving, Peter suggested building three shelters, not knowing what he was saying.

On a Tuesday. We want to stay on the mountaintop. But glory comes through the cross. Follow Jesus down into the valley. If you are living on the memory of a past spiritual high, thank God for it, and then ask what obedience he is calling you to in the valley this week. And if your prayers often fight sleep, take comfort: so did Peter’s. Keep coming.

For worship. The instinct to build something that will keep the moment is a permanent one, and it always fails for the same reason. The glory was never given to be housed. It was given for the road down. And the one whose glory they saw did not stay on the mountain either: he came down, set his face to Jerusalem, and went to the cross, so that one day we might dwell with him in a glory that will never end.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. A voice came out of the cloud, saying: this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him! When the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.

As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them. Peter is interrupted mid-sentence. It is the only answer his proposal gets. And the cloud is not weather. It is the cloud of God’s presence: the cloud that came down on Sinai (Exodus 24:15–18), that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35), that went before Israel in the wilderness, that filled Solomon’s temple until the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11). Israel had not seen it for centuries. Overshadowed (episkiazō) is the same word used of the Spirit coming on Mary (1:35): the power of the Most High will overshadow you. The same word, the same presence, at the conception and at the mountain.

And they were afraid as they entered the cloud. Of course they were. They entered the presence of God, and everything Israel knew said that men do not walk into that and come out.

And a voice came out of the cloud. The Father speaks twice in this Gospel and both times about the same person. At the Jordan it was spoken to Jesus: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). Here it is spoken to the three of them.

This is my Son. Not one of three, but the Son, unique. The answer to Peter’s three tents.

My Chosen One. Some manuscripts read my Beloved, as in Mark. Chosen One is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading: a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the wording at the baptism and in the other Gospels. And the phrase is deliberate. Chosen One echoes Isaiah 42:1: behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights. Jesus is the chosen Servant of the Lord, who will suffer (Isaiah 53). On a mountain where they have just been discussing his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant’s title. And the rulers will mock this very title at the cross: if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One (23:35).

Listen to him! Then the command, and it is the only command in the whole scene. Not, look at him, though the light was extraordinary. Not, build for him. Listen. It echoes Deuteronomy 18:15: the LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, and it is to him you shall listen. Jesus is that prophet, greater than Moses. And the command is aimed with precision at three men who have spent the last eight days failing to accept one particular thing he said: that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed and be raised. Listen to him, above all when he speaks of the cross (v. 22). Moses spoke and Elijah spoke and Israel was to hear them; the Father says the listening now goes to his Son.

And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. Moses and Elijah gone. Jesus only. The cloud lifts. There are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents. There is one, and he is the one they are to hear. The Law and the Prophets have said what they came to say and have stepped back, and what is left standing in the ordinary evening light is a man they are going to follow down the hill to Jerusalem.

And they kept silent and told no one in those days. Why did they tell no one? Jesus ordered them to tell no one until he had risen (Mark 9:9). Before the cross, the glory they had seen would only have fed the wrong hopes.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Through his word. The Son who spoke on earth now speaks through the Scriptures his Spirit inspired (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16). There is no need for a new voice from a cloud, and we should not seek one; the canon is closed, and Scripture is sufficient. Listen when you read the Bible, slowly and with prayer. Listen when it is faithfully preached. Listen especially to the parts you would rather not hear, as the three needed to hear about the cross. And listen in order to obey, for hearing in the Bible always means doing.

In a sentence. The cloud of God’s presence covered them, and the Father declared Jesus his Son, his Chosen One, and commanded them to listen to him, and then Jesus was alone.

On a Tuesday. God’s command to you today: listen to my Son. Open his word and hear him. Before you open your phone in the morning, open his word. And when other voices, even good ones, crowd in, remember the mountain: Moses and Elijah stepped back, and Jesus was found alone.

For worship. This is my Son, my Chosen One. The Father himself has spoken, from the cloud of his glory, and named his Son. Every other voice in history steps back before that one. Jesus only: our prophet, priest and king, the beloved of the Father, the chosen Servant who went down the mountain to die. Listen to him, and live.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “my Beloved” for “my Chosen One.”

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen
my chosen, in whom my soul delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets a father whose only child is seized by a spirit that convulses him — and the disciples who were not on the mountain had tried and failed.

The father's description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, then flattened exhaustion. So was the boy ill or possessed? Luke is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and he consistently keeps the categories apart: those sick with various diseases, and demons also came out of many (4:40-41); a crowd healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits (6:17-18). Jesus speaks the same way: “I cast out demons and perform cures” (13:32). Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this boy something else was behind them.

Two errors do real harm and Luke's care rules out both — that every seizure or darkness of mind is the enemy's work, and that “demon” was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose. But Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

“O faithless and twisted generation” is addressed to the whole scene, not the father — the word “twisted” is Moses' word for Israel in the wilderness (Deut. 32:5). And it is followed immediately by “Bring your son here.” He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy anyway.

Luke ends the miracle as he ended the one at Nain: “he gave him back to his father” (cf. 7:15). Not “the boy was healed.” A son handed back to the man who brought him.

Then, at the height of the crowd's enthusiasm, the second passion prediction — “let these words sink into your ears.” They did not understand, it was concealed from them, and they were afraid to ask. Afraid of the answer, almost certainly; Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32).

And what fills the silence is an argument about which of them is greatest. Jesus takes a child — a person with no legal standing and nothing to offer — and stands the child beside himself. Then John reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, and gives his reason: “he does not follow with us.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' failure at v.40, after their success in vv.1-6, raises the question of what changed. Matthew records Jesus naming it as “little faith” (Matt. 17:20). The lesson is what the whole chapter teaches: the authority delegated to them is not their own. It flows from the one who gives it and is sustained by the relationship of trust with him.

“Delivered into the hands of men” — handed over. There is a bitter wordplay the English keeps: the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of men.

Luke's “it was concealed from them” is a passive without an agent, and probably deliberately so. Two things are true at once: there is a hiddenness God appoints (cf. 19:42; 24:16), and there is a hiddenness they are manufacturing, since the next verse shows exactly what they were thinking about instead.

On “the one who is not against you is for you” — a reader will notice the apparent opposite at 11:23, “whoever is not with me is against me.” The difference is in the pronouns. There the subject is a man's own relation to Christ, where there is no neutral ground. Here it is one servant's judgement of another. About my own standing, assume nothing; about another doing good in his name, assume the best.
verseByVerse.examples:
The child placed beside Jesus is a searching challenge to every form of Christian leadership measured by influence, platform, numbers or reputation. A first-century child had no legal rights, no property, no voice, and no capacity to confer honour on anybody — which is exactly why he was chosen for an argument about greatness.

So the test is not how a man behaves towards those above him; everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats those who cannot advance him, repay him, report him, or do him any good at all. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching.

“I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not” is an honest report of ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed. It belongs in the Gospel and it is a comfort of a hard kind: the record of the church's work has always included the things that did not work.

And John's “he does not follow with us” — not “he does not follow you” — names the instinct precisely. It is the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition. Christ has servants who do not attend your church, use your vocabulary, or share your history, and they are not to be stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out: Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.

On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain. From glory to need. The mountain was last night. This is the morning, and the crowd is waiting at the bottom. Luke has built the contrast deliberately, and it is the same one Moses walked into. He came down Sinai carrying the words of God, and found the people round a golden calf (Exodus 32). Jesus comes down with the voice of the Father still in the disciples’ ears, and finds a boy in convulsions and a ministry that has failed.

Where Christian work is done. That descent is where nearly all Christian work is actually done. Not on the mountain, and not in the memory of it, but the next morning at the bottom of the hill, among people who were not there and have a problem that will not wait. The mountaintop prepares for the valley.

And behold, a man from the crowd cried out. Every word of what follows is a father’s. He cried out: he shouted over a crowd.

Teacher, I beg you to look at my son. He does not open with a theological claim or a request for a miracle; he asks Jesus to look at the boy. Look at means look upon with favour and compassion. He has stopped expecting anything and is asking for attention.

For he is my only child. And then the detail that does the work. Only Luke says only, and he has used that phrase twice already: the widow’s only son at Nain (7:12), Jairus’s only daughter (8:42). It is his way of saying there is nothing behind this. No other children, no second chance, and in that world no future for the family either. The depth of a father’s grief.

A father in a crowd. This man is not a disciple, and Luke does not tell us his name. He is a father in a crowd who has been living for years with a child who is destroyed in front of him at unpredictable intervals, and who has come, presumably having heard something, to a preacher’s followers, and been let down. Anybody who has cared for a severely ill or disabled child will recognise the exhaustion in the request. He does not ask for much. He asks to be looked at.

Does God see my child? Yes. The God who saw Hagar’s son crying under a bush in the wilderness (Genesis 21:17), and who looked on this boy through the eyes of his Son, sees every child and every parent. If you are caring for a child who is ill, disabled or far from God, you may feel unseen by everyone, including the church. Jesus is not like the crowd. Bring your child to him in prayer, as this father did, even if all you can manage is, Lord, look at my son. And ask your church family for help; they are meant to carry this with you (Galatians 6:2).

In a sentence. Coming down from the mountain, Jesus was met by a crowd and a father who begged him to look at his only son.

On a Tuesday. Bring your children to Jesus and ask him to look on them with favour. Pray for each one by name this week. And look out for the exhausted parents in your church, those caring for a sick or disabled child, and ask what one practical thing you could do for them.

For worship. The Son came down from the mountain of glory into a valley of need, and he has never stopped coming down. The Lord who looks on the humble from on high (Psalm 113:5–7) looked on a convulsing boy and his weary father. Blessed be the God who sees, and who does not leave the valley to its own devices.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.

And behold, a spirit seizes him. An evil spirit. The father’s description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it immediately: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, and then the flattened exhaustion afterwards. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, but the cause was demonic (v. 42).

And shatters him. Shatters (syntribon) means crushes, bruises, breaks him. Satan’s aim is destruction.

And will hardly leave him. Even between seizures, it barely lets him go.

Ill or possessed? So was this boy ill, or was he possessed? And behind that sits the sharper question people actually mean: were these pre-scientific people simply calling a disease of the brain a devil? The answer comes from Luke himself, and it is worth having, because he is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and his Gospel is full of his clinical eye: the woman who had spent all she had on doctors (8:43), the high fever (4:38), the sweat like drops of blood (22:44). And he consistently keeps the two categories apart. He writes that they brought Jesus those who were sick with various diseases, and that demons also came out of many (4:40–41). He describes a crowd who came to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits who were cured (6:17–18): two groups, named separately, in a single breath. Jesus himself speaks the same way: I cast out demons and perform cures (13:32). A man who thought every convulsion was a devil would not write like that. Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this particular boy something else was behind them.

Two errors. Two errors do real harm here, and Luke’s own care rules out both. The first makes every seizure, every darkness of the mind, a work of the enemy: a cruelty this Gospel forbids by the plain fact that its author lists sickness and spirits as different things. A Christian with epilepsy is not in the devil’s grip; he needs good medicine and the love of his church, not an interrogation about hidden sin. The second is the fashionable error, that demon was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose properly. But notice what happens in two verses’ time: Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not. That sentence has to be sat with, because it is the honest report of a ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed. The nine disciples who stayed below had failed, though Jesus had given them authority over all demons (v. 1). These are the same men who came back a chapter ago full of what they had done. Whatever happened in those villages was real. And here, at the bottom of the mountain, with a father watching, nothing worked.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? Jesus calls it faithlessness (v. 41), and in Mark he adds that this kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer (Mark 9:29). The authority they had been given was real, but it was derived, and they had stopped depending on the one who gave it.

What should I do when the church fails someone? Admit it honestly, as this father’s words force the disciples to. Churches and Christians do fail people: in counsel, in care, in prayer, in noticing. The answer is not to pretend otherwise, nor to give up on Christ because his people failed. The father did the right thing: when the disciples could not help, he took his son to Jesus himself. If you have been let down by Christians, do not let their failure keep you from the Lord. And if you are the one who failed, take it back to him in prayer, and learn dependence.

In a sentence. The father described how a spirit seized and convulsed his son, crushing him, and how the disciples had failed to cast it out.

On a Tuesday. Past success is no guarantee of present power. Every work of God needs fresh dependence on him. If you teach, lead, counsel or serve in any way, do not walk into this week on the strength of last week’s fruit. Pray before you begin, every time.

For worship. What his servants cannot do, he can. When our best efforts fail, Christ has not failed. The Lord of the mountain is also the Lord of the valley, and no work of the devil is too strong for him. He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here. While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marvelling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples:

O faithless and twisted generation. It is one of the sharpest things Jesus says in this Gospel, and the first question is who it is aimed at. Not the father. The man has done nothing wrong; he came, he asked, and he told the truth about what happened. Not the boy. The address is to a generation: the crowd, the disciples, the whole scene at the foot of the mountain. Addressed to all, including the disciples. Twisted (diestrammenē) means perverse, crooked: the word Moses used of Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:5).

How long am I to be with you and bear with you? And there is something in the tone worth noticing, because it is not simply anger. It is the sound of a man carrying something heavy: the weariness of the holy Son among unbelievers. He has come down from the light of his Father’s presence into a valley where nothing works, and he says so.

Bring your son here. Then, without pausing: and yet compassion. That is the whole answer to the question of whether the exasperation was the last word. He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy. He does not make the father’s help conditional on the crowd improving.

The demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. Its last attack, and it happens on the way. Luke wants it seen: the thing is at its worst in the final seconds before it is finished. That is not unusual, and it is worth knowing by anyone who has watched a besetting sin or a long oppression flare up hardest just as ground is being taken.

But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. Three verbs, and the third is the one Luke chose to end on. Luke tells it more briefly than Mark, but he keeps this. He gave him back to his father, exactly the phrase used at Nain, where he gave him to his mother (7:15). The same tender words. Not, the boy was healed; not, the demon departed. A son was handed back to the man who had brought him. Luke will not let a miracle be reported as an event when it can be reported as a gift, from one person to another, in front of witnesses.

And all were astonished at the majesty of God. Majesty (megaleiotēti) means greatness, magnificence. The crowd does not credit a technique or a healer. They saw God’s greatness in what Jesus did. The same word is used of the transfiguration (2 Peter 1:16). The majesty seen on the mountain is now seen in the valley: something of the size of God has been visible in a valley, in a boy who could stand up, in the arms of a father who had stopped hoping.

Does Jesus lose patience with me? He grieves over unbelief, and he says so; we should not pretend he is indifferent to it. But notice what he does with his weariness: he says, bring your son here. His patience is not endless in the sense that sin does not matter to him; it is endless in the sense that he goes on bearing with his people until he has finished his work in them. The same Lord who sighed over a faithless generation went to the cross for it. If you fear you have exhausted his patience, the very fear shows his Spirit is still at work. Bring your need to him.

In a sentence. Jesus lamented the faithlessness of his generation, then rebuked the spirit, healed the boy and gave him back to his father, and everyone was astonished at the majesty of God.

On a Tuesday. When the thing you are fighting flares up hardest, do not conclude you are losing. It may be the last throw of a defeated enemy. Keep bringing it to Christ. And when he answers, give him the glory: tell someone of the majesty of God you have seen.

For worship. The majesty of God is seen in Jesus’ compassion as much as in his glory. Worship him. The same splendour that shone on the mountain stooped down in the valley to lift a broken boy and put him into his father’s arms. Our God is great enough to rule the universe and gentle enough to give a son back to his father.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

The second passion prediction. While everyone was marvelling at his power (v. 43), Jesus speaks of his weakness. The timing is the point. The crowd is at the height of its enthusiasm (a boy has been restored, God’s greatness is on everyone’s lips) and Jesus turns away from all of it to tell his disciples something that will spoil it. Popular amazement would not last. The disciples must not be swept up in it.

Let these words sink into your ears. Literally, put these words into your ears. Pay close attention. Remember this. Set them down there. He is not making an announcement; he is asking them to store something they will need later and cannot use yet.

The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. This is the second passion prediction, much shorter than the first, and one word in it is new. Delivered (paradidosthai) means handed over, betrayed. It is the word that will be used of Judas throughout the passion, and the word Isaiah’s Greek text uses of the Servant who was handed over because of our sins (Isaiah 53:12). And there is a bitter play on words that the English keeps. The Son of Man into the hands of men. The one who came as the representative man is going to be handed over to men, by a man, and killed by them. The one who heals by his hands will be handed into human hands.

But they did not understand this saying. They could not reconcile a suffering Messiah with what they believed.

And it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. Only Luke says this. Concealed by whom? He does not say, and the passive is probably deliberate. Two things are true at once, and the Gospel holds both. There is a hiddenness that God appoints. God concealed it, not as punishment, but because the time for understanding had not yet come. Luke will say the same of the Emmaus pair, whose eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16), and their eyes would be opened only after the resurrection (24:31, 45). And there is a hiddenness the disciples are making for themselves, because the next verse shows exactly what they were thinking about instead, and it was which of them was greatest.

And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. There is the human half, stated plainly. They did not understand, and they did not ask, and Luke tells us why: they were afraid. Afraid of what? Almost certainly of the answer. There is a kind of not-understanding that is genuinely stuck, and there is a kind that has grasped enough to know it does not want the rest. Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32). They had understood more than they wanted to.

Why would God hide the meaning from them? For a time, and for their good. They could not yet bear the full truth of the cross, and they would understand it only in the light of the resurrection, when the risen Christ opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (24:45). God’s timing in revelation is wise. There are things in his word you may not understand yet, and some will become clear only through later experience, or in glory. That is no excuse for not asking; the disciples’ fear was their own fault. But it is a comfort when understanding is slow. He will finish teaching you.

In a sentence. While everyone marvelled, Jesus told his disciples to remember that he would be handed over to men, but they did not understand, because it was hidden from them, and were afraid to ask.

On a Tuesday. Do not be afraid to ask Jesus about the hard things in his word. Understanding is his gift. The question that most needs asking is very often the one nobody in the room will raise, not because it is difficult, but because everyone present suspects what the answer will cost. Ask it, in prayer and to people who know the Scriptures. And be wary of being carried along by enthusiasm without asking where Jesus is going.

For worship. The hands that had just lifted a broken boy would be handed over to the hands of men and nailed to a cross. He told them it was coming, and he went. The Son of Man was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). We understand now what they could not: that the delivering up was love, and the hands that were pierced are the hands that hold us.

parallels.desc: they understood none of these things

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side
verseByVerse.commentary:
An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side.

An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. Read that sentence with the previous one still in the air. He has just told them he is going to be handed over to men and killed. They did not understand it, and were afraid to ask. And what fills the silence is an argument about rank. Jesus speaks of being handed over; they argue about rank. Luke sets the two side by side without a word of comment, and the effect is devastating. The same argument will arise at the Last Supper (22:24).

What were they arguing about? The timing suggests an answer. Three of them had just been up a mountain and come back different, and would not say why (v. 36). Peter had been the one to name him the Christ. The nine had not managed to cast out the demon. Perhaps the choice of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy, or the failure of the nine. There was material for a dispute, and it was fresh. So this is not a general failing of ambitious men. It is what happened in the hours after the glory, among people who had been let in on something, which is precisely where this particular sin lives. Nobody argues about greatness who has not first been given something.

But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts. Luke does not say they told him. He knew what they were thinking (5:22; 6:8), and the phrase he uses is the reasoning of their hearts, which is where the argument actually was. Whatever was being said aloud, the thing being weighed was internal, and he could see it. That is worth pausing on before the child arrives. This is not a man detecting a squabble. It is the one who knew what was in man (John 2:25) reading the inner life of twelve people at once, including the parts they would not have admitted to each other.

Took a child and put him by his side. He does not answer the argument. He does not name a winner, or rebuke the ambition, or deliver a lecture on humility. He walks over, takes a child (paidion, a young one, small enough to be taken) and stands the child beside himself, in the place of honour. Children had no status in the ancient world. The picture is the argument. Twelve grown men are ranking themselves, and he places beside himself the one person present with no rank whatsoever.

Is it wrong to want to do well? No. Paul tells us to excel, to work heartily, to aim for the prize (1 Corinthians 9:24; Colossians 3:23). Ambition for God’s glory and for the good of others is a virtue. What Jesus exposes here is the desire to be thought greater than others: comparison, rank, the need to be ahead. The test is simple. Can you rejoice when someone else is honoured, chosen, or more fruitful than you (Romans 12:15)? Do you want to be great, or do you want Christ to be great? Pride hides easily in spiritual success, so watch especially after God has blessed you.

In a sentence. When the disciples argued about which of them was greatest, Jesus, knowing their thoughts, set a child beside him.

On a Tuesday. Pride is persistent, even in disciples. Watch for the desire to be thought greater than others. Notice this week when you mentally rank yourself against someone: a colleague, a fellow church member, a sibling. Confess it to God by name, and then do something to honour the person you were measuring yourself against.

For worship. The one who had every right to be called the greatest took the lowest place. Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7). While his disciples argued about rank, he was on his way to be handed over. And he put a child in the place of honour beside him, because that is the kind of King he is.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said to them: whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.

Whoever receives this child in my name receives me. To understand the force of this, the modern picture of childhood has to be set aside entirely. A first-century child was loved, certainly. But in law and in society a child was a person of no standing: no legal rights, no property, no voice, no capacity to confer honour on anybody. A child could do nothing whatever for a man’s position. That is why Jesus chose one to stand beside him in the middle of an argument about greatness. Receives is the key verb, and it is the language of hospitality: to welcome, to take somebody in. So the question is not, who is willing to be like a child?, though that is true elsewhere (18:17). The question here is: who will you make room for, when the person can do nothing for you? To welcome a person of no status, for Jesus’ sake, is to welcome Jesus himself. He identifies himself with the least.

And whoever receives me receives him who sent me. And so receives God. Then the chain, which is startling. Receive the child, and you receive Christ. Receive Christ, and you receive the Father who sent him. The one with the least standing in the room is connected, in three steps, to the throne of God. That is not sentiment. It is a claim about where Christ has chosen to be found, and it will be made again more sharply: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40).

For he who is least among you all is the one who is great. And there is the answer to their argument, and it is not that the argument was about nothing. He does not abolish greatness. He tells them the measurement is inverted, and then leaves them holding it. Greatness in the kingdom turns the world upside down. The least is the greatest. Not the one who seeks to be great, but the one who becomes small: who welcomes the unimportant and serves without seeking recognition (22:26–27).

Making it concrete. This is easy to admire and hard to live. The test is not how a man behaves towards those above him; everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats the people who cannot advance him, cannot repay him, cannot report him, and will never be in a position to do him any good at all. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching. Whatever is being said to them is being said to Christ, and whatever is being given them is going to the Father.

Does this mean children’s work in the church matters? Very much. Those who welcome, teach and care for children in Christ’s name are receiving Christ himself, though their work is often unseen and rarely thanked. The crèche rota and the Sunday school are not lesser ministries for those not gifted enough to preach. And the principle reaches further: the disabled, the elderly with dementia, the newcomer who does not fit, the person with nothing to give. A church’s greatness is measured by how it receives those who can do nothing for it.

In a sentence. Jesus taught that whoever welcomes a child in his name welcomes him and the Father, and that the least among them is the greatest.

On a Tuesday. Welcome someone today who can give you nothing in return. In them, you welcome Christ. On Sunday, speak to the child, the shy visitor, or the elderly member no one sits with. Thank someone who serves among the children. And if you are tempted to think your own hidden service is wasted, remember who is being received in it.

For worship. The God of glory has chosen to be found among the least. The Father sent his Son, the Son identifies himself with a child, and the welcome of a little one reaches the throne of heaven. He who was the greatest became the least of all, the servant of all, so that the least might be made great in him. What a Lord, who counts a cup of water to a child as given to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John answered: Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us. But Jesus said to him: do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.

John answered, Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name. The word answered is odd, because nobody had asked John anything. He is responding to what Jesus has just said about receiving a child, and what he offers, apparently as a contribution, is an account of something they did. The timing is not accidental and Luke has left it exposed. Jesus has just placed a child beside himself and said the least is the greatest. John, one of the three who went up the mountain, immediately produces an incident in which the disciples enforced a boundary.

What John reports. Now look at what he actually reports, because it is carefully worded. The man was casting out demons. It was working. Successfully, when the disciples had just failed at precisely this a few verses earlier (v. 40). And he was doing it in your name: not in his own, not as a rival, but under the authority of Jesus.

And we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us. So the ground for stopping him is not that he was a fraud, and not that he was doing harm. John states the reason himself, and it is the only reason he has. With us: not one of our group. Not, he does not follow you. Us. The same pride as the argument about greatness, now as group pride.

Do not stop him. Jesus corrects their exclusiveness, and the correction is immediate and unqualified.

For the one who is not against you is for you. A generous principle. Anyone genuinely working in Jesus’ name against Satan is on the same side. What is being corrected is a specific instinct, and it is thoroughly religious. It is the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition.

Against or with? A reader will notice that Jesus says something apparently opposite two chapters later: whoever is not with me is against me (11:23). The two are not in conflict, and the difference is in the pronouns. There, the subject is a man’s own relation to Christ, and there is no neutral ground: no one is uncommitted where he is concerned. Here, the subject is one servant’s judgement of another, and the presumption runs the other way. The first is a rule for how to view others; the second, a test for oneself. About my own standing before Christ, assume nothing. About another man doing good in his name, assume the best. Do not exclude genuine fellow workers; but you yourself must be wholly with Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who uses Jesus’ name is a true believer, or that doctrine does not matter (Matthew 7:22–23; Acts 19:13–16; Galatians 1:8). The issue here is group loyalty, not the truth of the gospel. The man in question was doing something unmistakably good in the name of Jesus. That is a long way from saying it does not matter what anyone believes.

How do I tell a fellow worker from a false teacher? Ask what he says about Christ and the gospel, not whether he belongs to your group. Does he confess Jesus as Lord and God, crucified for sinners and risen (1 John 4:2–3; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4)? Does he preach salvation by grace through faith, not by works (Galatians 1:6–9)? Does his life and teaching honour Christ? Where those are present, rejoice in his work, even if he baptises differently, governs his church differently or sings different songs. Where the gospel itself is denied, the name of Jesus is being used, not served, and love requires us to say so.

In a sentence. When John said they had tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name because he was not one of them, Jesus told them not to stop him, for whoever is not against them is for them.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice when Christ is served by believers outside your own circle. Think of a church or ministry in your town that is not yours but preaches Christ faithfully, and pray for it by name this week. Speak well of it. And watch for the moment when you are more pleased that your group succeeds than that Christ is honoured.

For worship. Christ has servants who do not attend your church, use your vocabulary, or share your history, and they are not to be stopped. The Lord of the harvest is bigger than our circles. His kingdom advances wherever his name is honestly served, and he will gather a people from every tribe and tradition to sing one song before his throne. Thank him that the kingdom is his, not ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” With that sentence Luke's narrative pivots. The Galilean ministry is over, and the journey that runs from here to 19:44 begins. Everything that follows — the parables, the healings, the controversies — happens on the road that leads to the cross.

“Taken up” reaches past the cross to the ascension. Luke has the whole arc in one word: the death, the rising, the going home.

“Set his face” is the language of the Suffering Servant: “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 50:7) — from a passage whose preceding verse reads, “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard.” He is not swept toward the cross by events, or cornered by his enemies. He turns and starts walking.

The route runs through Samaria, which some Jewish pilgrims avoided by going round through the Jordan valley. He goes straight through. And the village refuses him precisely because his face is set toward Jerusalem — the ancient dispute over Gerizim and Jerusalem. On the first day of the journey to the cross, what he is rejected for is going to the cross.

James and John ask to call down fire, reasoning from Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:10-12), and reasoning badly: Elijah faced armed men sent to seize a prophet, and these two are facing a village that declined to provide beds. Jesus rebukes the disciples, not the Samaritans, and they go on to another village. Samaritan villages like it would be evangelised within a few years (Acts 8:5-8, 25), and no one there was burned.

Three encounters close the chapter. A man volunteers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head — a saying that fits the refusal he has just met. A second is called and asks to bury his father first; in that world burial happened the same day, so the request may well mean “let me stay until my father dies,” an indefinite postponement. A third asks only to say goodbye — which is what Elisha was granted (1 Kgs. 19:20) — and is answered with a ploughing image, the difference being that Elisha destroyed his plough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The travel narrative beginning at 9:51 is Luke's unique structural contribution. Matthew and Mark move quickly from Galilee to Jerusalem; Luke devotes ten chapters to the journey. The structure is theological before it is geographical: to follow Jesus is to be on the road to Jerusalem, which is to say on the road to the cross. The whole of it is lived in the shadow of the set face of 9:51.
