“Leave the dead to bury their own dead” is among the most shocking sayings in the Gospels — an apparent violation of the fifth commandment and of an obligation so weighty that the Old Testament names its absence as a mark of judgement (Jer. 22:18-19). It is not an abolition of family duty. It is a refusal of one word, and the word is first. And the saying is wordplay, not cruelty: let those who are spiritually dead attend to the socially necessary; you have been called by the one who gives life.

“Fit for the kingdom of God” is the language of usefulness. It is not a statement about whether such a man is saved. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while facing the wrong way.

And the instinct James and John show — to destroy those who reject Jesus — is answered by the direction he is walking. The one who has set his face toward a cross does not call down fire on those who refuse him; he presses on toward the sacrifice that will make it possible for even Samaritans to receive him.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ancient plough was light, single-handled, and pulled through stony ground; it had to be held down with constant pressure and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A man who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment, and a crooked first furrow makes every furrow after it crooked, because they are all set by the first. The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

The three would-be disciples represent three ways of not following. The first underestimates the cost — “wherever you go” sounds easy until it means homelessness. The second and third both say first. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable, which is exactly what makes them so effective at postponing everything.

Luke does not tell us what any of the three decided. He never does. The stories are left open, which is itself the point: the road is still going, and the question is still standing.

And a comfortable church needs the first exchange plainly, because a certain kind of preaching promises the opposite — that coming to Christ secures a settled life. The one making the offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing.

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. He sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

The journey to Jerusalem. This is the hinge of Luke’s Gospel. Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins, running to 19:44, ten chapters. Everything from here on happens on a road, and the road has one destination. Much of Luke’s unique material is here: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus. The whole journey is lived in the shadow of the cross.

When the days drew near. Literally, the days were being fulfilled, filled up. Time is running out on purpose, and it is being counted.

For him to be taken up. Taken up (analēmpsis) is a noun used nowhere else in the New Testament. It means the taking up, and it reaches past the cross to the ascension: the same root as the verb in Acts 1, where he was taken up (Acts 1:2, 11, 22). Luke is describing the whole arc in one word, the whole of his departure: the death, the rising, and the going home to the Father. Jesus looks beyond the cross to the glory.

He set his face to go to Jerusalem. The phrase is Hebrew in shape, an expression of fixed determination, and it is not merely a decision. It is the language of the Suffering Servant: I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame (Isaiah 50:7). And it belongs to a passage in which the Servant says, in the verse before, I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). So the face that is set towards Jerusalem is set with Isaiah’s words already in it, and the man knows exactly what is at the other end. He is not swept toward the cross by events, or cornered by his enemies, or overtaken by a plot. He turns and starts walking. Jesus knows what awaits him in Jerusalem, and he goes there resolutely. Nothing will turn him aside.

And he sent messengers ahead of him. To arrange food and lodging for a large group. The route from Galilee to Jerusalem ran through Samaria, and many Galilean pilgrims went round it, down the Jordan valley and through Perea, east of the river, adding days to the journey rather than cross that ground. He goes straight through.

A village of the Samaritans. Samaria lay between Galilee and Judea. Samaritans were descendants of the northern Israelites who had intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses, and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem (John 4:20). The hostility was ancient and mutual. Jews and Samaritans despised each other.

But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. Because he was going to worship in Jerusalem, at the Jewish temple they rejected. Samaritans were often hostile to Jewish pilgrims passing through to Jerusalem. So the refusal is not personal. It is a village looking at a party of pilgrims heading for the wrong mountain, and declining to house them. And notice the irony. What he is rejected for, on the first day of the journey to the cross, is going to the cross.

Did Jesus know everything that would happen in Jerusalem? Yes. He had already told the disciples twice (vv. 22, 44), and he would tell them again in detail: he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon (18:31–33). He did not go to Jerusalem hoping for the best. He went as the Lamb who knew the altar. That is what makes his resolve so overwhelming. Every step south was taken with full knowledge, and every step was chosen. He was not a victim of circumstances but the willing Saviour.

In a sentence. As the time of his departure approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem, but a Samaritan village refused to welcome him because he was heading there.

On a Tuesday. Is there a hard thing God has made clear you must do: a conversation to have, a sin to confess, a duty to take up? Set your face. Do not wait for it to become easy. And when obedience costs you a welcome somewhere, remember that it cost him a bed on the first night of the road.

For worship. Jesus set his face to go to the cross for you. Nothing could turn him aside from saving you. Not the rejection of a village, not the failure of his friends, not the shadow of what was waiting. He saw the cross, and he saw beyond it to his taking up, and for the joy that was set before him he endured it (Hebrews 12:2). Our salvation rests not on our resolve but on his: the face set like a flint toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins. “Taken up” points to the ascension. Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea and were often hostile to pilgrims heading to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: I have set my face like a flint
Jews have no dealings with Samaritans

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his disciples James and John saw it, they said: Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.

James and John. Jesus called them Boanerges, Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17). Here we see why, and it is difficult to read this verse without concluding that the name was earned.

Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? And notice: they ask permission. They do not act. There is even a kind of deference in it, do you want us to?, which makes the request more disturbing rather than less, because they genuinely expect the answer might be yes. Their precedent is scriptural. Elijah, in this same region, called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent by the king of Samaria to arrest him (2 Kings 1:9–16). These two have recently come down a mountain where they saw Elijah in glory. And they had been given power (v. 1). Why not use it? They are not making it up; they are reasoning from the Bible, and reasoning badly. Because the situation is not the same at all. Elijah faced armed men sent by an idolatrous king to seize a prophet. James and John are facing a village that declined to provide beds.

But he turned and rebuked them. The one rebuked in this passage is not the Samaritans. Luke records no word to the village at all. The rebuke goes to the disciples. Jesus came to save, not to destroy. This is not the time for judgement, but for grace. The day of vengeance has not yet come (4:19).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add as Elijah did, and others add Jesus’ words: you do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them. These are probably not original, but they capture the meaning. They are absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, and the modern versions put them in a footnote, which is why one Bible may be shorter than another at exactly this point. Two things are worth saying, and they pull in opposite directions. The words are almost certainly not what Luke wrote: a scribe appears to have supplied the content of a rebuke Luke deliberately left unstated, and once written in a margin it moved into the text. But the sentence that was added is entirely true, and it is true from Luke’s own pages. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10) is in this Gospel in Jesus’ own words. And within one chapter the hero of his most famous story will be a Samaritan (10:33). The copyist guessed the theology exactly right. He simply had no business putting his guess into the Gospel.

And they went on to another village. No revenge. He simply went elsewhere. That is the whole response to rejection: no fire, no argument, no curse. They walked on.

The fire that did come. And Jesus would later send his gospel to Samaria (Acts 1:8), where it would be received with great joy (Acts 8:5–8, 14–17), and John himself would go there with Peter to lay hands on Samaritan believers so they would receive the Holy Spirit. The fire would come down on Samaria: the fire of the Spirit, not of judgement. The man who wanted to burn a Samaritan village lived to pray for Samaritans to receive the Spirit.

Will God never judge, then? He will. The day of vengeance is real, and Jesus himself speaks of it often (17:26–30; 21:22). Those who finally reject him will face God’s just and eternal judgement (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). But judgement belongs to God, not to us, and it belongs to the last day, not to this one. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Our task is to warn, to plead and to pray, never to wish destruction on those who reject us. Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord (Romans 12:19).

In a sentence. When James and John offered to call down fire on the Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them, and they went on to another village.

On a Tuesday. When people reject you or the gospel, resist the desire for revenge. Jesus came to save, and so should you. Notice when you enjoy imagining the downfall of someone who has mocked your faith, or a political opponent, or a church that has hurt you. Turn the thought into a prayer for them. And be careful of using Bible verses to justify the anger you already feel.

For worship. The Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them. The words may not be Luke’s, but the truth is his, and it is the heartbeat of the gospel. The Lord who could have called down fire chose instead to bear the fire of God’s wrath himself, on the cross, so that Samaritans and Galileans and we ourselves might receive the fire of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “as Elijah did,” and a further saying: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.”

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were going along the road, someone said to him: I will follow you wherever you go. And Jesus said to him: foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

Three would-be followers. Three men now meet him on that road, in three short encounters about the cost of discipleship (vv. 57–62), and Luke puts them together because between them they cover most of the ways a person fails to follow. Each shows a different obstacle.

I will follow you wherever you go. The offer is unprompted, enthusiastic, sincere, and unlimited, but perhaps impulsive. Nobody called this man. He volunteers, and he volunteers everything: wherever you go. Matthew tells us he was a scribe (Matthew 8:19), which adds something: a trained man, used to attaching himself to a teacher, and probably expecting the arrangement to look like the ones he knew. Does he know where Jesus is going? To Jerusalem, to the cross.

Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests. Even animals have homes. It is not a refusal. It is a disclosure, and it is worth noticing that Jesus does not respond to enthusiasm by taking advantage of it. He gives the man the one piece of information his offer did not account for. The comparison is exact and slightly bitter. Foxes have dens. Birds have nests. The animals of the land he made have somewhere to sleep.

But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. The Son of Man does not. Jesus had left his home in Nazareth, and had just been refused lodging in Samaria. The timing matters: this is not only a general statement about his way of life; it fits the refusal he has just met. The man has said wherever you go on a road where the last village would not have him. Following him means giving up security and comfort. Count the cost first (14:28).

What a comfortable church needs to hear. There is something in this that a comfortable church needs to hear plainly, because a certain kind of preaching promises the opposite: that coming to Christ secures a settled, prosperous life. The one making the offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing.

The open endings. Luke does not tell us what the man decided. He never does with any of the three. The stories are left open, which is itself the point: the road is still going, and the question is still standing, now for the reader.

Must every Christian give up their home? No. Jesus’ own followers included people with houses, like Martha (10:38), and Peter kept his house in Capernaum. Jesus was not laying down a rule that disciples must be homeless, but telling a volunteer the truth about the road. What every disciple must do is hold home, comfort and security loosely, ready to lose them if following Christ requires it, as many believers around the world do today. A Christian may have a home; he may not make it his foundation. The question is whether you would still follow if it cost you the house.

In a sentence. To a man who promised to follow him anywhere, Jesus warned that he, the Son of Man, had no home, unlike even foxes and birds.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus may cost you comfort and security. Are you willing? Before you make a large promise to God, count what it may cost, and then make it anyway, leaning on his grace rather than your enthusiasm. And if you are helping someone come to faith, tell them honestly about the road.

For worship. The Lord of heaven and earth, for whom all things were made, had nowhere to lay his head. He who owned the foxes’ holes and the birds’ nests chose homelessness for our sake, and on the cross he bowed his head (John 19:30) in the only rest the world gave him. And he has gone to prepare a place for us, so that we who follow him on the road will have a home with him for ever (John 14:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To another he said: follow me. But he said: Lord, let me first go and bury my father. And Jesus said to him: leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.

To another he said, Follow me. Jesus calls this one. He does not volunteer. He is called, with the same two words that were said to Levi at the tax booth (5:27), and to fishermen at a lakeside.

Lord, let me first go and bury my father. His reply sounds like the most reasonable sentence in the chapter. Burying a father was a sacred duty in Judaism, so important that it overrode other religious obligations, like reciting the Shema. A son who did not bury his father had failed at the commandment to honour him.

Was the father already dead? In that world burial happened the same day, or the next at the latest. If the father had just died, he would be burying him that day, at the tomb, not standing on a road listening to a travelling preacher. More likely, his father was still alive and the man meant: let me wait until my father dies, and I have my inheritance and have fulfilled my family duty, perhaps years from now. It is not a plea for three days off. It is a request for an indefinite postponement, a few years, perhaps many, until the duty is discharged and the inheritance settled and the man is free to go with nothing owing. Either way, he puts something else first. That is why the answer lands as it does. Jesus is not being cold about a coffin. He is refusing one word, and the word is first.

Leave the dead to bury their own dead. A shocking, deliberately paradoxical saying. It uses the word in two senses in a single line: let the spiritually dead bury the physically dead. Those who have not responded to the call of the kingdom can handle the affairs of this world. The village will manage the funeral. It cannot manage the proclamation. The kingdom is more urgent than even the most sacred family duty.

But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God. Your task is greater: to bring life to the spiritually dead. The commission is the reason for the severity. This is not a man being told to abandon his family for no purpose; he is being given a different one, and it is urgent.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should neglect their parents or refuse to attend funerals. Jesus condemned the Pharisees for using religion to avoid caring for parents (Mark 7:9–13). But no duty, however sacred, comes before Christ. Whatever you put first is your real lord.

What if my family really does need me? Then caring for them may be exactly the way you follow Christ. Scripture is clear that providing for your family and honouring your parents are Christian duties (1 Timothy 5:4, 8), and Jesus provided for his own mother from the cross (John 19:26–27). The man in this passage was not caring for his father; he was using his father as a reason to delay obeying Christ. The question to ask is not, do I have family duties?, but, am I using them to avoid something Christ has plainly told me to do? Duty done for Christ is following; duty used against Christ is the first that he refuses.

In a sentence. When a man called by Jesus asked first to bury his father, Jesus told him to let the dead bury their dead and go and proclaim the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. What do you want to do first, before following Jesus fully? Nothing should come before him. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable, which is exactly what makes them so effective. Name your first, and give it to him.

For worship. The Lord who calls is the Lord of life. He did not come to bury the dead but to raise them, and his call goes out to the spiritually dead with power to make them live. The kingdom does not take a place in the queue behind the rest of a life, because the King is worth more than everything else in the queue. He is the first and the last, and he gave his own first place up so that we could be brought in.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet another said: I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home. Jesus said to him: no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home. The third man volunteers like the first and asks for a delay like the second, and his request is the smallest of the three. He does not want to wait for a death or negotiate terms. He wants to go home and say goodbye. A reasonable request, it seems.

The precedent of Elisha. And there is a precedent for exactly this, which he may well have had in mind. When Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha at the plough, Elisha asked to kiss his father and his mother goodbye, and Elijah allowed it (1 Kings 19:19–21). He went back, slaughtered his oxen, burned his ploughing equipment for the fire, fed the people, and then followed. So the man is asking for what the prophet allowed. And this time the answer is no. Jesus demands more than Elijah, because he is more than Elijah.

No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back. Notice that Jesus answers him with a ploughing image, which suggests the Elisha story is in view on both sides. And the difference between the two cases is instructive: Elisha destroyed the plough. This man wants to keep the option of the house. The picture itself is precise and any farmer would have felt it. The ancient plough was light, single-handled, and pulled by oxen through stony ground. A light plough was guided by one hand while the other held a goad for the oxen. It had to be held down with constant pressure and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward to cut a straight furrow. A man who turns to look behind him loses the line in a moment. A divided heart, half looking back to the old life, cannot plough straight for the kingdom. Lot’s wife looked back (Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32). The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

Is fit for the kingdom of God. Fit (euthetos) means suitable, useful, well-placed for a purpose. Not that he cannot be saved, but that half-hearted discipleship is useless for kingdom work. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while he is facing the wrong way.

The three obstacles. Comfort (v. 58), duty (v. 60), and family affection (v. 61). All good things. But none can come before Christ. Jesus demands undivided loyalty, because he is Lord. The first would not count the cost; the second and third both said first. None of them is told he cannot come.

Is it wrong to miss my old life? Not in itself. Feelings of loss are human, and Christ is not offended by honest grief over what following him has cost. The danger is the backward look that wants to return: the heart that keeps the old life as an option, in case Christ does not prove worth it. Paul’s remedy was to count everything loss compared with knowing Christ, forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (Philippians 3:8, 13–14). The cure for looking back is not trying harder not to look, but fixing your eyes on what is ahead: on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2).

In a sentence. When another man wanted first to say goodbye to his family, Jesus said that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Are you looking back at your old life while trying to follow Christ? Fix your eyes forward on him. Is there an option you are keeping open, a relationship, a habit, a way back, in case following him does not work out? Close it this week, as Elisha burned his plough.

For worship. And so the chapter ends, on a road, with three unfinished conversations and a man walking towards Jerusalem. What each is told is that the road is going somewhere, and it is going there now, and the one leading it has already set his face. He never looked back. Through the rejection of the Samaritans, the failure of his friends, the agony of the garden and the darkness of the cross, he kept his hand on the plough until he could say, it is finished. Because he did not turn back, we can be brought home.
verseByVerse.note: A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward to cut a straight furrow.

parallels.desc: Elisha asks to kiss his parents goodbye

9.text: <sup>1</sup> And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, <sup>2</sup> and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. <sup>3</sup> And he said to them, “Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. <sup>4</sup> And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. <sup>5</sup> And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>6</sup> And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. <sup>7</sup> Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, <sup>8</sup> by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. <sup>9</sup> Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. <sup>10</sup> On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. <sup>11</sup> When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. <sup>12</sup> Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.” <sup>13</sup> But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.” <sup>14</sup> For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” <sup>15</sup> And they did so, and had them all sit down. <sup>16</sup> And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. <sup>17</sup> And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces. <sup>18</sup> Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” <sup>19</sup> And they answered, “John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” <sup>20</sup> Then he said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” <sup>21</sup> And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, <sup>22</sup> saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” <sup>23</sup> And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. <sup>24</sup> For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. <sup>25</sup> For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? <sup>26</sup> For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. <sup>27</sup> But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” <sup>28</sup> Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>29</sup> And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white. <sup>30</sup> And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, <sup>31</sup> who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. <sup>32</sup> Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. <sup>33</sup> And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he said. <sup>34</sup> As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. <sup>35</sup> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” <sup>36</sup> And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. <sup>37</sup> On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. <sup>38</sup> And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. <sup>39</sup> And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. <sup>40</sup> And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” <sup>41</sup> Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” <sup>42</sup> While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. <sup>43</sup> And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, <sup>44</sup> “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” <sup>45</sup> But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. <sup>46</sup> An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. <sup>47</sup> But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side <sup>48</sup> and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” <sup>49</sup> John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” <sup>51</sup> When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. <sup>52</sup> And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. <sup>53</sup> But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. <sup>54</sup> And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” <sup>55</sup> But he turned and rebuked them. <sup>56</sup> And they went on to another village. <sup>57</sup> As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>58</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>59</sup> To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>60</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” <sup>61</sup> Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” <sup>62</sup> Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
Chapter 10 gives us three of Luke's most theologically rich scenes — each one, in its own way, a complete world. The sending of the seventy-two (vv. 1–24) expands the mission beyond the twelve, shows what kingdom authority looks like in practice, and culminates in the most intimate expression of Jesus's joy in the entire Gospel. The parable of the Good Samaritan (vv. 25–37) is the world's most famous story about neighbourly love — and simultaneously one of its most searching challenges to religious self-justification. And the scene at the home of Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) is the New Testament's most precise statement about the one thing that is necessary in a life pulled in every direction by legitimate demands.

The chapter is the opening movement of the great travel narrative (9:51–19:44) — the long road to Jerusalem during which Jesus pours himself into his disciples and into the crowds that gather around him. The sending of the seventy-two models the missional multiplication that will characterise the church after Pentecost. The Samaritan parable models the ethics of the kingdom in the most concrete possible terms. The Mary-and-Martha scene models the devotional centre that makes the mission and the ethics sustainable. Together, the three scenes answer three questions: What does the kingdom produce in the world? What does the kingdom demand of its citizens? And what does the kingdom require of those who would receive it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others — beyond the twelve — and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town and place he is about to go.

If your Bible says seventy, nothing is wrong: the manuscripts divide almost evenly here and at v. 17, and both figures carry the same symbolism. Moses appointed seventy elders to help carry a burden he could not carry alone (Num. 11:16), and two more prophesied in the camp (Num. 11:26); and the nations listed in Genesis 10 come to about seventy. Either way, the expansion from twelve signals that the mission is wider than the twelve tribes.

They go two by two — the two witnesses the law required (Deut. 19:15) — and they go ahead of him. They are not independent agents but an advance party, and everywhere they arrive he is coming behind them.

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” inverts the instinctive picture. The field is not the problem; the field is ready. And faced with a labour shortage, Jesus does not say “go” but “pray” — and he says it to the seventy-two he is about to send out that hour. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the shortage is not finally ours to solve: it is “the Lord of the harvest” and “his harvest,” twice in one sentence.

“Lambs in the midst of wolves” is candid. A lamb among wolves is food; there is no version of that scene where the lamb wins. Jesus does not promise safety, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending.

The instructions echo those to the twelve, with additions. “Greet no one on the road” is not rudeness but urgency — an Eastern roadside greeting could consume a large part of a day, and Elisha said the same to Gehazi on an errand that would not wait (2 Kgs. 4:29). The “son of peace” is a Semitic idiom for a person already prepared to receive what is being brought; and where there is none, the peace “returns” — nothing is wasted.

“Eat what is set before you” is far more than manners. It sends Jewish men into households whose kitchens were the daily boundary of the covenant, and it plants the seed of Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10:14-15).

And the woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are among the most severe words in Luke's Gospel — aimed not at pagan cities but at the three villages where most of the ministry had happened.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chain of representation in v.16 — “the one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me” — governs all Christian mission. It rests on the ancient principle that an authorised envoy carries the standing of the one who sent him: insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king.

The comfort in that is enormous. A believer stammering through an explanation to a colleague is not offering a private opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The messenger's inadequacy does not degrade what is carried.

The weight is equally real. There is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken. But note the limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant: the chain runs through the message, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to shield leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. What could not be refused without consequence was a specific announcement: the kingdom of God has come near.

The woes introduce graduated accountability — judgement proportional to light received. Paul develops it (Rom. 2:12-16), and Hebrews applies it to those who have known the covenant (Heb. 10:26-31). The privileged place in the kingdom is also the most exposed position under judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Chorazin appears in the whole New Testament exactly twice — here and in the Matthew parallel — and not one miracle done there is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of “the mighty works done in you” as though his hearers knew what he meant. It is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books (cf. John 21:25): a town condemned for a history of miracles no evangelist thought to write down.

“It will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town” is not a claim that inhospitality outranks Sodom's sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in her streets announcing that the kingdom of God had come near.

And the last word a rejecting town hears is not a curse but the offer, repeated. “Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near” is almost word for word what the receiving towns were told (v. 9). The kingdom came as near to Chorazin as to anywhere — and nearness is not reception.

The principle bites hardest where most has been given (12:48), which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. He said to them: the harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest.

Meaning first. Only Luke records the sending of the seventy-two. The Twelve were sent in chapter 9; now a wider circle goes out ahead of Jesus as he sets his face toward Jerusalem. The mission is not only for apostles. The chapter then moves from the field to the heart: the joy of names written in heaven, the Son’s own exultation in the Father, a lawyer who wants to know how little love he can get away with, and a woman at Jesus’ feet who has found the one thing necessary. Running through it all is a single question: what does it mean to have the kingdom of God come near, and what do you do when it is standing at your door?

Seventy or seventy-two? If your Bible says seventy where this one says seventy-two, nothing is wrong and nothing much hangs on it. The manuscripts divide almost evenly, here and again at v. 17, and translators go different ways. Either figure carries the same symbolism, because the Old Testament supplies both. The elders Moses appointed number seventy (Numbers 11:16), but two more were left in the camp and prophesied anyway (Numbers 11:26); and the table of nations in Genesis 10 comes to seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek. A copyist working from either tradition could easily tidy the other toward it. What the number says is the same on both counts. Moses’ seventy were appointed to carry a burden he could not carry alone. Genesis’ seventy are the nations of the world. Twelve for the tribes of Israel; seventy-two for the whole earth. This mission is larger than the Twelve, and it is pointed outward.

Two by two. Not only for company, though that helps on a dark road. Under the law a matter was established by two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and what these men are carrying is testimony. Pairs make them harder to discredit and harder to discourage. One can pray while the other speaks; one can lift the other when he falls (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

Into every town and place where he himself was about to go. They are not independent operators. They are an advance party, like John the Baptist preparing the way, and everywhere they go he is coming behind them. That is the whole shape of Christian mission, and it has not changed: the messenger arrives first, and the Lord follows into the place the message has opened. No believer ever goes anywhere for Christ where Christ is not already on his way.

The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Turn that over, because it is the opposite of what most people assume. The instinctive picture of evangelism is a small harvest and a resistant field: a few interested souls in a world that has stopped listening. Jesus says the opposite. The field is not the problem. The field is ready (John 4:35–38). Harvest is also, in the prophets and in John the Baptist’s preaching, a picture of the end, when the wheat is gathered and the chaff burned (3:17). So the image carries both urgency and hope: the crop is ripe, and ripe crops do not wait.

Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. And here is the surprise. Faced with a shortage of workers, he does not first say go. He says pray, and he says it to seventy-two men he is about to send out that very hour. The people being sent are told to pray for more of themselves. “Pray earnestly” (deēthēte) means beg, plead. And the one being begged owns the field: the Lord of the harvest, and his harvest, twice in one sentence. That quietly settles a great deal of anxiety about Christian work. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the labour shortage is not finally our problem to solve. It is his, and he has told us how to raise it with him.

To send out. The verb (ekballō) is literally to throw out, to thrust out; it is the word used for casting out demons. Workers do not usually drift into the harvest. They have to be pushed, by a God who overcomes their reluctance, rearranges their lives and sometimes uses hardship to get them moving. And those who pray this prayer honestly often find they have become the answer to it.

What does praying for labourers look like in practice? Name real places and real people: your own church’s need for teachers and youth leaders, a missionary you know, an unreached people group, the street you live on. Pray for the sending of preachers and church planters, but also for ordinary believers in workplaces and families who will speak of Christ there. Pray for your own children and grandchildren to be among those sent, which is harder than it sounds. And hold your hands open while you pray, because the Lord of the harvest may answer by sending you, to the next room or the next continent.

In a sentence. Jesus sent seventy-two disciples ahead of him in pairs, telling them that the harvest is great but the workers few, and to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for God to send workers into his harvest, and be willing to be sent yourself. If you have stopped praying for the people around you because they seem uninterested, remember who said the field is ready. And if Christian work has become a weight you carry alone, hand the harvest back to its Lord: it was never yours to bring in by your own strength.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest is not short of anything. He owns the field, he ripened the crop, and he has a heart large enough to want the whole of it gathered in. He sent his Son into the field first, the true seed that fell into the ground and died so that it might bear much fruit (John 12:24). Every labourer he sends since then is following that Son into a harvest he has already secured, and the gathering in will be his glory, not ours.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy. The number may recall the nations listed in Genesis 10, or the seventy elders who helped Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.

Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. It is one of the most candid sentences he ever spoke, and it is worth noticing that he says it as he sends them, not afterwards. Take the picture seriously. A lamb among wolves is not an underdog with a fighting chance. It is food. There is no version of that scene in which the lamb wins, and no shepherd who ever put one there on purpose, which is exactly what he says he is doing. He does not promise it will be all right in the sense they would want. He does not say the wolves will turn out to be friendly, or that the lambs will be made into something more formidable. He says I am sending, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending. The lambs are sent by the Shepherd who will lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

The design, not a fault. There is something here that a comfortable church habitually softens. The vulnerability of the mission is not a design fault to be engineered out. It is the design. A church that has made itself safe, culturally powerful, financially insulated and politically protected, has not improved on this arrangement. It has swapped it for another one. The gospel has always travelled best in the hands of people who could be hurt.

Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals. The list is even shorter than the Twelve’s (9:3): no purse, no traveller’s satchel, no spare sandals, the ancient equivalent of no wallet, no bag and no change of shoes for a journey on foot. The point is total dependence on God, shown in the plainest way possible. They will eat because someone feeds them, and they will be fed because God has gone before them into the houses.

And greet no one on the road. This sounds rude until you know what a greeting was. An Eastern roadside greeting was not a nod; it was an extended exchange of embraces, enquiries after family, health and business, and invitations to stay, and it could consume a large part of a day. There is a precedent almost certainly in view. Elisha, sending Gehazi urgently to a dead child, told him not to greet anyone he met on the way, or answer anyone who greeted him (2 Kings 4:29). So it is not a rule about manners. It is a rule about urgency, and it is temporary and specific: a single sweep through the towns he is about to visit, with a deadline attached, and the men have been told not to let the ordinary courtesies of the road eat the daylight.

Does this mean Christian workers today should go without money or supplies? No. These were instructions for one short, urgent mission inside Israel, where hospitality to travelling teachers was expected. Later Jesus deliberately reverses them: now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack (22:35–36), because the situation has changed. Paul travelled with funds, received gifts and sometimes worked with his hands. What carries over is not the packing list but the posture: go in dependence on God, do not let comfort set the terms of obedience, and do not let lesser things crowd out what is urgent.

In a sentence. Jesus sent them out like lambs among wolves, with no money, supplies or spare sandals, and no time to stop for long greetings.

On a Tuesday. There are seasons when the ordinary good things have to give way to something that will not wait, and knowing which season you are in is most of the skill. Think of the thing God has plainly given you to do, a conversation you owe a friend, a reconciliation, a call to a lonely relative, and ask what small courtesies, hobbies and screens keep eating the daylight. And if you feel exposed as a Christian at work or at home, remember you were never promised the wolves would be tame. You were promised a Shepherd.

For worship. The Shepherd who sent lambs among wolves went among the wolves himself, and let them have him. He became the Lamb, led to the slaughter and silent before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7), so that no lamb of his would finally be lost. He sends from a place of having already been where he sends us, and he holds every one of his sheep in a hand from which no one can snatch them (John 10:28).
verseByVerse.note: Travellers’ greetings could be long and elaborate; there was no time for them.

parallels.desc: if you meet anyone, do not greet him

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever house you enter, first say: peace be to this house! And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the labourer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.

Whatever house you enter, first say, Peace be to this house! The greeting is shalom, and in Hebrew it never meant merely the absence of trouble. It means wholeness, everything in its right place, a life not at war with God or with itself. And in the mouth of a man sent by Jesus it is not a pleasantry. It is the peace the angels sang over the fields of Bethlehem (2:14), peace with God through the Messiah. Notice how the next sentence treats it: as something that goes somewhere, settles or does not, and can come back.

And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. “Son of peace” is a Hebrew idiom: a person characterised by the thing named, in this case one who belongs to the peace being offered and is ready for it. Somebody in that village has been prepared before the messengers arrive. That is worth registering by anyone who has ever felt that evangelism is a matter of manufacturing interest out of nothing. It is not. The instruction assumes there is already a person in the street whose heart has been made ready by somebody else, and the work is largely to find him. Lydia’s heart was opened by the Lord before Paul finished speaking (Acts 16:14). The blessing is effective: God’s peace actually comes.

But if not, it will return to you. Nothing is lost. Like the dove sent out from the ark that found no place to rest and came back to Noah’s hand (Genesis 8:9), a blessing offered to a house that will not have it is not wasted; it comes back to the one who offered it. That is a quiet mercy for every believer who has spoken and been rebuffed and felt they had spent something they could not get back.

And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide. Stay put. Do not go from house to house. The rule is the same as the Twelve’s, and for the same reason: a messenger who trades up for better hospitality has begun to be paid, and a man whose lodging depends on the standing of his host will eventually trim his message to keep it. Be content with what you are given.

For the laborer deserves his wages. There is a phrase here worth stopping on, because of what happened to it later. Paul quotes it in a letter to Timothy, and quotes it as Scripture: for the Scripture says, you shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain, and, the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:18). The first half is Deuteronomy 25:4. The second half is this verse. So within Paul’s lifetime the words of Jesus recorded by Luke were being set alongside the Law of Moses under the single heading the Scripture says. That is not a later church council conferring authority on a book. It is an apostle, writing to a colleague, treating what Jesus said exactly as he treats what God said through Moses, because he could see no difference. And the principle itself is plain: those who work for the gospel have a right to be supported by those they serve (1 Corinthians 9:14). It is not charity; it is wages earned.

Should I give to my church if I am not sure the money is well used? Give, and give gladly, because supporting those who teach you is obedience to Christ, not a favour to an institution (Galatians 6:6). But you are not asked to give blindly. A faithful church is open about its finances, and you may ask how money is spent. If you have real concerns, raise them with the elders, privately and kindly. What you should not do is let vague suspicion become a permanent excuse for keeping back what Jesus says the labourer deserves.

In a sentence. They were to greet each house with peace, which would rest on those open to it, and stay where they were welcomed, accepting food as a worker’s due wages.

On a Tuesday. Speak peace into the houses you enter this week, and mean it: a blessing on the household, a prayer for the family you visit, a kind word about Christ where the door is open. Watch for the person God has already prepared. And if you sit under faithful preaching, ask whether your giving treats your pastor as a labourer worthy of his wages or as a cost to be kept down.

For worship. The peace these men carried was not theirs to manufacture. It was bought at a price, by the one who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and it goes out still from his hand into ordinary houses. He is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Every time it rests on a son of peace, a war that began in Eden ends in one more heart.
verseByVerse.note: A “son of peace” means a person open to God’s peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them: the kingdom of God has come near to you.

Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. It sounds like a rule about manners, and it is a great deal more than that. These are Jewish men, sent by a Jewish teacher, into towns that would sometimes include households whose kitchens were not kept by the purity laws. The food laws were not a dietary preference; they were the daily, physical boundary of the covenant people. And he tells them to eat what they are given. Luke, writing for a Gentile church, knows exactly where that instruction is going. In his second volume Peter will be on a rooftop in Joppa, shown a sheet full of unclean animals and told to kill and eat, and he will protest that he has never eaten anything common or unclean, and be answered: what God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:14–15). Within days he will be in a Roman centurion’s house. The seed of that is here, in a travel instruction, years before anyone understood what it meant. Paul gives the same rule later: eat whatever is set before you without raising questions on the ground of conscience (1 Corinthians 10:27).

Receiving the person. There is a plainer point too, about the receiving end of hospitality. To eat what a poor household puts in front of you, without inspecting it, is to accept the person. Anybody who has been served a meal by people who had very little will know that scrutinising it would have been the one unforgivable thing.

Heal the sick in it and say to them, The kingdom of God has come near to you. The two go together, and in that order: the touch and then the word. The healing is not a strategy to earn a hearing, and the word is not merely an explanation of the healing. They are one announcement made in two ways. The healings are signs of the kingdom: the King has arrived, and wherever he goes, sickness and death begin to retreat.

Has come near. The announcement is precise: not that the kingdom of God will come, but that it has come near. The perfect tense means the nearness is a settled state: it has arrived and it is standing there, which is exactly what a village would conclude on watching its sick get up. In Jesus, God’s reign is at your door. It is close enough to be reached, and it demands a response.

Is “heal the sick” a command to the church today? It belonged to this particular mission, whose signs confirmed the arrival of the kingdom in Jesus. Many Christians hold that such healing gifts continue, and they should be heard charitably; the more likely reading is that the sign gifts belonged to that foundational time, when Christ and his apostles were establishing the word (Hebrews 2:3–4). But God still heals. The church still prays for the sick, the elders anointing and praying in faith (James 5:14–15), and God often answers, through medicine and sometimes beyond it. And the heart of the command, the message that the kingdom has come near, goes on until he returns.

In a sentence. In towns that welcomed them, they were to eat what was offered, heal the sick, and announce that the kingdom of God had come near.

On a Tuesday. The kingdom of God has come near in Jesus; tell someone today, simply. Pray for a sick friend by name, and visit if you can, because care for the body is part of the message. And when someone with little offers you hospitality, receive it gladly and without fuss. It is one of the ways the gospel crosses thresholds.

For worship. The kingdom that came near in Galilee came near in a Person. He touched lepers, ate with outcasts and made his home among the unclean, and the healings were the first light of a morning in which he will wipe away every tear and death shall be no more (Revelation 21:4). He who once said to a village that the kingdom had come near will one day say that the dwelling place of God is with man, and the nearness will never end.

parallels.desc: eat whatever is set before you

verseByVerse.quote: But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say: even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near. I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.

But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say. Notice that he does not tell them to leave quietly. He tells them to go out into the public street and make an announcement, which takes a good deal more courage than staying, and is the last thing a rejected messenger would naturally want to do.

Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. The gesture is the one the Twelve were given (9:5): the dust a devout Jew shook off at the border on returning from pagan ground. Performed in an Israelite street, it says something devastating: that this town has put itself outside, and the line no longer runs where they think it does. We want nothing of yours; you are under God’s judgement.

Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near. Look at what is added, because it changes everything about the tone. That is the same sentence they were told to say to the towns that received them (v. 9), almost word for word. The only real difference is the nevertheless. So the last thing a rejecting town hears is not a curse. It is the offer, repeated. Even in rejection the message stands: they cannot say they were not told, and it is a final warning that is still an invitation. The kingdom came near to that town exactly as near as it came to the village that took the messengers in, and nearness is not the same as reception. It came near, and they were standing there, and they said no. That is the whole tragedy of the verse. The kingdom of God is not a distant possibility that unfortunate towns never had a fair chance at. It walked up the street.

I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. Sodom is the Bible’s byword for a place beyond saving, a city destroyed by fire from heaven, whose name became shorthand for the outer limit of wickedness (Genesis 19). And a Galilean village that declined to receive two travelling preachers will fare worse. The logic is not that hospitality outranks Sodom’s sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in the streets of Sodom announcing that the kingdom of God had come near, and nobody healed her sick in the market square. These towns did have it, and they had it in daylight, and they preferred not to. Judgement is according to light received (12:47–48).

Degrees of judgement. Note the phrase “on that day”: a fixed, known day, the day of judgement. Whatever else is true of the last day, it is not a single undifferentiated verdict. It is weighed. There are degrees of punishment in the final judgement, according to privilege and knowledge (Matthew 11:22–24; Romans 2:12). Every sentence is just, every sentence is conscious and eternal, and no sentence is the same as another, because the Judge knows exactly what each person was given.

Is it right for Christians to walk away from people who reject the gospel? The gesture was a solemn act by commissioned messengers on a short, urgent mission, not a licence to write people off. We still warn plainly, and we may move on from those who will not hear when there are others waiting (Acts 13:51; 18:6). But we do not stop praying, and we leave the door open, because Paul himself had once been on the rejecting side. With friends and family, keep loving, keep living the gospel, and speak again when God gives an opening. Judgement belongs to God, not to our frustration.

In a sentence. In towns that rejected them, they were to wipe off the dust as a sign of judgement, warning that the kingdom had come near, and Jesus said Sodom would fare better at the judgement.

On a Tuesday. Hearing the gospel is a great privilege and a great responsibility. Ask how many times the kingdom has come near to you: in your upbringing, in sermons, in a friend’s witness, in a crisis. Every one of those was mercy, and every one is remembered. Do not treat it lightly. Answer it today.

For worship. The God who keeps such exact accounts is the same God who sent the offer to the town that would refuse it, and repeated it at the gate on the way out. His justice weighs every grain of light; his mercy keeps knocking after the door has closed. And the judgement that rejecting towns will bear was borne in full by his Son for everyone who receives him: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgement for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.

Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! Now the woes, among the most severe words in Luke’s Gospel, and it is worth being clear who is receiving them. Not Rome. Not the Sanhedrin. Not the towns that never heard. Three small towns at the north end of the Sea of Galilee, the places where he had lived and worked and where most of his ministry so far had happened.

The town with no recorded miracle. Here is something that ought to stop a careful reader. Chorazin appears in the whole of the New Testament exactly twice: here, and in the parallel in Matthew 11:21. Not one miracle done in Chorazin is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of the mighty works done in you as though everyone listening knew what he meant. It is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books. John says as much at the end of his Gospel: there are also many other things that Jesus did (John 21:25). Chorazin is the evidence: a town condemned for a history of miracles that no evangelist thought to write down.

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician port cities on the coast, wealthy, pagan, and denounced by the prophets for centuries for pride and cruelty (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28). A Galilean listener would have filed them under hopeless. Sackcloth, coarse cloth of goats’ hair, and ashes were the marks of mourning and repentance, as when the king of Nineveh came down from his throne (Jonah 3:6). And Jesus says they would have repented. Not might have: would have, and long ago. That sentence tells us something about the mind of God that is not comfortable and is not optional: he knows what people would have done under circumstances they were never given. It raises questions no one can fully answer. What it does not do is give anyone an excuse, because the towns being addressed are the ones that did get the circumstances.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. Capernaum was his base, the town he moved to after Nazareth threw him out (4:31), where he taught in the synagogue, healed Peter’s mother-in-law, and emptied a street of its sick in one evening. The most privileged town of all. And the language he uses about it is borrowed. It is the taunt Isaiah aimed at the king of Babylon, who said in his heart I will ascend to heaven and was told you are brought down to Sheol (Isaiah 14:13–15). The most privileged village in Galilee is addressed in the words written for the archetype of proud rebellion. Hades is the Greek name for the Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead; here it is the place of judgement. The ruins of Capernaum, Chorazin and Bethsaida still lie empty today.

If Tyre and Sidon would have repented, why did God not send them these miracles? God gives light as he wills, and owes it to no one: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Romans 9:15–16). We are not told why he chose Galilee and not Phoenicia, and Scripture does not pretend to tell us. But we are told enough to stop us accusing him. Those who received more are judged more strictly, and those who had less are judged by what they had. The towns that saw and did not repent are condemned for their own refusal, not for a decree they were trying to obey. The secret things belong to the LORD our God (Deuteronomy 29:29); what is revealed is that the light came, and they would not walk in it.

Everyone to whom much was given. The principle underneath is stated plainly later: everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (12:48). It cuts hardest at those who have had most, which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Galilean towns that saw his miracles and did not repent, saying that pagan cities would have repented and would fare better at the judgement.

On a Tuesday. If you have grown up hearing the gospel, you have great privilege. Do not let familiarity harden you to it. Ask honestly whether the things that once moved you now leave you unmoved, and whether you have more light than you are walking in. Capernaum’s danger was not open hostility; it was a town that had seen it all and stayed exactly the same.

For worship. These woes are spoken by the one who wept over Jerusalem (19:41). He does not pronounce them from a distance, as a judge glad to be rid of a case; he pronounces them as the one whose miracles were refused and whose love was spurned, and then he goes on toward Jerusalem to die for sinners no better than Chorazin. The same Lord who weighs light so exactly gave the greatest light of all, himself, and still says to every town and every heart: come.
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.

The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me. One sentence, and it holds the whole doctrine of Christian mission in a chain of links. Follow it backwards, because that is the direction the authority runs. The Father sends the Son. The Son sends the seventy-two. So what is done to the seventy-two is done to the Son, and what is done to the Son is done to the Father. When Saul persecuted the church, the risen Lord asked him: why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

The envoy. This rests on something older than the Gospel. In the ancient world an authorised envoy carried the standing of the man who sent him; the rabbinic principle was that a man’s representative is as the man himself. Insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king, and every court in the world understood it. What Jesus does here is put ordinary men in that position, men with no money, no bag and no spare sandals, and connect them by a direct line to the throne of heaven.

A comfort and a weight. Two things follow, and they pull hard in opposite directions. The first is an extraordinary comfort. A believer stammering through an explanation of the gospel to a colleague is not conducting a private conversation about a personal opinion. If the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The messenger’s inadequacy, and it is usually considerable, does not degrade what is being carried. Nobody ever thought less of a king because his letter arrived in the hands of a tired man. The second is a weight. There is no such thing as a neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken, and the person declining is not declining you. That distinction matters in both directions. It should stop a rejected Christian from taking it as a personal verdict on himself, and it should stop him from being casual about what has actually just happened in the conversation.

The authority of preaching. When the word of God is faithfully preached, Christ himself speaks: how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14–17); we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us (2 Corinthians 5:20). The preacher is not the source of the authority, but his message, if true to Scripture, carries Christ’s authority. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566) puts it boldly: the preaching of the word of God is the word of God.

What it does not mean. Notice one limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant. The chain runs through what the messenger says from Christ, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to protect leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. The seventy-two were carrying a specific message: the kingdom of God has come near. That is what could not be refused without consequence, not their preferences and not their opinions. A sermon carries Christ’s authority exactly as far as it says what Scripture says, and the Bereans were commended for checking Paul against it (Acts 17:11).

How do I tell when a preacher is speaking with Christ’s authority? Open your Bible during the sermon and ask whether the point is actually in the passage. Where it plainly is, receive it as Christ’s word to you, even if it is unwelcome and even if the preacher is not gifted. Where he adds his own views on politics, schooling or methods, weigh them as one man’s wise or unwise counsel. If he contradicts Scripture, speak to him privately, and if necessary to the elders. And do not treat a dull delivery as an excuse: the authority is in the word, not the voice.

In a sentence. Jesus told his messengers that whoever hears them hears him, and whoever rejects them rejects him and the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word is faithfully preached on Sunday, listen as to Christ himself: come prepared, pray before, and decide afterward what you will do. And when you speak of Christ to a friend this week, remember whose message you carry. You do not need to be impressive. You need to be faithful, and the King will stand behind his own word.

For worship. The Father sent the Son, and the Son has never stopped sending. Through weak voices and tired messengers, the eternal Word still speaks into towns and kitchens and offices, and to hear the faithful word is to hear him. How kind of God, that the voice which called the worlds into being should be willing to be carried by such as us, and that he should count the welcome given to his smallest messenger as a welcome given to himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventy-two return elated: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” The word even gives them away — they expected the preaching to work and did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name.

“I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” is one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels. It may look back to the primordial fall, or forward to the cross and the final defeat (cf. Rev. 12:9); but the tense and the context favour a comment on what has just happened. They came back talking about demons submitting, and his answer begins “I saw.” He is telling them what their preaching tour looked like from where he was standing.

Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. The Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning. There is no ordinary Christian work — only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it.

Then the authority over serpents and scorpions, and the promise that nothing shall hurt them — both of which have been badly misused and both of which the passage itself guards.

And then the redirection: “do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The joy was not wrong; it was aimed at the wrong thing. Authority is about what they can do, and anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance.

Jesus then rejoices in the Holy Spirit — one of the very few places where Luke tells us what he was feeling, and it is exultation. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father, and the occasion is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

The prayer thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and then makes one of the highest claims in the Synoptic Gospels: all things handed over, and a mutual knowing of Father and Son that admits no third party except by the Son's choosing.

Finally the private beatitude: “blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” Not blessed for perceptiveness — blessed for what happens to be in front of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The joy of Jesus “in the Holy Spirit” is a Trinitarian moment: the Son's joy is given in the Spirit and directed to the Father in prayer. The mutual delight of Father, Son and Spirit overflows into the mission and into the lives of those who share in it.

Verses 21-22 have long been called the Johannine thunderbolt, because they drop into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel. “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” is not authority in a defined area but everything. And the mutual knowing is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others; it is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door only he can open. That he opens it is why the prayer is joy rather than terror.

“The wise and understanding” are not scholars in general — the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived, and Luke, who records it, is the most educated writer in the New Testament. They are the professionally religious who have watched everything and concluded he is a problem. And the “little children” are the seventy-two.
