The dividing line is not intelligence but whether a man will come with empty hands; learning is no obstacle to that, it simply supplies one more thing to hold onto.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” reorients the worker's identity from achievement to grace. The image is a citizen register — the book of life in which names are written (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 21:27).

Every feature of it reverses what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else — and it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

This belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness. The minister whose standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children's faith as a report card on himself. The Christian who has been ill for two years, can no longer do any of the things he used to do, and quietly suspects he has become surplus.

And the beatitude of vv.23-24 is a rebuke to the boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time. Abraham died with one son of the promise and a burial plot. Moses asked to see God's glory and was shown a back. Isaiah described the Servant's wounds seven centuries early and never met him. Every one of them longed for this. Isaiah would have given everything he owned for an afternoon with a New Testament and a quiet room.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy-two returned with joy, saying: Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name! And he said to them: I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

The seventy-two returned with joy. Joy is one of Luke’s great themes, from the angels’ good news of great joy (2:10) to the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy after the ascension (24:52). Here it is the joy of men who have seen God at work through their own unremarkable hands.

Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name! The word “even” gives them away, and it is delightful. They expected the preaching to work. They expected the healings, more or less: those they had been told to do (v. 9). They did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name. Whatever the exhilaration, they have not confused whose authority it was.

I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. It is one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels, and the first question is when he saw it. Three readings are possible. It may look back to the primordial fall, the rebellion of the great adversary before human history began, which Scripture gestures at rather than narrates (Isaiah 14:12, the morning star fallen from heaven, is often read this way). It may look forward to the cross and the final defeat, seen in advance, as Revelation describes it (Revelation 12:9–11). Or it may be a comment on exactly what has just happened: as seventy-two unremarkable men walked through Galilean villages saying the name of Jesus, he watched the enemy’s position collapse. The context favours the third. They came back talking about demons submitting; his answer begins I saw. He is telling them what their preaching tour looked like from where he was standing. The kingdom of God is overthrowing the kingdom of Satan (11:20–22), and the decisive blow would fall at the cross, when the ruler of this world was cast out (John 12:31) and the powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15).

Like lightning. The image is exact in two ways. Lightning is sudden: not a slow retreat but a fall. And lightning comes down; whatever height the adversary held, he is not holding it.

There is no ordinary Christian work. What that does to the scale of the thing is the point. Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. That is what they experienced. And the Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning. There is no ordinary Christian work. There is only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it, which is why the report and the reply in these two verses hardly sound as if they belong to the same event.

If Satan is defeated, why is there still so much evil? Because he is defeated but not yet destroyed. The decisive battle was won at the cross, and his final end in the lake of fire is certain (Revelation 20:10). Between those two points he is like an enemy whose capital has fallen, still dangerous in retreat. He prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), and we are to resist him, firm in faith. But he cannot take back one person Christ has rescued, and every time the gospel is believed, his kingdom shrinks again. We fight from victory, not toward it.

In a sentence. The seventy-two returned joyfully reporting that even demons submitted to them in Jesus’ name, and Jesus said he had seen Satan fall from heaven like lightning.

On a Tuesday. Satan is a defeated enemy; serve Christ with confidence. The Sunday school lesson you teach, the verse you share, the prayer you pray for a neighbour may look tiny from where you stand. You are not the one who sees the true size of it. Do the small faithful thing, and leave its scale to the one who watches from heaven.

For worship. The Son who saw Satan fall is the Son who made him fall. He bound the strong man and plundered his house; he went to the cross, where the serpent bruised his heel, and crushed the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). The adversary who once stood in heaven to accuse the brothers has been thrown down, and they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 12:10–11). Every name of Jesus spoken in a Galilean village was a stone from that sling.

parallels.desc: how you are fallen from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.

Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. Two things in that promise need guarding, because both have been badly misused. The language comes straight from Psalm 91:13: you will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot. Serpents and scorpions are standard biblical shorthand for hostile and demonic power, reaching back to the serpent in the garden (Genesis 3:15) and the wilderness of fiery serpents and scorpions (Deuteronomy 8:15). And the sentence explains itself in its own next clause: and over all the power of the enemy. The enemy is Satan. The promise is primarily spiritual: authority over the forces of evil.

What it does not mean. Set beside the longer ending of Mark, they will pick up serpents with their hands (Mark 16:18), this verse has been made the charter of the snake-handling churches, where believers lift live rattlesnakes in worship to demonstrate their faith, and where people have died doing it. But Jesus is describing the authority the seventy-two have just been exercising over demons, not issuing an invitation to pick up vipers. And there is a sharper point still, from Luke’s own pages. Psalm 91 is the very psalm the devil quoted in the wilderness, urging Jesus to throw himself from the temple because angels would catch him, and Jesus refused with a single line: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (4:9–12). To engineer a danger in order to make God prove a promise is not faith; it is precisely the thing Jesus called temptation. A man who deliberately handles a rattlesnake to demonstrate his trust is not obeying this verse. He is repeating the devil’s use of Scripture.

And nothing shall hurt you. Read as bodily immunity, the phrase is contradicted by almost everyone who first heard it. James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2). Stephen was stoned. Paul was beaten, stoned and shipwrecked, and finally, according to the early church, beheaded, though he was also once shaken off a viper into a fire without harm (Acts 28:3–6), which shows that God can preserve, not that he always will. So what does the promise mean? Luke answers it himself, putting both halves in a single breath: some of you they will put to death, but not a hair of your head will perish (21:16–18). Both sentences are true at once, and that settles the sense beyond argument. The protection is not a guarantee that the body will be untouched. It is a guarantee that the enemy cannot finally destroy them: no spiritual power can separate them from the love of God or take away their salvation (Romans 8:35–39). Nothing done to a disciple’s body can undo what has been secured for his soul.

Does every believer have this authority over the enemy? The victory over Satan is real and secured (v. 18), and every believer is protected by Christ: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4), and the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20). We resist the devil by faith, prayer and the word, and he flees (James 4:7). But the particular commission and signs given to the seventy-two belonged to their mission. A Christian does not need special formulas, shouted commands or rituals to be safe. And Jesus himself immediately points them away from the power to the greater thing: their names are written in heaven (v. 20).

In a sentence. Jesus gave his disciples authority over all the power of the enemy, so that nothing could ultimately harm them.

On a Tuesday. In Christ you have nothing to fear from the powers of evil. If you are troubled by fear of curses, spirits or the occult, or haunted by a dark past, take your stand on Christ’s finished work, renounce any involvement plainly, and pray in his name; you do not need to perform anything. And do not test God by courting needless danger; trust him in the dangers that come to you in the path of obedience.

For worship. He gives authority over serpents because he has already trodden on the serpent. In the wilderness he would not use the promise to save himself; on the cross he would not come down to save himself; and so he saved us. Nothing shall hurt you is a promise only he could make, because he let everything hurt him, and rose. Our safety is his wounds.

parallels.desc: you will tread on the lion and the adder

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.

Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you. He has just confirmed the authority in the strongest terms. Now he tells them not to build their happiness on it. Note that he does not say the joy was wrong. He says it was aimed at the wrong thing, which is a much finer correction and a much more necessary one. What they came back rejoicing in was real, granted by him, and worth being pleased about. It is simply not what a person can stand on.

Why not? Because it is about what they can do. And anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance. There will be a day like the one at the foot of the mountain, where the disciples tried and nothing happened (9:40). There will be seasons when the work does not go. A joy founded on effectiveness is a joy on a schedule, and the schedule is not in your hands. Spiritual power can also feed pride, and there will be some on the last day who say, did we not cast out demons in your name?, and are told, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Power in ministry proves nothing about the heart.

But rejoice that your names are written in heaven. The perfect tense: they have been written and remain written. The image is a citizen register, the roll of a city listing those who belong to it. Scripture uses it repeatedly: the book of life, in which names are written (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12, 15; 21:27). And every feature of it is the reverse of what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent and is not being reviewed. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else, and, this is the part that carries the weight, it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

Election. The names are written by God. This points to God’s sovereign choice of his people and their security. Revelation speaks of names written in the book of life before the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 17:8), and Paul says God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Joy rests on grace, not on performance. Success in ministry can come and go; a name written in God’s book cannot be erased.

For those who measure themselves by usefulness. This verse belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness, and there are a great many. The minister whose sense of standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children’s faith as a report card on his own. The Christian who has been ill for two years and can no longer do any of the things he used to do for God, and quietly suspects he has become surplus. The word to all of them is that the thing worth rejoicing in was never the doing. It is a name, already written, in a book they cannot reach and cannot lose.

How can I know my name is written there? Not by trying to read the book, which God has not opened to us, but by looking at the Christ he has offered to you. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have turned from sin and are trusting Christ alone, your trust is itself the sign of the writing, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The fruit of the Spirit, love for other believers, and a growing hatred of sin confirm it (1 John 3:14). And if you are unsure, do not stare inward: come to him now. Nobody who comes is found missing from the roll.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to rejoice chiefly in their power over spirits, but that their names are written in heaven.

On a Tuesday. Notice what makes you happiest about your Christian life this week. If it is a good day of serving, a fruitful conversation, a well-received talk, thank God for it, and then lay it down beside the greater joy. And on the days when nothing goes well, when you are ill, or fruitless, or forgotten, rejoice anyway, because nothing about your name in heaven has changed since yesterday.

For worship. Before the seventy-two set out, before they were born, before the mountains were brought forth, a hand wrote their names. It is the hand of the Father who chose them in love, and the names stand in the book of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8), written in his blood and kept by his life. No failure on earth reaches that page. If you belong to Christ, your name is written in heaven, and the God who wrote it does not erase.

parallels.desc: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. Luke stops to tell us what Jesus was feeling, which he almost never does. The verb is ēgalliasato: not quiet contentment but exultation, the verb of Mary’s song, my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour (1:47), and its noun is used when the child leaped in the womb (1:44). And it happens in the Holy Spirit; only Luke mentions the Spirit here. This is one of the clearest windows in the Gospels into the life of God. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father: Father, Son and Spirit in one sentence, three persons, one delight. And the occasion for it is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth. Intimacy and sovereignty together. Father is the word of a son at home; Lord of heaven and earth is the title of the King of all things. Jesus holds both in one breath, and teaches us to do the same.

That you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children. He thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and that has to be faced rather than smoothed. “These things” are the truths of the kingdom: who Jesus is, and what his coming means. But notice who the wise and understanding are in this Gospel. They are not scholars in general, and this is emphatically not a commendation of ignorance: the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived, and Luke, who records it, is one of the most educated writers in the New Testament. The wise here are the professionally religious of Galilee and Jerusalem, men with the texts, the training and the standing, who have watched all of it and concluded he is a problem. And the little children (nēpioi, infants) are the seventy-two: fishermen and farmers who could not have argued a point of law and had just come back from casting out demons. So the dividing line is not intelligence. It is whether a man will come with empty hands. Learning is no obstacle to that whatsoever; it simply supplies one more thing that can be held onto. Not that intelligence is bad, but that pride blinds (1 Corinthians 1:18–31).

Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. “Gracious will” (eudokia) is good pleasure, the same word as the angels’ song of peace among those with whom he is pleased (2:14). God reveals and hides according to his sovereign good pleasure. Jesus does not merely accept the Father’s arrangement or complain about it. He is delighted by it. Election is a cause of praise.

All things have been handed over to me by my Father. Scholars have long called this passage the Johannine thunderbolt, because it drops into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel, and it is one of the strongest claims Jesus makes anywhere. All things: not some authority in a defined area. Everything, handed over.

No one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son. Then a mutual knowing that admits no third party: the Father knows the Son; the Son knows the Father; nobody else knows either except by the Son’s choosing. Only God can know God fully. That is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others. It is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door that only he can open. It is one of the clearest statements in the first three Gospels of Jesus’ deity and his unique relationship to the Father.

And anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. The only way to know God is through the Son’s revelation, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he chooses. Knowing God is a gift of sovereign grace (John 6:44; 14:6; 17:6). And he opens the door. That is the last clause, and it is why this prayer is joy rather than terror.

Does God, then, choose who will understand? Jesus says so plainly: the Father has hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children, for such was his gracious will, and the Son reveals the Father to anyone he chooses. The Reformed reading takes these words at face value: understanding is God’s gift, and no one can boast of having worked it out. Yet those who reject Jesus are responsible for it (vv. 13–16), and the invitation is to all: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden (Matthew 11:28), which in Matthew follows these very words. Both are true. If you want to know God, that desire is already the Son at work, so come.

Can people of other religions know God without Christ? They may know that God exists, for creation declares his power (Romans 1:20), and their consciences bear witness. But they do not know him as Father, and they cannot be saved by that knowledge. The saving knowledge of God comes only through the Son: no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). That is not narrowness for its own sake. It is the shape of reality, and it is why the church must go and tell, because the Son is willing to reveal the Father to anyone, from any nation, who comes to him.

In a sentence. Rejoicing in the Spirit, Jesus thanked the Father for revealing the truth to the humble rather than the wise, by his gracious will, and declared that only the Son knows the Father and reveals him to whom he chooses.

On a Tuesday. If you know God, it is because the Son chose to reveal him to you, and that leaves no room for looking down on anyone who does not yet see. Thank him today, by name, for opening your eyes. When you speak to a clever friend who scoffs, do not try to out-argue him into the kingdom; pray for him to be made a little child. And if you feel too ordinary to understand the Bible, take heart: these things are revealed to infants.

For worship. Here, for a moment, we overhear the joy at the centre of everything. The Father delights in the Son, the Son exults in the Father, the Spirit fills the Son with gladness, and the subject of their joy is the salvation of small and foolish people. God was not obliged to share that joy with anyone. He chose to open the door, and the Son who alone knows the Father has pleased to make him known to us. Rejoice and give thanks with Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning to the disciples he said privately: blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.

Then turning to the disciples he said privately. Luke marks it carefully: he turns, and he speaks to them alone. What follows is not for the crowd.

Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! Not blessed are you for being perceptive. Blessed are the eyes, for what happens to be in front of them. The blessing is entirely a matter of where they are standing in history, and they did nothing to arrange it. They are witnessing the fulfilment of everything the Old Testament promised: the Messiah, the kingdom, the defeat of Satan.

For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it. Put names to that and it becomes almost unbearable. Abraham, who was told that all nations would be blessed through his offspring and died with one son of the promise and a burial plot, yet rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56). Moses, who asked to see God’s glory and was hidden in a rock and shown his back. David, promised a son whose throne would stand for ever, who went to his grave a thousand years before the child was born. Isaiah, who described the Servant’s wounds seven centuries early, and never met him. Daniel, who saw one like a son of man receiving an everlasting kingdom, and was told to seal the book and go his way. The prophets searched and inquired carefully about this salvation (1 Peter 1:10–12). Every one of them wanted this. Not one of them got it. They all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). And a group of Galilean labourers had been walking around with him, eating with him, and coming home to tell him how the trip went.

Desired. Longed, yearned. These were not men with a mild curiosity. They spent their lives leaning toward something they were told they would not see.

The boredom of proximity. That puts a familiar problem in a hard light. There is a boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time: the sense that the gospel is a known quantity, the Bible a familiar book, the whole thing slightly worn. It is not usually unbelief. It is simply the effect of proximity on the extraordinary. And there is a further turn, because it goes further than the disciples. They saw him before the cross and understood almost nothing of it; anyone reading this has the finished account of the death and the rising, the whole of the Scriptures, and the Spirit given. Isaiah would have given everything he owned for an afternoon with a New Testament and a quiet room.

Were the Old Testament believers worse off in salvation? No. They were saved by the same Christ, through faith in the promise, as we are through faith in the fulfilment (Romans 4; Hebrews 11). Abraham was justified exactly as a believer is today. What they lacked was not salvation but sight: they saw the dawn from a long way off, and we stand in the morning. Our advantage is in clarity and fullness, which is why it is ours to be more grateful, not more proud.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples privately that they were blessed to see and hear what many prophets and kings had longed to see and hear.

On a Tuesday. Open your Bible today as if you were Isaiah given an afternoon with it. Read one Gospel passage slowly and say to yourself: prophets wanted to see this. If church has become routine, do not wait to feel differently; ask God to restore wonder, and keep looking at Christ until it comes.

For worship. The prophets and kings were not disappointed in the end. Abraham saw his day and was glad; Moses stood with him on the mountain and spoke of his departure (9:30–31); and all of them now see what they longed for, face to face. The Christ they strained toward has come, has finished the work, and has given us the whole story to hold in our hands. We live in the age every saint of old leaned toward. Blessed are our eyes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A lawyer — an expert in the law of Moses — stands up to test Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” The wording gives him away twice over. What shall I do assumes the answer is an action; and an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for, since it comes by belonging to a family. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence without noticing.

Jesus answers with two questions. “What is written in the Law?” asks for the text. “How do you read it?” asks for the man — and a reading is never neutral. The examination has quietly moved.

The lawyer's answer is superb: Deuteronomy 6:5 welded to Leviticus 19:18, the spine of the law in a sentence. And Jesus commends it: “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.”

Which is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. The catch is not in the offer but in the doer. Jesus is using the law as it was meant to be used — not a ladder to climb but a mirror to look into (Rom. 3:20; Gal. 3:24).

And it works. The lawyer does not go home content; he starts negotiating, “desiring to justify himself.” His question — “who is my neighbour?” — sounds like scholarly precision and is a search for a boundary. If neighbour has edges, there are people outside them, and a man can be entirely obedient and still walk past the rest. It was a live question with real answers on offer: neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite, and the Qumran sect required its members to hate the sons of darkness.

The story refuses him a category from its first line: not a Jew, not a Gentile, just “a man.” Stripped and beaten unconscious, he has lost the two things — clothing and speech — by which anyone could have identified him.

A priest passes. A Levite passes. Every listener now expects the third man to be an ordinary Israelite; that is the shape of the joke. What arrives is a Samaritan — and the hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. It is only a chapter since a Samaritan village refused Jesus a bed and James and John asked to burn it.

Then the reversal: not “who is my neighbour?” but “which of these three proved to be a neighbour?” The lawyer cannot say the word. He says “the one who showed him mercy.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The usual defence of the priest is ritual purity: contact with a corpse made him unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11-13), and he could not tell from a distance whether the man was dead. But note the direction of travel — he was going down, away from Jerusalem, towards Jericho, where many priests lived between rotations. His duty is behind him, not ahead.

And the law he was protecting had a clause about exactly this. The same Torah commands a man to help even his enemy's fallen animal (Ex. 23:4-5), and forbids standing by the blood of your neighbour (Lev. 19:16) — two verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

Luke offers the priest and Levite no mitigation whatever. He simply says they passed by on the other side, and adds of the second that he “came to the place” — he got closer, looked from nearer, and crossed anyway. The Samaritan, by contrast, “when he saw him, had compassion.” The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

The parable has been read allegorically since Origen: the traveller is humanity, the robbers the devil, the priest and Levite the law and prophets that cannot save, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, the two denarii the sacraments. The reading is not without insight — Jesus is indeed the one who binds wounds, pays the debt and promises to return. But the surface command is non-negotiable: “Go and do likewise.”
verseByVerse.examples:
“Had compassion” — compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses the word at three great moments: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20), and of the Samaritan.

The care is worth itemising, because Jesus itemises it. Bandages torn from his own clothing; his own oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, now gone; his own animal, which means he walked; a night spent nursing a stranger; two denarii, two days' wages, enough for a fortnight's board; and then an open-ended undertaking — “whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.” A blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despised him.

“Go and do likewise” is not “go and feel compassion,” which is sentiment, or “go and have good intentions,” which are cheap. It is the specific, costly, schedule-wrecking, wallet-opening action of the Samaritan.

Which is unbearable if read honestly — and that is the moment it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road, to where we were lying, when we were in no condition to ask; he paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy, but mercy received and then passed on (1 John 4:19). The command remains binding — and it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, 'Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He said to him, 'What is written in the Law? How do you read it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying: Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? He said to him: what is written in the Law? How do you read it?

And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test. A lawyer here is not an advocate in a court but an expert in the law of Moses, a scribe: a scholar of Scripture, a man whose whole training was in what God had said and what it required. And Luke tells us his motive before he opens his mouth. This is not an enquiry. It is an examination, conducted in public, by a professional, of a Galilean teacher with no formal qualifications. Students stood to ask a teacher a question, and the posture is respectful; the purpose is not.

Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? The question is enormous, the most important question there is, and the rich ruler will ask it in the same words (18:18). But the wording gives the man away. What shall I do? The assumption is already in place before the answer arrives: eternal life is a thing achieved by an action, and what he wants is the specification. And there is a second thing buried in it that only shows up on a second reading. He asks what he must do to inherit. An inheritance is the one thing nobody works for. It comes by belonging to a family, and the beneficiary contributes nothing but a relationship. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence and not noticed.

What is written in the Law? How do you read it? Jesus does not answer. He asks two questions back, and both are respectful: this man knows the law, and he is being invited to say so. Jesus always points to Scripture. But the second question is doing something the first is not. What is written asks for the text. How do you read it asks for the man. That distinction is worth having, because it is the difference between two things that are constantly confused. Two people in a disagreement about Scripture usually have the same words in front of them. What differs is the reading, and a reading is never neutral. It is done by a person, with a history and a set of interests, who wants some things to be true and others not to be. So Jesus has, in a handful of words, moved the examination. The lawyer came to test him on the content of the law. He is about to be tested on what he has been doing with it.

What does eternal life mean here? Not simply living for ever, which in one sense everyone will do, in joy or in judgement. Eternal life is the life of the age to come, the life of God’s kingdom, beginning now and completed at the resurrection. Jesus defines it elsewhere: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). So the lawyer is really asking how to belong to God for ever, and the answer will turn out to be a Person, not a performance.

In a sentence. A lawyer tested Jesus by asking what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus asked him what the law said and how he read it.

On a Tuesday. When you have questions about God, go to his word: what is written? Then ask the second question of yourself: how do I read it, and what do I want it to say? Notice the passages you instinctively soften, and read those twice.

For worship. The inheritance the lawyer wanted to earn is held out by the Father to children who cannot earn it. If children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The Son came down to make outsiders sons, and the eternal life no one can buy is the gift of his own life, shared.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And he said to him, 'You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbour as yourself. And he said to him: you have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.

You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself. The lawyer’s answer is superb, and it deserves saying so. He puts together Deuteronomy 6:5, from the Shema, which every Jew recited daily, and Leviticus 19:18, a single line in a chapter of miscellaneous statutes, and welds them into one command, as Jesus himself did elsewhere (Mark 12:29–31). Nobody had to teach him that. He has read the law and seen its spine. And the four terms are not a checklist of separate compartments; they are a way of saying all of you, with nothing held back. Heart, soul, strength, mind: the affections, the life, the effort, the thinking. There is no part of a man left over that is not commanded.

You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live. An echo of Leviticus 18:5: if a person does them, he shall live by them. And here is the question that ought to trouble anyone reading this with Paul in mind. Is Jesus really telling a man he can earn eternal life by keeping the law? Take the sentence at face value and it is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. God has never said otherwise. The catch is not in the offer. It is in the doer, and there has never been one, apart from the man saying it.

Law and gospel. So Jesus is using the law exactly as the law was meant to be used: not as a ladder to climb but as a mirror to look into. This is the first use of the law, to convict of sin: through the law comes knowledge of sin (Romans 3:20); all who rely on works of the law are under a curse (Galatians 3:10–12); the law was our guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). Its work is to bring a man to the end of himself so that he will look elsewhere. The perfect law demands perfect love. Only one man ever kept it, Jesus, and his perfect obedience is counted to those who trust him: by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19), for Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4–5).

Watch how well it works. Jesus says do this and you will live, and the lawyer does not say amen and go home content. The very next thing he does is start negotiating the terms, desiring to justify himself (v. 29). That is a man who has just felt the floor move. He asked how much he had to do, and has been handed a standard that leaves him nowhere to stand; and rather than fall, he reaches for a definition small enough to survive on. The parable that follows is not a softening of the demand. It takes his last handhold away.

If no one can keep the law, why should Christians still try to obey it? Because the law that could never save us now describes the life Christ has saved us into. Once we are justified by faith, the same commands become the shape of gratitude, and the Spirit writes them on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4). We obey not to be accepted but because we are accepted, and our obedience, though imperfect, is pleasing to the Father for Christ’s sake. The law still shows us our sin daily and sends us back to Christ; and it still shows us the path of love. A Christian does not throw away the map because he has stopped trying to earn the journey.

In a sentence. The lawyer summarised the law as loving God with everything and one’s neighbour as oneself, and Jesus told him that if he did this, he would live.

On a Tuesday. Measure yourself honestly against these two commands, not against other people. Have you loved God with all your heart today, or with a corner of it? Have you loved your neighbour as yourself, wanting his good as eagerly as your own? If not, do not reach for a smaller definition. Flee to the one who kept them, and then ask him for grace to love a little more today.

For worship. There was once a man who loved the Lord his God with all his heart, soul, strength and mind, every hour of his life, and loved his neighbour so much that he died for him. He did this, and he lived; and then he gave his life away, so that those who had not done this might live in him. The great commandment was fulfilled by the great Commander himself, and his righteousness is the robe we wear.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus: and who is my neighbour?

But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, And who is my neighbor? Luke gives the motive again, and this time it is the hinge of the whole chapter. Desiring to justify himself: wanting to come out of this conversation still standing, still right, still able to say that he had done what was required. Perhaps also to justify his question, since he already knew the answer. Self-justification is the instinct of the human heart: to define God’s law in a way we can keep. Jesus will later say to the Pharisees, you are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts (16:15). The question that produces the world’s most famous story is asked by a man looking for somewhere to hide.

A clever question. It is not evasive on the surface at all. It sounds like precision, the reasonable request of a careful scholar wanting to know the scope of a term before he applies it. Any lawyer would ask it. But run it out and see where it goes. If neighbour can be defined, then it has edges. If it has edges, there are people outside them. And if there are people outside them, then a man can love everyone inside the line, be entirely obedient, and walk past the rest with a clear conscience. That is what he is after. Not whom should I love? but whom am I permitted not to?

A live question. It was a live question with real answers on offer. The discussion of Leviticus 19:18 among the teachers turned on the surrounding phrase, the sons of your own people, so neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite; some excluded sinners and enemies too. Some communities of the period drew it tighter still: the Qumran sect taught its members to love the sons of light and hate the sons of darkness. Every one of those definitions gave a man a boundary and let him rest. The instinct is universal, and it does not present itself as wickedness. It presents itself as realism. Nobody can help everybody; a line has to be drawn somewhere; the question is where. And the moment a line is agreed, the people beyond it stop being a claim on anyone. Every version of that reasoning was standing behind this question, and Jesus is about to tell a story in which the line the lawyer most wanted, the racial and religious one, is crossed by the man he least wanted to admire. Jesus will not answer the question as asked. He will turn it around.

In a sentence. Wanting to justify himself, the lawyer asked Jesus who his neighbour was.

On a Tuesday. Do you try to limit God’s commands so you can keep them? Listen for the sentences that begin with but surely: but surely I am not expected to love him; but surely that does not apply at work. Let his word define the terms, not you. Name the person you have quietly placed outside the line, and pray for him by name today.

For worship. We came to God with our definitions and our boundaries, wanting to know how little we owed. He came to us with no boundary at all. While we were still sinners, while we were enemies, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8–10). The God who is love never asked who his neighbour was. He crossed every line to make himself ours.

parallels.desc: those who justify yourselves before men

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus replied, 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus replied: a man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.

The parable of the good Samaritan. Only Luke records it, and it is one of the best-known stories in the world. That familiarity is its danger: a story so famous that its name has become a word for kindness has lost, for most readers, the shock it was built to deliver.

A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Note what we are not told. No name, no trade, no nationality, no religion. He is simply a man, and the omission is deliberate: the lawyer asked for a category, and the first thing the story refuses him is a category. The road is real, and it was notorious. Jerusalem sits about 2,500 feet above sea level; Jericho lies roughly 800 feet below it, some seventeen miles (27 km) away. The road drops over three thousand feet (900 m) through limestone gorges and blind bends, with caves and rocks all along it. Jerome, living nearby centuries later, says it was still called the red or bloody ascent, and it was known as bandit country.

He fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Stripped, beaten and unconscious, unable to help himself, perhaps dying. That matters more than it looks, because those details remove the only two things a passer-by could have used to identify him. Clothing told you a man’s nationality and status; speech told you the rest. Naked and silent, he is unclassifiable. He is a human being in a ditch, and there is no way to work out whether he is one of ours.

Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. Why? Perhaps fear: the robbers might still be near. Perhaps ritual purity: contact with a corpse made a priest unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–13), and he could not tell from a distance whether the man was dead. Perhaps simple indifference. Jesus gives no reasons; excuses do not matter. But look at the direction of travel. He was going down, away from Jerusalem, toward Jericho, where a great many priests lived between their weeks of service. His duty is behind him, not ahead. Whatever else was in his mind, a defiling contact on the way home would have cost him a week of inconvenience, not a lost turn at the altar. And it is worth saying plainly that the law he was protecting had clauses about exactly this. The same Torah commands a man to help even his enemy’s fallen animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and forbids standing by while your neighbour’s life is in danger (Leviticus 19:16), two verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. Levites assisted the priests in the temple: religious, respectable, knowledgeable about the law. Luke adds a phrase for the second man: he came to the place. He got closer. He looked, from nearer, and crossed anyway. The two men who should have helped, who knew the law about loving one’s neighbour best, did nothing. Religion without love.

The shape of the story. And every listener now knows what comes next, because these stories run in threes and the third man is always the ordinary Israelite. Priest, Levite, layman. It is the familiar shape of every story anyone has ever told about the temple establishment failing while the common man does right. What arrives instead detonates the entire structure.

Is it always wrong to pass by someone in need? Not every passing by is sin. There are real dangers, prior duties and needs you cannot meet, and sometimes the loving thing is to call for help rather than to stop yourself. A woman alone at night is not commanded to pull over on a dark road. But the priest and Levite had no such reasons that Jesus thought worth mentioning; they simply did not want the cost. The test is honest: am I unable, or merely unwilling? Has God put this person in my path, and is there something I can actually do? If so, the ditch is my business.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man robbed and left half dead on the Jericho road, whom first a priest and then a Levite saw and passed by on the other side.

On a Tuesday. Who have you passed by on the other side? The colleague whose marriage is falling apart, the neighbour whose bins have not moved in a week, the widow at church who sits alone. Religious knowledge is no substitute for love, and a busy schedule of good things can make a very convenient other side of the road.

For worship. We were the man in the ditch, stripped and half dead, and no priest or Levite of the old order could lift us. The law passed by on the other side, not because it was evil, but because it had no power to heal. And then one came down the road from heaven to the place where we lay, and did not cross over. Blessed be the God who did not leave us there.
verseByVerse.note: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet in about 17 miles through barren, rocky country, and was notorious for robbers. Touching a dead body made a priest unclean.

parallels.desc: no priest shall make himself unclean for the dead

verseByVerse.quote: But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying: take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.

But a Samaritan. It is difficult now to feel what those words did to that audience. Jesus’ hearers would expect the third man to be an ordinary Jewish layman. Instead, a Samaritan. The hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. Samaritans were descended from the remnant of the northern kingdom, mixed with settlers brought in after the Assyrian conquest; they had their own temple on Mount Gerizim, their own edition of the five books of Moses, and no use for Jerusalem. Jews regarded them as heretics and half-breeds. Within living memory, Josephus tells us, Samaritans had scattered human bones in the temple courts at Passover to defile it. John records the flat statement that Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), and it is only a chapter since a Samaritan village refused Jesus a bed and James and John asked to call down fire on it (9:52–54). This is the man Jesus makes the hero of the story, to a Jewish scholar of the law, in answer to a question about who counts as a neighbour.

And when he saw him, he had compassion. All three saw. Only one had compassion. The verb is esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs: compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses it at three great moments: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal on the road (15:20), and here. Compassion is the heart of the story. And note the sequence, because it is the same sequence the priest and Levite had and broke. They saw and crossed over. He saw and was moved and went to him. The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then the care, and it is worth itemising, because Jesus itemises it. He bound up his wounds, with whatever cloth he had, since there is nothing else on that road. He poured on oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, wine to cleanse and oil to soothe, both of them his own travelling supplies, now gone. There is a quiet irony: oil and wine were also offerings in the temple the priest had just left. The Samaritan poured them out in the true worship, for I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6).

Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. Setting him on his own animal means the Samaritan walked, at the pace of an injured man, in robber country, for however many miles remained. He brought him to an inn and took care of him: that is a night, spent nursing a stranger.

Two denarii. In the morning: two denarii, two days’ wages for a labourer, enough to cover board for perhaps a fortnight. Then the sentence that goes furthest of all: whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back. Without payment, a penniless guest could have been held as a debtor. He has just written a blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despises him, and bound himself to return.

The cost of love. Time, effort, risk, money and inconvenience, for a stranger, and for one of a people who regarded him as an enemy. Love does not calculate. It does not ask whether the man will be grateful, or whether he deserves it, or what the neighbours will say. It sees, it is moved, and it goes.

Where Christians differ: Christ the Samaritan? From the early church onward (Origen, Augustine), many read the parable as an allegory of salvation: the man is Adam, the robbers are the devil, the priest and Levite are the law and the prophets, the Samaritan is Christ, the inn is the church, the two denarii the sacraments, and the return is the second coming. Verdict: the parable’s primary meaning, given by Jesus himself, is ethical: go and do likewise (v. 37). It answers the lawyer’s question, who is my neighbour?, and reading every detail as a code goes beyond the text. Yet there is a true echo: Christ is the supreme neighbour, who came to us when we were his enemies, half dead in our sins, and gave himself to save us (Romans 5:8–10). The parable both commands love and points to the love that makes it possible, and every Christian’s mercy flows from his.

What if helping someone could be dangerous or be taken advantage of? The Samaritan took a real risk, and love sometimes will. But wisdom is not the enemy of love. He did not hand the man his purse; he paid the innkeeper and arranged care, which is both generous and sensible. You may help through the right channels, involve others, set limits that protect your family, and decline to fund what would harm someone. What love may not do is use prudence as a disguise for indifference. Ask: what would genuinely help this person, and what part of that can I carry?

In a sentence. A despised Samaritan, moved with compassion, tended the man’s wounds, took him to an inn, cared for him, and paid for his ongoing care.

On a Tuesday. Love is costly and practical. Whose wounds can you bind up this week, whatever it costs? It may be an evening, a lift to hospital, a meal cooked, a bill quietly paid, a long conversation with someone whose politics or background you dislike. Notice whether there is a particular kind of person you would find it hardest to help, and ask God to make that the person you notice first.

For worship. The despised Samaritan is the clearest picture in the Gospels of the despised Saviour. He was despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3); they called him a Samaritan and said he had a demon (John 8:48). He came to where we lay, was moved with compassion, bound up the broken-hearted, paid our debt with his own blood, and has promised: I will come back. Every act of mercy we do is a small copy of the mercy that found us on the road.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage — two could cover some days at an inn.

parallels.desc: the captives clothed, anointed and carried on donkeys to Jericho

verseByVerse.quote: Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' He said, 'The one who showed him mercy.' And Jesus said to him, 'You go, and do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbour to the man who fell among the robbers? He said: the one who showed him mercy. And Jesus said to him: you go, and do likewise.

Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers? The question has been turned inside out, and that is the parable’s most important move. The lawyer asked, who is my neighbour?, which puts the other person under examination and the questioner safely in the chair. Jesus asks which of the three proved to be a neighbour, which puts the questioner in the road and asks what he did. It is no longer a question about the boundaries of obligation. It is a question about what kind of man is walking past. Neighbourliness is not defined by the other person’s status, but by my compassion.

He said, The one who showed him mercy. He cannot say it. The answer is a single word, the Samaritan, and he takes a whole phrase to avoid it. Luke leaves that exposed without a syllable of comment, and it is the most human moment in the chapter: a man who has understood the story perfectly and cannot get the word out of his mouth.

You go, and do likewise. And there the parable stops, which is unbearable if you have been reading honestly. The command is not lowered by an inch at the end. Stop asking whom you must love, and start loving whoever is in need, even your enemy. Go and be the Samaritan: cross a racial hatred, spend your own money, give your own time, take on an open-ended liability for a stranger who can never repay you. Anyone who finds that manageable has not understood it. Anyone who has understood it is standing exactly where the lawyer is standing, looking for somewhere to put his feet. If the lawyer is honest, he will find that he cannot love like this by his own strength. He needs a new heart. The law drives us to Christ.

Who is telling the story. This is the moment it matters enormously who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road than the one from Jerusalem to Jericho, to where we were lying, when we were stripped and half dead and in no condition to ask. He bound up the wounds at his own expense. He paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. And he is on the road to Jerusalem as he speaks, to settle the account himself.

Does this mean I must help everyone in need? The parable defines a neighbour as the one who shows mercy to the person in front of him, whoever he is. It does not tell us how to meet every need in the world, nor is it a programme for the state. You cannot help everyone, and God does not ask you to. But it forbids us to decide that someone in real need, whom God has put in our path, is not our concern because of who he is. Begin with the household of faith and those nearest you (Galatians 6:10), and let your circle of mercy keep widening.

Mercy received, then mercy passed on. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy. It is mercy received, and then mercy passed on: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Go and do likewise remains a command, and it remains binding. But it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch, and that is the only reason it is good news and not a sentence.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of the three had been a neighbour, and when the lawyer answered that it was the one who showed mercy, Jesus told him to go and do the same.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask who your neighbour is. Ask whose neighbour you can be today. Look for the person in your path whom you would naturally file under not my concern, and do one concrete merciful thing for him. And when you fail, as you will, do not reach for a smaller definition. Go back to the Samaritan who picked you up, and let his mercy send you out again.

For worship. The lawyer could not bring himself to say the name of the one who showed mercy. We may say it with joy. His name is Jesus, who had mercy on us when we were his enemies, and the mercy he showed is the mercy he sends us out to show. The command go and do likewise is spoken by the one who first went and did, all the way to a cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes in a house in a village — Bethany, though Luke does not name it — and the placing is deliberate. The Samaritan has just poured out his time and money on a road, with “go and do likewise” still in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something.

Martha “welcomed him into her house” — her house, Luke says, which is unusual enough to notice, and she received him as an honoured guest. She is not a woman lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching,” and both halves of that would have struck a first-century reader. Sitting at a teacher's feet is the technical posture of a disciple — Paul describes his own training as being brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3). And that place was not open to a woman. Mary sat down in it, Jesus let her, and in three verses he will defend her right to be there against her own sister. Luke reports it in a subordinate clause, as though it were ordinary — which, from now on, it is.

Martha is “distracted with much serving” — pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not being busy but being torn. And the thing tearing her is service: she is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for.

Her complaint takes three steps and each goes further. She interrupts his teaching; she accuses her sister in front of the guests; and then she accuses him. “Do you not care?” is not a request but a charge, levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed in — and then “tell her,” which does not even ask him to intervene but tells him what to say.

Every word of it is what an exhausted person says, and she is not wrong about the facts. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance — and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score.

“Martha, Martha” is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person: the same register as “Simon, Simon” (22:31), “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” (13:34), “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4). And the diagnosis is not of her workload but of her interior — “anxious,” the worry he will forbid his disciples (12:22-26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Mary sitting at the Lord's feet is the posture of discipleship, and Luke has used the phrase once already of the Gerasene man restored to his right mind (8:35). In the first century women did not ordinarily receive rabbinic instruction, and the posture of female discipleship was itself a quiet revolution. Jesus does not redirect Mary to help; he defends her right to receive what he is giving.

“The good portion” plays on a word for a share at a meal — and Martha, of all people, would have felt it, since she is in the kitchen dividing portions while Mary has taken the one that matters.

“Which will not be taken away from her” carries the force of a promise. What Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week's end; the word Mary is taking in is permanent, the living and abiding word of God (1 Pet. 1:23).

Some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one” at v.42; the shorter reading is very likely original and the sense is unaffected either way. What lasts defines what is necessary, and what is necessary defines what must not be sacrificed to the urgent.
verseByVerse.examples:
The scene speaks to the perennial tension between doing and being. It does not abolish the tension; it orders it. Martha's service is not wrong — her anxiety is. And this is not a rebuke of practical work: Luke has just spent a chapter praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills.

It is a statement about order. Martha's work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

“Do you not care?” is worth naming for anyone who has prayed like it, because a good many have. It is the same accusation the disciples threw at him in the boat (Mark 4:38) — what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

The Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where she is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping — including, in the end, with the Lord it was all being done for. The cure is not less service. It is the recovery of the one thing that makes service a gift rather than a grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. A woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. She had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his teaching.

The placing. After the parable about doing, love your neighbour, comes a story about listening. The two belong together: loving God by hearing his word, and loving neighbour by serving. The chapter has just finished with a Samaritan pouring out his time and money on a road, and go and do likewise is still hanging in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something. Anyone who thinks Luke has arranged these two stories carelessly has not read him. Martha and Mary show the balance, and the order.

Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. Luke does not name it. John does: Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, the home of Martha, Mary and their brother Lazarus (John 11:1; 12:1–3). Luke may leave it unnamed because in his ordering of the journey Jesus is not yet near Jerusalem.

And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. It is her house; Luke says so, and it is unusual enough to be worth noticing. Martha was apparently the head of the household. And she welcomed him as an honoured guest. In a culture where hospitality was a sacred obligation, a travelling teacher with his disciples, perhaps thirteen or more people, meant a great deal of work, and Martha opened her door to the lot of them. This is not a woman being criticised for lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his teaching. Two details, and a first-century reader would have caught both. Sat at the Lord’s feet is a technical phrase. It is the posture of a disciple under a rabbi. Paul describes his own training as being brought up at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and Luke has used the same phrase already, of the Gerasene man restored to his right mind (8:35). It does not mean Mary was sitting on the floor being decorative. It means she had taken a student’s place. And that place was not normally open to her. Women were taught the law as it applied to their duties, and the formal relationship of teacher and student was a male arrangement. Mary sat down in it, and Jesus let her, and in two verses’ time he will defend her right to be there against her own sister. Luke reports it without a flourish, in a subordinate clause, as though it were the ordinary thing. Which, from now on, it is. And she listened: the tense means she kept on listening.

Does Mary’s place at Jesus’ feet mean women may hold every office in the church? It means women are full disciples: called to learn, to know the Scriptures deeply and to sit under Christ’s word as fully as any man, which was a revolution in its day. That is the point Luke is making. The question of who may serve as an elder or preach to the gathered church is answered elsewhere, where the New Testament reserves that office to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). This app holds that complementarian view, with headship understood as self-giving service, never domination. Mary’s example rebukes any church that keeps women from learning deeply. It does not settle the eldership question either way.

In a sentence. In a village, Martha welcomed Jesus into her home, and her sister Mary sat at his feet listening to his teaching.

On a Tuesday. Make time today to sit at Jesus’ feet: open his word and listen before you speak or serve. If you are the one who always opens the door and does the work, thank God for that gift, and then make sure you also take the student’s place. And if you are a woman who has been told, in so many words, that deep study of Scripture is not really for you, know that Jesus defended your seat.

For worship. The Lord of glory sat in an ordinary house and taught a woman who was not supposed to be learning, and called it the good portion. He is the Teacher who welcomes every disciple to his feet, and his word is life. How gracious of the Son of God, on his way to the cross, to stop in a village kitchen and give himself to whoever would sit and listen.
verseByVerse.note: John places Martha and Mary in Bethany, near Jerusalem. Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the place of a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Martha was distracted with much serving. She went up to him and said: Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.

But Martha was distracted with much serving. The verb is periespato: literally to be pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not a word for being busy. It is a word for being torn. And the thing tearing her is much serving, diakonia, the word that will become the church’s term for ministry. She is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for doing. Her service was good, and necessary. So the problem in this house is not that Martha chose work over devotion. The problem is what the work has become inside her: it pulled her away from Jesus. Luke marks the moment it surfaces.

Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? She went up to him and said it, and added: tell her then to help me. Three things in one sentence, each a step further than the last. She interrupts his teaching. She accuses her sister in front of the guests. And, this is the sharp one, she accuses him. Do you not care? That is not a request. It is a charge, and it is levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed into her house. They are almost the words the disciples threw at him in the storm: teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). Anxiety turns into resentment, against others and against God. She has moved from serving him to reproaching him, and the distance between those two things was crossed in an afternoon, in a kitchen, doing a good thing. Then tell her: she does not even ask him to intervene. She tells him what to say. Busy, worried people often judge others who are not as busy.

Not hard on her. It would be easy to be hard on her, and it would be a mistake. Every word of her complaint is what an exhausted person says. She is not wrong about the facts: she is serving alone, and the meal does have to be produced, and somebody has to do it. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance, and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score. There is something worth naming for anyone who has ever prayed like this, because a good many have. Do you not care? is what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

Is it wrong to complain to God? Not to bring him your distress: the psalms are full of honest lament, how long, O LORD?, and he invites us to cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). What Martha shows is the moment honest weariness hardens into accusation, when do you not care is said as a verdict rather than a cry. The cure is to tell him the truth about how you feel, and then to let him tell you the truth about himself. He does care. That is precisely why he will not simply give Martha what she asks.

In a sentence. Martha, distracted by her many preparations, complained to Jesus that her sister had left her to serve alone and asked him to tell Mary to help.

On a Tuesday. Even good service for Jesus can distract you from Jesus. Notice when busyness turns into resentment: the sigh as you clear up after the church lunch, the mental list of who never helps, the irritation at the person who seems to have time to pray. Those are signals, not proofs that you are wrong to serve. Stop, sit down for five minutes with him, and let him take the score card out of your hand.

For worship. The Lord whom Martha accused of not caring was on his way to the clearest proof of care the world has ever seen. He was the true servant, who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life (Mark 10:45). He did all of it without a grievance, without a score card, for people who did not help, and he never once said to the Father, do you not care. He knew the Father did.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord answered her, 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord answered her: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.

Martha, Martha. The doubled name is not impatience. Luke records the same double address at other moments, and the register is always the same: Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you (22:31); O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children (13:34); Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). It is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person and is about to say something she needs and will not enjoy. A gentle rebuke, from love.

You are anxious and troubled about many things. Two verbs, and neither is busy. Anxious is merimnas, the word for the worry Jesus forbids in 12:22–26, the same root as the cares that choke the word in the parable of the soils (8:14). Troubled (thorybazē) means agitated, in an uproar, flustered. He is not diagnosing her workload. He is diagnosing her interior, and it is worth being clear that these are words he uses of a heart not resting in God rather than of overwork. She is not too busy. She is worried. Many things.

But one thing is necessary. If your Bible has a footnote here, it is a real one: some manuscripts read few things are necessary, or only one, as if Jesus were saying that a simple meal would do. The shorter reading, one thing, is very likely original, and the sense is unaffected either way. Not just one dish, but the one thing that matters most: listening to Jesus. David knew it: one thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD (Psalm 27:4).

Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her. Two words carry it. Portion (meris) is the word for a share at a meal, and there is a play on it that Martha, of all people, would have felt: she is in the kitchen dividing up portions, and Mary has taken the one that matters, the food of Jesus’ word. Man does not live by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3); Jesus said his own food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:32–34). And “will not be taken away” is a promise: what Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner Martha is making will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week’s end. The word Mary is taking in is permanent. Jesus defends her.

What it does not mean. This is not a rebuke of practical service, and Luke has just spent a parable praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills. It is not a recommendation of contemplation over action, or of the monastery over the kitchen. And it is certainly not an instruction that meals should go uncooked. Martha was not wrong to serve. It is a statement about order. Listening to Jesus comes first, and is the source of true service. Martha’s work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down. Service without listening becomes anxious and resentful. Hearing his word is the one thing necessary.

The servant who never receives. The Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where Martha is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping, including, in the end, with the Lord she is doing it all for.

With young children, a job and an elderly parent, how can I possibly sit at his feet? The good portion is not measured in hours, and Jesus is not asking a mother of three to keep a monk’s timetable. It is a matter of where your heart rests. Take what you can: ten minutes with a Psalm before the house wakes, a passage read aloud at breakfast, a sermon listened to while you drive, a prayer while you wash up. Guard the Lord’s Day as a time to receive. And let the busy hours themselves be done at his feet, in the sense of being done for him and in dependence on him. Little and real is better than much and anxious.

In a sentence. Jesus gently told Martha that she was anxious about many things, but only one thing was necessary, and Mary had chosen the best portion, which would not be taken from her.

On a Tuesday. What are you anxious and troubled about today? Write the many things down, and then put them aside for a few minutes while you read one passage and pray. The list will still be there; you will not be the same person facing it. Before the next busy week of serving begins, sit down first.

For worship. The one thing necessary is not a technique but a Person, and he is the good portion that cannot be taken away. The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I will hope in him (Lamentations 3:24).
