Meals are eaten and forgotten; kingdoms rise and fall; but the word of the Lord remains for ever, and the Lord himself is the inheritance of everyone who sits at his feet. Martha’s dinner was gone by nightfall. Mary’s portion is still hers, and it is the same one offered to us.

parallels.desc: one thing have I asked of the LORD
the LORD is my chosen portion

10.text: <sup>1</sup> After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. <sup>3</sup> Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <sup>4</sup> Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road. <sup>5</sup> Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ <sup>6</sup> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. <sup>7</sup> And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house. <sup>8</sup> Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. <sup>9</sup> Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ <sup>10</sup> But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, <sup>11</sup> ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ <sup>12</sup> I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. <sup>13</sup> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>14</sup> But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>15</sup> And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. <sup>16</sup> “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.” <sup>17</sup> The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” <sup>18</sup> And he said to them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. <sup>19</sup> Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. <sup>20</sup> Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” <sup>21</sup> In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>22</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” <sup>23</sup> Then turning to the disciples he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! <sup>24</sup> For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” <sup>25</sup> And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>26</sup> He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” <sup>27</sup> And he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>28</sup> And he said to him, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” <sup>29</sup> But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” <sup>30</sup> Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. <sup>31</sup> Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. <sup>32</sup> So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. <sup>33</sup> But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. <sup>34</sup> He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. <sup>35</sup> And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’ <sup>36</sup> Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” <sup>37</sup> He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said to him, “You go, and do likewise.” <sup>38</sup> Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. <sup>39</sup> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. <sup>40</sup> But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.” <sup>41</sup> But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, <sup>42</sup> but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

11.title: Prayer, Darkness, and the Woes of the Pharisees
11.overview:
Chapter 11 divides into three movements of escalating intensity. It opens with the disciples' request — “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples” — and Jesus's response: the Lord's Prayer and two parables about persistent asking. It continues with the controversy over Beelzebul, where Jesus is accused of casting out demons by the power of the prince of demons, and responds with the parable of the strong man, the sign of Jonah, and a warning about the darkness that replaces expelled light. And it closes with the most sustained series of woes in Luke's Gospel — six pronouncements against the Pharisees and lawyers that are simultaneously the most confrontational and the most sorrowful words Jesus speaks in public.

The chapter's movement from prayer (vv. 1–13) to spiritual warfare (vv. 14–36) to religious condemnation (vv. 37–54) is not a random sequence. The prayer section establishes the relationship with the Father that makes spiritual life possible. The Beelzebul controversy shows what happens when the kingdom's power is at work in the world — it provokes opposition, demands decision, and warns against the neutrality that is actually a form of hostility. And the woes reveal what becomes of religious life when it loses the relationship with the Father — when the form of religion remains but the substance has been evacuated, replaced by the performance of piety for the wrong audience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying, and when he finishes one of the disciples asks: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” Of everything on offer in three years beside the Son of God — the healings, the stilled storm, the knowledge of men's thoughts — the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father.

Luke's version is shorter than Matthew's (Matt. 6:9-13), and that difference has unsettled readers who learned the prayer by heart as children. Where is “who art in heaven”? Where is “thy will be done”? An older Bible will have them at this very verse and a modern one will not.

There is nothing sinister in it. Luke's prayer was always the shorter of the two, but the version the church actually prayed aloud, week after week for centuries, was Matthew's — and scribes copying Luke knew that fuller wording by heart. Line by line, over generations, they filled Luke out to match what their lips already said. It is one of the most understandable corrections in the history of copying and one of the easiest to detect: the earliest manuscripts of Luke are short, and the additions match Matthew word for word. Nothing was lost. Every phrase you were taught is genuinely the Lord's; it is simply Matthew who recorded it.

And Luke's shorter form is worth having in its own right, because two versions tell us something one could not. Jesus plainly gave this prayer more than once, and not in identical words. Matthew says “pray then like this”; Luke says “when you pray, say.” Set them side by side and the conclusion is unavoidable: this was never handed down as a formula to be recited syllable-perfect on pain of not counting. It is a shape for praying — a floor to build on, not a ceiling.

The prayer opens with one word that was a revolution. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation; what is almost entirely absent is an individual addressing him that way in prayer. The word Jesus himself uses in Gethsemane is the Aramaic Abba (Mark 14:36) — family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of that period addressed God with it in prayer.

Then five petitions: his name, his kingdom, our bread, our forgiveness, our protection. God first, then us — and the order is not decoration. A prayer that begins with God's honour can bring every human need afterwards without becoming a list submitted to a dispenser.
verseByVerse.theology:
The address “Father” is the theological revolution of this prayer. Paul will name what has happened: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'” (Rom. 8:15). The address is not a warmer name for the same relationship; it is a different relationship — the Son's own, opened to people with no natural claim to it.

“Hallowed be your name” asks that God be treated as holy, since his name cannot be made more holy than it is. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known, so the petition asks that he be known, honoured and reverenced as what he actually is — first by the one praying, and then by everybody else. It is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to.

“Your kingdom come” is the central petition and the shortest, and it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God's rule to come is to ask for one's own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he was hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

“Daily” bread — the ESV margin gives “our bread for tomorrow,” enough for the coming day. It is a small request, deliberately: enough for today, asked today, and again tomorrow.
verseByVerse.examples:
The “for” in “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive” has troubled readers, and it must not become a bargain. God's forgiveness is not purchased by ours; the prayer has just called him Father, which nobody earns.

What the clause does is make our forgiving the evidence that his has landed — a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot go on with a ledger open against his neighbour; and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all. Matthew makes the connection explicit (Matt. 6:14-15).

Note the tense, too: “we ourselves forgive,” present and continuing. Not “we forgave, once, years ago.” It is a standing policy.

And “lead us not into temptation” is not a fear that God might try to make us sin, which James forbids (Jas. 1:13). It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it — which is a far more realistic prayer than asking for strength to survive the edge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.

Meaning first. Luke 11 is a chapter about the God who hears and the people who will not. It opens with the disciples asking Jesus to teach them to pray, and he gives them the Lord’s Prayer, the parable of the friend at midnight, and the promise that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Then the mood darkens. Jesus casts out a demon and is accused of working by Satan; he answers that the kingdom of God has arrived, that a stronger one has come to plunder the strong man’s house, and that there is no neutral ground. He warns a sign-seeking generation that the only sign will be the sign of Jonah, and that the light they think they have may be darkness. The chapter ends at a Pharisee’s dinner table with six woes against religion that cleans the outside and leaves the heart full of greed, and with the scholars of the law beginning to hunt him. The thread through it all is the difference between knowing about God and knowing him as Father.

Now Jesus was praying in a certain place. Notice the order. He prays; they watch; and when he has finished, one of them asks. Luke shows Jesus at prayer more than any other Gospel: at the baptism (3:21), withdrawing to desolate places (5:16), all night before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before the great question about who he is (9:18), on the mountain where his face changed (9:28–29). He does not tell us what they saw in his praying, and he does not need to. Something about the way this man prayed was different enough that men who had grown up saying prayers several times a day concluded they did not know how.

Lord, teach us to pray. They had been with him long enough to have seen a great deal. They had watched him still a storm, feed thousands, raise the dead, and send a legion of demons out of a man with a word. Any one of those would have been worth asking about. What they asked for was this. Not teach us to preach, or teach us to heal, though they had just come back from a mission where both were happening. Of everything on offer in three years of walking beside the Son of God, the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father. It is a wise request. Prayer must be learned. It does not come naturally to sinners, and the best teacher is the one who prays perfectly.

As John taught his disciples. Teachers and movements had characteristic prayers; they functioned as a kind of identity, a way of marking out what a group was for. John had given his followers one, and Jesus’ disciples want the same from him: not merely instruction in the discipline, but a prayer that belongs to them, that expresses who they are as his.

Why does prayer feel so hard? Almost every Christian who has been at it for a while will admit, if pressed honestly, that prayer is the part that never quite settles. It is the first thing to go in a busy week and the last thing to come back. Part of the reason is that prayer is the one Christian activity with no audience and no visible result in the moment; part is that our flesh resists dependence; and part is that the enemy hates it. The answer is not a technique, and it is not more determination. It is what the disciple did here: to say out loud, to the one person who can do anything about it, that he does not know how. Then to start small and keep going, using the words Jesus gives.

In a sentence. After watching Jesus pray, one of his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, as John had taught his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Make the disciples’ request your own today, in so many words: Lord, teach me to pray. Then give him five unhurried minutes, perhaps praying slowly through the prayer that follows. If you have let prayer slide for weeks, do not wait until you feel worthy to start again. The disciples asked because they could not, and that is exactly the qualification required.

For worship. The Son of God, who had the Father’s presence every moment, still went away to pray. He prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (22:32), prayed in agony in the garden, prayed for those who crucified him, and he lives now to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). The one who taught us to pray is praying still, and our stumbling words reach the Father on the strength of his.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers commonly gave their disciples a characteristic prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: when you pray, say: Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.

The Lord’s Prayer. Luke’s version is shorter than Matthew’s (Matthew 6:9–13). Jesus probably taught it on more than one occasion, in slightly different forms. Luke’s has five petitions; Matthew’s seven. The ESV notes that some manuscripts expand Luke’s version to match Matthew’s. It is both a prayer to pray and a pattern for all prayer. Notice the order: God’s concerns first, then ours.

When you pray, say. A prayer to be prayed, not only a model. The church has prayed these words ever since.

Is this prayer a form to recite or a pattern to follow? Both. Luke says when you pray, say, and Matthew pray then like this (Matthew 6:9). Christians may pray these words together, as the church has done from the beginning, as long as they are prayed from the heart and not as empty repetition (Matthew 6:7). And they shape all our other prayers: praise before petition, God’s glory before our needs, forgiveness alongside bread. A believer who prays only these words has prayed well; a believer who never prays them has missed a gift.

Father. One word, and it was a revolution. Simply Father, without our or in heaven. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation: is not he your father, who created you (Deuteronomy 32:6); you, O LORD, are our Father (Isaiah 63:16). What is almost entirely absent is an individual Israelite addressing God that way in prayer. The standard addresses were LORD, God of our fathers, King of the universe: titles that keep a proper distance. Behind Luke’s Greek stands the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). It is not baby-talk, as is sometimes said; grown men used it of their fathers. But it is family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of that period addressed God with it in prayer. He hands it to them as the first word.

The Son’s own word, opened to us. Paul will later say exactly what has happened: you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The address is not a nicer name for the same relationship. It is a different relationship, and it is the Son’s own, opened to people who have no natural claim to it whatsoever. We pray as children, adopted by grace. This is the privilege of the gospel: the holy God is our Father.

What if my earthly father was absent or cruel? Then the word may at first bring pain rather than comfort, and you are not wrong to feel that. But Jesus is not asking you to picture God as your father was. He is showing you what fatherhood was always meant to be, and what your father failed to be. God is the Father from whom every family is named (Ephesians 3:14–15): faithful, patient, never abusive, never absent. Many believers with wounded histories have found that learning to say Father to God slowly heals what an earthly father broke. Begin by reading how Jesus speaks of him, and let that, not your memory, fill the word.

Hallowed be your name. “Hallowed” (hagiasthētō) means sanctified, treated as holy, honoured. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known: God’s name is God himself as he has revealed himself. And since God’s name cannot be made more holy than it is, the petition asks that he be treated as holy: known, honoured and reverenced as what he actually is, first by the one praying and then by everybody else (Ezekiel 36:23). That is a startling thing to put first. The prayer opens by asking that God’s reputation be honoured in a world that has trampled it, and it is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to. Not first my needs, but his glory.

Your kingdom come. The central petition of the prayer, and the shortest. God’s reign, which has come in Jesus (11:20), is still to come in fullness (22:18). Pray for it to spread now, as people turn to Christ, and to come finally, when Christ returns. It was the prayer of the early church: Maranatha, our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22; Revelation 22:20). And it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God’s rule to come is to ask for one’s own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he had been hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

In a sentence. Jesus taught his disciples to pray to God as Father, first asking that his name be honoured as holy and his kingdom come.

On a Tuesday. Begin your prayers with God, not yourself: his name, his kingdom. Before you list your needs today, spend a minute simply telling him who he is. Then pray your kingdom come over the specific places where you would rather keep your own rule: your money, your evenings, your temper, your plans for your children. And call him Father, out loud if you can.

For worship. The God whose name the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy has let us call him Father. It cost the Son everything to open that word to us: he who always had the right to say Abba cried my God, my God from the cross, so that rebels might be brought into his place at the Father’s table. Hallowed be the name of the Father who adopted us, and come quickly the kingdom of the Son who made us heirs.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s version of the Lord’s Prayer is shorter than Matthew’s; the ESV notes that some manuscripts add phrases from Matthew’s form. “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.

Body, past, future. Now the prayer turns to us, and it asks for three things: bread, forgiveness and protection. Body, past and future. There is nothing else a human being needs.

Give us each day our daily bread. Our physical needs, brought to God. The word behind daily is epiousios, one of the strangest words in the New Testament. It occurs here and in Matthew’s version and almost nowhere else in surviving Greek, so rare that Origen, a native speaker writing nearly two centuries later, thought the evangelists must have coined it. It may mean for today, or necessary for existence, or for the coming day. The point is clear: daily dependence on God for what we need, as Israel gathered manna day by day (Exodus 16:4). It is a small request, deliberately. Not a year’s security, not a pension, not the removal of uncertainty: enough for today, asked for today, and again tomorrow. Not riches, but enough (Proverbs 30:8).

A daily appointment. Anyone who has ever wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so that the matter could be closed and no longer prayed about, has been asking for something this prayer will not give. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight if they hoarded it (Exodus 16:19–20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment. “Each day” is only in Luke: pray every day. And notice us and our: we pray for others’ bread as well as our own.

Should Christians save and plan, if we pray for daily bread? Yes. Joseph stored grain for seven years of famine; the ant prepares her bread in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8); Paul tells believers to provide for their households (1 Timothy 5:8). This petition does not forbid savings, insurance or a pension. It forbids trusting them. The man with a full barn still prays for daily bread, because the barn, the health to use it, and the next breath are all from God (12:16–21). Plan wisely, give generously, and pray this prayer as honestly with money in the bank as without it.

And forgive us our sins. Matthew has debts; Luke has sins, making the meaning clear for Gentile readers. We need forgiveness as much as bread, every day. A sin is something owed and not paid.

For we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Here Luke keeps the image of debt. The “for” in the middle has troubled people, and it must not become a bargain. It does not mean God’s forgiveness is purchased by ours; the whole of Scripture forbids that reading, and this same prayer has just called him Father, which no one earns. What it does is make our forgiving the evidence that his has landed. It is a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has genuinely grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot go on with a ledger open against his neighbour, and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all (Matthew 6:14–15; 18:21–35). And note the tense: we ourselves forgive, present, continuing. Not we forgave, once, years ago. It is a standing policy. “Everyone”: no exceptions.

Does forgiving mean I must trust again or pretend it did not happen? No. Forgiveness means you release the debt: you give up the right to repay, and you hand the case to God, who judges justly (Romans 12:19). It does not mean the wrong was small, that consequences vanish, or that trust is instantly restored. Trust is rebuilt slowly, by changed behaviour. A victim of abuse may forgive and still rightly report the crime, keep away from the abuser and protect others; forgiveness never requires anyone to remain in danger, and abuse is never to be tolerated. And if the feelings lag behind, keep praying this prayer; forgiveness is often a decision renewed many times before the heart catches up.

And lead us not into temptation. “Temptation” (peirasmos) is the same word as at 4:2, covering both testing and enticement: the trials and situations that could lead us into sin or cause us to fall away. God does not tempt anyone to sin (James 1:13), but he does lead his people into trials, as the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness (4:1). The prayer is: Father, I am weak. Do not let me be put to a test I cannot bear, or let me fall when tested (22:40, 46; 1 Corinthians 10:13). It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it, which is a far more realistic prayer than asking for the strength to survive the edge. Matthew adds: but deliver us from evil.

In a sentence. Jesus taught them to ask for daily bread, for forgiveness as they forgive others, and to be kept from temptation.

On a Tuesday. Bring your daily needs, your sins and your weaknesses to your Father every day. Name the person you are still holding a ledger against, and before you pray for your own forgiveness tonight, release him to God. And think of the particular situation where you know you are weak, the screen late at night, the colleague who provokes you, the shop where you overspend, and pray specifically not to be led there, and then do not walk into it.

For worship. The Father who feeds the ravens feeds his children day by day, and has never yet run out of bread. The Son who taught us to pray forgive us our sins never needed to pray it for himself; he bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that the debt we ask to be forgiven has already been paid. And the Lord who teaches us to pray lead us not into temptation went into the wilderness and the garden in our place, met the tempter at his strongest, and did not fall. Every line of this prayer rests on what he has done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — Ask, and It Will Be Given
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two illustrations follow the prayer, and both argue from the lesser to the greater.

The first is the friend at midnight. To feel it you have to see the house: one room, the family asleep together on a raised platform, a single door barred at night with a beam that cannot be lifted quietly. Getting up wakes everybody. And there is no bread in the house, because bread was baked daily and eaten daily.

The man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. Hospitality in that culture was an obligation with the weight of law, and a traveller arriving at night was the whole village's guest; to fail him was a public disgrace. He asks a friend, at the worst possible hour, for three loaves — enough for one meal — and he asks to borrow them.

The sleeper's excuses are all true. The door is barred, the children are asleep, getting up will wake them. And he gets up anyway, “because of his impudence” — anaideia, shamelessness.

Whose shamelessness has been argued over. The traditional reading takes it as the asker's brazen persistence. A second reading, with a good deal to be said for it, takes it as the sleeper's — he rises to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. Both land in the same place: if even this man gives, how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced.

What the parable licenses is boldness. Most prayer dies of good manners, and this story was told to kill that.

Then “ask, seek, knock” — after that parable, keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking — and a promise unconditional in form: “everyone who asks receives.” Which raises the honest problem, because a great many people have read that verse and then buried someone they prayed for.

Jesus answers it with a picture of a father and a child. A fish and a snake are roughly the same shape; an egg and a coiled scorpion are roughly the same shape. What is described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he asked for and will hurt him — and no father does that.
verseByVerse.theology:
The three imperatives are in the present tense, implying continuous action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. And there is a progression. Asking is words; seeking involves the feet; knocking is standing at a closed door that has not yet opened, and staying there.

On the difficulty in v.10, three things have to be said. Scripture itself never treats the promise as a blank cheque and says so in the same breath: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14), and “you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (Jas. 4:3). Jesus himself prayed a prayer not granted in the form he asked it — “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). And the next three verses are his own commentary, which is where the weight lies.

A request denied is not a father who is deaf. It is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless, and it is not meant to. What it removes is the one conclusion that would be unbearable — that the silence means indifference.

And Luke's ending is his own. Matthew has “how much more will your Father give good things” (Matt. 7:11); Luke has “the Holy Spirit.” Luke's version tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance; it is himself, present, in a person.
verseByVerse.examples:
“You, who are evil” is dropped in without emphasis, as agreed common ground. He is talking to ordinary decent parents and takes it as obvious that they are bad — and that even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

The parable of the friend at midnight is also worth noticing for what the man needs. He is not asking for himself. He wants bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them — which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty.

And “give us each day our daily bread” has a hard edge for anyone who has wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so the matter could be closed and no longer prayed about. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight (Ex. 16:19-20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment.

For anyone praying about something that has not moved in years, this is where the passage lands. Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift explicitly promised to everyone who asks is God himself — and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.

The friend at midnight. Only Luke records this parable. It teaches persistence and boldness in prayer, and the goodness of God.

Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight. To feel this parable you have to see the house. A peasant home in a Galilean village was often a single room. The family slept together on a raised platform at one end, on mats, with the animals below. There was a single door, barred at night with a heavy wooden beam that could not be lifted quietly. Getting up meant waking everyone. And at midnight there was usually no bread in the house, because bread was baked in the morning and eaten through the day; by evening most had none left. Neighbours knew who had baked that day. Travellers often journeyed at night to avoid the heat, so the late arrival was not unusual.

A friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him. Here is the pressure the parable turns on, and a modern reader will miss it without help. Hospitality in that culture was not a courtesy. It was a sacred obligation, and it was not a private matter between host and guest; it was a village matter. A traveller arriving at night was in a sense the whole community’s guest, and to fail him was a public disgrace. So the man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. He is doing what any neighbour would expect. And the request is modest and specific: three small flat loaves, enough for one meal, and lend: he will bake tomorrow and return them.

A friend’s door. Notice too that he asks a friend. This is not a stranger’s door. There is an existing relationship, and he presumes on it at the worst possible hour, which is precisely what friendship is for. That is the picture Jesus has chosen for prayer, immediately after teaching them to say Father. Not a subject petitioning a distant monarch through the correct channels at an appointed hour. A man in the dark, out of bread, with somebody depending on him, walking round to a house where he knows he will be heard.

Asking for someone else. The need in the parable is also worth noticing. He is not asking for himself. He wants the bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them, which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty. The parent with a child in trouble, the friend sitting with someone grieving, the Sunday school teacher on Saturday night: I have nothing to set before him. That is not a reason to give up. It is the reason to knock.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who went to a friend at midnight to borrow bread because an unexpected guest had arrived and he had nothing to offer.

On a Tuesday. When you have nothing to give others, go to God, who has everything. Before the hard conversation, the visit to the hospital, the lesson you feel unready to teach, say it plainly: I have nothing to set before him. Then ask for bread, for them, and expect to be given it.

For worship. We come to a Friend whose house is never dark and whose bread never runs out. Jesus is himself the bread of life (John 6:35), and he has called us friends (John 15:15). The door we knock at was opened from the inside, at the cost of his own body broken, and he has never once told a needy friend to go away.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty; villagers baked daily, and a household might have nothing left at night.

verseByVerse.quote: and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he will answer from within: do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.

Do not bother me; the door is now shut. The excuses are entirely accurate. The door is barred with its heavy bolt; the children are asleep on the mat beside him; getting up, unbarring it and stepping over them will wake the whole household. Every word of it is true, and my children are with me in bed is the clinching one. I cannot means I will not.

This man is not God. It is worth saying plainly, before anything else. The parable is not a picture of a reluctant deity who has to be worn down. It is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and it works by contrast, not by comparison: if even this, how much more that. If a reluctant, sleepy neighbour will get up and give, how much more will God, who is not reluctant and never slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), give to those who ask him. God is not like the sleeper; he is the opposite.

Yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. The word is anaideia: literally shamelessness, the absence of the ordinary restraint that would stop a man knocking at midnight. Its sense here has been argued over for a long time. The traditional reading takes it as the asker’s: his brazen persistence wins. That is a natural reading, and it fits what follows: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking (v. 9). But there is a second reading with a good deal to be said for it. On this view the shamelessness, or the avoidance of shame, belongs to the sleeper: he gets up to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. In a village where everyone would hear about it by morning, his own honour is at stake. Both readings land in the same place, which is why the argument need not be settled here. Either the asker’s boldness prevails, or the host’s regard for his own name does. And in both cases the point is the same: how much more the Father, who is neither asleep, nor inconvenienced, and whose name is pledged to his promise.

Most prayer dies of good manners. What the parable licenses is the boldness. Not politeness, not the carefully worded petition submitted through proper channels: a man banging on a door in the dark because he has nothing and knows where the bread is. It is possible to be so respectful of God that nothing is ever actually asked for, and this parable was told to kill that. We do not have to wear God down. But we should pray with the boldness and persistence of someone who knows he has a real need and a friend who can meet it (18:1–8).

If God already knows what I need and wants to give it, why keep asking? Because prayer is not information for God; it is fellowship with him. He has chosen to work through the prayers of his people, as a father delights to hear his children ask even when he has already bought the gift. Persistent prayer also changes us: it clarifies what we truly want, exposes motives, deepens dependence, and keeps our eyes on him rather than on the problem. And Scripture simply commands it: pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). We keep knocking not to change his mind but because he has told us to, and because he is worth talking to.

In a sentence. Even if the friend would not get up out of friendship, he would get up and give everything needed because of the man’s shameless persistence.

On a Tuesday. Pray boldly and persistently. God is not reluctant, but he loves to see his children keep asking. Pick one request you gave up on because it seemed too long unanswered, a prodigal child, a friend’s salvation, a besetting sin, and start knocking again this week, every day, plainly and without apology.

For worship. Our Father does not barricade his door against midnight callers. He neither slumbers nor sleeps; his ear is open to the cry of his children at any hour; and he has staked his own name on hearing them. We knock on a door the Son has already opened, and we are welcomed by a Father whose honour is to give.
verseByVerse.note: A peasant family slept together in one room; opening the barred door would wake everyone. The ESV notes that “impudence” can also be rendered “persistence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. Three verbs, rising in intensity. Ask: make the request; that is words. Seek: search with effort; that involves the feet, what a man does when the thing is not lying where he can point at it. Knock: stand at a closed door that has not yet opened, and stay there, as the man in the parable did. The tense of each means keep on: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. That rules out the reading where a single well-formed request is submitted and the matter is closed. And three promises answer the three verbs: given, found, opened. God answers prayer.

For everyone who asks receives. Not a few privileged people, but everyone. Prayer is not reserved for the spiritual elite.

The honest problem. This must not be stepped over, because a great many people have read this verse and then buried someone they prayed for. The promise as it stands is unconditional in form. Everyone who asks receives. And a Christian who has asked for years for a marriage to be saved, a child to come home, a body to be healed, and watched none of it happen, is entitled to put the verse and the experience side by side and ask what is going on. Three things have to be said, and the third is the one that carries the weight. The first is that Scripture itself never treats this as a blank cheque, and says so close beside the promise. John writes: if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14). James is blunter: you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions (James 4:3). The New Testament that records this promise is the same New Testament that qualifies it, and it is not embarrassed to do both. The second is that Jesus himself prayed a prayer that was not granted in the form he asked: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). If everyone who asks receives meant what the anxious reading takes it to mean, that sentence could not exist. The third is that the next three verses are Jesus’ own commentary on this one, and he chose to answer the question with a picture of a father and a child.

What it does not mean. Not that God will give us anything we want, as if prayer were a blank cheque. God gives what is good (v. 13), according to his will. Sometimes his answer is not what we asked for, but something better. A good father does not give his child everything he asks for. But no prayer of his child goes unheard or unanswered.

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to keep asking, seeking and knocking, promising that everyone who does so will receive, find and have the door opened.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to keep asking God for? Write it down, and keep knocking. And if a prayer you prayed for years has been answered with a no, bring that grief to him honestly as well. Asking again is not unbelief; it is exactly what he told you to do.

For worship. The God who says ask, seek, knock is not hiding behind his door. He is the one who came seeking us before we ever sought him (19:10), knocking at our door before we knocked at his (Revelation 3:20). Every promise in this verse stands on the faithfulness of a Father who did not spare his own Son, and will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.quote: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!

What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? A second argument from the lesser to the greater: from earthly fathers to the heavenly Father. Two pairs, and both are chosen with care. A fish and a water snake look roughly alike; an egg and a curled-up pale scorpion, about the size of a fist, look roughly alike too. What is being described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he wanted and will hurt him. And every parent listening knows the answer instantly. Nobody does that. It is not even a temptation.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew 7:9. It was probably added to match Matthew.

If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children. A striking aside, dropped in without emphasis, as an agreed fact: you, who are evil. Not you, who are imperfect, or you, who mean well. He is talking to ordinary decent parents, and he takes it as common ground that they are sinful, for human nature is sinful even at its best (Romans 3:10–12). And even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

How much more will the heavenly Father. Who is perfectly good. Here is the answer to the difficulty in v. 10, and it is not a qualification of the promise but a description of who is keeping it. What a good father will not do is give a child something harmful that resembles what was asked for. So a request denied is not a father who is deaf; it is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless. It is not intended to. What it does is remove the one conclusion that would be unbearable: that the silence means indifference.

Give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! Matthew’s version ends differently: how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him (Matthew 7:11). Luke has the Holy Spirit, the greatest of all good gifts, the gift that includes all others. Both are the Lord’s words, and Luke’s tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance. It is himself, present, in a Person. Luke and Acts are full of the Spirit. The Father gives his Spirit to his children: to dwell in them, to make them holy, to help them pray (Romans 8:26), and to empower them for witness (Acts 1:8).

If every believer already has the Spirit, why ask? This is not a promise of a second blessing for some Christians. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). The disciples asking here were living before Pentecost, and the Father was eager to give. We ask now for his ongoing work: to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16), for his fruit, and for his help in our weakness. You will never ask for that and be handed a scorpion.

The gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape. This is worth holding by anyone praying about something that has not moved for years. Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift explicitly promised to everyone who asks is God himself, and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

In a sentence. If sinful fathers give their children good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

On a Tuesday. Ask your Father today for more of his Spirit: for love toward the person you find hardest, for self-control where you keep failing, for courage to speak of Christ. Ask specifically, and expect him to answer. And when he says no to something else you wanted, remind yourself out loud that he is not the father who hands out scorpions.

For worship. Your Father is better than the best human father. He gave the Son, who is the best of heaven, for children who were evil; he gives the Spirit, who is God himself, to all who ask. A Father like that has never once handed a child a serpent. Every good and perfect gift comes down from him (James 1:17), and the greatest gift he gives is himself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew.

parallels.desc: the gift of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–28 — Jesus and Beelzebul; True Blessedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus casts out a demon that has made a man mute, and the crowd marvels. Two responses come from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

The first is the Beelzebul charge — that he works by the prince of demons. Notice what it concedes: nobody disputes that the man is speaking, and nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source reassigned, which is in its way the strongest testimony in the chapter to the fact that it happened.

The second is a demand for “a sign from heaven” — a real one, not this business with a local demoniac. Made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, that is not scepticism; it is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable.

Jesus dismantles the charge twice over. A divided kingdom cannot stand, so Satan casting out Satan is destroying his own operation. And “by whom do your sons cast them out?” exposes a standard applied to him and not to their own exorcists — which means the objection is not the real reason.

Then his own account: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” The phrase occurs three times in the Old Testament — Pharaoh's magicians conceding they are out of their depth (Ex. 8:19), and the tablets written by God's own finger (Ex. 31:18; Deut. 9:10). Deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, in three words. And the verb is “has come upon you” — not near, as the seventy-two announced (10:9), but arrived.

The parable of the strong man is the interpretation of everything he has done. The strong man is fully armed, on his own ground, and while that holds his goods are safe. Then one stronger attacks, overcomes, strips the armour he trusted in, and divides the spoil. And the goods, in this context, are people.

The section closes with two warnings. Neutrality is abolished — “whoever does not gather with me scatters.” And the swept house: a life cleaned up and left empty is not a neutral state on the way to better. It is a vacancy, advertised.
verseByVerse.theology:
The warning about the returning spirit is the parabolic form of the New Testament's consistent warning against reformation without regeneration. Everything in the description is good news — swept, put in order, the mess dealt with, the habits sorted. One word is missing, and it is the whole point: nobody is living there.

Jesus's assessment of that condition is not “an improvement, as far as it goes.” It is “worse than the first,” because an empty swept house has been made attractive. The remedy is not more sweeping but occupation — and Luke has just named who is available, and how he is described: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either; he was found sitting at the feet of Jesus (8:35).

“Whoever is not with me is against me” must be read alongside 9:50, “the one who is not against you is for you,” and the two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There the subject is you — the disciples' judgement of a stranger. Here it is me — a person's own standing before Christ. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

And note what Jesus assumes in passing while making his argument: that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom — organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against. He says it as something too obvious to argue.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's beatitude on Jesus's mother is well meant and entirely ordinary in that culture: praise the son by praising the woman who produced him. Elizabeth said something very like it in this Gospel's first chapter (1:42).

The word “rather” is doing careful work in the reply. It is not a contradiction but a redirection, and it refuses the assumption underneath the compliment — that blessedness is a matter of proximity. If that were true the whole thing would be closed to everybody else, since there is exactly one womb that bore him.

What he offers instead is open to the entire crowd: “hear the word of God and keep it” — two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth. And Mary is the outstanding instance of exactly that: “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38). The correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

And the swept-house warning is worth turning into a question by anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing. Not “what have you got rid of?” but “who lives there now?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. But some of them said, 'He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,' while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marvelled. But some of them said: he casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.

Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. Luke’s phrasing is compressed: the demon is named by its effect. The man could not speak, and when the demon went out he did. Matthew adds that he was blind as well (Matthew 12:22).

And the people marveled. The crowd’s reaction is the same as everywhere else: wonder, which is not the same as faith and never has been. Then come two responses from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Notice what this concedes. Nobody disputes that the man is speaking. Nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source is reassigned, which is in its way the strongest testimony in the chapter that it happened. His enemies were reduced to explaining it, not denying it. Better to call God’s work demonic than to admit Jesus came from God.

The name. Beelzebul is a name for Satan, and it has a history. Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron whom a king of Israel once sent to consult instead of the LORD, and Elijah met the messengers on the road with a message about it (2 Kings 1:2–3). The name probably means lord of flies, and Jews may have mocked it into lord of dung; Beelzebul may also mean lord of the dwelling. By the first century it had become a title for the chief of the demons. So the charge is as serious as a charge can be. Not he is mistaken, not he is unqualified, but the power in him is the enemy’s. And they are saying it about a man who has just given a mute person his voice back.

While others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. The second response is subtler, and it is worse. They want a sign, a real one, from the sky, something spectacular and undeniable, on their terms, not this business with a local demoniac. It is a way of not counting what has just happened in front of them. The demand for further evidence, made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, is not scepticism. It is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable, and it is available to anyone at any time, because there is always one more thing that could be asked for. Luke says they were doing it to test him, which is what Jesus refused, in the wilderness, to do to his Father (4:12). He will answer the demand in vv. 29–32.

Is it wrong to want evidence for faith? No. Christianity is not a leap in the dark; God has given abundant evidence, and Luke wrote his Gospel so that Theophilus might have certainty (1:4). The resurrection was public, with many witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Honest questions are welcome, and Christians should answer them patiently. What Jesus refuses is the demand that God perform on our terms after he has already spoken. If you are genuinely seeking, read the evidence that exists, the Gospels themselves, and ask God to show you the truth. If you find you would not believe whatever you were shown, the problem is not the evidence.

In a sentence. When Jesus cast out a demon that made a man mute, some accused him of doing it by the power of Satan, and others demanded a sign from heaven.

On a Tuesday. People who do not want to believe will always find an explanation. Notice where you do it yourself: the conviction you explain away, the answered prayer you put down to coincidence, the clear command you are still waiting for more light on. Do not demand more evidence than God has given. Act on what you already know.

For worship. The Lord who opened a mute man’s mouth is the same Lord who will one day open every mouth to confess that he is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11). His enemies could not deny his works, and they still cannot. He bore their slander patiently, and went on doing good, and the tongue he set free that day joined the praise that will never end.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, 'Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them: every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.

But he, knowing their thoughts. Again he reads hearts. Some made the Beelzebul charge, others demanded a sign; whether either was said to his face, Jesus answers what is in the room.

Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. The first answer: the charge is illogical. He begins with a proposition nobody would dispute, drawn from politics and from family life, two things everybody in that crowd had watched fail. Civil war destroys a kingdom.

And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? The logic is simple and airtight. If the prince of demons is expelling demons, he is dismantling his own operation. No commander destroys his own positions. Notice what is assumed along the way, because it is easy to miss under the argument. Jesus takes it as given that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom: organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against (4:5–6). That is a good deal more than most modern readers assume, and he says it in passing as something too obvious to argue.

And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? The second answer: inconsistency. “Your sons” means your followers, your own people. Jewish exorcists were active at the time; Luke records an instance in his second volume (Acts 19:13–14), and the practice was not controversial among the Pharisees. So the critics have a standard they apply to Jesus and do not apply to their own. If you accept their exorcisms as from God, why not mine?

Therefore they will be your judges. Your own people’s practice condemns your double standard. And the shape of the thing is worth naming because it recurs. The objection is not being applied consistently, which means it is not really the reason. Something else is doing the work, and the argument has been assembled afterward to justify a conclusion already reached. There is a hard word in this for anyone who has ever constructed a reason for not accepting something they did not want to accept. The reasoning is usually sound. It simply is not what is actually going on.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that Satan would not fight against himself, and that their own exorcists exposed their double standard.

On a Tuesday. Watch for double standards in how you judge others’ ministries: the church across town whose fruit you dismiss while excusing the same weaknesses in your own, the preacher you criticise for what you praise in your favourite. And when you find yourself with an airtight argument against something God is plainly doing, ask what you are afraid of losing.

For worship. The Lord who knows our thoughts is not deceived by our reasons. He sees through every argument we build against him, and still he answers us patiently, with truth. His kingdom is not divided; Father, Son and Spirit are one in purpose, and the work of salvation that the Father planned, the Son accomplished and the Spirit applies cannot be overthrown.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” means the critics’ own followers.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons. Having dismantled the alternative, he states his own account of what is happening, and he does it with a phrase that would have gone off like a bell in that crowd. Matthew reads by the Spirit of God (Matthew 12:28), which is the same thing said plainly. Luke keeps the Exodus wording, and the phrase occurs three times in the Old Testament, each worth having. The first is in Egypt. Pharaoh’s magicians have matched Moses trick for trick: the staffs, the blood, the frogs. Then comes the plague of gnats, and they cannot reproduce it, and they go to Pharaoh and say: this is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19). It is the moment the opposition concedes it is out of its depth, spoken by professional practitioners of the dark arts about a power they recognise and cannot copy. The other two are the tablets of stone, written with the finger of God (Exodus 31:18; Deuteronomy 9:10). So the phrase carries deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant in a few words, and Jesus takes it, in a Galilean street, in an argument with men who have just accused him of witchcraft, and applies it to what he has done for one mute man. It means the direct power of God. His exorcisms are as clearly God’s work as the plagues of Egypt, and like them, they show God liberating his people from a tyrant.

Then the kingdom of God has come upon you. This is one of the most important sentences in Luke, and the verb (ephthasen) is the point: has arrived, has overtaken you. Not is near, which is what the seventy-two were sent to announce (10:9). Has come upon you: arrived, landed, already here. The kingdom of God is not, in the first instance, a place or a programme or a future era. It is God reigning; and where the King acts, the reign is present. That is why the evidence he offers for its arrival is not a throne or an army but a man who can suddenly talk. And note the pronoun: upon you, spoken to the people accusing him. The kingdom had arrived in their street, on their afternoon, in front of them. They were standing in it.

Already and not yet. God’s reign has broken in. Satan’s kingdom is being invaded and overthrown. Yet the kingdom has not come in its fullness: we still pray your kingdom come (v. 2), and we still live among sickness, sin and death. This is the already and not yet of the kingdom. It came in the King’s first coming; it grows as the gospel spreads and hearts bow to him; and it will be complete when he returns and every enemy is put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:24–26).

Where is the kingdom of God today, if not in exorcisms and healings? Wherever Christ reigns. It is present whenever a sinner repents and believes, because that is a captive set free; whenever the word is faithfully preached and the church lives under it; whenever a believer forgives, gives, or resists sin in Christ’s strength. It is not a political programme or a territory, though it will one day fill the earth. Look for it where people bow to Jesus, and pray for it there first.

In a sentence. If Jesus casts out demons by God’s own power, then the kingdom of God has arrived.

On a Tuesday. The kingdom of God has come in Jesus; live today as a subject of the King. When you face a temptation that has mastered you for years, remember that the finger of God is stronger than that habit. And when you pray for someone bound by addiction or despair, pray as one who believes the King has already invaded the enemy’s territory.

For worship. The finger that wrote the law on stone and humbled Pharaoh touched a mute man in Galilee, and he spoke. That same power raised Christ from the dead and is at work in all who believe (Ephesians 1:19–20). The kingdom has come in a Person, and it cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28). Rejoice that God reigns, and that Satan’s power is broken.
verseByVerse.note: “The finger of God” is what Pharaoh’s magicians said of the plague of gnats, which they could not copy.

verseByVerse.quote: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armour in which he trusted and divides his spoil.

When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe. A short parable, and it is the interpretation of everything he has just done. Take the picture as it stands. The strong man is Satan. He is not weak, and he is not asleep. He is fully armed. He is in his own house, on his own ground, guarding property he regards as his. And Jesus grants the premise: while that arrangement holds, his goods are safe. His captives, those he holds in bondage, cannot escape by their own strength. That is a sober assessment of the world before he came. The human race was not neutral territory awaiting instruction. It was occupied, and the occupier was armed, and the goods were secure.

But when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him. The stronger one is Jesus. John had said: he who is mightier than I is coming (3:16). Jesus has come to attack Satan’s kingdom, overpower him, and set his captives free (4:18). Four verbs follow, each worse than the last for the strong man. Attacks: the initiative is not his. Overcomes: it is not a contest; it is a result. This victory began in the wilderness (4:1–13), continued in the exorcisms, and was won decisively at the cross, where he disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15) and destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14–15).

He takes away his armor in which he trusted. The man is not merely beaten but disarmed, and Luke adds that this was armour in which he trusted, so what is removed is also his confidence.

And divides his spoil. The property is not merely recovered; it is distributed, handed out, given away. Isaiah said of the Servant: he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death (Isaiah 53:12). Then note what the goods in this parable are. Not gold. The context is exorcism, and the thing carried out of the strong man’s house is a human being who could not speak. So this is what a healing means, seen from above. Every demon evicted, every sinner forgiven is plunder: property taken off an armed occupier by someone who walked in and was not stopped. The spoil is the people freed from Satan, who become Christ’s own.

No struggle recorded. There is no struggle recorded anywhere in this Gospel. He speaks and it is over. The demons in Luke do not fight him; they beg (8:28, 31). The strong man in this parable never lands a blow, until the cross, where the blow he landed was his own undoing. Here, then, is what was actually happening in a village street while men argued about the source of his power. The house of the great occupier was standing open, the armour he had trusted in was on the floor, and the goods he had held for the whole of human history were being carried out and handed back.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. A believer belongs to Christ and is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19); he has been delivered from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). The strong man cannot move back into a house the stronger one now owns. Christians can certainly be tempted, deceived and oppressed by the devil, and must resist him (Ephesians 6:10–18), but not owned. If you are a believer troubled by dark thoughts or fears, you need not look for an exorcist. Confess any sin, renounce any occult involvement, and stand on what Christ has done.

In a sentence. Jesus compared Satan to a strong man guarding his palace, and himself to a stronger one who overpowers him, strips him of his armour and plunders his goods.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the people you love who are still in the strong man’s house, by name, as people the stronger one can carry out. And when your own past accuses you, remember whose property you are now. If you are a Christian, you are part of the spoil.

For worship. We were the goods in the strong man’s palace, safe in his keeping and hopeless in our chains. Then one stronger came. He walked into the house of death, broke its doors, stripped the enemy of every weapon, and carried us out on his shoulders. He poured out his soul to death, and now divides the spoil. Thank him for your freedom: you are his treasure, bought with his blood.

parallels.desc: he shall divide the spoil with the strong

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.

Whoever is not with me is against me. The middle ground is abolished in one sentence, and it is worth seeing why it is placed here. Two groups have just been described. One accused him of working by Beelzebul; the other wanted a further sign. Neither has committed to anything. The second group in particular would have thought of itself as open-minded: not hostile, merely waiting for more evidence. Jesus tells them there is no such position. In the war between Christ and Satan there is no neutral ground. You are on one side or the other. Those who stand back and criticise are, in fact, on Satan’s side.

And whoever does not gather with me scatters. The reason is in the second half, and the image is agricultural, a harvester gathering a crop or a shepherd gathering a flock. Gather and scatter are harvest words, and the harvest has already been named a chapter earlier: the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few (10:2). There is a gathering going on. Anyone not part of it is, by the simple fact of standing in the field doing nothing, part of the loss. That is the sharp edge of the saying, and it has nothing to do with hostility. Scattering does not require malice; it requires only absence. Grain left ungathered is lost by exactly the same amount whether it was trampled deliberately or simply not picked up.

But did Jesus not say the opposite in 9:50? A reader with a good memory will object. Two chapters ago John reported that they had stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name, and was told: do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you (9:50). The two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There, the subject was you: the disciples’ judgement of a stranger. Here the subject is me: a person’s own standing before Christ. And the two run in opposite directions on purpose. About somebody else, doing good in Christ’s name outside your circle: assume the best, and do not stop him. About yourself, in relation to Christ: assume nothing, because neutrality is not on offer. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

In a sentence. There is no neutrality with Jesus: anyone not with him is against him, and anyone not gathering with him scatters.

On a Tuesday. Are you with Jesus, gathering with him? Ask what you are actually doing for the harvest: praying for the lost by name, supporting gospel work, speaking of Christ when the door opens, welcoming newcomers at church. Sympathetic spectating is not a third option. And be as generous to other believers as you are strict with yourself.

For worship. Christ is the great Gatherer. He came to gather the lost sheep of Israel and the scattered children of God from every nation into one (John 11:52), and he will not lose one of them. To gather with him is the highest honour a sinner can be given: to be taken into the work of the Lord of the harvest, whose kingdom is advancing and whose gathering will fill heaven.

parallels.desc: the one who is not against you is for you

verseByVerse.quote: 'When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says: I will return to my house from which I came. And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.

When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person. A strange little story, a warning that follows the point about neutrality, and one of the most searching things in the chapter. Deliverance from evil is not enough by itself.

It passes through waterless places seeking rest. Desert places were thought to be the haunt of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). Demons are restless; they want a home in a person.

I will return to my house from which I came. Note the pronoun the spirit uses: my house. It has been evicted and it has not conceded ownership. And it comes back to inspect.

And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Everything in that sentence is good news, and that is what makes the story so unsettling. Swept: cleaned. Put in order: tidied, arranged, set right. This is not a person who relapsed. This is a person whose life visibly improved: the mess dealt with, the habits sorted out, the household running properly. And there is one word missing, which Matthew supplies: empty (Matthew 12:44). Reformed, but not occupied by anyone new. Nobody is living there. The person has been cleaned up, morally improved, but Christ has not come to live there.

Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself. Seven: complete possession. The house was not merely available. It had been made attractive.

And the last state of that person is worse than the first. This is the warning, and it is aimed squarely at something religion produces in quantity: reformation without regeneration. A man gives up the drink, or the affair, or the temper. He tidies the house. He is, by any external measure, better than he was, and everyone around him says so, which makes it harder rather than easier to see what has not happened. What has not happened is that anyone has moved in. And Jesus’ assessment of that condition is not an improvement, as far as it goes. It is worse than the first. An empty swept house is not a neutral state on the way to something better. It is a vacancy, advertised. Moral reformation without Christ leaves a vacuum that evil fills. This applied to the people of Jesus’ generation, stirred by John and Jesus but never committed to him (Matthew 12:45), and it applies to anyone who makes a fresh start without Christ.

The remedy is occupation. The remedy is not more sweeping. It is occupation, and Luke has just told us in the same paragraph who is able to do it: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either. He was found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind (8:35). It is not enough to get rid of evil; the heart must be filled with Christ and his Spirit.

Can a Christian be repossessed? No. This parable describes a life cleaned up but left empty, someone reformed but not converted. A believer is not an empty house; the Holy Spirit lives in him, and what Christ has taken he keeps (John 10:28). But the warning is still for church members, because it is possible to sit in church for years, clean and orderly, without ever having received Christ. The question to ask is not whether you have stopped doing bad things, but whether Christ himself lives in you by faith.
