In a sentence. Jesus warned that a person cleaned of an evil spirit but left empty will be reoccupied by worse spirits, ending worse than before.

On a Tuesday. Self-improvement is not salvation. Anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing should read this paragraph slowly. The question it puts is not what have you got rid of? but who lives there now? When you put off an old habit, ask what you are putting on in its place: prayer where there was the screen, generosity where there was grasping, fellowship where there was isolation. Do not just sweep your house clean; invite Christ to live in it.

For worship. Christ does not merely clean the house; he moves in. The Father and the Son make their home with those who love him (John 14:23), and the Spirit dwells in them as in a temple. A heart he occupies is never empty again, and no spirit, however many it brings, can drive out the stronger one who lives there.
verseByVerse.note: Waterless places were thought to be the haunt of demons.

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, 'Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!' But he said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him: blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed! But he said: blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!

A woman in the crowd raised her voice. Only Luke records this. It is one of the most human interruptions in the Gospels: in the middle of an argument about demons and kingdoms, a woman shouts a blessing on his mother. A spontaneous cry of admiration.

Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed! A common way of praising a man in that culture: praise the son by praising the mother who produced him. How blessed she must be to have such a son. It is entirely well meant, and it is also true. Elizabeth said something very like it, filled with the Holy Spirit (1:42), and Mary herself sang that all generations would call her blessed (1:48).

Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it! “Rather” (menoun) is doing careful work: yes, but more than that. It is not a contradiction; it is a redirection: here is where the blessing actually lies. Jesus does not deny that his mother is blessed. What he refuses is the assumption underneath the compliment: that blessedness is a matter of physical proximity, and that the closest person to Jesus of Nazareth is necessarily the most blessed. If that were true, the whole thing would be closed to everybody else. There is exactly one womb that bore him. Nobody else can compete for that, and nobody else can have it. What he offers instead is open to the entire crowd, including the woman who shouted. Hear the word of God and keep it: two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth. It is the same point as 8:21, where he redefined his family as those who hear the word of God and do it.

Mary heard and kept. It is worth adding, because it is often missed in the anxiety to keep Mary in her place, that she is the outstanding example of the very thing he commends. When the angel finished speaking she said, let it be to me according to your word (1:38). Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed (1:45), and twice Luke tells us she treasured these things in her heart (2:19, 51). She heard the word of God and kept it. So the correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

Where Christians differ: devotion to Mary. Roman Catholic and Orthodox devotion gives Mary a unique place of honour and intercession: praying to her, and calling her Queen of Heaven and Mediatrix. Verdict: Jesus himself redirects attention from his mother’s physical role to the blessing of obedience, which she shares with all believers. Mary is rightly called blessed, and is a great example of faith. But she is not to be prayed to or venerated. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

In a sentence. When a woman called Jesus’ mother blessed, he said that those who hear God’s word and keep it are more blessed still.

On a Tuesday. The blessing of hearing and keeping God’s word is open to you today. Read it, and do it. Choose one verse this morning and carry it into the day, and tonight ask yourself what difference it made. That small, repeated habit is the blessedness Jesus means.

For worship. How generous is this Lord, who will not let the greatest blessing be the privilege of one woman, but throws it open to everyone who hears and keeps his word. Mary bore the Word made flesh; every believer receives the same Word by faith and carries him in the heart. The blessedness of Nazareth is offered to the whole world.

parallels.desc: all generations will call me blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — The Sign of Jonah; The Light in You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowds are increasing — and Luke notes it, because that is when Jesus says “this generation is an evil generation.” Popularity has never once altered what he told people.

They want a sign from heaven, and he refuses; but the refusal is not of evidence. It is of evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count. A sign given to someone resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain — which is exactly what happened fifteen verses earlier when an exorcism was credited to Beelzebul.

The sign of Jonah works two ways, and they are not rivals. Jonah himself was a sign to Nineveh: a foreigner walking into the greatest city of the ancient world with a single sentence of judgement and no miracle whatever, and the city repented (Jon. 3:4-9). And behind that stands what happened before he arrived, which Matthew makes explicit — three days in the belly of the fish, and three days in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12:40). Luke leaves it unstated and lets the reader who knows Jonah do the arithmetic.

Two witnesses are then called, and both are chosen to sting. The Queen of Sheba travelled over a thousand miles by camel, on a rumour, under no obligation to anybody's God. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria — the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, a byword for a people beyond hope — and it repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there and was furious when it worked.

Neither had a fraction of the light this generation has. And twice the refrain: “something greater than Solomon is here… something greater than Jonah is here.” Not someone greater but something — broader and stranger. No prophet in Israel's history ever spoke about himself like that.

The lamp sayings close the section. The lamp is not hidden; it has been on a stand in Galilee for three years. So the problem cannot be the lighting — it is the window. “Your eye is the lamp of your body,” and its two conditions are not merely medical: Scripture speaks of “a bountiful eye” for a generous man (Prov. 22:9) and, as the ESV margin renders it, “a man whose eye is evil” for a stingy one (Prov. 28:22; cf. Deut. 15:9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The queen and the Ninevites will rise at the judgement and condemn this generation, because both responded to far lesser messengers. It is the graduated-accountability principle of the woes on Chorazin and Bethsaida, sharpened: it will not be the ignorant who are condemned by Nineveh, but the well-informed.

“Something greater than Solomon” is worth weighing. Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived, and Wisdom itself is standing in the street. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. Jesus does not argue for it; he says “behold,” and leaves it there.

The eye sayings are not about eyesight or intellect. Ancient thinking often understood the eye as a window through which light entered and filled the person — so the picture is a house with a window: clear, and the house is bright; blocked, and the house is dark however strong the sun outside.

Which explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person's capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true — and nobody ever thinks that is happening to them.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Be careful lest the light in you be darkness” is the warning that ought to keep a religious person awake. It does not say “be careful in case you are in the dark” — a man in the dark generally knows it and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you have been navigating by is itself darkness.

That is a different order of danger. It is not the traveller who knows he is lost; it is the traveller with a compass that is wrong, walking confidently in the wrong direction, and getting further away the harder he tries. Be careful — look carefully, examine. It is an instruction to inspect the instrument.

The context names who it is for. The next paragraph is a dinner party with a Pharisee that ends in six woes. The people at greatest risk are not the irreligious but those with the most exposure — long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two feel identical.

And then, after the warning, the promise, which is unexpectedly warm. “Having no part dark” is the condition — not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut. And the result is not an impressive person but a useful one: “as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” A life fully lit becomes a lamp, and a lamp is not for the room it stands in.

verseByVerse.quote: When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, 'This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowds were increasing, he began to say: this generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.

This generation is an evil generation. Luke marks the moment carefully: the crowds were increasing, and that is when he said it. Popularity does not impress Jesus; it has never once altered what he told people. This generation is evil because it does not repent, despite seeing God’s works.

It seeks for a sign. They had asked for a sign from heaven (v. 16). He refuses, and the refusal is instructive, because he has spent the chapter performing signs. A mute man is standing there talking. What is being refused is not evidence but evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count: a sign that would remove the need for faith. And there is a reason that request can never be satisfied. A sign given to someone who has resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain, which is precisely what happened fifteen verses ago when the exorcism was credited to Beelzebul.

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. How was Jonah a sign to Nineveh? Two answers, and they are not rivals. The obvious one is his preaching. Jonah walked into the greatest city of the ancient world with a single sentence of judgement and no miracle whatever, and the city repented, king, nobles and commoners, in sackcloth (Jonah 3:4–9). The prophet himself was the sign: a foreigner arriving with a word from a God they did not worship. The Ninevites did not see a miracle; they heard a message, and repented. The other is what happened before he arrived. Jonah came to Nineveh as a man who had, in effect, come back from the dead after three days in the fish (Jonah 1:17), and Matthew’s parallel makes the link explicit: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). A man swallowed by death and given back.

So will the Son of Man be to this generation. Luke leaves the resurrection unstated, which is characteristic; he lets the reader who knows Jonah do the arithmetic. But the shape is unmistakable. Jesus himself, his preaching, and above all his resurrection, is the sign. The sign this generation is being promised is not something they will be shown next week. It is a grave outside Jerusalem, and it is the only sign that will ever be given, and it is enough.

How was Jesus three days and three nights in the earth if he died on Friday and rose on Sunday? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day and night. Esther called for a three-day fast, night and day, and went in to the king on the third day (Esther 4:16; 5:1); an Egyptian had not eaten for three days and three nights and it was the third day (1 Samuel 30:12–13). Friday, Saturday and Sunday make three days. The phrase is an idiom, not a stopwatch, and the first readers would have heard no contradiction.

In a sentence. Jesus called his generation evil for demanding a sign, and said the only sign given would be the sign of Jonah: the Son of Man himself, and his resurrection.

On a Tuesday. You have the greatest sign of all: the risen Christ. If you are still waiting for God to prove himself in some more convenient way, the proof has been offered, once, in public, and it involved a tomb. And if you are praying for a friend who keeps asking for one more argument, do not despair: give him the Gospels, and pray that he will hear the message, as Nineveh did.

For worship. The sign of Jonah is the deepest mercy in the Bible. Jonah went down into the deep because he ran from God; Christ went down into death because he ran toward us, bearing the judgement Nineveh deserved and we deserve. And on the third day he came back, not reluctant and resentful, but rejoicing, to preach peace to the very city that rejected him. The empty tomb is God’s final answer to every demand for a sign.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South will rise up at the judgement with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgement with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.

Two witnesses. Two witnesses are called, and both are chosen to sting: a pagan queen and a pagan city.

The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them. The queen of Sheba, probably from south-west Arabia, modern Yemen: a journey of well over a thousand miles by camel, undertaken on a rumour, by a foreign monarch under no obligation to anybody’s God. She came to test Solomon with hard questions, and she listened, and she said the half had not been told her (1 Kings 10:1–7). At the final judgement she will be a witness against them. She travelled a vast distance to hear Solomon; they had a greater one in their midst and would not listen.

Something greater than Solomon is here. “Something” is neuter, and the wording is worth noticing. Not someone greater but something greater, which is broader and stranger: the kingdom, the wisdom of God, present in the person of Jesus. It is not merely that a better teacher than Solomon has turned up. Something of a different order is present. Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived, and Wisdom itself is standing in the street. He is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30), in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom and deported ten tribes, whose armies were remembered for cruelty long afterward. If a first-century Jew had a byword for a people beyond hope, it was these. They repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there, who had run in the opposite direction, preached judgement with no promise of mercy, and was furious when it worked (Jonah 3:5–10; 4:1).

Something greater than Jonah is here. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. He does not argue for it. He says behold, and leaves it there, and no prophet in Israel’s history ever spoke about himself like that. If pagans repented at Jonah’s preaching, how much more should Israel repent at his?

The point. Two Gentiles, a queen and a city, will condemn Jesus’ generation. Neither had a fraction of the light this generation has. Sheba had a rumour about a king’s wisdom. Nineveh had one sentence from an unwilling foreigner. The men listening to Jesus have him. The warning underneath is the one from the previous chapter, sharpened: privilege increases responsibility, and judgement is proportional to light (10:13–15). It will not be the ignorant who are condemned by the Ninevites, but the well-informed. A pagan queen who travelled a thousand miles for a rumour of wisdom will stand up at the last day beside people who could not be troubled to cross a room.

Will the queen of Sheba and the Ninevites be in heaven? Jesus does not say, and we should not speculate beyond him. His point is not their final destiny but their response: they answered far smaller light with seriousness, and that response will expose those who answered the greatest light with indifference. The Ninevites’ repentance was real enough to turn away a temporal judgement (Jonah 3:10). Whether any of them came to saving faith in the God of Israel is known to God. What is certain is that no one is saved apart from the grace of God revealed in Christ, and that we, who have heard him, have no excuse.

In a sentence. The queen of Sheba, who travelled far to hear Solomon, and the Ninevites, who repented at Jonah’s preaching, will condemn this generation at the judgement, because one greater than Solomon and Jonah is here.

On a Tuesday. You have far more than Solomon’s wisdom or Jonah’s preaching: you have Christ, the whole Bible, and the Spirit. Ask what you would cross a thousand miles for, and whether you would cross the room for a Bible study or the road for a prayer meeting. Listen, and repent, and do it today.

For worship. Something greater than Solomon is here: the King whose wisdom made the worlds, whose throne is for ever, whose kingdom has no end. Something greater than Jonah is here: the Prophet who did not run from his mission but embraced it, who went down into death willingly and rose again. And this greater one has not stayed in a distant palace for us to travel to. He came all the way to us.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, probably in south-west Arabia. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.

No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand. The saying has been used before in this Gospel (8:16), and its placing here gives it a different edge. He has just said that something greater than Solomon and Jonah is here. That is the lamp, and it has not been hidden. It has been standing on a stand in the middle of Galilee, healing people in daylight, in front of crowds, with witnesses. So the problem in this generation cannot be the lighting. The problem is not lack of light but lack of sight.

Your eye is the lamp of your body. The image shifts, and it takes a moment to follow. The lamp on the stand is outside; now there is a lamp inside, and it is the eye. Ancient thinking about vision often pictured the eye as a window through which light entered and filled the person. So the picture is of a house with a window: if the window is clear, the house is bright; if it is blocked, the house is dark, however strong the sun outside. Spiritually, the eye is the heart’s ability to perceive God’s truth.

When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light. “Healthy” (haplous) means single, sincere, undivided, and in the wider usage of the day, generous: a single-minded focus on God. You receive the light and live in it.

But when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. “Bad” (ponēros) means evil, diseased. In Jewish idiom a bad or evil eye meant a grudging, envious, tight-fisted disposition (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22; Matthew 20:15). So this is not really about eyesight or even about intellect. It is about whether a person is undivided and open-handed, or grasping and calculating, and Jesus says that condition determines what light can get in. A heart that is double-minded, greedy or hostile cannot see the light, however brightly it shines.

A blocked window. That explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person’s capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true. Nobody ever thinks that is happening to them. The crowd’s problem was not that Jesus was unclear, but that their eyes were bad.

How can I tell if my eye is bad? Watch for the things that make Scripture suddenly unclear to you. When a plain passage about money, sex, forgiveness or anger seems strangely complicated, ask whether the difficulty is in the text or in what obeying it would cost. Notice envy, which turns other people’s blessings into grievances, and greed, which makes generosity feel foolish. Then ask God to heal your sight: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). A single eye is not a perfect one; it is one turned wholly toward God and willing to see.

In a sentence. The light has been given openly, and a healthy, sincere eye lets it fill the whole person, but a bad eye leaves the whole person in darkness.

On a Tuesday. Is your eye single toward God? Pick one area where you have been calculating rather than trusting, and make one generous, open-handed choice there this week. Ask him to heal anything in your heart that keeps you from seeing his light.

For worship. God has not hidden his light. He set it on a stand for the whole world to see: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). And the God who said let light shine out of darkness is the God who opens blind eyes to see it. The light and the sight are both his gifts.
verseByVerse.note: A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess or an evil desire.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.

Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. Of all the warnings in Luke’s Gospel, this is the one that ought to keep a religious person awake. It does not say be careful in case you are in the dark. A man in the dark generally knows it, and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you have been navigating by is itself darkness. That is a different order of danger entirely. It is not the traveller who knows he is lost; it is the traveller with a compass that is wrong, walking confidently in the wrong direction, and getting further away the harder he tries. Be careful: look carefully, examine. It is an instruction to inspect the instrument. The Pharisees thought they saw (John 9:39–41). Self-deception is the worst blindness.

Who is it for? The context answers. The next paragraph begins a dinner party with a Pharisee and ends with six woes. The men being warned are the most religiously informed people in the country, men who could recite the law, tithed their garden herbs, and had built their whole lives around getting this right. So the people at greatest risk from this verse are not the irreligious. They are the ones with the most exposure: long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two can feel identical.

If I cannot tell from the inside, how can I ever be sure? Not by staring inward, but by letting something outside you test you. Measure yourself by Scripture, not by your feelings or your church’s customs. Invite honest friends to tell you what they see. Look at fruit: does your knowledge make you humbler, kinder and more prayerful, or prouder and colder? And above all, pray as David did: search me, O God, and know my heart, and see if there be any grievous way in me (Psalm 139:23–24). The man who asks God to show him his darkness is not the man this verse describes.

If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright. And then, after the warning, the promise, and it is unexpectedly warm. Having no part dark is the condition. Not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut; the whole of it, with nothing held back, no dark corner reserved.

As when a lamp with its rays gives you light. The result is not a person who has achieved something impressive. It is a person who has become useful: someone others can see by. That is where the paragraph has been going since v. 33. The lamp is put on a stand so that those who enter may see. A life fully lit becomes a lamp, and a lamp is not for the room it stands in. A life fully open to God’s light shines.

In a sentence. Jesus warned them to make sure that what they thought was light in them was not darkness, for a life fully open to the light will shine.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to search you and show you any part of your life you have kept dark: the room you never let anyone into, the habit you have never confessed, the attitude you have learned to call by a nicer name. Then open that door to one trusted believer this week. Light gets in where doors are opened.

For worship. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). He does not leave us steering by a broken compass. He sent his Son, the light of the world, so that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life (John 8:12). The light that searches us is the same light that saves us, and it shines from the face of a Saviour who loves us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–54 — Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to dine, and he goes. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel and every one ends badly — and Jesus accepts every invitation. Whatever is said in this room is said by a guest who came when he was asked.

He does not perform the ritual handwashing, and the omission may well be deliberate. That washing was not hygiene and it was not in the law of Moses; nothing in the Torah requires an ordinary Israelite to wash before eating. The Pharisees had taken the priestly standard and applied it to everybody, all the time — a serious and, in its way, admirable ambition. They wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

His answer takes their own debating point about the cleansing of vessels and turns it on them. A cup polished outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup; it is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse, because it gets the cup put back on the table. And the first word for what is inside is greed — the grasping that takes. Something is being taken.

“Give as alms those things that are within” is his prescription, and it is remarkable: they asked how to be clean and the answer is not a better ritual but to give the contents away. The remedy for greed is not scouring the cup; it is giving away what was grasped.

Then six woes — three against the Pharisees and three against the lawyers. The word itself needs setting straight: ouai is the prophets' word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict, the sound a man makes watching somebody walk towards a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later in this Gospel (19:41).

They tithe mint and rue and neglect justice and the love of God — and “these you ought to have done” refuses to abolish the small duty. They love the best seat and the public greetings. They are unmarked graves. The lawyers load burdens they will not touch, build the tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and have taken away the key of knowledge.

And it hardens them. The chapter ends with respectable men following a guest out of a house, firing questions to get a sentence they can use.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tithing woe turns on a trade nobody consciously makes. The law required a tithe of grain, wine and oil (Deut. 14:22-23); it said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. These were not lazy men — they were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt. And “these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” is regularly ignored: he does not condemn the herb-tithing.

The mechanism is universal. The measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off, and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off — and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will find he has run out before he reaches the things that do not.

The unmarked-grave woe depends on a detail of the law. Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Num. 19:16), so graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover, conspicuously, so pilgrims could see them and go round. The marking was a public service; it kept people clean. An unmarked grave is the exact opposite — one a man walks straight over and finds out afterwards, if he finds out at all.

And “the key of knowledge” is the heaviest charge. The knowledge in question is not information about God but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce. These men were the keyholders legitimately — and they did not enter themselves, and they blocked the door for people who were already moving towards it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lawyer's interruption — “in saying these things you insult us also” — is wonderfully revealing. He does not say “that is untrue.” He concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone, which is one of the commonest ways a person defends himself against a word he cannot answer: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite.

The burdens woe puts a simple test to anyone who teaches. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself. Set it against “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

The tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet; he has stopped saying the things that got him killed. Meanwhile a living one is at the table, and they are about to arrange his death. Every generation of the church admires the awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. A dead prophet requires a subscription; a live one requires repentance.

And the key-of-knowledge woe puts a question to anyone who teaches anything to anybody. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine; he transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine. Not whether what you say is correct, which is the easier test — whether someone who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder.

verseByVerse.quote: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.

While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him. Two things to register before the confrontation starts. The first is that a Pharisee invited him, and he went. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel (7:36; here; 14:1), and every one of them ends badly, and Jesus accepts every invitation, as he accepted the tax collectors’. Whatever is about to be said in this room, it is being said by a guest who came when he was asked. That is worth holding on to when the woes arrive, because it decides how they should be heard. This is not a man denouncing his enemies from a safe distance. It is a man eating their food. The word for the meal is literally the morning or midday meal.

So he went in and reclined at table. Reclining tells you the kind of meal. Reclining on couches around a low table was the posture of a formal meal with guests, which means there was an audience, and the whole exchange took place in front of the Pharisee’s friends.

The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. The washing was not hygiene. It was a ritual of purity before a meal (Mark 7:3–4): water poured over the hands in a prescribed way to remove any ceremonial defilement picked up in the course of the day, particularly from contact with people or things outside the community of the observant. And it was not in the law of Moses. Nothing in the Torah requires an ordinary Israelite to wash before eating; the rules were for priests handling holy things. It was the tradition of the elders. What the Pharisees had done was to take the priestly standard and apply it to everybody, all the time, a serious and, in its way, admirable ambition. They wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

Deliberate. Jesus does not wash, and Luke says the Pharisee was astonished. It may well have been deliberate, to provoke the conversation that followed. His disciples had done the same in front of a delegation from Jerusalem, and he had defended them (Mark 7:1–5), and he knew exactly what omitting it would say at a formal dinner. He is not being careless or rude. He is declining, in front of witnesses, to endorse a system, and he is about to explain why.

Should a Christian accept invitations from people who disapprove of him? Jesus did, again and again, knowing the hostility at the table. Accept them where you can, and be a gracious guest; meals are one of the best places for real conversation. But do not buy peace by pretending to agree with what you believe is wrong. Jesus was courteous enough to come and honest enough to speak. You can be both: thankful for the food, kind to your host, and clear about Christ when the moment comes.

In a sentence. Jesus accepted a Pharisee’s invitation to dinner, and his host was surprised that he did not perform the ritual washing first.

On a Tuesday. Be careful about judging others by human traditions rather than by God’s word: how people dress for church, which translation they use, how they school their children, whether they raise their hands. Ask of each of your own standards: is this commanded, or only customary? Hold customs lightly and commands firmly.

For worship. The Holy One of Israel sat down unwashed at a Pharisee’s table, and he was the only clean person in the room. He needed no ritual, because he had no defilement. And he came to make the unclean clean, not by water poured on hands, but by his blood poured out for sinners, which cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).
verseByVerse.note: The washing was a ritual of purity before a meal, not hygiene.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said to him, 'Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord said to him: now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.

Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish. He answers the unspoken criticism with an image drawn from the table in front of him. The picture is exact, and it was not merely rhetorical. The Pharisees had detailed rules for washing vessels (Mark 7:4), and rabbinic law discussed whether the inside and outside of a cup could be clean or unclean independently of each other. Jesus takes their own debating point and turns it on them. They make the outside of their lives clean, ritually and morally, before people.

But inside you are full of greed and wickedness. A cup polished on the outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup. It is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse rather than better, because it gets the cup put back on the table. And note the two words for what is inside. “Greed” (harpagē) is plunder, robbery, rapacity. It is a startling charge to bring against the most scrupulous men in the country, and it means the problem is not merely that they are inwardly unimpressive. Something is being taken. Religion that cares about appearances but not the heart is worthless.

You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? “Fools” (aphrones) means senseless: a strong word. The argument is from creation, and it is unanswerable. The same God made the visible and the invisible parts of a man. He cares about both, and he sees the inside: the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). A religion that attends to one and not the other has not understood who it is dealing with, as though God could see the hands and not the heart.

If Jesus warns against calling a brother a fool, how can he say it here? There (Matthew 5:22) he forbids the angry insult that despises a person. Here he gives the Lord’s verdict on teachers who ignore the God who made the inside as well as the outside (v. 40), as the prophets did before him. He is the Judge, and he sees hearts; we do not. So we may name folly in what people teach and do, but we must never use contempt as a weapon against a person, and never imagine that our anger shares his perfect knowledge.

But give as alms those things that are within. This is a genuinely difficult sentence, and translators differ over it. The likeliest sense is: give what is inside, the contents of the cup and dish, the food and the wealth it stands for, to the poor, instead of being greedy. That is a remarkable prescription. They had asked, in effect, how to be clean, and the answer is not a better ritual. It is: give the contents away. And it goes straight at the word he has just used. The inside is full of greed; the remedy for greed is not scouring the cup but giving away what was grasped. Generosity is the exact opposite of grasping, and it reaches the place where the actual defilement is. Love for the poor is the inward cleanness God looks for (Micah 6:8).

And behold, everything is clean for you. When the heart is right, the ritual rules do not matter. Mark notes that in teaching like this Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

Does this mean that almsgiving cleanses a person? No. The phrase is hard, and has been read as give the contents of your cups as alms or give from within, from the heart. On either reading Jesus is not teaching salvation by charity. He is telling men obsessed with outward purity that a heart turned outward in generous love is what God calls clean. Only the blood of Christ cleanses a sinner before God; but a heart he has cleansed will show it by opening its hands.

A practical test. There is a sharp practical test buried in this, and it is not comfortable. It is entirely possible to be meticulous about religious observance and tight-fisted, and Jesus treats the second as the diagnosis and the first as the cover.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for cleaning the outside of the cup while their insides were full of greed, and told them to give generously from the heart, and then everything would be clean for them.

On a Tuesday. God sees your heart. Do not just look good on the outside; let him clean the inside. Look at your bank statement alongside your church attendance and ask which one tells the truer story about your heart. Then give something away this week that you would rather keep.

For worship. He who made the outside made the inside also, and he did not leave either to rot. The Creator came as Redeemer, to give us a new heart and put a new spirit within us (Ezekiel 36:26). He cleans from the inside out, and what he cleans, he fills with his own generosity: the generosity of the one who, though he was rich, for our sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

parallels.desc: to the pure, all things are pure

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

But woe to you Pharisees! Six woes follow, three on the Pharisees (vv. 42–44) and three on the lawyers (vv. 46–52), and the word itself needs setting straight before any of them are read. “Woe” (ouai) is not a curse and not an insult. It is the prophets’ word, Isaiah’s, Amos’s, Habakkuk’s, a cry of lament as much as a verdict of judgement. It is the sound a man makes looking at somebody walking toward a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later in this Gospel (19:41), and the woe and the weeping come from the same heart.

For you tithe mint and rue and every herb. The law required a tithe, a tenth, of the produce of the field: grain, wine, oil, the fruit of the land (Deuteronomy 14:22–23). It said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. The Pharisees, wanting to be certain they had not fallen short anywhere, tithed the garden herbs too, the tiniest plants, counting out every tenth leaf. There is something genuinely admirable in that, and it should be admitted before it is criticised. These were not lazy men. They were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt.

And neglect justice and the love of God. And there it is. The same men counting mint leaves were failing at the two largest things in the law, the weightier matters (Matthew 23:23). Justice: fair dealing with others, especially the poor. The love of God: loving him with the whole heart. The two great commandments (10:27). Careful about tiny details, careless about the heart of the law.

These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. This clause matters enormously and is regularly ignored. Jesus does not abolish the herb-tithing. He says they were right to do it. What he condemns is the trade: the quiet substitution of the small and achievable for the large and demanding. The small things must not replace the great ones.

How the trade happens. The mechanism is universal, and it is not hypocrisy in the ordinary sense. Nobody decides to swap justice for mint. What happens is that the measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off, and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off, and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will find he has run out before he reaches the things that do not. The modern equivalents write themselves. Attendance is countable. Reading plans are countable. Positions on secondary matters are defensible. Whether I am just, and whether I love God, are neither, and they are the two things this verse says were being neglected.

Where Christians differ: the tithe today. Some teach that Christians must give a tenth of their income, as a binding law. Others say the tithe belonged to the old covenant, and the New Testament gives no fixed percentage. Verdict: the New Testament does not command a tithe for Christians, but calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate, sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Jesus was speaking here to Jews under the law, before the cross. A tenth is a wise starting point, and many will give more. The heart matters more than the percentage, and the point of this verse is the weightier matters: justice and the love of God.

What does justice look like for an ordinary Christian? Paying your workers and your bills fairly and on time. Telling the truth in business, on forms and in references. Refusing to exploit someone’s weakness, ignorance or poverty. Speaking up for the person who is being treated unfairly at work or in church, especially the one with no voice. Treating the cleaner and the director with the same respect. And caring about the poor with your money and your time, not just your opinions (Proverbs 31:8–9). Justice is love in the shape of fairness, and it is checked daily, not annually.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees for scrupulously tithing tiny herbs while neglecting justice and the love of God.

On a Tuesday. Are you careful about small religious details and careless about justice and love? Put first things first. Keep your quiet time, keep your giving, keep your church commitments; and then ask whether anyone you dealt with today was treated unjustly by you, and whether you loved God at your desk as well as in your pew.

For worship. Only one man ever did both the weightier matters and the smaller ones, without neglecting either. He tithed what the law required, and he did justice, loved mercy and walked humbly with his God every day of his life. Then he gave not a tenth but all of himself, for people who had neglected justice and the love of God. His righteousness covers our counted herbs and our forgotten weightier matters alike.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to garden herbs such as mint and rue.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.

Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. The second woe is about seating arrangements, and it is more searching than it sounds. The best seat was a real and visible thing: a bench at the front, facing the congregation, near the chest where the scrolls were kept. To sit there was to be seen by everyone for the whole service, and to be seen in the act of being religious. And greetings in the marketplaces: the elaborate public respect, with honorific titles, paid to a recognised teacher in the open square, where the transaction could be observed by passers-by.

The word is love. Notice what is not being condemned. Not the seats: somebody has to sit at the front, and honouring teachers is not wicked. The word is love. What is diagnosed is an appetite: love of prominence and recognition. Their religion served their pride. They wanted to be seen and honoured by people (Matthew 6:1–5; 23:5–7). The problem is not the seat or the greeting, but the love of it.

The second audience. It is worth being exact about what that appetite does, because it is not merely vanity. A man who loves the front seat has acquired a second audience, and the second audience is standing between him and the first. Every act of piety now has two possible payments, and one of them arrives immediately, which is precisely the problem Jesus names elsewhere: they have received their reward (Matthew 6:2). The reason this is a woe and not a scolding is that it is self-defeating in a way the man cannot see. He is doing genuinely good things and being paid for them in the wrong currency, and the payment is instant and pleasant and leaves nothing outstanding.

What if I recognise this in myself? Two things are worth saying. The first is that the desire to be well thought of is not curable by pretending not to have it. Public modesty about one’s own achievements is one of the front seats. The second is where the actual remedy lies, and it is not in trying harder to be humble. It is in the fact that a man who already has the approval he most needs stops shopping for the substitute. The prayer at the top of this chapter begins Father, and a person who has heard that word settle on him has considerably less use for a bench at the front. Practise doing some good things in secret, where only he sees (Matthew 6:4), and let him be enough.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees for loving the places of honour and public recognition.

On a Tuesday. Do you love recognition in church? Notice the small sting when your contribution goes unthanked, or the glow when your name is mentioned from the front. Do one helpful thing this week that no one will ever know about, and tell no one. Seek God’s approval, not people’s honour.

For worship. The one who truly deserved every seat of honour took the lowest place. He was born in a stable, washed his disciples’ feet, and was lifted up not to a throne but to a cross, despised and rejected. Therefore God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name (Philippians 2:9). In him we have the Father’s approval, the only honour that lasts, and it frees us from needing anyone else’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.

Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it. The third woe is the worst of the three, and it depends entirely on a detail of Jewish law that a modern reader has to be told. Under the law, touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). It was one of the most serious defilements available, and it disqualified a man from worship until the full ritual of purification had been completed. Because of this, graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover, painted a conspicuous white so that pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem could see them and go round (compare Matthew 23:27). The marking was a public service. It kept people clean. An unmarked grave is therefore the exact opposite: a grave a man walks straight over, and finds out afterward, if he ever finds out at all.

Devastating in three ways. First, they are graves: whatever is on the surface, the contents are dead. He has just said the inside of the cup is full of greed; now he says what is inside the man. Second, they defile. This is not a criticism of their private spiritual condition. Contact with them makes other people unclean, and Jesus is talking about the effect of these men’s ministry on the people they teach. The Pharisees thought they were the guardians of purity, keeping people clean. In fact they were sources of defilement. Third, and worst, nobody can tell. They are unmarked. There is no warning, no visible sign, nothing about their bearing or reputation to make a person step round. The whole reason the damage is done is that they look entirely safe. People thought they were being led to holiness, and were being led to death.

Not obvious hypocrites. This is not a description of obvious hypocrites, who are much less dangerous because everybody eventually spots them. It is a description of respected men, whose seriousness about God is genuine, whose knowledge is real, whose lives are outwardly admirable, and who are quietly transmitting something that kills. What passes over the grave is very often the sincere. A young believer takes his cue from the most impressive religious person he knows, and if what that person actually has is scrupulosity without justice and knowledge without love, that is what he will catch, and he will catch it without any idea that a transfer has taken place.

How do I protect myself and my children from unmarked graves? Test every teacher, however respected, by Scripture and by fruit (Matthew 7:15–20; 1 John 4:1). Watch whether a ministry produces love, humility and joy in Christ, or fear, pride and harshness. Be wary of anyone who cannot be questioned. Do not take your whole picture of the Christian life from one impressive person; let your children see many ordinary faithful believers. And where you find real spiritual abuse, name it and bring it into the light; protecting victims always matters more than protecting a reputation.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees as unmarked graves that unknowingly defile those who walk over them.

On a Tuesday. Your influence affects others, more than you know. Think of the people who take their cue from you: your children, a younger believer, a colleague who knows you go to church. What are they catching from you, beneath the surface? Make sure it leads them to life, not defilement, and ask God to deal with what lies hidden before it spreads.

For worship. There was once a grave that defiled no one, because it could not hold its occupant. Christ entered the place of death and corruption and came out on the third day, and since then a grave is no longer the end for those who are his. He touches the dead and makes them clean; he turns tombs into doorways. In him there is no hidden corruption, only life.
verseByVerse.note: Touching a grave made a person unclean; an unmarked grave defiled people without their knowing it.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: One of the lawyers answered him, 'Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.' And he said, 'Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the lawyers answered him: Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also. And he said: woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.

Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also. It is a wonderfully revealing interruption. The lawyers were experts in the interpretation of the law of Moses, the scholars behind the Pharisees’ practice; many lawyers were Pharisees, and the Pharisees followed their interpretations. They have been listening to three woes aimed at somebody else, and one of them speaks up to point out that the criticism is landing on his profession too. He hoped, perhaps, that Jesus would distinguish the experts from the Pharisees. Note what he does not say. Not that is untrue. Not you have misunderstood us. He says you insult us, which concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone. That is the response of a man who has heard something true and has decided to be offended rather than to look. It is one of the commonest ways a person defends himself against a word he cannot answer: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite. He might have hoped the interruption would end it. It doubles it. Jesus does not back down.

Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear. The picture is of pack animals and their drivers. These men had built an elaborate structure of rulings around the law, the oral tradition that specified exactly how each command was to be kept, and the ordinary Israelite was expected to carry it. Countless rules made obedience impossible for ordinary people. Peter would later call the law as they handled it a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10).

And you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. Either they found clever ways to avoid their own rules, or they did nothing to help others carry them. The heavier charge is the second: no allowance made, no weight shared, no interest in whether an ordinary man with a farm and five children could actually do it. They imposed burdens without compassion. Set that against what Jesus says about himself: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30). The contrast is the point of the woe.

Does this mean Christian teachers should not preach high standards? No. Jesus set the highest standard of all: be perfect, love your enemies, deny yourself. The difference is that his standards come with grace to keep them and forgiveness for failing them, and he himself carried the heaviest load. The test for anyone who teaches is uncomfortable and simple. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself, and whether he points people to Christ who bears it.

In a sentence. When a lawyer protested, Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for loading people with impossible burdens while not lifting a finger to help them.

On a Tuesday. Do not load others with rules God has not given. Help them carry the burdens they have: the young mother overwhelmed by advice, the new believer drowning in expectations, the friend who feels he can never do enough. Lift a finger. And when you receive a hard word, ask first whether it is true before you ask whether it was gentle.

For worship. The lawyers would not touch the burdens with one finger. Christ took the whole weight on his shoulders. He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isaiah 53:4); he carried the curse of the law to the cross and nailed our debt there. And now he offers a yoke that is easy and a burden that is light, because he is the one pulling it with us.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.

Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. The fifth woe has a sting that takes a moment to feel. Building and beautifying prophets’ tombs was a genuine piety of the period, and monuments to great figures of Israel’s past were being built in Jesus’ day. On the face of it, it is the most respectful thing imaginable: honouring the men their ancestors murdered, publicly, at their own expense. It seemed like repentance for their ancestors’ sin. And Jesus calls it complicity.

So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. The logic is compressed, and there is a bitter play in it: the fathers put the prophets in the ground, and the sons put up the masonry over them. One buries, the other seals. The joint operation is complete. They honour dead prophets, but reject the living one, as their fathers did; and they will kill the greatest prophet of all.

Safely over. The real charge is deeper than wordplay: the tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet. The dead prophet has stopped saying the things that got him killed. His words have been polished into Scripture, quoted approvingly, and inscribed on the monument these men are paying for. There is no danger anywhere in it. Meanwhile a living prophet is sitting at their table telling them that their religion is an unmarked grave, and they are about to arrange his death. That is what makes the monument an endorsement rather than a repudiation. A man who says he would never have joined the mob, while queuing to join this one, has not broken with his fathers. He has simply arrived late.

The pattern in every generation. The pattern outlives the first century entirely. Every generation of the church admires the reformers, martyrs and awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. The reason is not always hypocrisy. It is that a dead prophet requires a subscription and a live one requires repentance. Honouring dead prophets is easy; listening to living ones costs.

Are there prophets today whom we must heed? Not in the sense of new revelation: the prophets and apostles laid the foundation once for all, and the canon of Scripture is closed (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But God still sends faithful preachers and believers who apply his word to us with uncomfortable accuracy: the pastor who preaches on the sin our church tolerates, the friend who tells us the truth. The test is not whether they claim a new word from God, but whether what they say is what Scripture says. When it is, we must not honour the Bible on the shelf while silencing the person reading it to us.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for building tombs for the prophets their fathers killed, because by rejecting God’s messengers they share in their fathers’ guilt.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to honour the great Christians of the past while ignoring the uncomfortable message of God’s word today. Think of the last time someone applied Scripture to you in a way that hurt. Did you check whether they were right, or only whether they had the standing to say it? Go back to that word and weigh it honestly.

For worship. Every prophet the fathers killed was pointing to one Prophet, and when he came, he too was killed. But his tomb could not be sealed. The stone was rolled away, the grave was empty, and the one whom the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). We do not build monuments to a dead Christ. We worship a living one.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore also the Wisdom of God said: I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute, so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.

I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute. The quotation matches no known book exactly, and the likeliest explanation is the plainest: Jesus is speaking as the Wisdom of God, the one who sent the prophets, and summarising in his own words what that sending has always cost. Perhaps it means that God, in his wisdom, decreed this. Matthew puts the words directly in Jesus’ own mouth: I send you prophets (Matthew 23:34). Jesus is the Wisdom of God. And note the word apostles. He is not only reviewing history; he is looking at the men who will be sent after him. Some will be killed: Stephen (Acts 7:58–60), James (Acts 12:2).

So that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation. The generation that rejects the Messiah fills up the measure of all its ancestors’ guilt (Matthew 23:32). It is the climax of a long history of rejection.

From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. The two names are the bookends of the Hebrew Bible. Abel is the first murder in Genesis (Genesis 4:8). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court, on the king’s orders, for rebuking the people (2 Chronicles 24:20–22); his is the last recorded murder in Chronicles, which stands last in the Hebrew ordering of the books. So from Genesis to Chronicles: from the first page to the last, the whole of the Old Testament. As he died, Zechariah said: may the LORD see and avenge! And he perished in the temple court, between the altar and the sanctuary.

Is God punishing men for what their ancestors did? That is the hardest question in the paragraph, and Scripture appears to forbid exactly that. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20); children shall not be put to death because of their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). If this verse meant inherited guilt, it would contradict the law and the prophets outright. It does not, and Jesus has already said why, one verse earlier: you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers (v. 48). Nothing is charged to these men that they have not personally ratified. The guilt is not inherited down a bloodline; it is incurred by choosing, in your own generation and with your own eyes open, to do the identical thing. And there is a reason the reckoning falls here. This is the generation to whom the Son himself has come, the one to whom every murdered prophet was pointing. A long account is closed not because these men are worse than their ancestors but because they have more light than any of them and are about to do worse with it. The judgement is proportional to the privilege, exactly as at Chorazin (10:13–15).

Which Zechariah? Matthew calls this Zechariah the son of Barachiah (Matthew 23:35), while 2 Chronicles 24:20 names his father as Jehoiada. Luke gives no father’s name. Jehoiada may have been his grandfather, or the name may reflect a confusion with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). Either way, Jesus means the last murder in the Hebrew Bible’s order, as Abel’s was the first.

It will be required of this generation. This was fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (19:41–44; 21:20–24), within forty years of these words.

What it does not mean. This verse and others like it have been quarried for centuries to justify appalling treatment of Jewish people. Note who is addressed: not a nation and not a race, but the scribes and lawyers in that room, whose conduct Jesus has just described. The speaker is himself a Jew, as are his disciples, as is every prophet whose blood he invokes, and later in this Gospel he will weep over this city rather than gloat over it (19:41). To take a rebuke that a Jewish prophet delivered to Jewish leaders about the killing of Jewish prophets, and turn it into a charge against Jewish people as such, is to misread it so completely as to end up standing exactly where the men being rebuked are standing. Christians owe Jewish people love, gratitude for the Messiah who came from them, and the gospel offered humbly.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the generation which rejects God’s messengers will be held responsible for the blood of all the prophets murdered from Abel to Zechariah.

On a Tuesday. Rejection of God’s word accumulates. Each time you hear a clear word and set it aside, it becomes easier to do again. Do not harden your heart today. Name the truth you have been putting off, and obey it before the week is out.

For worship. Abel’s blood cried out from the ground for vengeance; Zechariah’s prayed that the LORD would see and avenge. There is another blood, shed by this same generation, that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). It cries not for vengeance but for pardon. Father, forgive them, said the one whose blood it was. The account of all the prophets’ blood was settled in full, and for everyone who trusts him it is settled in mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.

Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. The last woe is the heaviest, and the image is worth taking slowly. There is a door. Behind it is the knowledge of God: not information about him, but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce, knowing him. And there is a key. These men were the keyholders. That was precisely their office. They had the texts, the training and the languages; they were the ones ordinary people came to when they wanted to know what God had said. The key was in their hands legitimately. The key of knowledge is the right understanding of Scripture, which points to Christ (24:27, 44–45; John 5:39). You have taken away the key: not lost it, not misplaced it, but removed it. By their traditions and false interpretations they had locked the door that God had provided a way through.

You did not enter yourselves. They had the key and never used it. They did not come to Jesus. A lifetime handling the Scriptures of the living God, and they never went in. That is possible, and it is possible in every generation, and it is one of the strangest facts about religious work.

And you hindered those who were entering. Note the wording: people were on their way in. Not people who might have thought about it, but people already moving toward the door. And these men got in the way, by their teaching and their opposition. How? The whole chapter has shown it. By burying the law under rulings so that no ordinary person could carry it (v. 46). By making the entry requirements ceremonial rather than moral (v. 39). By modelling a religion of counted herbs and front seats. By teaching so that God came out looking like the sort of person these men were. That last is the real mechanism, and it is why this is the final and worst woe: false teachers who block the way to God. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine. He transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine.

How do I know whether my teaching opens or shuts the door? Ask whether people leave your teaching seeing Christ more clearly, and wanting him more. Ask whether you point to the cross and the empty tomb, or mainly to rules and techniques. Ask whether ordinary, struggling people find in you a way in or a wall. Teach the Bible as a book about Christ, not a manual of performance. And be in the room yourself: the surest way to open the door for others is to be someone who has gone through it and is still delighting in what is inside.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for taking away the key to understanding Scripture, neither entering the kingdom themselves nor letting others enter.

On a Tuesday. If you teach God’s word to anyone, a Sunday school class, your children, a small group, ask whether somebody who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder. Make sure your teaching opens the door to Christ, not shuts it. And pray for faithful teachers in your church by name.

For worship. The lawyers took away the key; Christ is the door (John 10:9), and he holds the key of David, who opens and no one will shut (Revelation 3:7). He opened the Scriptures to two disciples on the Emmaus road until their hearts burned within them (24:32), and he still opens them to anyone who asks. No keyholder on earth can lock out a sinner whom he has let in.

verseByVerse.quote: As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard. The dinner is over. He has said everything, and Luke records what it produced. Not repentance. Not even argument. Something colder. “Press him hard” (deinōs enechein) means to be bitterly hostile, to hold a grudge. The opposition hardens.

And to provoke him to speak about many things. Firing questions at him, as a witness is pressed until he says something usable.

Lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say. The verbs end as hunting words: lying in wait is the vocabulary of an ambush, hunters setting traps for an animal. They were not seeking truth, but evidence against him. So the scene at the end of chapter 11 is a group of respectable men following a guest out of a house, firing questions, not to learn anything but to get a sentence they can use.

The turn. This is a turning point. Up to now the opposition in Luke has been sceptical, then hostile, then organised. From here it is a hunt with a purpose, and it will run without interruption to a courtyard and a trial and a cross.

Truth softens or sets. It is worth sitting for a moment with what has just happened, because it is one of the most sobering things in the Gospel. The word of God had been spoken to these men as clearly and as directly as it has ever been spoken to anybody. Every woe was accurate. Every one of them was delivered by a guest at their own table who had come when he was invited. And it hardened them. That is not an accident, and it is not a failure of the message. Scripture has said from early on that this happens: Pharaoh, whose heart set harder with every plague; the commission given to Isaiah, that this people would hear and not understand (Isaiah 6:9–10); and Luke’s own account of a word that falls on a beaten path where nothing can get in (8:12). The truth is never neutral. It softens or it sets, and which one it does is decided by what it lands on. These men had heard the finest teaching ever given, delivered in person, in their own dining room, and they left the house looking for a way to kill him.

Why does the same word soften some and harden others? Because the word meets hearts in different conditions, and because God in his sovereign mercy opens some hearts (Acts 16:14) and in his justice leaves others to the hardness they have chosen (Romans 9:18). No one who hardens himself can blame God; no one who is softened can boast. The practical lesson is for us: when the word cuts, do not reach for a reason to resent the one who spoke it. Bring the wound to God and ask him to soften you. A heart that asks to be softened is already being softened.

In a sentence. After this, the scribes and Pharisees became fiercely hostile, firing questions to trap him in something he might say.

On a Tuesday. When you are criticised for faithfulness to Christ, remember that he was too. Speak the truth with wisdom, and do not be surprised when not everyone thanks you. And when the word of God corners you this week, notice the impulse to hunt for a flaw in the messenger, and let the word do its work instead.

For worship. They lay in wait to catch him in his words, and they never could, because he never spoke a false word. When at last they took him, it was not because he slipped, but because he gave himself up, the Good Shepherd laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). The hunters thought they had trapped him. In fact he was walking into the trap on purpose, to spring it on death itself, and to rescue the very men who were hunting him.

parallels.desc: to trap him in his talk

11.text: <sup>1</sup> Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. <sup>3</sup> Give us each day our daily bread, <sup>4</sup> and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, <sup>6</sup> for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; <sup>7</sup> and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>10</sup> For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>11</sup> What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; <sup>12</sup> or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? <sup>13</sup> If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” <sup>14</sup> Now he was casting out a demon that was mute.
