When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. <sup>15</sup> But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,” <sup>16</sup> while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. <sup>17</sup> But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. <sup>18</sup> And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. <sup>19</sup> And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>20</sup> But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>21</sup> When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; <sup>22</sup> but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil. <sup>23</sup> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>24</sup> “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ <sup>25</sup> And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. <sup>26</sup> Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” <sup>27</sup> As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!” <sup>28</sup> But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” <sup>29</sup> When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. <sup>30</sup> For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. <sup>31</sup> The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>32</sup> The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>33</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>34</sup> Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. <sup>35</sup> Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. <sup>36</sup> If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” <sup>37</sup> While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. <sup>38</sup> The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. <sup>39</sup> And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. <sup>40</sup> You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? <sup>41</sup> But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you. <sup>42</sup> “But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>43</sup> Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. <sup>44</sup> Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.” <sup>45</sup> One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” <sup>46</sup> And he said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. <sup>47</sup> Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. <sup>48</sup> So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. <sup>49</sup> Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ <sup>50</sup> so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, <sup>51</sup> from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. <sup>52</sup> Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.” <sup>53</sup> As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, <sup>54</sup> lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

12.title: Fear, Greed, Anxiety, and the Coming Fire
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is one of the most urgent chapters in Luke's Gospel — a sustained call to a particular quality of life in the light of the coming judgment. Jesus addresses a massive crowd (v. 1 — “so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another”) and then moves between the crowd and the disciples in a series of teachings that together form a comprehensive call to undivided allegiance. Do not fear those who can kill the body; fear the one who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Do not covet or stockpile; the rich fool who planned bigger barns died the night he planned them. Do not be anxious about food and clothing; seek the kingdom first. Be dressed for action, with lamps burning, waiting for the master to return.

The chapter's emotional register is high throughout. Jesus speaks of fire he has come to cast on the earth and a baptism he has to undergo before it — and he is distressed until it is accomplished. He warns that he has not come to bring peace but division — a division that runs through the family. He rebukes the crowd for its ability to read the weather and its inability to read the present moment. And he calls everyone to settle accounts with their adversary before they arrive at the judge — because once you are before the judge, the outcome is fixed. The urgency is eschatological: the crisis of the kingdom's arrival is not a background hum; it is the defining emergency of every human life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Fear God, Not Man; Acknowledge Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowd is so large that people are being trampled — and in the middle of it Jesus turns his back on the thousands and addresses the handful. This is a word for those inside about a temptation specific to religious people.

“The leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” Leaven was a lump of soured dough kept back from the last batch: small, invisible once mixed in, working by itself, changing everything it touches. And Luke alone gives us Jesus's own definition. Hypocrisy is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part.

The argument against it is not moral but practical: “nothing is covered up that will not be revealed.” The performance has a fixed run and a closing date. Whether that sentence is the most frightening in the chapter or the most liberating depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

The teaching on fear is the application. Do not fear those who kill the body — after that, Jesus says, they have nothing more. The threat runs out. What is commanded instead is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror; and the effect is the opposite of paralysis, since a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else. Every tyranny in history has run on the fear of what can be done to a body, and this sentence cuts the supply line.

Which is why “fear him” is followed two verses later by “fear not.” The bridge is a bird nobody wanted: sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, and Matthew's parallel prices them two for a penny (Matt. 10:29), so two pennies buys five — the fifth thrown in free, because it is not worth counting. Not one of them is forgotten.

Then the stakes rise. To acknowledge Christ before men is to be acknowledged before the angels of God; to deny him is to be denied. And then the hardest verse in the chapter — the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — followed immediately by the promise that in the hour of trial the Spirit himself will supply the words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word for hell is Gehenna, and it is not a mythological invention. It is a place: the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under two of Judah's worst kings (2 Kgs. 23:10; Jer. 7:31), and which the prophets turned into a byword for judgement. Everyone listening could have pointed at it.

The one to be feared is God, not the devil — Scripture never gives the enemy authority to cast anyone anywhere, and nowhere are believers told to fear him. And the whole force of the passage depends on the fact that the one who has authority over death is the same one who does not forget a sparrow and knows a number about you that you do not know yourself.

On the blasphemy against the Spirit, the context is decisive. This saying stands in Matthew and Mark immediately after the Beelzebul accusation — which Luke gave us in the previous chapter (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work in the open and called it the devil, and Mark states the reason plainly: “for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit” (Mark 3:30).

It is not a word said in a bad moment. It is the settled, eyes-open decision to call the light darkness. And since the Spirit's work is to convict of sin and point to Christ (John 16:8-14), a man who has finally refused that work has stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. The anxiety itself is therefore the disproof: nobody who has committed this sin is afraid of it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light” uses the architecture everyone lived in. The “private rooms” are the windowless inner storeroom where valuables were kept — the one place a conversation could not be overheard; the housetops were flat, adjoining, and where public announcements were made. The most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town.

The saying cuts both ways, and the context decides which is uppermost. Much of what Christians say for Christ is said quietly, in rooms with no audience, and looks unrecorded; Jesus says it is being minuted. But the primary force here is the other: everything a man is when nobody is watching is going to be read out. And a man who has decided in advance that everything will be known has no further use for the machinery of managing an impression — which is a considerable amount of energy returned to him.

The confession sayings must not become a performance requirement, and the safeguard is in the Gospel itself: Peter denied him three times, in public, and was restored on a beach. What is described is a settled position, not a single failure of nerve. Yet it should not be softened into nothing either. Very few Western Christians will stand in a court; the moments that count are the conversation at work, the family gathering where silence is taken for agreement, the friendship of a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned.

And “the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour” is not a licence for unprepared preaching — the situation named is arrest and interrogation — nor a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen made the longest speech in Acts under exactly this promise and was stoned at the end of it. What is promised is not acquittal but that the right words will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, 'Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.

Meaning first. Luke 12 is Jesus teaching his disciples how to live in the open before God while the world presses in. It gathers teaching on fearless faithfulness, money and anxiety, readiness for Christ’s return, and the urgency of the present time. Most of it is addressed to the disciples, with the crowds listening. Beware hypocrisy, because everything hidden will be revealed. Do not fear those who can only kill the body; fear God, and then fear nothing, because the God who holds hell in his hand counts the hairs on your head. Guard against greed, because life is not possessions, as the rich fool learned on the night his soul was called in. Do not be anxious, because your Father knows what you need and delights to give you the kingdom. Be ready, because the Master is coming at an hour you do not expect, and the Master who comes will put on an apron and serve his servants. And read the times: the fire is about to be kindled, the baptism of the cross is near, and today is the day to settle with God on the road.

The setting. Chapter 12 gathers teaching on fearless faithfulness, money and anxiety, readiness for Christ’s return, and the urgency of the present time. Most is addressed to the disciples, with the crowds listening.

When so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another. Literally tens of thousands. Luke sets the scene with a detail nobody would invent: the crowd is so large that people are being walked on. This is the height of his popularity, and it comes immediately after a dinner that ended with the religious establishment following him into the street to trap him (11:37–54). Jesus is not impressed by numbers.

He began to say to his disciples first. In the middle of that crush, he turns from the thousands and addresses the handful. The warning is for his own followers. Note who is being warned: not the Pharisees, but the disciples. This is a word to people already inside, and it is the first thing he says to them after watching what religion had done to the men at that dinner table. The disciples are not immune.

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Leaven in the ancient world was not a sachet of yeast. It was a lump of dough kept back from the last batch and left to sour, then worked into the new one. Its properties are the point of the image: it is small, it is invisible once mixed in, it works by itself, and it changes everything it touches. A little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6). Hypocrisy is like that: it starts small and spreads through a life and a community. And Luke alone gives us Jesus’ own definition: which is hypocrisy. The word had a specific origin: a hypokritēs was a stage actor, a man who spoke his lines from behind a mask. It is not the same as inconsistency, and it is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, which is the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part: pretending to be what you are not.

Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. Here is the argument against it, and it is not first moral. It is practical. He does not say that hypocrisy is wrong, though it is. He says that it does not work: the performance has a fixed run and a closing date, and everything behind the mask is going to be public. God sees everything, and at the judgement everything will be exposed (8:17; 1 Corinthians 4:5). The mask will come off. That is either the most frightening sentence in the chapter or the most liberating, and which it is depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

If I struggle with sin I have not overcome, am I a hypocrite? No. A hypocrite is not a person who fails; he is a person who pretends. The believer who fights a sin, confesses it to God and perhaps to a trusted friend, and keeps getting up again is not acting a part. He is being honest about a war. Hypocrisy begins when you cultivate an image you know is false: hiding what you are, performing what you are not, and condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The cure is not to stop striving for holiness until you are perfect. It is to walk in the light (1 John 1:7): honest before God, honest with someone, and humble about yourself.

In a sentence. With vast crowds around him, Jesus warned his disciples to beware of the spreading influence of the Pharisees’ hypocrisy, because everything hidden will be revealed.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to seem more spiritual than you are? It is often in small things: the prayer said in a voice you never use alone, the Bible-reading habit described as more regular than it is, the marriage presented as better than it is. Be real before God and people. Tell one trusted believer the truth about where you actually are, and find how much energy it frees.

For worship. The Lord who warns us against masks wore none. What he was in public he was in private; what he said in the temple he said in the garden. And he came to save hypocrites, because he knew everything behind every mask and loved us still. On the day when all is revealed, those who are in him will not be found out. They were found out long ago, at the cross, and covered.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; here it pictures hypocrisy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.

Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light. Private words will be made public; every careless word will be judged (Matthew 12:36). The picture is precise, and it uses the architecture everyone in that crowd lived in.

And what you have whispered in private rooms. Literally inner rooms: the innermost storeroom of a house, the windowless space at the back where valuables were kept, and the one place where a conversation could not be overheard through a doorway.

Shall be proclaimed on the housetops. The housetops were flat, used for sleeping and drying grain, and in a village where the roofs adjoined, a man standing on his could be heard by the whole street. It was where public announcements were made, like a town crier. So: the most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town. What is said in the first is going to be repeated from the second. There are no secrets from God.

A double meaning. Which way does this cut? Both ways, and the context decides which is uppermost. It is an encouragement: the disciples are about to be told they will be hauled before synagogues and rulers (v. 11), and much of what they say for Christ will be said quietly, to individuals, in rooms with no audience. That work looks small and unrecorded. Jesus says it is being minuted, and the gospel they now hear privately will be preached publicly to the world. But the immediate context is a warning about hypocrisy, and the primary force is the other one. Everything a man is when nobody is watching, the private appetites, the things said about people who are not in the room, the version of himself that exists only behind a closed door, is going to be read out.

The gap is temporary. Most people maintain a gap of some size between the public self and the interior one, and manage it so habitually that they no longer notice they are doing it. This verse says the gap is temporary. And there is one entirely practical consequence. A man who has decided in advance that everything will be known has no further use for the machinery of managing an impression, which is a considerable amount of energy returned to him for other purposes.

Will my forgiven sins be broadcast at the judgement? Scripture’s emphasis for believers is that their sins are blotted out, cast into the depths of the sea, remembered no more (Hebrews 8:12; Micah 7:19). Whatever is opened on that day will be opened as the record of grace, not as evidence for condemnation, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The warning here presses hardest on the hidden life that is being kept from God now. Bring it into the light today, in confession, and it will never be used against you.

In a sentence. Everything said in secret will be heard openly and announced from the rooftops.

On a Tuesday. Speak in private as you would if it were broadcast; God hears it all. Notice the conversation where you say about someone what you would never say to them, the message you would hate to see forwarded, the comment made only because the door is shut. And take courage from the other side of it: the quiet word for Christ to one person, which nobody else heard, has been heard in heaven.

For worship. The God who hears every whisper in every inner room is not a spy but a Father. He hears the gossip and the groaning alike, the curse and the prayer too deep for words. And the Son who will one day proclaim from the housetops is the Son who already speaks for us in the highest court of heaven. Everything hidden will be revealed, and for those who are his, the last thing revealed will be how much they were loved.
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!

I tell you, my friends. He has never called them that before in this Gospel; it is the only time in the first three Gospels that Jesus calls his disciples friends (compare John 15:14–15). The placing is deliberate. He is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, preparing them for persecution, and he opens by naming the relationship it is being said inside.

Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. Hypocrisy very often comes from fear of people, and Jesus addresses the root. Take the sentence at its full weight. He is not saying that persecution will not come. He is saying that when it comes, and does its worst, it will have reached the end of its resources, and that its worst is death. That is a startling assessment of what the powers of this world can actually do to a Christian. They can kill him. After that, Jesus says, they have nothing more. The threat runs out. Death is not the end, and they cannot touch the soul.

Fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Who is meant? The devil, some have suggested; but Scripture never gives him authority to cast anyone anywhere, and nowhere are believers told to fear him. The one who has authority over both death and what follows it is God. He alone has power over eternal destiny. The word for hell is geenna, Gehenna, and it is not a mythological invention. It is a place: the Valley of Hinnom, on the south side of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under two of Judah’s worst kings (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), and which the prophets turned into a byword for judgement. Everyone listening could have pointed at it. Jesus uses it of the place of final, conscious punishment.

Yes, I tell you, fear him! Repeated for emphasis. The fear of God drives out the fear of people: do not fear what they fear; the LORD of hosts, him you shall regard as holy, let him be your fear (Isaiah 8:12–13); the fear of man lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25). If you fear God, you need fear nothing else. And this awe is the beginning of wisdom.

Are Christians meant to be afraid of God? A sensitive reader will stop here. The answer is that this is spoken to my friends, and the two things are not in tension. The fear of God is not cringing terror for his children, but reverent awe of the one who holds all power, including over eternity. What is commanded is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror. And the effect is the exact opposite of paralysis: a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else, because the worst any human power can do to him has been placed in its true proportion. A child can be in awe of his father’s strength and run into his arms in the same moment. That is why the next thing Jesus says is fear not.

Cutting the supply line. Every tyranny in history has run on the same fuel, which is the fear of what can be done to a body. This sentence cuts the supply line. The martyrs who sang in the arena were not reckless. They had simply been told the truth about who held the final authority.

In a sentence. Jesus told his friends not to fear those who can only kill the body, but to fear God, who has authority to cast into hell.

On a Tuesday. Whose opinion do you fear most? Your manager’s, your family’s, the group chat’s? Name the person whose disapproval most shapes what you say about Christ. Then put that fear next to the fear of God, and watch it shrink to its true size. Fear God, and you will be set free from the fear of people.

For worship. The God who has authority to cast into hell sent his Son into the place of judgement for us. The fire that we feared fell on him; the One with authority over death went down into it and came out holding its keys (Revelation 1:18). So the God we fear is the God we flee to. He is holy beyond imagining, and he has called us friends.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.

Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Two verses after fear him comes fear not, and the bridge between them is a bird nobody wanted. The detail is exact. Sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, food for the very poor. And there is a touch in the arithmetic. Matthew records the price as two sparrows for a penny (Matthew 10:29). Luke says five for two pennies: buy four, and the fifth is thrown in free, the one with no value at all, added because it is not worth counting.

And not one of them is forgotten before God. Including that one. Notice the form of the statement, because it is unexpected. He does not say God feeds them, or watches them, or values them. He says none of them is forgotten, which is the language of memory, and it means that the death of a bird thrown in free with a purchase is registered. God’s care extends to the smallest and least valuable creature.

Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Not counted once, at some point. The perfect tense means the number is known and stands known: a figure that changes daily and is never out of date. It is the most useless piece of information imaginable, and that is precisely the point. Nobody needs to know how many hairs are on a man’s head. The fact that God does tells you not that the information is important but that the attention is total. God knows you in the tiniest detail, more than you know yourself.

Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. The God to be feared (v. 5) is the God who cares; the same God. Holy fear and trusting confidence go together. Here is the answer to the fear of what men can do. It is not that the danger has been overstated: he has just conceded that they can kill you. It is that the God who has authority over death is the same God who does not forget a sparrow, and who knows a number about you that you do not know yourself. If God cares for sparrows, he cares far more for his children. Even if they kill your body, it is not outside his care. Nothing happens to you that he does not know and allow, and he works all of it for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). That is why the two commands sit two verses apart without contradiction. The one to be feared and the one who counts the hairs are the same person, and the second fact is what makes the first bearable.

If God cares so closely, why did he let this happen to me? Jesus does not promise that sparrows never fall; Matthew says not one falls to the ground apart from your Father (Matthew 10:29). The promise is not that nothing painful will happen, but that nothing will happen unknown, unnoticed or outside his purpose. You may not see the reason this side of glory, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend the pain is small. It asks you to trust the character of a Father who counts hairs, who did not spare his own Son, and who will one day wipe every tear away. Bring the question to him honestly; the psalms give you words for it.

In a sentence. God does not forget even the cheapest sparrow, and knows the number of hairs on your head, so do not fear, for you are worth more than many sparrows.

On a Tuesday. You are known and cared for by God in every detail. When you feel overlooked, at work, in church, in your family, look at a sparrow on a fence and remember that it is remembered. Face today without fear, and bring the smallest worry to him, because nothing about you is too small for his attention.

For worship. The Lord of the universe keeps a register of sparrows and a count of hairs. Nothing is beneath his notice, and nothing is beyond his power. And the Father who forgets no sparrow did not forget us: he gave his Son, of infinitely more value than all the sparrows and all the worlds, so that we might never be forgotten before him.
verseByVerse.note: Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; Matthew says two for a penny, Luke five for two, as if the fifth came free.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.

Everyone who acknowledges me before men. The word (homologēsē) means confesses, openly declares loyalty. The construction is literally confesses in me, an unusual phrase that suggests not merely stating a fact about him but declaring an allegiance to him. In the face of fear of persecution, the disciple publicly owns Jesus. And the setting for both halves is public: before men, then before the angels of God. So there are two courtrooms, and what happens in the second corresponds exactly to what happened in the first.

The Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God. At the judgement, Jesus will say: this one belongs to me. Note that Jesus is the judge; his acknowledgement decides eternal destiny. And the promise on this side is worth as much as the warning. Whatever is said for him in a difficult room is said again, by him, in front of the angels of God.

But the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. Measure for measure (9:26).

What it does not mean. Not that a single failure means final rejection. The man who made the sharpest denial in the New Testament was forgiven and restored and became a leader of the church. Peter denied Jesus three times, in public, in a courtyard (22:57–62), and was recommissioned on a beach (John 21:15–19). So the saying is not describing a single failure of nerve. The warning is against a settled refusal to acknowledge him: the person who, over a life, will not own him. And the warning itself is one of the means God uses to keep us faithful.

The smaller moments. It should not be softened into nothing either, because the context makes the intended situation exact. The disciples are about to be dragged before synagogues and rulers (v. 11). The confession in view is the one made when it costs something, and it is not a confession at all if it is only made where it is free. Very few Western Christians will ever stand in a court. The moments that count are smaller and more frequent than that: the conversation at work where the subject comes up and it would be easier to say nothing; the family gathering where a view is expressed and the silence is taken for agreement; the friendship maintained for a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned. None of those is a denial in the courtroom sense. But a man can spend his whole life quietly declining to be identified, and never once decide to.

If I stayed silent when I should have spoken, have I denied Christ? Probably you failed, as Peter did, and the answer is the same as his: go back to the Lord, confess it, and be restored. He looked at Peter, and Peter wept, and that look was mercy (22:61–62). A single silence is not a settled life of denial. But do not leave it there: ask God for the next opportunity, and take it. Often the best repair is simply to go back to the person and say, I wanted to tell you what Christ means to me, and I did not. That is how a failure becomes a confession.

In a sentence. Jesus will acknowledge before God’s angels all who openly acknowledge him before others, and deny those who deny him.

On a Tuesday. Where can you acknowledge Jesus openly today, at work, with friends, online? Think of one friendship in which Christ has never been mentioned, and look for a natural way to mention him this week. It need not be a sermon. A plain sentence will do: I am a Christian, and this is why.

For worship. Before the angels of God, the Son of Man will speak our names. He was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), though we have so often been ashamed of him. He confessed the good confession before Pontius Pilate (1 Timothy 6:13), and went to the cross rather than deny the Father’s will. And on the last day, in front of the whole host of heaven, he will say of trembling, failing disciples: this one is mine.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.

Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. This is the verse that has caused more terror in sincere Christians than any other in the Bible, and it must be handled slowly. Start with what is being contrasted. A word spoken against the Son of Man is forgivable, and that is an extraordinary concession, since Jesus has spent this Gospel demonstrating who he is. Men can insult him, mock him, misjudge him, and be forgiven if they repent. Paul once blasphemed Jesus and persecuted the church in an organised way (1 Timothy 1:13). Peter denied him. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (23:34), and many of the people who called for his death were saved at Pentecost (Acts 2:36–41).

But the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. What is it? The context supplies it, and it is the context that unlocks the verse. In Mark and Matthew this saying comes immediately after the accusation that Jesus cast out demons by Satan (Mark 3:28–30; Matthew 12:31–32), and Luke has just given us that accusation (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work through Jesus, in the open, and called it the devil. Mark records the reason plainly: for they were saying, he has an unclean spirit (Mark 3:30). That is the sin: calling the Spirit’s work the devil’s work. It is not a word said in a bad moment. It is a deliberate, settled, persistent rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ, in full knowledge, calling God’s light darkness.

Why can it not be forgiven? Not because God’s grace is insufficient, but because the Spirit is the one who brings people to repentance. His work is to convict of sin and to point to Christ (John 16:8–14). To reject him finally is to cut oneself off from the only way to forgiveness. It is not that someone wants to repent and cannot be forgiven, but that he no longer wants to repent. A man who has finally and permanently refused the Spirit’s work has, by definition, stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. He does not lie awake. He has no interest in the question.

Where Christians differ, and a pastoral word. Some have taught that the unforgivable sin is a specific act, such as suicide or a particular blasphemous word. Verdict: it is not a single act or careless word, but a final, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ. Anyone who is worried that they have committed it has not, because the very worry shows the Spirit is still at work in them. Those who have committed it do not care.

The anxiety is the disproof. So if you are reading this with your stomach tight, and have been for years: that tightness is not the symptom. It is the disproof. The fear of having committed this sin is a fear the Spirit produces, and he does not trouble the hearts he has stopped working on. The unforgivable sin has never once been committed by a person who wanted to be forgiven.

What about blasphemous thoughts that come into my mind against my will? Many tender believers are tormented by sudden, horrible thoughts about God or the Spirit, which they hate even as they arrive. Those thoughts are not the sin Jesus describes; they are temptations or intrusive thoughts, and the distress they cause shows your heart is on God’s side. Do not argue with them endlessly or try to prove you did not mean them. Bring them to Christ, tell him you hate them, and turn your attention to his promises. If they are persistent and consuming, speak to a wise pastor, and do not be ashamed to see a doctor too.

In a sentence. Those who speak against Jesus can be forgiven, but those who finally reject the Holy Spirit’s testimony will not be forgiven.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you are beyond forgiveness, the fear itself shows you are not. Come to Christ, who forgives everyone who comes. And if you know someone haunted by this verse, do not leave them with it: sit with them, read John 6:37 aloud together, and remind them that the door is open.

For worship. How patient is the Son of Man, who let himself be slandered, mocked and crucified, and prayed for his enemies. How gracious is the Spirit, who keeps convicting and drawing hard hearts for years, until they bow. The God who warns of the unforgivable sin is the God who has forgiven every sin of everyone who comes to Christ, and he casts none of them out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.

And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities. Not if. When. He tells them plainly that this is coming, and Luke’s second volume shows it happening repeatedly: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4), Stephen before the council (Acts 7), Paul before governors and a king (Acts 24–26). And note the range: synagogues, the religious courts, and rulers and authorities, the civil ones, Jewish and Gentile. Opposition will come from both, and sometimes from both at once.

Do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say. The word for defend yourself (apologēsēsthe) is the root behind apologetics, and in that world a technical term for a courtroom defence speech. A man in the dock had to make one, and men trained for years to do it well. They are told not to worry about it.

For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say. The Spirit who is blasphemed by unbelievers (v. 10) helps believers. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke boldly before the council, and they were astonished at uneducated, common men (Acts 4:8–13). Stephen spoke with a wisdom they could not withstand (Acts 6:10).

What it does not mean. Two things need guarding, because this verse has been misused in both directions. It is not a licence for unprepared preaching or careless thinking. The situation named is precise: arrest, trial, an official interrogation about the faith. It has nothing to do with a man who has not opened his Bible all week and intends to trust the Spirit at eleven o’clock on Sunday. Paul, who lived through more of these trials than anyone, is also the man who told Timothy to do his best to present himself to God as one approved, rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15), and Peter tells every believer to be prepared to make a defence (1 Peter 3:15). And it is not a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen made the longest recorded speech in Acts under exactly this promise and was stoned at the end of it. What is promised is not acquittal. It is that the right words will be there.

The ordinary comfort. The actual comfort is worth naming for a much more ordinary situation than a courtroom. The dread of not knowing what to say, at a hospital bedside, in a conversation that has suddenly turned serious, in front of someone hostile, is one of the commonest reasons Christians stay quiet. The promise here is not that you will be eloquent. It is that in the hour, and not before it, you will not be alone in the room.

In a sentence. When believers are put on trial for Christ, they need not worry about their defence, because the Holy Spirit will teach them what to say.

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians standing trial today, that the Spirit would give them words; find one name or country and pray for it specifically. And when you dread a conversation about Christ, prepare what you can, then go into it trusting that you will not be alone. Short, true and kind is enough.

For worship. The Spirit who hovered over the waters, who spoke by the prophets, and who filled Jesus at the Jordan, stands beside the weakest believer in the dock. Christ himself stood silent before his accusers so that we might never stand alone before ours. The church has never lacked a defender, because its Defender is God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Parable of the Rich Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man interrupts a discourse on hell and martyrdom to ask for help with a family estate — and it was not an unreasonable request in that world, since rabbis routinely arbitrated inheritance disputes. But notice what he actually asks: not “settle the dispute between us” but “tell my brother.” He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Jesus refuses, and the address is cold — “Man,” not “friend” — with an echo of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt (Ex. 2:14). Then he diagnoses the plaintiff and says it to the whole crowd, so the man is not singled out: “be on your guard against all covetousness.” Not merely the greed a man would recognise as greed, but every form of it — including the perfectly legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed. This man had a case. He may well have been in the right.

The parable is not a warning against prosperity or against prudent planning. Notice how it opens: not “a rich man made a fortune” but “the land produced.” He did not do it. The harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange — which is the first thing he forgets.

Then the pronouns. In three verses of soliloquy he says I or my eleven times, and God is mentioned by nobody but God. There is no wife in this man's head, no labourers, no neighbour, and above all no giver. The question “what shall I do?” had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. There were poor people within a mile of that farm.

And then the strangest thing in the parable: he opens a conversation with his own soul, which is what a person does when there is nobody else — and tells it that its needs have been met by grain. Every clause is a category error. Ample goods; many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry. He is treating the ache of the soul as a supply problem.

The thing to see is that it very nearly works. He is not miserable. He had done it, and he was content, and he went to bed satisfied. And God's first word is “Fool.”
verseByVerse.theology:
“Fool” in Hebrew thought is not an insult about intelligence. The fool of the Psalms is the man who says in his heart “there is no God” (Ps. 14:1) — which is not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist. He simply ran his entire life without reference to anybody but himself.

“This night your soul is required of you” — demanded back, as a lender demands what is his. Which reframes everything he has said. He has spent the parable talking about what is his, and the soul he was addressing turns out to have been on loan the whole time.

And note the timing against his own words: he said “many years,” God says “this night.” The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

“Rich toward God” is the positive alternative and one of the most compact phrases in Luke. It is worth noticing that the alternative is not poverty. Jesus does not say “so is the one who is rich.” He says “so is the one who lays up treasure for himself” — rich in the wrong direction. To be rich toward God is to live in the awareness that every good thing was received and is to be used toward his purposes; the opposite is to treat what one has as one's own achievement, for one's own use, accountable to nobody.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man's problem is not the abundance; it is the accounting. He has a genuine agricultural difficulty and his solution is reasonable, practical, and completely self-oriented. There are exactly two things a man can do with a surplus — distribute it or store it — and he never considers the first. He demolishes serviceable barns to build larger ones, which is a considerable investment of time and money in the business of retention.

Watch also what happens to the ownership across the parable. It begins as “the land” producing. It becomes “my barns,” “my grain,” “my goods.”

“And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” is left unanswered, and it is devastating precisely because everyone knows the answer is “somebody else's.” He tore down good barns for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once in five verses.

Which leaves a test that takes about a minute and is uncomfortable. Not “how much have I got?” but: if my accumulation were described out loud by somebody else, in whose direction would it be pointing?

verseByVerse.quote: Someone in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.' But he said to him, 'Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?' And he said to them, 'Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Someone in the crowd said to him: Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. But he said to him: man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? And he said to them: take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.

Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. It is one of the strangest interruptions in the Gospels. Jesus has just been talking about hell, martyrdom, the unforgivable sin and the courts, and a man in the crowd wants help with a family estate. It was not an unreasonable request in that world. Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes, and the law had detailed provisions, with the eldest son taking a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). Perhaps the elder brother was refusing to divide the estate. Notice, though, what the man actually asks for. Not settle the dispute between us. Tell my brother. He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? The address is cool, man, not friend, and the refusal is flat. And there is an echo in it of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt: who made you a prince and a judge over us? (Exodus 2:14). Why refuse? Not because the grievance was necessarily unjust; Jesus never enquires. He declines because this is not what he came to do. He did not come to sort out property disputes, but to deal with the heart, and becoming the arbiter of one man’s estate would have made him a functionary in somebody’s dispute rather than the Lord of both brothers. The man’s real problem is not his brother, but his greed.

Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness. He refuses the case and diagnoses the plaintiff, and then turns to the whole crowd and says it to everybody, so the man is not singled out. Two warnings, doubled for emphasis: watch out, and guard yourselves. It is the language for a threat that is not obvious. “Covetousness” (pleonexia) is the desire for more, greed. And all covetousness: every kind, including the respectable kinds, not merely the greed a man would recognise as greed, but the perfectly legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed. Covetousness is a sin people rarely confess. It is forbidden by the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17), and Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5). That is the sting. This man had a case. He may well have been in the right. And what Jesus saw, watching him push through a crowd of thousands to raise it, was not a wronged brother but a man whose grip had closed.

For one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions. Life is not measured by what you own. Possessions cannot give life, or keep it, or satisfy it. True life is found in God.

Is it wrong to seek justice in a money dispute? Not in itself. Scripture values justice, and Paul himself appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 25:11). There are times when a fair settlement should be sought, especially to protect the vulnerable. But Jesus’ warning cuts close to every inheritance quarrel: ask what is happening in your heart. Is the money worth the brother? Christians should be slow to take one another to court (1 Corinthians 6:1–8), quick to seek reconciliation, and willing, sometimes, to be wronged rather than lose a relationship. Where you must pursue a claim, pursue it without bitterness, and be ready to let go of more than you think you can.

In a sentence. Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, Jesus refused and warned against all greed, because life does not consist in an abundance of possessions.

On a Tuesday. Is there a possession or an amount of money you think would make your life complete? Guard your heart against greed. Where this saying applies: the quiet resentment over who got what in a will, the endless browsing for the next upgrade, the sense that a little more would finally be enough. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to shame a widow for seeking what she needs to live, or to tell a poor family that wanting a decent wage is covetous. Greed is the grip, not the need.

For worship. The Lord who would not divide this man’s inheritance has given his people an inheritance that cannot be divided, an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). He is himself our portion. And he who owned everything became poor, so that brothers who quarrel over fields might become fellow heirs of a kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes. The law gave the eldest son a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable, saying, 'The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable, saying: the land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself: what shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?

Only Luke. Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool.

The land of a rich man produced plentifully. Notice how the parable opens. Not a rich man made a fortune. The land produced. He did not do it. He may have ploughed and sown and hired well, but the harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange, under a sun he had no hand in. A good harvest is God’s gift: he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons (Acts 14:17). Every Israelite knew this; it is why the firstfruits were brought to the temple, and why the law required the edges of the field to be left for the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10). He was already rich, and God gave him more. And it is the first thing the man will forget.

And he thought to himself. Literally he dialogued with himself. He talks only to himself: not to God, not to his neighbours, not to the poor. There is nobody else in this man’s head. No wife, no children, no labourers who brought the harvest in, no neighbour, and above all no Giver. And there is something almost claustrophobic in the phrase, because the whole discussion of what to do with an enormous surplus takes place inside one man’s skull. He has more than he can hold and nobody to talk to about it, which is not an accident of the story. It is what the surplus has done to him.

What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops? His problem is real. He is not a fraud or an oppressor; the parable gives him no vices at all. He is a competent farmer with a genuine logistical difficulty, and the question he asks is the sensible one. A good question, with a wrong answer. The question had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. He could have shared with the poor (3:11); there were poor people within a mile of that farm. Notice: my crops. Everything is mine. In the three verses of his soliloquy he will say I or my again and again, and God will be mentioned by nobody but God.

A decent man. One further thing is worth registering before the parable turns. Jesus does not say the man was dishonest. He is not an oppressor, not a swindler, not a defrauder of labourers, which would have been the easy way to tell it, and would have let every hearer off. He is a competent farmer having a good year. That is the whole of his character, and it is precisely why the parable is dangerous. It removes every handhold a decent person might reach for.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man whose land produced a huge harvest, who asked himself what to do with it.

On a Tuesday. When God blesses you with more than you need, ask him what to do with it, not just yourself. The pay rise, the bonus, the inheritance, the unexpected refund: before it is absorbed into a larger lifestyle, stop and ask God and someone wise what it is for. Notice too who is in your head when you make money decisions. If the answer is only you, invite others in.

For worship. Every good harvest is a letter from God. He sends rain on the just and the unjust, crowns the year with his bounty, and fills our hearts with food and gladness. And beyond every harvest stands the Giver himself, who did not keep his riches to himself but gave his Son. The God of abundance is the God of open hands.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool.

parallels.desc: I must leave it to the man who comes after me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.

I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones. The solution is entirely rational and entirely revealing. He has a surplus. There are exactly two things a man can do with a surplus: distribute it or store it. He never considers the first. And note that he does not merely keep the barns he has and fill them. He demolishes serviceable buildings in order to construct larger ones, which is a considerable investment of time and money in the business of retention. More storage for more stuff. In this short speech, I and my come over and over: utterly self-centred. And notice what has quietly happened to the ownership. It began as the land producing (v. 16). It is now my barns, my grain, my goods.

And I will say to my soul. This is the sentence the parable is built to reach, and it is the strangest thing in it. The man opens a conversation with his own soul, as if it could be satisfied with grain. That is what a person does when there is nobody else. He has been talking to himself for two verses, and now he addresses the last available party, and what he tells his soul is that its needs have been met.

Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry. Take the promise apart, because every clause is a category error. Ample goods: quantity, offered as an answer to a soul. Laid up for many years: a guarantee about a future he does not own; he assumes he has many years. Relax, eat, drink, be merry: comfort, appetite and cheerfulness, which are all real goods and not one of which a soul can live on. It is the philosophy of the world: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (Isaiah 22:13; 1 Corinthians 15:32). He is doing what every wealthy society trains its people to do: treating the ache of the soul as a supply problem, and answering it with more. Retirement as the goal of life. And the thing to see is that it very nearly works. He is not miserable. There is no suggestion that he was unhappy or unfulfilled or secretly hollow. He had done it, and he was content, and he went to bed satisfied.

Was his sin saving and planning ahead? No. Scripture commends the ant that stores up food in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8), and a man who does not provide for his family has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). The rich fool’s sin was not the barns but the heart: everything was my crops, my barns, my goods, his future taken for granted and God left out. Saving for old age is wise; living as if the savings were your life is folly.

Is it wrong to look forward to retirement? Not at all. Rest after a lifetime of work is a good gift, and age brings real limits. The question is what retirement is for. The rich fool’s plan was to stop being useful and start consuming. A Christian’s later years can be some of his most fruitful: time to pray, to serve the church, to help grandchildren and neighbours, to give generously, to mentor younger believers. Plan for rest, enjoy it with thanks, and keep asking how you can be rich toward God with the time and money you have saved.

In a sentence. The rich man planned to build bigger barns to store everything for himself, and then to tell his soul to relax and enjoy itself for many years.

On a Tuesday. Are your plans for the future all about I and my? Bring God and others into them. Look at your pension, your savings, your long-term goals, and ask a simple question: whom is this for? Where this applies: a plan that hoards, assumes many years, and leaves God out. Where applying it would be wrong: shaming a careful family for saving for their children’s needs or their own old age, which Scripture commends.

For worship. Our souls were never made to be satisfied with grain. God made us for himself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in him. And he has spread a feast for the soul that no barn could hold: the bread of life, broken for us; the living water, poured out for us. Whoever comes to him shall not hunger.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God said to him: fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

But God said to him, Fool! The first word God speaks in this parable is the last word the man expected, and the timing is the whole point: it comes in the same breath as be merry. He had left God out of his plans. Now God speaks. He has not been called wicked. He is called a fool, and in the Bible that is not an insult about intelligence. The fool is the one who says in his heart, there is no God (Psalm 14:1): one who lives as if there were no God. That is not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist. He was clever, successful and prudent by the world’s standards. He simply ran his entire life and made every plan as if God did not exist, and as if he would never die.

This night your soul is required of you. “Required” (apaitousin) is a financial word: demanded back, as a loan is recalled. That reframes everything the man has said. He has spent the parable talking about what is his, and the soul he was addressing turns out to have been on loan the whole time, lent to him by God, and it is being called in tonight. Note the timing against his own words. He said many years. God says this night. The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

And the things you have prepared, whose will they be? The question is left unanswered, and it is devastating precisely because everyone knows the answer is somebody else’s. He cannot take any of it with him (Psalm 49:16–17; Ecclesiastes 2:18–19; 1 Timothy 6:7). He tore down good barns to build larger ones for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once. Perhaps it went to the very kind of inheritance dispute that began this conversation (v. 13).

So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. The two phrases define each other. For himself is the diagnosis; rich toward God is the alternative. And the alternative is not poverty. Jesus does not say so is the one who is rich. He says so is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God: rich in the wrong direction. To be rich toward God is to use what you have for him: for his kingdom, for the poor, for eternal treasure (v. 33; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). Not wealth itself, but wealth hoarded for oneself, is the folly.

What does being rich toward God look like? It begins with knowing God himself as your treasure, and then it shows in how you use everything else. It means giving regularly and generously to the church and to gospel work; caring for the poor and the stranger; being hospitable; supporting family members in need; and holding your possessions as a steward, ready to release them. It also includes being rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:18): time, attention and love spent on others. A poor widow with two small coins can be richer toward God than a millionaire (21:1–4).

In a sentence. God called the rich man a fool, for his life was demanded that very night, and his hoard would go to others, as it does for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.

On a Tuesday. If tonight were your last night, would you be rich toward God? Use what you have for his purposes today. A test that takes about a minute: if your accumulation were described out loud by somebody else, in whose direction would it be pointing? And make sure your will, your giving and your plans would read differently from the rich fool’s.

For worship. The God who called in the fool’s soul holds every breath we draw. Our times are in his hand. And the Son of God, who was truly rich, made himself poor and laid down his life, so that people who had laid up treasure for themselves might be made rich toward God and rich in him. There is no fool so foolish that Christ cannot make him wise unto salvation.
verseByVerse.note: In the Bible a fool is not unintelligent but one who lives as if there were no God.

parallels.desc: the fool says in his heart, “There is no God”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties this to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson drawn is not “store less” but “worry less” — aimed at a different group. The parable was for a crowd with a covetous man in it; this is for disciples, most of whom had nothing to store. And the two problems are the same underneath: both are attempts to secure a life by managing supplies.

Note what is named — food and clothing, not luxuries. This is spoken to people who might actually go hungry.

The ravens are chosen deliberately. They were unclean under the law (Lev. 11:15), they are scavengers, and there is a psalm about exactly this — “he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry” (Ps. 147:9; cf. Job 38:41). The argument is set at the lowest available point. And the ravens are not idle; they fly all day looking. What they lack is a storehouse.

“Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” is an audit. Anxiety presents itself as responsible — the alert mind doing necessary work — and the question exposes the claim. And then the sharper turn: he calls adding an hour to a life a small thing. From where we stand it is not small at all; it is what a person at a bedside would give everything for. He calls it the little end of the problem.

The lilies are probably the wild anemones that carpet the Galilean hillsides in spring, and the two activities they do not do — toil and spin — were the two halves of a household's labour. And the argument turns hard on where the grass ends up: gathered as fuel, because wood was scarce, and burned in a peasant oven within the week. God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will heat somebody's bread.

Then the alternative, and it is not serenity but a different pursuit: “seek his kingdom.” And behind it the tenderest address in the Gospel — “fear not, little flock” — with a gift that is not a wage but the kingdom itself, given because the Father enjoyed giving it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The argument from ravens and lilies is not an argument for passivity. The ravens still fly; the lilies still grow; the farmer still plants. What is addressed is not the activity of provision but the anxiety about it — the energy spent worrying about what worry cannot secure.

“O you of little faith” is a name Jesus uses only of disciples. It is never aimed at outsiders; nobody is called little-faith who has none. And the diagnosis is worth noting: not “you have too much to do” and not “your circumstances are difficult,” both of which may be true. The problem named is a shortage of faith in the character of a particular Father — which makes anxiety a theological condition rather than a temperamental one.

“Nor be worried” in v.29 names the mind that will not settle — up in the air, unanchored. Anybody who has lain awake at three in the morning will recognise the picture.

“The nations” is not an insult but a description of a real difference. The pagan world had a crowded pantheon of local deities who had to be managed — offerings at the right time, none of them notably fond of you, none reliable. Anxiety in that setting is not a failure of nerve; it is a rational response to the facts as understood. If nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better.

Against which stand seven words: “your Father knows that you need them.” Not a force, not a committee of powers. He knows — so it does not have to be brought to his attention, and a great deal of anxious praying is really lobbying. And the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual.
verseByVerse.examples:
Knowing that anxiety is useless does not cure it. Nobody was ever argued out of worry by being told it achieves nothing; anxious people generally know. What the argument does is clear the ground, so the question becomes the right one: not “how do I stop worrying?” but “what am I going to trust instead?”

“Little flock” is an honest name — a small group in an occupied province with the authorities already hunting their teacher. He does not tell them they are stronger than they look. He tells them who the shepherd is, and the word carries the whole weight of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, where God says “I myself will search for my sheep.” And “good pleasure” means it delighted him.

“Sell your possessions” must be faced, because it is not a metaphor — and Luke supplies the answer across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half and salvation comes to his house that day (19:8-9). The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of means they must therefore still have had. And Peter's rebuke to Ananias turns on it: “while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (Acts 5:4). The selling was never compulsory; the sin was the lie.

So the command is a transfer of ownership, not a rule about percentages. What it can never mean is a Christian who has settled the matter, drawn a line, and considers the rest his own. Ask not what proportion you have given away, but whether there is anything left that you would refuse him.

And “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” reverses the order everyone assumes. We think the heart chooses and the money follows. He says the heart goes after the treasure — which means the affections can be steered, and that there is a reliable way of finding out what you actually love. Not the confession of faith. The bank statement, and the diary.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to his disciples: therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!

Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious. The therefore ties this directly to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson drawn is not store less but worry less, which is a different point, aimed at a different group. The parable was for a crowd with a covetous man in it. This is for disciples, and most of them had nothing to store. The rich fool trusted in his possessions. The poor can be just as preoccupied with possessions, through anxiety. The rich man’s problem and the anxious disciple’s problem look opposite and are the same: both are trying to secure a life by managing supplies. Both are forms of unbelief.

Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. “Anxious” (merimnate) means worried, divided in mind, distracted: the same word as Martha’s (10:41), and the same danger as the thorns that choke the word in the parable of the soils, the cares and riches and pleasures of life (8:14). Food and clothing are not luxuries but the two irreducible necessities, and for most of his hearers a genuine daily question. This is not a rebuke to the comfortable for fretting about trivialities. It is spoken to people who might actually go hungry.

For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. A short sentence doing heavy work. God gave you life and a body, the greater gifts; will he not give the lesser ones? Whatever life is, it is not the sum of what sustains it, and the proof is that a man can have all the food and clothing he needs and be, as the last parable showed, a fool who dies that night.

Consider the ravens. “Consider”: look carefully, think about it. The choice of bird is not random and would have registered. Ravens were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:15), scavengers, the least regarded. Matthew says birds of the air (Matthew 6:26); Luke names the bird nobody wanted. And there is a psalm about exactly this: he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry (Psalm 147:9); Job is asked, who provides for the raven its prey? (Job 38:41).

They neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Unlike the rich fool with his barns. So the argument is deliberately set at the lowest available point. If God feeds the birds nobody wants, on ground he owns, without a barn between them, how much more his children.

Of how much more value are you than the birds! If God feeds unclean ravens, how much more his children.

What it does not mean. Not that we should not work or plan. The ravens are not idle; they fly all day looking. What they do not have is a storehouse. Paul says: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). The point is not idleness but trust: work, but do not worry. The verse is not against work. It is against the belief that security comes from the size of the reserve.

Is anxiety a sin, then, and is every anxious believer of little faith? Jesus is speaking to worry about food and clothing that springs from not trusting the Father. But some anxiety has roots in the body and the mind, and it is a real illness. Elijah despaired (1 Kings 19:4), the psalmist wrestled with his troubled soul (Psalm 77), and they were not cast off. Seeking help from a doctor or counsellor is not a lack of faith. The command still invites every anxious believer to bring the fear to the Father who knows what we need (v. 30).

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to worry about food or clothing, for life is more than these, and God, who feeds even the ravens, values them far more.

On a Tuesday. What are you anxious about? Consider the ravens: God feeds them; he will feed you. Where this saying applies: the late-night spiral about bills you have already planned for, the fear that God will not provide when he always has, the constant checking of a balance that has not changed. Where applying it would be wrong: telling someone with a diagnosed anxiety disorder that they simply need more faith, or telling a family with no food to stop worrying instead of helping them. The church is often the Father’s answer to the raven’s cry.

For worship. The Lord who feeds the ravens has never once forgotten a single bird. He opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing (Psalm 145:16). And the Father who feeds scavengers fed his Son’s people in the wilderness with manna, and feeds them still with the bread of heaven. We are of more value than the birds: the price of the Son proves it.
verseByVerse.note: Ravens were unclean birds — yet God feeds them.

parallels.desc: he gives to the young ravens that cry

verseByVerse.quote: And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?

And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? Having argued from the birds, he now argues from the results, and the question is not rhetorical decoration. It is an audit. Anxiety makes an implicit claim. It presents itself as responsible, as the alert mind doing necessary work on a problem, and it feels like a form of preparation. The question exposes the claim. What has it ever produced? The ESV notes that the phrase can also be read a single cubit to his stature, about eighteen inches to a height. Either way the answer is the same: not one person in the history of the world has ever managed it by worrying. It cannot lengthen your life (if anything, it shortens it), or make you taller.

If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? And there is the second turn, the sharper one. He calls adding an hour to a life a small thing. Read that again, because it inverts the whole scale. From where we stand, an extra hour of life is not a small thing at all; it is precisely what a person at a bedside would give everything for. Jesus calls it the little end of the problem, and if a man cannot manage the little end, the anxiety about food and clothing is aimed at something he is even less able to control. Worry is useless. It does not change tomorrow; it only spoils today. And it forgets God, who controls what we cannot.

Clearing the ground. This is the actual argument, and it is not a comfort exactly. It is a demolition. Anxiety is not being described as unpleasant or unhealthy, though both are true. It is being described as ineffective: a machine that runs continuously, consumes an enormous amount of fuel, and produces nothing. And knowing that does not cure it. Nobody was ever argued out of worry by being told it was useless; anxious people generally know. What the argument does is clear the ground, so that the question becomes the right one: not how do I stop worrying? but what am I going to trust instead? The next verses answer that, and the answer is not a technique. It is a Father.
