What is the difference between worry and responsible concern? Concern looks at a real problem, does what can be done, and then leaves the rest with God. Worry keeps turning the problem over long after anything can be done, and treats the turning as if it were doing something. A parent who books a doctor for a sick child is concerned; a parent who lies awake rehearsing every terrible outcome is worried. Paul’s cure is specific: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:6–7). Do the next thing, pray about the rest, and give thanks.

In a sentence. Worry cannot add a single hour to your life, so if you cannot do something so small, why worry about anything else?

On a Tuesday. Has worrying ever changed anything? Take the thing you are anxious about and divide it into two lists: what I can do today, and what only God can do. Do the first list. Pray over the second, by name, and then deliberately give thanks for one thing. Give your worries to God in prayer instead.

For worship. Our days are numbered by God, not by us. He wrote every one of them in his book before one of them came to be (Psalm 139:16), and not one hour can be added or taken without him. The Lord who holds the span of our lives laid down his own life at the appointed hour, and took it up again. Our times are in his hand, and his hand was pierced for us.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.”

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!

Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin. Consider: study them, take them in properly. The lilies are probably not the cultivated flower but the wild blooms that carpet the Galilean hillsides in spring with brilliant colour: anemones most likely, irises, poppies, scarlet and brief. And the two activities named are the two halves of a household’s labour in that world: men toiled in the field, women spun thread for cloth. Making clothes was hard work: spinning thread, weaving cloth. The flowers do neither, which is to say they do not work for a living and they do not make their own clothes.

Yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Solomon is the highest available standard, the richest, most splendid king in Israel’s history. His court was so magnificent that a foreign queen was left breathless (1 Kings 10:4–5), and the phrase in all his glory is the summit of what human wealth can dress a man in. And a weed on a hillside beats it: a flower that grew where the seed happened to fall, was dressed by nobody, and will be gone in a fortnight. His royal robes were nothing compared with the beauty God gives a wildflower.

But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. Now the argument turns hard, and the detail is deliberately unglamorous. Those hillsides dried out; the stalks were gathered as fuel, because wood was scarce, and a peasant’s clay oven was fired with dead grass and thorns. They last a day. So the sequence is: God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will be burned to heat somebody’s bread. Not preserved, not admired, not even noticed by most people who walked past. Burned, within the week.

How much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! You are eternal; they are temporary. The rebuke at the end is gentle, and it is a rebuke. Little-faith ones is a single word, one Jesus uses only of disciples. It is never aimed at outsiders. Nobody is called little-faith who has none. Anxiety is a sign of little faith: not no faith, but small faith that does not take God at his word. And notice what the diagnosis is. Not you have too much to do, not your circumstances are difficult, both of which may be perfectly true. The problem named is a shortage of faith in the character of a particular Father, which means anxiety is, at root, a theological condition and not only a temperamental one.

How can little faith grow? Not by staring at your faith, but by looking at God. Faith grows as it feeds on his promises and remembers his past faithfulness. Read the Psalms that recount what he has done. Keep a record of answered prayer. Sit under the preaching of his word. Take small steps of obedience that require trust, and watch him keep his word. And pray as the father of the epileptic boy did: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not reject that prayer. He answered it.

In a sentence. If God clothes short-lived wildflowers more beautifully than Solomon, how much more will he clothe his people, who have so little faith.

On a Tuesday. Look at a flower today and remember: your Father clothes it, and he will clothe you. When you worry about how you look, what you can afford, or whether your children will have enough, go and look at the hedgerow. Then say to him plainly what you are afraid of, and thank him for the last time he provided.

For worship. The God who paints anemones for a single week has clothed his people in something better than Solomon’s robes: the righteousness of Christ, a garment of salvation, a robe that will never wear out or be thrown in the oven. He takes delight in beauty, and he has determined to make his people beautiful for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.

And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink. Do not make these the goal of your life.

Nor be worried. The word is curious: meteōrizesthe, used in Greek of a ship tossed on the swell, or of something suspended in mid-air; it is where the English meteor comes from. To be up in the air, unanchored, in suspense, going wherever the next wave puts you. Anybody who has lain awake at three in the morning will recognise the picture with some precision. The mind is not thinking; it is being moved about.

For all the nations of the world seek after these things. The nations is the standard Jewish term for the Gentiles, the peoples outside the covenant, and it is not being used as an insult. It is a description of a real difference in situation. Consider what the pagan world actually had: a crowded pantheon of local deities who had to be managed, gods of the harvest, of the weather, of the household, each requiring the right offering at the right time, none of them notably fond of you, and none of them reliable. Provision had to be negotiated, and the negotiation never ended. Anxiety, in that setting, is not a failure of nerve. It is a rational response to the facts as they were understood. If nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better. The pagans, who do not know God as Father, live for food, drink and clothing. It is all they have. Worry about possessions is pagan, not Christian.

And your Father knows that you need them. The decisive reason, and every word of it bears weight. Your Father: not a force, not a committee of powers, not a proprietor; the word he taught them to pray with (11:2). You are not an orphan in a hostile world. Knows: so it does not have to be brought to his attention. A great deal of anxious praying is really lobbying, conducted on the assumption that the case has not yet been properly presented. That you need them: the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual. He does not say the disciples are above such things. Food and drink are real needs, and he says so. That is the whole answer, and it is not a technique for calming down. It is a fact about who is in charge of the supply, offered to people who had been living as though nobody was.

If my Father already knows, why pray about my needs? Because he tells us to ask: give us each day our daily bread (11:3). Prayer is not briefing God; it is trusting him out loud. Asking reminds us that every meal is a gift, keeps us dependent, and turns anxiety into conversation. The difference between pagan prayer and Christian prayer is not that one asks and the other does not. It is that the pagan asks in order to persuade a reluctant power, and the Christian asks as a child whose Father already knows and already cares.

In a sentence. Do not make food and drink your goal or worry about them, as the pagans do, for your Father knows you need them.

On a Tuesday. Notice where your worries sound exactly like those of people who do not know God. Then talk to your Father about them as a child, not a lobbyist. Your Father knows exactly what you need. Thank him today, and trust him with tomorrow.

For worship. We are not orphans in a universe of indifferent powers. We have a Father in heaven who knows every need before we ask, who has numbered our days and counted our hairs, and who has shown his heart by giving his Son. The gods of the nations had to be bargained with. Our Father gives freely, and delights to.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. 'Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.

Instead, seek his kingdom. Make God’s reign the goal and centre of your life. Matthew adds: and his righteousness (Matthew 6:33). This is not something extra special, but an ordinary life lived God’s way, asking first what he wants (see the note on Matthew 6:33).

Not seek nothing. The energy is not to be switched off; it is to be redirected. He has just said the nations seek after food and drink, and now uses the same verb: go after this instead. That matters, because the alternative to anxiety in this passage is not serenity. It is a different pursuit. A man who has stopped chasing security and started chasing the kingdom has not become calmer by relaxation; he has become calmer because his attention has gone somewhere it can actually get purchase. And the pursuit is ordinary: the next duty done for him, the next choice made his way, the next person loved because he loves them.

And these things will be added to you. Food and clothing, as extras. Not riches, but what you need. God gives the kingdom, and throws the rest in. Added is the language of a bonus thrown in on top of a transaction: not the object of the deal, but not withheld either. It is worth guarding this from a promise it does not make. It is not an undertaking that a Christian will never be hungry. Paul knew what it was to be in need and to go without (Philippians 4:12), and Hebrews remembers believers who were destitute (Hebrews 11:37). What is promised is that the Father who knows will not forget, not that the provision will always look like comfort.

Fear not, little flock. Only Luke records this tender saying. Of all the things Jesus called his disciples, this is the tenderest. Little flock is an honest name: a small, weak, vulnerable group in an occupied province, with the religious establishment already hunting their teacher, like sheep among wolves (10:3). He does not tell them they are stronger than they look. He tells them who the shepherd is. The word flock carries the whole weight of Psalm 23, of Isaiah 40:11, where he gathers the lambs in his arms, and of Ezekiel 34, where God says he himself will search for his sheep. Jesus is their shepherd, and God is their shepherd.

For it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom. “Good pleasure” (eudokēsen): it delighted him; his gracious will. The same root as the voice at the Jordan, with you I am well pleased (3:22). God is not reluctant. He delights to give. And the gift is not a wage or a supplement. It is the kingdom, the whole of it, the thing they had been told to seek, handed over to a frightened handful because their Father enjoyed doing it. If he gives you the kingdom, will he not give you bread? He who did not spare his own Son, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Romans 8:32). A man who is given a kingdom by somebody who enjoyed giving it has been told everything he needs to know about whether his next meal is in doubt.

So what does seeking the kingdom look like on an ordinary day? Mostly it looks like the day you already have, lived under a different King. At breakfast it is thanking him and asking what he wants of you today. At work it is honest effort and fair dealing, done as for the Lord. At home it is patience with a tired spouse and time for a child. In money it is giving first and spending carefully. When you are wronged it is forgiveness; when you fail it is confession. It also means gathering with his people on the Lord’s Day and sharing Christ when the door opens. It rarely feels dramatic. It is ordinary walking in God’s will, one decision at a time, with his kingdom, not your comfort, as the question you ask first.

In a sentence. Seek God’s kingdom, and he will add what you need, so do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father delights to give you the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Before your next decision today, a purchase, a reply, a plan for the evening, ask first: what does my King want here? Where this saying applies: the choice between a promotion that would swallow your family and church life and a slower path that keeps them; the decision to give before you spend. Where applying it would be wrong: thinking you must leave your job for full-time ministry to really seek the kingdom, or neglecting your family’s needs for a church project. The kingdom is sought in the ordinary calling God has given you.

For worship. Your Father delights to give you the kingdom. Rest in his good pleasure, and seek his kingdom first today. The Shepherd who calls us little flock is the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep, and the Father who gives the kingdom gives it gladly, because it pleased him to. We do not earn it, we do not bargain for it, we do not fight for it. We are given it, by a Father who smiles as he gives.

parallels.desc: he will tend his flock like a shepherd
the kingdom given to the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. The command has to be faced, because it is not a metaphor. It is the opposite of the rich fool. Since God gives you the kingdom, you are free to give away earthly things, and some early Christians did exactly this (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–37). Does the Lord require every Christian to liquidate everything?

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must sell everything. The rich ruler was told to (18:22); Zacchaeus gave half (19:8); the women of 8:3 used their means to support Jesus. The early church’s sharing was voluntary (Acts 5:4). But every Christian must hold possessions loosely, give generously, and be willing to sell anything for Christ.

A transfer of ownership. Luke is the last man to let us dodge the question, and he is also the one who supplies the answer, spread across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half his goods, and Jesus says salvation has come to his house that very day (19:8–9): half, not all, and it was accepted. The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of their means, which they must therefore still have had. Martha keeps a house he visits and is glad of. And in Acts, when Ananias lies about the price of a field, Peter’s rebuke turns on this: while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? (Acts 5:4). The selling was never compulsory; the sin was the lie. So the command is not a rule about percentages. It is a transfer of ownership. The disciple is not asked to reach a particular balance and stop; he is asked to stop being the owner, so that whatever is still in his hands is held at the Master’s disposal and can go the moment it is called for. For one man that will mean selling the lot, as it did for the rich ruler, precisely because his possessions owned him. For another it will mean an open house, a funded ministry, a quietly emptied account nobody hears about. What it can never mean is a Christian who has settled the matter, drawn a line, and considers the rest his own.

Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old. Leather purses wore out and got holes. Note that he is not against investment. He is against bad investment.

With a treasure in the heavens that does not fail. What is given to God and the poor is stored up in heaven, safe for ever (1 Timothy 6:18–19). Treasure in heaven is mostly ordinary: kindness, generosity, faithful work and care for others, done for Christ (see the note on Matthew 6:20).

Where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat, or as coins and goods, which thieves could steal. The three things that destroyed stored wealth in that world, the purse that wears through, the thief and the moth in the stored cloth, are simply named, and an alternative offered.

For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. Your heart follows your treasure. What you spend money on shows what you love, and also shapes what you love. And here is the reason this is in a chapter about anxiety, and it is the most practically useful sentence in it. The order is not what anyone expects. We assume the heart chooses and the money follows. He says the opposite: the heart goes to where the treasure already is, and it follows it there. That means the affections can be steered, and that the steering wheel is a chequebook. A man who cannot make himself care about something can move his money into it and find, some months later, that his heart has gone after it. Invest in heaven, and your heart will be drawn there. It also means there is a reliable way of finding out what you actually love, as distinct from what you say you love. Not the confession of faith. The bank statement, and the diary.

How much should I give, and to whom? The New Testament sets no fixed figure, but it asks for regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7). Begin with your own church, which feeds you; then the needy around you, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10); then gospel work further afield. Many find a tenth a wise starting point and grow from there. Give in a way that costs you something, plan it rather than leaving it to impulse, and do it quietly. If you are in debt or poverty, give what you can with a glad heart; the widow’s two coins counted most of all.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to sell their possessions and give to the poor, storing up lasting treasure in heaven, because the heart follows the treasure.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement. Where is your treasure? Give something away today, and see your heart follow. Where this applies: the possession you could not bear to lose, the account you never touch, the room full of things you have not used in years. Where applying it would be wrong: selling the family home without your spouse’s agreement, giving away what your children need to live, or treating a tired single mother’s modest savings as a sin. Hold everything open-handed, and let love, not guilt, decide what goes.

For worship. The Lord who told us to sell our possessions sold everything himself. He left the riches of heaven, had nowhere to lay his head, and was stripped of his last garment at the cross. And because he did, we have a treasure in heaven that does not fail, kept for us by him, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. He is the treasure. Where he is, our hearts are drawn.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three parables of readiness, and they describe the church living between the two advents.

“Stay dressed for action” is, as the ESV margin gives it, “let your loins stay girded” — the long outer robe pulled up and tucked into the belt, so that a man could run or work. It has a history: Israel ate the first Passover with belts fastened and sandals on, dressed to leave a country that night (Ex. 12:11). And the lamp kept burning through the dark hours required somebody awake to trim the wick — readiness is not a state achieved and possessed but maintained, hourly, by somebody who has not gone to sleep.

The servants are waiting on the night of somebody else's wedding feast, which could run for days. They have no timetable, and their whole readiness reduces to one small thing: whether the door opens at once. Not whether they achieved anything in his absence. Whether, when he knocked, somebody was still expecting him.

Then the sentence nothing in the ancient world prepares anybody for: he will gird himself, sit them at his table, and serve them. That does not happen — the whole architecture of that society rested on the distinction between those who recline and those who serve. And Luke proves it is not a flourish: “I am among you as the one who serves” (22:27), and on the same night John records him tying a towel round himself and washing feet (John 13:4-5).

The watches named are the second and third — roughly ten till two, and two till dawn. Not the early evening when staying up is easy, and not the last hour when the end is in sight. The dead middle, which is where most Christian waiting is actually done.

The thief image changes the register entirely: same arrival, opposite colour, and the difference is wholly in the state of the person inside. The walls were mud brick; a thief had no need to force the door.

Peter asks whether the parable is for the Twelve or for everyone, and gets no answer — only another parable, this one specifically about a man with responsibility over others. So the answer is yes, especially you, but not in the direction the question hoped.
verseByVerse.theology:
The returning master who serves his watching servants is the most counter-cultural image of authority in the ancient world. It is the enacted theology of the whole ministry — “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45) — and of the ascended Lord who gives the Spirit, intercedes, and prepares a place. He has never stopped serving those he loves.

The oikonomos of v.42 is a steward, usually himself a slave, placed over the household with the keys and the accounts. He owns nothing and can be dismissed. And his one named duty is not “increase the estate” or “keep order” but “give them their portion of food at the proper time” — which is the same commission Peter himself will receive on a beach: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep (John 21:15-17).

Two adjectives govern it. Faithful — trustworthy with what is not his; and wise — the practical sense to know what the household needs and when. Either without the other is useless.

The reward for faithfulness is startling in its logic: he is set over all the master's possessions. The reward for a job well done is a bigger job — not release from service, not a pension. Which cuts against a picture most people carry without examining it: the New Testament nowhere describes the life to come as retirement. Its images are of reigning, of serving, of being given cities to look after (19:17).

And the unknown hour is the arrangement, not an inconvenience in it. If the hour were knowable, readiness could be scheduled — and everyone would schedule it late, which is exactly what the wicked servant does when he concludes the master is delayed.
verseByVerse.examples:
The servant's ruin begins with a private conclusion about a timetable, said “to himself.” There is no moment of rebellion. And the conclusion is not even wrong — the master is delayed. What is wrong is what he does with an accurate observation.

Then two directions, and they are the two ways a leader goes bad. He turns on the household — and these are his fellow servants, not his property. Authority given to feed people is used to hit them, which does not usually involve fists: the pulpit used to settle a score, the discipline that is really about control, the counselling relationship in which one person is always the one who has to change. And he turns to himself: “eat and drink and get drunk,” an echo of the rich fool's “relax, eat, drink, be merry.” The food he was appointed to distribute is going down his own throat.

The two beatings settle something readers often pass over. Scripture does not teach that judgement is a single undifferentiated verdict falling equally on everyone; it teaches degrees (cf. 10:12-14). Perfect justice is exact, and exactness means proportion. But note what is not said: the second servant is not acquitted. Ignorance reduces the sentence; it does not produce innocence.

And the closing principle falls hardest not on the ignorant but on the well-taught. The wording — “was given,” “they entrusted” — points past the servant to the one who gave, which means every item is a deposit and not an achievement: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible, a church down the road, forty years of clear preaching. None of them is a reward. Every one raises the bar. A lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter; it is an account.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.

Readiness for Christ’s return. From possessions, Jesus turns to his return. The two are linked: those who store up treasure on earth are not ready for him, and those whose treasure is in heaven are already leaning toward the day it is opened.

Stay dressed for action. Two images, and both are physical. The first is literally let your loins stay girded, as the ESV notes. Men wore a long outer robe, and to do anything requiring movement, running, working, fighting, it had to be pulled up and tucked into the belt. To be girded was to be unable to lounge. The dress itself was a decision. And it has a history. Israel ate the first Passover with belts fastened, sandals on their feet and staff in hand (Exodus 12:11), dressed to leave a country that night. Jesus is putting his disciples in the posture of a people about to be brought out.

And keep your lamps burning. The second image is a lamp kept burning through the dark hours, which required somebody awake to trim the wick and top up the oil. A lamp does not stay lit by itself, and that is the point of using it. Readiness is not a state a person achieves and then possesses; it is maintained, hourly, by somebody who has not gone to sleep.

And be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast. The picture is a household staff on the night of somebody else’s celebration. A wedding feast in that world could run for days, and there was no way to know which night the master would come back or at what hour. The servants have no timetable. What they have is a duty that continues regardless.

So that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. Not keeping him waiting. The whole of their readiness reduces to one small thing: whether the door opens at once. That is the test the parable sets, and it is a modest one. Not whether they achieved anything in his absence. Not whether they were impressive. Whether, when he knocked, there was somebody on the other side of the door who was still expecting him.

The delay is built in. It is worth noticing what this implies. There is a delay, it is unspecified, and it is long enough that staying awake is difficult. Jesus builds the waiting into the parable from the start. He never suggested it would be short.

What does being ready actually mean? Not living in a constant state of alarm, or giving up ordinary work to watch the sky. It means being a true believer, trusting Christ now, with nothing between you and him that you would be ashamed for him to find. It means keeping short accounts with God and others, confessing sin quickly and putting wrongs right. And it means being about your Master’s business: faithful in the work, the family and the church he has given you. A ready servant may be found asleep in bed at night; what matters is that he is the Master’s, and expecting him.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to be dressed and ready with their lamps lit, like servants waiting to open the door at once when their master returns.

On a Tuesday. Are you ready for Christ’s return, if he came today? Ask what you would want to put right first, the unconfessed sin, the unreconciled friend, the neglected duty, and put it right now. Then go about your ordinary work with your belt fastened, as one who expects a knock.

For worship. The Master is coming home. He went away to prepare a place for us, and he will come again and take us to himself (John 14:3). The long night of waiting has a morning, and the knock will be the voice of the Bridegroom. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the literal wording, “Let your loins stay girded” — the long robe tucked into the belt for work.

parallels.desc: your belt fastened, ready to leave

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!

Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Faithful, watchful. And then the sentence that ought to stop the reader, because nothing in the ancient world prepares anybody for it.

Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. An astonishing reversal. The master ties up his own robe, the same girding the servants were told to do in v. 35, sits them down at his table, and waits on them. Nothing like this happens. Not in Roman households, not in Jewish ones, not anywhere. The whole architecture of that society rested on the distinction between those who recline and those who serve, and it did not bend. A master returning at midnight expects his meal; that is what servants staying up are for (17:7–8). And the Truly, I say to you is Jesus flagging that he knows how this sounds. He uses that formula when he is about to say something the hearer will not otherwise credit.

Picture or promise? Both, and Luke will prove it twice. At the Supper he says it about himself in plain words: who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves (22:27). And on the same night John records him rising from the meal, tying a towel round himself, and washing his disciples’ feet (John 13:4–5), girded, exactly as here. He came not to be served but to serve. So the image is not a flourish. It is what he is like, and it is what he did. The Lord of glory will serve his people at the banquet of the kingdom.

If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! The night was divided into watches, and the second and third covered the middle of the night, roughly nine in the evening to three in the morning. The hardest time to stay awake, and the least expected time to come. Not the early evening when staying up is easy, and not the last hour when the end is in sight. The dead middle. That is where most Christian waiting is actually done. Nobody finds the first years hard. What is hard is year twenty, in the dark, with no sign of anything, holding a lamp. He does not merely say those servants will be commended. He says the master will put on an apron for them.

Will Christ really serve us in heaven, rather than we serving him? Both. Scripture says his servants will worship him (Revelation 22:3), and we will gladly serve him for ever. But the deepest truth of the kingdom is that he serves us first and always: he feeds us at his table, wipes away our tears, and gives us himself. Our service is only ever a response to his. Heaven is not a place where Christ finally gets the reward of being waited on by us. It is the place where we discover the full extent of how he loves to give.

In a sentence. Blessed are the servants the master finds awake, for he himself will serve them at table, however late he comes.

On a Tuesday. If you are in the dead middle of a long night, a long illness, a long wait for a prodigal, a long season of dryness, keep your lamp lit for one more hour. Do the next small faithful thing. The Master who is coming is not a harsh inspector but the one who will tie on an apron and serve you.

For worship. The Lord who will return will serve you at his table. Wait for him with joy. Think of it: the King of kings, before whom angels veil their faces, will gird himself and bring the dishes to tired servants who managed to stay awake. He washed feet on the night he was betrayed; he will serve the feast on the day he returns. There is no master like this Master.
verseByVerse.note: The second and third watches covered the middle of the night.

parallels.desc: he dressed himself and washed their feet

verseByVerse.quote: But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.

But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming. The register changes completely, and it is meant to. A few verses ago the arrival was a master coming home from a wedding, and the servants were waiting to open the door. Now the arrival is a burglary, and the householder is asleep. Same event, opposite emotional colour, and the difference is entirely in the state of the person inside. Thieves do not announce their arrival.

He would not have left his house to be broken into. Literally dug through, which is exact: the walls of an ordinary house were mud brick, and a thief did not force the door. He made a hole in the wall. And note where the argument sits. The householder is not blamed for being asleep at night, which is what nights are for. He is caught out because the one thing he needed, the hour, was the one thing unavailable.

You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. Not that Christ is a thief, but that his coming will be as unexpected. The image is used elsewhere in the New Testament for the same event, and always the same way: the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 3:3; 16:15). It is never about his character. It is about the timing. No one can know the date (Mark 13:32). So be ready always.

Why the hour is hidden. The logic is worth stating plainly, because it cuts through a great deal of unprofitable speculation. If the hour were knowable, the readiness could be scheduled, and everyone would schedule it late. That is precisely what the servant in the next parable does when he concludes the master is delayed. The unknowability is not an inconvenience in the arrangement; it is the arrangement, and it is what makes readiness a way of living rather than a task to be done nearer the time. It is also the standing answer to every attempt to calculate the date. A man who has worked out when the thief is coming has not increased his readiness. He has explained why it can wait. And there is a mercy in it that is easy to miss. Because the hour is unknown, no Christian is ever asked to be ready later. He is only ever asked to be ready now, which is the only thing anybody can actually do.

Will Christ come secretly first and take believers away before the end? This app holds that he will not. The New Testament describes one visible, public return of Christ at the end of the age, when the dead are raised, believers are gathered to him, and the world is judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). His coming is unexpected in its timing, like a thief, but not hidden in its manner: every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). That is why the call is simply to be ready, all the time, for the day itself.

In a sentence. As a homeowner would guard his house if he knew when a thief was coming, so be ready always, because the Son of Man will come when you do not expect.

On a Tuesday. Live each day as if Christ might return today. When you hear someone predicting a date, do not be drawn in; ask instead what you would change if he came this afternoon, and change it. Unknown timing is not a reason for anxiety but for steady faithfulness.

For worship. The Lord who comes at an unexpected hour is the Lord who has never once been late. He came in the fullness of time; he rose on the third day as he said; he will return on the day the Father has fixed. We do not know the hour, but we know the One who is coming, and to those who love his appearing, his coming will be no thief’s surprise but a homecoming.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had walls of mud brick that a thief could dig through.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said, 'Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?' And the Lord said, 'Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said: Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? And the Lord said: who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?

Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? It is a very Petrine question, and Luke keeps it because of what it exposes. What is Peter actually asking? Almost certainly this: is the standard the same for the Twelve as for the crowd, or is there a separate arrangement for us? He has heard a warning about servants and unexpected arrivals, and he wants to know which category he is in.

Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household? Jesus does not answer the question directly. He does something better and more uncomfortable: he tells another parable, and this one is especially for people with responsibility over others. So the answer is yes, it does apply especially to you, Peter, but not in the direction the question was hoping. The manager is an oikonomos, a steward, often himself a trusted slave, but one placed over the whole household and its supplies, with authority to run it (16:1). He held the keys and the accounts. He was not the owner of anything, and he could be dismissed. The word is used of church leaders: stewards of the mysteries of God, of whom it is required that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Titus 1:7).

To give them their portion of food at the proper time. His one named duty is worth pausing on, because it is not what anyone would nominate. Not to increase the estate. Not to keep order. To give them their portion of food at the proper time. Feeding the household. That is the job description of Christian leadership as Jesus states it: to feed God’s household with his word, faithfully and at the right time. It is the same commission Peter himself will be given on a beach three times over: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep (John 21:15–17); and Paul and Peter will hand it on to the elders (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2).

Faithful and wise. Two adjectives govern it. Faithful: trustworthy with what is not his. Wise: the practical sense to know what the household needs and when. Either without the other is useless: a reliable man with no judgement will feed them the wrong thing, and a shrewd one who cannot be trusted will feed himself. And the whole thing turns on at the proper time. The steward is not asked to produce food from nowhere. He is asked to distribute what the master has provided, on time, to people who are hungry now.

If I am not a church leader, is this for me? Yes, in its own measure. Every Christian is a steward of something: a family to feed spiritually as well as physically, a Sunday school class, a friend who looks to you, gifts and money and time (1 Peter 4:10). Parents especially are managers of a household, given the task of feeding their children with God’s word at the proper time. The questions are the same for you as for a pastor: am I faithful with what is not mine, and wise about what the people in my care need now?

In a sentence. When Peter asked whom the parable was for, Jesus described the faithful and wise manager whom the master puts in charge of feeding his household.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who lead your church, that they would be faithful managers, feeding God’s household; tell your pastor this week that you are praying for him. And ask who in your own household or circle is hungry for something from God that you could give them at the proper time: a verse, a prayer, an hour of your attention.

For worship. The Master of the house is himself the bread. He feeds his people with his own body and blood, given for them, and he appoints under-shepherds to set that bread before his household week by week. He never forgets the portion of the smallest servant. The Good Shepherd feeds his flock like a shepherd, and gathers the lambs in his arms.
verseByVerse.note: A household manager was often a trusted slave put in charge of the other servants.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.

Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. The blessing is not attached to results. Not whom his master finds having built up the estate, and not whom the household speaks well of. So doing: not just watching, but still working faithfully at the thing he was left to do, on the day the master happens to arrive. Readiness is faithfulness in the task given. That is a considerable relief to anyone in Christian work, because it removes the metric most people are quietly measuring themselves by. The steward is not accountable for the size of the household or its enthusiasm. He is accountable for whether the food went out on time. And it removes the other anxiety too. He does not have to be found doing something impressive at the moment of arrival. He has to be found doing the ordinary thing, which means the aim is not a heroic finish but an unbroken habit.

Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. The reward is startling, and its logic is worth following. He was set over the household; he is now set over everything. The reward for having been trusted with a job is a bigger job. Not release from service, not a pension, not an easier post: more responsibility, and permanently (19:17). In the kingdom, faithful servants will share Christ’s reign (22:29–30; 2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 3:21).

Not retirement. That tells you something about what heaven is, and it cuts against a picture most people carry without examining it. The New Testament nowhere describes the life to come as idle retirement. Its images are of reigning, of serving, of being given cities to look after (19:17), of a servant entering into his master’s joy, which is the joy of somebody who is still doing something.

All his possessions. There is one further thing in the phrase. The steward began as a slave with no property at all, managing what belonged to another. He ends with the run of the entire estate. Nothing has become his by right; everything has been entrusted to him. That is what being an heir means, and Paul says it in so many words: if children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The man who was faithful with somebody else’s bread is handed the house.

Are rewards in heaven earned? No. Every reward is grace upon grace: God gives the gifts, the strength to use them, and then rewards the use as if it were ours (1 Corinthians 4:7; 15:10). Salvation itself is never earned; it rests on Christ alone. But Scripture does promise real, differing rewards to faithful servants, and Jesus means us to be encouraged by them. There will be no envy in heaven, because every servant will be full, and every crown will be cast at his feet (Revelation 4:10).

In a sentence. Blessed is the servant the master finds faithfully at work when he comes, for he will put him in charge of everything he owns.

On a Tuesday. What has the Master given you to do? Be found doing it when he comes. It is probably not glamorous: the nappies, the spreadsheet, the hospital visit, the Bible study preparation, the care of an ageing parent. Do today’s portion of it faithfully, and stop measuring yourself by results he has not asked you for.

For worship. The Master who rewards faithfulness is himself the faithful Servant, who finished the work the Father gave him to do and was set over all things. Every reward we receive is a share in his. And the God who could have run his household without us chose to entrust it to us, and then to make the stewards heirs. Such is the generosity of the Lord of the house.

verseByVerse.quote: But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if that servant says to himself: my master is delayed in coming, and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.

But if that servant says to himself, My master is delayed in coming. Everything that follows comes out of that one sentence, and it is worth noticing that it is said to himself. Nobody announces it. There is no moment of rebellion, no decision to become a tyrant. There is a private conclusion about a timetable. And the conclusion is not even wrong. The master is delayed: the whole point of the previous parables is that he takes longer than expected. What is wrong is what the servant does with an accurate observation. This is the danger of the delay of Christ’s return. People begin to think he will never come (2 Peter 3:3–4), and live accordingly.

And begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk. Two things, and they are the two directions in which a leader goes bad. He turns on the household: abuse of power, a leader who mistreats those in his care. And note that these are his fellow servants, not his property. Authority given to feed people is being used to hit them. That is the permanent temptation of religious office, and it does not usually involve fists: the pulpit used to settle a score, the discipline that is really about control, the counselling relationship in which one person is always the one who has to change. And he turns to himself: self-indulgence. Eat and drink and get drunk echoes the rich fool’s relax, eat, drink, be merry. He has begun to consume the master’s stores. The food he was appointed to distribute (v. 42) is going down his own throat. Both are what the delay makes possible. Not causes them: makes them possible. A man who genuinely expects his employer within the hour does not start drinking the cellar.

The master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know. Sudden and unexpected.

And will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. The phrase is violent, and its exact sense is disputed, possibly meaning cut him off; but the verdict is not. The language shows how seriously God judges unfaithful leaders. He is put with the unfaithful, with unbelievers, which is the real sentence, and it means he is finally classified with the people he showed himself to be one of. He had the keys. He held the office. He was called a servant to the last line of the parable. And the accounting placed him where he had actually been standing all along.

Is this servant a true believer who loses his salvation? The more likely reading is that he is a professing servant, a leader in the household, whose conduct shows he never truly knew his master; Matthew says he is put with the hypocrites (Matthew 24:51). Cut in pieces is a picture of severe judgement. A true servant may fail and be disciplined, but those who belong to Christ endure to the end because he keeps them.

What should a church do about a leader who abuses those in his care? Take it seriously and act, because Jesus does. Abuse of any kind, physical, sexual, emotional or spiritual, must never be tolerated or covered up to protect a ministry’s reputation. Crimes should be reported to the civil authorities; victims should be believed, protected and cared for; and the leader should be removed from office while the matter is examined honestly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). A leader is a servant over the household, never its owner. A church that protects the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable has taken the side of the servant in this parable.

In a sentence. A servant who assumes his master’s delay means he can abuse others and indulge himself will be severely punished when his master returns unexpectedly.

On a Tuesday. The delay of Christ’s return is not a licence for unfaithfulness. He is coming; live accordingly. Ask where the long delay has made you careless: in your use of authority over others at home or work, in your appetites, in what you excuse because judgement feels far away. If you lead anyone, ask the people under you whether you serve them or use them, and listen to the answer.

For worship. The Master who will return is just. He sees every hand raised against the weak, every servant beaten in his house, every store wasted by those who should have fed his people, and he will put it right. He is also the Master who never once abused his authority, who used his power only to serve, and whose rule over his household is gentle and lowly in heart. Blessed are those who live under such a Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That servant who knew his master’s will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.

And that servant who knew his master’s will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. Deliberate disobedience in full knowledge brings greater judgement.

But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Two servants, the same offence, and different sentences, and the difference is entirely what each of them knew. Readers often pass over this, and it should not be passed over, because it settles something. Scripture does not teach that judgement is a single undifferentiated verdict falling equally on everyone outside Christ. It teaches degrees. Jesus has already said it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for the Galilean towns that watched him work and shrugged (10:13–14), and more bearable for Sodom than for a village that turned away his messengers (10:12). Perfect justice is exact, and exactness means proportion. There are degrees of guilt and punishment, according to knowledge (Numbers 15:27–31; Romans 2:12). And note carefully what is not being said. The second servant is not acquitted. He did what deserved a beating, and he receives one. Ignorance does not excuse; he still did wrong and is punished. Ignorance reduces the sentence; it does not produce innocence. There is no group in this parable that gets away with it.

Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required. A principle of God’s justice, and one of the most sobering sentences in the Gospel, not least because of whom it is aimed at. Privilege brings responsibility. The passive verbs, was given, they entrusted, are the reverent Jewish way of saying God gave without using the name. That means every item on the list is a deposit, not an achievement: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible in a language you can read, a church down the road, forty years of clear preaching, health, education, money, time. None of those is a reward for anything. Every one of them raises the bar. Those who have heard the gospel, those who know the Bible, those who lead in the church, will be judged more strictly (James 3:1). This applies to Christians in wealthy and free countries, who have so much.

An account, not a shelter. This word falls hardest not on the ignorant but on the well-taught. The man who has heard the gospel explained plainly for four decades and has never done anything about it is not in the safer category. He is the servant who knew his master’s will, and on the parable’s own reckoning he is nearer the severe beating than the light one. It is a strange thing to have to say, but there it is: a lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter. It is an account.

Does this mean people who never heard the gospel will be saved by their ignorance? No. The servant who did not know still receives a beating; ignorance lessens judgement but does not remove guilt, because all have sinned against the light of creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). Salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–15), which is exactly why the church must send preachers. God will judge everyone with perfect fairness, according to what they knew. Infants who die in infancy, who cannot hear or believe, are in the hands of a merciful God, and we may trust that his elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit.

Should I avoid learning more of the Bible so as to be judged less? That would be to choose darkness so as not to be blamed for it, which is itself a sin against light. The goal is not to know less but to obey what you know. Every truth learned is a gift to be lived, and the same God who requires much gives grace to do it. A believer who keeps learning and keeps obeying, however imperfectly, is not storing up judgement but growing in Christ.

In a sentence. Those who knew their master’s will and ignored it will be punished severely, those who did not know, less severely, for much is required of those to whom much is given.

On a Tuesday. You have been given much. Ask what God requires of you in return. List three things you have been given that most of the world has not: a Bible, a church, freedom, money, education. For each, ask one concrete question: what is this for, and what does my Master want me to do with it this week?

For worship. The Judge of all the earth will do right. He weighs every privilege and every refusal with perfect justice, and not one person will be treated unfairly. And the same Lord who requires much has given most: he gave his Son, the greatest gift of all, and he gives his Spirit to make his servants faithful. Everything he requires of us, he first gave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–59 — Fire, Division, and the Urgent Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with three sayings of escalating urgency, and the first is the most emotionally exposed moment in Luke outside Gethsemane.

“I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled!” The fire is most likely the one John announced at the start of this Gospel — “he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (3:16) — and Luke's second volume opens with tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). It is also the fire of judgement and purifying, and the two are not separable: the same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on.

“I have a baptism to be baptized with.” To be baptized is to go under — and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. In the Psalms the waters are often death: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Ps. 42:7). He is talking about the cross, and calling it a drowning.

And “how great is my distress” is the cry of a man hemmed in, pressed on every side. Read the two verses together and the shape is precise: the fire cannot be lit until the baptism is finished, and the baptism is Calvary. Pentecost waits on Golgotha, and he is pressed between them.

Then the division saying, which shocks — not least because angels announced “on earth peace” over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14). Both are true. What he brings is peace with God, which every human being needs and cannot manufacture. What he never promised is the peace of everybody getting along, which was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked. The household list is quoted from Micah 7:6, where it describes a society coming apart — and every pair is named in both directions.

Finally the weather. West of Israel is the Mediterranean, so cloud coming inland meant rain; a south wind off the desert meant the scorching sirocco. Two confident readings, and Jesus grants they are right. These people are competent. And they will not apply the skill where it matters.
verseByVerse.theology:
“How great is my distress until it is accomplished” is not a man dreading the cross and hanging back — Gethsemane will show that the dread was real, and this shows what was underneath it. He wants what is on the far side badly enough that the waiting is a torment. He went to that cross wishing it were already over, not because the pain was unendurable but because he could not wait to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.

The charge of hypocrisy at v.56 is precise. It is not that the crowd is stupid; it is that they are perfectly capable of reading evidence and drawing conclusions, and have declined to apply the skill in the one place it matters. A man who cannot read anything is not a hypocrite but illiterate. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what stands in front of him has made a choice and is pretending it was a limitation.

And the evidence he expects them to have read is not a secret sign. The “present time” is the whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor given good news, thousands following, and the authorities plotting a death.

“Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?” assumes the resources for the judgement are already in their possession. It needs a guard — Scripture is emphatic that a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Prov. 14:12; Jer. 17:9) — so the question is not “why not decide what suits you?” It is narrower: given what you can already read, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? And the answer, in nearly every case, is that the conclusion would cost something.
verseByVerse.examples:
The division saying has real pastoral weight, because someone reading it is living inside it. He does not say the division is good. He says it is what happens — and he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold when he was converted has very often concluded that he handled it badly, or that a wiser person would have avoided it. This verse says the fracture was in the nature of the case.

Every generation is expert at reading something — markets, politics, the mood of a culture, the trajectory of a career — and the skill is genuine. The same person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never once asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or in his own house. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

And “you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny” has carried theological weight it was never built to bear — one of the two verses historically cited for purgatory. But this is practical advice about a lawsuit used to illustrate urgency, and doctrine cannot be quarried from an illustration's scenery. A man in a debtors' prison could not earn, which was the point of the prison; “until you have paid the last penny” is the ordinary way of saying he is not getting out. And a doctrine supplying a further opportunity to settle after death removes the urgency of the only sentence that mattered. Settle now, on the road — and know that the settlement is not a schedule of payments but an amnesty, purchased at the judge's own expense (7:41-42; Col. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: 'I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptised with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!

I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! For two verses the mask of the teacher comes off, and Luke lets us hear what it was like inside him. What fire? Fire in Scripture pictures judgement (3:9, 17) and purifying (Malachi 3:2–3), and the Holy Spirit. John the Baptist announced at the start of this Gospel that the Messiah would baptise with the Holy Spirit and with fire (3:16), and Luke’s second volume opens with tongues as of fire resting on each of the waiting disciples (Acts 2:3). The same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on. Jesus came to bring the fire of God’s judgement and refining, and the fire of the Spirit, and all of it would be set alight by his death and resurrection. Would that it were already kindled: the Greek is an unfinished exclamation, and translators have struggled with it because it is not a tidy sentence. It is a man wishing out loud. Jesus longs for the completion of his work.

I have a baptism to be baptized with. The word means to be plunged, immersed, submerged, and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. To be baptised, in the Old Testament’s imagery, is to go under the waters, and the waters in the Psalms are often death: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Psalm 42:7); save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck (Psalm 69:1–2). He is talking about his death (Mark 10:38), and he is calling it a drowning: being overwhelmed, plunged into suffering, under the judgement of God against sin.

And how great is my distress until it is accomplished! “Distress” (synechomai) means to be gripped, hemmed in, pressed on every side. Luke uses it elsewhere of being seized by a high fever (4:38) and of a besieging army closing on a city (19:43). It is the word for something with no room left in it. A glimpse of Jesus’ inner anguish on the road to the cross, anticipating Gethsemane (22:42–44).

Pentecost waits on Golgotha. Read the two verses together and the shape is unbearable and precise. The fire he longs for cannot be lit until the baptism is finished, and the baptism is Calvary. He cannot have the one without going through the other, and he is pressed between them. He must first be overwhelmed by the judgement of God against sin. So this is not a man dreading the cross and hanging back. Gethsemane will show that the dread was real, and this shows what was underneath it. He wants what is on the far side badly enough that the waiting is a torment. He went to that cross wishing it were already over, not because he was looking for a way out but because he could not wait to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.

Does this baptism tell us anything about Christian baptism? Indirectly, yes. Jesus calls his death a baptism, and Paul says that believers are baptised into his death, buried with him and raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3–4). That is why this app holds believer’s baptism by immersion: going under the water pictures union with Christ in the death he describes here, and coming up pictures resurrection. Our paedobaptist brothers see the same union signified in the baptism of infants, and we honour their faith. But the reality behind every baptism is this one, which Jesus endured alone.

In a sentence. Jesus longed for the fire he came to bring to be kindled, and was deeply distressed until his baptism of suffering was accomplished.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to treat your Christian life as routine, read these two verses and remember what it cost. Pray for the Spirit’s fire in your own heart and church: a holy love that burns away sin and warms cold faith. And when you are pressed by suffering you cannot escape, remember that your Lord knew what it is to be hemmed in, and went on for you.

For worship. Jesus felt the weight of the cross long before he reached it, and went on anyway, for you. He walked toward the flood with his eyes open, longing for it to be over and longing even more for what lay beyond it: a church set on fire with the Spirit. The breakers and waves went over him so that they would never go over us. And the fire that fell at Pentecost has never gone out.
verseByVerse.note: Fire can picture judgment or purifying; “baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed by suffering.

parallels.desc: the baptism with which I am baptized

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.

Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? The sentence is a shock, and it is meant to be, not least because the angels announced on earth peace over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14), and Zechariah sang that he would guide our feet into the way of peace (1:79). Both are true, and the resolution is not a compromise between them. Jesus does bring real peace: peace with God, which is the thing every human being most needs and cannot manufacture (Romans 5:1), and peace between those who belong to him. What he does not bring, and never promised, is the peace of the world, a peace without truth, the peace of everybody getting along, which was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked.

No, I tell you, but rather division. The effect of his coming is to divide people by their response to him. Simeon said it over the infant: this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many (2:34–35). Everyone must decide, and families split over him.

For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. Five is a household: father, mother, son, daughter, and daughter-in-law, the son’s wife living with them. And the arithmetic is deliberately awkward. Three against two, then two against three: the same fracture described from both sides, because in a divided house both halves feel like the ones being left.

Father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law. The list is quoted, and the source matters. It is Micah 7:6, where the prophet describes a society coming apart in a time of judgement: the son treats the father with contempt, and a man’s enemies are the men of his own house. In Micah it is a picture of national breakdown. Jesus says it will happen because of loyalty to him. And note that every pair is named in both directions. There is no suggestion that the believing half will find it easy or behave well.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should seek conflict, or be needlessly divisive, or neglect their families. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). A great deal of family division is caused by Christians being insufferable rather than by Christ. But when others reject Christ, conflict may come, and loyalty to Christ must come first (14:26).

The mercy of a warning. Someone reading this is living inside it. Jesus does not say the division is good. He says it is what happens, and he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold when he was converted has very often concluded that he handled it badly, or that a wiser person would have avoided it. This verse says the fracture was in the nature of the case. When everything has been done gently and the division comes anyway, it is not evidence of failure. It is the thing he warned about, happening.

How do I love a family that opposes my faith? Honour your parents in everything that does not require disobeying Christ. Be the kindest, most helpful person at the family table, and let your life speak before your words. Do not preach at every gathering; do answer honestly when asked. Pray for them faithfully, sometimes for decades. Keep the door open, and refuse bitterness when they mock. Where there is real danger or abuse, you may need distance for safety, and that is not unloving. And remember that God has often used one believer’s patient faithfulness to bring a whole household to Christ (Acts 16:31–34).

In a sentence. Jesus said he came not to bring peace but division, which would split even families as people responded differently to him.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has divided your family, he foretold it. Love them, pray for them, and stay faithful. Where this applies: the parent who disowns a child for being baptised, the spouse who mocks every prayer. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to excuse rudeness, harshness or neglect, or to justify cutting off a family that simply finds your faith strange. Ask whether the offence is Christ, or you.

For worship. The Prince of Peace accepted being the cause of division, because the only peace that lasts is peace with God, and it cannot be had on any terms but his. He was himself rejected by his own household, who thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and he gathers into his family everyone who does the will of his Father. In him the lonely believer has a household that can never be divided.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the crowds, 'When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also said to the crowds: when you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, a shower is coming. And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, there will be scorching heat, and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?

When you see a cloud rising in the west. He turns from the disciples to the crowds, and begins with the weather, which in that country was entirely predictable if you knew the geography. West of Israel is the Mediterranean. Cloud building over the sea and coming inland meant rain, as Elijah’s servant saw from Carmel (1 Kings 18:44), and the peasant standing in his field did not need to think about it. A shower is coming, he says at once, and so it happens.

And when you see the south wind blowing. South is the Negev and the Arabian desert; a south wind meant scorching heat that could strip a crop in a day. Two signs, two confident readings, and Jesus grants that they are right: and it happens. These people are competent. They were good at reading the weather, and their instincts about the sky are reliable and hard-won.

You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky. The charge is precise. It is not that they are stupid. It is that they are perfectly capable of reading evidence and drawing conclusions, and have declined to apply the skill in the one place it matters. They claim not to be able to see, when they can see perfectly well; they just do not want to. What makes it hypocrisy rather than error is that the failure is selective. A man who cannot read anything is not a hypocrite; he is illiterate. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what is standing in front of him has made a choice, and is pretending it was a limitation.

But why do you not know how to interpret the present time? “The present time” (kairos) is this decisive moment, the time of God’s visitation. And notice what he expects them to have read. Not a secret sign. The whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor being told good news, thousands following, and the religious authorities plotting a death. The Messiah was among them. Any of it could have been interpreted by a man who reads clouds for a living. But they would not read it, and he will weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:44).

Turning it on ourselves. It is worth turning this on ourselves before it is enjoyed at their expense. Every generation is expert at reading something: markets, politics, the mood of a culture, the trajectory of a career. The skill is genuine. And the same person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never once sat down and asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or in his own house, or in the last five years of his own circumstances. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

Does this mean I should try to match news events to Bible prophecy? Not in the way that often happens. Jesus’ point is that the decisive time had already arrived in his own coming, and his hearers were ignoring it. The present time, for us, is the age between his first and second comings: the day of salvation, when the gospel goes to the nations and he could return at any hour. Reading the times means recognising that, and responding with repentance, faith and readiness, rather than building charts of headlines. Discernment is spiritual, not speculative.

In a sentence. Jesus called the crowds hypocrites, because they could read the weather but would not read the signs of the time in which God was visiting them.

On a Tuesday. Can you read the signs of what God is doing? Take ten minutes and ask: where has God been at work in my life in the last year, in a trial, an answered prayer, a conviction that will not go away? Do not be skilled in everything except spiritual discernment.

For worship. The Lord of the seasons sends the rain from the west and the heat from the south, and he sent his Son in the fullness of time. He has never been unclear about his visitations; the clouds of mercy have been rising over this world since the manger. And the God who gave us eyes to read the sky has given us his Spirit to read his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Clouds from the west came off the Mediterranean with rain; the south wind blew hot off the desert.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?

And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? One short question, and it deserves an entry of its own because of what it assumes. He has just told them they can read the sky and will not read the times. Now he asks why they do not work it out themselves. You have the evidence; you do not need anyone to tell you. Use your own judgement, honestly, and you will see who I am, and what you must do. The time for decision is now, and it leads into the parable that follows.

Not for want of a teacher. The failure is not for want of a teacher. They are not being told to go and consult somebody. They are being told that the resources for the judgement are already in their possession, and that they are declining to use them. The verb is the one for reaching a verdict, and for yourselves puts the responsibility exactly where the crowd would least like it. They had spent the chapter asking him to settle things: adjudicate my inheritance (v. 13), give us a sign (11:16), tell us whether this parable is for us (v. 41). He hands it back.

What it does not mean. This needs a guard, because it is not an invitation to make it up.
