Scripture is emphatic that the human heart is unreliable and that a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Proverbs 14:12; Jeremiah 17:9). The question is not why not decide what suits you? It is narrower and harder: given what is in front of you, the evidence you can already read, the conscience you already have, the Scriptures you already possess, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? And the answer, in nearly every case, is that the conclusion would cost something. The crowd’s problem is not a shortage of light but an unwillingness to act on what the light shows. That is why the next two verses are about a man on his way to court, running out of road.

The habit of waiting to be told. There is a particular kind of religious passivity that this question is aimed at, and it survives well in churches. It is the habit of waiting to be told: of treating every question as one for the experts, so that nothing is ever settled and nothing therefore has to be done about it. Jesus calls it what it is by asking why.

Should I not rely on my pastor and church to tell me what is right? Listen to them, gratefully: God gives teachers to the church, and you should be humble enough to be taught (Hebrews 13:17). But no teacher can believe for you, repent for you or obey for you. The Bereans checked even Paul against Scripture (Acts 17:11). On the plain things, who Jesus is, what sin is, what he commands, you already know enough to act. Take your questions to your pastor, but do not hide behind them.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why they could not judge for themselves what was right.

On a Tuesday. Do not wait for others to decide for you. Weigh the evidence about Jesus for yourself, and act. Is there a question you keep postponing, whether to be baptised, whether to make things right with someone, whether to give up a known sin, because you are waiting for someone to tell you? You already know. Do it this week.

For worship. God has not left us in the dark. He has written his law on our hearts, set his creation before our eyes, given us his word in our hands and sent his Son into our world. The light is enough. And the God who asks why do you not judge? is the God who opens blind eyes to see and gives willing hearts to act.

verseByVerse.quote: As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.

As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way. The picture is a lawsuit already in motion: a man on his way to court with a debt he cannot pay, and the case certain to go against him. The two parties are walking to court together, which is how it worked, the plaintiff bringing the defendant himself, and the road is the last stretch of time in which anything can be done. Make an effort is a strong verb: work at it, put yourself into it. Settle out of court while you still can. Once you reach the judge, it will be too late.

Lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. Three handovers in a row, and the man is passed down the chain like a parcel: debtors’ prison. Once the process starts, he has no further say in it, which is exactly the point. On the road he is a man who can negotiate. In the courtroom he is a case.

I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny. The penny (lepton) was the smallest coin in circulation. Every last coin.

The meaning. In context (vv. 54–57), this is a parable about the coming judgement of God. We are all on our way to court, with a debt we cannot pay. Now, on the way, is the time to be reconciled with God, through Christ. Once we stand before the Judge, it will be too late. And the debt cannot be paid by us; we would never get out.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. Roman Catholic teaching has sometimes cited this verse in support of purgatory, a place where souls pay for their sins after death before entering heaven. Verdict: the parable is about urgent reconciliation before judgement, not about a process of purification after death. Scripture teaches that Christ’s sacrifice has paid the debt of believers in full (Colossians 2:13–14; Hebrews 10:14), and that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). For those who reject Christ, the debt can never be paid.

Three reasons the purgatory reading fails. The last clause has carried a great deal of theological weight it was never built to bear. With its parallel in Matthew 5:26, it is one of the verses historically cited for purgatory: the word until seems to promise a way out at the end of the paying, and a prison that is temporary is not hell. Three things make that reading impossible. First, look at what this is: practical advice about a lawsuit, used as an illustration of urgency. Doctrine cannot be quarried from the scenery of an illustration. Push the method and Luke’s parable of the persistent widow would make God a judge who grants justice only to stop being pestered (18:1–8), which nobody believes and Jesus never meant. The magistrate, the officer, the prison and the penny are the furniture of the story, not a floor plan of eternity. Second, the idiom runs the other way. A man in a debtors’ prison could not earn; that was the entire point of the prison. To say he will not get out until he has paid the last penny is not to hold out a release date; it is the ordinary way of saying he is not getting out at all. Third, and most decisively, it reverses what this passage exists to say. Every line presses one point: act now, because afterward is too late. A doctrine that supplies a further opportunity to settle the account after death takes the urgency out of the only sentence that mattered. If there were a way to pay later, the advice to settle on the road would be optional.

An amnesty, not an instalment plan. And what of the debt itself? Luke answered that five chapters back, in a house where a woman wept over Jesus’ feet. Two debtors owed sums they could not repay, and when they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both (7:41–42). The record of debt that stood against us was not put on an instalment plan. It was set aside, nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). So take the urgency with full seriousness: settle now, on the road, while it is still called today. But know what the settlement is. It is not a schedule of payments. It is an amnesty, and it was purchased at the Judge’s own expense.

How do I settle with God? Not by offering to pay, because the debt is beyond you, and not by promising to do better, because that adds nothing to what is owed. You settle by agreeing with God about your sin, turning from it, and trusting Jesus Christ, who died to pay that debt in full and rose again. Tell him so, in your own words, today. Then you are no longer on the way to court as a debtor; you are walking home as a child. If you are already his, the parable also has a horizontal echo: where you have a quarrel with someone, settle it quickly (Matthew 5:23–25).

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to settle with their accuser on the way to court, before it was too late, a picture of the urgency of being reconciled to God before judgement.

On a Tuesday. Today is the day to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20; 6:2). Do not wait until you stand before the Judge. Where this saying applies: anyone who has put off the question of God for years, assuming there will be time later; and, by its echo, a believer with an open quarrel he keeps meaning to resolve. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to frighten an assured believer into thinking he must keep paying for forgiven sin, or to pressure someone into a settlement that lets an abuser off. Christ has paid; settle by trusting him.

For worship. We were on the road to court with a debt we could never pay, and the Judge himself came down to meet us on the way. He did not reduce the charge or offer easier terms. He paid the very last penny with his own blood, tore up the record, and set the prisoners free. There is no purgatory for the forgiven, because there is nothing left to pay. It is finished.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” was the smallest coin in circulation.

12.text: <sup>1</sup> In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. <sup>2</sup> Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>3</sup> Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops. <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>6</sup> Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. <sup>7</sup> Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>8</sup> “And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, <sup>9</sup> but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. <sup>10</sup> And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>11</sup> And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, <sup>12</sup> for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” <sup>13</sup> Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” <sup>14</sup> But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?” <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” <sup>16</sup> And he told them a parable, saying, “The land of a rich man produced plentifully, <sup>17</sup> and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’ <sup>18</sup> And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. <sup>19</sup> And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ <sup>20</sup> But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ <sup>21</sup> So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. <sup>23</sup> For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. <sup>24</sup> Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! <sup>25</sup> And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>26</sup> If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? <sup>27</sup> Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>28</sup> But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! <sup>29</sup> And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. <sup>30</sup> For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them. <sup>31</sup> Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. <sup>32</sup> “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. <sup>33</sup> Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. <sup>34</sup> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <sup>35</sup> “Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, <sup>36</sup> and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. <sup>37</sup> Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. <sup>38</sup> If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! <sup>39</sup> But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. <sup>40</sup> You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” <sup>41</sup> Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?” <sup>42</sup> And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time? <sup>43</sup> Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>44</sup> Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>45</sup> But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, <sup>46</sup> the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. <sup>47</sup> And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. <sup>48</sup> But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more. <sup>49</sup> “I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! <sup>50</sup> I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! <sup>51</sup> Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. <sup>52</sup> For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. <sup>53</sup> They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.” <sup>54</sup> He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. <sup>55</sup> And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. <sup>56</sup> You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time? <sup>57</sup> “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? <sup>58</sup> As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. <sup>59</sup> I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

13.title: Repent or Perish; the Narrow Door; Jerusalem's Lament
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is structured around the call to repentance and its refusal — three overlapping statements that together describe what happens when the opportunity for repentance closes. It opens with Jesus's response to news of a Galilean massacre and the fall of the tower of Siloam — two disasters that the crowd assumes were punishments for exceptional sinfulness. Jesus refuses the assumption and turns both events into a summons to universal repentance: “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” Then he tells the parable of the fruitless fig tree — one more year of patient cultivation before the axe comes. Then on a Sabbath he heals a woman bent double for eighteen years, and the synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus names the synagogue ruler's hypocrisy before the entire crowd.

The middle section (vv. 18–30) moves through the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven — the kingdom's hidden but irresistible growth — to the question about the number of the saved, and Jesus's answer: “Strive to enter through the narrow door.” The door will close. The day will come when the master of the house rises and shuts the door, and those who knock and say “we ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets” will hear “I do not know where you come from.” Familiarity with Jesus is not relationship with Jesus; proximity to the gospel is not reception of it.

The chapter ends with one of the most heartrending passages in the Gospel: the lament over Jerusalem. Some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him; Jesus refuses to be deflected (“I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem”). And then he speaks to the city itself: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” The willingness is on his side; the unwillingness is on theirs. And the house will be left desolate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Repent or Perish; the Barren Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The massacre Pilate carried out on Galilean pilgrims is recorded nowhere else in ancient literature — which is itself telling, since this is exactly the kind of local atrocity that filled a province and left no trace in the histories. It fits everything known about the man.

The crowd assumes the victims' fate was a verdict on their exceptional sinfulness, and Jesus brings the assumption into the open before they can state it: “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners…? No, I tell you.” Flat, immediate, unqualified.

That was not a fringe view he was demolishing. It was the working theology of the ancient world — Job's friends spent most of a book on it, and the disciples will ask it about a blind man (John 9:2). It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong.

He then supplies a second case himself, and the choice is deliberate because it is a different kind of disaster. The first was murder; the second is an accident — masonry giving way near the pool of Siloam. Between them the two cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did. And the answer is identical, word for word, twice, so that neither case is left open.

The parable of the fig tree extends the urgency and adds the intercession. The tree is planted in a vineyard — prime cultivated ground, occupying space that would otherwise carry vines. Three years is not impatience: a fig takes about three years to bear at all, and the law required the first three years' fruit to be left untouched (Lev. 19:23), so the owner has waited the full statutory period and then come three times on top of it.

And the charge is precise. Not that the tree has done harm, but that it is “using up the ground.” Barrenness here is not a neutral condition; a tree that produces nothing is consuming, and what it consumes belongs to somebody else.

The vinedresser disputes none of it. He accepts the whole case and asks for time — and offers to do the work himself: digging round compacted roots, and dunging. Heavy, unpleasant labour on a tree that has given him nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus's answer refuses both the question and the assumption behind it. He does not say “God never punishes” — the Old Testament would contradict that. He says this is not the special punishment of especially sinful people. All are sinners; all face mortality; all need to repent.

So the disasters are not explanations of why those particular people died. They are reminders to the living that they are not exempt from the mortality those people have just experienced. The right response to someone else's death is not theological analysis of their sins but examination of one's own soul while there is time.

The fig tree and the vineyard together would have been unmistakable. Israel is the vineyard of Isaiah 5 — “he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes” — and Israel is the fig tree in which God came looking and found nothing (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13; Mic. 7:1). The one who stands between the tree and the axe, asking for another year and offering to do the digging himself, is standing in that room saying it.

But the intercession has a term. The vinedresser does not ask for indefinite reprieve; he names the period and concedes the outcome. Which puts this parable in its proper relation to the two disasters: those verses said the axe is real, and this one says the axe is being held — and by whom. Separating the two halves ruins the passage in one direction or the other. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Take this into the real world, because it will be needed there. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, or a driver crosses a line, two sentences will be offered and this passage forbids them both.

The first is the one Jesus is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly, and about both kinds of death. Never say it, and never let it be said to the bereaved. The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either — he does not remove these deaths from his Father's world; he refuses to let us read them as verdicts.

Between those two errors is where a Christian must stand, and it is a narrow place: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it. The honest answer to why them? is that we are not told; the answer we are given instead is that our own footing is no firmer than theirs was.

And there is a sting in the wording. “You will all likewise perish” was heard by a generation that would watch Roman soldiers kill worshippers in the temple courts and walls come down on Jerusalem within forty years. It came true in the very forms they had just been discussing.

The vinedresser's response to three barren years is the model of patient labour with an apparently hopeless case — a church that has not grown, a child who will not turn. He neither writes the tree off nor pretends there is fruit. He asks for another year and goes and gets the spade.

verseByVerse.quote: There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And he answered them, 'Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. He answered them: do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

Meaning first. Luke 13 is a chapter about time running out and grace still running. It opens with two disasters in the news and Jesus refuses to read them as verdicts on the dead; he reads them instead as a summons to the living: repent, or you will likewise perish. Then a fig tree that has had every advantage and borne nothing is given one more year, because someone pleads for it and takes up the spade. In a synagogue he straightens a woman bent double for eighteen years, and a religious official is angry at the date on the calendar. The kingdom, he says, starts as small as a seed and as hidden as yeast, and it will fill the world. But the door into it is narrow, and one day it will be shut, and people who ate in his presence will be left knocking while strangers from every direction sit down with Abraham. And the chapter ends with Jesus walking towards the city that kills prophets, weeping over it like a hen with her wings spread, and promising a day when it will say, blessed is he who comes. Judgement is real, the patience is real, and the one who holds both is walking to Jerusalem to die.

The setting. Jesus had just urged the crowds to read the signs of the times and be reconciled to God before judgement (12:54–59). Some in the crowd respond with a news item.

There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. The incident is recorded nowhere else in ancient literature, which is itself worth noting: this is exactly the kind of local atrocity that filled a province and left no trace in the histories. It fits everything known about Pilate. Josephus records several incidents in which Pilate provoked riots and had his soldiers put them down brutally. Some Galileans, perhaps suspected of rebellion, were killed in the temple courts while offering sacrifices, probably at Passover, when laymen slaughtered their own lambs. Their blood mixed with the blood of the animals. It was a sacrilege and an atrocity at once: men killed at the altar, in the act of worship, by the governor of a pagan empire.

Why do they raise it? Luke does not say, and the silence is suggestive. They may be testing him. A Galilean teacher’s opinion on a massacre of Galileans would be useful to somebody: condemn Pilate and he is a rebel; say nothing and he has no sympathy for his own people. Perhaps they wanted him to say the victims deserved it. But the answer Jesus gives tells us what they were actually thinking.

Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? There it is, and he brings it out into the open before they can say it. The assumption behind the report is that the manner of a man’s death is a comment on his life. That was not a fringe view. It was the working theology of the ancient world. Job’s friends spent most of a book on it (Job 4:7). The disciples will ask it about a blind man: who sinned, this man or his parents (John 9:2)? It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong.

No, I tell you. Flat, immediate, unqualified. He does not say probably not, and he does not explore the possibility. Suffering is not always a sign of special guilt. The victims were not worse than others. The equation is broken.

But unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. And then the turn nobody was ready for. He does not merely deny that the dead were worse. He tells the living they are in the same position, and the only difference between them and the men on that temple pavement is a matter of timing. Don’t speculate about others’ sins. Look to your own. The real question is not why they died, but whether you are ready to die. Everyone is a sinner, and everyone will perish unless they repent. The question they brought was about somebody else’s guilt. He has handed it back with their own name on it. And “likewise” may be meant quite literally. Forty years later, many Jews died at Roman hands in the temple courts during the siege of Jerusalem, their blood mingled once again with the place of sacrifice.

What does perish mean here? More than dying, since the Galileans have already died and his hearers will die too whatever they do. To perish is to be lost before God: to die unreconciled and come under his judgement, for ever (John 3:16, where perishing is the opposite of eternal life). Jesus is not threatening that the unrepentant will all be killed by Pilate. He is saying that what happened to the bodies of those men is a picture of what will happen to every soul that meets God without repentance: sudden, unprepared and final. That is why the warning is urgent and not merely sad.

What is repentance? Repentance is turning from sin to God. It begins by seeing your sin as God sees it, not only as harmful to you but as an offence against him, and grieving over it. It takes hold of his mercy in Christ, because repentance without hope only drives a person away. And it turns: you forsake the sin and set yourself to walk with God in new obedience (Westminster 15.2). It is not a single event at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life, and it is never too late to begin it while you are still breathing.

In a sentence. When told of Galileans killed by Pilate in the temple, Jesus denied that they were worse sinners than others, and warned that all must repent or perish.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of disasters, don’t ask what the victims did. Ask whether you are ready to meet God. Notice the reflex next time the news breaks: the faint relief that it was over there, the quick search for what they did differently. Jesus will not let that reflex stand. Let every report of sudden death send you, not into judging, but to your knees, and to the one honest prayer the news can produce: Lord, I am no safer than they were; have mercy on me.

For worship. The Lord of life does not use the dead to make the living feel secure. He tells the truth, and he tells it because he loves the people he is warning. He spoke these words on the road to Jerusalem, where his own blood would be shed at the Passover, not mingled with the sacrifices but made the sacrifice, so that those who repent will never perish. The one who said unless you repent is the one who makes repentance possible, and who receives every repenting sinner with joy.
verseByVerse.note: This massacre is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits what is known of Pilate’s brutality. Many assumed disaster was punishment for a particular sin.

parallels.desc: who that was innocent ever perished? see: John 9:1–3 = who sinned, this man or his parents?

verseByVerse.quote: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them. He supplies a second case himself, and the choice is deliberate, because it is a different kind of disaster altogether. The first was murder: a cruel man with soldiers, doing something wicked on purpose. The second is an accident. Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam at the south end of Jerusalem (John 9:7). Perhaps a tower in the city wall gave way, possibly during building work on the aqueduct that Pilate built, and eighteen people were underneath it. Again, it is recorded nowhere else. Between them the two cases cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did. Whatever category a bereaved person’s loss falls into, one of these two covers it.

Were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? The word for offenders (opheiletai) means debtors, the word Jesus taught them to use in prayer (11:4). Were they greater debtors to God? The question assumes there is a ledger, and that the falling masonry was the bailiff calling in one particular account. Jesus agrees there is a ledger. He denies that the tower was a reading from it.

No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Word for word, twice, which is Jesus making certain that neither case is left open. Whether by human evil or natural disaster, death comes to everyone, often unexpectedly. The only safety is repentance.

Disasters and God. Scripture teaches that God is sovereign over all things, including disasters (Amos 3:6; Isaiah 45:7). But it does not teach that every disaster is a punishment for the particular sins of those who suffer. Rather, every disaster is a reminder that we live in a fallen world under the curse of sin (Romans 8:20–22), that life is short and death is certain, and that all of us need to repent.

Two sentences this passage forbids. Take this into the real world, because it will be needed there. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, or a driver crosses a line, two sentences will be offered. The first is the one he is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly, and about both kinds of death. Never say it, and never let it be said to the bereaved. The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either. He does not remove these deaths from his Father’s world; he refuses to let us read them as verdicts. Between those two errors is where a Christian must actually stand, and it is a narrow place: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it.

So what may be said to the grieving? Very little about the dead, and a great deal to the living. The honest answer to why them is that we are not told. Do not offer explanations God has not given, and do not hurry anyone through their grief. Sit with them, weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), pray with them, and speak of the God who is not distant from suffering because his Son entered it. The word Jesus gives here, that our own footing is no firmer than theirs, is not a change of subject but the only useful thing that can be said to people standing near a fresh grave and quietly assuming they are safe. It is usually a word for the preacher and for your own heart before it is a word for a widow.

And what about my own suffering? Is God punishing me? If you are in Christ, no. The punishment your sins deserved was laid on him, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). God does discipline his children, but discipline is a father’s training, not a judge’s sentence, and its aim is our holiness and good (Hebrews 12:5–11). You may not be able to say what a particular trouble is for. You can say what it is not: it is not God paying you back. It may be a call to search your heart, and it is always an invitation to draw near.

In a sentence. Jesus also denied that those killed when a tower fell in Siloam were worse sinners than others in Jerusalem, and repeated his warning to repent or perish.

On a Tuesday. Every news report of sudden death is a call to repentance. Are you ready? And there is a sting in the wording worth remembering when the headlines come. You will all likewise perish was heard by a generation that would watch Roman soldiers kill worshippers in the temple and walls come down on Jerusalem within forty years. The warning came true in the very forms they had just been discussing. The next disaster you read about is not a puzzle to solve. It is a mercy aimed at you, while there is still time.

For worship. God is sovereign over towers and governors, over accidents and atrocities, and nothing in this world falls outside his hand. And he is good: he does not leave us to guess our standing from what happens to us, but tells us plainly, and then provides the way of escape. When the tower of his judgement fell, it fell on his own Son at Calvary, so that everyone who shelters in him will never be crushed by it. Blessed be the God who warns, and who saves.
verseByVerse.note: Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem; the tower’s collapse is otherwise unknown.

parallels.desc: not wishing that any should perish

verseByVerse.quote: And he told this parable: 'A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told this parable: a man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser: look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?

The parable of the barren fig tree. Only Luke records it. It explains the warning to repent: why the axe has not yet fallen, and why it will.

A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. Notice the setting before anything else. A fig tree in a vineyard, not wild on a hillside. Fig trees were often planted in vineyards, in the best soil. This one has been deliberately planted in prime cultivated ground, and it is occupying space that would otherwise carry vines. Which is the first half of the case against it: this tree has had every advantage. And the two images together would have been unmistakable to anyone who knew the prophets. Israel is the vineyard of Isaiah 5, where God looked for grapes and found wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7), and Israel is the fig tree of the prophets, in which God came looking and found nothing (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). God had planted Israel in the best place, with every privilege.

And he came seeking fruit on it and found none. Fruit means righteousness, justice, repentance and faith, the fruits in keeping with repentance that John the Baptist demanded at the start of this Gospel (3:8). Not leaves, not size, not a pleasant shape: fruit, which is the only thing a fig tree is for.

For three years now. Three years is not impatience. A fig takes some years from planting to bear at all, and the law required that the fruit of the first three years be left untouched in any case (Leviticus 19:23). So the owner has waited and then come three times on top of it. A fig tree that had not borne fruit after so long probably never would. Some see a reference to the length of Jesus’ ministry, though that is uncertain. What is certain is that this is a man who has given the tree every year it was owed and several it was not.

Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground? And here is the charge, stated exactly. Not that it has done harm, nor that it is diseased. It is using up the ground. The verb (katargei) means to waste, to exhaust, to make idle. A fruitless tree draws water and nutrients out of good soil, takes the light, and occupies a space where something fruitful could stand. Barrenness in this parable is not a neutral condition. A tree that produces nothing is not simply failing to help; it is consuming, and what it consumes belongs to somebody else. Judgement was deserved.

What fruit is God looking for in me? Not a religious performance, and not a quota of activity. Jesus means the life that grows from a heart turned to God: repentance, trust in Christ, and the fruit of the Spirit that follows, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), along with honest dealings and mercy to the poor (3:10–14). Fruit is quiet and grows over time. You will often see it more clearly in others than in yourself, and a believer who fears he has none is often bearing more than he knows. The barren tree in the parable is not a struggling Christian; it is a life that has had every privilege and given nothing back to God at all.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a vineyard owner who came for three years seeking fruit on a fig tree, found none, and ordered it cut down.

On a Tuesday. God has planted you in good soil, with every privilege: an open Bible, perhaps a Christian home, a church where the gospel is preached, the prayers of people who love you. What fruit is he finding in your life? Ask it of the last year rather than of your whole life, because the whole is too large to see. What has God’s word actually produced in you since this time last year? The question the owner asks is not whether the tree has done wrong. It is what the tree is for.

For worship. The Lord of the vineyard is not careless with his ground. He plants with purpose, he comes looking, and he has every right to expect fruit from what he has made. And he is astonishingly patient. Three years, and he comes again; generations, and he sends again. The God who seeks fruit is the God who gives the sap, the sun and the soil, so that every fig his people ever bear is grown from his own goodness and offered back to his glory.
verseByVerse.note: Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: the vineyard that yielded wild grapes

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he answered him: sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.

Sir, let it alone this year also. The vinedresser does not dispute the verdict. He does not argue that the tree is fruitful, or that the owner has been hasty. He accepts the whole case and asks for time. It is a picture of intercession, and of God’s patience (2 Peter 3:9). And the identification is not difficult. The one who stands between the tree and the axe, asking for another year, is the one telling the story. Jesus intercedes for his people, and he is standing in that very crowd saying it.

Until I dig around it and put on manure. Notice what he offers along with the request. Not merely a delay: let it alone is only half his sentence. He undertakes to work: to dig round the roots, breaking up compacted ground so water can reach them, and to dung it. That is heavy, unpleasant, unglamorous labour on a tree that has given him nothing for three years, and he volunteers for it. Every possible help. God gives every opportunity to repent: his word, his messengers, his Son.

Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good. The sentence in Greek is broken off: if it bears fruit next year, and then nothing, as if the outcome is left open. Will it? The translators supply well and good; Jesus leaves a silence.

But if not, you can cut it down. Patience has an end. The time of grace is limited. Judgement is delayed, not cancelled. And here the parable does something most of its readers would rather it did not. The intercession has a term. The vinedresser does not ask for indefinite reprieve; he names the period, and he concedes the outcome if nothing changes.

The point. God’s patience is great, but it is not endless. The extra year is a gift: use it to repent (Romans 2:4). The parable ends without telling us what happened, because the hearers must decide. And it stands in its proper relation to the two disasters that preceded it. Those verses said the axe is real. This one says the axe is being held, and by whom. Both halves are needed, and separating them ruins the passage in one direction or the other. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years’ time. Jesus puts them in the same paragraph.

Does this mean a Christian can be cut down and lost? The parable is spoken first to Israel, and then to everyone who has privilege without fruit: the person who has heard the gospel all his life and never truly turned. It does not teach that those who belong to Christ can be cut off. Jesus says his sheep will never perish and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6). But it does warn that a fruitless profession is not safe, because fruit is the evidence of life (Matthew 7:16–20). If the warning troubles you, that is not a sign the axe is at your root. It is the vinedresser’s spade, and the right response is to turn to Christ now.

How do I pray for someone who seems hopeless? Like the vinedresser. His response to three barren years is not to write the tree off and not to pretend there is fruit. It is to ask for another year and go and get the spade. So pray specifically and persistently for the child who will not turn, the friend who shrugs, the church that has not grown. And add to your praying whatever digging is yours to do: the patient kindness, the honest conversation, the invitation, the Bible left open. The results belong to God. The asking and the labour belong to us.

In a sentence. The vinedresser pleaded for one more year to tend the tree, after which, if it still bore no fruit, it would be cut down.

On a Tuesday. God’s patience with you is a call to repent, not a reason to delay. This may be your extra year. If there is a sin you have been meaning to deal with, a reconciliation you have been putting off, a call to Christ you have been answering with later, the parable is talking to you, and its message is: now, while the ground is being dug for you.

For worship. The Son of God came down into the vineyard and took up the spade himself. He pleads for barren trees before the Father, and he works the soil of hard hearts with his own hands. And when the axe did fall, it fell on him: the one truly fruitful tree was cut down, hanged on a tree and made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that barren trees might be spared and made fruitful. Every year of grace you have had has been bought by his blood and asked for by his prayers. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

parallels.desc: God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A Woman with a Disabling Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke notes almost in passing that Jesus is teaching in a synagogue — the last time in this Gospel he is recorded doing so. The doors are closing.

The woman had been bent double for eighteen years and could not straighten herself. Luke the physician gives the clinical picture in a line. Consider what it means: she has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body, and has not looked another adult in the face in nearly two decades. She sees feet, floors, and the lower half of the world.

And she is in the synagogue. Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped coming — eighteen years of asking and receiving nothing, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict — and she is in her place. She asks for nothing when he arrives, which is what makes everything that follows one-sided.

Three things happen and all three are his: he saw her, in a crowded room, teaching, with a woman folded double probably out of everyone's sightline; he called her over, which made her healing public when it could have been quiet; and he touched her, which nobody had needed to do for a long time. “You are freed from your disability” — released, and the release stands; four verses later he calls it being “loosed from this bond.”

She stands up straight for the first time since the middle of another decade, and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look for eighteen years.

The synagogue ruler is indignant, and he does not address Jesus. He addresses the people — public instruction aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target. And his argument is not stupid: the fourth commandment says what he quotes. What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Which produces the sentence that gives the whole thing away: “come on those days and be healed.” He is proposing a schedule for a miracle, to a woman who has not been healed on any working day of any week for eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
“A disabling spirit” should not be flattened either way. Luke does not call her possessed or record a demon being cast out; Jesus says Satan had bound her — and chapter 11 showed a stronger one overpowering the strong man (11:21-22). What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it: the fallen world's disorder, exploited.

“Daughter of Abraham” occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation; the title is handed to a bent, unnamed, ceremonially awkward woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Luke will pair it later with Zacchaeus — “he also is a son of Abraham” (19:9).

The argument from lesser to greater is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice. An animal tied in a stall cannot reach water, and leaving it thirsty for a whole day was not an option any farmer would entertain; the rulings of the period permitted untying and leading, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering.

And the final word is the one they thought was the problem: “on the Sabbath day.” Not in spite of it. Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of slavery is the day for a knot to be undone.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ruler's manoeuvre is worth naming because it is recognisable. Public instruction, aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the target — the sermon everyone knows is about one person, the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

And underneath it is the real failure, which is not legalism exactly: he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem. There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure, and it does not feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness.

The woman glorifies God before anyone can tell her what she should feel — not the carefully considered religious expression calibrated for an audience, but the overflow of a life that has just been changed.

Two responses close the section, set side by side in a single verse: the adversaries put to shame, the people rejoicing. Nothing in the evidence separated them. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up, and what divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

And there is a small mercy at the end. Being put to shame is not the end of a man; shame is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.

Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. Only Luke records this healing. Luke notes the setting almost in passing, and it is the last time in this Gospel that Jesus is recorded teaching in a synagogue. The doors are closing.

And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. The behold is Luke pointing. She is not mentioned by anyone else in the room. The phrase is literally a spirit of weakness. Her condition was caused by Satan (v. 16), though she is not described as possessed, and Luke does not say a demon was cast out of her. What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it: the fallen world’s disorder, exploited. Satan can cause physical affliction (Job 2:7; 2 Corinthians 12:7). Not all illness is caused directly by Satan, but some is.

She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. Luke the doctor describes it precisely, in a line, with the eye of a man who has examined such people. Perhaps a fusion of the spine. She is folded forward and cannot lift herself upright. Consider what that means for eighteen years of ordinary life. She has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body. She has not looked another adult in the face; every conversation of nearly two decades has been conducted with the top of her head. She sees feet, floors and the lower half of the world. Eighteen years is longer than a childhood.

And she is in the synagogue. That is the thing to sit with. Eighteen years bent double, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict, and she is still coming to worship on the Sabbath. Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped coming. Luke does not tell us she prayed for healing, and she asks for nothing when Jesus arrives. It is likely she had stopped expecting anything, which is what makes what happens next entirely one-sided. And nobody in that synagogue had done anything about her. She had presumably been coming for most of those years, past the same faces, and she had become the settled furniture of the place: the bent woman at the back, whom everybody knew and nobody expected to change.

Is sickness caused by Satan? Here Luke says this woman’s condition came from a spirit, and Jesus calls her one whom Satan bound (v. 16). But Scripture never teaches that every illness is demonic: the man born blind was not (John 9:3), and Paul’s thorn was a messenger of Satan that God used for his good (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). A believer cannot be owned by Satan, though God may permit him to be afflicted. The ordinary response to illness is prayer and medicine, not exorcism.

In a sentence. While Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, a woman was there who had been bent double by a spirit of weakness for eighteen years.

On a Tuesday. Faithful in worship despite long suffering. Keep coming to God, whatever your burden. And look around your own church for the person who has become furniture: the one with the long illness, the one who comes alone, the one everybody knows and nobody expects to change. Jesus saw her. Ask him to give you eyes like his.

For worship. The Lord sees the ones who have stopped expecting to be seen. Eighteen years did not exhaust his attention, and a crowded room did not hide her from him. He is the God who lifts up those who are bowed down (Psalm 146:8), and he came into a synagogue that had forgotten her because he had not.

parallels.desc: another synagogue healing on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, 'Woman, you are freed from your disability.' And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her: woman, you are freed from your disability. And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.

When Jesus saw her, he called her over. Three things happen in that half-verse, and all three are his. She did not ask. He saw her. In a crowded synagogue, teaching, with a woman folded double and probably out of the sightline of everyone facing the front, he noticed her. Luke uses the same verb of him seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), and it always precedes an action. He called her over, which means she had to cross the room, slowly, bent, with every eye following her, and it means he made her healing a public event when he could have done it quietly. Whatever else is coming, nobody in that building will be able to say afterwards that they did not see it. He took the initiative, as he always does with those he saves.

Woman, you are freed from your disability. The verb (apolelysai) is a perfect passive: you have been released, set loose, and the release stands. It is the vocabulary of untying, and it is the same idea Jesus will use three verses later of the ox untied from its manger. He does not say be healed. He says the knot has been undone. It is the language of liberation he announced in Nazareth: liberty to the captives (4:18).

And he laid his hands on her. He touched her, which nobody may have done for a long time. A healing touch, and also a human one.

And immediately she was made straight. After eighteen years, she could stand upright and look up. Eighteen years, and it takes one sentence and a pair of hands. The Lord lifts up those who are bowed down (Psalm 146:8).

And she glorified God. The first thing she does with her new body, and the tense suggests she kept on doing it. Not only thanks, though presumably she thanked him; Luke records that the first use she made of standing upright was worship. For eighteen years she had not been able to lift her face towards heaven in a building built for lifting faces towards heaven. She stands up straight for the first time in nearly two decades, and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look all that time.

Why does Jesus heal some and not others, and should I expect healing? In the Gospels his healings are signs that the kingdom has come and that the one who will undo every curse is here. He did not heal every sick person in Israel, and he does not promise every believer healing in this life; Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God still heals today, in answer to prayer and through medicine, and we should ask him freely (James 5:14–15). But the miraculous gifts that marked the apostles were signs for the founding of the church, and we hold, charitably, that they are not given in the same way now. What every believer is promised is the final straightening: a resurrection body with nothing bent in it (Philippians 3:21). Ask boldly, and rest in that.

In a sentence. Seeing her, Jesus called her, declared her free, laid his hands on her, and she was straightened at once and praised God.

On a Tuesday. If you have been bent under something for years, an illness, a grief, a habit, a long loneliness, bring it to him again. You do not need to have the words; she had none. And when he lifts something off you, do what she did first. Before you tell anyone else, before you plan what to do with the freedom, look up and glorify God.

For worship. Jesus lifts up those who are bowed down. He saw her before she saw him, he called her before she asked, and he undid in a moment a knot Satan had tied for eighteen years. He is the stronger man who binds the strong (11:21–22), the Saviour whose touch makes straight what is crooked. Whatever is bending you low, bring it to him, and look up, because one day every one of his people will stand upright before him and see his face.

parallels.desc: the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down

verseByVerse.quote: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, 'There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people: there are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.

But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. The ruler of the synagogue was the man responsible for organising its services (8:41). A woman has just stood upright for the first time in eighteen years and is praising God at the front of his synagogue, and this man is angry. Not glad that a woman was freed after eighteen years, but angry that a rule had been broken. Religion without love.

Said to the people. Notice who he speaks to. Not to Jesus, who did it. To the people, and effectively to her, since she is the one being told when to come for healing. Too cowardly to rebuke Jesus directly, he lectures the congregation. That is a recognisable manoeuvre and it is worth naming: public instruction aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target. The sermon that everyone knows is about one person; the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

There are six days in which work ought to be done. He is quoting the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:9; Deuteronomy 5:13). And his argument is not stupid. He is right that the Sabbath forbids work, and he is not inventing a rule. What he has done is classify a healing as work. True, but misapplied.

Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day. Say it slowly and it collapses. He is instructing a woman who has been bent double for eighteen years, who has not been healed on any of the six working days of any week for nearly two decades, to come back on Monday. He is proposing a schedule for a miracle, as though healing were a service to be booked on weekdays, and the only issue were the opening hours. And as if a woman who had waited eighteen years could not wait one more day. Underneath that is the real failure, and it is not exactly legalism. It is that he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem.

How do I know if I am like this man? There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure. It is not rare, and it does not usually feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness. Ask yourself what your first reaction is when God moves in an unexpected way: in a person you had written off, in a church tradition not your own, in a service that ran late. Is it gladness, or a list of objections? Order matters, and Scripture asks for it (1 Corinthians 14:40). But when your love for the way things are done is stronger than your joy that a sinner is helped, the rule has taken the place of the Lord who gave it.

In a sentence. The synagogue ruler, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, told the people to come for healing on the other six days.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let love for rules make you angry at God’s grace. And if you have a grievance with someone, take it to that person, not sideways to everyone else (Matthew 18:15). The next time you feel the urge to make a pointed general remark, stop and ask whether you are teaching or merely hiding.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath is not a keeper of opening hours. His mercy does not wait for Monday. He gave the commandment as a gift of rest, and he came in person to give the rest the commandment promised. The God who rested on the seventh day is the God who does not rest from doing good (John 5:17), and his grace overflows every timetable we try to set for it.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord answered him, 'You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Lord answered him: you hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?

You hypocrites! The plural is deliberate. One man spoke; Jesus answers a whole way of thinking, and everyone in the room who agreed with him is included.

Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? The argument is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice, and everybody present did it. An animal tied in a stall cannot get to water, and animals could not go a day without it. Leaving a beast thirsty from Friday evening to Saturday evening was not an option any farmer would have entertained. Even the strictest rules of the period allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath; untying and leading were permitted, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering. Jesus is not asking them to adopt a new rule. He is asking them to apply the one they use every week of their lives.

And ought not this woman. Now the comparison, which is the sharpest thing in the chapter, and every term is chosen. The word for ought (edei) means must, it was necessary: the word of divine necessity that runs through Luke. It was not merely permitted to heal her; it was required. And this woman, set over against his ox or his donkey. The animal has an owner who will take trouble for it. The woman has been in that congregation for years.

A daughter of Abraham. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. A member of God’s covenant people, an heir of the promises, like Zacchaeus, a son of Abraham (19:9). Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation. The title is being handed to a bent, unnamed woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Of more value than an ox.

Whom Satan bound for eighteen years. The real cause. He names the one who tied the knot: the strong man of chapter 11, whom a stronger one overpowers (11:21–22). This is not merely a medical misfortune. It is an occupation, and someone is being dispossessed. Eighteen years, against the ox’s overnight thirst.

Be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day? A play on words: you untie your animals; should I not untie this woman? They untie; he unties. And the final word is the one they thought was the problem. Not in spite of the Sabbath, but on it. The Sabbath was the most fitting day for it. The Sabbath was given as a sign of God’s rest and of his liberation of Israel from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). What better day to free a captive of Satan? Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of bondage is the day for a knot to be undone. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ’s liberation.

Does the Sabbath still bind Christians? Christians who love the Bible answer this differently. Many, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment remains, moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day, so that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, kept holy for worship and works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, the true rest, so that no day binds the conscience in itself (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5), while Christians gladly gather on the Lord’s Day as the apostles did. Both agree on what this passage teaches: the day of rest is a day of mercy, deeds of kindness are never a breach of it, and its meaning is found in Christ, who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28).

In a sentence. Jesus called them hypocrites, since they untie their animals to water them on the Sabbath, and argued that a daughter of Abraham bound by Satan for eighteen years should certainly be freed on the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Look at the rules you live by, the good ones included, and ask whether you apply them more gently to your own convenience than to other people’s needs. Then think of the person in your church who is still bent under something, and ask what knot it is in your power to help untie this week: a visit, a meal, a lift, an hour of listening. Mercy is always in season.

For worship. The Lord’s Day is the day of liberation. On the first day of the week Christ rose from the dead, having broken the bonds of death itself, and every Lord’s Day since is a festival of untying. He is the one who proclaims liberty to the captives, and the knots of Satan cannot hold against his word. Rejoice in the freedom Christ gives, because he counts his people of more worth than the whole world, and he paid for their release with his life.
verseByVerse.note: Even the strictest rules allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath.

parallels.desc: he also is a son of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.

As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame. One verse, two reactions, and Luke sets them side by side without comment. The adversaries are those set against him, opponents in a case; the synagogue ruler is no longer merely indignant, he belongs to a party. And they had no answer. Humiliated by exposure: not shouted down, but shown up. Nobody argued them into silence; the argument and the standing woman did it between them. It is an echo of Isaiah 45:16 in the Greek: all who are incensed against him shall be put to shame.

And all the people rejoiced. The ordinary people saw it rightly. The crowd, who had nothing invested in a ruling about Sabbath work, are simply delighted.

At all the glorious things that were done by him. The word (endoxois) is unusual for a healing. It is the word used of God’s mighty acts at the exodus (Exodus 34:10, in the Greek). They have not merely observed something useful. Something of the weight of God has been visible in their synagogue, and they know it. Jesus’ works are God’s works.

Two responses to one event. This is the point of putting them in one sentence. Nothing in the evidence separated these people. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up. What divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel and for the rest of the story: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

Is there hope for the man who was put to shame? Yes. Being put to shame is not the end of a man. Shame is what a person feels when he has been shown to be wrong, and it is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the synagogue ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed. If you have been shown up by Christ, in your pride or your hardness, the shame is not meant to drive you away from him. It is meant to bring you to him.

In a sentence. His opponents were humiliated, but the people rejoiced at all the glorious things Jesus did.

On a Tuesday. When God does something good that you did not plan, someone converted whom you had given up on, a gift in someone you had underrated, notice which reaction rises in you first. Make a habit of rejoicing out loud at the glorious things Christ does, in your home and in your church, so that gladness becomes your instinct rather than suspicion.

For worship. Rejoice today at the glorious things Christ has done, including for you. The same weight of glory that rested on the exodus rested on a village synagogue that Sabbath, and it rests on every sinner he lifts. His works are glorious because he is glorious, and his enemies will one day be put to shame and his people will rejoice for ever in all that he has done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Narrow Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties the parables to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, been attacked for it, and sent a happy crowd home — and it is a fair question whether that is what the kingdom of God amounts to.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing anyone handled. And it is sowed in his garden — deliberately put in the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort. Black mustard grows fast and reaches ten or twelve feet; calling it a tree is a stretch, and probably meant to be.

Because the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not invented here. It is Ezekiel's and Daniel's, and it always means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6; Dan. 4:12). Jesus takes the image of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins; this starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.

The leaven parable ought to bring a reader up short, since one chapter ago leaven was the picture of everything that ruins (12:1). That is its usual role in Scripture — scoured out before Passover (Ex. 12:15), and Paul's image for malice and evil (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

But the sentence refuses the warning reading. Jesus does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says it is like leaven — the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading, and everything that makes it a good image for hypocrisy makes it a good image for the kingdom.

Then someone asks whether the saved will be few, and gets no number. “Strive to enter through the narrow door” — strain, exert everything, as an athlete does in a contest. And the door is narrow: not locked, not hidden, not high. Narrow says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The question “will those who are saved be few?” was a live one in the rabbinic schools, and notice how it is framed — a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking has placed himself outside the calculation.

That is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. There is a particular safety in the general: as long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing. And Jesus's reply is to them, plural, though one man asked.

If striving is required, is salvation earned? No — and notice what the striving is for. Not to become worthy, and not until enough has been done. Strive to enter. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13-14), and the dying criminal with nothing to offer is told “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). Nobody buys this door open — but plenty intend to go through it later, and later is a door that shuts.

“I do not know where you come from” is not a failure of memory. To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational (Amos 3:2), and “where you come from” is a householder's question about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house?

The closing vision fulfils Isaiah's feast on the mountain for all peoples (Isa. 25:6-8) and the gathering from far off (Isa. 49:12). The seats do not stand empty; the table is full of people nobody in that synagogue expected to see there.
verseByVerse.examples:
The plea of those outside is entirely true and entirely beside the point. They had eaten in his company — very possibly at one of the meals Luke has been recording — and he had taught in their streets and they were there. These are not people making things up.

But every claim is about proximity. We were near you. We were in the room. We were in the town where you preached. Nobody says we trusted you — and a modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years; I sat under good preaching; I took communion. All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

Which raises the question that keeps people awake: how do I know I am inside? The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing the entering all along in ordinary people. The centurion who says “say the word” (7:7). The woman told “your faith has saved you; go in peace” (7:50). The leper who came back (17:19). The blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38-39). Not one was admitted for being impressive; each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside.

And “some are last who will be first” should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog. What determines the order is not disadvantage but grace — and grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore, 'What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore: what is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.

He said therefore, What is the kingdom of God like? The therefore ties this to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, and been attacked for it, and the crowd went home happy. Now he explains what that was. In the light of the healing and of the opposition, the kingdom is present, in small beginnings, and it will grow. It is a fair question to have been asking. If this is the kingdom of God arriving, it does not look like much. One woman. One synagogue. One argument won against a minor official, and the establishment more hostile than it was that morning.

It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, the standard picture of the negligible, and Jesus uses it that way himself when he talks about faith (17:6). The kingdom began with one man from Nazareth and a handful of followers, and seemed insignificant. And note that it is sown in his garden: not scattered in a field, not dropped by accident. Somebody deliberately put a thing that small into the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort.

And it grew and became a tree. The mustard plant by the Sea of Galilee can grow taller than a man, ten feet (3 m) or more, large enough for birds to perch and shelter in.
