Guests reclined on couches arranged around tables, with the most important nearest the host: a visible ranking of the room that everybody present could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself. Honour in that culture was public and finite; it was gained and lost in front of witnesses, and a man’s standing was whatever the room said it was.

A parable. Not just social advice, but a picture of how God deals with people. It opens as pure etiquette, the sort of thing a wise uncle might say, and it ends with a statement about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited. And arrive later. Important guests often arrived last. The scenario is entirely realistic and would have made everyone wince.

Give your place to this person. Public humiliation. Follow the mechanics of it, because Jesus has thought it through. The man is not merely demoted. He has to get up, in front of everybody, and walk the length of the room.

And then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. By then, all the middle places are taken. You go to the very bottom, and every guest between the top and the bottom watches you go past. And begin with shame is exact. The shame is not a moment; it starts, and it goes on for the rest of the evening while he sits where everyone can see he ended up. Proverbs had said it long before: do not put yourself forward in the king’s presence, for it is better to be told, come up here, than to be put lower in the presence of a noble (Proverbs 25:6–7). That is what the grasping actually costs, and the parable has not yet said a word about God.

Is it wrong to want to be recognised? The desire to be honoured is not itself evil: God made us for glory, and he promises honour to those who seek it by patient well-doing (Romans 2:7). What Jesus condemns is seizing it, ranking yourself above others and pushing for the place. The question is who you want the honour from. If you live for the room’s estimate, you will always be anxious about the next guest through the door. If you live for God’s, you can sit anywhere, and let him do the honouring in his own time.

In a sentence. Seeing guests choose the best seats, Jesus told them not to take the place of honour, in case someone more important came and they were moved down in shame.

On a Tuesday. Don’t push yourself forward for recognition. Let others, and God, do the honouring. Notice the small seat-grabbing moves you make: steering the conversation to your achievements, needing to be thanked, quietly resenting the person who got the credit. Each is a scramble for a couch. Let it go.

For worship. The true guest of honour at that dinner had taken the lowest place long before he walked in. He left the highest seat in heaven and came down to the bottom of the table, born in a stable and laid in a manger, and he would go lower still. Every honour we scramble for, he laid aside, so that we might be called up to sit with him at his Father’s table.
verseByVerse.note: Places at a banquet were ranked by closeness to the host.

parallels.desc: better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be put lower

verseByVerse.quote: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you: friend, move up higher. Then you will be honoured in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place. Choose humility. The advice is exactly reversed.

So that when your host comes he may say to you, Friend, move up higher. The host honours the humble. And if it stopped here it would be a piece of shrewd manoeuvring: take the bottom seat as a tactic, and enjoy being moved up in front of everybody. Anyone who has read it that way has been outmanoeuvred by the parable, and the next verse is what closes the trap.

Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. Real honour comes from the host, not from self-promotion. Only the one who gave the feast can say where you belong at it.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. The principle. The passive voice means: humbled by God, exalted by God. This is not about how the evening goes. It is a statement about who runs the seating of the universe. It is a central truth of the kingdom, repeated in 18:14 (the Pharisee and the tax collector). Mary sang it (1:52). Jesus himself lived it: he humbled himself to the cross, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:5–11).

What it does not mean. Not false humility, a clever tactic to be noticed. Taking the lowest place in order to be promoted is pride in disguise. True humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less, and leaving your honour to God (1 Peter 5:5–6).

Why humility is accuracy. This is where the parable turns from advice into gospel. It cannot be obeyed as a technique. It can only be obeyed by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing, and there is exactly one thing that produces that, which is knowing what your actual standing is. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat. He is being accurate. There is no lower place in that room than the one he already occupies before God, and he is at the table by invitation and not by merit. Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it, and an evening spent at the bottom of the table costs him nothing at all.

Does humility mean I should never accept a responsibility or say I can do something well? No. Humility is not pretending to be less gifted than you are, and refusing a task God plainly calls you to is not modesty but disobedience. Paul could say he worked harder than all the apostles, and add at once that it was the grace of God with him (1 Corinthians 15:10). Humility is honest about gifts, because it knows they are gifts (1 Corinthians 4:7). It serves without needing the credit, rejoices when others are honoured, and does not grasp. You may sit at the head of the table if the host puts you there. Just do not put yourself there.

In a sentence. Take the lowest place, so that the host may call you higher, for whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

On a Tuesday. Where can you take the lower place today, and leave your honour in God’s hands? Let someone else have the parking space, the last word, the credit for the idea. Do one piece of good this week that nobody will ever know was yours.

For worship. The one who said this was on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is. He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:8–9). He went to the bottom of the table so that sinners could hear the Host say, Friend, come up higher. All our exaltation is his gift, and all the glory of it is his.

verseByVerse.quote: He said also to the man who had invited him, 'When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said also to the man who had invited him: when you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbours, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.

He said also to the man who had invited him. Having dealt with the guests, he turns to the host, at the host’s own table, having eaten his food. It is one of the least comfortable moments in the Gospels.

Do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors. Not a prohibition of ever inviting family and friends. A Hebrew way of saying: not only these, but rather. The four categories are the entire ordinary guest list.

Lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return. Hospitality was a social exchange, building status and alliances. An invitation created a debt, and the debt was discharged by a return invitation of matching quality. A dinner party was a transaction with a settlement date. That is not grace; it is business (6:32–34).

Invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind. Those who could never repay, and who were often excluded from religious gatherings, as the Qumran community excluded the lame and blind from its meals. The very people God will bring to his banquet (v. 21). The four categories here are the exact opposite of the first four: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none.

And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. The blessing is in giving without return. The reason given is not that they are more deserving. It is precisely that they cannot repay you: the inability is the qualification. This is how God gives: to those who cannot repay.

For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just. God will repay. The resurrection of the just is the resurrection to life of the righteous at the last day (Acts 24:15; John 5:29). Not you will not be repaid. The account is not cancelled; it is moved. And see what the host is being offered: a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection, which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

So am I forbidden to have my family round for Christmas dinner? No, and the same chapter tells you why. A dozen verses on, Jesus will say that a disciple must hate his father and mother (v. 26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends; it is do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends, at Levi’s feast, in Martha’s house, and at this very Pharisee’s dinner while he said it. So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does.

Does giving in hope of a heavenly reward spoil it? No. Jesus himself sets the reward before us, so it cannot be wrong to want it (Hebrews 11:6). What spoils giving is wanting the return from people: thanks, status, an invitation back. To give looking to God for your reward is to give freely to people, since you need nothing from them. And the reward itself is a gift of grace, not wages earned. God crowns in his children what his Spirit has worked in them, and the greatest part of the reward is the Giver himself.

In a sentence. Jesus told his host to invite to his feasts not those who could repay, but the poor and disabled who could not, and God would repay him at the resurrection.

On a Tuesday. Who could you invite to your home who could never invite you back? Put the two lists side by side, those your table has served this year and those Jesus names, and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so. Start with one name: the widower from church, the international student, the family that is struggling, the man nobody sits with.

For worship. This is how God gives. He spread his table for people who had nothing to bring and could never invite him back. We were the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, and he did not wait for us to become worth inviting. The whole of salvation is a feast given to those who cannot repay, by a God who needs nothing from us and delights to give. And the one who tells the host to do it is the Host who has already done it, at the cost of his own body and blood.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return.

parallels.desc: the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow shall eat

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Parable of the Great Banquet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A guest breaks the silence with something entirely correct: “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” The picture he invokes was the settled hope of Israel — the feast on the mountain, rich food for all peoples, death swallowed up (Isa. 25:6-8).

So why does Jesus answer with a parable about people who refuse an invitation? Listen to the sentence again. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense, and nobody in the room is implicated by it. Jesus has just told them to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them — both remarks about this table, tonight — and what comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

The parable changes the tense. And it turns on a custom: a formal banquet involved two invitations, the first well in advance so the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals, the second on the day to say it was ready. So these guests are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They accepted weeks ago, and the host has slaughtered on the strength of it.

“Come, for everything is now ready” is the gospel in six words. Not would you consider coming? The work is done, the cost has been met, and the only thing missing is the guests. And notice who carries it — not the host but a servant, sent on foot to men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own.

Then the excuses, and not one is disreputable. A field already bought; five yoke of oxen already bought; a new marriage. Property, work, family — every one a good thing, and not one a sin. Nobody says “I do not want to come.” They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home.

Which is the form the rejection of the gospel almost always takes. Very few people ever say “I refuse Christ.” A great many say “not now — there is something I have to deal with first,” and go on saying it politely for forty years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The master's anger is the only emotion attributed to him, and it is easily made into something it is not. It is not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. He has been given his guests' word and spent accordingly — and in that economy a great banquet meant slaughtered animals that could not be kept, so the cost was already unrecoverable. What has been refused is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were both unanimous and casual. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved.

But the anger does not cancel the banquet; it redirects it. And the four categories the servant is sent to fetch are the same four Jesus gave the host eight verses earlier (v.13) — which is the parable's quiet accusation to a room that had just heard the instruction and let it pass. God does exactly what he told them to do.

The parable's geography follows the movement of Acts: the original guests, then the streets and lanes of the city, then the highways and hedges outside it — Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. The original guests are the religious establishment that has had the invitation through the whole Old Testament and is declining it with polite excuses; the poor and lame of the city are the tax collectors and sinners responding to his ministry; the people beyond the walls are the Gentiles.

And the exclusion is stated without qualification: “none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.” The feast does not wait indefinitely, and the door does not stay open after the house is full.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room” is the most hopeful sentence in the parable. The servant has swept every street and every alley and brought in everyone he found, and the hall is not full. Whatever else this house is, it was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come.

One phrase has done real damage and should be handled plainly: “compel people to come in.” Augustine, pressed by the Donatist controversy, used it to justify the state coercing schismatics back to the church, and it was quoted for centuries afterwards in defence of forced baptisms and penal laws.

Which is exactly the opposite of force. Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will. If the verse presses anything on the church, it is urgency in persuading the people who assume the gospel cannot possibly be for them.

And “that my house may be filled” is the heart of it. Not that the food may not be wasted. He wants the room full.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, 'Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him: blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!

Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God! Somebody breaks the silence, and what he says is entirely correct. A pious remark, perhaps to ease the tension, or to show his own piety. The picture he is invoking was the settled hope of Israel: the messianic banquet, the great feast at the end of the age, when the LORD of hosts would spread a feast of rich food for all peoples and swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8), the feast Jesus had spoken of on the road (13:29). Every devout Jew at that table believed it and looked forward to it. He assumes he will be there. The parable that follows asks: will you?

Why does Jesus answer a true remark with a warning? Listen to the sentence again and the reason surfaces. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense: blessed is everyone who will eat. Nobody in the room is implicated by it. It is the kind of thing a man says at a dinner table when the conversation has become uncomfortable and he wants to return it to safe and elevating ground. And the timing gives it away. Jesus has just told this room to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them. Both remarks were about this table, tonight. What comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

A manoeuvre worth recognising. It is very hard to object to. Nothing false has been said. The speaker has agreed enthusiastically with the general direction of everything, and in doing so has moved the entire discussion somewhere it can cost him nothing. Jesus’ reply changes the tense. The parable that follows is not about who will be blessed at a future feast. It is about a banquet that is ready now, a servant already at the door, and a set of men who all had something else on. The man wanted to talk about the guest list of the kingdom. He is about to be told that the invitations have gone out and the replies are coming in.

In a sentence. One of the guests exclaimed how blessed are those who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to speak warmly about heaven. Make sure you have accepted the invitation. Watch for the moments when you change the subject to something true and general because the specific was getting close: a sermon applied to someone else, a conversation about the church’s needs that never reaches your diary. The kingdom is not only a hope to admire. It is an invitation to answer.

For worship. Blessed indeed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God, and the blessing is real because the King himself has made it so. He is the bread of life, broken for his guests, and at his table death will be swallowed up for ever and every tear wiped away. To sit at that feast will be the joy of eternity, and every seat at it was paid for by the Host.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to him, 'A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to him: a man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited: come, for everything is now ready.

A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. God, preparing the feast of the kingdom. A great banquet, for many. Note the two stages, because the custom matters and the parable turns on it. In that world a formal banquet involved two invitations. The first went out well in advance, and it was accepted or declined then; the host needed to know the numbers before he killed the animals, since meat could not be kept. The second was sent on the day, when everything was ready, to tell the guests who had already accepted that it was time to come, since there were no clocks. So the people in this story are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They said yes weeks ago. The host has bought and slaughtered on the strength of it. The first invitation had been accepted. Israel had been invited long ago, through the prophets.

And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant. That is the second summons. And notice who carries it. Not the host. A servant, sent out on foot to the houses of men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own. The servant is Jesus, or those who preach the kingdom. That is the shape of every gospel errand since. The servant does not prepare the feast, cannot add to it, and has nothing to offer but the message that it is ready, and the message is the whole of his commission.

Come, for everything is now ready. Hear what it actually says. Not would you consider coming, not are you free. Everything is now ready: the work is done, the cost has been met, the table is laid, and the only thing missing is the guests. The kingdom is ready now. Everything has been prepared. All they need to do is come. The gospel invitation. That is the gospel in a sentence, and it is why the parable is not really about hospitality at all. The invitation Jesus brings is never an invitation to do something. It is the announcement that something has been done and is finished, and that the only remaining question is whether a man will come and sit down.

What does it mean for me to come? To come is to trust Christ: to stop relying on anything you bring and to rely on what he has done. It is not first a matter of feelings or of cleaning yourself up; the guests at this feast are fed, not inspected. You come by turning from your sin and resting on Christ, telling God in your own words that you have nothing and asking him to receive you for his Son’s sake. And having come, you keep coming: to his word, his table and his people. The banquet is ready today, and the invitation is addressed to you.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who gave a great banquet and, when it was ready, sent his servant to tell the invited guests to come, for everything was prepared.

On a Tuesday. If you speak to anyone about Christ this week, remember what you are carrying. Not a programme of self-improvement or a set of conditions, but news: everything is ready. You are a servant with a message, not a salesman with a pitch, and you need add nothing to it.

For worship. God has prepared everything for your salvation. Come, for everything is now ready. The Father planned the feast before the foundation of the world, the Son paid for it with his own blood and cried it is finished, and the Spirit goes out still with the summons. Nothing is left undone. There is no gift more complete, no Host more generous, and no table more full.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him: I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused. And another said: I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused. And another said: I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.

But they all alike began to make excuses. All alike: with one accord, as though it had been arranged. And these are men who had already accepted. To refuse after accepting an invitation was a grave insult. And their excuses are flimsy. Three are given as samples, and the striking thing about them is that not one is disreputable.

I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Possessions. Who buys a field without seeing it first? The transaction is already complete; in that world nobody purchased land unexamined. Going out to look at it now is pleasure, not necessity, and it would still be there tomorrow.

I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Business, and the same shape. Ten oxen: a wealthy man, farming on a substantial scale. Again, you would test them before buying, and trying them out could be done any morning that week.

I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. Family, and this one is different in tone. The first two say please have me excused, which is at least polite. This one does not ask. He states it as a fact. And there was a legal provision he may be leaning on: the law excused a newly married man from war and public duty for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5). But a banquet is not a war, and the law he is standing on was given to protect a marriage, not to excuse a man from a feast.

The point. Possessions, work, and family: all good things. But they become excuses for refusing God’s invitation. Not wicked things, but good things put first, keep people out of the kingdom (8:14; 9:57–62). Which is why the parable is more searching than a story about wicked men would have been. Nobody here says I do not want to come. Nobody attacks the host. They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home.

The form refusal takes. That is the form the rejection of the gospel almost always takes. Very few people ever say I refuse Christ. A great many say not now: there is something I have to deal with first. And they go on saying it, politely, for forty years. Jesus classifies that answer without hesitation. It is not a postponement. It is the refusal.

But surely my family and work are things God gave me? They are, and that is exactly what makes them dangerous as excuses. God gives fields, oxen and wives so that we might enjoy them with thanksgiving under him (1 Timothy 4:4). Coming to Christ does not take them away; it puts them in their place, and they are better there. The trouble begins when a gift is used to keep the Giver at arm’s length. If your reason for not coming to Christ, or not following him fully, is something good, you are in precisely the position of these men. Bring the field and the oxen and the marriage with you to the feast. Do not send them as your apology.

In a sentence. The invited guests all made excuses: one had bought a field, another oxen, and another had just married.

On a Tuesday. What good thing in your life is your excuse for not coming fully to God? Listen for your own version of I must go and see it: the work that crowds out prayer, the weekend plans that keep you from worship, the family schedule that leaves no room for Christ. None of those is wicked. Any of them can be an apology sent to the King.

For worship. The God who gives fields and oxen and marriages is better than all of them, and he invites us to himself. How patient he is with polite refusals, how generous to keep his table spread after insults. And the Son who told this story was himself refused by the guests his Father had invited, and went on to the cross to make a place for those who had refused him before. Better is one day in his courts than a thousand elsewhere (Psalm 84:10).
verseByVerse.note: The law excused a newly married man from war for a year — but not from a feast.

parallels.desc: a newly married man free at home one year

verseByVerse.quote: So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant: go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.

So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry. Rightly. His generosity had been insulted. The anger is worth stopping at rather than hurrying past, because it is the only emotion attributed to the host in the whole parable and it is easily made into something it is not. It is not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. He has been given his guests’ word. He has spent accordingly. Then, on the day, with the food on the table, every one of them sent back a message about a field. What has been refused is not an evening’s entertainment. It is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were both unanimous and casual.

Is God really angry with people who decline his invitation? Yes, and it would be a lesser God who were not. His anger is not a loss of temper but the settled response of holy love to generosity treated as an inconvenience. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved. That is sobering for anyone who has been treating the gospel as an offer with no deadline. But notice what the anger does next. It does not cancel the feast. It sends the servant out again, to people nobody else wanted. God’s anger at refusal and his eagerness to fill his house stand together.

Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city. And then the astonishing turn: the anger redirects the banquet. Quickly, because the food is ready and the evening is going ahead. The streets and lanes are the public thoroughfares and the narrow back alleys, the town’s back streets where the outcasts lived. This is where a man goes to find people who have nowhere else to be. Within Israel: the tax collectors, sinners, the poor, those excluded by the religious elite.

And bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame. Exactly the list of verse 13. God does what he told the host to do. The kingdom is filled with those who have nothing to offer. That is the parable’s quiet accusation, delivered to a room that had just heard the instruction and let it pass. The people who cannot repay him are the ones who end up at the table, not as a second-best arrangement forced on him by circumstances, but because that was always the kind of guest list he wanted.

What if I feel too broken to belong at God’s table? Then you are exactly the kind of guest this verse describes. The poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame were not brought in because they had recovered; they were brought in as they were. Your sense of unworthiness is not a barrier to coming. It is, in this parable, the very mark of those who are carried in. Come as you are, and he will make you what he wants you to be.

In a sentence. The angry master sent his servant to bring in the poor and disabled from the city streets instead.

On a Tuesday. Who in your town is in the streets and lanes: those who would never think a church was for them, those on the edges of your own congregation? Go to them quickly, with the same message the servant carried, and bring them in. Make your church a place where the poor and broken are not tolerated but wanted.

For worship. You were invited when you had nothing. Thank God for his grace to the poor and broken. He went into the back streets of the world to find us, and he did not ask us to tidy ourselves first. The King of glory fills his house with beggars and calls them his guests, and the joy of the feast is that every person there knows he had no right to be.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant said: sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room. And the master said to the servant: go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.

Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room. The most hopeful sentence in the parable, and it is spoken by the servant. He has swept the city, every street and every alley, and brought in everyone he found, and the hall is not full. God’s house is large. Whatever else this house is, it was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come. There is room for more.

Go out to the highways and hedges. Now he is sent outside the town altogether. The highways are the roads between towns; the hedges are the field boundaries and hedgerows where travellers and vagrants sheltered, where a man with no roof sleeps. These are not the poor of the city. These are people with no address at all, and to the men listening, they are foreigners. The Gentiles, outside Israel. This is the mission of Acts, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8; 13:46).

And compel people to come in. Compel means urge them strongly, press them to come. Strangers would not believe such an invitation, and would be reluctant. In Middle Eastern culture, a guest would politely refuse and have to be urged. A man summoned from a hedgerow to a nobleman’s banquet would assume a mistake had been made, and would need pressing hard before he believed the invitation was meant for him. The compulsion in view is a servant taking a beggar by the arm and saying: no, truly, he means you. The invitation is so generous it must be pressed on people.

Where Christians differ: compel them to come in. Augustine used this verse to justify using the power of the state to force heretics (the Donatists) back into the church, and it was later used to justify forced conversions and persecution. Verdict: this is a grievous misreading. The compulsion is the urgency of love and persuasion, not force. Faith cannot be coerced. The gospel is to be pressed on people earnestly, but never by violence (2 Corinthians 5:11, 20). Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will.

How do I urge someone without being pushy? Urgency and respect belong together. Speak plainly about Christ, and do not be embarrassed to ask someone to come, more than once if need be: to church, to a Bible study, to Christ himself. Tell them the invitation is truly for them, especially if they think they are too far gone. But never manipulate, never bully, and never use pressure that bypasses the conscience; God opens hearts, and we only persuade (Acts 16:14). Pray before you speak, listen as much as you talk, and let your life make the invitation believable. Love presses; it does not coerce.

That my house may be filled. God is determined that his banquet will be full. His purpose will not be thwarted by refusal. Not merely that the food may not be wasted: he wants the room full. Every seat at that table has a name on it, and the Master will not rest until every one is taken (John 6:37–39).

For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet. Those who refused will be shut out (13:28). By their own choice. And the last line is spoken in the plural, to somebody other than the servant, which is Jesus stepping out of the parable and addressing the dinner party he is sitting at.

In a sentence. When there was still room, the master sent his servant to the country roads to urge people to come in until his house was full, declaring that none of the first guests would taste his banquet.

On a Tuesday. There is still room. Urge others to come to Christ, earnestly and lovingly. Think of the person you have assumed would never be interested, the one beyond the hedges of your usual circle, and tell them, kindly and plainly, that the invitation is for them. And pray for the missionaries who are going to the highways of the world where the name of Christ is still unknown.

For worship. Still there is room: the most hopeful words a sinner can hear. The Father’s house has many rooms, and the Son has gone to prepare them (John 14:2). His grace has run out to the hedgerows of the Gentile world and found us there, and it will not stop until the house is full. Glory to the God whose mercy is larger than all our refusals, and whose banquet will never be short of a single guest he has chosen.
verseByVerse.note: “Compel” means press them to come — the invitation is so generous it must be urged.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Great crowds are travelling with him, and he turns round and says the hardest thing in the Gospel — which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a following.

“Hate” is Semitic idiom for loving less by comparison, and the usage is well attested: Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah,” and in the next verse Leah is described as “hated” (Gen. 29:30-31). Matthew records the same saying in the plainer form — “whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

The idiom explains the word, but the softer reading is not a rescue operation; it is the only one the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity — when the scribes devised Corban to avoid supporting aged parents, he called it making void the word of God (Mark 7:9-13), which is precisely the manoeuvre a literal reading of this verse would license. He kept the commandment himself in his last hours, giving his mother to John (John 19:26-27). And Paul states it flatly: a man who does not provide for his household “has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

And note the last name on the list, which governs the rest: “and even his own life.” Family is not being singled out for sacrifice; the self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation.

The cross image was not a metaphor to that crowd. A cross-bearer was a specific sight: a condemned man, already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets, with the jeering going on around him. It carries finality, shame, and submission — and the man saying it was going to do it himself within the year.

Then two parables, both beginning “sit down first.” The tower is probably a farm watchtower, not a monument, and the failure is public and permanent: an abandoned foundation sits in the field for as long as anybody remembers, and Jesus supplies the sentence the neighbours will say. The king's case adds a third option the builder does not have — sue for peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cost teaching is addressed to those already following, already enthusiastic, already in the crowd. They are not being warned before they commit; they are being warned that what they think they have committed to may not be what discipleship requires. The danger is not the uncommitted outsider but the enthusiastic follower who has not counted the cost.

He is not recruiting. He has just watched thousands attach themselves to his procession and his response is to tell them to stop and calculate — the exact opposite of every technique for gathering a following that has ever been used. A crowd that has not counted the cost is not an asset; it is a field full of abandoned foundations waiting to happen.

The king's parable changes the register. The builder's alternatives are to finish or be mocked; the king can send a delegation and ask for terms. And who is the greater king in that picture? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. What is left is the delegation — going out, while there is still distance, and asking for terms. That is not defeat in this parable; it is the only wise move on the board, and it is what the counting of the cost is actually for.

“Renounce” is not primarily get rid of but let go of: a man at a door, releasing his hold on what he is leaving behind.
verseByVerse.examples:
What the hate-saying means is a matter of collision, not everyday temperature. Most of the time there is no conflict at all — loving Christ makes a man a better son, husband and father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured: when following Jesus will cost you your family's approval, or your inheritance, or your place at their table.

If you are living inside that collision, take two things from it. The cost is real and Jesus never pretends otherwise — he has already said he came to divide households (12:51-53), and he says this to a crowd, not to specialists; the grief you feel is not a sign you have done something wrong. And the command does not license coldness. Nothing here permits writing your family off, arguing at every meal, or making your faith a weapon. You go on loving them, and usually better than before; you simply stop letting their approval decide what you do with Christ.

“Renounce all that he has” is comprehensive in a way that goes past property — reputation, plans, the rights a man believes his circumstances have granted him, the future he has drawn up. Here is a test that is not about percentages: think of the thing you are most certain God would never ask you for. Not the hardest to lose — the thing quietly filed as not up for discussion. Whatever came to mind has not been renounced.

And the salt saying is the chapter's last word on what a half-committed disciple is for. The salt of Palestine was gathered from Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum; if the sodium leached out with damp it left a white powder that looked exactly like salt and did nothing. Still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt — and it has stopped working.

verseByVerse.quote: Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them: if anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.

Now great crowds accompanied him. Popular. But Jesus is not interested in crowds; he wants disciples. The setting is the point. He has an enormous following, and he turns round and says the hardest thing in the Gospel, which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a crowd.

And he turned and said to them. Deliberately, to the whole crowd. He has been walking ahead, and they have been following, and he stops the procession to tell them what following means.

If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother. A shocking statement. Hate here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less, a comparison. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and in the next verse the text says Leah was hated (Genesis 29:30–31; see also Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13). Matthew’s parallel gives the plainer form: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). Jesus demands first place, above every other love.

And wife and children and brothers and sisters. The closest relationships, named one by one, so that no one can think his own case is the exception.

Yes, and even his own life. Even self. The last name on the list governs the rest. Family is not being singled out for sacrifice. The self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation of the two.

He cannot be my disciple. Not may not be a very good disciple, but cannot be. Jesus claims a loyalty that only God has the right to claim. Either he is God, or this is outrageous. No prophet ever said, love me more than your mother. Moses said, love the LORD your God with all your heart (Deuteronomy 6:5). Jesus puts himself where Moses put God.

Is this not a convenient softening? The idiom explains the word, but a reader may still suspect the explanation of being a rescue operation, a hard saying softened because we do not like it. It is not; it is the only reading the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity. When the scribes devised Corban, a way of declaring money dedicated to God so that it need not support aged parents, Jesus said they were making void the word of God by their tradition (Mark 7:9–13). That is precisely what a literal reading of this verse would license, and he condemned it. He kept the commandment himself at the last possible moment, giving his mother into John’s care from the cross (John 19:26–27). And Paul says that anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

What it does not mean. Not literal hatred, or neglect of family. Jesus commands honouring parents (18:20) and loving wives (Ephesians 5:25). But when love for family conflicts with loyalty to Christ, Christ must win. Compared with our love for him, every other love should look like hatred. And in fact, loving Christ most makes us love others better.

When does the conflict actually come? Most of the time there is no conflict at all: loving Christ makes a man a better son, a better husband, a better father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured. A convert from another faith whose family cuts him off. A believer whose spouse demands that she stop going to church. A son whose father insists he join a dishonest business. A parent who must choose between a child’s approval and the truth. In those moments Jesus must win, gently and without contempt, and with the door kept open. And where a family relationship involves abuse, putting Christ first never means submitting to it; it may mean seeking safety and help.

In a sentence. Jesus told the crowds that anyone who does not love him more than family and even his own life cannot be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. Who or what do you love more than Jesus? Put him first, and every other love will find its right place. Ask a hard question: if following Christ cost you the approval of the person whose approval you most want, would you still follow? Pray for the grace to answer yes, and then go home and love your family better than you did yesterday, for his sake.

For worship. Only one who is God can ask for this, and only one who loves like God would deserve it. Christ asks for first place because he gave up his first place: he left his Father’s side and laid down his own life for us. He is worthy to be loved above mother and father, wife and child, and life itself, because he is the source of every good love and the fountain of all joy. Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Psalm 73:25).
verseByVerse.note: “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Matthew’s parallel says “loves father or mother more than me.”

parallels.desc: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah — “Leah was hated”

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

Whoever does not bear his own cross. He has said this before, after Peter’s confession (9:23), and there it was daily. Here it is put differently: not take up but bear, and not his cross but his own cross. Bear is the ordinary word for carrying a load, not a single act of lifting but the sustained business of walking under a weight. And his own makes it particular. There is no generic cross issued to disciples in one size. Each man carries the one that has his name on it, and it will not look like anybody else’s.

What the image meant. It was not a metaphor to that crowd, and it has been worn smooth by two thousand years of use. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. A cross-bearer in the Roman world was a specific sight: a man already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets, with the jeering going on all around him. Everyone in that crowd had probably seen it. So the picture is not hardship. It is a man walking to his death in public, and it carries three things. Finality: nobody carrying a crossbeam is coming back down that road. Shame: crucifixion was designed to be degrading, reserved for slaves and rebels. Submission: a man carrying his cross has stopped fighting; he is going where he is being taken. To bear your cross is to accept rejection, shame and death for Jesus’ sake, as a way of life.

And come after me. Follow him on the road to Jerusalem and the cross. The cross is not carried in a circle; it is carried behind someone.

Cannot be my disciple. The second cannot. There is no cross-less discipleship.

Is my cross the illness or difficulty I have? Not exactly. Every Christian suffers the ordinary troubles of a fallen world, and God uses them; but the cross Jesus means is what comes to you because you follow him. It is the cost of saying no to yourself and yes to Christ: the career move declined because it meant dishonesty, the friendships lost because you would not join in, the mockery at work, the sin you go on refusing year after year, the persecution that in many lands means prison or death. A cross is chosen in the sense that you could put it down by abandoning Christ. Bearing it means you will not.

In a sentence. Whoever does not carry his own cross and follow Jesus cannot be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. What cross are you carrying for Jesus today? Name the place where following him costs you something this week, and do not quietly lay it down. And if nothing about your Christian life costs you anything at all, ask whether you are following closely enough to be noticed.

For worship. The man saying it was going to do it himself within the year: through those same streets, condemned, shamed, submitting. He never asks anyone to walk a road he has not walked first. He bore not only his own cross but our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), and what he carried was the full weight of the wrath we deserved. Our crosses are light beside his, and every one of them is carried behind a risen Lord who has already walked the road to the end and out the other side.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying: this man began to build and was not able to finish.

For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost? Having said what discipleship costs, he insists that people work out whether they can pay. A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm (Isaiah 5:2), or be a farm building: not a great civic monument but an ordinary piece of work that an ordinary landowner might undertake. And the verb is sit down. Not consider in passing. Stop, sit, and do the arithmetic before the first stone is laid. Wise planning: do I have enough to finish?

This man began to build and was not able to finish. A half-built tower was a monument to foolishness, mocked by all. The failure described is public and permanent. An abandoned foundation does not go away. It sits in the field, visible from the road, for as long as anybody in the district remembers, and Jesus supplies the sentence the neighbours will say, which is the detail that makes it sting.

The point. Before you follow Jesus, think about what it will cost. Don’t start enthusiastically and give up halfway (8:13). The crowds were following without thinking.

He is not recruiting. This is a startling thing to say to a crowd that is following him. He has just watched thousands of people attach themselves to his procession, and his response is to tell them to stop and calculate whether they can afford it, which is the exact opposite of every technique for gathering a following that has ever been used. He is not after numbers. A crowd that has not counted the cost is a field full of abandoned foundations waiting to happen. That has something uncomfortable to say about how conversions are sometimes sought. There is a kind of appeal that works by keeping the cost out of sight until the decision is made: get them in, and explain later. Jesus does the reverse, in public, to the largest crowd he ever had.

If I must count the cost, how can anyone afford it? No one can pay it in his own strength, and that is part of what the counting reveals; the next parable will say so. The cost is real: Christ asks for everything. But the one who calls also supplies. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), and those who build on him are kept by his power, not their own (1 Peter 1:5). The counting is not meant to deter anybody. It is meant to make the commitment real, so that what begins actually gets finished, and so that the tower, when it is up, is a witness rather than a joke.

In a sentence. As a builder first counts the cost of a tower to make sure he can finish it, so a would-be disciple must count the cost of following Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Have you counted the cost of following Jesus? It is everything, and he is worth it. When you speak to others about Christ, tell them the cost honestly as well as the joy. And if you have stalled halfway, with a foundation laid years ago and little built since, come back to him today. He finishes what he starts.

For worship. Jesus counted the cost before he laid the first stone of our salvation. He sat down in eternity and knew exactly what it would take, the manger, the cross, the grave, and he did not turn back. He set his face to go to Jerusalem, and he finished. It is finished, he said, and the tower of our redemption stands complete, a monument not to foolishness but to the wisdom and love of God.
verseByVerse.note: A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm.

verseByVerse.quote: Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.

Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate? A second parable. A greater matter: a war, not a building. The change of scale is deliberate, from a farmer with a half-built shed to a king with an army, from money to survival. Sit down first again: the same instruction as the builder’s. Do the sum before you move.

Whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Outnumbered two to one. Not hopeless, but the kind of arithmetic that requires an honest man to face a difficult conclusion.

He sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. Wise surrender, while there is still time, while the other is yet a great way off. Here the two parables part company, and the difference is the whole point. The builder’s alternatives are to finish or to be mocked. The king has a third option, and it is the one Jesus names: he can sue for peace. He sends envoys before the armies are in sight of each other, and asks what the terms are.

The point. Two possible readings, both true. First, as with the tower: count the cost of discipleship. Second: God is the king coming against you with superior force. You cannot win against him. Make peace with him now, while he is still far off, by surrendering everything to him (12:58).

Who is the greater king? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size, in a chapter about what it costs to follow Jesus, is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. He cannot. Nobody can. What is left is the delegation: going out, while there is still distance between you, and asking for terms. And that is not defeat in this parable. It is the only wise move on the board, and it is the one the king is commended for making. The disaster is not surrender; the disaster is a man who marches out with ten thousand against twenty thousand because he never sat down and did the sum. Which is what the counting of the cost is actually for. It is not to establish that you can afford discipleship. It is to bring you to the point of sending the delegation.

What are the terms of peace? Astonishingly generous. The King who comes against us does not demand that we make up our losses or pay reparations. He has already provided the peace himself. In Christ, God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and he has sent ambassadors to plead: be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:19–20). The terms are unconditional surrender to his Son and trust in what his Son has done. We give up our arms; he gives us his friendship. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1).

In a sentence. As a king facing a stronger army sits down to consider whether he can win, and if not, seeks peace while there is time, so a person must consider the cost and make peace with God.

On a Tuesday. You cannot fight God and win. Surrender to him on his terms, and find peace. Is there a part of your life where you are still at war with him: an area where you keep your own counsel, a command you resent, a providence you will not accept? Send the delegation today. Tell him you give it up, and ask for his peace.

For worship. The King who could have crushed us sent his own Son as the embassy of peace. He did not wait for us to sue for terms; while we were still enemies, Christ died for us (Romans 5:10). He made peace by the blood of his cross. There is no stronger King, and none more willing to receive those who lay down their arms. Blessed are those whose rebellion has ended at his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.

So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has. The so therefore ties this to both parables. This is the conclusion the builder and the king were drawn for. The verb (apotassetai) is worth having exactly. In ordinary Greek it meant to take leave of somebody, to say goodbye, to part with, to give up. Luke uses it that way five chapters back, of the man who wanted to say farewell to those at home (9:61). So it is not primarily get rid of. It is let go of. The picture is of a man saying goodbye at a door, releasing his hold on what he is leaving behind. Not necessarily literally to sell everything, but to give up ownership of everything to Christ, holding it all at his disposal. Everything you have belongs to him.

Cannot be my disciple. The third cannot (vv. 26, 27, 33). Three conditions: Christ above family, above self, and above possessions.

Must I sell everything I own? No, and Luke himself will not allow that reading. Zacchaeus gives half and is told salvation has come to his house (19:8–9). The women of 8:3 funded the ministry out of means they must still have had. Peter’s rebuke to Ananias turns on the fact that the property was his to keep (Acts 5:4). What is required is that a man stop holding. Some are called to give up a great deal literally; all are called to hold everything open-handed, as stewards and not owners, ready to give whatever he asks. The test is not what percentage you give but whether anything you have is off limits to him.

What it does not mean. Not that discipleship earns salvation, or that only those who take a vow of poverty can be saved. But a disciple is someone who has surrendered everything to Christ, and will let go of anything he asks.

All that he has. The phrase is comprehensive in a way that goes past property. It reaches reputation, plans, the rights a man believes he has been granted by his circumstances, the future he has drawn up: everything the sentence this is mine can be said about. Here is a test that can be run without much difficulty. Think of the thing you are most certain God would never ask you for. Not the thing you would find hardest to lose; the thing you have quietly filed as not up for discussion. Whatever came to mind has not been renounced. It is still being held, and this verse says so.

The freedom of letting go. There is a mercy in the severity, which the chapter has already supplied. A man who has let go of everything cannot be robbed, cannot be blackmailed, and cannot be moved from the low seat because he has nothing to defend. The renunciation is not a fee charged at the door. It is what makes a man free enough to walk through it.

In a sentence. Anyone who does not give up everything he has cannot be Jesus’ disciple.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you have not yet surrendered to Christ? Give it to him today. Say it in prayer by name: my savings, my plans for retirement, my children’s futures, my reputation, my time. Then live this week as a steward of what you have handed over: give generously, hold loosely, and ask before you spend what is his.

For worship. Christ asks for all because he gave all. Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He let go of heaven’s glory and of his own life, and in return he gives us himself and an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade. What we renounce for him is nothing beside what we receive from him, and he is the treasure for which a wise man sells everything with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

Salt is good. Salt preserved, flavoured, and was used as a fertiliser in small amounts. In that world it was genuinely valuable: it kept meat, seasoned food, and was scattered on the dunghill and dug into fields. It was one of the few things a poor household could not do without. The saying closes the chapter, and it is not a change of subject. The crowd has just been told what discipleship costs; this is what happens to a disciple who will not pay it.

But if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? Pure salt cannot lose its taste. But the salt of Palestine was not pure. Impure salt, collected from the Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum and other minerals, could have its salt leached out by moisture and lose its taste, leaving a useless white powder. Which is the whole force of the image. This is not salt that has disappeared. It is salt that is still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt, and it has stopped working.

It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. Not even good enough to be mixed with manure as fertiliser. Luke’s detail is the sharpest of the three Gospels. Even the dunghill will not take it.

It is thrown away. Worthless. And that is a fair description of what a half-committed disciple is for. Not wicked. Not an enemy of anybody. Simply useless for the one thing that was the point of him, because a follower who has kept his own life, his own family loyalties and his own possessions out of the arrangement has retained the appearance and lost the function.

The point. A disciple who loses what makes him a disciple, his wholehearted commitment to Christ, is useless, like saltless salt. Discipleship that is not costly is not discipleship. And a church that has lost its distinctiveness is useless to the world.

Where Christians differ: can a true Christian lose his saltiness and be thrown away? Arminian Christians read the verse that way: a real disciple may fall away and be finally lost. Verdict: Jesus is warning those who follow at a distance without counting the cost. A disciple in name who will not carry his cross shows that he never truly had the salt (1 John 2:19; John 15:6). Those whom Christ has truly made his own he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real, and it is one of the very means by which Christ keeps his true disciples faithful: they hear it, and they hold on to him.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Pay attention. This is serious. Jesus called out the same words after the parable of the soils (8:8), and it is the same demand. Anybody can take in a saying about salt. What is being asked for is the hearing that goes past the surface and lets the thing in. And it is a good sentence to end on, because it hands the whole chapter back to the reader. A man has counted a cost or he has not; a table serves people who can repay or people who cannot; a seat has been grasped or given up. The teaching has been given. What is left is the hearing.

I feel I have lost my saltiness. Is there hope? Yes. The very fact that you feel it and care about it is a sign that the Spirit is still at work in you. Salt that has truly lost its savour does not grieve over it. Return to Christ, confess where you have grown cold or compromised, and ask him to restore the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12). Saltiness is not something you manufacture by trying harder to be different. It comes from closeness to Christ, and it returns as you return to him: to his word, to prayer, to his people, and to the cost you had begun to avoid.

In a sentence. A disciple who loses his distinctiveness is like salt that has lost its taste: useless and thrown away.

On a Tuesday. Is your discipleship salty: distinctive, costly, wholehearted? Don’t lose your saltiness. Ask where your life has become indistinguishable from the people around you who do not know Christ: your speech, your spending, your entertainment, your ambitions. Choose one place this week to be different for his sake, quietly and gladly.

For worship. Christ is the salt that never loses its savour. He was wholly given to his Father’s will from the manger to the cross, and nothing in him was ever half-hearted. He seasons a corrupt world through a people who belong to him, and he keeps them by his Spirit so that his savour is never finally lost in them. He who calls us to everything gives us everything, and his own faithfulness is the reason ours does not fail.
verseByVerse.note: Impure salt could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

14.text: <sup>1</sup> One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy. <sup>3</sup> And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?” <sup>4</sup> But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away. <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?” <sup>6</sup> And they could not reply to these things. <sup>7</sup> Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, <sup>8</sup> “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, <sup>9</sup> and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. <sup>10</sup> But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. <sup>11</sup> For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>12</sup> He said also to the man who had invited him, “When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. <sup>13</sup> But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, <sup>14</sup> and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” <sup>15</sup> When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” <sup>16</sup> But he said to him, “A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. <sup>17</sup> And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ <sup>18</sup> But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ <sup>19</sup> And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ <sup>20</sup> And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’ <sup>21</sup> So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’ <sup>22</sup> And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ <sup>23</sup> And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. <sup>24</sup> For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’” <sup>25</sup> Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, <sup>26</sup> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. <sup>27</sup> Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. <sup>28</sup> For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? <sup>29</sup> Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, <sup>30</sup> saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ <sup>31</sup> Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? <sup>32</sup> And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. <sup>33</sup> So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. <sup>34</sup> “Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? <sup>35</sup> It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

15.title: Lost and Found: The Three Parables of Grace
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the theological heart of Luke's Gospel — the chapter that more than any other earns Luke the title “the Gospel of grace.” It contains three parables told in response to a single complaint: the Pharisees and scribes grumble that “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” The three parables are Jesus's answer to the grumbling — not an argument but a story, or rather three stories that together form a single, overwhelming answer to the question: why does the Son of God eat with sinners? Because this is what God is like. He is the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep. He is the woman who lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house until she finds the one lost coin. He is the father who runs to meet his returning son while he is still a long way off.

The three parables form a crescendo: from a sheep (something lost through its own wandering nature), to a coin (something lost through its owner's carelessness, possibly), to a son (someone lost through deliberate, calculated rebellion). The lostness becomes more personal, more chosen, more culpable at each step — and the joy at the finding becomes more extravagant, more communal, more absolutely centred on grace rather than on the condition of the lost. The sheep does nothing to return; it is carried home. The coin does nothing; it is found. The son turns around and prepares a speech about his unworthiness — and the father interrupts the speech with the best robe and the ring and the sandals and the fatted calf. The grace always exceeds the repentance.

The chapter's most searching moment is the elder son (vv. 25–32) — the one who has never left, who has served faithfully, who is furious at the welcome given to the prodigal. He is the Pharisees in the parable — the ones whose complaint prompted all three parables. And the father's final words to him are the most tender and most open-ended in the chapter: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” The chapter ends without the elder son's response. Luke does not tell us whether the Pharisees came in to the feast. The question is left open — which is where Jesus leaves the invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Parable of the Lost Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Everything in this chapter depends on the first two verses. Tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to hear him — a settled pattern rather than one occasion — and the Pharisees and scribes grumble.

Grumbling is what Israel did over and over in the wilderness (Ex. 16:2, 7-8). It is not argument; it is a noise made at the back of a crowd by people who have decided not to engage.

“This man receives sinners and eats with them” is meant as an accusation and is completely accurate. The charge is not that Jesus preaches to sinners — nobody objected to that. It is the table. A shared meal in that world was the single clearest social statement a person could make about who his people were, and he was making it, often enough for everyone to have noticed.

What follows is his answer: three parables, all about something lost, all ending in a party — and the charge is never denied. Luke calls them one parable (v.3), singular, which is worth noticing. They are one argument in three movements.

He begins by putting his critics inside the story. “What man of you” compels agreement: any shepherd here would do this. He is not defending an eccentric practice but describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to.

The detail is realistic. A hundred sheep is a substantial flock, likely with hired help, so leaving the ninety-nine “in the open country” is not the recklessness it sounds. And a lost sheep is genuinely lost: sheep have no homing instinct, and a separated animal will lie down and refuse to move.

“Until he finds it” governs the whole search — there is no clause allowing the shepherd to come home empty. And he does not drive the animal back; an exhausted sheep cannot be herded, so he hoists seventy or eighty pounds across his shoulders and carries it home over the same country he searched, rejoicing.

Then he throws a party, over one sheep out of a hundred, quite possibly at a cost exceeding what the sheep was worth. The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.
verseByVerse.theology:
The shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine is the most dramatic possible image of divine initiative. The sheep does not seek the shepherd; the shepherd seeks the sheep. This is the consistent pattern of grace: “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19); “no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). The lost sheep contributes nothing to its rescue — it is found, lifted, carried.

Note also where the word repents falls. It appears in the application, not in the story. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried. The repentance and the being-found are the same event seen from two sides.

The phrase “ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” can be taken two ways and both are held by serious readers. It may be straightforward: there really are people already safe in the fold, and no slight is intended.

But remember who Jesus is answering. On the lips of the men grumbling at verse 2, “righteous persons who need no repentance” is exactly how they would have described themselves — and by the end of this chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an elder brother standing outside his father's house. Read against that ending, the phrase carries a dry edge: there is no joy in heaven over the ninety-nine, not because they are secure, but because nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.
verseByVerse.examples:
