The ninety-nine left “in the open country” looks irresponsible, and it reveals something about the community that belongs to the shepherd: they are safe in his care even while he is searching for the one. The gathered community is not threatened by the shepherd's pursuit of the wanderer; it is the context from which he goes and to which he brings the found sheep.

The church that begrudges the energy spent on the lost has misunderstood its own situation. It was once the one, and is now among the ninety-nine.

And the arithmetic of the parable is the thing to sit with, because it is deliberately disproportionate. Heaven does the sum the shepherd did. One sheep out of a hundred, and the whole neighbourhood is called in.

If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, it is worth asking which number you have quietly assigned yourself. The men it was told to were quite certain they were among the ninety-nine, and the parable was constructed so that they would agree with every word of it right up to the moment it closed on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying: this man receives sinners and eats with them.

Meaning first. Luke 15 is Jesus’ answer to a complaint: this man receives sinners and eats with them. He does not deny it. He tells three stories of lost things found, a sheep, a coin and a son, and each one ends in a party. In each, the one who has lost goes looking, or watching, and will not stop until the lost is home; and in each, the finding produces a joy so large it has to be shared. The shepherd carries the sheep, the woman sweeps the house, the father runs down the road. Heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. And the last story turns, at the end, to the son who never left: the respectable older brother who stands outside the feast, angry that grace has been given to someone who did not deserve it, while his father comes out and pleads with him too. The chapter shows us the heart of God towards sinners of both kinds, and leaves the door of the feast open.

The gospel within the gospel. Chapter 15 has been called the heart of Luke’s Gospel. Three parables of lost things found: a sheep, a coin, and a son. Each ends with joy. All three answer one complaint: why does Jesus welcome sinners? Everything in this chapter depends on these two verses, and a reader who skips them will misread all three parables.

Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. The verb means they were drawing near and kept doing it. This is not one occasion. It is a settled pattern, and by this point in the ministry it has become the most conspicuous fact about him. All: in large numbers. Tax collectors were Jews who had contracted with Rome to collect its revenue, and were regarded as traitors as well as extortioners. Sinners is broader: the word covered the openly immoral, but it was also used by the scrupulous of anybody who did not keep the purity code, which meant most ordinary working people. And note why they came: to hear him. Not for bread, not for healing. They came to listen to a preacher, which is the last thing anyone would have predicted of that crowd. The outcasts were drawn to Jesus. Something in him made sinners feel welcome.

And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled. The verb (diegongyzon) means muttered among themselves, the word the Greek Old Testament uses over and over of Israel grumbling in the wilderness about the water and the bread (Exodus 16:7–8). It is not argument. It is a noise made at the back of a crowd by people who have decided not to engage.

This man receives sinners and eats with them. It is meant as an accusation, and it is completely accurate. Receives (prosdechetai) means welcomes, accepts, takes to oneself. And eats with them was the part that mattered most, because a shared table in that world was not a casual thing. Eating together signalled acceptance and friendship; that was the offence. To eat with a man was to accept him, his standing and his reputation attached to yours for the evening. To the Pharisees, a holy man should keep away from sinners. So the charge is not that Jesus preaches to sinners; nobody objected to that. It is that he sits down and eats with them. Their complaint is the gospel: Jesus receives sinners. It is the most wonderful thing about him. What follows is his answer, and the charge is never denied.

Does receiving sinners mean Jesus approves of sin? No. He receives sinners in order to save them, and the word that runs through the chapter is repentance (vv. 7, 10). The doctor sits with the sick because he means to heal them (5:31–32). Jesus never said to a sinner that what he had done did not matter; he said that their sins were forgiven, and called them to follow him, as he did Levi (5:27–28). His welcome is not an endorsement of the far country. It is the open door out of it. That is the pattern for his church: a table open to any sinner, and a gospel that calls every sinner home.

So should Christians spend time with people whose lives are a mess? Yes, gladly, as Jesus did, with the aim of drawing them to him. That means real friendship, meals, hospitality and patience, not a project kept at arm’s length. It also means wisdom: you go as one who belongs to Christ, not to join in the sin, and if a friendship is pulling you away from him rather than drawing them towards him, something needs to change (1 Corinthians 15:33). But the danger in most churches is not that we are too close to sinners. It is that we are as far from them as the Pharisees were.

In a sentence. When tax collectors and sinners crowded to hear Jesus, the Pharisees and scribes grumbled that he welcomed sinners and ate with them.

On a Tuesday. Who are the tax collectors and sinners in your world: the colleague with the scandalous life, the neighbour who has been in prison, the relative everyone avoids? Ask whether they would find you as approachable as they found Jesus. Invite one of them to eat with you.

For worship. This man receives sinners. Thank God that he received you. The holiest man who ever lived was the one sinners most wanted to be near, because his holiness was full of grace. He did not keep his distance from us; he came and sat at our table, and then he spread his own table and invited us to it. The accusation of his enemies is the song of his people: he receives sinners, and he eats with them.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together signalled acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: So he told them this parable: 'What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he told them this parable: what man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.

So he told them this parable. To the grumblers. Singular: Luke calls the whole of what follows one parable, though three stories are coming. They are one argument in three movements, perhaps one parable with three panels.

What man of you, having a hundred sheep. He begins by putting his critics inside the story. What man of you: the question is framed to compel agreement. Any shepherd would do this; the answer is obvious. Which is the move that traps them. He is not defending an eccentric practice. He is describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to. Shepherds were despised by the Pharisees, but Jesus asks them to imagine being one. And God is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34). A hundred sheep is a modest flock for a family, perhaps with hired help.

If he has lost one of them. One percent. Hardly worth worrying about, you might think. But every sheep matters to the shepherd. And a lost sheep is genuinely lost: sheep have no homing instinct, and a separated animal will often lie down and refuse to move.

Does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country. Presumably with other shepherds, or safely gathered. They are in pasture, and there is somebody with them, so this is not the recklessness it sounds.

And go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? The shepherd takes the initiative. The sheep does not find its way back; the shepherd seeks it. Until he finds it: four words that govern the whole search. Not until dark. Not until it seems hopeless. There is no clause in this sentence that allows the shepherd to come home empty. This is God’s seeking love. God had promised through Ezekiel that he himself would search for his sheep and seek the lost (Ezekiel 34:11, 16). And Jesus: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).

He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. A lost sheep is often frightened, exhausted, and lies down and refuses to move. A frightened animal cannot be herded, so the shepherd hoists it across his neck, front legs in one hand and back legs in the other, and carries it home over the same country he searched. The shepherd carries it home. No scolding, no punishment, only joy. And the word Luke attaches to that is rejoicing. Not exhausted, not relieved, though he must have been both. The whole weight of the animal that caused the trouble is on his shoulders, and he is glad about it all the way home. Isaiah had seen it: he will gather the lambs in his arms (Isaiah 40:11).

If the shepherd does all the work, what do I do? You are found. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried, and that is a true picture of salvation: God seeks us before we seek him, and we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Our coming to him, our repentance and faith, is real, and we must do it; but it is the sheep’s response to the shepherd’s arms, not its own way home. If you have come to Christ, you can trace it back to his seeking. If you are still lost, know that he is the one who goes looking. Cry out to him, and you will find you have been sought.

What about the ninety-nine? Does God care less about faithful believers? No. The ninety-nine are not abandoned; they are left safe in the pasture. The parable is not ranking the sheep. It shows how much one lost sheep matters to a shepherd who already loves all of them. If you have been in the fold for years and feel overlooked, remember that you, too, were once the one he went after, and the joy over your finding was no less. The shepherd who carried you home has not put you down.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of them, losing one sheep out of a hundred, would not leave the ninety-nine to search for it until he found it, and carry it home with joy on his shoulders.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person who has wandered: a friend who has stopped coming to church, a child who has turned away. Go after them, in prayer first and then in person, gently, without scolding. A phone call, a meal, a note: the shepherd’s work is often as plain as that.

For worship. Jesus is the shepherd who came looking for you, and carries you home. Rejoice that you have been found. He left the ninety-nine of heaven’s glory and came down into the wilderness of our world, and he searched until he found us. And the shoulders that carried us home are the shoulders that carried a cross. He is the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and no sheep he has lifted will ever be dropped.

parallels.desc: I myself will search for my sheep
he will carry them in his bosom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbours, saying to them: rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost. Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.

And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors. Joy must be shared. He throws a party: over one sheep out of a hundred, and quite possibly at a cost exceeding what the sheep was worth. That is the thing the shepherd does that nobody would predict, and it is the one that answers the grumbling of verse 2. The Pharisees have objected to a man who eats with sinners. Jesus has just described a man who, having recovered what was lost, cannot keep it to himself and calls in the neighbours for a meal. The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.

Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost. My sheep: it belonged to him all along. It was his while it was lost, and that is why he went after it.

Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven. In heaven: in God’s presence, a reverent way of saying God himself rejoices. The Pharisees grumble; heaven celebrates. God’s heart is the opposite of theirs. And the application is deliberately disproportionate. Heaven does the arithmetic the shepherd did.

Over one sinner who repents. Repentance is the sheep being found. Notice: in the parable, the shepherd does all the work. In reality, repentance is the sinner’s response to being found by God. The word repents appears here for the first time, in the application, not in the story. The repentance and the being found are the same event seen from two sides.

Than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. Irony. There are no righteous people who need no repentance (Romans 3:10, 23). But the Pharisees thought they were such people (18:9). So heaven has no joy over them, because they will not repent. Remember who Jesus is answering. Righteous persons who need no repentance is exactly how the grumblers would have described themselves, and by the end of this chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an older brother standing outside his father’s house, refusing to come in. There is no joy in heaven over the ninety-nine, not because they are secure, but because nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.

Does God really feel joy? Yes. Scripture does not picture God as cold or unmoved. The LORD your God will rejoice over you with gladness and exult over you with loud singing (Zephaniah 3:17). His joy is not like ours, needy or fluctuating; he is eternally blessed in himself. But he truly delights in mercy (Micah 7:18), and the repentance of a sinner is the occasion of real gladness in heaven. If you have come to Christ, you were the cause of God’s rejoicing. That is not sentiment. It is what Jesus said.

In a sentence. As the shepherd calls his friends to rejoice with him, there is more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner than over ninety-nine who think they need no repentance.

On a Tuesday. When a sinner repents, heaven rejoices. Share in God’s joy when someone comes to Christ. If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, ask which number you have quietly assigned yourself. And when you hear of someone converted, especially someone you thought unlikely, let your first response be gladness, out loud, rather than a question about whether it will last.

For worship. The joy of heaven is the joy of the Shepherd over what he has found. God is not grudging in mercy; he delights in it. The whole host of heaven breaks into celebration over one sinner brought home, because the Son has done what he came to do. Every conversion in the history of the church has been a feast in heaven, and the Shepherd’s joy over his sheep will never end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Parable of the Lost Coin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman — deliberate, and not likely to be accidental in the Gospel that records more about women than any other. God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a housewife on her hands and knees.

The coins are drachmas, each roughly a day's wage. Ten is not a fortune, but for a peasant household it is ten days' living. It may be more serious still: in some parts of that world a woman's ten coins were her dowry, strung together and worn on her headdress — both her security and the visible sign of her marriage, so that the lost coin is a gap in something she wears.

Every detail of the search is exact for the house she lived in. A peasant home had few windows and a beaten earth floor, so even at midday the corners were dark — hence the lamp. And the sweeping is not tidying; it is dragging a broom across the floor to hear the coin move, because in that gloom you would find it by sound before you found it by sight.

“Until she finds it” is the shepherd's clause again, and the same refusal to stop. And the ending is the same: friends and neighbours called in, and a party quite possibly costing more than a drachma.

One difference from the first parable deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin can do nothing at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, under something, and no amount of time will improve its position. Whatever contribution the sheep made to being found — and it made almost none — the coin makes less.

The application changes in two small ways. The tense moves from future to present: not “there will be joy” but “there is joy,” now, and every time. And the location becomes “before the angels of God” — which puts the angels in the position of onlookers, watching somebody else be glad.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whose joy are the angels watching? The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already answered it. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted.

So the picture is this: somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round — and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

That is a very long way from the God the grumblers at verse 2 were defending, and a long way from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable, and disappointed. Nothing in these parables is grudging. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

The angels are elsewhere described as “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14). They are not detached observers of the gospel; they are invested in its outcomes. The finding of one lost sinner is a cosmic event, celebrated at every level of the created order that understands what was lost.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's method is the model of the kind of prayer and pastoral work that refuses to give up. She does not glance round and conclude it is not there. She lights the lamp — creating the conditions for seeing clearly. She sweeps — removing what might be covering it. And she seeks diligently until the finding.

Intercession for the lost follows the same method: create the conditions for light, remove what obscures the gospel, and keep at it. And the sweeping is worth holding on to, because it is the least glamorous part and the part that actually finds the coin. It is repetitive, unremarkable work done on hands and knees in a dark room, and it is how the thing was recovered.

And the completeness of the coin's helplessness is a comfort rather than an insult. Anyone who has watched a person they love become entirely unable to help themselves — through addiction, or illness of the mind, or a hardness they cannot seem to break — is looking at the coin. It cannot call out. It cannot move towards the light.

What the parable says is that this changes nothing about the search.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbours, saying: rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.

Or what woman, having ten silver coins. The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman. Luke’s pairing again: a man and a woman (13:18–21). God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a woman searching her house, on her hands and knees. Luke, who records more about women than any other evangelist, is not likely to have included it by accident.

The coins. The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius, a day’s wage. Ten coins: perhaps her savings, or her dowry, worn on a headdress. In some parts of that world a woman’s coins were strung together and worn as both her security and the visible sign of her marriage. On that reading the lost coin is not merely money. It is a gap in something she wears. Losing one was a real loss for a poor woman.

Does not light a lamp and sweep the house. Every detail is exact for the house she lived in. A poor house had few or no windows, and a beaten earth floor, perhaps covered with straw, so even at midday the corners were dark: hence the lamp. And the sweeping is not tidying. Finding a small coin meant lighting a lamp and sweeping carefully, listening for the clink, because in that gloom you would find it by sound before you found it by sight.

And seek diligently until she finds it. Again, persistent searching, until. The same clause as the shepherd’s, and the same refusal to stop.

Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost. The same joy, the same sharing. And the same ending: a party, and quite possibly one costing more than a drachma.

The difference. A sheep wanders away by its own folly; a coin is lost through no will of its own; a son will walk away deliberately. All lost; all sought; all found. And the coin deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin cannot do anything at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, under something, and no amount of time will improve its position. Whatever contribution the sheep made to being found, and it made almost none, the coin makes less. It is simply lost, and then it is simply found, and everything in between was done by somebody with a lamp.

Is it right to picture God as a woman? The parable pictures God’s searching love through a woman’s action, as Scripture elsewhere compares his care to a mother’s (Isaiah 49:15; 66:13), and Jesus has just compared himself to a hen (13:34). These are images of what God does, and they are precious. But Scripture never addresses God as mother or calls him she. He reveals himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and we name him as he has named himself. We can rejoice in every likeness Scripture gives, and still pray, as Jesus taught us, Our Father.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a woman who lost one of her ten silver coins and searched her house carefully until she found it, then called her friends to rejoice with her.

On a Tuesday. God searches diligently for the lost. Be part of his search: pray for and seek those who are lost. The lamp and the broom are ordinary tools; so are a Bible, a conversation and an open home. And if you feel as helpless as a coin under the furniture, unable to do anything to get yourself found, take heart: that is precisely the kind of lost thing this woman went looking for.

For worship. God lights the lamp. He shines into the dark corners where we lie, unable to move, and he sweeps the whole house until he finds us. The light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ has shone in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6), not because we went looking for it, but because he came looking for us. Praise the God who does not rest until what he has lost is in his hand again.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius — about a day’s wage. Houses were dark, with small windows and earthen floors.

verseByVerse.quote: Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.

Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God. The same application as the sheep, with two changes, and both repay attention. The first is the tense. Over the sheep it was there will be more joy in heaven, future. Here it is there is joy, present. Not a celebration held later when the accounts are settled; it is happening now, and it happens every time. The second is the location: before the angels of God. Not exactly that the angels rejoice, though they surely do, but that there is joy in their presence, the joy of God himself. It puts the angels in the position of onlookers watching somebody else be glad.

Whose joy are they watching? The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already told us. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. And in the parable still to come, a father will run down a road and kill the best animal on the farm. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted. So the picture is this. Somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round, and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

Over one sinner who repents. Every single one matters. The arithmetic never changes: one sheep out of a hundred, one coin out of ten, one sinner of no particular importance to anybody, whose repentance stops heaven in its tracks. That is a very long way from the God the grumblers were defending, and from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable and disappointed. Nothing in these parables is grudging. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

Do the angels know when someone is saved? The verse says there is joy in their presence, and Scripture elsewhere shows angels longing to look into the gospel (1 Peter 1:12) and serving those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). It is natural to think they share heaven’s gladness. But we should not speculate beyond what is written, and the point is not the angels but the God before whom they stand. The joy that fills heaven at a sinner’s repentance is first and most of all his.

In a sentence. There is joy in the presence of God’s angels over every single sinner who repents.

On a Tuesday. If you think your repentance is too small to matter, or your life too ordinary to interest heaven, read this verse again. And when you pray for someone far from God, remember what you are asking for: an occasion of joy in the presence of the angels.

For worship. Heaven rejoiced when you repented. Let that thought fill you with joy. The God who is surrounded by angels, before whom the seraphim cover their faces, bends down to delight in one sinner turning home. His joy is not a reaction to our worth but an overflow of his love, and every repenting sinner is a fresh display of the riches of his grace before the watching host of heaven (Ephesians 3:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–32 — The Parable of the Prodigal Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“There was a man who had two sons.” The story is announced as being about two — worth remembering, since it is usually preached as though it were about one.

The younger son's request is difficult to convey in its full shock. An estate passed at the father's death; a son had no standing to ask early, and the request carried an unmistakable meaning: I want what I will get when you are dead, and I do not want to wait for you to die. And he calls it “the share that is coming to me” — not a gift but something owed.

The father grants it without a recorded word. Note the plural: “he divided his property between them.” Two-thirds went to the elder son on the spot, and he never asked — which will matter enormously when he stands in a field complaining that he has never been given anything.

Liquidating that land was a public act. Land in Israel was the family's portion in the inheritance of God's people, with laws to keep it in the family (Lev. 25:23-28), so the whole district watched the transactions and drew the obvious conclusion. And the far country is not chiefly a place. It is wherever a man can go to be unobserved.

The descent is calibrated: the money goes, then a famine removes any possibility of recovery, then he attaches himself to a Gentile who sends him out of sight to feed pigs — the floor, for a son of Israel — and then he is hungry enough to envy the carob pods and cannot get them. “No one gave him anything.” The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

“He came to himself” is exact. He does not become someone else; he comes round, the way a man does after a blow to the head — which says that everything from verse 12 onwards was the aberration, and repentance is sanity returning.

His prepared speech gets two things right and one wrong. He names it as sin, against God first and his father second. Then he proposes to work his way back as a hired labourer — he has understood his guilt and entirely misunderstood his father.

And the father, seeing him a long way off, runs.
verseByVerse.theology:
The father running is the most shocking thing in the parable. An elderly man of standing in a Middle Eastern village did not run; it required gathering up the robe and exposing the legs, which was humiliating, and dignity was the currency such a man lived on. He deliberately and publicly makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village.

And he may have had a further reason. The boy had sold family land to Gentiles and lost it, and could expect a hostile reception. The father reaches him first, on the road, before anyone else can get to him. The same logic runs through the fattened calf: everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father's verdict on his son, and it is very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Every gift is a specific restoration. The best robe is the finest in the house and probably the father's own — so anyone entering afterwards sees a son of the house and nothing else. The signet ring is authority, the instrument for sealing contracts in the father's name, handed to the one member of the family who has proved beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money. Slaves went barefoot; the shoes settle the question the boy had rehearsed all the way home.

An objection has to be met here, because it is raised by critics and by thoughtful believers alike: there is no atonement in this parable. No sacrifice, no blood, no mediator — the father simply forgives. Some have built on that silence the claim that the doctrine of atonement was a later invention laid over a simpler gospel.

But the parable is not costless; we have been reading it from the son's side. The younger son's portion was real property, squandered and not coming back — the father is permanently poorer for having let him go. And the robe, the ring, the sandals and the calf all come out of what remains. The father does not forgive at no cost. He absorbs the entire cost himself, in silence, and never once mentions it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The boy did not come home because he missed his father. He came home because he was hungry, and the text is entirely candid about it — so a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold. I turned to God when my marriage collapsed. I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real?

Watch what the father does with it. He does not interrogate the motive or wait at the gate to establish whether the boy has come for love or for supper. He sees him a long way off and runs. Luke has been showing this all through: the tax collector who could not lift his eyes came out of sheer misery and went home justified (18:13-14); the criminal on the cross came with a few hours left and nothing else on earth to try (23:42-43).

Nobody's repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace — the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards.

Then the elder brother, and the parable's real target. He describes his life in his father's house as service — “these many years I have served you” — and thinks he is stating a credential. He wanted a goat to celebrate with his friends; even his imagined party does not have his father in it. And the complaint is false: two-thirds of that estate had been legally his since verse 12, and he could have killed a goat any week he liked.

He cannot say “my brother.” The servant managed it without effort; the elder son says “this son of yours.” And he supplies the prostitutes, which Luke never mentioned and which he was several days' journey away from witnessing — resentment filling in the blanks in the worst available way and calling it honesty.

The parable then stops. A man standing in the dark outside a lit house, being begged by his father, with the music still playing. Jesus told this to the men who grumbled at verse 2, and left them on the doorstep. The ending was theirs to write.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: there was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father: father, give me the share of property that is coming to me. And he divided his property between them.

The parable of the two sons. Often called the prodigal son, but it is really about a father and two sons. The younger son represents the tax collectors and sinners (v. 1); the older son represents the Pharisees and scribes (v. 2). The father represents God. The story is left open at the end, because the older son, the Pharisees, must decide.

There was a man who had two sons. Only Luke records this parable. Eight words, and everything in the chapter has been leading to them. Note that the story is announced as being about a man and two sons, which is worth remembering when it is preached, as it usually is, as though it were about one.

Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me. It is difficult to convey how shocking that sentence was, and the shock is the doorway into the whole parable. A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive one-third (the elder received a double portion, Deuteronomy 21:17). A father could distribute property early, but the son had no standing to ask. To ask for it now was shocking. It was like saying: I wish you were dead. I want your things, not you. A son making this request would expect his father to strike him and throw him out. And the word he uses is careful. He asks for the share that is coming to me, which he calls his by right. He has not asked for a gift. He has asked for what he considers already owed. What he is really asking for is his father’s death without the inconvenience of a funeral.

And he divided his property between them. Astonishingly, the father agrees, without a recorded word. That silence is one of the most extraordinary things in the parable. There is no argument, no attempt to talk him out of it, no condition attached. He does not force his son to stay. He lets him go, though it breaks his heart. And note the plural: between them. The elder son receives his share too, though he never asked, and he says nothing in defence of his father. That will matter enormously at the end of the story, when he stands in a field complaining that he has never been given anything. Everything both sons will need is already in their hands. What remains to be seen is what kind of man each of them is when he has it.

The picture. This is what every sinner does to God: takes his gifts (life, health, abilities) and wants to live without him. Sin is not first breaking rules, but breaking a relationship, wanting God’s gifts without God.

Why does God let people walk away from him? The father does not hold his son by force, and God does not drag sinners into his house against their will. He lets people have what they insist on, and sometimes that is the most terrible judgement there is (Romans 1:24). But the letting go is not indifference. The father’s eyes are on the road from the day the boy leaves. God’s patience gives a sinner room to discover what the far country is really like, and his providence, as the next verses show, is at work even there. If someone you love has walked away, the parable does not tell you to stop loving or praying. It tells you to keep watching the road.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man with two sons, the younger of whom insulted his father by demanding his inheritance at once, and the father divided his property between them.

On a Tuesday. Are you enjoying God’s gifts while keeping him at a distance? That is the heart of sin. Look at the good things in your hands today, your health, your money, your time, your mind, and ask whether you are using them with him or without him. The request of verse 12 is rarely made out loud. It is made in the way we spend a Saturday.

For worship. Every good gift we have ever squandered came from a Father who gave it freely. He gave the younger son his share, and he gives sun and rain to the just and the unjust. He is generous even to those who wish him gone. And the Son who told this story would one day stand in the place of rebels, despised and rejected, so that sons who had wished their Father dead might be brought home alive. Who is a God like him?
verseByVerse.note: A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive a third — the elder son had a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.

Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had. He did not even wait. He sold his share of the estate, turning land into cash, as quickly as possible. Selling family land was itself shameful. Land in Israel was not merely an asset; it was the family’s portion in the inheritance of God’s people, held in trust across generations, and there were laws to keep it in the family (Leviticus 25:23–28). To sell up was a public act, and the neighbours would have watched every transaction and drawn the obvious conclusion about what the boy thought of his father. By the time he left, the whole district knew. Gathered all he had: everything convertible, converted. Nothing left behind that could bring him back.

And took a journey into a far country. Gentile land, far from his father, his family, his people, and his God. Distance was the point. Not the next town, where he would be known, but a far country, where nobody had heard of his father and nobody would report on him. Which is the honest anatomy of the thing, and it is why the parable has never dated. The far country is not chiefly a place. It is wherever a man can go to be unobserved, and every generation has its own version, and the current one has more of them than any before it.

And there he squandered his property. The verb (dieskorpisen) means scattered, wasted, like seed thrown to the wind. It is the verb Mary sang of God scattering the proud in the thoughts of their hearts (1:51).

In reckless living. The word (asōtōs) means wastefully, without restraint, literally unsavingly: without keeping anything back, without a thought for what comes next. The root is less about a particular vice than about the absence of any brake. Luke does not itemise. His brother will say: with prostitutes (v. 30), and Luke does not confirm it. Freedom from his father became slavery to his appetites.

What is my far country? It may not involve travel at all. It is anywhere you go to be out of your Father’s sight, or so you think: the screen at midnight, the second life at a conference, the hidden spending, the resentment nursed in private, the corner of your heart where God is not consulted. It always begins with wanting the gifts without the Giver, and it always promises freedom. Name it honestly before God. The first step home is admitting where you are.

In a sentence. The younger son soon turned his inheritance into cash, went to a distant country, and wasted it all on reckless living.

On a Tuesday. The far country promises freedom, but delivers emptiness. Where is your far country? Notice the places in your life where you most want not to be seen, and ask why. Then bring them into the light, to God first, and if need be to a trusted Christian friend (James 5:16).

For worship. There is no country so far that the Father’s love does not reach it. He saw his son leave, and he never stopped being his father. The Son of God went into the far country of our sin and death, further than any prodigal ever travelled, to bring his brothers home. He scattered nothing of his Father’s wealth; he spent himself entirely for us, and his riches are still undiminished.
verseByVerse.note: A far country is Gentile land.

parallels.desc: a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.

When he had spent everything. The money ran out, and so did his friends. Watch the sequence, because it is the ordinary sequence and it is merciless. First the money runs out, which was always going to happen.

A severe famine arose in that country. Circumstances turned against him. The famine arrives on top of the spending, and the two together remove any possibility of recovery. A man with capital can survive a famine; a man in a famine cannot rebuild capital. And notice how much of this he did not choose. He chose the far country and the spending. He did not choose the famine. Sin puts a man in a place where circumstance can destroy him, and then circumstance does not require his permission. God often uses hardship to bring sinners to their senses.

And he began to be in need. From wealth to want.

He hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country. Literally glued himself, clung to him. This is not applying for a post. It is a starving man fastening himself to a stranger who does not want him. Desperate, he attached himself to a Gentile. And the employer’s response reads as a way of getting rid of him.

Who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. The lowest point imaginable for a Jew. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7). A Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had fallen as low as a person could go: cut off from his people, his religion and his God. A rabbinic saying pronounces a curse on the man who raises pigs. For a son of Israel this is the floor.

And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate. Carob pods, the long dark seed pods of the carob tree, fed to animals and eaten by the very poorest in hard times. Coarse and barely nourishing, and he cannot get them. He is not eating them; he is longing to. He envied the pigs. He left home with a third of an estate, and he now ranks below the livestock.

And no one gave him anything. No one cared. The far country does not care for its slaves. There were plenty of people around him while the money lasted. The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

Is God behind the famine? God rules over famines as over everything (Psalm 105:16), and in this story the hardship is the very thing that turns the son homeward. That does not mean every hardship is a punishment for a specific sin, as Jesus has just insisted (13:1–5). But it does mean that the bottom of the pit is never outside God’s reach, and that he often uses empty hands to make a sinner look up. If you are at the bottom now, your misery may be the severe mercy that brings you home. Do not waste it.

In a sentence. When his money was gone and famine struck, he hired himself out to a Gentile to feed pigs, and was so hungry he longed to eat their food, but no one gave him anything.

On a Tuesday. Sin promises much and leaves you envying pigs. If you are at the bottom, the way home is still open. And if someone you love is in the pigsty, do not be in a hurry to rescue them from every consequence; pray that the famine will do its work, and be ready for the day they come to themselves.

For worship. The God who lets the far country show its true face is the God who never stops providing for those who come home. The far country gives nothing; he gives everything. And the Son, who had every right to the Father’s table, was made poor and hungry and an outcast for us, so that no one who turns to him need ever go hungry again (John 6:35).
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean under the law; a Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had sunk as low as possible. The pods were probably carob pods, used as animal feed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he came to himself, he said: how many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.

But when he came to himself. One of the most exact phrases in the Gospels: came to his senses, woke up. He does not become someone else. He comes to himself, which is what we say of a man recovering from a faint, or coming round after a blow to the head. The implication is that everything from the request in verse 12 onwards was the aberration, and that this is the boy waking up. Sin is a kind of madness; repentance is coming back to sanity. It begins with seeing clearly: where I am, and where I could be.

How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread. He remembers his father’s goodness. His first clear thought is about bread, and about his father’s household, and the detail he remembers is that even the lowest grade of worker on the estate has more than enough. He is remembering the one thing he had never valued. Remembering God’s goodness draws sinners back (Romans 2:4).

But I perish here with hunger! Honest about his condition.

I will arise and go to my father. Repentance is a decision, followed by action: turning around, going back. There is no agonising. He has been in the pigsty long enough.

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. Against heaven: against God. All sin is first against God (Psalm 51:4). And against his father. Genuine confession, without excuses or blaming others. He does not blame the famine, or his friends, or his father. He names it as sin, not misfortune, and he names it against God first and his father second, which is the correct order.

I am no longer worthy to be called your son. True. He has forfeited every right.

Treat me as one of your hired servants. Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family, hired in the morning and paid at night. Not even a household slave. He plans to work off his debt, to earn his way back. His repentance is real, but he still thinks in terms of earning. He has not yet understood his father’s heart. He has understood his guilt and has entirely misunderstood his father.

Was his repentance real if he only came home because he was hungry? This troubles more honest Christians than almost any other question. The boy did not come home because he missed his father; the text is candid that he came because he was starving. So a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold: I turned to God when my marriage collapsed; I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real? The truth is that nobody’s repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace, the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards. And motives are purified on the way, as the father’s embrace is about to show.

In a sentence. Coming to his senses, he remembered that even his father’s hired workers had plenty, and resolved to go home, confess his sin, and ask to be treated as a hired worker.

On a Tuesday. Come to your senses. Confess your sin to God, honestly and without excuse. And then go home. Make the confession specific: not I have not been very good, but the thing itself, by name. And notice if you are rehearsing a hired servant’s speech, planning how you will make it up to God. He is not looking for a labourer. He is looking for his son.

For worship. The Father’s goodness is so great that even the memory of it, in a pigsty, draws a ruined man home. His house is full of bread; his servants have more than enough; his mercy is from everlasting to everlasting. And the Spirit who brings sinners to themselves is the Spirit of the Father who has never stopped watching the road. Every homeward thought a sinner ever had was first a gift from him.
verseByVerse.note: Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family.

parallels.desc: against you, you only, have I sinned

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.

And he arose and came to his father. He did what he said. Luke gives the journey half a sentence. Whatever it cost him to walk back into that village with the smell of pigs on him, past the neighbours who had watched him sell the land, it is not described.

But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him. Which tells you what the father had been doing. You do not identify a figure at that distance unless you are looking, and you do not look unless you have been looking for a long time. The father had been watching, waiting, looking down the road every day. Nothing in the parable says the father knew he was coming. The old man had been watching a road for a boy who had every reason never to appear on it. He saw his son before his son saw him.

And felt compassion. The word (esplanchnisthē) means moved in his innermost being, the compassion that turns over inside a person. It is the word used of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the good Samaritan (10:33): three great moments in Luke.

And ran. Two words, and it is the most shocking thing in the parable. In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run. He would have to hike up his robe and show his legs, a disgrace, and dignity was the currency such a man lived on. Aristotle had said the great-souled man moves slowly. So the father, seeing his son on the road, deliberately and publicly makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village. And there may be a reason beyond simple joy. The village would have seen the son coming back in rags, and might have abused him; according to some customs, a son who lost his inheritance among Gentiles could be cut off by the village. The father ran to reach him first, taking the shame on himself, protecting his son.

And embraced him. Literally fell on his neck, as Esau embraced Jacob (Genesis 33:4) and Joseph his father (Genesis 46:29). He is filthy, he stinks of a pig field, and he is ceremonially unclean. The father has him by the neck before a word has been said.

And kissed him. Again and again; the verb is intensive. A sign of acceptance, forgiveness and reconciliation (2 Samuel 14:33). Before the son could say a word of his confession.

The heart of God. This is the centre of the parable, and the answer to the Pharisees’ complaint. God is not a reluctant judge who must be persuaded to forgive. He is a father who runs to meet repentant sinners, while they are still far off. This is why Jesus receives sinners.

If God runs to forgive, does it matter how I live? It matters more, not less. The son who has been met on the road like this does not go back to the pigs; he has found his father’s heart, and the far country has lost its charm. Grace that is truly received produces a new life, because it changes what we love (Titus 2:11–12). Paul faced this objection directly: shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). The father’s running is not permission to leave again. It is the most powerful reason never to want to.

In a sentence. While the son was still far off, his father saw him, was filled with compassion, ran to him, threw his arms around him and kissed him.

On a Tuesday. If you have been putting off coming back to God because you think you must first clean yourself up, or because you dread the reception, look at this verse. The Father is already running. And when someone who has hurt you comes back, be quick to go out to meet them.

For worship. This is how God receives you when you turn to him: he runs to you, embraces you and kisses you. Worship the running Father. And see in his running the shadow of a greater shame: the Son of God, stripped and lifted up outside the city, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), so that the Father could run to us without compromising his holiness. The God of all majesty set aside his dignity to embrace a sinner. There is no other God like this.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run.

parallels.desc: Esau ran to meet him and embraced him
you who once were far off

verseByVerse.quote: And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the son said to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. He makes his confession. Repentance is still necessary, even after the embrace. He is not embraced into a situation where nothing needs to be said; he says it, and both statements are entirely true.

I am no longer worthy to be called your son. True.

What he does not say. He leaves out the last line of his prepared speech: Treat me as one of your hired servants (v. 19). Perhaps the father interrupts him. Perhaps, embraced and kissed, he realises he cannot bargain. Grace does not negotiate. You cannot earn your way back to a father who has already forgiven you. He comes as a son, or not at all.

Two readings, both worth having. He may have been interrupted. He is speaking into his father’s shoulder, being kissed, and the next verse begins but the father said to his servants, which reads like a man not waiting for the end of a sentence. Or he may have stopped himself. A boy who arrived planning to negotiate terms of employment may have found, with his father’s arms round him, that the offer had become absurd. Either way, the plan to work his way back never gets said out loud, and the parable is careful about that. Everything the son had worked out in the far country about how to be received is left unspoken, because it was answered before he opened his mouth.

Why confess, if I am already forgiven? Because confession is not payment; it is honesty. Grace is sometimes preached in a way that makes confession unnecessary, and the son shows otherwise: he says the words. What he does not get to do is set the terms on which he will be taken back. For the believer, daily confession is not a way of earning back a lost sonship. It is a child being truthful with his Father, and receiving again the assurance of a pardon already given (1 John 1:9). There is only one thing a returning sinner has to bring, and he brought it: an honest account of himself. Everything else in this scene is supplied by somebody else.

In a sentence. The son confessed his sin and unworthiness to his father, but did not finish his offer to become a hired worker.

On a Tuesday. When you confess your sins to God, stop at the end of the confession. Do not add the bargain: the promises to make up for it, the penance you set yourself, the quiet sense that you must earn your way back into favour. Say what is true, and let your Father answer.

For worship. Confess your sins to God, and then stop trying to earn his favour. He has already welcomed you as a son. His mercy is before our words, his embrace before our confession, his love before our coming. We bring nothing but our sin; he supplies everything else, and he does it with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the father said to his servants: bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.

But the father said to his servants. He does not even reply to the confession. He acts. He turns and gives orders about clothing, and every item is a restoration of something specific.

Bring quickly. No delay, no probation period, no conditions. Quickly comes first, and it governs the rest. Nobody is sent to wash first.

The best robe. Literally “the first robe”: the finest in the house, perhaps the father’s own. The robe honoured him. It covered his rags, and showed everyone in the village that he was restored to honour. That is the point in the story: a full, free welcome back, not a probation. Jesus does not say what the robe stands for, and the parable is about the Father’s joy over a returning sinner (vv. 7, 10), not about how forgiveness is achieved. But the Old Testament often pictures God clothing his people with salvation (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5), and the rest of the New Testament shows that God clothes sinners with Christ himself (Galatians 3:27). So Christians have rightly heard in the robe an echo of the righteousness God gives in Christ, as long as we remember that this comes from the rest of Scripture, not from the parable alone.

What the village saw. The boy is dressed in his father’s best, and the rags of the far country disappear underneath. Anyone entering the room afterwards would see a son of the house, and would see nothing else.

And put a ring on his hand. A signet ring, used to seal documents, gave him authority to act on his father’s behalf (Genesis 41:42; Esther 3:10). Full restoration as a son, with a son’s rights. It is not jewellery. It is authority, handed to the one member of the family who has demonstrated beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money.

And shoes on his feet. Sandals marked a free man; slaves went barefoot. Not a servant, but a son. It is a small detail and it settles the question the boy had been rehearsing all the way home. He had come to ask for a place among the hired men. Before he can propose it, his father has put shoes on him.

Three gifts at the gate. Between them they restore his standing, his authority and his freedom, immediately and without a single condition attached. Not one of them is deserved, and everybody watching knows it. That is what makes the scene so uncomfortable and so exactly like the gospel. The father does not restore him gradually as he proves himself. He restores him completely at the gate, before the boy has done one honest day’s work, and then lets him live the rest of his life as what he has been declared to be.

Is the prodigal a believer who fell away? The parable is aimed at the Pharisees’ complaint about tax collectors and sinners (vv. 1–2), and the younger son stands for sinners coming home to God. He is a son throughout; the father calls him my son (v. 24). It may also comfort a believer who has wandered for a season, but it does not teach that sonship can be lost and regained. If you are a Christian who has drifted, the way back is the same road: come to yourself, confess, and go home. You will find your Father has not changed.

In a sentence. The father ordered the best robe, a ring and sandals for him at once, restoring him fully to honour, authority and sonship.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, live today as what you have been declared to be. You are not a hired servant on probation, anxiously working to stay in favour; you wear the robe, the ring and the sandals of a son. And treat returning sinners the same way: when someone comes back to church after years away, do not put them on probation. Welcome them as the Father welcomed you.

For worship. God does not just forgive you; he welcomes you home fully, as his child, without probation. And in Christ he has clothed you in a righteousness not your own. Rejoice in your robe. I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall exult in my God, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation (Isaiah 61:10). The Son was stripped so that we might be clothed; he was treated as a slave so that we might wear the sandals of sons. Every gift at that gate was paid for by the Father’s own Son.
verseByVerse.note: The robe honoured him, the ring gave him authority, and sandals marked a son, not a barefoot slave.

parallels.desc: Pharaoh gives Joseph his ring and garments

verseByVerse.quote: And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to celebrate.

And bring the fattened calf and kill it. A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations. A peasant household did not eat meat often, and this was one animal, grain-fed and kept back for a single great occasion: a wedding, or a visit from someone important. Enough meat to feed the whole village. The father throws a feast, not for the son only, but for the community, to restore him publicly. So this is not a family supper. The father is calling in the same village that had watched the boy sell his father’s land and leave. Which is a further piece of protection. Everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father’s verdict on his son. It becomes very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Let us eat and celebrate. Eating together: the very thing the Pharisees complained about (v. 2). Jesus eats with sinners because God celebrates their return.

For this my son was dead, and is alive again. My son: not a hired servant. The boy had just finished saying he was no longer worthy to be called it. The father does not argue the point. He simply uses the word. Dead and alive: the language of resurrection. In that culture a son who had done what this one did was reckoned dead to the family, and the father takes the household’s own language and reverses it. Repentance is passing from death to life (Ephesians 2:1–5; Colossians 2:13).

He was lost, and is found. Like the sheep and the coin. Here the three parables of the chapter close into one. A sheep was lost and found; a coin was lost and found; a boy was lost and found, and every one of them ended in the same thing, which is a party.

And they began to celebrate. Joy, as in the first two parables. And Luke’s phrasing is worth noticing: they began. The celebration is under way and is not finished when the chapter ends. It is still going on in the last verse, with music audible from the field, and one son standing outside it.

Where Christians differ: forgiveness without a cross? Some liberal theologians have argued that this parable shows God forgives freely, without any need for atonement: the father simply forgives, with no sacrifice. Verdict: a parable teaches one main point, not every doctrine. This one shows God’s welcome to repentant sinners, in answer to the Pharisees. It does not explain how forgiveness is possible for a holy God. The rest of Scripture does: Jesus came to give his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45), his blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins (22:20; Matthew 26:28), and Luke ends with the Christ who must suffer so that forgiveness may be proclaimed (24:46–47). The father’s running, at cost to his own honour, is a hint of the cost God himself bore. And the one telling the story was on his way to Jerusalem to die.

Who paid for the calf? Somebody paid for it, and it was not the boy, who came up the road with nothing but the smell of pigs on him. Every single thing he receives in this scene is drawn from his father’s own resources, and the father never once mentions the cost. That is the gospel’s logic, and the cross is where the bill was met: God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, to show his righteousness, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).

In a sentence. The father ordered the fattened calf killed for a feast, because his son had been dead and was alive, lost and was found, and they began to celebrate.

On a Tuesday. Make your church and your home a place where returning sinners are celebrated, not merely tolerated. When someone is baptised, or comes back after years away, show up, rejoice, and eat with them. And if you have never quite believed that God is glad you are his, read verse 24 slowly, with your own name in it.

For worship. You were dead and are alive, lost and found. Join heaven’s celebration. The Father has spread a feast that will never end, and the music has been playing since the first sinner came home. Christ is the sacrifice and the host, the price and the welcome. One day the whole family will sit down together at the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the joy that began on that road will fill the new creation.
verseByVerse.note: A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him: your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.

The second half. The story could have ended with the feast. But Jesus tells it to the Pharisees (v. 2). Now comes their part. The camera turns, and everything from here is about the son who never left.

Now his older son was in the field. Working, dutiful, as always. It is where he has been all day and every day. Whatever else is true of him, he is not a bad son by any ordinary measure. He is out working while his brother is being kissed at the gate.

He heard music and dancing. Celebration. He hears it before he understands it: music from his own house, and he has no idea why. That detail is doing work. It means nobody sent for him. A party is under way at his father’s expense, involving the whole village, and the elder son of the household learns about it by getting close enough to hear the band.

And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. He does not go in. He stands outside and asks. He does not go in and ask his father; he stops outside, gets hold of a servant and interrogates him. Which is the first sign of the distance, and it is a considerable one. He is standing in his own yard, treating his own home as somewhere he needs to be briefed about before entering.

Your brother has come. The servant says your brother, without hesitation. The elder son will refuse the word in three verses’ time. The servant’s answer is entirely artless and entirely accurate, and it contains every fact the elder brother will later distort.

Because he has received him back safe and sound. The word (hygiainonta) means healthy, whole. The father’s joy is simply that his son is back. That is the reason given, and it is worth weighing. Not because your brother has proved himself, not because he has paid anything back. The stated cause of the celebration is simply that he is home and he is well. A servant who has been in that house all his life has understood the father exactly. The son standing in the yard is about to demonstrate that he never has.

Can someone be in the church and still outside the feast? Yes, and this is the most searching part of the chapter. The older son lives on the estate, works the fields and keeps the rules, and he does not know his father’s heart. It is possible to grow up in a Christian home, serve faithfully for decades, hold sound doctrine, and still relate to God as an employer rather than a Father, and to grace as something for other people. The test is not how long you have been in the field. It is whether the music of grace makes you glad.

In a sentence. The older son, returning from the field, heard music and dancing, and was told his brother had come home and his father was celebrating his safe return.

On a Tuesday. When others come to Christ, do you join the celebration or stand outside asking questions? Notice your first reaction the next time you hear of someone’s conversion or restoration, especially someone who hurt others or who seems not to have paid for it. If it is suspicion, go in anyway, and ask God to tune your heart to the music.

For worship. The Father’s house is full of music because the Father is full of joy. He does not need a reason beyond this: the lost is home, safe and sound. And the Son who tells this story is the true elder brother, who did not stand outside resenting us but left the Father’s side to come and find us, and brought us in to the feast himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him.

But he was angry and refused to go in. Both verbs matter and neither is a passing mood. He was angry, a settled state rather than a flash, like the Pharisees’ grumbling (v. 2). And he refused to go in, which is an act, and a public one. To refuse to attend a father’s feast was a public insult, as great as the younger son’s demand. Every guest at that party knows the elder son is outside and will not come. The younger son had shamed his father by leaving; the elder is now shaming him by standing in the yard.

Two sons outside. Now he is the one who is shut out, by his own choice. The lost son is inside; the good son is outside. The symmetry has been building all along. Two sons, both outside the father’s house, both by their own decision. One went to a far country; one is standing just outside the door. The distance is not measured in miles.

His father came out and entreated him. The father goes out again, this time to the older son. For the second time in one evening, the old man leaves his house and goes out to a son who has humiliated him. He humbles himself a second time, leaving his guests. It is the same movement as the running in verse 20: he does not summon the boy, or send a servant, or wait for him to see sense. He walks out of his own celebration, in front of everybody, and goes to find him. Entreated (parekalei) means urged, begged, pleaded. There is no command in it. The father, who has every right to order his son indoors, stands in the dark asking. God’s love pursues the self-righteous as well as the openly sinful. Jesus is pleading with the Pharisees, through this very parable.

Is God kind to sinners and severe to the religious? Not in this parable. The father goes out twice, and the second time is harder, because the second son does not want to be found. Whatever else the elder brother is about to say, he says it to a father who came out and asked. And there is a warning in the staging for anyone who has ever been the one outside. Standing in the yard feels like taking a position. It usually is just standing in a yard, in the dark, near a house where people are happy, waiting to be persuaded to enjoy something you have already decided not to enjoy. The father will not force him in. The door is open, the music is audible, the invitation has been delivered in person, and after that the yard is a choice.

In a sentence. The older son was angry and refused to go in, so his father came out and pleaded with him.

On a Tuesday. If you are standing in the yard about something, resentful of how God has blessed someone else, angry that grace has gone where you think it should not, recognise the father’s voice pleading with you. Go in. And if you lead or love someone who is standing outside, go out to them as the father did, gently and more than once.

For worship. God pursues the respectable as well as the rebellious. If you have been standing outside, he is pleading with you too. The same love that ran down the road walks out into the dark yard. There is no one too far gone for him, and no one too proud for him to plead with. Such is the patience of the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not want the elder son any more than the younger to be left outside.

verseByVerse.quote: but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he answered his father: look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!

Look. No respectful Father. The younger son began Father; the older son does not.

These many years I have served you. The word (douleuō) means I have slaved for you. Not lived with, not worked alongside. He thinks of himself as a slave, not a son. He describes his life in his father’s house in the vocabulary of a servant, and he thinks he is stating a credential. He has been working for wages, not living in love. It is the whole tragedy in one verb: he has been a son for the entire story and has experienced it as employment. The younger son wanted to come back as a hired servant; the older son had been living like one all along.

And I never disobeyed your command. Outward obedience, like the rich ruler (18:21) and Paul before conversion (Philippians 3:6). But his heart was far from his father. He was as lost as his brother, though he never left home.

Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. He wanted to celebrate, but with his friends, not his father. Even his imagined party does not have his father in it. And note the scale. A young goat is a modest animal, and this is a small grievance carefully preserved. He feels he has earned more, and been cheated. And the complaint is, as a matter of fact, false. Two-thirds of that estate had been his since verse 12. He could have killed a goat any week he liked. He had been living on his own property, asking permission he did not need, and resenting a father who had already given him everything. Self-righteousness is always resentful of grace.

But when this son of yours came. Not my brother, but this son of yours. He disowns his brother. The servant managed the word without effort; the elder son cuts the boy out of his own family.

Who has devoured your property with prostitutes. The worst interpretation, perhaps exaggerated, publicly announced. He wants his brother’s sin remembered. Luke never said that. Verse 13 says reckless living and nothing more. He may be right. He does not know, and the detail he reaches for is the one that will do the most damage, which is what resentment does when it finally gets to speak. It fills in the blanks in the worst available way and calls it honesty.

You killed the fattened calf for him! He cannot bear grace being given to someone who does not deserve it. This is the Pharisees’ complaint: this man receives sinners. Not a complaint about justice. A complaint about somebody else’s welcome.

How do I know if I am an older brother? Watch for the signs this verse gives. You keep score of your service and feel God owes you. You find obedience a grind, done for reward rather than love. You resent it when God is generous to people with worse records. You find it easy to remember other people’s sins in detail and hard to call them brother. You enjoy your friends more than your Father. Most of us find some of this in ourselves. The cure is not to try harder at being a good son. It is to see that you, too, have needed grace every day, and that everything the Father has was always yours as a gift.

In a sentence. The older son complained that he had slaved for his father for years without reward, while the father had killed the fattened calf for this son of his who had wasted everything on prostitutes.

On a Tuesday. Do you resent God’s grace to others? Do you obey God as a slave seeking wages, or as a son who loves him? Self-righteousness can keep you out of the feast as surely as rebellion. Think of one person whose sins you rehearse, aloud or in your head, and this week call them brother or sister in your prayers, and ask God to bless them.

For worship. The Father bears with the insults of both his sons, the one who wished him dead and the one who served him as a slave. He is not a hard master.
