He is the giver of every goat and every calf, the owner of the cattle on a thousand hills, and he gives himself to his children. And the true Son, who alone could have said I never disobeyed your command, and said it truly, did not resent the Father’s welcome of sinners. He died to make it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.

Son. The word (teknon) means child, the tender word, the one a parent uses. Despite the insult, the father speaks with love. After everything that has just been said in the yard, the father’s first word is an endearment.

You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. Everything he wanted, he already had: his father’s presence, and the whole estate. He did not need to earn it. He only had to enjoy it as a son. You are always with me: that was the elder son’s privilege, and he had experienced it as a sentence. He has had, every day for years, the one thing his brother threw away, nearness to his father, and he has been counting goats. And all that is mine is yours: a flat statement of fact, and it demolishes the complaint. The Pharisees had the Scriptures, the covenants, the temple, God’s presence (Romans 9:4–5). All theirs. But they lived as servants, not sons.

The sharpest thing in the parable. It is not aimed at the disreputable. A man can live in his Father’s house for forty years, keep every rule, resent the whole arrangement, and never once take anything out of a storehouse he has always owned.

It was fitting to celebrate and be glad. The word (edei) means it was necessary, it was right: the word of divine necessity Luke has used all through this Gospel of what God’s purpose requires. How could anyone not celebrate this? Not it was generous of me, and not I hope you will understand. Given what has happened, a party was the only proper response, and any other response would have been wrong.

For this your brother. Not this son of yours, but your brother. The father reminds him of the relationship he has disowned. He hands the word back, corrected. There is only one relationship in dispute here, and it is not the one between the father and the younger boy.

Was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found. The refrain repeated.

The open ending. Jesus does not tell us whether the older son went in. The story stops. Because the Pharisees and scribes, listening, had to decide: would they come in to the feast, and rejoice that sinners were coming home? Or would they stay outside? Every self-righteous person faces the same choice. Luke ends the chapter with a man standing in the dark outside a lit house, being begged by his father, with the music still playing. That is not an oversight. Jesus has put the grumblers of verse 2 on the doorstep of the party and left them there. The ending was theirs to write. It still is.

What does all that is mine is yours mean for me as a Christian? It means that in Christ you are an heir, not a hired hand. All things are yours, Paul says, whether the world or life or death or the present or the future, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). The Father’s presence, his promises, his Spirit, the riches of his grace, and an inheritance kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4) are already yours, not as wages but as a son’s portion. So pray as a child who has access, give as one who cannot be impoverished, and serve as one who is already loved.

In a sentence. The father told his older son that he had always been with him and owned everything, but they had to celebrate, because his brother had been dead and was alive, lost and was found.

On a Tuesday. Take something from the storehouse today. Thank God for one specific blessing you have always had and never enjoyed. Spend time with your Father not because you must, but because you may. And when you hear that a lost brother or sister has come home, go in to the feast.

For worship. If you are a Christian, all that is God’s is yours. Enjoy it as a son or daughter, and rejoice whenever a lost brother or sister comes home. The Father who ran to the younger son and walked out to the elder is the God who has given us his Son, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32). His house is never full of servants only. It is full of children, and the music has not stopped.

parallels.desc: to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants

15.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. <sup>2</sup> And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” <sup>3</sup> So he told them this parable: <sup>4</sup> “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? <sup>5</sup> And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. <sup>6</sup> And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ <sup>7</sup> Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. <sup>8</sup> “Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? <sup>9</sup> And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ <sup>10</sup> Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” <sup>11</sup> And he said, “There was a man who had two sons. <sup>12</sup> And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them. <sup>13</sup> Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. <sup>14</sup> And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. <sup>15</sup> So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. <sup>16</sup> And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. <sup>17</sup> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! <sup>18</sup> I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. <sup>19</sup> I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”’ <sup>20</sup> And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. <sup>21</sup> And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ <sup>22</sup> But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. <sup>23</sup> And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. <sup>24</sup> For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate. <sup>25</sup> “Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. <sup>26</sup> And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. <sup>27</sup> And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ <sup>28</sup> But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, <sup>29</sup> but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. <sup>30</sup> But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’ <sup>31</sup> And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. <sup>32</sup> It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’”

16.title: Money, the Law, and the Great Divide
16.overview:
Luke 16 is one of the most challenging chapters in all the Gospels. It contains two sustained teachings — the Parable of the Dishonest Manager and the story of the Rich Man and Lazarus — that bracket a cluster of sayings about the law, divorce, and divine valuation. What holds it together is money as a spiritual diagnostic: how a person handles wealth reveals the true condition of their heart before God.

The Parable of the Dishonest Manager shocks its hearers because Jesus appears to commend a fraudster. The commendation, however, is carefully qualified: the manager is praised not for his dishonesty but for his shrewdness — his ability to think clearly about the future and use present resources to secure it. Jesus turns the parable into an indictment of disciples who exercise less practical wisdom in spiritual things than worldly people do in material ones.

The story of the Rich Man and Lazarus is the only parable in which a character has a proper name, and it closes the chapter with one of Scripture's most sobering statements: if people will not be persuaded by Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. This is both a claim about the sufficiency of Scripture and a prophecy about the response to Jesus's own resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Parable of the Dishonest Manager
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus tells this to his disciples while the Pharisees are also listening (v.14), which is why the chapter ends where it does.

The manager is an oikonomos — the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts and ran the property in his master's name. And what he had been doing is what the prodigal did in the far country (15:13). The parable opens with a second man squandering another man's property.

Note the order of the dismissal: he is sacked first and the audit demanded second, which means he is finished and the paperwork is a formality. What that gives him is a gap — no longer trusted, not yet stripped of authority, the debtors not yet told, the seal still in his hand. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application.

His options are closed: he cannot dig, and he will not beg — and the difference in the two clauses is a fair sample of the man. He is not able to dig; he is ashamed to beg. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

What he then buys is not money. He does not embezzle; what he wants is houses — an open door somewhere when he has nothing. He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships, and that the wealth can be converted into them while he still controls it.

The reductions are uneven — fifty per cent on oil, twenty on wheat — which is the clue. If he were simply defrauding his master the discounts would be arbitrary; that they differ by commodity suggests he is removing something that varied by commodity, and the obvious candidate is his own commission. On that reading he waives his fee and takes a large personal loss, which would explain the otherwise baffling commendation.

It cannot be settled with certainty and the parable does not require it. What is commended is neither the honesty nor the dishonesty but the structure of the act: he took a resource about to stop being his and spent all of it, immediately, on the only thing that would outlast the deadline.
verseByVerse.theology:
The commendation is careful about what it does and does not say. He is still called the dishonest manager. What is praised is his shrewdness: practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act. A commander can admire an enemy's manoeuvre without approving the war.

“Sons of light” was a term the devout used of themselves — the Qumran community wrote a whole scroll about the war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at reading a situation and acting in time.

The observation is simply true, which is what makes it sting. A man will plan a pension he may never draw, take advice about a mortgage, insure a house he expects to keep. Set beside that the way the same qualities are deployed in the things of God by people who genuinely believe they will stand before him: the forward thinking stops, and a man who would never let a financial decision drift leaves the whole of his spiritual life to it.

The three descriptions of money in vv.10-12 are each deflating. It is unrighteous — the currency of a fallen order, and nobody's money is clean all the way back. It is a very little, said to people for whom it was the difference between eating and not eating. And it is another's. But the promise on the other side is easily missed: the true riches, and that which is your own. There is something coming that will actually belong to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 9 is the hardest sentence in the chapter and needs facing. Read flatly it appears to say a man can purchase his welcome into heaven — and it has been read that way in defence of almsgiving as accumulated merit.

Who are “they”? Three readings are held by careful Christians: the friends themselves, the angels, or — most likely — God himself, whose name the wording leaves unspoken.

And on whether salvation is for sale, the verse answers itself in three words that are easy to read past: when it fails. The money is explicitly the thing that runs out. Whatever else a currency guaranteed to become worthless may be, it is not the purchase price of eternity — and in this very chapter a rich man's fortune procures him not one drop of water.

What the verse teaches is that generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with “you cannot serve God and money,” which is where the saying is travelling.

And that closing sentence is a statement about what is possible, not advice about priorities. A man may hold two jobs; nobody has ever had two owners. Note too that both outcomes are the same outcome — whichever way it falls, one master gets the loyalty and the other the contempt. Most people serving money would sincerely say they love God, and the conflict only becomes visible when the two masters give conflicting orders.

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the disciples, 'There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also said to the disciples: there was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him: what is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.

Meaning first. Luke 16 is about money, and through money about the heart, about eternity and about the word of God. It has three movements: a dishonest manager who acts shrewdly before his dismissal takes effect (vv. 1–13); the money-loving Pharisees who sneer, and the permanence of God’s law (vv. 14–18); and a rich man and a poor man whose places are reversed at death (vv. 19–31). The parable of the dishonest manager is one of the most puzzling in the Gospels, but read carefully its point is clear: everything we hold belongs to Someone else, the arrangement is ending, and the wise use what they still control for what will last. The chapter ends at a grave that someone was about to leave, and with a Bible in the reader’s hands.

The setting. Chapter 15 was aimed at the grumbling Pharisees, with three stories of the lost being found. This chapter is spoken to the disciples, the men who follow him, though verse 14 tells us the Pharisees were still listening, which is why the chapter ends where it does. The same word ties the two chapters together. The manager here is wasting his master’s possessions, and the word, diaskorpizōn, scattering, is the one Luke used of the younger son squandering his inheritance in the far country (15:13). The parable opens with a second man scattering another man’s property, which is no coincidence in a Gospel arranged as carefully as this one. The prodigal was welcomed home by a father; the manager will have to find a welcome by his wits.

There was a rich man who had a manager. The manager is an oikonomos, the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or a freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts, lent goods, collected rents and ran the property in his master’s name. He was not a servant among servants. He had the seal and the keys, and absentee landlords were common in Galilee: the owner might see the place twice a year. A man in that position could do a great deal of good or a great deal of damage, and nobody would know until the books were opened.

Charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. Whether by incompetence or dishonesty, the property was leaking away. And notice what the man does not do when he is confronted. He does not dispute the charges. Luke never says whether they were true, but the manager’s silence, and his immediate move to plan for unemployment, answer the question well enough.

Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager. Two things, and the order matters. The dismissal is announced first and the audit demanded second, which means he is finished, and the paperwork is a formality. What that gives him is a gap. He is no longer trusted and not yet stripped of authority; the debtors have not been told; the seal is still in his hand. He has a short, precisely bounded interval in which he can still act in his master’s name. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application. Every person in this chapter is holding something on somebody else’s behalf, has been told the arrangement is ending, and has an unspecified amount of time left in which the seal still works.

Who is the manager meant to be? Not a cipher for any one person, and the parable does not need us to decide whether he stands for the Pharisees, for Israel’s leaders or for the disciples. He is a picture of every human being before God. Everything you have, your money, your body, your time, your gifts, your years, belongs to God, and you are its steward (1 Corinthians 4:2, 7). The notice of dismissal has already been served: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). The only open question is what you will do with the time in between.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man who, hearing that his manager was wasting his property, dismissed him and demanded his accounts.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement, your diary and your mirror, and say over each of them: this is not mine, I am managing it. Then ask the question the manager was forced to ask, the one that most people leave until a hospital corridor: when the books are handed in, what will they show? You do not need to be afraid to ask it. Asking it now, while the seal still works, is the whole point of the story.

For worship. There has only ever been one Steward who was never accused of wasting his Master’s goods. The Son received everything from the Father and lost none of it: this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me (John 6:39). He rendered his account in full, with nails in his hands, and it was found perfect. And the astonishing thing is that the account he rendered is the one God now reads over the wasteful stewards who trust him. We scattered our Master’s goods; he gathered us.
verseByVerse.note: A manager (steward) ran an estate for his master, often with wide powers to make deals in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The manager said to himself: what shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.

And the manager said to himself, What shall I do? The parable now goes inside his head, which is where Luke has taken us twice already: the rich fool talking to his own soul (12:17), and the prodigal coming to himself in the pigsty (15:17). It is the same construction each time, and it is always a man at the end of his options. But this man, unlike the rich fool, thinks ahead.

I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. Two doors, and both shut. He cannot dig. A steward’s life was clerical, not physical, and he is honest about what a lifetime of it has done to him: a middle-aged administrator suddenly facing labouring work, poorly paid and hard, and knowing his back will not last a week. And he will not beg. Note the difference in the two clauses: he is not able to dig, and he is ashamed to beg. The first is a limitation and the second is a decision, and it is a fair sample of the man. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

I have decided what to do. A sudden idea, and he has it all at once. The tense suggests a flash of clarity: I know what I will do.

So that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses. There is the plan, and the thing to notice is what he is actually buying. Not money. He does not embezzle for himself; a man with a bag of stolen silver would be in a far worse position than a man with friends. What he wants is houses: an open door somewhere, hospitality, a place at a table when he has nothing. He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships, and that the wealth, while he still controls it, can be converted into them. That is the entire insight of the parable, and Jesus is about to say so. What is striking is how late it comes. He has run that estate for years with the whole apparatus of value in his hands, and it took a dismissal notice to make him ask what any of it was for.

Is it wrong to plan for my future, or to save for retirement? No. The manager is not blamed for planning; he is held up as an example of it. Scripture commends the ant that stores in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and calls a man who will not provide for his household worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). The rich fool of chapter 12 was not condemned for having barns but for being rich toward himself and not toward God (12:21). The question this verse presses is not whether you plan but how far ahead. Most people plan carefully for thirty years and not at all for eternity. Prudent saving is stewardship; a pension that has become your security in place of God is idolatry, and only you and he know which yours is.

In a sentence. The manager, unable to dig and ashamed to beg, came up with a plan to make people welcome him into their homes after he lost his job.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself the manager’s question, but further out: when I am removed, not from a job but from this life, who will receive me, and into what? Then notice whether you have actually given that question a single hour of the planning you have given your holidays this year.

For worship. The manager had to scheme for a house to receive him, and was ashamed to beg. We are received on other terms. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (9:58), was cast out of the city, and was laid in a borrowed tomb, so that the beggars who come to him with nothing are given a room in his Father’s house that he went ahead to prepare (John 14:2). We do not have to be shrewd enough to secure a welcome. He has secured it.

verseByVerse.quote: So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Summoning his master’s debtors one by one, he said to the first: how much do you owe my master? He said: a hundred measures of oil. He said to him: take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty. Then he said to another: and how much do you owe? He said: a hundred measures of wheat. He said to him: take your bill, and write eighty.

So, summoning his master’s debtors one by one. One by one, and quickly, before the news gets out. These are not petty debtors; the quantities are enormous. They are tenant farmers who paid rent in produce, or merchants who had bought on credit, and they have serious contracts.

A hundred measures of oil. The ESV notes the size: a hundred measures of oil was about 875 gallons (3,300 litres), the yield of perhaps 150 olive trees. A hundred measures of wheat was about 1,000 bushels, the crop of something like a hundred acres. Each debt represents years of a labourer’s wages.

Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty. The debtor writes it himself, in his own hand, on his own bond, which is important. What the manager produces is a document that looks entirely legitimate and carries no trace of him. The reduction on the oil is fifty measures, worth about 500 denarii, more than a year and a half’s wages; the reduction on the wheat, write eighty, is twenty measures, worth about the same. Each debtor now owes the manager a very large favour.

Was it dishonest? The reductions are curiously uneven: fifty per cent on the oil, twenty per cent on the wheat. That unevenness has led some scholars to suggest that the manager was removing something that varied by commodity: his own commission, the surcharge a steward customarily added to a contract, or the interest that the law forbade charging to fellow Jews (Deuteronomy 23:19). On that reading he is waiving his own fee to buy goodwill. But Jesus calls him dishonest (v. 8), and the simplest reading is that he cheated his master to make friends of the debtors, who would now be grateful and in his debt. It cannot be settled with certainty, and the parable does not require it to be. Jesus commends neither the honesty nor the dishonesty. What is commended is the structure of the act.

The structure of the act. He took a resource that was about to stop being his, and spent all of it, immediately, on the only thing that would still exist after the deadline. And notice the tempo, because it is part of what is being praised. Sit down quickly. He summons them one by one and gets it done before the news travels, because the window is measured in hours and he knows it. Nobody in this parable is described as clever. He is described as fast.

In a sentence. The manager called in his master’s debtors and quickly had them reduce their bills, making them indebted to him.

On a Tuesday. The world is quick about its own interests. A man who learns that his firm is closing does not drift; he updates his CV that night. Ask what you know about eternity that you have been treating as if there were all the time in the world. A reconciliation postponed, a sin you meant to deal with, a gift you meant to give, a conversation about Christ you meant to have with your father: write one down, and do it before the week is out.

For worship. Here is a man who reduced other men’s debts to save himself. The gospel turns the picture inside out. Our Master did not trim our bill from a hundred to fifty; he took the bond, a record of debt that stood against us, and cancelled it entirely, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). And he paid it from his own account, not his Father’s. The manager wrote fifty to buy friends; Christ wrote nothing, because he paid everything, and called us his friends (John 15:15).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the size of these debts: a hundred measures of oil was about 800–900 gallons, a hundred measures of wheat about 1,000–1,200 bushels. Cutting them won the debtors’ gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.

The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. The surprise of the parable, and the sentence is careful about what it does and does not say. He is still called the dishonest manager, literally the steward of unrighteousness, a man characterised by it. The commendation does not rehabilitate him. What is praised is that he acted phronimōs: with prudence, practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act on it. A commander can admire an enemy’s manoeuvre without approving of the war, and that is roughly what is happening here. The master, a man of the world, recognised a clever move when he saw one, even at his own expense.

Who is the master who commends him? Most likely the rich man in the story, since Jesus speaks in his own voice in the next sentence and again in verse 9 (and I tell you). Some take it as the Lord himself. Either way, what is praised is the manager’s foresight, not his dishonesty.

For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. Here is the sting, and it is one of the most uncomfortable sentences Jesus ever spoke about his own people. The sons of this world are worldly people, who live for this age. The sons of light are God’s people (John 12:36; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). It was a title the devout used of themselves; the Qumran community wrote a whole scroll about the war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at this. Better at what, exactly? At dealing with their own generation: at reading a situation, seeing where it is going, and acting in time.

The ordinary competence of the world. The observation is simply true, which is what makes it sting. A man will spend real effort on a pension he may never draw, take advice about a mortgage, insure a house he expects to keep, plan a career over decades. He thinks forward, calculates, and acts while he still can. Now set beside that the way the same qualities are usually deployed in the things of God, by people who genuinely believe they are going to stand before him. The forward thinking stops. The strategy disappears. A man who would never leave a financial decision to drift leaves the whole of his spiritual life to it. Jesus is not asking his disciples to become worldly. He is asking them to become as intelligent about eternity as they already are about money.

What it does not mean. Jesus is not commending dishonesty, or teaching that the end justifies the means. A parable can use a bad man to make a good point. Luke will do it again with the unjust judge, who gives a widow justice only to be rid of her (18:1–8). The argument in both runs from the lesser to the greater: if even a scoundrel acts decisively to secure a few years of comfort, how much more should the sons of light act for eternity. The point is the manager’s urgency and foresight, not his ethics.

How would I actually be shrewd about eternity? The same way a sensible person is shrewd about anything: by looking at where things are going and acting now. Shrewdness for the kingdom looks like setting your giving before you see what is left, not after. It looks like choosing a church, a house and a job with an eye on what they will do to your soul and your children’s, not only on salary and schools. It looks like investing in people, in friendships with believers, in hospitality, in the young, because people are the only part of this world that goes on into the next. And it looks like dealing with sin today rather than meaning to, because the window is not as wide as it seems.

In a sentence. The master praised the dishonest manager for his shrewdness, for worldly people are often shrewder in their affairs than God’s people are in theirs.

On a Tuesday. Pick one area of your life where you are clearly competent: your work, your finances, your garden, your fantasy football. Notice the planning, the attention, the willingness to act. Then put the same intelligence to one eternal thing this week: your prayer, your children’s souls, your giving, a neighbour who does not know Christ. Be as thoughtful, decisive and wise in eternal matters as worldly people are about money and career.

For worship. The wisest Son of Light who ever lived did not merely see a crisis coming; he walked into it on purpose. He set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), knowing the hour and the cost, and spent everything he had, his reputation, his body, his life, on the one thing that would still exist after the deadline: a people for his Father. No one has ever been as shrewd for eternity as Jesus was for us.
verseByVerse.note: The master praises the manager’s shrewdness, not his dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth. The application, and the hardest sentence in the chapter, so it needs facing rather than hurrying past. Unrighteous wealth renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions; literally, the mammon of unrighteousness. It does not necessarily mean wealth gained dishonestly. It means wealth that belongs to this unrighteous world, the currency of a fallen order, which so often leads to sin and is inevitably entangled with things God hates. Nobody’s money is clean all the way back. And Jesus says: use it. Use it wisely, to make friends, by giving to the poor and supporting the work of God.

So that when it fails. Three words that are easy to read past. When money runs out, or when you die and it is useless to you. The money is explicitly described as the thing that fails. Whatever else a currency guaranteed to become worthless may be, it is not the purchase price of eternity.

They may receive you into the eternal dwellings. The manager made friends who would receive him into their houses; you can make friends who will welcome you into eternal homes. Who are they? Some take it of the friends themselves: those you have helped with your money, the poor and those who came to faith through the gospel you supported, standing at the door of the next life, glad to see their benefactor arrive. Some take it of angels, who will carry Lazarus a few verses later. And many take it as the Semitic way of saying you will be received without naming God directly, a reverent third-person plural. Luke has used the identical idiom already: this night your soul is required of you (12:20), where the Greek literally reads they require your soul, and nobody supposes a committee. Either way the point is the same: use money now with an eye on eternity. Lay up treasure in heaven (12:33).

What it does not mean. Not that you can buy your way into heaven. Read flatly, the verse appears to say a man can purchase his welcome by spending money on the right people, and it has been read that way, in defence of almsgiving as a work that accumulates merit. Luke will not let that stand. The tax collector who could offer nothing but his beaten breast went home justified (18:13–14); the criminal a few hours from death bought nothing whatever and was told he would be with Christ in Paradise that day (23:43); and in this very chapter a rich man’s fortune procures him not one drop of water. If money could buy an eternal dwelling, the man in torment was the best-funded soul in the story. Salvation is by grace. But how you use money shows where your heart is, and true faith is generous. Generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with you cannot serve God and money, which is where this saying is travelling: how a man treats his wealth shows which master owns him.

So how much should I give, and to whom? Scripture sets no fixed percentage for the Christian, but it sets a direction and a spirit. Give regularly and in proportion to what you have been given (1 Corinthians 16:2); give cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7); give first to the ministry of the word in your own church (Galatians 6:6) and to the poor, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). Many Christians find a tenth a sensible starting place, not a ceiling. The test of this verse is simple: ten years from now, will there be people, in heaven or on the way there, who are there partly because of what you did with your money? If the honest answer is no, start this month with something that costs you.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to use worldly wealth to make friends, so that when it runs out they will be welcomed into eternal homes.

On a Tuesday. Take your last three months of spending and divide it, roughly, into what will be gone when you die and what will not. A meal shared with a lonely widow, the support of a missionary, a gift to a struggling family in your church, a Bible for a new believer: these go on. Most of the rest does not. How could you use your money this week in a way that will matter in eternity?

For worship. There will be faces at the door. That is the quiet glory of this verse: heaven is not an empty hall but a household, and those who come in are received by people. And over all of them is the Host himself, who became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). We spend the mammon that fails; he spent the riches that never fail, and spent them on us. Every eternal dwelling was bought with his blood, and every welcome at its door is an echo of his.
verseByVerse.note: “Unrighteous wealth” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: rich in good works, storing up treasure

verseByVerse.quote: 'One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?

One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much. The parable is finished and the application widens, and this is the principle underneath it. Character does not change with scale. The way a man handles a small thing is not a warm-up for how he would handle a large one; it is a sample of it. Faithfulness is not a matter of the size of the task.

And one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. Small dishonesty reveals a dishonest heart. Which cuts against a very common self-assessment. Most people privately believe they would be generous if they had more, honest if the stakes were higher, disciplined if the work were more important. Jesus says the evidence is already in, and it is in the small things, and it has been all along. The expense claim rounded up, the hours padded, the change not returned, the excuse that was not quite true: none of these is small in what it reveals.

If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? Three descriptions of money follow, and each is deflating. It is unrighteous wealth: the currency of a fallen world. It is a very little. That is an extraordinary thing to say to people for whom money was the difference between eating and not eating, and Jesus says it anyway. Whatever the sums involved, compared with eternal things they are small. And the true riches are the spiritual riches of the kingdom: God’s word, his grace, responsibility in his kingdom, eternal reward. How we handle money is a test of whether we can be trusted with greater things.

If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own? And money is another’s. Not yours. It belongs to God, and you are the steward of the parable, running an estate you did not buy, and the audit is coming. Then the promise on the other side, which is easily missed under the warnings: that which is your own. There is something coming that will actually belong to you, an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). Everything held now is on loan and will be handed back; what is being trained for is an inheritance that cannot be taken away, and the training ground is a bank account.

Why would God care so much about money? It seems beneath him, and in one sense it is: he owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10) and does not need a penny of yours. He is not interested in the money. He is watching what a man does with a small sum of somebody else’s cash, because that is the most reliable evidence available of what he would do with anything. Money is concentrated life: hours of work, choices, security, pleasure, power, all in a form you can count. What you do with it shows what you love, and God cares very much about what you love.

Does this mean I earn my place in heaven by being faithful? No. That which is your own is a gift, an inheritance, and an inheritance is never earned by the heir. But God is pleased to reward the faithfulness that his grace produces, and Scripture speaks plainly of rewards differing (19:17; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). The believer is not saved by his faithfulness; he is saved for it, and then, in a kindness that is almost embarrassing, rewarded for what God himself worked in him. As Augustine said, when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts.

In a sentence. Faithfulness in small things like money shows whether someone can be trusted with the true riches of the kingdom, which will be their own.

On a Tuesday. Be faithful in small things: your money, your time, your promises. They reveal and shape your character. This week, put right one small dishonesty you have let stand, the overcharge, the borrowed thing not returned, the claim that was not quite accurate. Nobody else may notice. That is exactly why it matters.

For worship. The Lord who says this was faithful in a very little for thirty years. He worked at a bench in Nazareth, made yokes that fitted, gave honest measure, and nobody wrote any of it down, and the Father said: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). And because he was faithful in much as well, all the way to the cross, the true riches are now his to give. That which is your own is waiting, and it is safe, because it is kept by the faithful One who never lost anything entrusted to him.

verseByVerse.quote: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.

No servant can serve two masters. Servant here is oiketēs, a household slave, and that settles the argument before it starts, because a man may hold two jobs but nobody has ever had two owners. A slave’s time, body and will belonged wholly to one person. Two owners would make impossible, conflicting demands. So the sentence is not advice about priorities. It is a statement about what is possible.

For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. Both outcomes are the same outcome. Whichever way round it falls, one master ends up with the loyalty and the other with the contempt. There is no third arrangement in which both are served. Hate and love is the Hebrew idiom for preference (14:26): one will always come first. But the strength of the language is deliberate. Not prefer and neglect, but love and hate, devoted and despise. The divided man does not end up mildly disappointing one of his masters; he ends up with something like contempt for him.

The conflict that rarely surfaces. Most people who are serving money would say they love God, and they would say it sincerely. What Jesus is describing is not what they would say but what is actually happening, and it becomes visible only when the two masters give conflicting orders. The promotion that would mean leaving a faithful church. The giving that would mean a smaller car. The Sunday shift that pays double. That is why so much of life passes without the conflict ever surfacing, and why, when it does, a man often discovers which master he had been serving all along.

You cannot serve God and money. The ESV notes that money renders mammon, an Aramaic term for wealth or property, and Jesus treats it here as a name. Not a thing you own but somebody who owns you. He has personified it, and the personification is the point: money is not a neutral tool in this sentence. It is a rival lord, and it makes demands, and it has slaves. It promises security, power and happiness, the things only God can give. Then the flat impossibility: you cannot. Not should not, and not will find it difficult. Money is a wonderful servant, but a terrible master. You must choose.

The compromise that is not one. The division most people are actually attempting, God at the centre and money in a firm second place, both properly managed, is not a compromise between two positions. It is one of them, held by a man who has not noticed which.

How do I know which master I serve? Ask what you worry about, because worry is the prayer we pray to the god we fear will fail us. Ask what you would find hardest to give up if God asked. Ask whether your giving is the first line of the budget or the last. Ask whether money decides where you live, what church you attend and how much time you have for your family, or whether God does. And ask how you feel when the markets fall. A Christian may feel the loss; but if a bad month on the statement shakes your peace more than a month without prayer, mammon has a stronger claim on you than you thought.

Is it wrong to be rich? No. Abraham was very rich, and he is the host at the banquet a few verses later. Joseph of Arimathea was rich and a disciple (Matthew 27:57). Paul tells the rich not to be haughty or to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–18). It is not wrong to have money; it is fatal to serve it. But Jesus speaks of the danger of wealth far more than of its blessing, because wealth makes the service so easy to slide into and so hard to notice.

In a sentence. No one can be a slave to two masters, and so you cannot serve both God and money.

On a Tuesday. Which master do you serve? Your bank statement and your diary will tell you. Read last month’s as if they belonged to a stranger and ask what that stranger loves. Then do one thing this week that only a servant of God would do with money: give something away that you will notice.

For worship. There is a Master worth serving with everything, and he is not a hard one. Mammon takes everything and gives back anxiety; this Lord gave everything and gives back rest. He was sold for thirty pieces of silver by a man who chose the other master, and he did not curse the bargain. He let himself be bought so that we might be bought back. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matthew 11:29).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — The Law, the Kingdom, and Human Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees are described as lovers of money, which is a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. But it was not a secret vice among them and did not feel like a vice at all, because the theology of the day connected prosperity with divine approval. A wealthy Pharisee could regard his estate as a testimonial.

Their response is not argument. They ridiculed him, and that is the tell. There is no counter-exegesis, no appeal to Scripture. Ridicule is the cheapest defence available and the most effective: it requires no reasoning and lets a whole room off the hook at once by making the speaker faintly absurd.

Jesus goes past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. “You justify yourselves before men” describes the exhausting business of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience. And “abomination” is a heavy word, not chosen loosely — in the Old Testament it is a standard word for idols. He is not saying human and divine values sometimes differ. He is putting visible success, honour and social standing in the same category as an idol.

Then two verses that must be held together. “The Law and the Prophets were until John” dates an era, and John stands on the seam — the last of the old order and the herald of the new (cf. 7:28). But “not one dot of the Law” will become void: the dot is the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another, and Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does.

The word holding them together is fulfilment. The Law's era as the way God's people related to him has closed; the Law itself has been kept — by the man saying this — and its moral claim stands exactly where it stood. What has changed is not the standard but who has met it.

Which is why the divorce saying follows, and the placing is not a change of subject. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things, by the party of permissive divorce rulings. He takes the point where their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law and shows who is actually relaxing it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Everyone forces his way into it” is a strange phrase and the translations divide: everyone is pressing in, or, as the ESV margin gives it, everyone is forcefully urged into it. Either way the point stands and it is not gentle: since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is entered the way a man presses through a closing door (cf. Matt. 11:12).

There is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone, spoken to men who have just sneered. Tax collectors and prostitutes are shoving their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

The two verses guard against two opposite errors that are always with the church. One man reads “the Law and the Prophets were until John” and concludes the commandments no longer trouble him — that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity. Verse 17 exists to stop him. Another reads verse 17 and concludes nothing has changed at all — that he is still under a covenant of works and must produce a righteousness of his own. Verse 16 exists to stop him: the good news is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.

And the permanence of the Law is why the sexual ethic is not negotiable. The Pharisees were known for liberal divorce interpretations — Hillel's school allowed it for almost any reason — and Jesus reaffirms the original design of Genesis 2:24 as the Law's continuing moral claim, not as something the kingdom relaxes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke gives the divorce saying flat, with no exception attached, and a reader who has only Luke will conclude that every divorce and remarriage is adultery. Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in: Matthew records the same teaching twice with an exception for sexual immorality (5:32; 19:9), and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Cor. 7:15). On that basis the Reformed churches have historically recognised two grounds, and that is the position confessed in the Westminster standards.

Luke leaves the exception out because he is giving the rule, not the case law — which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says “never take this on an empty stomach” is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. The exceptions are narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

But there is a further question, and it is the one that keeps people out of church: what about the man or woman already divorced and already remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18) — he calls them husbands, names the truth exactly, and does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage; it is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that exists and carries real obligations.

Where there was sin it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and then left at the cross rather than dragged out every morning. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: “and such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Cor. 6:9-11).

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them, 'You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them: you are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things. Luke tells us two things and the second follows from the first. Lovers of money is philargyroi, literally silver-lovers, and it is a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. Not all Pharisees were wealthy, but it was not a secret vice among them, and it did not feel like a vice at all, because the theology of the day connected prosperity with divine approval. The covenant blessings promised fruitful fields and full barns to the obedient (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and it was a short step to reading the balance sheet as a certificate of righteousness. Money and piety went together, they thought. A wealthy Pharisee could regard his estate as a testimonial.

And they ridiculed him. The verb is vivid: literally they turned up their noses at him. A poor teacher from Galilee, with nowhere to lay his head, telling them about money! And that is the tell. They do not argue. There is no counter-exegesis, no appeal to Scripture, no attempt to show that the teaching is wrong. They sneer, which is what people do when something has landed and cannot be answered. Ridicule is the cheapest defence available and the most effective. It requires no reasoning, it costs nothing, and it lets a whole room off the hook at once by making the speaker faintly absurd.

You are those who justify yourselves before men. He goes straight past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. They made themselves look righteous in people’s eyes; their wealth and religious reputation impressed others. To justify yourself before men is the effort of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience, which is exhausting, and which is the only thing sustaining the position they have just defended with a sneer. It is the opposite of the tax collector who will stand at the back of the temple two chapters later, with no audience and no defence, and go home justified by God (18:14).

But God knows your hearts. He sees through appearances: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). The verdict of the audience and the verdict of God are two different courts, and only one of them is final.

For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. Abomination, bdelygma, is a heavy word and it is not chosen loosely. In the Greek Old Testament it is the standard term for idols and for the practices of the nations, the things that provoked God to jealousy, and it is used of the proud in heart (Proverbs 16:5). So the sentence is stronger than it first appears. He is not saying that human values and divine values sometimes differ. He is saying that the thing this society most admires, visible success, honour, religious reputation, the standing these men had spent their lives accumulating, when it flows from pride and self-love, is in the same category as an idol.

Does God hate success, then? No. God gives wealth, skill and honour, and Scripture praises the man skilful in his work (Proverbs 22:29). What is an abomination is the exaltation: success turned into a throne, reputation turned into a righteousness, the applause of men treated as the verdict of heaven. The same promotion can be received with gratitude by one man and worshipped by another. The question is not what you have achieved but what you are leaning on, and whose praise you are living for (John 5:44).

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely. A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches (Proverbs 22:1), and an elder must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). But reputation is a by-product of faithfulness, not its goal. The danger begins when the audience becomes the judge: when you would rather be thought generous than be generous, thought godly than be godly. A simple test: what do you do when no one will ever know? Jesus told us to give, pray and fast in secret, and promised that the Father who sees in secret will reward (Matthew 6:4).

In a sentence. When the money-loving Pharisees sneered at him, Jesus said that they justified themselves before people, but God knows their hearts, and what people prize is detestable to God.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of the three things you most admire in other people, the qualities that make you think, I wish I were like that. Then hold each one up to the cross and ask whether God values it. Money, looks, wit, influence and confidence may come out quite differently from humility, faithfulness, and kindness to people who cannot repay. And notice when you reach for ridicule. Mockery of something true is often the sound of a conscience defending its savings.

For worship. God knows your hearts. To the Pharisees that was a threat; to the broken it is the most comforting sentence in the Bible. The God who sees through every pretence also sees through every despair, and is not fooled by our failures any more than by our successes. He knows the heart, and he gives a new one. The Lord whom they sneered at was exalted by God to the highest place precisely because he refused every exaltation among men (Philippians 2:8–9). What men despised, God crowned.

parallels.desc: the LORD looks on the heart

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.

The Law and the Prophets were until John. A hinge verse, and it divides history in two. The Law and the Prophets is the standard way of naming the whole Old Testament, and Jesus dates its era: until John. Not abolished at John, and the next verse will make that emphatic. But the age in which the Scriptures pointed forward to something not yet arrived, the time of promise, has closed, because the thing they pointed to has come. John stands on the seam. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the herald of the new, the bridge between the ages, which is what Jesus meant when he said no one born of women is greater than John, and yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he (7:28).

Since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached. A new era has begun: the time of fulfilment. The kingdom has come in Jesus. And notice how it comes. Not argued, not required: announced, as news is announced. The verb is euangelizetai, the gospel is preached. The kingdom is not a programme for people to implement but a report of what God has done.

And everyone forces his way into it. A difficult phrase, worth a pause, because the Greek verb can be read more than one way and the translations divide. It may be middle voice: everyone is pressing urgently to enter, with the earnest striving of 13:24 (strive to enter through the narrow door), as the tax collectors and sinners are doing. Or passive: everyone is being urged in, pressed to come, like the guests compelled in from the highways (14:23); the ESV notes this in its margin. Or, as in Matthew 11:12, it may speak of the kingdom suffering violence from its opponents. In Luke’s context, the first is most likely: people of all kinds are pressing into the kingdom, while the Pharisees stay outside.

Entered like a closing door. Either way the point stands, and it is not gentle. Since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is not drifted into. It is entered the way a man presses through a closing door: with decision, urgency, and everything he has. And there is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone, spoken to the men who have just sneered. Tax collectors and prostitutes are pushing their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

Does this mean I get into the kingdom by my own effort? No. The kingdom is preached as good news, and good news is received, not earned. The striving here is not the effort that earns entry but the urgency of a man who will not let anything keep him from the gift: not pride, not fear of what people think, not the pleasures he must leave behind. Those who press in are precisely those who have stopped trusting their own righteousness. And behind every human pressing in is the God who draws: no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). The urgency is ours; the power is his.

In a sentence. The era of the Law and the Prophets lasted until John; since then the good news of the kingdom is preached, and people are pressing into it.

On a Tuesday. Which is worth turning on any settled congregation, and on any settled heart. The kingdom in this verse is not a place people are gently ushered into over a lifetime of respectable attendance. It is somewhere people are visibly fighting to get. If you have been standing at the door for years, interested, sympathetic, attending, but never actually coming to Christ yourself, this verse is for you. Enter the kingdom with urgency. Do not stand at the door.

For worship. For centuries the Law and the Prophets stood at the window and looked down the road. Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56); the prophets searched and inquired what person or time the Spirit was indicating (1 Peter 1:10–11). And then he came. We live on the far side of the seam, in the age of the announcement, when what kings and prophets longed to see is preached in every village (10:24). The King has come, the door is open, and the most unlikely people in the world are pouring through it. Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.

But. In case anyone thought the new era meant the law was abolished. Immediately after saying that an era has ended, he says the Law is untouchable, and the but is there to stop exactly the conclusion a hearer would otherwise draw.

It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away. The most permanent things imaginable. The sky over Galilee and the hills under it had been there since creation, and Jesus says they are less secure than what God has written.

Than for one dot of the Law to become void. The dot is the keraia, literally a little horn: the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. In Hebrew script the difference between certain letters is a mark smaller than the head of a pin, and Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does. The law stands for ever. Not one word of God’s law will fail.

How the law continues. So the two verses have to be held together, and they are held together by one word: fulfilment. Jesus did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17–18). The Law’s era as the way God’s people related to him has closed. The Law itself has not been cancelled; it has been kept, by the man saying this, and its moral claim stands exactly where it stood. What has changed is not the standard but who has met it. Its moral demands remain, summed up in love for God and neighbour. Its ceremonial laws, such as the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, are fulfilled in Christ, who is their reality (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). Its promises are kept in him. Nothing of God’s word is lost; it all reaches its goal.

Must Christians, then, keep the Old Testament law? Reformed Christians distinguish three kinds of law in the Old Testament. Its ceremonial laws, the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, are fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind us (Hebrews 9–10). Its civil laws were given to Israel as a nation and expired with that nation, though their general equity still teaches wisdom (Westminster 19.4). Its moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still guides believers, not as a ladder to climb to God but as the shape of the life he has given us (Westminster 19.5–6). Not a dot of the law fails, because Christ fulfils all of it, some by completing it and some by writing it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

Two opposite errors. There is a word here for two errors that are always with the church. One is the man who reads the Law and the Prophets were until John and concludes that the commandments no longer trouble him, that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity. Verse 17 exists to stop him. The other is the man who reads verse 17 and concludes that nothing has changed at all, that he is still under the covenant of works and must produce a righteousness of his own. Verse 16 exists to stop him. The good news of the kingdom is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.

Why does the next verse jump to divorce? It is not a change of subject. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things; the Pharisees who sneered at his teaching on money were also the party of permissive divorce rulings. So he takes the point at which their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law, and shows who is actually relaxing it. Verse 18 is an example of verse 17.

In a sentence. Heaven and earth would sooner pass away than the smallest stroke of God’s law fail.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is more permanent than the universe. Build your life on it. When a commandment is inconvenient this week, and one will be, notice the instinct to treat it as a dot that surely does not matter: a small lie, a small lust, a small theft of time. Then remember the One who kept every dot for you, and keep it for love of him.

For worship. Every stroke of the law pointed somewhere, and every one of them arrived. The lamb on the doorpost, the scapegoat in the wilderness, the bread in the holy place, the blood on the mercy seat: not one was a wasted pen stroke, because all were sketches of him. And the moral law, which condemned us to the last dot, was kept to the last dot by the Son, and its curse borne by him to the last drop. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away (21:33). We stand on a foundation more stable than the ground.
verseByVerse.note: The “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.

Why here? An example of the permanence of God’s law (v. 17), aimed at the Pharisees, who used the law to allow easy divorce. Deuteronomy 24:1 permitted a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce if he found some indecency in her, and the school of Hillel read that so broadly that a burnt dinner, or a prettier woman, could count. They justified themselves (v. 15) by quoting Moses, while breaking the deeper intent of God’s law for marriage. And perhaps there is a pointed reference to Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias, his brother’s wife, and had imprisoned John for saying so (3:19–20).

Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery. In God’s eyes the marriage bond still holds, so remarriage is adultery (Mark 10:11–12). Divorce in that world was a man’s prerogative: he wrote the certificate, and she was put out. Jesus will not let the paperwork dissolve what God has joined. The man who discards his wife for another woman has not left a contract; he has broken a covenant.

And he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. The second husband too. The sin is not confined to the man who started it; it reaches everyone who treats the first marriage as though it had never been.

The exceptions. Luke, like Mark, gives the saying flat, with no exception attached, and a reader who has only Luke might conclude that every divorce and every remarriage without qualification is adultery. Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in. Matthew records the same teaching twice and both times includes an exception for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:32; 19:9). Paul adds a second case: if an unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer is not enslaved (1 Corinthians 7:15). Why then does Luke leave the exception out? Because he is giving the rule, not the case law, which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says never take this on an empty stomach is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. Luke’s flat form is the shape of the thing: marriage is for life, and the exceptions are exceptions, narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced person ever remarry? As at Mark 10:10–12. Some Christians hold that there is no ground for remarriage while a former spouse lives, reading this verse without exceptions. Others allow divorce and remarriage on wider grounds, such as incompatibility or the breakdown of love. Verdict: the Westminster position (Westminster 24.5–6) is best: marriage is for life, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied by the church or the civil authority, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and, after the divorce, remarry as if the offending party were dead. Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and Paul for desertion by an unbeliever (1 Corinthians 7:15); Luke gives the principle, and Matthew and Paul give its exceptions. Those who have sinned in divorce and remarriage can find full forgiveness in Christ.

What about the person already divorced and remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? This is the question that keeps people out of church. Is every day of the new marriage a fresh sin? Is the only repentance available to break the second home apart? No. Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18); he calls them husbands, he names the truth exactly, and he does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage. It is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that now exists and carries real obligations to a real spouse and real children. Where there was sin, it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and then left at the cross, not dragged out and re-committed every morning. If that is your history, the word to you is not go back. It is be washed, and be faithful now.

Such were some of you. Paul lists adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: and such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). None of this is a loophole, and it must not be heard as one. The fence stands exactly where Jesus put it, and he put it there to protect something, chiefly the wife who in that world could be dismissed at her husband’s convenience and left with nothing. But a fence is not a cage, and the gospel does not leave a man locked outside his own forgiveness.

What if my spouse is abusing me? Then this verse is not a chain to keep you in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated, in the church or in the home, and nothing in Jesus’ words requires a husband or wife to remain under the same roof as someone who threatens, beats or terrorises them. Get yourself and your children to safety; tell your elders and, where a crime has been committed, the police (Romans 13:4). Separation for protection is not the sin this verse condemns. Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse has broken the marriage in the way Scripture recognises, by the abuser’s wilful abandonment of the covenant’s every duty, is a question to be weighed carefully with faithful elders, and many Reformed churches have judged that it can. What is never right is to tell a victim that God wants her to stay and suffer. Jesus’ words protect the vulnerable; they were never meant to be turned against them.

What if I was the one who sinned in my divorce? Yes, and the way is the same as for every other sin: confess it to God without excuse, put right what can still be put right, and receive his forgiveness fully. That may mean seeking reconciliation with a former spouse if both are unmarried and it is possible; it will certainly mean honesty, humility, and faithfulness to the obligations you still have, especially to your children. It does not mean living for ever under a cloud. David, who took another man’s wife and killed him to cover it, wrote the psalm the church still prays: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Psalm 51:7).

In a sentence. Jesus declared that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, as does the man who marries a divorced woman.

On a Tuesday. Honour marriage as God designed it. If you are married, do one thing this week that strengthens the wall rather than tests the doors: an apology you owe, an evening together protected from screens, a prayer for your spouse by name. If you are unmarried, honour other people’s marriages in what you say and what you allow yourself to think. And if you have failed here, there is forgiveness in Christ, full and free, and a church that should be the first place to say so.

For worship. Behind this hard saying stands a Bridegroom who has never once divorced his bride. Israel went after other lovers, and the LORD said through Hosea that he would allure her and speak tenderly to her, and betroth her to himself for ever (Hosea 2:14, 19). The church is no better, and he gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Every human marriage is a small picture of that one. When ours are broken, his is not. He hates divorce because he is faithful, and he is faithful to us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The most extended treatment of life after death in the Synoptics, told as the direct sequel to the teaching on money.

Every detail of the opening is a price tag. Purple came from the murex shellfish and took thousands of them to colour a garment; the fine linen was a costly luxury cloth, and he feasted every day, not on feast days when ordinary people ate meat.

Lazarus was laid at the gate — passive, because he could not get there himself — and the gate is the great portal of a walled estate, which means the rich man could not enter or leave his own property without passing him. He wanted what fell: not a place at the table but the scraps on the floor. And he did not get them. The dogs are not a comfort but the final degradation — scavenging pariah animals reaching him when no human being would.

Then the reversal, and it is total. Lazarus is carried — the same passivity as at the gate, and he does nothing in either case. “Abraham's side” is, as the ESV margin gives it, his bosom: at a formal meal guests reclined on their left elbows, so the guest of honour lay with his head near the host's chest, which is the phrase John uses of the beloved disciple (John 13:23). The beggar who longed for what fell from a table is in the place of honour at the greatest table there is.

The rich man is buried — a few words, and the last good thing that happens to him. And the first thing he sees from Hades is Lazarus: the one face he had trained himself not to register, and he knows his name. He had always known his name.

Everything he then says shows that nothing has been learned. He pleads descent — “Father Abraham,” exactly what John the Baptist warned against (3:8) — and twice says “send Lazarus,” still treating him as somebody who ought to be running errands.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story teaches several interlocking truths. There is conscious existence after death, prior to the resurrection: the rich man sees, recognises, feels pain and argues. This is consistent with 23:43 and with Paul (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:23). The final state of the wicked involves real torment. And it is irreversible — the chasm “has been fixed,” established and standing established, and it is described as working in both directions. That second clause rules out something a sentimental reading would like: it is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him.
