One caution on reading the scene rightly. Jesus is not drawing a surveyor's map of the afterlife. He speaks in the vivid imagery his hearers already knew to press home truths that stand however the scene is pictured: death settles our destiny beyond changing, the comforts and miseries of this life can be exactly reversed by God's justice, and no messenger from the dead will persuade those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets. The imagery serves the warning; it was never meant to be quarried for geography.

But the warning must not be softened by that caution — and the gulf of verse 26 is not a new thing. There was a gulf in verses 19 to 21 as well. It was a gate, and it could be crossed by anybody who chose to. One man had the power to cross it every day of his life and never did.

Abraham's “Child, remember” is tender and it is not an accusation. Nothing new is introduced; no list of sins is produced. He simply asks the man to recall a life in which he received his good things — got exactly what he had chosen, all of it, for as long as he lasted.
verseByVerse.examples:
One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story's shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything, and the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns.

That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was wealthy. Note also the one name in the story: the rich man, who had every name worth having in this life, is anonymous, and the beggar is called Lazarus — named, and known. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily; what saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

“They have Moses and the Prophets” is one of the most important sentences in Luke. They had not been left without warning: the Law commands provision for the poor at your gate (Lev. 19:9-10; Deut. 15:7-11), and the Prophets say almost nothing more often — Amos on those who lie on beds of ivory and are not grieved, Isaiah on fasting that does not share bread with the hungry (Amos 6:4-6; Isa. 58:6-7). The rich man heard it read every Sabbath of his life, walked home past Lazarus, and had dinner.

And the final line is devastating for two reasons. The problem is never a shortage of evidence but an unwillingness to hear — miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it. And somebody did rise from the dead. When another Lazarus was raised at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him too (John 12:10). The test was run, and it went exactly as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: 'There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.

The rich man and Lazarus. Only Luke records this story. It illustrates the danger of wealth (v. 13), the reversal promised in the beatitudes and woes (6:20–26), and the sufficiency of Scripture (vv. 29–31). It also answers the Pharisees who had just sneered: they loved money and thought it a sign of God’s favour, and here is a man who had all of it.

There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen. Every detail is a price tag. Purple dye came from the murex shellfish, and it took thousands of them to colour a single garment; it was so costly that some societies restricted it by law to royalty. The fine linen was a luxury cloth, worn by the very rich. And he is unnamed. Tradition calls him Dives, Latin for rich, but Jesus gives him no name at all. The man who had every name worth having in this life has no name before God.

And who feasted sumptuously every day. Not on feast days, which is when ordinary people ate meat. Every day. Constant luxury, and the word suggests not just plenty but display: he made merry, splendidly.

And at his gate was laid a poor man. The verb is passive: he was laid there, thrown down, dumped, by somebody, because he could not get there himself. And the gate is not a garden gate. It is the great portal of a walled estate, which tells you the rich man could not enter or leave his own property without passing him. He was impossible to miss.

Named Lazarus. The only character in any of Jesus’ parables to be given a name. Lazarus, from Eleazar, means God helps, or God has helped. No one else did. The poor man has a name; the rich man does not. God knows the poor by name, and the name is the single hint the parable gives about where this man’s hope actually lay.

Covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table. Ulcerated, perhaps from malnutrition. He wants what falls: not a place at the table, the scraps that go on the floor, like the prodigal longing for the pigs’ pods (15:16). Diners used pieces of bread to wipe their hands and threw them under the table. Even those were not given to him.

Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. The dogs are not a comfort. They are the scavenging street dogs of a Near Eastern town, unclean animals, and they can reach him when no human being will. He was too weak to keep them off. It is the final degradation, and Luke means it as one. Perhaps the dogs showed him more attention than the rich man did.

The rich man’s sin. Not that he was rich, nor that he had done anything to Lazarus. He did nothing. He walked past the poor man at his gate every day and ignored him. His sin was neglect, indifference, the failure to love his neighbour, and behind it the failure to love God, because a man who loves God cannot step over his image every morning.

What it does not mean. One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story’s shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything; the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns, and a poor man is safe on the strength of his sores. That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was a wealthy man. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily. What saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

Who is the Lazarus at my gate? Usually someone you pass so often you have stopped seeing him. It may be the homeless man outside the station, but it is just as often the widow two doors down who has not had a visitor in a month, the colleague whose marriage is collapsing, the asylum-seeking family at the back of church, the believer in your congregation who cannot pay the gas bill. Your gate is wherever your daily path brings you within reach of real need. You cannot meet every need in the world, and God does not ask you to. He asks you not to step over the one he has laid where you will see him.

Should I give to every beggar who asks? Not necessarily, and wisdom is not the opposite of love. Giving cash to someone feeding an addiction may not help him, and Scripture expects the able to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). But the rich man’s problem was not careless giving; it was no giving and no seeing. A good rule is never to walk past without at least seeing the person: a word, a name asked, a meal bought, a referral to a church or charity that can do more than you can. And support, regularly, those in your church and town who do this work well. Love may be wise; it may not be blind.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man who lived in daily luxury while a poor, sick man named Lazarus lay at his gate, longing for scraps, with dogs licking his sores.

On a Tuesday. Who is lying at your gate: someone in need whom you see every day and ignore? Walk your ordinary route this week with your eyes open, the commute, the school gate, the church foyer, the street where you park, and ask God to show you one person you have trained yourself not to register. Then learn his name.

For worship. There is a God who knows the names of those whom the world steps over. He counts the hairs of the beggar’s head and records the tears of the forgotten in his book (Psalm 56:8). And the Son of God did not stay inside the gate. He came out to where we lay, covered with sores we could not heal, and he did not lick them like a dog or pass them like a rich man. He took them on himself: by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The God who helps is not a hint in a name. He is a Man with scars.
verseByVerse.note: Purple dye was costly and fine linen a luxury — the clothing of the very rich. Lazarus, the Greek form of Eleazar, means “God has helped”; he is the only character in Jesus’ parables, apart from Abraham, who is given a name.

parallels.desc: whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.

The poor man died. Luke does not say he was buried. A man in his condition, with nobody to claim him, would have gone into a common pit outside the walls, a pauper’s grave, and the parable simply passes over it, because something else was happening that nobody at the graveside could see.

And was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. He was carried. The same passivity as verse 20, and the same helplessness: he was laid at a gate by men, and he is carried through death by angels, and he does nothing in either case. The ESV notes that Abraham’s side is literally Abraham’s bosom, which is the language of a banquet. At a formal meal guests reclined on their left elbows, so the person in the place of honour lay with his head near the chest of the host. It is the phrase John uses of the beloved disciple at the Last Supper (John 13:23). It is a picture of paradise, the blessed rest of the righteous with the father of the faithful, at the messianic banquet where many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (13:28–29). So the beggar who longed for what fell from a table is now in the place of honour at the greatest table there is.

The rich man also died and was buried. A few words, and they are the last good thing that happens to him. He got what Lazarus did not: a funeral, and given his wealth, presumably an impressive one. But death came to him too, and his wealth could not save him. The burial is the final entry in the ledger of a life that had everything the world can supply, and the sentence moves straight past it.

And in Hades, being in torment. Hades is the Greek term for the realm of the dead, used in the Greek Old Testament for the Hebrew Sheol; here it is the place of punishment for the wicked. Torment, basanois, is torture, agony. And what the parable describes is conscious existence: he sees, he recognises, he is in pain, he will shortly argue. The reversal is complete: the rich man has nothing, Lazarus has everything. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53).

He lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. He can see what he has lost. Then the detail that finishes him. The first person he picks out is Lazarus. The man he had walked past at his own gate, every day, for years, the one face he had trained himself not to register, is the first thing visible from where he now is. And he knows his name. He had always known his name.

Where Christians differ: parable or history? And what happens after death? Some argue this is a literal description of the afterlife; others that it is a parable using popular imagery, and should not be pressed for details. It begins like other parables, there was a rich man, but names Lazarus, which no other parable does. Some, holding soul sleep or annihilationism, deny that the dead have conscious existence, or that the lost suffer for ever. Verdict: it is a parable, and its details (seeing across the chasm, speaking, a drop of water) are pictures, not a map of the afterlife. But Jesus would not use a picture that taught falsehood. The story teaches clearly that at death there is conscious existence, that the righteous are comforted and the wicked suffer, immediately after death, that there is a fixed separation, and that destiny is settled at death. The fuller picture comes at the resurrection and final judgment, when Hades itself gives up its dead (Revelation 20:13–15) and the lost go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The punishment is conscious and it is without end.

Hades and Abraham’s side. Hades here is the place of the dead before the final judgment, not yet the lake of fire, and Abraham’s side is the blessedness of believers with God, the same Paradise Jesus promised the dying thief that very day (23:43). The souls of the righteous, says the Westminster Confession, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, and the souls of the wicked are cast into hell, where they remain in torments and utter darkness, reserved to the judgment of the great day (Westminster 32.1). Then the bodies are raised, and soul and body together enter their final state.

When a Christian dies, does he sleep until the resurrection? No. The body sleeps in the grave, which is why the New Testament can call death falling asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). But the soul does not. Lazarus is carried at once to Abraham’s side; the thief is with Christ today; Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Your believing mother, your child who trusted Jesus, the friend you buried last year: they are not unconscious and they are not waiting in some grey place. They are with Christ, awake, at rest and rejoicing, and they await only the resurrection of their bodies.

Is there a purgatory, a place where souls are cleansed before heaven? No. Lazarus goes straight from the gate to the banquet, and there is no third place in the story, only comfort and torment. Christ’s blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). Nothing remains to be paid off. Believers are made perfect in holiness at death and pass immediately into glory (Westminster 32.1). Purgatory would add our sufferings to Christ’s sacrifice, as though his were not enough. It was enough.

In a sentence. When Lazarus died, angels carried him to Abraham’s side, but when the rich man died, he found himself in torment in Hades, seeing Lazarus far off with Abraham.

On a Tuesday. Death reveals what was true all along. Where you spend eternity is decided by how you respond to God now. Think of the two funerals: one with no mourners and angels in attendance, one with every honour and none of the things that mattered. Then ask which of the two your life is preparing. And if you are grieving a believer this week, read this verse slowly. They were carried.

For worship. The angels who carried Lazarus had once sung over a manger, and they are servants of the One who lay in it. He is the true Host of Abraham’s banquet, the one at whose side the beloved disciple reclined, and he has prepared a table for his poor. He went down into death himself so that for those who are his it would no longer be a pit but a doorway. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15). No believer dies unattended. No beggar of his is buried without being carried home.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom” — the place of honour beside the host at a banquet. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called out: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame. But Abraham said: child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.

Father Abraham, have mercy on me. Two things in that request tell you the man has not changed at all. The first is Father Abraham. He is pleading descent, which is exactly what John the Baptist had warned against at the start of this Gospel: do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father (3:8). Physically, yes; in faith, no. His claim is ancestry, and it is the only one he makes. And have mercy on me: he never showed mercy to Lazarus. Now he begs for it.

And send Lazarus. The second is worse. He knows the name, he can see the man in the place of honour beside Abraham, and his instinct is to have him fetched, like a servant, to bring water. Even now, he thinks of Lazarus as somebody who ought to be running errands for him. Nothing has been learned. Hell does not reform; it reveals.

To dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue. And note how small the request is. Not release, not reversal. The end of a finger, dipped. A single drop. He who feasted every day now begs for one drop of water, the exact reversal of the scraps from his table. Even that is refused.

For I am in anguish in this flame. Fire is a picture of the suffering of the lost, used by John the Baptist and by Jesus himself (3:17; Mark 9:43–48). Whether or not the flame is physical, what it pictures is real, and Jesus chose the most terrible image available because nothing less would be true.

Child, remember. Abraham’s answer opens with Child. There is no cruelty in this scene, and no gloating. The word is tender. But the answer is no. And what he says is not an accusation. It is an accounting, and it turns on one word: remember. Memory remains, and memory is a torment in itself. Nothing new is being introduced. Abraham does not produce a list of sins; he asks the man to recall his own life.

That you in your lifetime received your good things. And the possessive is exact. Your good things. He had his comfort in this life, and chose it as his portion: woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation (6:24). He lived for himself, and got what he lived for, and he had all of it, and it lasted exactly as long as he did.

And Lazarus in like manner bad things. Not that Lazarus was saved because he was poor. His name, God helps, suggests he trusted God. But in this life, he received evil, and he did not get it back.

But now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. The great reversal. Which is the whole indictment, and it does not require a single charge to be laid. The rich man had received everything he wanted. The tragedy is not that he was punished for enjoying it. It is that he wanted so little.

How can heaven be happy if people we love are in hell? This is one of the hardest questions a Christian carries, and Scripture does not answer it with a formula. But it gives us this: in the parable, Abraham is neither cruel nor tormented. He speaks with tenderness and with perfect agreement with God’s justice. In glory we will see as God sees, and we will love what he loves; no one will be in hell whom God has wronged, and no one in heaven will doubt that the Judge of all the earth has done right (Genesis 18:25). Until then, the question should drive us to pray and to speak to those we love while the door is open, and to trust that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

In a sentence. The rich man begged Abraham to send Lazarus with a drop of water, but Abraham reminded him that he had received his good things in life, and now Lazarus was comforted and he was in anguish.

On a Tuesday. If your good things are all in this life, you have nothing left for eternity. Store up treasure in heaven. Make a short list of the good things you most enjoy, your home, your holidays, your health, your comforts, and thank God for each one. Then ask, over each: is this my portion, or a gift on the road to my portion? The difference shows in what happens to your heart when one of them is taken away.

For worship. There was One who did cry out in anguish and thirst, and whose request was met with sour wine. I thirst, he said on the cross (John 19:28), and he drank the cup of wrath to its last drop, so that no one who trusts in him will ever beg for a drop of water in the flame. The rich man received his good things in his lifetime; Christ received our bad things in his, so that we might be comforted for ever. Lord, you are my portion (Psalm 119:57), and the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places.

parallels.desc: men whose portion is in this life

verseByVerse.quote: And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.

And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed. A second reason, on top of the first, and this one is not about what the man deserves. It is about what is possible. Has been fixed, estērktai, is perfect tense: it was established, and it stands established, firmly and permanently. Somebody fixed it, and there is no doubt who. By God.

In order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us. And the barrier is described as working in both directions: nobody crosses from there, and nobody crosses from here, not even out of compassion. That second clause is worth registering, because it rules out something a sentimental reading would like. It is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him. It is that the door is shut, and it is shut from the side that had every reason to want it open. And no one crosses from there to us: there is no escape from punishment.

No second chance. After death, destiny is fixed. There is no crossing, no purgatory, no second chance: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). This is the parable’s answer to the hope that there might be another opportunity after death, and it is the plainest statement of it in the Gospels. Whatever was decided in the life is now settled. The time to repent is now: behold, now is the favourable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Not a surveyor’s map. One caution on reading the whole scene rightly. Jesus is not drawing a map of the afterlife. He speaks in the vivid imagery his hearers already knew, Abraham’s side, a fixed gulf, a cry across the divide, to press home truths that stand however the scene is pictured: death settles our destiny beyond changing, the comforts and miseries of this life can be exactly reversed by God’s justice, and no messenger from the dead will persuade those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets. The imagery serves the warning; it was never meant to be quarried for geography. But the warning itself must not be softened by that caution.

The same chasm. And this is the reason the parable exists in a chapter about money. The gulf in verse 26 is not a new thing. There was a gulf in verses 19 to 21 as well, and it was a gate, and it could be crossed by anybody who chose to. The rich man had a chasm at his gate, between himself and Lazarus, which he could have crossed any day. One man had the power to cross it every day of his life and never did. He is now on the far side of a chasm he cannot cross, and it is the same chasm.

What about people who never heard the gospel, or who died as infants? The parable is spoken to people who had Moses and the Prophets, and its warning is aimed at those who hear and will not listen. Scripture is clear that salvation is only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17), which is why the church must send preachers, not wait for the dead to be given a second hearing. Those who never heard are judged by the light they had, and all have sinned against that light (Romans 1:20; 2:12). Infants who die in infancy are a different case: Scripture gives grounds for hope, and the confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3). Neither case offers a second chance after death.

In a sentence. A great chasm has been fixed between the blessed and the lost, so that no one can cross from one side to the other.

On a Tuesday. Now is the time to cross the chasm between you and those in need, and between you and God. After death, it will be too late. Which gate are you walking past? Which call to repentance have you been putting off? And whom do you love who is not yet in Christ? Pray for him by name today, and look for the conversation; the chasm is not fixed yet.

For worship. There was one chasm wider than this, and only one person has ever crossed it. The gulf between a holy God and a sinful race was not bridged by anything we could build. The Son came down across it, took flesh, and bore in his body the wrath that fixes chasms, so that the door could be opened from heaven’s side. I am the door, he said; if anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9). Everyone who crosses into Abraham’s side crosses on him.

parallels.desc: to die once, and after that comes judgment

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: then I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment. But Abraham said: they have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.

Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house. The second request, and it is usually read as the one decent thing the man does. He has given up on himself and is thinking of his family. There is something in that, and it should not be dismissed. He does not want them where he is, and the sentiment is real. But notice that it is still send him. Twice now, and both times the same instinct: Lazarus is a resource, an errand boy, to be dispatched. And notice which house he wants him sent to: his father’s house, where his brothers are presumably still feasting sumptuously and stepping over somebody at the gate.

For I have five brothers. Living as he had lived.

So that he may warn them. Warn, diamartyrētai, is to testify earnestly, solemnly. And there is something in the request that reads, very faintly, like a complaint, a hint of self-justification: if only I had been warned properly, I would not be here. That is not stated, and it is worth not pressing too far, but Abraham’s answer meets it exactly.

They have Moses and the Prophets. That is the answer, and it is one of the most important sentences in Luke’s Gospel. Moses and the Prophets means the Old Testament Scriptures. They have not been left without warning. They have everything they need, and the Scriptures are full of this. The Law commands that the poor at your gate be provided for and that the corners of your field be left for the poor and the sojourner (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 15:7–11). The Prophets say almost nothing more often: Amos on those who lie on beds of ivory and are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph; Isaiah on the fast that shares bread with the hungry and brings the homeless poor into the house (Amos 6:4–7; Isaiah 58:6–7). And the Scriptures point beyond care for the poor to repentance and faith in the Messiah they promise.

Let them hear them. Listen and obey. The rich man had all of it. He heard it read in synagogue every Sabbath of his life, walked home past Lazarus, and had dinner. So the request for a messenger is not really a request for information. Nobody in that house lacks information. What is being asked for is something more compelling than the word of God, and Abraham’s reply is that they already have the word of God, and it is enough, and the problem was never the evidence.

The sufficiency of Scripture. God’s word is enough to bring people to repentance and salvation. The sacred writings are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). They do not need a special messenger from the dead. The whole counsel of God is either set down in Scripture or deduced from it, and nothing is ever to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or traditions of men (Westminster 1.6).

Should I look for visions, dreams or messages from the dead to guide me? No. The story gives no warrant for contact between the living and the dead, and Scripture forbids seeking it (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Isaiah 8:19). The rich man’s request is refused, and the point is that the living have the Scriptures. God has spoken, finally and fully, in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the canon of his word is closed. If you want to hear God speak, open the Bible: he will not say anything there that contradicts it, and he will not say anything outside it that you need more.

In a sentence. The rich man begged Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers, but Abraham said they had the Scriptures and should listen to them.

On a Tuesday. You have the Scriptures. Listen to them. They are all you need. You have more than the five brothers had: the Law and the Prophets, and the Gospels and the letters as well. Ask honestly whether you are waiting for something more before you obey: a sign, a feeling, a clearer word. Then take the next plain command you find in the page this week and do it.

For worship. God has not left us to guess. He has spoken, in a book that has outlasted every empire that tried to burn it, and in it he has told us everything we need to know about himself, our sin and our Saviour. The Word who spoke Moses and the Prophets became flesh, and they all testify about him (John 5:39). Every page is a warning from love and an invitation from mercy. Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Psalm 119:105).
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and the Prophets” means the Old Testament Scriptures.

parallels.desc: if you believed Moses, you would believe me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: no, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent. He said to him: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.

No, father Abraham. He contradicts Abraham flatly, which is a remarkable thing to do from where he is standing, and entirely in character. He has been managing people all his life and is still doing it. Scripture is not enough, he thinks.

But if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent. A spectacular sign would convince them. And his theory is one that a great many people hold: the common belief that if only there were more evidence, people would believe. The Scriptures are not enough; what would really work is something dramatic. A miracle. A visitation. Some undeniable event that would settle the question. It is worth admitting how reasonable that sounds. Most Christians have thought it about somebody they love: if he could only see something, he would believe.

If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets. The problem is not lack of evidence, but hardness of heart. A man who will not be moved by the word of God will not be moved by anything, because the resistance is not located in his mind. Miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it; they only raise the stakes.

Neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead. A haunting prophecy, and the reason this sentence ends the chapter. Somebody did rise from the dead: Jesus himself. Not long after this was spoken, a man came out of a tomb outside Jerusalem, and the leaders who had heard this kind of teaching were not convinced. They paid the soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15). And in John’s Gospel, when another Lazarus was raised from the dead at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him and Jesus too (John 11:43–53; 12:10–11). The test was run. It went exactly as he said.

How faith actually comes. Miracles do not create faith in those who reject God’s word. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), by the work of the Spirit. When the dead do come to life, it is not because a ghost has visited them but because God has spoken through his word and opened their hearts, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14). That is why the church preaches rather than performs: the power is in the message, because the Spirit works with the word.

Should I pray for a sign for a relative who will not believe? Pray for him, constantly and by name; but pray above all that God would open his heart to the word, because that is how God saves. A sign without a new heart would only harden him further, as this verse warns. So put the word in front of him: your life, which he reads first, then your words about Christ, a Gospel to read, an invitation to hear the Bible preached. And do not despair if nothing seems to happen. The Spirit is not in a hurry, and many who resisted for decades were finally won by a verse they had heard a hundred times.

In a sentence. When the rich man insisted that someone returning from the dead would make his brothers repent, Abraham replied that if they would not listen to Scripture, they would not be convinced even by someone rising from the dead.

On a Tuesday. There is no further evidence coming. What we have is Moses and the Prophets, and now the record of the one who rose, and if that is not heard, nothing else will be. There is no dramatic sign that will do what a page of Scripture, honestly attended to, is able to do. So stop waiting for one, for yourself or for anyone else. Open the Gospel of Luke this week, read one chapter slowly, and ask the risen Christ to speak.

For worship. Someone has risen from the dead. Not a beggar sent back on an errand, but the Lord of glory, who went down into the realm of the dead and came out holding its keys (Revelation 1:18). The rich man asked for a messenger; God sent his Son, and raised him on the third day, just as Moses and the Prophets had said (24:27, 44). He is the final word, the last evidence, the only door. Listen to the Scriptures that point to him, and believe, and you will find that he has been standing at your gate all along, not as a beggar, but as a King with his hands full of mercy.

parallels.desc: after Lazarus of Bethany is raised, they plot to kill Jesus

16.text: <sup>1</sup> He also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. <sup>2</sup> And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’ <sup>3</sup> And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. <sup>4</sup> I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’ <sup>5</sup> So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ <sup>6</sup> He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ <sup>7</sup> Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’ <sup>8</sup> The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. <sup>10</sup> “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. <sup>11</sup> If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? <sup>12</sup> And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own? <sup>13</sup> No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.” <sup>14</sup> The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. <sup>16</sup> “The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it. <sup>17</sup> But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void. <sup>18</sup> “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. <sup>19</sup> “There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. <sup>20</sup> And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, <sup>21</sup> who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. <sup>22</sup> The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, <sup>23</sup> and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. <sup>24</sup> And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ <sup>25</sup> But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. <sup>26</sup> And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’ <sup>27</sup> And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— <sup>28</sup> for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ <sup>29</sup> But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’ <sup>30</sup> And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ <sup>31</sup> He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’”

17.title: Forgiveness, Faith, Gratitude, and the Coming Son of Man
17.overview:
Luke 17 gathers teachings that might appear loosely connected but share a common thread: the shape of life in the kingdom as it moves toward its final consummation. Disciples are warned about causing others to stumble, commanded to forgive repeatedly, confronted about the nature of faith, and then — after the extraordinary healing of ten lepers — taught about gratitude. The chapter then pivots to sustained teaching about the coming of the Son of Man: apocalyptic instruction that would be at home in the Olivet Discourse.

The healing of the ten lepers is one of the most poignant episodes in Luke, precisely because of what does not happen: nine healed men simply walk away. The one who returns is a Samaritan — an outsider — and his return becomes the occasion for Jesus to say something remarkable: “your faith has made you well” — or, as the ESV margin gives it, “has saved you.” The nine received physical healing; the one received something more.

The eschatological teaching (vv. 20–37) is deliberately disorienting. The kingdom does not come with observable signs (v. 20); it is already in your midst (v. 21). Yet the day of the Son of Man will come with lightning-like sudden visibility (v. 24). The tension is not a contradiction: the kingdom is already present in the person of Jesus, but its final manifestation remains future — and when it comes, it will be unmistakable, inescapable, and final.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, Faith, and Duty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Four short teachings, each pressing the disciples on a different part of their calling.

The ESV margin gives “temptations to sin” as “stumbling blocks” — not primarily an enticement but an obstacle set in somebody's path. Drowning carried a particular horror for a Jew who expected burial in his own ground, and it is offered as the preferable outcome.

The weight of the saying falls on the influential, because nobody trips a person who is not following them. The “little ones” include children and reach wider: the young in faith, the recently converted, anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

The forgiveness command opens with “pay attention to yourselves,” and the order governs everything after it — a man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not. Seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, and it is meant to kill the arithmetic: anyone who apologises seven times before evening for the same thing is, by any ordinary judgement, not sincere, and Jesus takes that objection away by naming the number himself. The test is not whether the repentance convinces but whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

The apostles respond “Increase our faith!” — and note when. Not before a storm or a demon. They have been told to forgive, and they say they have not got enough of whatever it takes. The answer is not what they asked for: he tells them the quantity was never the issue.

Then the servant parable, which checks the pride that obedience produces. And note the condition: “when you have done all that you were commanded” — this is the sentence for the best possible day, with nothing outstanding. Even then there is no credit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The forgiveness teaching anticipates the Lord's Prayer — “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (11:4). This does not make forgiveness a condition of justification; it describes the effect of justification on a heart. Those forgiven much love much (7:47).

The mulberry saying needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and made into a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough — and the corollary follows at once about the tumour and the child. It cannot be got out of this text.

Start with where it sits: the apostles asked for help to forgive, and this is his answer about that. Then consider that Luke wrote the sequel — if this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it claimed, and men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer offered in perfect faith: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). Nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small.

Achreioi — “unworthy” — means unprofitable, contributing no surplus. It does not mean worthless in God's sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. And it must be guarded from the opposite error, because the same Lord says he will gird himself and serve his watching servants (12:37) and set the faithful man over ten cities (19:17). There is no wage; there is a Master who pays anyway.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents and leaves the other case open. What if he never says “I repent”? That silence is where most real wounds live.

The answer begins with a distinction: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart — releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury. Jesus does this from the cross for men who had not repented and never would (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and Jesus attaches it to “if he repents.” You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally; you cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends.

That protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

And the servant parable has a reader for whom the whole scene will sting: anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement, doing the work that is simply expected and eating after everybody else. Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. He has already said that when the master comes he will gird himself and have them recline at table and serve them (12:37). Both pictures are his, and the second one is the ending.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to his disciples: temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.

Meaning first. Luke 17 moves from the life of the church to the end of the world, and the same Lord is in charge of both. It opens with four short teachings for the disciples on life together: do not cause others to stumble, rebuke and forgive without limit, use the faith you have, and serve without seeking credit (vv. 1–10). Then ten lepers are cleansed and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks, and is told that his faith has saved him (vv. 11–19). Finally, asked when the kingdom will come, Jesus says it is already standing among them in his own person, and then tells his disciples how his return will come: suddenly, visibly, after his suffering, on a world as busy and ordinary as Noah’s and Lot’s (vv. 20–37). The thread through it all is a question of direction: who turns back to Christ, and who looks back to the world.

The setting. After the parables about money and the Pharisees in chapter 16, Jesus turns to his disciples. The journey to Jerusalem goes on (9:51), and Luke gathers sayings that teach a community how to live while its Lord walks towards the cross.

Temptations to sin are sure to come. The word is skandala, and it is not primarily about enticement. A skandalon was the baited trigger-stick of an animal trap: the innocent-looking thing that brings the whole apparatus down. What is being described is not a tempting offer but a snare somebody has set, anything that trips a person into sin or out of faith. And the first half is a flat acknowledgement of the world as it is. In a fallen world they are inevitable. Jesus does not promise a church in which nobody is ever tripped up, and a man who expects one will be disillusioned within a year.

But woe to the one through whom they come! But inevitability does not excuse responsibility. Each person who causes another to fall is accountable. And Luke’s woe is the prophets’ word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict. Judas was the stumbling block God had foretold, and still the Son of Man said woe to that man by whom he is betrayed (22:22). God’s sovereignty over sin never turns the sinner into a victim.

It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea. The image is deliberately extreme. The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill, a wheel of rock turned by a donkey, which no man could lift. Drowning with it would be a terrible death, and it carried a particular horror for a Jew, who expected burial in his own ground: a body that could not be buried. This is being described as the preferable outcome. Better that than the judgment that awaits whoever destroys the faith of another.

Than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin. Who are the little ones? The phrase can cover children, and it certainly includes them. But in this context it reaches wider: humble, ordinary believers, the young in faith, the recently converted, the tax collectors and sinners who have just come to Jesus (15:1), anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

The weight falls on the influential. Nobody trips a person who is not following them. So this is a word for parents, and for anyone who teaches, leads, or is simply admired by a younger believer, and its terms are severe beyond anything else Jesus says about the consequences of a bad example. To ruin your own soul is a catastrophe. To be the stumbling block under somebody else’s is worse, and he measures it with a millstone.

How might I cause someone to stumble without meaning to? Most stumbling blocks are not set deliberately. A church leader whose private life contradicts his preaching. A parent who teaches prayer and never prays, or who mocks other Christians at the dinner table. A mature believer who flaunts a freedom, in drink or entertainment or speech, in front of someone fresh out of the very thing (Romans 14:13–21). Harsh legalism also trips people, by teaching them that God is impossible to please. And in its gravest form, it is the abuse of a child or a vulnerable person by someone they trusted, which has driven many out of the faith and is exactly what this millstone is for. Such abuse must be reported, never hidden to protect a church’s name.

What if I have caused someone to stumble? Then repent, and do not let the millstone become despair. The warning is spoken to disciples, to bring them to their senses, not to push them past forgiveness. Confess it to God, and where possible go to the person, own it without excuse, and ask how you can help put it right. Then live differently in front of them. Peter denied his Lord three times in front of servants who were watching, and was restored to feed the very lambs (John 21:15–17). The blood of Christ covers the sins of influence too.

In a sentence. Stumbling blocks are inevitable, but woe to the person who causes one of Jesus’ little ones to fall, for drowning would be a better fate.

On a Tuesday. Your example is watched by others. Never be the reason a weaker believer falls. Think of three people younger in faith or in years who watch you: a child, a new Christian, a colleague who knows you go to church. Ask what they have learned about Christ from you this month, from your speech, your temper, your screen, your use of Sunday. If one of those lessons is false, correct it in front of them.

For worship. Look at how much Jesus loves his little ones. He measures the danger to them in millstones and seas, because to him they are not little at all. Not one of the weakest believers is beneath his notice or outside his protection: my sheep hear my voice, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:27–28). And he himself became a stone of stumbling to the proud (1 Peter 2:8) so that he could be the cornerstone for the weak, the one Rock on which no little one who trusts him will ever fall.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, I repent, you must forgive him.

Pay attention to yourselves! The imperative comes first and it governs everything after it. Watch yourselves: your own example, and your own heart. Before a word is said about rebuking anybody, the man doing the rebuking is told to look at himself.

If your brother sins, rebuke him. Three obligations follow, and the middle one is the least popular. Love does not ignore sin. A fellow believer who sins should be lovingly confronted, privately first (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). The rebuke is not optional and it is not unkind; it is what love does when it sees somebody going wrong and would rather they did not arrive. Silence is not always kindness. What makes it bearable is the order. A man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not.

And if he repents, forgive him. The goal of rebuke is restoration, not humiliation. A rebuke that does not hope for repentance is only an attack.

And if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, I repent, you must forgive him. Seven is the number of completeness. Not a limit, but limitless forgiveness: the same limitless forgiveness Jesus gives Peter, seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:21–22). And seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, meant to kill the arithmetic. Anyone who apologises seven times before evening for the same thing is, by any ordinary judgment, not sincere, and Jesus takes that objection away by naming the number himself. Even if his repentance seems unconvincing, if he says he repents, forgive. The test is not whether the repentance convinces. It is whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrong was not wrong, or always restoring full trust at once, or removing all consequences. A treasurer who stole may be forgiven and still not be given the chequebook again. But forgiveness means letting go of the debt and of revenge, and being ready to restore the relationship.

What if he never says he repents? Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents, and leaves the other case open, and that silence is worth pressing, because that is where most real wounds live. The answer begins with a distinction Luke’s own wording invites: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart: releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury, declining to make yourself the creditor. Jesus prays for this from the cross for men who had not repented (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and that takes two; Jesus attaches it to if he repents. You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally. You cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends. And that protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from the cruelty of having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for.

And if the sin is serious and goes on? This private rebuke is the first step Jesus describes more fully in Matthew 18:15–17, where unrepentant sin is taken to one or two others and then to the church. Forgiveness in your heart does not mean the church must look away. And where the sin is a crime, abuse of a spouse or a child, or anything that endangers others, forgiving does not mean staying silent or staying in danger. Report it, protect the vulnerable, and let the elders and the civil authorities do their work. You can release your own claim to revenge and still insist that justice be done.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to rebuke a sinning brother and to forgive him whenever he repents, even seven times in a day.

On a Tuesday. Is there a brother or sister you need to confront lovingly, or forgive again? Name the person in prayer first, and ask God to show you your own part. Then either go and speak, gently and privately, or, if he has already said he is sorry, tell him plainly: I forgive you, and I will not bring it up again. And hold the two together, because the opening command does its work here. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

For worship. Count how many times a day you turn back to God and say, I repent. Seven would be a good day. And he has never once run out. As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12). The Lord who tells us to forgive seven times a day forgives us seventy times seven, and he does it at his own cost, from a cross, for people who were still driving the nails. Every time we forgive a brother, we are only passing on a sliver of what we have been given in full.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' And the Lord said, 'If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles said to the Lord: increase our faith! And the Lord said: if you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, be uprooted and planted in the sea, and it would obey you.

The apostles said to the Lord, Increase our faith! Note when they say it. Not before a storm, not facing a demon, not in front of a crowd of five thousand. They have just been told to forgive a brother seven times in a day, and their response is that they have not got enough of whatever it takes. They feel unable. It is an honest request and a good prayer, and they were right to be daunted.

If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed. The answer is not what they asked for. They wanted more; he tells them the quantity was never the issue. The mustard seed is the smallest seed (13:19), the standard image of the negligible. Jesus does not say they need more faith, but real faith. The size of faith matters less than its object. Tiny faith in a great God can do great things.

You could say to this mulberry tree. The mulberry, or sycamine, tree, the black mulberry of Palestine, has a deep, spreading root system and was very hard to uproot. It was proverbially long-lived, said to stand for six hundred years.

Be uprooted and planted in the sea, and it would obey you. A deliberately impossible picture, and doubly absurd: a tree that cannot be moved, put where nothing grows. Faith does the impossible, because God does. Forgiving seven times a day may feel like uprooting a mulberry tree; faith in God makes it possible.

What it does not mean. The verse needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and turned into something else: a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough, and the corollary follows at once, that the tumour did not shrink and the child did not recover for the same reason. That has been preached to a great many people at the worst hour of their lives, and it cannot be got out of this text. Start with where the saying sits. The apostles have not asked for power to work wonders. They have asked for help to forgive, and the mulberry tree is his answer about that. To pull it out and make it a lever for moving circumstances is to use a sentence about pardoning your brother as a technique for rearranging your life.

The prayer that was not granted. Consider that Luke wrote the sequel. If this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it claimed, and in the whole of that book, men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer in history offered in perfect faith: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). The cup was not removed, and nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small. What is promised is not that faith is a force whose output rises with its volume, but that its power lies in what it is attached to.

My prayer was not answered. Was my faith too small? No. If your faith was the size of a mustard seed, it was enough, because the power never lay in your faith but in God. When he does not do what we asked, it is not because we failed a test of believing hard enough; it is because our Father, who loves us and knows what we do not, has a better purpose, as he had for Paul, whose thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Faith is not the confidence that God will do what I want. It is trust that he is good, and wise, and will do what is right, and the willingness to keep obeying while I wait.

So how does my faith grow? Not mainly by trying to feel more certain, but by looking at the One you trust. Faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), so read and hear it. It grows by use, like a muscle: the next time you forgive when it is hard, or give when it is costly, you will find that God was there. It grows in the fellowship of believers and at the Lord’s Table, where Christ is set before us. And it grows by asking: the apostles’ prayer, increase our faith, is one God loves to answer.

In a sentence. When the apostles asked for more faith, Jesus said that even faith as small as a mustard seed could uproot a tree and plant it in the sea.

On a Tuesday. Take the thing that feels impossible this week, the person you cannot forgive, the habit you cannot break, the obedience you cannot face, and stop measuring your faith. Bring what you have, however small, to God, and act on it today. What you already have, actually used, is enough for the seventh apology today.

For worship. Bring your small faith to a great God. He does the impossible. The mustard seed does not move the tree; the One it trusts does, the One who spoke and the sea obeyed, who said to a fig tree wither and it withered, and who uprooted the tree of our sin and planted it in the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19). He never asks us to bring great faith. He asks us to bring our faith to him, and he is great.
verseByVerse.note: The mulberry (sycamine) tree has a deep, spreading root system.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will any one of you who has a servant ploughing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field: come at once and recline at table? Will he not rather say to him: prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterwards you will eat and drink?

Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep. The question expects the answer no, and every man listening would have given it without hesitation. Picture the household. This is a small farm, not a great estate: a small farmer with one slave, who does the ploughing by day and the shepherding, and works in the house in the evening. There is no second slave in the kitchen. When he comes in, the supper has not been made, because he is the one who makes it.

Say to him when he has come in from the field, Come at once and recline at table? Recline at table is the posture of a guest at a formal meal. The suggestion is not that the master might let him sit down; it is that he might treat him as an honoured visitor in his own master’s house. No master would serve his slave first. That was not how things worked.

Will he not rather say to him, Prepare supper for me. The slave’s duty continued. The arrangement is not cruel by the standards of that world, and Jesus is not commending it as a model for employment. It is simply how a household ran, and everybody knew it. Dress properly is, in the ESV margin, gird yourself: tuck up the robe for work, as the servants waiting for their master did in chapter 12.

And afterward you will eat and drink. Note the last clause, because it is easy to miss under the severity. The servant is not going hungry. He eats; he simply eats second. Which is worth holding, because this parable is about to say something very hard about deserving, and it says it inside a picture where the servant is fed.

The point. The parable is not about how masters should treat slaves, but about the disciple’s attitude to God. A slave does not expect special reward for doing his duty. Elsewhere Jesus says the Master will serve his faithful servants (12:37): that is grace, not obligation.

Does Jesus approve of slavery here? No. He uses the household as his listeners knew it to make a point about God, just as he uses a dishonest manager and an unjust judge without approving of them. Slavery in that world was a fact of life, and the gospel set to work on it from inside: Paul tells a master to receive his runaway slave no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), and the Bible condemns man-stealing outright (1 Timothy 1:10; Exodus 21:16). The parable’s subject is not human employment but the relation of a creature to his Creator, who owns us by right and whom we can never put in our debt.

For the one who serves unseen. There is a reader for whom the whole scene will sting, and it is worth saying now rather than at the end. Anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement will recognise this household exactly: the work that is simply expected, the meal made after everybody else has eaten. Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. He has already said, in this same Gospel, that when the master comes he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them (12:37). Both pictures are his, and the second one is the ending.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether a master would invite his slave to sit and eat when he came in from the field, rather than expecting him to prepare and serve his master’s meal first.

On a Tuesday. Serve God without expecting thanks or reward for doing what you should. Notice this week the small resentment that rises when your service goes unseen: the rota nobody else fills, the meal nobody thanks you for, the prayer meeting nobody else attends. Then do the next thing anyway, as for the Lord and not for men (Colossians 3:23), and leave the thanks to him.

For worship. Here is the wonder. The Master in the parable would never serve the servant. Our Master did. On the night he was betrayed he rose from supper, tied a towel around his waist and washed his servants’ feet (John 13:4–5). I am among you as the one who serves, he said (22:27). And at the end of the age he will do it again: he will seat his tired servants at his table and come round to serve them himself. No earthly master ever behaved like that. Only the King of glory would.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say: we are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.

Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? Again the answer is obvious and again it is no, not because thanks would be wrong, but because thanks are for something over and above. A slave doing his job puts no one in his debt. Nobody is owed gratitude for meeting the terms.

So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded. Note the condition attached. This is not addressed to a man who has failed. It is the sentence he is to say on the day he has done everything: the best possible day, with nothing outstanding. And no one has ever had that day (Romans 3:23). Even then there would be no credit. Not a small credit; none. Duty done is duty done.

Say, We are unworthy servants. Unworthy, achreioi, means unprofitable, contributing no surplus, not deserving special merit, owed nothing. It does not mean worthless in God’s sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. It means having no claim on the Master: at the end of the accounting there is nothing on the credit side that God did not first supply.

We have only done what was our duty. Obedience to God is our duty, not a favour to him. We cannot put God in our debt: who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? (Romans 11:35). This destroys the idea of earning salvation or merit by good works. Even our best obedience earns nothing; we owe God everything. Any reward he gives is pure grace.

Why this parable sits here. Chapter 17 has just demanded three enormous things: do not trip the weak, forgive seven times a day, exercise the faith you have. A disciple who manages any of that will feel something rise in him, and what rises is the thought that God now owes him a little. That thought is the target.

Where Christians differ: merit. Medieval theology developed a doctrine of merit, including works of supererogation, good works beyond what is required, which built up a treasury of merit in the church that could be applied to others. Verdict: this verse refutes it. No one can do more than duty requires. Even after doing everything, we are unworthy servants. Reward is grace. The Reformers saw it clearly: we cannot by our best works merit pardon of sin or eternal life, and when we have done all we can, we have done but our duty and are unprofitable servants (Westminster 16.5, which echoes this very verse).

What it does not mean. This saying needs guarding from the opposite error, because it has been used to flatten people who were already flat. It does not mean God is indifferent to what his servants do, and Luke will not allow that reading. The same Lord says he will serve his watching servants (12:37), and that the faithful man will be set over ten cities (19:17). He is generous past anything owed. The two sit together without strain once the direction is right. There is no wage. There is a Master who pays anyway, and the whole point of the parable is that the second sentence is a gift and not an invoice.

Then why bother working hard for God? Because love does not work for wages. A son does not help his father in order to be paid; he helps because he is a son, and because he loves him. Freed from the need to earn, the Christian can serve with joy instead of anxiety, and God, who owes us nothing, has promised to reward even a cup of cold water given in Christ’s name (Matthew 10:42). As Augustine put it, when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts. We work hard because we are already accepted, not in order to be.

In a sentence. When disciples have done everything commanded, they should say they are unworthy servants who have only done their duty.

On a Tuesday. Catch the quiet bookkeeping in your heart this week: I have served on the rota for three years, I tithe, I gave up that job for the church, surely God will see me right. Name it, and hand the ledger back to him. Then do your duty gladly, and when a blessing comes, receive it as a gift, not a payment.

For worship. You can never put God in your debt. Serve him gladly, and receive his rewards as gifts of grace. There was only one Servant who did all that was commanded, every command, every day, without a single failure, and who could have claimed a wage. And he did not claim it for himself. He was counted unworthy, numbered with transgressors, so that unprofitable servants like us could hear at the end: well done, good servant (19:17). Every reward we will ever receive is his merit, spent on us.

parallels.desc: who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is in the border country where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory — a detail that will matter in five verses.

The ten stand at a distance because the law required it: a man with the disease lived outside the camp, in torn clothes, calling “unclean” as anyone approached (Lev. 13:45-46). “Leprosy” covered a range of skin conditions, but the social consequence was the same whatever the diagnosis — total exclusion from worship, family, work, and touch.

And ten of them are together, which tells its own story. Whatever each had been before, the disease had stripped it off and left them with the one thing they now had in common. Which is what makes verse 16 so striking: one of these ten is a Samaritan. Nine Jews and a Samaritan are living together outside a village, because the disease has done to their divisions what nothing else could.

“Master” is, everywhere else in this Gospel, on the lips of disciples. And they ask not for cleansing but for mercy, leaving the content of it to him.

He does not touch them and does not pronounce them clean. He gives them an errand that only makes sense afterwards — the inspection of Leviticus 14 is what you go for when the disease has gone. So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence.

“And as they went they were cleansed.” Not before they went. There would have been a stretch of that road during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed.

One turns back — and it is worth being clear that the other nine were obeying. Until a priest certified them they could not go home or touch their children. Nine men are hurrying towards the thing they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told. One of them stops.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story illustrates the difference between receiving a benefit from God and responding to God himself. All ten received cleansing; only one responded to the Giver. And the nine were not ingrates by worldly standards — their failure was not defiance but distraction. They moved from the gift to the system without pausing to return.

The Samaritan's outsider status is theologically loaded in Luke, who shows Samaritans in a positive light three times: the good Samaritan (10:33), this leper, and Samaria as the first step beyond Jerusalem in Acts (1:8; 8:5).

And the point is sharper than it first appears. The nine were going to the priests in Jerusalem — to the temple, the sacrifices, the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. He could not have gone with them. So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place open to him, and it turned out to be the right one.

“Foreigner” at v.18 is allogenēs, a word found only here in the New Testament — and it is the word carved on the stone barrier in the temple court warning Gentiles not to pass beyond on pain of death. That inscription has been dug up. Jesus names this man by the very status the sign held against him, and the only man in the story fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Your faith has made you well” — or, as the ESV margin gives it, “has saved you.” Luke has used those words to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48).

Which answers the obvious difficulty: all ten were cleansed, so what is left for this man to receive? Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved. A man can receive a great deal from Christ and never arrive at Christ, and this is the clearest picture of it in the Gospels.

And notice what his faith actually consisted of, because it was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men, obeyed an instruction that made no sense, and when he saw what had happened, turned round and went back to the one who did it. There is no impressive spiritual content anywhere in his story.

The three questions at v.17 are among the few places where Jesus expresses something like disappointment at how he has been treated. He does not do it elsewhere for himself — not when a village will not house him, not when a Pharisee omits the courtesies at dinner.

And the nine are not villains but ordinary. Nobody in that group decided to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight to the next necessary thing, and the next, and by evening it was a fortnight ago. A family prays for a sick child and the child recovers; within weeks the thankfulness has given way to relief and resumed normal life. The story calls ordinary people to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance.

On the way to Jerusalem. The journey continues (9:51). Luke reminds us of the destination again, and only Luke records this healing. Every step of the story that follows is taken by a Man walking towards a cross.

He was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. Luke gives us the geography: the border country, the strip where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory, where Jews and Samaritans lived near each other. It is a detail that will matter in five verses. Border regions are where mixed populations live, and where the ordinary boundaries are thinner than they are further in.
