And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers. They are outside the village, which is where the law required them to be. Lepers lived together outside towns, cut off from society: Leviticus put a man with the disease outside the camp, in torn clothes, with his hair loose, calling out unclean, unclean as anyone approached (Leviticus 13:45–46). Leprosy in that world covered a range of skin conditions, not only the disease that now bears the name. But the social consequence was the same whatever the diagnosis: total exclusion from worship, from family, from work, from touch.

A colony of the excluded. Ten of them are together, which tells its own story. Whatever they had been before, farmer, father, householder, the disease had stripped it off and left them with the one thing they now had in common. And Luke saves a detail for verse 16: one of these ten is a Samaritan. A Jew and a Samaritan did not eat together, worship together or share a cup. But nine Jews and one Samaritan are living together outside a village, because shared misery has done to their divisions what nothing else could. It is a bleak observation and a true one. There are forms of suffering severe enough to dissolve hatreds that no argument would ever have touched.

Who stood at a distance. Lepers were required to keep their distance and cry out a warning. They could not approach. That is the last thing said about them before they speak, and it is where every one of them had been standing for years.

Is leprosy a picture of sin? In a sense, yes, and the church has long read it that way, though carefully. The leper was not more sinful than his neighbours; his disease was not a punishment for a particular sin (John 9:3). But the law made leprosy a living parable of uncleanness: it spread, it disfigured, it cut a man off from God’s house and God’s people, and no one could cure it but God (2 Kings 5:7). That is what sin does to every one of us. And Jesus, who could not be made unclean by touching lepers, made them clean, which is exactly what he does with sinners.

In a sentence. On the way to Jerusalem, on the border of Samaria and Galilee, Jesus was met by ten lepers who kept their distance as the law required.

On a Tuesday. Suffering often breaks down barriers that pride builds. Jesus meets the outcasts on the edges. Ask who in your town stands at a distance: the long-term ill, the person with a disfiguring condition, the prisoner’s family, the one everyone avoids at the school gate. Then go nearer than is comfortable, because your Lord did.

For worship. Jesus walks the border country. He is not afraid of the edges where the clean and the unclean meet, and he does not wait for the excluded to make themselves acceptable. The holy Son of God entered a world of lepers and became, on the cross, the one cast outside the camp (Hebrews 13:12–13), so that people who had stood at a distance all their lives could be brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: Lepers were required to keep their distance and cry out a warning.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: and lifted up their voices, saying, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.' When he saw them he said to them, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' And as they went they were cleansed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And lifted up their voices, saying: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. When he saw them he said to them: go and show yourselves to the priests. And as they went they were cleansed.

And lifted up their voices, saying, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. They shout, because they have to. The distance the law imposed is the reason the request is delivered at the top of ten voices. Master is epistata, a word only Luke uses, and everywhere else in this Gospel it is on the lips of disciples (5:5; 8:24; 9:33). These men are not disciples. They have picked up the word from somewhere and are using it correctly. And note what they ask for: not cleansing but mercy. It is the cry for mercy that echoes through Luke, from the tax collector in the temple to the blind man on the Jericho road (18:13, 38). They do not specify the terms. They ask him to be merciful and leave the content of it to him.

When he saw them he said to them, Go and show yourselves to the priests. He does not touch them, which he had done for the leper in chapter 5. He does not pronounce them clean. He gives them an errand. And the errand only makes sense afterwards. A priest had to declare a leper clean before he could rejoin society, and Leviticus 14 lays down a detailed procedure for a man whose leprosy has healed: he presents himself to the priest, is examined, and after the offerings is certified clean and readmitted to the community (Leviticus 14:2–32; compare 5:14). It is the inspection you go for when the disease has gone. So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence. Jesus tells them to go before they are healed. A test of faith: will they go, still leprous, trusting his word?

And as they went they were cleansed. There it is, and the timing is the whole point. Not before they went. As they went, as they obeyed. Every one of them had to turn round and walk towards a priest while still covered in the disease, having been given nothing but a sentence. There would have been a stretch of that road, a hundred yards, half a mile, during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed. Faith acts on Christ’s word before seeing the result, like Naaman, who was healed when he obeyed and washed (2 Kings 5:14).

The shape of the Christian life. Which is a fair description of most of the Christian life, and it is why this detail is worth stopping at. The instruction is given first and the evidence arrives on the way. A man who waits to see the change before he starts walking will not see it, because the walking is where it happens.

Does this mean I must obey before I am saved? No. The order in salvation is grace first: God gives life, and faith and obedience flow from it. These men did not earn their cleansing by walking; their walking was their faith, trusting a word that had already been spoken by the one with power to fulfil it. That is what faith always does. It hears Christ’s word and acts as if it were true, because it is. You do not need to feel forgiven before you believe you are forgiven; you take him at his word, and the feelings come on the road.

In a sentence. The lepers cried for mercy, and Jesus told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went, they were healed.

On a Tuesday. Obey Christ’s word before you see the result. Blessing often comes on the way. Is there a plain command you are waiting to feel ready for: to forgive, to confess, to be baptised, to give, to speak to a neighbour about Christ? Start walking this week, on his word alone, and watch what he does on the road.

For worship. Here is a Lord whose word is enough. He does not need to touch, or to wave a hand, or even to be present: he speaks, and leprosy dissolves on a dusty road half a mile away. It is the same voice that said let there be light, and there was light. And every sinner who has ever cried Jesus, Master, have mercy on us from a distance has found that the mercy came before the asking was finished, because it was already on its way from a cross.
verseByVerse.note: A priest had to declare a leper clean before he could rejoin the community.

parallels.desc: he shall be brought to the priest

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.

Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back. He is the only one who stops. Before reaching the priest, he could not wait to give thanks. And it is worth being clear about what the other nine were doing, because they are usually described as ungrateful and it is not quite that simple. They were obeying. They had been told to go to the priests, and they went, and until a priest certified them they were not legally clean, could not go home, could not enter the synagogue, could not touch their children. Nine men are hurrying towards the thing they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told. One of them turns round.

Praising God with a loud voice. Loudly, as loudly as he had cried for mercy. In verse 13 they lifted up their voices from a distance for mercy. The same volume, redirected.

And he fell on his face at Jesus’ feet. Which is not the posture of gratitude but of worship. He gives glory to God, and does so at Jesus’ feet. Praising God and thanking Jesus are the same act, done in the same breath. He has not merely worked out that a benefit came from somewhere. He has worked out where. And Luke lets that stand without comment, as he does every time someone falls at Jesus’ feet, because the only fitting response to God present in the flesh is to worship him.

Giving him thanks. The word is eucharistōn, from which comes Eucharist, the church’s ancient name for the Lord’s Supper, the meal of thanksgiving. This man is the first eucharist on the Samaritan border: a cleansed sinner on his face before the One who cleansed him.

Now he was a Samaritan. The punchline, delayed for effect, and it detonates the whole story. Samaritans and Jews despised each other; to a Jew a Samaritan was a heretic and a half-breed. The nine were going to the priests in Jerusalem, to the temple, to the sacrifices, to the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. He could not have gone with them; the priest would not have received him. So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place that was open. And it turned out to be the right one.

The story Luke keeps telling. The despised outsider is the only one who returns. The Samaritan on the Jericho road was the one who showed mercy (10:33); Samaria is the first stop beyond Jerusalem in Luke’s second volume (Acts 1:8; 8:5). The man with the fewest religious options in the group is the one who ends up on his face in the right place.

Why do outsiders so often respond better than insiders? Because they have nothing to lean on. The insider has his upbringing, his church, his knowledge, his standing, and it is very easy to receive a blessing and file it with the rest. The outsider knows he deserves nothing, so a gift astonishes him. That is why Jesus could say that tax collectors and prostitutes were going into the kingdom ahead of the religious (Matthew 21:31). The cure for a church full of insiders is not to become less churchly but to remember what we were, and where we would be if he had not turned to us first.

In a sentence. One of the ten, seeing he was healed, came back praising God loudly and fell at Jesus’ feet to thank him, and he was a Samaritan.

On a Tuesday. Take one specific mercy from the last year, an answered prayer, a recovery, a reconciliation, a provision, and turn back with it. Not a general thank you, but this one, named, out loud, to Christ. Say it on your knees if you can. Then tell one other person what he did.

For worship. Have you come back to thank Jesus for what he has done? Do it now. And look at whom he receives at his feet: the foreigner, the heretic, the one with the wrong temple and the wrong family. He receives him without a word of reproach, because the One who was born in Bethlehem came for exactly such men. In Christ there is neither Jew nor Samaritan; there is only a crowd of cleansed lepers at his feet, and the song never ends: worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:12).
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other; shared misery had joined these ten.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus answered, 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus answered: were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?

Then Jesus answered, Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Three questions, and they are not rhetorical flourishes. Something is being registered. Jesus notices. He notices our gratitude, and our ingratitude. And it is one of the few places in the Gospels where Jesus expresses something like disappointment about how he has been treated. He does not do it for himself elsewhere: not when a village will not house him, not when a Pharisee omits the courtesies at dinner. Here he asks where the other nine are.

Every one of them got what he asked for. The arithmetic is stated plainly: were not ten cleansed? The healing was not withheld from the ungrateful, and it is important to see that. All ten were cleansed before any of them had shown what he would do about it. God is kind to the ungrateful and the evil (6:35).

Where are the nine? Down the road, doing what they were told, about to be certified, perhaps rushing home to their families. Not villains. Ordinary. Which is what makes the question searching rather than merely sad. Nobody in that group made a decision to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight on to the next necessary thing, and the next, and by evening it was a fortnight ago. But they did not return.

Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner? Foreigner, allogenēs, is a startling word to find here, because it names exactly what the stone barrier in the temple court was built to keep out: it is the word on the temple inscription that warned foreigners not to pass into the inner courts on pain of death. That inscription has been dug up. Jesus names this man by the very status the sign held against him. The only man in the story who was fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to God, to Jesus, the true temple, to worship.

A matter of direction. Jesus does not say the nine failed to feel grateful. He says nobody was found to return. The failure named is a matter of direction: nine men were walking one way and one man turned round. Which is worth having, because gratitude is usually discussed as a feeling and this passage will not let it be one. All ten were presumably delighted. Only one of them changed course.

The lesson. Ingratitude is common. Many receive God’s blessings and never return to thank him. Paul traces the whole downward slide of humanity to exactly this: although they knew God, they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him (Romans 1:21). Ingratitude is not a small fault of manners. It is the root of idolatry, the refusal to let the Giver be seen behind the gift. And outsiders often respond better than insiders.

Does God really mind if I forget to say thank you? Yes, because he loves you, not because he is touchy. A father minds when his child takes his gifts and never looks up at him, not because he needs the thanks but because the child is missing the father. Thanksgiving is how a gift becomes a meeting. And the habit protects us: the heart that gives thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18) is guarded against both pride, which thinks it earned its blessings, and despair, which forgets it ever had any.

In a sentence. Jesus asked where the other nine were, and why only this foreigner had returned to give praise to God.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of God’s blessings this week, and thank him for each one. Begin with the ones you take most for granted: breath, sight, the people at your table, the Bible on your shelf, the church that will gather on Sunday. Then add the great one, the cleansing of your soul. You will find that the list does not end, and that the act of writing it turns you round.

For worship. Were not ten cleansed? Christ is the God who heals the ungrateful too. He sends rain on the just and the unjust, feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies, and keeps giving to a world that rarely looks up. And he remembers every face. He counted to ten on that road, and he knows exactly who came back. The God who notices the nine who left notices the one who returns, and is glad.

parallels.desc: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.

Rise and go your way. He is not kept there. He is sent home like the others, on to the priests and to his new life, with a certificate no priest issued and a body no priest examined.

Your faith has made you well. Start with the difficulty, because it is a real one. All ten were cleansed; Luke says so twice (vv. 14, 17). So what is left for this man to get? The answer is in the verb. For made you well the ESV margin gives has saved you: sesōken. Luke has used the phrase twice before, and both times about something more than a body: to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48). The word can mean physical healing and it can mean salvation, and Luke’s usage here is deliberate. Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved.

Physical blessing is not the same as salvation. The nine received physical healing; the Samaritan received more: salvation, a restored relationship with God through Christ. The difference was faith that returned in worship. And it sharpens the question about the nine. They received a genuine, enormous, undeserved gift from Jesus of Nazareth and went home with it. There is no suggestion anywhere that it was taken back. But a man can receive a great deal from Christ and never arrive at Christ, and this passage is the clearest picture of it in the Gospels.

What his faith consisted of. It is worth noticing, because it was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men. He obeyed an instruction that made no sense. And when he saw what had happened, he stopped, turned round, and went back to the one who did it. That is all of it. There is no impressive spiritual content anywhere in this man’s story. Saving faith is not a great achievement of the soul. It is an empty hand that comes back to Christ.

Can a person enjoy God’s blessings and still not be saved? Sadly, yes, and this is one of the most searching truths in the Gospels. Answered prayers, a healed body, a happy family, even religious experiences: all of these can be received from God by people who never bow to his Son (Matthew 7:22–23). The test is not what you have received but whether you have come back to the Giver. If you are uncertain, do what the Samaritan did. Do not wait to feel worthy. Turn round, go to Jesus, fall at his feet and thank him, and hear him say what he said to that man.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Samaritan to rise and go, for his faith had saved him.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly: of all that God has given you, how much has actually brought you back to Jesus himself? Pick the blessing you are most grateful for and let it lead you to the Person, not just the gift. Spend ten minutes this week not asking for anything, only adoring him.

For worship. The greatest gift is not healing but salvation. If you have it, thank him with your whole life. Nine men were given their lives back and walked on. One came back to say thank you, and was told his faith had saved him, which means that turning round is a good deal more than a courtesy, and that the distance between the nine and the one is not gratitude. It is where each of them ended up standing. And the One at whose feet he stood would soon be nailed up outside the city, unclean and cast out, so that a Samaritan leper could rise and go his way, saved for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — The Kingdom and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees ask when the kingdom is coming, and the question assumes a datable event that can be worked out by people currently standing outside it.

“Not coming in ways that can be observed” rules out surveillance for signs, which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

“The kingdom of God is in the midst of you” has probably been misquoted more than any other line in Luke. The King James renders it “within you,” and that has been carried off to mean that the kingdom is an inner glow native to every human heart. The ESV margin allows “within you,” so the translation is not dishonest — what settles it is who he is addressing. He is answering the Pharisees, who have been lying in wait to catch him (11:53-54). He is not telling them the kingdom is glowing inside their hearts; he is telling them it is standing in the room.

Turning to the disciples, he warns of days when they will long to see one ordinary day of his presence and will not. The longing is named and allowed — and then he deals with the danger it creates, because a man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will travel to where somebody says he has. The lightning settles it: nobody has ever been told where the lightning was.

Then, dropped into the middle of it, verse 25: first he must suffer. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man about to be spat at and hung up outside a city wall, and he will be that first.

The Noah and Lot examples select, out of everything available, the ordinary: eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting and building. Not one is a sin. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tension between “the kingdom of God is in the midst of you” and “the days of the Son of Man are coming” is the foundation of the New Testament's already-not-yet. The kingdom has come in the person and work of Jesus; it has not yet come in fullness. Believers live in the overlap.

“Revealed” at v.30 means unveiled — which says something precise about what is coming. It is not that the Son of Man will arrive from elsewhere like a visitor; he will be uncovered, and the implication is that he is not absent now, merely unseen. The day does not change where he is; it changes what can be seen.

On the missing verse 36: your Bible may go straight from 35 to 37, or may print a verse 36 reading “two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left.” Nothing has been removed. The line is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of Luke and appears to have been copied in from Matthew 24:40 by a scribe who borrowed Matthew's “two men in the field” to bring Luke's two examples up to three. Modern versions drop it to a footnote and keep the old numbering rather than renumber the chapter, which is why the gap is visible — honest bookkeeping, with the workings printed rather than tidied away.

On “taken”: popular retellings fix the picture so that the taken are caught up to safety. But two paragraphs earlier the examples were Noah and Lot, and in both it was the judgement that did the taking — the flood swept them all away, and the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was left alive outside it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Remember Lot's wife” is one of the shortest verses in Luke, and it does not need the story told. She had been brought out by the hand — the angels seized Lot and his wife and set them outside the city, “the LORD being merciful to him” (Gen. 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger. And she looked back.

Her looking back was not curiosity. Everything she had was in that town — her house, her daughters, the whole shape of a life. She was out of Sodom and Sodom was not out of her.

Which is worth taking personally rather than eschatologically. There is a kind of Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward; he is not looking forward. And Jesus does not say “remember Sodom.” He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

“Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it” is a statement about how reality is constructed rather than a piece of moral advice, and everybody knows a version of it. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the man who protects his reputation above everything is left with nothing but a reputation. The grip is what loses the thing.

And the disciples' “Where, Lord?” is our instinct exactly. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want is the geography. He answers with a proverb that tells them nothing useful about location, and the uselessness is the sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, 'The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them: the kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, look, here it is! or there! For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.

Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come. The question assumes a great deal, and the assumptions are what Jesus answers. It assumes the kingdom is a future event with a date; that the date can be worked out; and that the people asking are not currently in any relation to it except waiting. The Pharisees expected a visible, political kingdom, with signs announcing it: the defeat of Rome and the restoration of Israel.

The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed. The word is paratērēsis, and it belonged to two vocabularies at once: the physician’s, for watching a patient for symptoms, and the astronomer’s, for observing the heavens. It means surveillance for signs. You cannot calculate it by signs. He is not saying the kingdom is invisible. He is saying it is not the kind of thing you detect by scanning for indicators, which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

Nor will they say, Look, here it is, or there. It is not a place you can point to on a map. The pointing is the giveaway. Anything requiring a guide is not it.

For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you. This verse deserves a note, because in its older wording it has probably been misquoted more than any other line in Luke. The King James renders it the kingdom of God is within you, and that sentence has been carried off to mean something Jesus never said: that the kingdom is an inner spiritual glow native to every human heart, that God’s reign is simply the divinity we already carry, that religion is a journey inward needing no king outside us at all. The Greek word entos can indeed mean within, and the ESV notes that alternative, so the translation is not dishonest. What settles it is who Jesus is talking to. He is answering the Pharisees, the men who have been lying in wait to catch him (11:53–54), in whose hearts the kingdom certainly was not. Most scholars therefore prefer in the midst of you, or among you. He is not telling them that the kingdom of God is glowing quietly inside their hearts. He is telling them it is standing in the room.

The King in front of them. The kingdom is present in the person of Jesus, the King, standing among them, and in his works: if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (11:20). They are looking for signs, and the King is in front of them. It is a far sharper word than the one that usually replaces it. The kingdom is not a feeling located by looking inward. It is a Person they have so far managed to look straight past, and they are asking him when he is going to arrive. And the kingdom is also present wherever God reigns in human hearts, because the King has taken his throne there by his Spirit.

Is the kingdom present or still to come? Both. It is in the midst of you because the King is standing among them. Yet in the very next verses Jesus speaks of the day of the Son of Man still to come (vv. 22–37). The kingdom has begun in Christ and his people, and it will be revealed in its fullness at his return. Theologians call this the already and the not yet. We live between the two comings: the King has come, won his decisive victory at the cross and the empty tomb, and reigns now from heaven; and he will come again to finish what he began, raising the dead, judging the world and making all things new.

So is the kingdom of God a political programme? No. Christians should be good citizens, work for justice and love their neighbours in public life, and the gospel has transformed whole societies. But the kingdom is not built by votes, revolutions or legislation, and it is never identical with any nation, party or movement. My kingdom is not of this world, Jesus told Pilate (John 18:36). It comes where Christ is preached and believed, and it will come in fullness only when he returns. A church that confuses the kingdom with its politics will be disappointed by every election and will lose its message in the process.

In a sentence. Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom would come, Jesus said it would not come with observable signs, for the kingdom of God was already in their midst.

On a Tuesday. Don’t look for the kingdom in political movements or spectacular signs. It is found where Jesus reigns. Look for it this week in the places it actually grows: a heart bowing to Christ in your small group, a quarrel ended in your family, a neighbour asking about your faith, the word preached on Sunday. And ask whether it is growing in you: where does Jesus reign in your life, and where are you still waiting for him to arrive?

For worship. The kingdom of God has a face. The rule of heaven, longed for by prophets and kings, did not come as a weather pattern or a political event but as a Man who could be touched, who ate with sinners and wept at graves. They were looking past him for signs, and he was the sign. And he is still among his people, wherever two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). The King is here, and his kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the kingdom of God is within you”; “in the midst of you” fits the setting — the King stood among them.

parallels.desc: the kingdom has come upon you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the disciples, 'The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to the disciples: the days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, look, there! or, look, here! Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.

And he said to the disciples. The audience changes. What follows is not for the Pharisees but for the men who will still be here when he is not. The kingdom is present (v. 21), but its fullness is still to come, at the return of the Son of Man.

The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. A tender sentence and a bleak one. After Jesus’ departure, in times of persecution and waiting, his disciples will long for his presence, or for his return, and it will not come as soon as they wish. And Luke’s readers were living in it. There will be a time when they will want one day back. Not only the second coming; one of the days, an ordinary day of walking about with him. And they will not get it. He says so plainly rather than promising them a substitute.

For the believer who feels far from God. This is worth registering by anyone who has known a season of unusual nearness to God and now does not. The longing is not a fault, and it is not answered here with a technique for recovering the feeling. It is named, and allowed, and then he moves straight to what to do about the danger it creates. The Lord is not absent because you cannot feel him. He has promised to be with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20), and the longing itself is a sign of his Spirit in you. Keep to the means he has given, his word, prayer, the Supper, the fellowship of his people, and wait for him. He will come.

Do not go out or follow them. They will say to you, Look, there! or Look, here! Do not go out after them, because that is what longing makes a person vulnerable to. A man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will get in a car and drive to where somebody says he has. These are false claims about Christ’s return, or false messiahs (21:8; Matthew 24:23–26). The instruction is blunt and it is doubled: do not go out, and do not follow. Not weigh the claim carefully. Do not go. Don’t be deceived.

For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. And there is the test, and it is beautifully simple. Nobody has ever been told where the lightning was. Nobody has ever had to travel to see it, or been let in on it by a teacher with special knowledge, or missed it because he was facing the wrong way. It fills the sky from one horizon to the other, and everybody in the country sees it at once. His return will be sudden, visible to all, unmistakable, universal. No one will need to tell you where he is. Every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7).

Anything that has to be pointed out is not it. Every claim that Christ has returned quietly, or secretly, or to a particular place, or to a particular group, is refuted by one sentence about weather, and the refutation was issued in advance, by him, precisely so that his people would not spend the centuries chasing rumours. The cults that announced his invisible return in a particular year, the self-proclaimed messiahs in compounds and on screens, the date-setters with their charts: all of them are answered here.

What about people who predict the date of his return? Do not follow them. Jesus said that concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only (Matthew 24:36), and that it is not for us to know times or seasons (Acts 1:7). Every date ever set has passed, and many who trusted them were shipwrecked in faith. The right posture is not calculation but readiness: live every day so that you would be glad to see him come that evening. Watchfulness is a way of life, not a reading of the news.

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples that they would long for his coming and should not be deceived by claims that he had appeared somewhere, for his coming would be as visible as lightning across the sky.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be taken in by anyone who claims to know where or when Christ will return. When he comes, everyone will know. If you find yourself drawn to the latest prophecy video or end-times chart, close it and open the Gospel instead. And if you are in a dry season, longing for one day back, tell him so. He hears, and he is not far.

For worship. He will not come quietly. The One who was born unnoticed in a stable, who came into Jerusalem on a donkey, who was carried out of the city to die between thieves, will come the second time in a glory that splits the sky from east to west. There will be no need to tell anyone. Every knee will bow, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). The lightning is his, and so is the day.

verseByVerse.quote: But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

But first. Before the glory, the cross. One sentence, dropped into the middle of a discourse about the end, and it changes the shape of everything around it. Before the lightning, before the day, before any of it: this.

He must suffer many things. Must is dei, the divine necessity, God’s plan, that has run through this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). The suffering is not a setback on the way to the glory. It is on the schedule (9:22). The way to glory goes through suffering: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (24:26).

And be rejected by this generation. Note who does the rejecting. Not Rome, though Rome will drive the nails. This generation: the people of his own time, the people he is standing among, including the Pharisees he was answering five verses ago and the crowds who have followed him from Galilee. Luke has recorded the prediction twice already (9:22; 9:44), and both times the disciples failed to take it in. Here it arrives without warning, in the middle of a different subject, and moves on without elaboration.

Why put it here at all? Because the disciples have just been told about a day of unmistakable, sky-filling glory, and a man can build a very attractive religion out of that alone. Jesus will not let the second coming be detached from the first. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man who is going to be spat at, flogged, and hung up outside a city wall, and he is going to be that first. Any expectation of his return that skips the cross has the wrong person coming back.

A word about taste. There is a word here for the way Christians think about the future generally. It is possible to be genuinely thrilled by prophecy and entirely unmoved by Calvary: to find the trumpet stirring and the crown of thorns merely sad. That is a taste, not a theology, and this verse is placed exactly where it is to correct it.

Why must he suffer? Why could God not simply forgive? Because God is just as well as merciful, and sin is a real debt against a holy God. He cannot pretend it does not matter without ceasing to be good. At the cross the Son bore the penalty our sins deserved, so that God could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). He was pierced for our transgressions, and the punishment that brought us peace was laid on him (Isaiah 53:5). The must is not a cruel necessity imposed on an unwilling Son; it is the plan of the Father and the Son together, freely embraced in love for us.

In a sentence. But before his glorious coming, the Son of Man must first suffer and be rejected by his generation.

On a Tuesday. If you think more often about the end of the world than about the cross, turn it round this week. Read one of the passion narratives slowly, Luke 22 and 23, and ask the Spirit to move you by the suffering as much as by the glory. And if you are suffering for Christ, remember the order: first the cross, then the crown, for him and for you.

For worship. The one who will come like lightning first came to suffer for you. Worship him for both. The road to the day of the Son of Man runs through Jerusalem, and he was walking it while he said this. He knew the scourge and the spittle and the nails, and he did not slow his pace. The Lord of glory chose rejection by his own generation so that a rejected generation could be received by his Father. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, and worthy is the Lamb who is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.

Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. The first of two examples, from Genesis 6–7, and Jesus treats Noah and the flood as real history. The thing to notice is what he does not say about Noah’s generation. Genesis is not gentle about them: the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and every intention of the thoughts of their hearts was only evil continually (Genesis 6:5, 11). Jesus could have made that the point. He does not.

They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage. Four activities, and not one of them is a sin. Eating, drinking, arranging weddings. Ordinary life. Nothing wrong with any of these things. This is ordinary life in a village, and it is the picture of a world that is not doing anything unusual at all. The problem was that they were absorbed in them, and ignored God’s warnings through Noah, a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). Life went on as normal, as if judgment would never come.

The warning people do not expect. And that is the warning, quite different from the one people expect. The danger is not that the world will become monstrous and everybody will see it coming. The danger is that it will look exactly like this. Supermarkets open, weddings booked, the school run, the football on Saturday.

Until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. Two clauses, and the order is the point. The ark had been under construction for years, in public, by a man who preached while he built. Everybody knew. And then one day Noah went inside, and the LORD shut him in (Genesis 7:16), and the day he went in was the day it came. Sudden. Too late. The door was shut. Note the phrase destroyed them all. Luke does not soften it, and he will use the identical phrase about Sodom two verses later.

They were not short of warning. Noah’s generation had a preacher, and a boat going up in their own neighbourhood, and decades to think about it, and they went on eating and drinking, not because they had considered the evidence and rejected it, but because life was going on and it always had. That is the exact position of the modern world with respect to the return of Christ, and it is why the illustration is here. Nobody in Noah’s village decided to drown. They simply had a normal week, and then another one, until the last one.

Is it wrong, then, to enjoy ordinary life? No. Eating, drinking and marriage are good gifts of God, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), and Jesus himself came eating and drinking (7:34). The Christian does not escape ordinary life; he lives it before God, with an eye on the door. The difference between Noah and his neighbours was not that Noah stopped eating. It was that he believed God’s word and built accordingly. Enjoy your meals, your marriage, your work; just do not let them become a reason to ignore the one who gave them, or the day he has appointed.

In a sentence. The Son of Man’s coming will be like the flood in Noah’s day, when people carried on with ordinary life until the flood suddenly destroyed them.

On a Tuesday. Are you so absorbed in ordinary life that you have forgotten Christ is coming? Look at your week: is there one hour in it given to getting ready for that day, in prayer, in the word, in speaking to someone who is not in the ark? And if you know someone who is not, do what Noah did: keep building and keep preaching.

For worship. There is an ark, and its door is still open. God, who shut Noah in with his own hand, has provided a refuge from the wrath to come in his Son: Christ, the ark of our salvation, who took the waters of judgment over his own head so that those inside him would rise above them. The patience of God that waited while the ark was being built (1 Peter 3:20) is waiting still, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Come in.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot (they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulphur rained from heaven and destroyed them all), so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.

Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot. The second example, from Genesis 19, and Jesus adds it because the first could be dismissed. Noah’s flood was a unique event at the dawn of history; Sodom was a town, in living memory of the patriarchs, in country his hearers could have walked to.

They were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. Six activities this time, and again not one is wicked. Business as usual: commerce, agriculture, construction. The busyness of a prosperous city, with no thought of God. Two of them, planting and building, are the most hopeful things a person can do, because both are investments in a future. And that is what makes the list so bleak. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards and laying foundations.

What Jesus selects. Sodom was notorious for its wickedness, and Genesis records it: the city is a byword for a particular sin, and elsewhere Scripture names its pride, excess of food, prosperous ease and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49). Jesus mentions none of it. What he selects, out of everything available, is the property market and the planting season. He emphasises its ordinariness.

But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom. The same structure as Noah, and the same hinge: the rescue of the righteous man and the arrival of the judgment are the same day. The moment the righteous were removed, judgment fell. Genesis is explicit that the angels could do nothing until Lot was out: escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there (Genesis 19:22).

Fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all. Sudden and complete. The phrase is the same as for the flood, and the point is the same: no one in the city expected it that morning, and no one escaped who had not left.

So will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. And there is the application, and one word in it is worth stopping at. Revealed, apokalyptetai: unveiled. It is not that the Son of Man will arrive from somewhere else, like a visitor. He will be uncovered, and the implication is that he is not absent now, merely unseen. He is present now, hidden, reigning at the Father’s right hand; then he will be revealed in glory. The day does not change where he is. It changes what can be seen. And the reason the world will be caught eating and drinking is not that a stranger turned up unannounced, but that the one who was there all along stopped being invisible. And judgment will be as sudden and complete.

Will Christians be taken out of the world before the judgment, like Lot? Lot was rescued on the very day the fire fell, not years before it; Noah entered the ark on the day the flood came. That is the pattern of Christ’s return: one public day on which his people are gathered to him and the world is judged (2 Thessalonians 1:6–10). Believers are not promised escape from all suffering before that day; Jesus told them to expect tribulation (John 16:33), and they have always had it. But they are promised that not one of them will be lost when the day comes. The same Lord who took Lot by the hand will not forget a single one of his own.

In a sentence. The Son of Man’s coming will be like the destruction of Sodom, which fell suddenly on people busy with everyday business the day Lot left.

On a Tuesday. Business and building are not wrong. But don’t let them make you forget the day of the Lord. When you sign a contract, plant a garden or plan an extension this year, add a sentence to the plan: if the Lord wills (James 4:15). It changes nothing in the paperwork and everything in the heart.

For worship. He is here, unseen. The Son of Man is not an absent landlord who will one day return to an empty estate; he is present now, upholding the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), watching over his people in every city of the plain. And one day the veil will be drawn back, and we will see him as he is. For those who love him, that day is not a terror but the unveiling of the One we have trusted without seeing, and we will be like him (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife.

On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away. The picture is exact for a Palestinian village. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair; people slept, dried grain and sat in the cool up there. So a man on the roof can get to the street without entering the house at all, which is what makes the instruction possible and what makes it cost something. He must leave with what he is wearing.

Not this, but the end. Similar words in 21:21 and Mark 13:15–16 concern the flight from Jerusalem before its fall in AD 70. Here the point is different: on the day of Christ’s coming, there will be no time to save possessions, and no point. The pattern is the same; the event is the last. Attachment to things will be fatal.

And likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Not even for the cloak he took off at the end of the row. The urgency is total, and the thing being forbidden is not sin but retrieval. Don’t look back to what you are leaving: no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (9:62).

Remember Lot’s wife. Three words, and the shortest verse in Luke. He does not tell the story; he does not need to. She had been brought out by the hand: the angels seized Lot and his wife and daughters and set them outside the city, the LORD being merciful to him (Genesis 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger. And she looked back to Sodom as she fled, and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26).

What her looking back was. It sounds like a small thing punished enormously. It was not curiosity. Everything she had was in that town: her house, her possessions, the whole shape of a life. To turn round was to have her heart still in it. She was out of Sodom and Sodom was not out of her. She was saved from the city, but lost because she could not let go of it. A warning to those who follow Jesus but whose hearts are attached to this world.

Half-turned. Which is the warning to a disciple, and it is worth taking personally rather than only as prophecy. There is a kind of Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the relationship broken off and still visited in the imagination, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward. He is not looking forward. And Jesus does not say remember Sodom. He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

Can a true believer be lost like Lot’s wife? No one whom Christ has truly saved will finally perish (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6); God keeps his own to the end. But that promise does not make warnings like this unnecessary. They are among the very means by which God keeps us, waking us up when our hearts drift back. Lot’s wife shows what an outward rescue without an inward change looks like: someone who left Sodom with her feet but not with her heart. If this verse troubles you, that is a mercy. Turn your face to Christ, and keep it there.

In a sentence. On that day, no one should go back for possessions or turn back, but remember Lot’s wife, who looked back and was destroyed.

On a Tuesday. What are you tempted to look back to? Remember Lot’s wife, and fix your heart on Christ. Name it: the habit, the relationship, the ambition, the city you left. Then tell God what it is, ask him to break its pull, and do one thing this week that puts it further behind you.

For worship. There was One who set his face like flint and never looked back. He left the glory of heaven and did not return for it until his work was done; he left his mother, his home, his trade, and walked into Jerusalem without a backward glance. For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). Because he did not look back, we can look forward, and the hand that pulled Lot out of Sodom is the hand that holds ours now.
verseByVerse.note: Lot’s wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.

Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it. He has said this before, after Peter’s confession (9:24), and it is worth noticing where it is repeated. There it followed the first passion prediction and the call to take up a cross daily. Here it follows a man on a roof being told to leave his possessions and a woman being remembered for looking back. The principle is the same; the application has moved from a lifetime to a moment. Lot’s wife tried to hold on to her old life, and lost everything. Those who cling to this world will lose it, and their souls.

Seeks to preserve. To secure as one’s own possession. And that is the link with the two verses before it. The man on the roof who goes back for his goods is trying to preserve; so is Lot’s wife. What they are trying to keep hold of is not merely property. It is the arrangement: the shape of a life that has been built and is now being taken away. And the sentence says the attempt is self-defeating in the strictest sense. Not that it is wrong, or greedy, or short-sighted. That it does not work. The grip is what loses the thing.

How reality is built. This is a statement about how reality is constructed, not a piece of moral advice, and it applies well outside the day of the Son of Man. Everybody knows a version of it. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the person who cannot bear to be disliked ends up with no friendships of any weight; the man who protects his reputation above everything is eventually left with nothing but a reputation.

But whoever loses his life will keep it. Keep is zōogonēsei: preserve alive, literally give it life, make it alive. Those who give up their lives to Christ gain eternal life. So the alternative is not a heroic sacrifice with nothing on the other side. It is the only route by which anything survives at all. The man who lets go is not choosing loss over gain; he is choosing the one grip that does not crush what it holds.

What does losing my life look like for an ordinary Christian? Rarely martyrdom, though for some it is, and has been for millions. More often it is the daily surrender of what you would hold on to for yourself. It is choosing obedience when it costs you a promotion; telling the truth when it costs you a friend; giving away money you could have kept; opening your home when you would rather close the door; being known as a Christian at work. And at the end, it is dying in faith, letting go of everything into the hands of Christ. None of it is wasted. All of it is kept alive in him.

In a sentence. Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will preserve it.

On a Tuesday. What are you clinging to? Let go of it for Christ, and you will find true life. Open your hand, literally if it helps, in prayer, and name what is in it: your plans, your children, your health, your money, your reputation. Give each one back to him. You will find he does not take them away so much as hold them better than you could.

For worship. The whole of it is settled by who said it. He was on the road to Jerusalem, on his way to demonstrate both halves there. He did not seek to preserve his life. He laid it down, and no one took it from him; and on the third day he took it up again (John 10:18). He lost his life, and kept it, and now holds the keys of death. Everyone who loses his life for his sake will find it, because it is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), and nothing can touch it there.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.' And they said to him, 'Where, Lord?' He said to them, 'Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left. And they said to him: where, Lord? He said to them: where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.

I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. The coming of the Son of Man will divide people who were closest: a household at night, husband and wife, or two companions. A sudden separation, with no warning. Outwardly the same, inwardly different.

There will be two women grinding together. Two women working side by side at a small hand mill, sitting opposite each other, grinding grain, a daily task done at dawn. Night and day: whenever he comes. The nearest possible proximity in both cases, and identical circumstances. And one of each pair is taken.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36: Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left. A reader comparing Bibles will find the verse number missing in one and present in another. Nothing has been removed. The line is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of Luke and appears to have been copied in from the parallel in Matthew 24:40 by a scribe who wanted to bring Luke’s two examples up to three. Modern versions drop it to a footnote and keep the old numbering rather than renumber the whole chapter, which is why the gap is visible. It is a small piece of honest bookkeeping, and it is worth knowing that the workings are printed rather than tidied away. No teaching of Scripture depends on it.

Taken and left. A word on taken, because most readers arrive at this verse already certain which they would rather be. Popular retellings have fixed the picture: the taken are caught up to safety and the left are abandoned to disaster. That reading belongs to a particular scheme of the end times held sincerely by many Christians, and nothing here needs to be unkind about it. But notice what Jesus has just been talking about. Two paragraphs earlier the examples were Noah and Lot, and in both, it was the judgment that did the taking. The flood swept them all away (Matthew 24:39); the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was spared outside it.

And they said to him, Where, Lord? Where will they be taken? And there it is: the disciples’ instinct, and ours. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want to know is the geography.

Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. A proverb. As certainly as vultures gather around a dead body, judgment will fall wherever there is spiritual death. He answers with a proverb that tells them nothing useful about location, and the uselessness is the sermon. The question where is pointless; judgment will come where it is deserved, as visibly as vultures circling. When the thing is ready, the gathering happens, and nobody has to be told where. Those taken are taken to judgment, to the vultures.

Where Christians differ: one taken, one left. Dispensationalists teach that one will be taken describes the secret rapture of believers before a tribulation, as in the novels and films about being left behind, reading it alongside the catching up of believers to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17) and his promise to take them to himself (John 14:3). Verdict: in context, the comparisons with Noah and Lot (vv. 26–30) show that those taken are taken in judgment, like those swept away by the flood, while those left are like Noah and Lot, spared. And the vultures (v. 37) show that being taken means death. There is no secret rapture here. Christ’s coming will be visible like lightning (v. 24), and will bring both the gathering of his people and judgment, at one public return. The point is the same on any reading: be ready, because no one will be warned in advance.

Then what do I make of the catching up in 1 Thessalonians 4? It is real and glorious, but it is not secret. Paul describes it with a cry of command, the voice of an archangel and the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16), about as loud an event as can be imagined. At Christ’s one return the dead in Christ rise, the living believers are caught up to meet him in the air, and they come with him as he arrives in judgment, as citizens go out to meet a king and escort him into the city. Believers are not left behind, and they are not taken away years early. They are gathered to their Lord on the day the whole world sees him.

Will my believing spouse or parent save me on that day? No. Two in one bed, two at one mill: the nearest relationships on earth, and one is taken and the other left. You can sleep beside a believer, work beside one, be raised by one, and still be lost. Faith is personal: each must come to Christ himself. That is not a cold truth but an urgent invitation. If you have been sheltering under someone else’s faith, come to Christ for yourself today. And if you love someone who is not yet his, pray, and speak, while it is still today.

In a sentence. At the Son of Man’s coming, people side by side will be separated, one taken and one left, and judgment will come wherever it is due, as surely as vultures gather over a corpse.

On a Tuesday. Being near a believer will not save you. Make sure you are ready for his coming yourself. The question is not which group you would prefer. It is whether the day, arriving in the middle of an ordinary night, would find you facing the right direction. Tonight, before you sleep, tell the Lord where you stand with him, and if you are not sure, ask him to receive you.

For worship. The same day that brings the vultures brings the Bridegroom. For those who are in Christ there is no fear in that night, only the voice they have been waiting for. He will send out his angels and gather his elect from the four winds (Matthew 24:31), and not one of his sheep will be missing. The Judge at whose coming the earth trembles is the Saviour who was judged in our place. So we pray, with the whole church through the ages, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! (Revelation 22:20).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36, “Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left,” and that “vultures” may also be rendered “eagles.”

If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, <sup>4</sup> and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.” <sup>5</sup> The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you. <sup>7</sup> “Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? <sup>8</sup> Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’? <sup>9</sup> Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? <sup>10</sup> So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’” <sup>11</sup> On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. <sup>12</sup> And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance <sup>13</sup> and lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” <sup>14</sup> When he saw them he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went they were cleansed. <sup>15</sup> Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; <sup>16</sup> and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Where are the nine? <sup>18</sup> Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” <sup>20</sup> Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, <sup>21</sup> nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to the disciples, “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. <sup>23</sup> And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. <sup>24</sup> For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. <sup>25</sup> But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. <sup>26</sup> Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. <sup>27</sup> They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. <sup>28</sup> Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, <sup>29</sup> but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— <sup>30</sup> so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. <sup>31</sup> On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. <sup>32</sup> Remember Lot's wife. <sup>33</sup> Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it. <sup>34</sup> I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. <sup>35</sup> There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.” <sup>37</sup> And they said to him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.”

18.title: Prayer, Humility, Children, Wealth, and Sight
18.overview:
Luke 18 is constructed around a series of contrasts: persistent widow versus unjust judge; Pharisee versus tax collector; those who would keep children from Jesus versus Jesus who receives them; a rich ruler who becomes very sad versus disciples who have left everything; a blind beggar who cries out versus those who rebuke his cry. In each pair, the unexpected person receives what they need — and the principle is always the same: those who come to God with empty hands receive; those who come convinced they already have what is required leave empty.

Luke tells us explicitly why Jesus told the opening parables. The widow-and-judge parable is told to show that “they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (v. 1). The Pharisee-and-tax-collector parable addresses “those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (v. 9). Together they define authentic prayer: persistent, humble, directed entirely toward a God who can do what we cannot.

The final section (vv. 31–43) contains the third passion prediction — which the disciples cannot understand — and closes with a blind beggar, a man who cannot see physically but sees Jesus with perfect spiritual clarity: “Son of David, have mercy on me.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us the point before the story starts — something he rarely does — which suggests he was not prepared to risk it being missed. And the two halves of the purpose are the same thing from two sides: “always to pray” and “not lose heart,” where the second word means to grow weary, to give out. The alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting.

Note where it sits. The previous paragraph closed with a discourse about a day that comes without warning after a long wait. This parable is what to do in the meantime.

The judge is described comprehensively: he neither feared God nor respected man, which is the whole of the Old Testament's requirement for the office (cf. 2 Chr. 19:6-7). He is not corrupt — a bribe would be a lever, and a lever would work. He simply does not care, and Luke says so twice, once as narrator and once in the man's own mouth, so nobody can call it a hostile characterisation.

The widow is the other end of the scale. Without husband, father or male relative she had no standing in a court at all, no money for a lawyer and no influence. And the law was emphatic about her: God “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deut. 10:18), and cursed is the man who perverts it (Deut. 27:19). The one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.

What she asks for is not charity but a verdict — “give me justice” — vindicate me. And the judge's phrase for what she is doing to him is violent: she will beat him down. He is not worn down by sympathy or shamed into it. He is being hit, repeatedly, in the same place.

So justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason, by a man who cared nothing about it, because one powerless woman would not go away. Which is the setup for the argument, and the argument runs by contrast: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer is not a mechanism for overcoming divine reluctance. The unjust judge is the contrast, not the model — this is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and every term in v.7 is set against him. He had no fear of God; this is God. The widow was a stranger; these are “his elect.” She was a nuisance at a door; they “cry to him day and night,” which is the language of the Psalms and of a people in exile.

And Jesus raises the delay himself rather than pretending it is not there. The parable assumes a widow who has been coming a long time. What is denied is not the delay but its meaning: the widow's problem was that her judge did not care, and that was the only reason for her wait. Whatever the reason for yours, it is not that one — because the one you are asking chose you.

“Speedily” does not promise a quick answer. It means without dawdling — that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end. And notice what the elect are crying for: not relief but justice, the setting right of all things, which arrives in full at the coming of the Son of Man named in the very next line. Some prayers are answered in this life; every prayer of God's people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable ends with a question, and it is the reverse of the one everybody arrives with. We come asking whether God will keep faith with us; he settles that flatly and moves on. What he asks is whether he will find faith in us — and he leaves it open, which is more unsettling than any answer would have been.

The “nevertheless” is doing the work. Justice is certain; the perseverance of the people waiting for it is not. Which is exactly the danger the parable was told to address: the risk is not an unanswering God but a widow who stops coming.

So if you are still praying after eleven years and have concluded that the long silence is evidence of being ignored, read the last line again. The thing he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

And there is a word here for the man whose prayer life has quietly collapsed — who prays in a crisis but finds sustained daily prayer pointless, since God knows what he needs anyway. The purpose of persistent prayer is not to overcome divine ignorance. It is to keep the heart oriented toward the right Source, and to sustain the posture of a person who genuinely believes help is coming from outside himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said, 'In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said: in a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.

Meaning first. Luke 18 is a chapter about how people come to God, and the answer is the same every time: with nothing in their hands. A widow with no power keeps coming to a judge who does not care, and Jesus says God is nothing like him (vv. 1–8). A Pharisee lists his virtues and a tax collector begs for mercy, and only the second goes home justified (vv. 9–14). Babies who can do nothing are welcomed, and the kingdom is said to belong to such (vv. 15–17). A rich ruler who has kept the commandments goes away sad, and Jesus says salvation is impossible with man but possible with God (vv. 18–30). Then Jesus tells the Twelve for the third time that he will suffer, die and rise, and they understand nothing (vv. 31–34), while a blind beggar outside Jericho sees exactly who he is (vv. 35–43). Those who come with nothing receive everything; the one who came with much went away with nothing.

The link. Jesus has just spoken of the days before the Son of Man comes, when disciples will long for him and not see him (17:22), and of a day that will come without warning after a long wait. How should they live while waiting? By prayer. The previous paragraph closed with two people in one bed and the disciples asking where, Lord? This parable is what to do in the meantime.

And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. Luke does something here he rarely does: he tells us the point before the story starts. Usually a parable is left to do its own work; this one comes with the moral attached at the front, which suggests he was not prepared to risk it being missed. Always means persistently, continually. And the word for losing heart, enkakein, means to give up, to grow weary, to give out, to become discouraged. The two halves of the purpose are the same thing described from two sides. Which tells you that the alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting. Nobody stops praying because they have found something better to do with the time. The great danger in the long wait is to stop praying.

In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. The description is devastating and it is comprehensive. The whole of the Old Testament’s requirement for a judge is contained in two things: he must fear God, and he must have some regard for the people in front of him. In Israel, judges were to judge fairly (Deuteronomy 16:18–20), and Jehoshaphat’s charge to the judges of Judah says exactly this: consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD; let the fear of the LORD be upon you (2 Chronicles 19:6–7). This man has neither. He is a godless judge, accountable to no one, moved by nothing. And Luke says so twice, once here and once in the man’s own mouth at verse 4, so nobody can suggest it is a hostile characterisation. He is the worst judge imaginable, and that is the point of him. He is in the story to be the opposite of somebody.

What does always to pray actually mean? It cannot mean doing nothing but pray, since Jesus also worked, ate, slept and taught. It means never giving up, and living in a settled habit of turning to God. Paul says the same: pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). In practice that means fixed times, morning and evening, when you deliberately bring your needs and other people’s to God; short prayers through the day as things happen; and refusing to drop a request just because the answer is slow. It is not a feeling of constant devotion. It is a direction of the heart that keeps coming back.

In a sentence. Jesus told a parable to teach that his disciples should always pray and not give up, about a judge who neither feared God nor cared about people.

On a Tuesday. Have you given up praying for something? This parable is for you. Write down the request you have quietly stopped making, the prodigal, the illness, the marriage, the salvation of a parent, and put it back on your list this week, by name, every day.

For worship. Before Jesus tells us a single thing about the judge, he tells us that we ought to pray, and that alone is a revelation of God. The Lord of heaven wants to be asked. He has not set up a universe that runs without him and left us to cope; he has opened his door to the weak and told them to keep knocking. And the One who taught this parable practised it: he rose before dawn to pray, spent whole nights on the mountain, and prayed for his enemies from the cross. He lives for ever to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). Our prayers go up on the back of his.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying: give me justice against my adversary. For a while he refused, but afterwards he said to himself: though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.

And there was a widow in that city. The other end of the scale, and the pairing is deliberate. A widow in that world was the standard biblical shorthand for defencelessness. She had no husband to represent her, and unless a son or a brother-in-law took up her case she had little standing in a court. She had no money for a bribe and no man to speak for her. And the law singled her out for protection: God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18; Exodus 22:22–24), and cursed is the man who perverts it (Deuteronomy 27:19). The prophets return to it constantly (Isaiah 1:17, 23). So the one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.
