If it has cost you little, ask whom you could be family to this week: the student far from home, the convert disowned by his parents, the widow with no children nearby. Set an extra place at your table.

For worship. No one has ever outgiven Christ. Every disciple who has left anything for him has found it returned many times over, in brothers and sisters, homes and tables, peace and joy, and at the end, life without end. He himself left the Father’s side and the worship of angels, and he did it for the sake of the kingdom: for us. And he has not been short-changed either. He shall see his offspring; out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:10–11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–43 — Third Passion Prediction and the Blind Man at Jericho
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third and fullest of the passion predictions, and the only one that explicitly grounds the events in Scripture: “everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.” What is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan; it is a text being fulfilled, and the text was written centuries before.

Every item can be traced. Isaiah's Servant gave his back to those who strike and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6); he was despised and rejected (Isa. 53:3-5). The psalmist is mocked and surrounded (Ps. 22:7-8). And “delivered over to the Gentiles” is new: the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests.

Notice how much of the list concerns humiliation rather than pain — mocked, shamefully treated, spat on — and Luke will record every one of them happening.

Then the incomprehension, stated three times in one verse so the reader cannot soften it. Jesus has given six specific things in plain language with no parable attached, and twelve men who had been with him three years took in nothing.

And the juxtaposition that follows is deliberate and devastating. The disciples, who have eyes, cannot see what he has just told them plainly. A blind beggar outside Jericho, working from one sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right — and “Son of David” is a messianic title, the first time in this Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud.

The crowd tells him to be silent, using the same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the babies two dozen verses earlier. And the people doing it are “those who were in front” — the ones nearest to Jesus.

He cries out all the more, and the widow at the top of the chapter would have recognised him exactly.
verseByVerse.theology:
A reader with three Gospels open will stop at v.35, and the difficulty is worth facing because sceptics have made a good deal of it. Luke has the healing “as he drew near to Jericho” and then has Jesus entering the town (19:1); Matthew and Mark both have it as he was going out (Matt. 20:29; Mark 10:46). Matthew reports two blind men where the others report one, and only Mark supplies a name.

The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives a name and a father's name — “Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus” — which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask.

The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart: the ancient city standing as a ruin on its old mound, and the splendid new town Herod the Great had built to the south with his winter palace, with the road running between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. Both are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon.

What looks like three writers contradicting each other is the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there produce exactly these.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's threefold statement that the disciples understood nothing is a mercy to the reader as well as astonishing. These are the men who would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony. Nobody inventing an account of the founding apostles makes them this stupid, and nobody who had merely persuaded himself of a resurrection afterwards would write down that he had been told in advance and had not understood a word.

And there is something here for anyone who has read a passage repeatedly and got nothing from it. They heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity; it arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45).

“And Jesus stopped” is worth the whole paragraph. He is on the last stretch to Jerusalem, has just described in detail what is waiting there, and the entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for a beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

“What do you want me to do for you?” is on the face of it unnecessary — anybody could name the need. But being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. And the mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

He was not told to follow, and he followed. The first thing he does with working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the twelve, he said to them, 'See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the Twelve, he said to them: see, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spat upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.

The third passion prediction. The last and fullest of these announcements (9:22, 44), and he takes the Twelve aside to give it. What follows is not for the crowd.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. Jerusalem sits high, and pilgrims always went up to it; but the word carries more here, because Luke has had his face set that way since 9:51. This is the last stretch.

Everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. Only Luke adds this. And the framing is prophetic. Not this will happen, but everything written will be accomplished, brought to completion. Which means what is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan. It is a text being fulfilled, and the text was written centuries before. The cross is the fulfilment of Scripture: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, and much more. Jesus will explain it after his resurrection, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (24:25–27, 44–46).

For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles. To Pilate and the Roman soldiers. Handed to Rome, which is new information; the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests.

And will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. Shamefully treated, hybristhēsetai: insulted, outraged, abused. Every item can be traced. Isaiah’s Servant gave his back to those who strike and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6); he was despised and rejected, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:3–5). The psalmist is mocked, surrounded, and has his garments divided (Psalm 22:7–8, 18). And notice how much of the list is about humiliation rather than pain. Mocked, shamefully treated, spat on: three of the six items concern what will be done to his dignity, and Luke will record every one of them happening.

And after flogging him, they will kill him. Roman scourging, with whips weighted with bone and metal, then crucifixion, the death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels.

And on the third day he will rise. Always the promise of resurrection. He does not stop at the death. He has never once announced it without the rising in the same breath.

The turn in the verbs. One thing more is worth registering about the pronouns. Every verb in this list is passive or has somebody else as its subject. He will be delivered, mocked, treated shamefully, spat on, flogged, killed: things done to a man who is not doing anything. And then the last clause turns: he will rise. Active, and his own. Everything up to the grave happens to him; the thing after it is something he does.

If he knew all this, why did he go? Because he chose to. No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). He went up to Jerusalem not as a victim caught by events but as the Lamb walking to the altar, because the Father’s will and his own love were one. He knew every blow in advance and went anyway, for the joy set before him: the joy of bringing many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). The prophecy is not a fate he was trapped in; it is a promise he came to keep.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Twelve that in Jerusalem everything the prophets wrote about him would be fulfilled: he would be handed to the Gentiles, mocked, abused, spat on, flogged and killed, and rise on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Read Isaiah 53 this week, slowly, and then Luke 23, and put a mark beside every place where the one fulfils the other. Let the precision of it steady your faith: the God who kept these promises to the letter will keep every promise he has made to you.

For worship. Every detail of his suffering was foretold, and he went knowingly, for you. The spit, the mockery, the whip and the nails were written down centuries before, and he read them in the synagogue as a boy and knew they were about him. And still he set his face to go up. The Son of God walked into the darkest chapter of the prophets with his eyes open, because on the far side of it was the third day, and on the far side of the third day was us.

verseByVerse.quote: But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.

But they understood none of these things. Three statements of the same fact in one verse: they did not understand, it was hidden, they did not grasp. That is Luke making certain the reader does not soften it. Not little, not imperfectly. None. Partly because it is astonishing, and Luke knows it. Jesus has just given a list of six specific things, in plain language, with no parable attached, and twelve men who had been with him for three years took in nothing.

This saying was hidden from them. A divine passive, as at 9:45. Luke does not say who hid it, but the phrase points to God, and he will say something like it of the Emmaus pair whose eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16). God concealed its meaning until the time was right. After the resurrection, the risen Christ will open their minds to understand the Scriptures (24:45). Understanding the cross is God’s gift.

And they did not grasp what was said. It is worth asking what was actually blocking them, because it was not stupidity. These men had a settled picture of what Messiah meant, and it had no room in it for a crucifixion. The words went in and found nowhere to lodge. That is how most misunderstanding of Scripture works. Not a failure to hear the sentence, but a frame that will not accommodate it, and the frame is invisible to the person holding it.

A mercy to the reader. There is a second reason for the threefold statement. These are the men who would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony. Nobody inventing an account of the founding apostles makes them this slow. And nobody who had merely persuaded himself of a resurrection afterwards would remember, and write down, that he had been told in advance and had not understood a word. They did not see it coming, which means that when they did come to believe, it was not because they had been expecting it.

The contrast. In the next scene a blind man will see. The disciples, who can see, are still blind to the cross.

Why do I read the Bible and sometimes get nothing from it? The disciples heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity. It arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45). So keep reading, and pray before you read: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Ask what frame you might be bringing that the text does not fit. Read with others, and sit under preaching. The Spirit who wrote the word is the one who gives light to it, and he delights to answer that prayer, often in a quiet moment long after the reading.

In a sentence. The disciples did not understand any of this, because its meaning was hidden from them.

On a Tuesday. Before you open your Bible this week, pray the psalmist’s prayer for opened eyes. And be patient with others who do not yet see what you see. The apostles themselves heard the gospel three times from Jesus’ own lips and understood none of it, until God opened their eyes.

For worship. If you understand the cross, it is because God opened your eyes. Thank him. You were no cleverer than the Twelve. For God, who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Every believer who has ever looked at the cross and seen love there is a miracle as great as the beggar outside Jericho.

verseByVerse.quote: As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. They told him, 'Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. They told him: Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.

As he drew near to Jericho. Jericho lay about 17 miles (27 km) by road east-north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan, the last stop before the climb to the city. And a reader with three Gospels open will stop at that first line, and the difficulty is worth facing squarely because sceptics have made a good deal of it. Luke says the healing happened as he drew near to Jericho, and then opens the next chapter with Jesus entering the town (19:1). Matthew and Mark both say it happened as he was going out of Jericho (Matthew 20:29; Mark 10:46). On top of that, Matthew reports two blind men where Mark and Luke report one, and only Mark supplies a name, Bartimaeus.

One man or two, entering or leaving? The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives not just a name but a father’s name, Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask; he had evidently become known in the church, and both Mark and Luke follow the man who mattered to the tradition, while Matthew notes there were two. The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart. The ancient city stood as a ruin on its old mound; Herod the Great had built a splendid new town to the south with his winter palace, and the road ran between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes, and Jesus may have been between them. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. Both are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon.

Independent witnesses. What looks like three writers contradicting each other is the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there, or who talked to people who were, produce exactly these. The Gospels are not identical because they are honest.

A blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. Pilgrims for Passover passed by in crowds, and were generous at festival time. For a blind beggar this road in this week was the best pitch of the year.

And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. He cannot see, so he asks, and the detail is the point of him. He has to work out from sound alone that something is happening, and he does not let it pass.

They told him, Jesus of Nazareth is passing by. The crowd’s name for him. The description is accurate and small: a place and a name, what everybody knew. And the blind man is about to say something better with less information. And he is passing by: this was his one chance. Jesus would never walk that road again.

In a sentence. Near Jericho, a blind beggar heard the crowd and was told that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.

On a Tuesday. When Jesus passes by, don’t miss the moment. It may be a sermon that lands, a friend’s invitation, a crisis that opens your heart, a verse that will not leave you alone. Do not tell yourself there will be a better time. Behold, now is the favourable time (2 Corinthians 6:2).

For worship. Jesus of Nazareth passed by, and the word is tender as well as urgent. He passes by where the beggars sit. He took the Jericho road on purpose, the road through the poor and the blind and the shouting, on his way to give his life. He is the God who passed by Moses in the cleft of the rock, proclaiming the LORD, merciful and gracious (Exodus 34:6), and in Christ that same God passes by our roadside, and stops.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 17 miles by road east-north-east of Jerusalem. Mark names the man Bartimaeus; Matthew mentions two men.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, 'Son of David, have mercy on me!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he cried out: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more: Son of David, have mercy on me!

And he cried out, Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! He was told Jesus of Nazareth. What comes back is Son of David. That is a messianic title, the promised king from David’s line (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and it is the first time in Luke’s Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud. Gabriel spoke of the throne of his father David (1:32); the genealogy runs through David; but no one in this book has looked at Jesus and said it until now. And it is a blind beggar sitting in the dust outside a town. The blind man sees what the crowd does not. And he knows what the Messiah was to do: give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1; 4:18).

The blind who see. Set that against the paragraph immediately before it. Twelve men who could see, who had been given the plainest possible account of what was about to happen, understood none of it. A man who cannot see, working from a sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right. Luke has put the two side by side and he means it to hurt.

Have mercy on me! The tax collector’s prayer again (v. 13). A beggar, with no claim, only need. Not a diagnosis and not a request for anything specific: the same plea the tax collector made in the temple twenty-five verses ago. He asks for mercy and leaves the content of it to Jesus.

And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. The same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the infants (v. 15). The crowd is doing again what the disciples had just been corrected for doing: clearing the road of people with no standing so that the important business can proceed. And notice who they are: those who were in front. The people nearest to Jesus are the ones telling this man to be quiet.

But he cried out all the more, Son of David, have mercy on me! He does not lower his voice; he raises it. Nothing about his social position, his blindness or the public rebuke is enough to make him stop, because he has worked out that this is the only chance he is going to get and there is not going to be another crowd. The persistence of the widow (vv. 1–8). She would have recognised him exactly.

What if the people around me discourage me from coming to Jesus? Do what the blind man did: cry out all the more. Sometimes it is friends who mock, family who think you have gone too far, a culture that tells you faith is foolish. Sometimes, sadly, it is people in the church who make the needy feel unwelcome. Jesus is not like the people at the front. He hears the voice they tried to silence. And if you are one of those at the front, near Jesus, make sure you are not the one standing between him and someone crying for mercy.

In a sentence. The blind man cried out to Jesus as the Son of David for mercy, and when told to be quiet, cried out all the more.

On a Tuesday. Cry to Jesus for mercy, and don’t let anyone silence you. Bring him the need you have been embarrassed to mention, and keep bringing it. And look round your church on Sunday for the person on the edge whom no one is listening to, and be the one who brings him nearer.

For worship. The blind beggar called him by his true name, and heaven agrees. Jesus is the Son of David, the King of Israel, the Lord of the everlasting throne, and he is the King who has mercy. David’s greater Son does not rule from a distance; he rules from a roadside, from a cross, from the right hand of God, and everywhere he hears the cry of the poor. The LORD opens the eyes of the blind; the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down (Psalm 146:8).
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, 'What do you want me to do for you?' He said, 'Lord, let me recover my sight.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him: what do you want me to do for you? He said: Lord, let me recover my sight.

And Jesus stopped. Three words, and they are worth the whole entry. He is on the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem. He has just told the Twelve, in detail, what is waiting for him there. There is a crowd around him, a procession moving, and a fixed appointment at the far end of it that everything in this Gospel has been travelling towards since 9:51. And he stops, because somebody is shouting. Luke does not decorate it. The entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for one blind beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

And commanded him to be brought to him. Note who is now employed on the errand. Those who tried to silence him now bring him. Mark records them saying take heart; get up, he is calling you (Mark 10:49), which must have been a considerable adjustment.

And when he came near, he asked him, What do you want me to do for you? Which is, on the face of it, an unnecessary question. The man is blind and has been begging by a roadside; anybody could name the need. So why ask? Partly because being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. Nobody in that town had put a question to him in a long time. But mostly because a request has to be made. Jesus asks him to say it. He will not heal him over his head either. The mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

Lord, let me recover my sight. And he asks. Plainly, without preamble, without qualifying it or hedging it or asking whether it is too much. Lord: he recognises Jesus’ authority. Simple, direct faith. It is worth setting that beside the ruler at verse 18, who came asking what he must do. The ruler wanted to do something; the blind man asks Jesus to do something for him. This man asks for what he needs.

If God knows what I need, why should I ask? Because he wants us to. You do not have, because you do not ask (James 4:2). Asking is not informing God; it is trusting him, and it brings our needs out of the vague background of worry into the light of his face. Jesus knew exactly what the blind man wanted and still made him say it, because the asking was part of the healing: a beggar who had always been spoken about was spoken to, and answered. So be specific in prayer. Name the thing. Your Father knows what you need before you ask him (Matthew 6:8), and he still loves to hear you say it.

In a sentence. Jesus stopped, had the man brought to him, and asked what he wanted, and he asked to see again.

On a Tuesday. Jesus asks you too: what do you want me to do for you? Tell him. Sit quietly this week, imagine the question put to you directly, and answer it honestly. You may be surprised what you say. Then say it to him, plainly, and leave it with him.

For worship. On his way to Jerusalem and the cross, he stops for one blind beggar. Nothing in heaven or on earth is more important to him than the next sinner who cries for mercy. The King of kings, with the salvation of the world on his shoulders, stood still on a dusty road and asked a beggar what he wanted. He still stops. He has never once been too busy, never once walked past, never once told a crying sinner to be quiet. Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up (Psalm 68:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.' And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: recover your sight; your faith has made you well. And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

And Jesus said to him, Recover your sight. A word of command. No touch, no clay, no procedure. One word in Greek and it is done.

Your faith has made you well. And the second half is the phrase Luke keeps for the moments that go past the body: has saved you, sesōken, the same words spoken to the sinful woman weeping at his feet (7:50), to the woman with the bleeding in the crowd (8:48), and to the Samaritan leper who came back (17:19). The verb is sōzō, and it means both healed and saved. Body and soul. Something has happened here that is more than a pair of eyes.

What his faith was. Which is worth examining, because there was not much of it and it was not sophisticated. He had heard a name, shouted a title, refused to be silenced, and asked for the obvious thing. That is the whole content. No theology, no track record, no promise about what he would do afterwards, and Jesus calls it faith and says it has saved him.

And immediately he recovered his sight. At once, completely.

And followed him. On the way to Jerusalem. He was not told to. There is no instruction here, and Jesus had told others to go home (8:39). This man simply falls in behind the procession, and everybody knows where it is going. The first thing he does with a pair of working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one to Jerusalem. The rich ruler would not follow (v. 22); the beggar does at once. He is a picture of true discipleship.

Glorifying God. As the Samaritan did (17:15). The gift turns into worship, and the worship is directed to God through the One who gave it.

And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God. His healing leads others to praise. The chapter that began with a widow being ignored ends with a whole crowd praising God, including the people who had told the man to be quiet.

The chapter’s pattern. Throughout chapter 18, those who come with nothing receive everything: the persistent widow, the tax collector, the infants, the blind beggar. The one who came with much went away with nothing.

Does Jesus still heal the blind today? He can, and God still answers prayer for the sick, sometimes wonderfully. But this healing was a sign of who Jesus is, the Messiah who opens blind eyes as Isaiah promised, and Scripture does not promise that every prayer for healing will be granted now. The gifts of miraculous healing given to the apostles confirmed their message and are not, in our judgment, the normal pattern for the church today (a cessationist view, held charitably towards brothers who see it differently), though God remains free to heal as he pleases, and we should pray for the sick in faith (James 5:14–15). The greater miracle, which he does every day, is the opening of blind hearts to see his glory. And the full healing of every believer’s body is certain, at the resurrection.

In a sentence. Jesus told the man to see, for his faith had saved him, and he saw at once and followed Jesus, praising God, and all the people praised God too.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus has opened your eyes, follow him, and let your life lead others to praise God. Tell someone this week what Christ has done for you, simply, like a man describing the day he first saw. And follow him where he is going, even when the road leads up to Jerusalem.

For worship. Here, then, is how the last stage of that journey begins. The Son of Man has set out for a city where he will be handed to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged and killed, and he has told his friends so, and they have not understood a word of it. And on the way he stops for one man nobody wanted him to hear, gives him his eyes, and gains a follower who walks the rest of that road with him. Nothing in Jerusalem was going to be turned aside. But there was time, on the way to it, for a beggar who would not stop shouting. And there is time still. Amazing grace: I once was lost, but now am found, was blind, but now I see.

18.text: <sup>1</sup> And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. <sup>2</sup> He said, “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. <sup>3</sup> And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ <sup>4</sup> For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, <sup>5</sup> yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “Hear what the unrighteous judge says. <sup>7</sup> And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” <sup>9</sup> He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: <sup>10</sup> “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. <sup>11</sup> The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. <sup>12</sup> I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’ <sup>13</sup> But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ <sup>14</sup> I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>15</sup> Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. <sup>16</sup> But Jesus called them to him, saying, “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>17</sup> Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>18</sup> And a ruler asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>19</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>20</sup> You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>21</sup> And he said, “All these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>23</sup> But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich. <sup>24</sup> Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, “How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup> For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup> Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup> But he said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” <sup>28</sup> And Peter said, “See, we have left our homes and followed you.” <sup>29</sup> And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, <sup>30</sup> who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.” <sup>31</sup> And taking the twelve, he said to them, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. <sup>32</sup> For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. <sup>33</sup> And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.” <sup>34</sup> But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said. <sup>35</sup> As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. <sup>36</sup> And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. <sup>37</sup> They told him, “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.” <sup>38</sup> And he cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>39</sup> And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, <sup>41</sup> “What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, let me recover my sight.” <sup>42</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.” <sup>43</sup> And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

19.title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the Triumphal Entry
19.overview:
Luke 19 is a chapter of arrivals. Jesus arrives at Jericho and finds Zacchaeus — a chief tax collector who has climbed a tree to see him and who will descend, transformed, to receive salvation in his house. Then Jesus tells the Parable of the Ten Minas — a kingdom parable about accountability and fruitfulness during the time of the absent king. Then Jesus arrives at Jerusalem itself, riding on a colt, welcomed by his disciples with praise, weeping over the city as he approaches it, and then cleansing the temple. The chapter is a compressed journey from private transformation (Zacchaeus) to public confrontation (the temple), with the parable providing the theological framework for understanding the entire sequence.

Zacchaeus is one of Luke's most vivid portraits of salvation. He is a chief tax collector, wealthy, despised, short of stature, and apparently desperate to see Jesus. He runs ahead and climbs a tree — an undignified act for a man of his status. Jesus's response is overwhelming: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” The word dei (must) is a divine necessity — the same word used for the Son of Man's suffering. Salvation has come to this house; the Son of Man has come to seek and to save the lost.

The Triumphal Entry (vv. 28–44) contains one of the most emotionally powerful moments in all of Luke: Jesus weeping over Jerusalem. The parade of praise, the disciples crying out about the king who comes in the name of the Lord — and then Jesus stopping on the descent and weeping, because she did not know “the things that make for peace.” This is not despair; it is the grief of the shepherd for the sheep who will not come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus was passing through Jericho — not stopping. The whole story turns on that clause, and on a man who got in the way of it.

Zacchaeus is described with three details that should make him unsympathetic. He is a chief tax collector — architelōnēs, a word that appears nowhere else in surviving Greek literature and may be Luke's own coinage. It means he held the district contract and had other collectors under him, taking a percentage of each man's takings. And Jericho was no backwater: it sat on the trade route from the east, in a plain famous for balsam and dates, at the crossing into Judea. That customs post was one of the most lucrative in the country.

He is rich, and by this point in Luke that word has weight — a rich man in torment three chapters back (16:19-31), a rich ruler grieving one chapter back (18:23-25), and a camel that will not go through a needle. The disciples had asked, reasonably, “then who can be saved?” The next rich man in this Gospel is up a tree.

And he is small in stature, which the crowd exploits. A short man can usually reach the front of a gathering; a short and thoroughly hated man in the town where he holds the tax contract will find that nobody moves.

So he runs — humiliating for a man of standing, since it meant hitching up the robe — and climbs a fig-mulberry, which is a boy's activity in full view of the street. Dignity is the first thing that goes. It nearly always is.

Then Jesus stops, looks up, and uses his name. Nothing in the story explains how he knew it. He announces rather than asks — “I must stay at your house today” — which is a mercy, because a man in Zacchaeus's position does not issue invitations and had learned not to put himself where he could be refused.

The crowd grumbles, all of them. And Zacchaeus stands and gives away half of everything and repays fourfold, and Jesus says salvation has come to the house.
verseByVerse.theology:
The episode is a case study in sovereign grace. Jesus announces the visit before any repentance has occurred; the restitution follows the encounter and is the fruit of salvation received, not the ground of it. It is the exact pattern of chapter 15 — the shepherd finds the sheep, and the sheep does not find its way home.

A crux has to be faced at v.8, because a good many modern commentators press it. Both verbs are present — “I give,” “I restore” — and a present can describe a habitual practice. On that reading Zacchaeus is not promising but defending himself: I already give half away; the grumbling is unjust.

It is possible and should be rejected, for three reasons drawn from the passage. Luke has told us the man was rich, and a chief tax collector who gave away half his income and repaid fourfold every disputed claim would not have stayed rich for a season. Jesus's reply is “today salvation has come to this house,” which is a strange thing to say to a man who has just proved he was fine all along. And the present is also the ordinary form for a promise made on the spot — I give you my word, or a man at an altar saying I take you.

The numbers are not arbitrary either. Half is far beyond anything the law required, and fourfold is the penalty for the aggravated case, a stolen sheep slaughtered or sold (Ex. 22:1); ordinary restitution was the sum plus a fifth (Lev. 6:5). He sentences himself at the highest rate on the books.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Son of Abraham” is a deliberate provocation, because it is precisely what the grumblers would have denied. A tax collector had forfeited his place in the popular reckoning, and some rabbinic rulings treated his repentance as practically impossible, since he could never trace everyone he had defrauded. Jesus hands the title back — as he did six chapters earlier to a bent woman nobody had helped in eighteen years, “a daughter of Abraham” (13:16).

And v.10 is the sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel. It answers the grumbling completely: they objected that he had gone in to a sinner's house, and he replies that this is the errand. Not a regrettable necessity, not an exception made for a promising case — the stated purpose of the coming. The verbs are the shepherd's from chapter 15: to seek, and to save.

Zacchaeus climbed a tree to get a look at somebody who had come to that town looking for him.

The story is also addressed to the crowd. A man in a congregation has a reputation; everyone knows what he was before — the financial impropriety, the trail of damage. He is welcomed into membership and watched carefully, with a persistent sense that his inclusion is provisional. Those who murmur at Christ's table fellowship with notorious sinners share the theology of the men in this street. He does not.

verseByVerse.quote: He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.

The climax of the journey. Zacchaeus is the last person Jesus meets before Jerusalem in Luke’s travel narrative, and his story sums up the whole Gospel (v. 10). Only Luke records it.

He entered Jericho. Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich town on a major trade route between Judea and the east, with balsam groves and palm plantations. A key customs post.

A man named Zacchaeus. A Hebrew name, from Zakkai, meaning “pure” or “righteous”. An irony: he was anything but.

He was a chief tax collector. The only time this title (architelōnēs) appears in Greek literature. He was in charge of others who collected tolls and taxes, probably buying the right to collect them from Rome and employing others. He took a cut of everything.

And was rich. From cheating his own people. He would be hated as a traitor and a thief. After the rich ruler who went away sad (18:23), and after Jesus said it is impossible for the rich to enter the kingdom, except with God (18:24–27), here is a rich man. What God can do.

In a sentence. As Jesus passed through Jericho, there was a rich man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond the reach of Christ’s grace: not the richest, not the most hated.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich town on a major trade route. A chief tax collector oversaw other collectors and profited from all of them.

parallels.desc: how difficult for those who have wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.

He was seeking to see who Jesus was. More than curiosity. Perhaps he had heard that Jesus was a friend of tax collectors (7:34), and that one of the Twelve was a former tax collector (5:27).

But on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. The crowd would not let him through. Who would make way for the town’s most hated man?

So he ran on ahead. A rich, important man running, in public: undignified (15:20).

And climbed up into a sycamore tree. The sycamore here is the sycamore-fig, a tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb. A ridiculous sight: a rich official up a tree like a boy. He was willing to look foolish to see Jesus.

In a sentence. Zacchaeus wanted to see Jesus, but was too short to see over the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree on Jesus’ route.

On a Tuesday. Are you willing to look foolish to see Jesus? Don’t let pride or the crowd keep you from him.
verseByVerse.note: The sycamore here is the sycamore-fig, a tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.' So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him: Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today. So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.

When Jesus came to the place, he looked up. Zacchaeus was seeking Jesus, but Jesus was seeking him (v. 10). Jesus stops at exactly that tree.

And said to him, Zacchaeus. He knows his name. No one had told him. Jesus knows his sheep by name (John 10:3).

Hurry and come down. Urgency.

For I must stay at your house today. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, the same word used of the cross (9:22). This meeting is part of God’s plan. “Today”: Luke’s word for the present moment of salvation (2:11; 4:21; 23:43). Of all the houses in Jericho, Jesus chooses the house of the most notorious sinner. He invites himself. To stay in someone’s house was a public sign of friendship and acceptance.

So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. “Received” (hypedexato): welcomed as a guest. “Joyfully”: the joy of the found (15:5–7). The rich ruler went away sad; Zacchaeus receives Jesus with joy.

In a sentence. When Jesus reached the tree, he looked up, called Zacchaeus by name, and told him to come down at once because he must stay at his house today, and Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed him with joy.

For worship. Jesus knows your name and wants to come to your house today. Welcome him with joy.

parallels.desc: I will come in to him and eat with him

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they all grumbled, 'He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.' And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they saw it, they all grumbled: he has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner. And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.

They all grumbled. “All”: not only the Pharisees (15:2), but the whole crowd, perhaps even the disciples. The same word as Israel in the wilderness.

He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner. By staying with him, Jesus was associating himself with his sin, and would be ceremonially defiled.

And Zacchaeus stood. A formal act, perhaps at the meal, a public declaration.

Behold, Lord. Zacchaeus calls Jesus “Lord”.

The half of my goods I give to the poor. The present tense: I am giving, from now on. Spontaneous, not commanded. The rich ruler could not give anything; Zacchaeus gives half, unasked. This is the camel going through the eye of the needle (18:25–27). Grace transforms his attitude to money at once.

And if I have defrauded anyone of anything. “If”: he knows he has. “Defrauded” (esykophantēsa): extorted by false accusation (3:14).

I restore it fourfold. The law required a thief to repay a stolen sheep fourfold (Exodus 22:1). For fraud, the law required only the amount plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7). Zacchaeus goes far beyond what the law required. With half his goods given away, and fourfold restitution from the rest, he would be left with little. True repentance shows itself in restitution: putting right what you can.

What it does not mean. Not that his giving earned salvation. Salvation came to his house when Jesus came (v. 9). His giving was the fruit, not the root. Grace came first; generosity followed.

In a sentence. When the crowd grumbled that Jesus had gone to a sinner’s house, Zacchaeus stood and declared he would give half his wealth to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had cheated.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you need to put right with someone you have wronged? True repentance makes restitution.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a thief to repay a stolen sheep fourfold; for ordinary wrongs, the amount plus a fifth.

parallels.desc: restore it in full and add a fifth

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said to him: today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.

Today salvation has come to this house. “Today” again. Salvation came when Jesus came. Salvation is not a thing but a person: Jesus himself (2:30). “This house”: Zacchaeus and his household.

Since he also is a son of Abraham. The crowd had excluded him as a sinner, no true Israelite. Jesus restores him: he is a son of Abraham, by birth and now by faith, sharing Abraham’s faith (3:8; 13:16; Galatians 3:7).

For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Key verse. The purpose of Jesus’ whole mission, in one sentence. An echo of Ezekiel 34:16: I will seek the lost. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son (chapter 15), and now Zacchaeus. Jesus came to seek: he takes the initiative. And to save: he does the saving. And the lost: not the righteous, but those who know they are lost (5:32). This is the answer to the grumbling. This verse is often seen as the key to Luke’s whole Gospel.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that salvation had come to Zacchaeus’ house that day, for he too was a son of Abraham, and the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.

For worship. Jesus came to seek and to save you. Praise him for finding you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–27 — The Parable of the Ten Minas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us exactly why the parable is given, and there are two reasons: they were near Jerusalem, and they supposed the kingdom was about to appear immediately. Seventeen miles from the city, at Passover, behind a man who raises the dead — every expectation they had was about to be fulfilled, and they were sure of it.

So everything in the parable is arranged to insert a delay where they expected a coronation: a departure, a long absence, an accounting on the return. And the shape is strange as a picture of the Messiah and exactly right — the King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem but in a far country, and comes back. Which is precisely what Luke's second volume describes (Acts 1:9-11).

Ten servants, ten minas — one each. Worth registering, because Matthew's cousin-parable of the talents distributes different amounts according to ability (Matt. 25:15). Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity; where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did. And a mina was about three months' wages — modest, and that is the point.

The subplot of the rebel citizens is borrowed from living memory. In 4 BC Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed, and a delegation of fifty Jews followed to argue against it (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). They failed; he came back with power and dealt with them. Jericho of all towns would have felt it — Archelaus rebuilt it and had a palace there.

The first two servants are rewarded proportionately and without comparison. The third produces the mina intact, wrapped in a handkerchief, and explains that he was afraid — and his accusation is turned against him. If the master really were what he says, the sensible course would have been the bank.

And the parable ends with the enemies. It is the hardest sentence in Luke.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable teaches two related truths. The kingdom has a “not yet”: the King goes away and returns, and faithful servants must live faithfully in the in-between. And stewardship in the in-between is not optional maintenance — “engage in business” is a commercial verb, and it is not “look after this.”

“Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little” is worth weighing for the disproportion. The master calls the mina — everything the servant had for the whole absence — a trifle, and gives ten cities in return. The exchange rate is absurd, and meant to be.

And notice what the reward is: more responsibility, on an enormously larger scale. Not rest, and not a payment. Which says something about heaven that cuts against the popular picture, since Scripture's images run the other way — “his servants will worship him… they will reign forever and ever” (Rev. 22:3-5).

“To everyone who has, more will be given” is not a celebration of the rich getting richer. It is a description of how entrusted things behave: capacity grows by use and atrophies without it. And note the last clause carefully — “from the one who has not.” The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master's reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for a whole absence is not a possession but an absence dressed up as one.

A reader with Matthew open should also know this is not the parable of the talents, though the two are cousins. Matthew's setting asks what you did with what you were given. Luke's, told on the road up to Jerusalem, asks that and one thing more — whether you wanted the King at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The third servant's fear is not reverence, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey — he was too frightened to act, which is a different thing entirely, and he had been calling it caution for the whole of the absence.

And his accusation is untrue, as the parable has already shown. This is a master who handed money to ten men with no supervision and no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. The servant constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about.

The word “wicked” lands where a reader might not expect it. He has not stolen the money or wasted it or run off with it. He is called wicked for laying it away in a cloth — and there is a category of failure here that comfortable religion rarely counts as sin at all. Nothing bad was done; that is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is condemned. A life that has carefully avoided doing anything wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

Verse 27 should not be hurried past. Two things keep it in place. These are words spoken by a character inside a parable, borrowed wholesale from a tyrant's homecoming, and not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task is to trade. And the horror of the image is the point rather than an embarrassment — Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway, and the tears of vv. 41-44 are fourteen verses off. A judgement described in terms this stark, by a man crying about it, is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

verseByVerse.quote: As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore, 'A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore: a nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.

Because he was near to Jerusalem. About 17 miles (27 km). The end of the journey.

And because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. They expected Jesus to arrive in Jerusalem and set up the kingdom at once, overthrowing Rome. Luke tells us why the parable was told: to correct this expectation. The kingdom will come fully only after a period of absence.

A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. Local rulers went to Rome to have their kingdoms confirmed. This had happened in recent memory: when Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus went to Rome to be confirmed as king of Judea, and a Jewish delegation of fifty followed him to oppose it (Josephus). Archelaus returned, with a lesser title, and took revenge on his opponents. Archelaus had built a palace at Jericho. Jesus’ hearers would know the story.

The meaning. Jesus is the nobleman. He is about to go away, to the Father, through death, resurrection and ascension, to receive the kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14), and then he will return.

In a sentence. Because the crowds expected the kingdom to appear at once, Jesus told a parable of a nobleman who went to a distant country to be made king, and then return.

On a Tuesday. Christ has gone to receive his kingdom, and he will return. Live in the meantime as his faithful servant.
verseByVerse.note: Local rulers went to Rome to have their kingdoms confirmed. Herod’s son Archelaus did so in 4 BC, and a Jewish delegation went after him to oppose it.

parallels.desc: will you at this time restore the kingdom?

verseByVerse.quote: Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them: engage in business until I come.

Ten of his servants. His slaves, trusted to manage his affairs.

He gave them ten minas. One each. The ESV notes that a mina was about three months’ wages for a labourer (100 denarii). Not a huge amount for a nobleman: a test of faithfulness in small things (16:10). This differs from the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30), where the amounts were enormous and differed for each servant. Here everyone receives the same. Perhaps it pictures what all disciples equally receive: the gospel, the opportunity to serve.

Engage in business until I come. Trade with it, invest it, put it to work. The task of the disciple in the time between Christ’s going and coming: not waiting idly, but working.

In a sentence. The nobleman gave ten servants a mina each, telling them to put it to work until he returned.

On a Tuesday. What has Christ entrusted to you? Put it to work for him until he comes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a mina was about three months’ wages for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying: we do not want this man to reign over us. When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.

But his citizens hated him. As the Jews sent a delegation against Archelaus.

We do not want this man to reign over us. A picture of those who reject Christ’s rule: the Jewish leaders who are about to reject him in Jerusalem (John 19:15: we have no king but Caesar), and all who refuse his reign.

When he returned, having received the kingdom. Christ’s return in glory, as King.

That he might know what they had gained. The judgement: an accounting (2 Corinthians 5:10; Romans 14:12).

In a sentence. His citizens hated him and sent a delegation saying they did not want him as king, but he returned as king and called his servants to account for what they had gained.

On a Tuesday. Do you want Christ to reign over you, in every area of your life?

parallels.desc: we have no king but Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first came before him, saying: Lord, your mina has made ten minas more. And he said to him: well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.

Your mina has made ten minas more. A thousand percent return. Notice: “your mina”. He does not take credit; it was the master’s money that produced it.

Well done, good servant! The master’s praise. The greatest reward: to hear Christ say “well done” (Matthew 25:21).

Because you have been faithful in a very little. A mina was little to a king.

You shall have authority over ten cities. The reward is out of all proportion: from a mina to ten cities. And the reward for faithful service is greater responsibility. In the kingdom, faithful believers will share in Christ’s reign (22:29–30; 2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 2:26; 3:21).

In a sentence. The first servant had made ten minas from one, and the king praised him and gave him authority over ten cities.

For worship. Long to hear Christ say to you: well done, good servant.

verseByVerse.quote: And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the second came, saying: Lord, your mina has made five minas. And he said to him: and you are to be over five cities.

Your mina has made five minas. Less than the first, but still faithful.

And you are to be over five cities. Reward in proportion to faithfulness. There are degrees of reward in the kingdom (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). Notice: no “well done” is recorded, though the reward is generous.

In a sentence. The second servant had made five minas, and was given five cities.

On a Tuesday. God rewards faithfulness according to what you have done with what you have been given. Be faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then another came, saying: Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.

Then another came. Literally “the other”, the third of the ten Jesus describes, representing the unfaithful.

Here is your mina. Nothing gained, nothing lost.

Which I kept laid away in a handkerchief. A handkerchief was not a safe place for money; burying it was the recognised safe method. He did not even take proper care of it. Laziness.

For I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. “Severe” (austēros): harsh, strict, exacting. He had a false view of his master, and it paralysed him.

You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow. He accuses his master of being a hard, grasping man who profits from others’ work. An insult, and an excuse. His fear was really unbelief, and his view of his master a slander.

In a sentence. The third servant returned the mina he had wrapped in a cloth, saying he was afraid because his master was a harsh man who took what was not his.

On a Tuesday. A false view of God leads to fear and paralysis. God is not harsh; he is generous. Serve him without fear.
verseByVerse.note: A handkerchief was not a safe place for money; burying it was safer.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to him: I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?

I will condemn you with your own words. His own excuse condemns him.

You wicked servant! Not just lazy, but wicked. Doing nothing with what God gives is sin.

You knew that I was a severe man? The master does not accept the description, but argues on its terms. If you really believed that, you should have done something.

Why then did you not put my money in the bank. The very least he could have done. “Bank” (trapezan): a moneychanger’s table. It would have earned interest with no effort or risk.

The point. The unfaithful servant did nothing. Not because he was afraid of failure, but because he did not care about his master’s interests. He represents those who receive God’s gifts and do nothing with them, perhaps outwardly religious but not truly serving Christ.

In a sentence. The king condemned the servant by his own words, asking why, if he thought his master so demanding, he had not even put the money in the bank to earn interest.

On a Tuesday. Doing nothing with God’s gifts is not neutral. What small step could you take today to use what he has given you?

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to those who stood by: take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas. And they said to him: Lord, he has ten minas! I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

Take the mina from him. He loses even what he had.

And give it to the one who has the ten minas. The faithful receive more.

Lord, he has ten minas! The bystanders object: it seems unfair.

To everyone who has, more will be given. The principle of 8:18. Those who use what God gives receive more; those who neglect it lose it. This is true of spiritual gifts, opportunities, and understanding of God’s word.

But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. The unfaithful servant had only what he had not used, and he loses it. He had nothing of his own.

In a sentence. The king ordered the mina taken and given to the servant with ten, because those who have will be given more, and those who have nothing will lose even what they have.

On a Tuesday. Use it or lose it. Put God’s gifts to work, and he will entrust you with more.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.

These enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them. The citizens of v. 14. Not the unfaithful servant, but open rebels.

Bring them here and slaughter them before me. A shocking end. Archelaus did execute his opponents. The picture is of final judgement on those who reject Christ’s kingship. It points first to the destruction of Jerusalem (vv. 41–44), and ultimately to the last judgement (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9).

Three groups. The faithful servants (rewarded), the unfaithful servant (loses everything), and the enemies (destroyed). Christ’s return will bring reward and judgement.

In a sentence. The king ordered his enemies, who had refused his reign, to be brought and executed before him.

On a Tuesday. Rejecting Christ’s reign is not a neutral position. Bow to the King now.

parallels.desc: kiss the Son, lest he be angry

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Triumphal Entry and Jesus Weeping over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He goes on ahead, leading — and “going up” is exact: Jericho lies 800 feet below sea level, Jerusalem 2,500 above, so the seventeen miles climb over three thousand feet through desert.

The Mount of Olives is not incidental scenery. Zechariah had said the LORD's feet would stand on it (Zech. 14:4), and from that ridge a king approaching Jerusalem first sees the city laid out below.

The instructions about the colt are startlingly specific, and Luke will not settle whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge. What it establishes is that nothing about the next hour is improvised. And “on which no one has ever yet sat” is not about comfort: an animal never worked was the requirement for sacred use — the cart that carried the ark (1 Sam. 6:7), the red heifer (Num. 19:2).

He has walked everywhere for three years. On the one occasion he rides, he sends for a specific animal, and the animal is the prophecy: “humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zech. 9:9). A king entering a capital rode a horse, and a horse was the animal of war.

The cloaks on the road are a coronation gesture, not enthusiasm — when Jehu was proclaimed king the officers put their garments under him on the steps and blew the trumpet (2 Kgs. 9:13). And a cloak was a poor man's blanket and often his most valuable possession, so protected in law that a creditor could not keep one overnight (Ex. 22:26-27).

Luke alone specifies who is shouting: “the whole multitude of his disciples.” And the reason is backward-looking — “for all the mighty works that they had seen.”

Then, at the point on the descent where the whole city comes into view at once, he weeps aloud.
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' shout alters Psalm 118:26. The psalm reads “blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD” — the greeting pilgrims received at the festivals. They insert one word: “blessed is the King who comes.” That is not a liturgical greeting any more but a public claim, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem — which is exactly why the Pharisees object. And it echoes what Jesus said at 13:35: they would not see him again until they said it.

“Peace in heaven and glory in the highest” closes a circle Luke opened in chapter 2. The angels sang “glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (2:14); the disciples sing it back with the terms reversed. Which is exact, and not sentimental. There will be no peace on earth this week — there will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution. What is settled in heaven is another matter, and it is being accomplished by the very week that is about to look like total defeat.

“If these were silent, the very stones would cry out” has roots in Habakkuk, where the stone cries out from the wall against injustice (Hab. 2:11) — stones as witnesses that cannot be silenced. And there is a bitter appropriateness in the choice: he is looking at magnificent stonework, and within four verses will say not one of those stones will be left on another.

The prophecy of vv.43-44 was fulfilled with precision. In AD 70 Titus built a wall of circumvallation right round the city — some four and a half miles, thrown up in three days — to stop anyone getting out or supplies getting in. Josephus, who was there, describes it. The temple was burned and then dismantled, and the great platform stones were levered off the walls into the street below, where they are still lying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's verb for the weeping is not the quiet one. Greek has two words: one for silent tears, used of Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), and this one — eklausen, to wail aloud, the word used of the mourners at Jairus's house (8:52) and of Peter after the cock crowed (22:62). So the sound coming from the middle of that procession is a man sobbing audibly, and the singing does not appear to have stopped.

And the sentence he speaks breaks off unfinished in Greek — an exclamation that starts and does not complete, exactly as a sentence does when the person speaking cannot finish it. “Even you” is emphatic and heartbreaking: of all the cities on earth, this one did not know the things that make for peace.

A pastor preaching this every Palm Sunday finds it tempting to stop at the shouting. The passage insists on including the tears. Palm Sunday is not unambiguously triumphant; it is triumphant and heartbroken at once.

“Visitation” is episkopē — God coming to see about his people, the word Zechariah used in the Gospel's first chapter: “he has visited and redeemed his people” (1:68). The visitation happened. That is what makes the sentence unbearable. And the word cuts both ways, because a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue: the same coming that saves those who know it for what it is condemns those who do not — not by a change in God, but because there is nothing else left when the visit has been made and refused.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying, 'Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying: go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, why are you untying it? you shall say this: the Lord has need of it.

He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. Leading, resolute (9:51; Mark 10:32). The climb from Jericho to Jerusalem rises about 3,500 feet (1,000 m).

Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet. Villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. The Mount of Olives was associated with the coming of the Lord (Zechariah 14:4).

You will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. An animal used for a sacred purpose had to be one that had never been put to ordinary use (Numbers 19:2; 1 Samuel 6:7). Jesus knows it will be there, by foreknowledge or arrangement. He is in control.

The Lord has need of it. “The Lord” (ho kyrios): its owner, and the Lord of all.

In a sentence. Jesus went on ahead toward Jerusalem, and near the Mount of Olives sent two disciples to bring an unridden colt, telling them to say the Lord needed it.

On a Tuesday. The Lord has need of what you have. Hold it ready for him.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, 'Why are you untying the colt?' And they said, 'The Lord has need of it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them: why are you untying the colt? And they said: the Lord has need of it.

And found it just as he had told them. Jesus’ word comes true exactly (22:13).

Its owners said to them. Only Luke says “owners” (kyrioi, literally “lords”). A play on words: the owners (lords) ask, and the answer is, the Lord needs it. The greater Lord.

And they said, The Lord has need of it. And that was enough.

In a sentence. The disciples found the colt as Jesus said, and when its owners asked why they were untying it, they answered that the Lord needed it.

On a Tuesday. Trust Christ’s word in small things, and you will learn to trust it in great things.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.

They set Jesus on it. The King mounts. A deliberate fulfilment of Zechariah 9:9: Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. A king of peace, not a warrior on a horse. Solomon rode David’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33–40).

They spread their cloaks on the road. Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king (2 Kings 9:13). Luke does not mention palm branches.

In a sentence. They brought the colt, put their cloaks on it and set Jesus on it, and as he rode, people spread their cloaks on the road before him.

For worship. The humble King comes riding on a donkey. Lay down your cloak before him: give him your honour.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was drawing near, already on the way down the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen.

On the way down the Mount of Olives. The road from the Mount of Olives descends into the Kidron Valley, with a magnificent view of Jerusalem and the temple across the valley.

The whole multitude of his disciples. Not just the Twelve, but the many followers who had come with him from Galilee. Luke says “disciples”, not the crowd.

Began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice. Joy and praise, as at his birth (2:13–14, 20).

For all the mighty works that they had seen. The healings, exorcisms, the raising of the dead, the blind man at Jericho.

In a sentence. As Jesus came down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of his disciples began to praise God loudly for all the mighty works they had seen.

For worship. Praise God loudly today for the mighty works you have seen him do.
verseByVerse.note: The road from the Mount of Olives descends into the Kidron Valley, with the city and temple in full view.
