verseByVerse.quote: saying, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saying: blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!

Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Psalm 118:26, the pilgrim psalm sung at Passover. Luke adds “the King”, making the messianic meaning explicit. The parable of the nobleman (vv. 11–27) has prepared for this: the King is coming, and some will reject him.

Peace in heaven and glory in the highest! An echo of the angels’ song at his birth: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace (2:14). The angels sang of peace on earth; the disciples sing of peace in heaven. Peace on earth is about to be rejected (v. 42). Only Luke omits “Hosanna”, a Hebrew word his Gentile readers might not understand.

In a sentence. They praised Jesus as the blessed King who comes in the name of the Lord, and proclaimed peace in heaven and glory in the highest.

For worship. Sing to the King who comes in the name of the Lord. He is your King.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
glory in the highest, peace on earth

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, rebuke your disciples.' He answered, 'I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him: Teacher, rebuke your disciples. He answered: I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.

Teacher, rebuke your disciples. They object to Jesus being called King. It sounded like blasphemy, and political danger, with Roman soldiers watching.

If these were silent, the very stones would cry out. The praise is so right, so necessary, that if people did not give it, creation itself would. The time has come; the King must be acknowledged. And perhaps a hint of judgement: Habakkuk 2:11 speaks of stones crying out against injustice. The stones of Jerusalem, about to be thrown down (v. 44), would testify.

In a sentence. When some Pharisees told Jesus to silence his disciples, he said that if they were silent, the stones would cry out.

For worship. If the stones would praise him, how can you be silent? Praise him.

parallels.desc: the stone will cry out from the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, 'Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying: would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.

And saw the city. From the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem spread out before him, the temple gleaming.

He wept over it. Only Luke records this. “Wept” (eklausen): wept aloud, sobbed. In the middle of the triumphal procession, with the crowds singing, the King weeps. Not for himself, though he knew he was going to his death, but for the city that would reject him. As he lamented in 13:34. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11).

Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! “Peace” (eirēnē), a play on the name Jerusalem, which was popularly understood as “city of peace”. The things that make for peace: Jesus himself, the King of peace, and the peace with God he brings. “On this day”: the day of God’s visitation. Now, at last, the King has come.

But now they are hidden from your eyes. Judicial blindness: because they had rejected the light, it was now hidden from them (8:10; John 12:37–40; Romans 11:7–10).

In a sentence. When Jesus saw Jerusalem, he wept over it, lamenting that it had not recognised on that day the things that would bring it peace, and now they were hidden from it.

For worship. Jesus wept over those who rejected him. Weep for those you know who are rejecting him, and pray for them.

parallels.desc: that I might weep day and night

verseByVerse.quote: For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.

The days will come upon you. A prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem.

When your enemies will set up a barricade around you. The Romans besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, building a siege wall around the city to starve it out. Josephus describes it: the Roman general Titus had a wall built around the entire city, nearly five miles (8 km) long, in three days, so no one could escape.

And surround you and hem you in on every side. The siege lasted about five months. Famine killed vast numbers.

And tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. “Tear you down” (edaphiousin): dash to the ground (Psalm 137:9; Hosea 10:14). The city was destroyed, and huge numbers killed or enslaved.

They will not leave one stone upon another in you. As Jesus said of the temple (21:6). Fulfilled precisely.

Because you did not know the time of your visitation. “Visitation” (episkopēs): God’s coming, to save (1:68, 78; 7:16). God visited his people in Jesus, and they did not recognise him. The judgement was the consequence of rejecting the Messiah.

In a sentence. Jesus foretold that Jerusalem’s enemies would besiege it, destroy it and its people, and leave no stone on another, because it had not recognised the time of God’s coming.

On a Tuesday. Don’t miss the time of God’s visitation. If he is calling you, respond today.
verseByVerse.note: The Romans besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, building a siege wall round it, and destroyed the city and temple. A “visitation” is God coming in mercy or judgment.

parallels.desc: I will encircle you with towers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–48 — The Cleansing of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's account is the briefest of the four — one clause for the action, no overturned tables, no whip of cords. He is not interested in the drama. He gives the words.

The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles, the great outer platform, and it was not in itself illegitimate: pilgrims from a distance needed sacrificial animals, and needed foreign coinage changed into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax. Somebody had to provide both. What had happened was that the provision had taken over the place — and the place it had taken over was the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

The two quotations are not equally weighted. The first is Isaiah 56:7, and the full verse matters: “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it.

The second is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah's temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety — “the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD” — while cheating and oppressing outside it. It ended by announcing that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh, which was to destroy it. So Jesus, two verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

And note the exact charge. Not “you have made it a market.” A den of robbers is not where robbery happens; it is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards.

Then he stays. Having cleared the court he takes up residence in it, teaching daily — which is the behaviour of an owner, not a protester.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cleansing is a prophetic act, not a reform. Jesus is not trying to improve the temple's efficiency; he is enacting in symbol what he has just prophesied in words. The combination of texts is deliberate: Isaiah 56:7 describes the eschatological temple as a house of prayer for all nations, and Jeremiah 7:11 the corrupt pre-exilic temple. You were called to be one; you have become the other.

“A den of robbers” names a use religion has never stopped being put to — a system that people use to feel secure while their lives are indefensible. That is what Jeremiah's hearers were doing with the first temple, and it is the charge here.

The closing two verses describe the strangest week in history in a single sentence. The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him — not because he is hiding but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds who will not leave. Luke's phrase is worth having: the people were “hanging on his words,” suspended from him.

What finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly, away from the people (22:6). Which settles something about how this ends. The authorities did not overpower him, and Luke says so plainly.
verseByVerse.examples:
A church becomes known primarily for its events, its café, its networking and its programmes — all good things in themselves, which have gradually crowded out sustained corporate prayer. The cleansing is not a template for expelling coffee shops from church lobbies; it is a question every community of faith must ask about its primary purpose and what has displaced it.

And the specific displacement here is worth naming, because it was not frivolous. Everything in that court served the sacrificial system. The animals were for worship; the money-changing existed so that the temple tax could be paid in the right coin. This was religion crowding out prayer, not entertainment crowding out religion — which is much harder to see from the inside and a great deal more common.

It also matters where it happened. Of all the spaces on that platform, the trade had colonised the only one open to Gentiles — so the practical effect of a thoroughly religious arrangement was that the people furthest from God found the door blocked by the machinery of worship.

That is a question worth putting to any congregation. Not whether the activity is legitimate, but whether a stranger walking in could find room to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them, 'It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them: it is written, my house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.

And he entered the temple. The King comes to his temple. Malachi 3:1: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.

And began to drive out those who sold. Luke tells it briefly (Mark 11:15–17). The traders in the Court of the Gentiles, selling animals for sacrifice and changing money, under the control of the high priests.

My house shall be a house of prayer. Isaiah 56:7. “My house”: the temple belongs to God, and Jesus claims it.

But you have made it a den of robbers. Jeremiah 7:11, from Jeremiah’s sermon predicting the first temple’s destruction. A den is where robbers hide. The leaders used the temple as a safe haven while robbing the people. And judgement would follow, as in Jeremiah’s day.

In a sentence. Jesus entered the temple and drove out the traders, quoting Scripture: God’s house is a house of prayer, but they had made it a den of robbers.

For worship. The church is God’s house of prayer. Make it a place of true prayer, not commerce or show.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

And he was teaching daily in the temple. Every day of his last week (21:37–38). The cleansed temple becomes a place of teaching. Jesus took over the temple courts.

The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people. The leaders: priests, experts in the law, and the leading laymen, the elders. The three groups of the Sanhedrin.

Were seeking to destroy him. The plot (6:11; 11:53–54) now becomes determined.

But they did not find anything they could do. They could not arrest him publicly.

For all the people were hanging on his words. “Hanging on” (exekremato): literally “hung upon” him, listening intently, spellbound. The people protected him, for now. Within days they would be shouting “Crucify him”.

In a sentence. Jesus taught in the temple every day, and the leaders wanted to destroy him but could find no way, because all the people hung on his every word.

On a Tuesday. Hang on Jesus’ words today. Read them as if your life depended on them, because it does.

19.text: <sup>1</sup> He entered Jericho and was passing through. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich. <sup>3</sup> And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. <sup>4</sup> So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way. <sup>5</sup> And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” <sup>6</sup> So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. <sup>7</sup> And when they saw it, they all grumbled, “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.” <sup>8</sup> And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. <sup>10</sup> For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” <sup>11</sup> As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. <sup>12</sup> He said therefore, “A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. <sup>13</sup> Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’ <sup>14</sup> But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ <sup>15</sup> When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business. <sup>16</sup> The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ <sup>17</sup> And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ <sup>18</sup> And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’ <sup>20</sup> Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; <sup>21</sup> for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ <sup>22</sup> He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? <sup>23</sup> Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’ <sup>24</sup> And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ <sup>25</sup> And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ <sup>26</sup> ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>27</sup> But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’” <sup>28</sup> And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. <sup>29</sup> When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, <sup>30</sup> saying, “Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. <sup>31</sup> If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’” <sup>32</sup> So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. <sup>33</sup> And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” <sup>34</sup> And they said, “The Lord has need of it.” <sup>35</sup> And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. <sup>36</sup> And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road. <sup>37</sup> As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, <sup>38</sup> saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” <sup>39</sup> And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” <sup>40</sup> He answered, “I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” <sup>41</sup> And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. <sup>43</sup> For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side <sup>44</sup> and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” <sup>45</sup> And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, <sup>46</sup> saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>47</sup> And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, <sup>48</sup> but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

20.title: Authority, Parables, and Traps in the Temple
20.overview:
Luke 20 records a sustained series of confrontations between Jesus and the religious authorities in the temple precincts during what we call Holy Week. Three major challenges are mounted: the question of authority (by what right does Jesus act?), the parable of the wicked tenants (Jesus's own counter-attack in story form), and a series of trick questions — the tribute to Caesar, the Sadducees' resurrection riddle, and the question about David's son. Each challenge is designed to trap Jesus; each is turned back on its questioners.

The chapter is a masterclass in Jesus's handling of religious and political hostility. He does not evade, capitulate, or compromise. He answers each question in a way that exposes the questioner's bad faith, defends the truth, and advances his own mission. The parable of the wicked tenants is the most sustained theological statement: it is a compressed history of Israel's relationship with God, a prophecy of Jesus's rejection and death, and an announcement of the judgment that will fall on those who reject the cornerstone.

The chapter closes with Jesus warning about the scribes — those who love the long robes and the best seats and the deferential greetings, who devour widows' houses and for a pretence make long prayers. The contrast with the genuine piety of the widow in 21:1–4 is deliberate and damning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chief priests, scribes and elders — between them, the Sanhedrin — approach Jesus while he is teaching in the temple and ask by what authority he does “these things.” The phrase is left unspecified and everyone knows what it means: he had ridden in as a king a few days earlier and then cleared the traders out of the temple court, and stayed.

The question is not unreasonable in itself. The temple was under their jurisdiction, and a man who takes public action in a place you are responsible for can properly be asked who authorised it. But the trap is well made and both jaws are shut: claim human authority and they can produce the records showing he has none; claim divine authority and they have a charge of blasphemy.

And notice the presumption underneath it. Nobody enquires whether the temple needed cleansing, or whether the trade had displaced the prayer it existed to serve. The question is entirely about credentials — which is the standard refuge of an institution that does not want to discuss the substance.

Jesus answers with a question, which was normal rabbinic practice and is not evasion. It is precision, because the two questions are the same question: John's ministry raised the identical issue, and they had never answered it. And the connection runs deeper — John had pointed at Jesus, so if John's baptism was from heaven, the man John pointed at needs no further credentials.

Which makes this more generous than a debating manoeuvre. He is giving a hostile delegation a genuine route to the truth that does not require them to capitulate in public.

They will not take it, and the reason is stated out loud by themselves. Luke lets us hear the huddle, and there is no question about truth in it anywhere — only about consequences. So they answer that they do not know, which is a lie, and Jesus declines to tell them what they have just refused to work out.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus's authority is not an administrative question but the central question of the Gospels. By what right does he cleanse the temple, teach, heal, forgive sins? The answer they are trying to avoid is divine right — the right of the Son sent by the Father.

Their counter-question strategy is itself an answer: those who cannot acknowledge John's prophetic authority cannot acknowledge the one John announced. Unwillingness to face the truth is not an epistemic failure but a moral one.

And the principle behind the refusal in v.8 runs right through Scripture. God does not supply further light to people who have refused what they already have — “to the one who has, more will be given” (8:18), and the reverse holds. A man who will not act on what he knows is not helped by being told more.

There is also a price the council paid that is easy to miss. These are the official teachers of Israel, and they have just declared publicly, in the temple, that they cannot tell whether a major prophetic movement was from God. Whatever they saved by that answer, they paid for it with the only thing their office was for. A man who will not risk being wrong ends up unable to say anything at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The deliberation in vv.5-6 is worth reading twice for what is absent from it. Not one clause considers what John's baptism actually was. The entire discussion is about what happens to us if we say this or that.

The manoeuvre survives in every institution including the church, and it never feels like dishonesty from the inside. It feels like responsibility. There is always a reason why the honest answer would be unhelpful just now, and a man can spend a whole career calculating the reception of his answers without noticing that he has stopped asking whether they are true.

The test is simple and uncomfortable. When a hard question arrives, is the first thing that moves in you an assessment of what is true, or an assessment of what it will cost?

And v.8 bears on a common modern situation. There are people who genuinely do not know and are asking, and Jesus deals with them all through this Gospel with enormous patience — the centurion, the woman in the crowd, the thief on the cross. And there are people whose questions are a way of not arriving anywhere. The tell is not the difficulty of the question but what happens to the answers: whether each one is weighed, or simply replaced by the next question. Jesus can be asked anything. What he will not do is join a conversation designed never to end.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him, 'Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him: tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.

Setting. Jesus’ last days of public teaching in the temple (19:47). Chapter 20 records a series of challenges from the leaders, each meant to trap him, and each turned back on them.

Teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel. “Preaching the gospel” (euangelizomenou): Luke’s favourite word. Even in the temple, in the last week, it is good news.

The chief priests and the scribes with the elders. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council. An official delegation.

By what authority you do these things. “These things”: the triumphal entry, the clearing of the temple, the teaching. The temple was under the high priest’s authority. Who gave this Galilean the right? A trap: if he claims divine authority, they can charge him with blasphemy; if not, they can dismiss him.

In a sentence. As Jesus taught and preached the gospel in the temple, the leaders of the Sanhedrin demanded to know by what authority he acted.

On a Tuesday. The question of Jesus’ authority is the question for every life. Does he have the right to command you?
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, 'I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered them: I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?

I also will ask you a question. A recognised method of rabbinic debate. The answer to his question answers theirs.

Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? “From heaven”: from God. John’s ministry pointed to Jesus (3:16) and was confirmed at Jesus’ baptism (3:21–22). If John was from God, so was Jesus’ authority. The two stand or fall together.

In a sentence. Jesus answered with a question: was John’s baptism from God or from men?

On a Tuesday. Have you responded to the light God has already given you?

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, 'If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They discussed it with one another, saying: if we say, from heaven, he will say, why did you not believe him? But if we say, from man, all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.

And they discussed it with one another. Not “what is true?” but “what is safe?”

Why did you not believe him? They had rejected John (7:30).

All the people will stone us to death. Only Luke records this fear. Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy and false prophecy; the crowd might regard denying a true prophet as blasphemy.

For they are convinced that John was a prophet. John, a martyr, was revered.

In a sentence. They reasoned that whichever way they answered, they would be trapped: either convicted of unbelief or stoned by the people.

On a Tuesday. Don’t decide what to believe by asking what is safe. Ask what is true.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them, 'Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them: neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

They did not know where it came from. The religious authorities, whose duty was to judge true and false prophets, confessed they could not judge the greatest prophet of their age. They disqualified themselves.

Neither will I tell you. Not evasion, but refusal to cast pearls before those who had already decided (Matthew 7:6). Yet he does answer, in the parable that follows: he is the beloved Son.

In a sentence. They said they did not know, so Jesus refused to tell them the source of his authority.

On a Tuesday. “I don’t know” can be evasion. Be honest about what you know to be true about Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He turns from the delegation to the people and tells a story about the delegation, in their hearing — and they understand every word of it (v.19).

The opening line is a quotation. Isaiah's song of the vineyard ends with its own interpretation stated flatly: “for the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:1-7). So the identifications come attached, from a passage everyone knew.

And the arrangement is entirely ordinary — absentee landlords letting estates to tenant farmers for a share of the crop were common in Galilee. But hold on to what it means: the tenants did not plant the vineyard, clear the ground, or build the winepress. Everything they work with was made by somebody else and handed to them on terms.

The escalation is exact: beaten; beaten and treated shamefully, which in that culture was the worse injury; then wounded and thrown out. And running alongside it is the stranger thing — a landlord who keeps sending. Any man with sense would have gone to law after the first assault. He sends a second, and a third, because he keeps wanting the relationship rather than the redress.

The servants are the prophets, and the compression is the point: “the LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers… but they kept mocking the messengers of God” (2 Chr. 36:15-16). The men hearing this were standing in a building where some of it had happened.

Then the son — “my beloved son,” the phrase from heaven at the Jordan (3:22). And the tenants' reasoning, said aloud among themselves, is the oldest reasoning there is: remove the owner's representative and the property is ours.

Luke has the order deliberately: thrown out of the vineyard, and then killed. Jesus was crucified outside the wall (Heb. 13:12), and he is telling this three days before it happens, with the geography included.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is one of the most explicit statements in Luke of Jesus's divine sonship. The son is not one more servant in a long series but the heir — the beloved son, whose rejection is categorically different from the rejection of the prophets.

“Perhaps they will respect him” puzzles thoughtful readers and has been pressed into service to prove something it does not prove. Does it mean God did not know? Some have read it so. But the same Scripture says the Son was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has already told his disciples three times how this would end.

The perhaps is spoken from the owner's side of the story — the language of a genuine appeal, not a report of divine ignorance. Its point is not what God did not know but what the tenants cannot claim: that the offer was real, that every possible envoy was sent, that the last was the owner's own beloved son. God knew exactly what they would do and sent the Son anyway — which is not a father caught out, but a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that nobody could ever say the door was never knocked upon.

The verdict — the vineyard given to others — must not be misused. It is not a statement that God has finished with the Jewish people; Paul asks exactly that question after the resurrection and answers it flatly, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Rom. 11:1). The tenants are the leadership, and Luke names the men Jesus was looking at in verse 19.
verseByVerse.examples:
Psalm 118:22 is quoted from the same psalm the disciples had been shouting a few days earlier on the road down the Mount of Olives — verse 26 of it (19:38). He quotes their processional hymn back to the authorities, four verses earlier.

And the image is precise. The cornerstone sets the angle and the line for two walls at once, so everything built after it is squared by it; and a builder examining stones on site rejects the ones that will not do. So the picture is of professionals doing their job — men whose whole competence is judging stone, whose professional judgement was that this one would not do. Then the turn: it has become the cornerstone. Their verdict was simply overruled.

Verse 18 turns the image twice, drawing on Isaiah's stone of stumbling (Isa. 8:14-15) and Daniel's stone that grinds a statue to powder (Dan. 2:34-35). To fall on the stone is to trip over it and be broken — bad, and survivable, since broken things can be mended. When the stone falls on a man, it crushes him to dust. The stone cannot be avoided: it can be built on, tripped over, or fallen under, and nobody in this passage walks past it.

And the parable is fulfilled in the hearing of the parable. They grasped it immediately — which answers a question people often put to Scripture, why God does not simply tell people plainly what they are doing. He did, and it produced a decision to do it sooner.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to tell the people this parable: 'A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to tell the people this parable: a man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

He began to tell the people this parable. To the people, with the leaders listening (v. 19).

A man planted a vineyard. The vineyard is Isaiah’s picture of Israel (Isaiah 5:1–7). God planted his people and did everything to make them fruitful.

And let it out to tenants. The tenants are Israel’s leaders. Absentee landlords leasing to tenant farmers were common in Galilee.

For a long while. Only Luke adds this: the long centuries of God’s patience.

He sent a servant to the tenants. The prophets, God’s servants.

But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Israel’s history of rejecting the prophets (2 Chronicles 36:15–16; Nehemiah 9:26).

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and sent a servant for his share of the fruit, but the tenants beat him and sent him away empty.

On a Tuesday. God looks for fruit from what he has given you. What is he receiving?
verseByVerse.note: The vineyard is Isaiah’s picture of Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.

Another … a third. The owner’s patience, beyond what any landlord would show. God sent prophet after prophet.

Treated him shamefully. Insulted, dishonoured.

This one also they wounded and cast out. Increasing violence. In Luke’s version, no servant is killed until the son, which makes the son’s death the climax.

In a sentence. The owner sent a second and third servant, and the tenants beat, insulted, wounded and threw them out.

For worship. Thank God for his patience with rebellious people, including you.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the owner of the vineyard said: what shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him. But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves: this is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.

What shall I do? Only Luke records this deliberation. The heart of God, pondering how to reach his rebellious people.

I will send my beloved son. The words of the Father at the baptism and transfiguration (3:22; 9:35). Jesus answers the question of his authority: he is the beloved Son, not another servant.

Perhaps they will respect him. The extraordinary hope of love.

This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours. They recognise him and kill him for that reason. The leaders wanted to keep control of God’s people for themselves. And Jesus foretells his death to their faces.

In a sentence. Finally the owner sent his beloved son, hoping they would respect him, but the tenants decided to kill the heir and seize the inheritance.

For worship. God sent his beloved Son to rebels, knowing what they would do. This is love (1 John 4:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.' When they heard this, they said, 'Surely not!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others. When they heard this, they said: surely not!

They threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Luke (with Matthew) has “threw out, then killed”, matching Jesus’ crucifixion outside the city wall (Hebrews 13:12–13).

He will come and destroy those tenants. Judgement on the leaders, fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

And give the vineyard to others. To new leaders, the apostles, and to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46; 28:28). God’s people continue under new tenants.

Surely not! Only Luke records this. Literally “may it not be!” (Paul’s favourite phrase in Romans). The people are horrified at the thought of judgement on Israel and the vineyard being given to others.

In a sentence. The tenants killed the son, so the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others, and the people were horrified.

On a Tuesday. Privilege is no guarantee. What God gives, he can give to others if it bears no fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: But he looked directly at them and said, 'What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he looked directly at them and said: what then is this that is written: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone?

But he looked directly at them. A penetrating look (22:61).

What then is this that is written. If judgement cannot happen, what does Scripture mean?

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Psalm 118:22, from the psalm the crowds had sung at his entry (19:38). The builders are the leaders, who rejected Jesus as useless. But God made him the cornerstone, the most important stone in the building, which holds it all together. Fulfilled in the resurrection (Acts 4:10–12; 1 Peter 2:4–8).

In a sentence. Looking straight at them, Jesus quoted Scripture: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.

For worship. The rejected Christ is the cornerstone of God’s temple. Build your life on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.

Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces. Isaiah 8:14–15: a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling … many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken. Those who stumble over Jesus, rejecting him, will be broken.

And when it falls on anyone, it will crush him. Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45: the stone cut without hands that strikes the statue of the world’s kingdoms and crushes it, and becomes a great mountain filling the earth: the kingdom of God. Christ will come in judgement and crush all who oppose him.

The point. No one can be neutral toward Jesus. He is either the cornerstone on which you build, or the stone that breaks you. Only Luke (and some manuscripts of Matthew) records this saying.

In a sentence. Everyone who stumbles over the stone will be broken, and anyone it falls on will be crushed.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is either your foundation or your judge. Build on him.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.

Sought to lay hands on him at that very hour. Doing exactly what the parable described.

For they perceived that he had told this parable against them. They understood it perfectly.

But they feared the people. The crowds still protected Jesus (19:48).

In a sentence. The leaders wanted to arrest him at once, knowing the parable was against them, but feared the people.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word exposes you, repent rather than resent it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — The Question about Tribute to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The direct approach has failed twice, so the tactics change. Spies are men planted, and they “pretended to be sincere” — actors playing devout enquirers. Luke gives the object before the question: a capital charge Rome will act on, because Pilate does not care about blasphemy.

The flattery is a trap in itself. If he is a man who “shows no partiality,” he cannot now give a diplomatic answer — they have publicly committed him to fearless speech before asking the dangerous question. And the terrible thing is that every word of the compliment is true. They have described him accurately as a means of destroying him, which is only possible for people who know exactly who he is and have decided against him anyway.

The tribute was the poll tax, a denarius a head, levied since Judea became a Roman province in AD 6 — and it had provoked an armed revolt at the time. Say yes and he endorses the occupation before a Passover crowd of patriots; say no and there are witnesses ready to report a man inciting tax refusal, which is exactly the charge they will eventually bring (23:2).

He asks for a coin, and does not have one — the man they are trying to trap on taxation has to borrow the currency from his accusers. And somebody produces one immediately, in the temple. The denarius bore the head of Tiberius with an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus, and Pontifex Maximus on the reverse: a portrait, which offended the second commandment, and a claim of divinity in writing.

“Caesar's” is the only possible answer and it concedes the whole question. The trap has been sprung without a word of doctrine, and it took one question about a coin.
verseByVerse.theology:
The verb in v.25 is not give but render — pay what is owed. It is the word for settling a debt, not making a donation, which quietly answers the first half: if the coin is Caesar's, handing it over is returning property.

But the weight falls on the second clause. He has just established the principle by which ownership is determined — whose likeness and inscription does it bear? So the question the second half silently asks is: what bears the image of God? And every person listening knew the answer from the first page of their Scriptures (Gen. 1:27).

The coin is stamped with Caesar and belongs to Caesar. The man holding it is stamped with God.

Two things follow, and the church has often held one without the other. The civil authority is legitimate — Jesus does not tell them to stop paying, and Paul develops it at length (Rom. 13:1-7). And the civil authority is bounded: Caesar gets what has his image on it and nothing more, so the moment he asks for worship, conscience, or the ultimate allegiance of a life, he is asking for property that is not his.

The “two kingdoms” principle drawn from these verses has been foundational for Reformed political theology. But the passage presses beyond institutional analysis to the personal: if you bear God's image, you belong to God — completely, with no reservation, because the image is not stamped on part of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian facing a regulation he considers unjust can think clearly from this. There is a legitimate sphere of civil authority, and there is an authority that is absolute. The question is not whether to comply with any government but whether the specific demand crosses into what belongs exclusively to God.

Note also what the borrowed coin exposes. The men who came to catch him on faithfulness to God were carrying Caesar's portrait and Caesar's divine title in their purses, in the temple courts, and one of them had it out in seconds. Whatever the question was really about, it was not scruple.

And “marveling at his answer” is a surprising word for men who came to destroy him. It is possible to admire the truth and remain entirely unmoved by it — Herod was glad to see Jesus and questioned him at length (23:8-9). There is a way of appreciating the quality of an answer that functions as a substitute for obeying it, and it is common among people who take religion seriously enough to enjoy a good argument about it.

Which is a hard lesson for anyone who assumes a sufficiently good answer will settle a matter. Jesus gave the best answer anyone ever gave to a hostile question, in public, and the men who heard it admired it, went quiet, and had him killed on Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. So they asked him, 'Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. So they asked him: Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?

And sent spies, who pretended to be sincere. Hypocrites, actors.

So as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. Only Luke states their aim so plainly. They wanted a political charge Pilate would act on.

Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly. Flattery. Every word true, but insincere.

Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not? The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. It provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). The trap: if Jesus says yes, he loses the crowd; if no, he is a rebel to be reported to Pilate. Ironically, they will later accuse him of forbidding the tax anyway (23:2).

In a sentence. The leaders sent flattering spies to trap Jesus into a statement they could report to the governor, asking whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar.

On a Tuesday. Beware of flattery that leads into a trap. Ask God for wisdom.
verseByVerse.note: The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason before the governor.

parallels.desc: forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, 'Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?' They said, 'Caesar's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them: show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have? They said: Caesar’s.

He perceived their craftiness. “Craftiness” (panourgian): cunning, trickery, the serpent’s skill (2 Corinthians 11:3).

Show me a denarius. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage. The coin bore the emperor’s head, Tiberius, and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. To strict Jews, a graven image and a claim to divinity.

Caesar’s. And they had one, so they used his coinage and benefited from his rule.

In a sentence. Seeing their trick, Jesus asked for a denarius and whose image and inscription it bore, and they said Caesar’s.

On a Tuesday. Wisdom often lies in looking carefully at what is in front of you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage. The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and his titles.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. “Render” (apodote): give back, pay what is owed. The coin bears Caesar’s image; give it back to him. The state has legitimate authority in its sphere, and taxes are owed (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17).

And to God the things that are God’s. What bears God’s image? You (Genesis 1:26–27). Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, wholly. And Caesar’s claims are limited by God’s: Caesar is owed taxes, not worship. When Caesar demands what belongs to God, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Verdict. As at Mark 12:17: Jesus does not make God and Caesar equal partners. All authority is under God. Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes and honouring rulers, but their final loyalty is to God alone.

In a sentence. Jesus said to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and God what belongs to God.

On a Tuesday. Pay your taxes honestly, and give yourself wholly to God, whose image you bear.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marvelling at his answer they became silent.

They were not able in the presence of the people to catch him. The trap failed.

Marveling at his answer they became silent. Silenced, amazed. Jesus is the wisdom of God.

In a sentence. They could not trap him in front of the people, and, amazed at his answer, they fell silent.

For worship. Christ’s wisdom silences every opponent. Trust it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–47 — Sadducees on Resurrection, the Son of David, and Scribal Warning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sadducees were the aristocratic party — the chief priestly families and wealthy landowners who ran the temple and managed the relationship with Rome. They accepted the five books of Moses and treated the rest as secondary, and from that drew the conclusions Acts states fully: “the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit” (Acts 23:8). Which limits the field for Jesus: he cannot answer from Daniel 12 or Isaiah 26, and will have to find the resurrection in Moses.

Their riddle rests on a good law. Deuteronomy 25:5-10 provided that if a married man died childless his brother should marry the widow, and the first son would carry the dead man's name and inherit his portion — so no family line or allotted land in Israel would be extinguished. It is the law behind Boaz and Ruth, and it was designed to protect a widow from destitution.

They turn it into a joke. Seven brothers, one after another, each obeying Moses, each dying childless. And notice what the story does to the woman: she is unnamed, unnumbered, given no words, and exists purely as contested property. The question at the end is not “what became of her?” but “whose will she be?”

The argument is a reductio, and it rests on one assumption the Sadducees have never noticed they are making — that the age to come is this age carried on, the same arrangements made permanent. So the answer is not a solution to the puzzle. Jesus dismantles the premise and the puzzle goes with it.

He then proves the doctrine on their own ground, from the burning bush; the scribes commend him; and nobody dares ask anything further. Which leaves him free to ask his own question, about Psalm 110 — and to close with a warning about the men who had been asking all day.
verseByVerse.theology:
“They cannot die anymore” is the reason marriage does not continue. Marriage in this age carries the future of the race: where people die, people must be born. Remove death and the mechanism for replacing the dead is no longer needed — the way scaffolding is no longer needed. And “equal to angels” does not mean disembodied; the resurrection is precisely of the body, and Luke's own last chapter has the risen Christ eating fish to prove it (24:41-43). The comparison is specifically to deathlessness, and Jesus says so in the same breath.

The argument from Exodus 3:6 turns on a tense. God does not say “I was the God of Abraham” but “I am” — four hundred years after Abraham was buried. And to be somebody's God is covenant language: to have bound yourself to a person and promised him a future. So if God is still Abraham's God, then either the covenant is with a handful of dust, which is no covenant at all, or Abraham is alive.

Note what the argument does not rest on. Not the immortality of the soul, which is a Greek idea and appears nowhere in the reasoning. It rests entirely on the character of God: he does not enter a binding relationship with a man and then let death end it, because that would make him unfaithful. The ground of resurrection hope is not something in us but something in him — which is why the last clause is one of the great sentences of Scripture: “for all live to him.”

Psalm 110:1 became the most quoted Old Testament text in the New (Acts 2:34-35; 1 Cor. 15:25; Heb. 1:13; 10:12-13). In that world honour ran upward — a man addressed his forebears as “my lord,” never the reverse — so a psalm in which David calls his own descendant “my Lord” is upside down, unless the descendant is more than a descendant.
verseByVerse.examples:
All of the resurrection teaching is true, and none of it is what the widow in the third pew is asking. She has buried a husband she loved for forty years, reads “neither marry nor are given in marriage,” and hears the one thing she was most afraid of.

For marriage was never the destination. Paul says the whole thing was pointing somewhere: “this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Eph. 5:31-32). Every good marriage has been a signpost, and nobody keeps reading the signpost after arriving at the city. What waits at the end of this age is a wedding (Rev. 19:6-9) — and marriage is not carried into it because it was too little, not too much. It was the picture; that is the reality.

The chapter closes with predation rather than vanity. Long robes and good seats are appetite; devouring widows' houses is theft — and the two halves of v.47 belong together, because the long prayers are not a separate failing but the instrument. The reputation for piety is what gets a man access to a widow's confidence and her accounts. The prayer is the cover.

Which is a word for anybody holding spiritual standing over others. It is possible to use the things of God to get things from people, and Scripture reserves its severest language for it. And Luke sets the next scene immediately: a widow at the treasury, putting in everything she had (21:1-4).

verseByVerse.quote: There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, 'Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying: Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.

Some Sadducees. The priestly, aristocratic party, who controlled the temple. They accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative.

Those who deny that there is a resurrection. Luke explains. They also denied angels and spirits (Acts 23:8).

Moses wrote for us. Deuteronomy 25:5–10, the law of levirate marriage, which kept a dead man’s name and inheritance in his family.

In a sentence. Some Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, came with a question based on Moses’ law that a man should marry his dead brother’s childless widow.

On a Tuesday. Scepticism about the resurrection is nothing new. Jesus’ answer still stands.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterward the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterwards the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.

Seven brothers. An absurd case, probably a standard argument the Sadducees used to ridicule the Pharisees’ belief in resurrection.

In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? Their assumption: resurrection life would be like this life. If so, the law of Moses would create an absurdity, so Moses could not have believed in resurrection.

In a sentence. They told of seven brothers who married the same woman in turn and died childless, and asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection.

On a Tuesday. Clever objections often rest on false assumptions. Look for the assumption.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: the sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die any more, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.

The sons of this age marry. Marriage belongs to this present age.

Those who are considered worthy to attain to that age. Only Luke has this fuller form. “That age”: the age to come. “Considered worthy”: by God, through grace.

Neither marry nor are given in marriage. Resurrection life is not this life continued. Marriage’s purposes are fulfilled.

For they cannot die anymore. Only Luke gives this reason. Marriage and children are needed in a world of death, to continue the human family. In the resurrection there is no death, and so no need for levirate marriage. The Sadducees’ whole puzzle falls apart.

Because they are equal to angels. Like angels, immortal, not that they become angels.

And are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. Children of God by resurrection, sharing his life (Romans 8:23; 1 John 3:2).

What it does not mean. Not that married love is lost or forgotten, but that it is taken up into something greater: the marriage of Christ and his church, to which every marriage points (Ephesians 5:31–32; Revelation 19:7–9).

In a sentence. Jesus answered that marriage belongs to this age, but those raised to the age to come do not marry, because they can no longer die, being like angels and children of God.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you are a son or daughter of the resurrection. Death has no future for you.

verseByVerse.quote: But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.

Even Moses showed. From the books the Sadducees accepted.

In the passage about the bush. Exodus 3, the burning bush. Before chapter and verse numbers, passages were located like this.

The God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Exodus 3:6, spoken centuries after they died. God still calls himself their God.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. A covenant relationship with God cannot be broken by death. If God is their God, they live to him, and he will keep his promises to them, body and soul.

For all live to him. Only Luke adds this. All who belong to God are alive to him, even now, after death (Romans 14:8). And they await bodily resurrection.

In a sentence. Jesus showed from the burning bush that God is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and so they live, for he is God of the living, and all live to him.

For worship. If God is your God, you will live for ever. Worship the God of the living.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes answered, 'Teacher, you have spoken well.' For they no longer dared to ask him any question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of the scribes answered: Teacher, you have spoken well. For they no longer dared to ask him any question.

Teacher, you have spoken well. Scribes who were Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection, were pleased to see the Sadducees defeated.

For they no longer dared to ask him any question. Every trap has failed. Jesus has answered the Sanhedrin, the Pharisees with the Herodians, and the Sadducees.

In a sentence. Some scribes praised his answer, and no one dared ask him any more questions.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s answers are sufficient. Bring your questions to him in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'How can they say that the Christ is David's son? For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to them: how can they say that the Christ is David’s son? For David himself says in the Book of Psalms: the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.

Now Jesus asks. Having answered every question, he asks the decisive one.

How can they say that the Christ is David’s son? All agreed that the Messiah would be a descendant of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). True, but is that all he is?

For David himself says in the Book of Psalms. Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New.

The Lord said to my Lord. In Hebrew: Yahweh said to my Adonai. God speaks to David’s Lord.

Sit at my right hand. The place of supreme honour and authority, sharing God’s throne.

In a sentence. Jesus asked how the Messiah could be David’s son, when David himself in Psalm 110 calls him Lord, seated at God’s right hand.

For worship. Jesus is seated at God’s right hand now. Worship him there.

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.’ David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until I make your enemies your footstool. David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?

Until I make your enemies your footstool. A conquered king’s neck could be used as a footstool, a picture of total victory (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns until every enemy, including death, is under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son? A father did not call his son “lord”. If David calls the Messiah Lord, the Messiah must be greater than David. The answer: he is David’s son by human birth, and David’s Lord as the eternal Son of God (Romans 1:3–4). Fully man and fully God. Jesus is pointing to himself.

In a sentence. Since David calls the Messiah Lord, who will rule until all enemies are under his feet, how can he be merely David’s son?

For worship. Jesus is both David’s son and David’s Lord. Worship him as fully man and fully God.
verseByVerse.note: A conquered king’s neck could be used as a footstool — a picture of total victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, 'Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples: beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honour at feasts.

In the hearing of all the people. Publicly.

Beware of the scribes. A warning against their example (11:43).

Who like to walk around in long robes. Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

And love greetings in the marketplaces. Respectful titles.

The best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts. Love of status (14:7).

In a sentence. Jesus publicly warned his disciples against the scribes, who love fine robes, public honour and the best seats.

On a Tuesday. Watch your heart for the love of recognition, especially if you serve in church.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who devour widows’ houses and for a pretence make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.

Who devour widows’ houses. Exploiting the most vulnerable: by charging for legal services, managing their estates dishonestly, or living off their generosity. God especially protects widows (Exodus 22:22–24).

And for a pretense make long prayers. Long public prayers to appear holy, while robbing the defenceless.

They will receive the greater condemnation. Greater because they knew better, and used religion to cover their sin (12:47–48; James 3:1).

The link. In the next scene (21:1–4), a poor widow gives her last coins, perhaps a victim of such men.

In a sentence. The scribes exploit widows and pray long prayers for show, and will receive greater condemnation.

On a Tuesday. Never use religion to cover selfishness. God sees and will judge.

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

20.text: <sup>1</sup> One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up <sup>2</sup> and said to him, “Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.” <sup>3</sup> He answered them, “I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, <sup>4</sup> was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?” <sup>5</sup> And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ <sup>6</sup> But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” <sup>7</sup> So they answered that they did not know where it came from. <sup>8</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” <sup>9</sup> And he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. <sup>10</sup> When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>11</sup> And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>12</sup> And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out. <sup>13</sup> Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ <sup>14</sup> But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’ <sup>15</sup> And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? <sup>16</sup> He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “Surely not!” <sup>17</sup> But he looked directly at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? <sup>18</sup> Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>19</sup> The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people. <sup>20</sup> So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. <sup>21</sup> So they asked him, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. <sup>22</sup> Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” <sup>23</sup> But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?” They said, “Caesar's.” <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.” <sup>26</sup> And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent. <sup>27</sup> There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, <sup>28</sup> and they asked him a question, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>29</sup> Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. <sup>30</sup> And the second <sup>31</sup> and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. <sup>32</sup> Afterward the woman also died. <sup>33</sup> In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, <sup>35</sup> but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, <sup>36</sup> for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. <sup>37</sup> But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. <sup>38</sup> Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.” <sup>39</sup> Then some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well.” <sup>40</sup> For they no longer dared to ask him any question. <sup>41</sup> But he said to them, “How can they say that the Christ is David's son? <sup>42</sup> For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>43</sup> until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>44</sup> David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?” <sup>45</sup> And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, <sup>46</sup> “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>47</sup> who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.”

21.title: The Widow's Offering and the Olivet Discourse
21.overview:
Luke 21 opens with a scene that provides the perfect contrast to the scribes condemned at the end of chapter 20: a widow who puts into the temple treasury two small copper coins — “everything she had to live on.” Then, as Jesus leaves the temple and a disciple admires its magnificent stones, he delivers the Olivet Discourse — his most extended eschatological teaching, covering the destruction of Jerusalem, the sufferings of the disciples, the fall of the city, and the coming of the Son of Man.

The Olivet Discourse in Luke (parallel to Matthew 24 and Mark 13) is notable for several features. Luke emphasises the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 more explicitly than the other Gospels, and the discourse includes several passages that apply specifically to that historical event. At the same time, the coming of the Son of Man in glory transcends any single historical event — it is the final, universal, unmistakable arrival of the Kingdom in its fullness.

The chapter closes with a pattern that defines the final days of Jesus's ministry: he teaches in the temple by day; the people come early to hear him; at night he goes out to the Mount of Olives. This is the rhythm of the last week — teaching, opposition, and solitary prayer, all moving toward the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 20 ended with Jesus warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses and for a pretence make long prayers. Chapter 21 opens with a widow whose house has been devoured, giving away the last of it. Luke has put the two paragraphs side by side on purpose.

Jesus is sitting in the Court of the Women, where thirteen trumpet-mouthed chests stood against the wall, built so that a coin rang all the way down. He looks up and watches the rich putting in their gifts — nothing is said against them, and nothing should be read in. Then he sees a poor widow put in two lepta, the smallest coin minted, together worth about a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage.

His verdict is that she has put in more than all of them, and the reason he gives is arithmetical: they gave out of their abundance, their overflow, what they would not miss; she gave out of her poverty, and she gave all she had to live on. The measure is not the size of the gift but the size of what remains.

There is a real difficulty in the sequence, and it is worth facing rather than smoothing over. Jesus has just condemned the men who run this temple, and five verses later he will say the building is coming down to the last stone. Is he praising a woman for handing her last coin to a doomed and corrupt institution? Some read the passage as a lament rather than a commendation. But his own words settle it — this poor widow has put in more than all of them is praise, not mourning. He is not endorsing the temple. He is telling us what God saw at the treasury.

Which is the comfort in it for every believer who has given, served and poured out small resources inside a church that was flawed, or failing, or would not outlast them. The worth of the gift was never in the soundness of the institution that received it.
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the divine valuation of giving, and it runs on a different ledger from ours. The rich men’s gifts are not condemned; they are revalued. What looked large is revealed to be cheap, and what looked negligible is revealed to be everything, because heaven measures the cost to the giver and not the benefit to the fund.

Behind that lies a deeper principle: God does not need our money. The temple did not stand or fall on the widow’s two coins, and the kingdom does not advance on donations. What God seeks in giving is the giver — which is why proportion tells the truth about a heart and totals do not.

And the scene is a small portrait of the cross, days before it. She gave her whole livelihood; he was about to give his whole life. She trusted God for the next meal with nothing left in reserve; he would go into the dark with nothing held back either. Complete self-giving is not a heroic exception in the kingdom of God. It is the shape of the King.
verseByVerse.examples:
The test in v. 1 is easy to run and hard to survive. Think of the last thing you gave to God’s work, and ask not how much it was but what you went without because of it. If nothing in the month changed, the answer has already been given.

A church announces the total of a giving campaign with celebration — a large figure, mostly from prosperous members. The pastor privately knows the costliest single gift came from a widow on a fixed income who gave her entire discretionary fund for the month. He has to decide whether the celebration names the total or the sacrifice, and this passage tells him which one heaven has already recorded.

And for anyone whose giving is small: she is remembered in every language on earth two thousand years later, and the names of the wealthy donors that morning are gone without trace — because the Lord noticed, and said so. Nothing done for him is unwitnessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box.

The link. Straight after the warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47), Jesus sees a widow.
